275784.evidence: So they finally discussed it with the girl singer, Doris Robbins, and they left California and went to New York
275784.subject: Bob Haggart
275784.audit: {"change": "verbatim fix", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: BH
sources.text: The Pollack band? Ben Pollack? Well that’s what happened. The Ben Pollack guys all left him because they weren’t getting any work. He was trying to get his wife, who was the girl singer, he was trying to get her into pictures. And so the band had these long layoffs and they got sick and tired of waiting around to work. So they finally discussed it with the girl singer, Doris Robbins, and they left California and went to New York and stuck together and rehearsed and did some recording dates and looked around for a leader, a new leader. So they wanted Jack Teagarden, but they couldn’t get him because he was signed up with Paul Whiteman at that time. So they came across, somebody suggested Bob Crosby would be a good choice because of his brother Bing being so famous, people would want to see what his kid brother looked like. And so we went on the road in 1935 and we did big business, always did, because of the name. And the band happened to be damn good, you know? So we formed a corporation and I was asked, I was the only non-Pollack guy, I just joined after. I never was with Pollack. But they let me come in too, so I was a member of the corporation. But the problem there was that the guys that weren’t in the corporation, it made it kind of sticky because they felt like second class citizens you know? Actually they were making more money than the guys in the corporation, because we had expenses that came out first and so there was never any kind of split, we were just on a salary and that was it. The corporation never meant anything. It was just that we’d have a meeting once in a while and we’d sit around listening to Gil Rodin talk. That was about it. Gil Rodin was really the guy who was really the brains behind the Pollack band too. He played lead alto and he was the businessman in the crowd. He could have been a lawyer I think, but he used to handle all the song pluggers and the bookers and so he really ran the band, because Bob Crosby knew nothing about that. So without Gil Rodin it wouldn’t have stuck together very long I’m afraid. But he kept everybody feeling optimistic and he’d make all the promises to everybody when they’d come in the band, and make sure they were happy with how much money they were going to make. So Gil Rodin was the brains behind the whole thing.

275784.evidence: He and Flip Phillips play
275784.subject: Bob Haggart
275784.audit: {"change": "Howard Alden plays with Flip Phillips, not Haggart", "previous": {"relation": "played with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "played unison lines together"}}

sources.speaker: BH
sources.text: Well, I’ve written a bass method book that’s out of print, and has been for a long time, but Ray Brown studied out of my book, and when I met Ray Brown he was playing with Dizzy Gillespie’s big band on 52nd street. And I think it was the first time Ray Brown had ever been to New York. I don’t know were he’s from originally, but he was a marvelous player at that time. He was about eighteen years old. And he came over to the table and my wife and I were there listening to Louis’, uh, Dizzy’s big band, and Ray Brown said, “I studied out of your book, Mr. Haggart.” He called me Mr. Haggart. I said, “I better go take another look at that book, I must have missed something.” Because he was playing all over that bass, stuff that he never found in that book, that’s for sure. So but you can’t really learn to play out of books I don’t think. I think it’s good to get you started, find out where the notes are so that when the time comes and you have to read a bass part. You seldom read what’s there anyway, you have to use your ear and play what you think it should be. As long as you know what chords are happening, and the way the tune is constructed, those are things you learn when you’re a kid you see, how to train your ear and to remember chord sequences. You have to store all those tunes in your head so that when they call out a tune you can’t say, “I don’t know it, what else do you know, what else?” And then you say, “Well I don’t know that either—what else?” You’ve got to know everything. If you’re going to play in a band you have to know every tune. I don’t know how you do that. It’s just something that takes a long time. Now these kids today, they know all those tunes, the ones I mentioned before, you know? Howard Alden, he’s got some kind of a brain because he not only remembers the tunes but he remembers all the choruses that Lester Young played. He’ll play them all. He and Flip Phillips play © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

275784.evidence: Then there was Bill Evans, he always had marvelous bass players, he had Scott LaFaro

275784.audit: {"change": "narrated tie", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: BH
sources.text: Yes. He’s supposed to be an accompaniment. It’s an accompaniment instrument. Once in a while I get a chance to solo, that’s great, but you don’t solo in every tune. I think what started that is all the duos — the piano and bass — because the clubs couldn’t afford any more than two men, and they wanted some kind of entertainment in a bar to attract people, so they’d get a very good piano player and he gets the best bass player he likes to work with. Piano and bass duos — like Ray Brown and Oscar Peterson. Start there. And then all over the world there’s these piano and bass duos, no drums, can’t afford it. Then there was Bill Evans, he always had marvelous bass players, he had Scott LaFaro, and they always had a quiet drummer. And that was it, the trio. You don’t find many piano and guitar trios, because they duplicate each other and they have to give in to each other all the time. They have to work out things together in order to have, you know—

275784.evidence: It’s like Lawrence Welk today. He was the Lawrence Welk of those days, Guy Lombardo.
275784.subject: Bob Haggart

sources.speaker: BH
sources.text: Well I guess the most famous was “South Rampart Street Parade.” That’s the one that’s played most today. They made a stock orchestration out of it. And so that got around. It’s a New Orleans march, you know, which isn’t everybody’s dish of tea to play a New Orleans march because it’s not exactly a thing for dancing but even Guy Lombardo, that was his big number. He’d play “South Rampart Street Parade,” with Guy Lombardo and they’d get hot on it. But you know that’s not a jazz band. Lombardo was a very sweet, they called it “sweet music” in those days. There was “hot music” and there was “sweet music.” And this had a nice tempo and everything, and then all the old people loved to dance to Guy Lombardo. It’s like Lawrence Welk today. He was the Lawrence Welk of those days, Guy Lombardo. “Sweetest music this side of heaven” that was their logo. Ours was “the greatest Dixieland band in the land,” the Bob Crosby band.

275784.audit: {"change": "verbatim fix", "previous": {"relation": "in music group with", "direction": "na", "proposed": "member of the small band for the Bob Crosby band's Sunday afternoon kids' show in Chicago, 1939"}}

sources.speaker: BH
sources.text: He was the whole show and you’d go hear the show and you’d remember him because the way he played the drums, he was an act in himself. Wonderful. He could dance. But we were doing a number for the kids from Winnetka. There were a lot of kids from, it was a suburb of Chicago. The kids were in there to hear the band on a Sunday afternoon and we had a radio broadcast coming up as I remember it was at 5:00. And we used to put on a show for the kids with the small band, come down off the stand and had trumpet, trombone, clarinet, tenor, it was Yank Lawson and then Eddie Miller and Matty Matlock and Smitty. And they’d pull out a little upright piano for Bob Zerke and another set of drums for Ray Bauduc would slide out on a little dolly on the dance floor, and I’d bring my bass down. And we’d play three or four tunes, and the kids all sat on the dance floor. Bob Crosby would say, “Now everybody sit down.” And this one day he said, “Well here’s Ray Bauduc and Bobby Hackett and they’re going to do the ‘Big Noise from Winnetka.’” So we just went into something, made it up as we went along, because we had some time to kill before going on the radio, see. And we had just done a thing called the “Big Crash from China.” That was the drum solo we used to play, something written by Ray Bauduc and with the Bobcats. And he played a lot of stuff with a big Chinese crash cymbal at the end, “Big Crash from China.” And so here’s the “Big Noise from Winnetka.” He just made up the title, see, and so we made up something to go with it. And then the next week we went into the studio to do an album and we said, “What did we do the other day — we’ve got to do that number.” So we tried to remember what we did. The gimmick is he plays on the G string of the bass with his sticks — tic-a-tic-a-tic- a-tic-a — and then I’d play up and down — ding-a-ding-a-ding-a-ding-a-ding-a-ding-a — and that was the gimmick.

275784.evidence: when I met Ray Brown he was playing with Dizzy Gillespie’s big band on 52nd street.
275784.subject: Bob Haggart
275784.audit: {"change": "verbatim fix", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: BH
sources.text: Well, I’ve written a bass method book that’s out of print, and has been for a long time, but Ray Brown studied out of my book, and when I met Ray Brown he was playing with Dizzy Gillespie’s big band on 52nd street. And I think it was the first time Ray Brown had ever been to New York. I don’t know were he’s from originally, but he was a marvelous player at that time. He was about eighteen years old. And he came over to the table and my wife and I were there listening to Louis’, uh, Dizzy’s big band, and Ray Brown said, “I studied out of your book, Mr. Haggart.” He called me Mr. Haggart. I said, “I better go take another look at that book, I must have missed something.” Because he was playing all over that bass, stuff that he never found in that book, that’s for sure. So but you can’t really learn to play out of books I don’t think. I think it’s good to get you started, find out where the notes are so that when the time comes and you have to read a bass part. You seldom read what’s there anyway, you have to use your ear and play what you think it should be. As long as you know what chords are happening, and the way the tune is constructed, those are things you learn when you’re a kid you see, how to train your ear and to remember chord sequences. You have to store all those tunes in your head so that when they call out a tune you can’t say, “I don’t know it, what else do you know, what else?” And then you say, “Well I don’t know that either—what else?” You’ve got to know everything. If you’re going to play in a band you have to know every tune. I don’t know how you do that. It’s just something that takes a long time. Now these kids today, they know all those tunes, the ones I mentioned before, you know? Howard Alden, he’s got some kind of a brain because he not only remembers the tunes but he remembers all the choruses that Lester Young played. He’ll play them all. He and Flip Phillips play © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

275784.evidence: You learn those three chords you can play almost anything, until you get into Cole Porter.
275784.subject: Bob Haggart

sources.speaker: BH
sources.text: Second chorus you’ve forgotten what you did the first chorus. Yeah. Well, you have to store up all these tunes in your head. You have to like it. You’ve got to like those songs. Irving Berlin, you know how many songs Irving Berlin wrote? More than anybody. I think I know them all, just because I was around when they came out, a lot of them. Even “Alexander’s Ragtime Band” that was way before my time but you learned that right away, you know. It’s a very simple song. Any fool can play it though [hums]. 1-4-5, it’s all based on. The rock & roll has those three chords, 1, 4 and 5. You learn those three chords you can play almost anything, until you get into Cole Porter. George Gershwin gets a little more, you know, Harold Arlen, it gets a little more sophisticated and you’ve got to learn all those other little side turns. Jerome Kern, “The Song Is You.” I mean it separates the men from the boys when you learn the release to “The Song Is You,” it goes into all kinds of strange levels, you know? You start in C and then you go into E and you go into G# minor and, you know. So it helps to study all those chords. Study harmony. Study composition, the way chords are constructed. Bass lines, and the little cello line. The melody and the bass line, and then one other line inside there, the tune is constructed on those three lines. The melody and the bass, even in Beethoven or Bach, that’s still a fundamental that goes through any music. You have the melody and then have the bass, and then you have all the stuff in between, that’s just the icing on the cake. But the fundamental thing is the bass line and the melody. Am I making any sense at all?

sources.text: Well I was, I started playing in high school actually. He had just switched from cello and he tuned his bass in fifths, which I had never heard of that before. I was just learning how to. In high school I just picked up the bass, of course tuned in fourths, as it still is. But in fifths means it’s like the cello, C-G-D-A, and the same as tenor banjo tuning too, which only would be up an octave with the banjo of course. 275787.proposed: drummer (then vibraphonist) in the Les Hite band backing Louis Armstrong in California, c. 1930; recorded 'Memories of You' with him
275787.evidence: at 17 years old I used to be a drummer for Louis Armstrong
275787.subject: Lionel Hampton
275787.audit: {"change": "Hampton drummed and recorded vibes behind Armstrong; old proposed 'late 1930s' was wrong", "previous": {"relation": "played under", "direction": "target", "proposed": "drummer in Louis Armstrong's band, late 1930s"}}

sources.speaker: LH
sources.text: Yes. I’ll tell you, it was quite an ordeal having these great stars to work with me. Well that’s what I’ve been working with all my life. But I started out when I was a youngster, at 17 years old I used to be a drummer for Louis Armstrong.

sources.speaker: LH
sources.text: Yeah. And that was just like heaven. Playing with Louis Armstrong was a great big ordeal.

sources.speaker: LH
sources.text: music. So they were having bands to do auditions to play behind Louis Armstrong, who was coming out to be the star, at this place called Frank Sebastian’s Cotton Club. And so we did an audition and Louis’ manager liked us so we got the job. So Louis Armstrong was in New York with his band, but he was trying to be commercialized, and picking a band out to play behind Louis. And this Les Hite’s band was a bunch of youngsters, and we all could read music like mad, and we could play like mad. We had a terrific band. And so Louis Armstrong came out and he liked us so well back then that they took him on a recording session with him, and when we got to the recording session, there was a set of vibes in the corner of the studio. And Louis asked me what was the name of the instrument and I told him it was a new instrument and that this had been added to the percussion family, and they called it a vibraharp. One company makes this instrument, and they called it a vibraharp. Then another company made the same instrument and they called it the vibraphone.

sources.speaker: LH
sources.text: So I got a little head start on jazz, see? So I played something for a song that Louis had made a record on, called “Chinese Chop Suey.” And Louis liked it so well, he said, “I’ll tell you, you keep the vibraphone out there, and we’re going to have you record with us.” So Eubie Blake, the big solo player and piano player at that time sent Louis arrangements to record for him. And the name of the tune was “Memories of You.”

275788.proposed: pianist in Miles Davis's band for five and a half years from 1963
275788.evidence: Probably because I had been a former member of Miles’ band and they could trust that I knew how to deliver that.
275788.subject: Herbie Hancock
275788.audit: {"change": "Old evidence spliced from several blocks; replaced with a single verbatim quote. '1960s late' claim in proposed was wrong (he joined at Seven Steps to Heaven).", "previous": {"relation": "played under", "direction": "target", "proposed": "joined Miles Davis' band in the late 1960s, playing piano for five and a half years"}}

sources.speaker: HH
sources.text: Well by the time I was able to give Miles the Lifetime Achievement Award from, I guess that was from NARAS from the Grammy Awards Ceremony. NARAS is the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences. It’s the Academy Award for the recording industry. Anyway, by that time I had my own career going. I had even done some acting on television. I think I had already had a T.V. show called “Rock School” at the time, which came, and we did a couple of seasons of that and then that went. There was another show I had too, called “Coast to Coast” it was on Showtime. I’m not sure whether that was before my presenting this award to Miles or not, but anyway I’m just saying that by then I’d kind of grown up and had my own things going and had been a presenter several times also for the Grammys. So I was selected by Mike Green, who is the President of NARAS and, I think he was president at that time, and maybe there was a committee, but I was asked to do that. Probably because I had been a former member of Miles’ band and they could trust that I knew how to deliver that.

sources.speaker: HH
sources.text: So Donald introduced me to Miles about a year and a half or two years prior to my joining Miles’ band. But the way I actually got into Miles’ band, I had been hearing rumors that Miles was looking for me. And finally I had started hearing so many rumors that I began to believe it because at first I said, “Come on, get out of here, Miles Davis calling me?” Forget it. That will never happen. I mean I had never even dreamed of playing with Miles. That was beyond my fondest dreams. And anyway so Donald Byrd, again, because he was my roommate, said, “If Miles calls you, tell him you’re not working with anybody.” I said, “But Donald, I owe you so much.” He said, “Shut up, man.” He said, “I would never stand in the way of you having such a great opportunity like that.” He says, “Tell him you’re not working with anybody.” And it was almost within about an hour, the phone rang and it was Miles. First question Miles asked was, “Are you working with anybody?” And I looked at Donald and I said, “No.” And then he invited me to his house the next day at 2:30 I think it was. Click. And he hung up the phone. I didn’t know his phone number. Fortunately I knew Donald Byrd knew where he lived, but I started to panic. And then a half hour later, Tony Williams, a great drummer, called me. And it turned out that Miles had called him too. And he had Miles’ address and everything, so the next day we went to Miles’ place. And Miles ushered us into his basement, his rec room there. And Ron Carter the bassist was there, and George Coleman, the tenor saxophonist, he was there. And Tony Williams and myself. And Miles. And Miles didn’t pick up his horn. He just said, “Play some of these” I think he got Ron to kind of lead this, what I thought was an audition, and he says, “Play some of these tunes.” There were some new tunes they were working on I guess. And then Miles split. He went upstairs somewhere. And so we started playing these tunes and they had music there. This went on for three days. And I saw Miles maybe twice in those three days. And once Gil Evans and Philly Jo Jones came down. Gil Evans, who did these incredible arrangements of “Porgy & Bess” and “Sketches of Spain,” “Miles Ahead,” a bunch of things. Anyway and Philly Jo Jones, who was Miles’ former drummer. They came down. And by the way I found out much later that Miles was upstairs in one of his other rooms listening to us play over the intercom. So I think he suspected that if he had been there we would have felt intimidated. So he wasn’t there, he was away, we didn’t even know where he was. So he could really hear what we could do. Anyway, after the third day, he came downstairs and he said, “Okay, tomorrow we meet at 3:30 at Columbia Studios on 30th Street.” And that was a very famous recording studio. I knew © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

sources.speaker: HH
sources.text: that studio, but I’d never recorded there. And I said, I was just shocked. And I said, “Miles, does that mean I’m in the band?” And he said, “You’re making the record.” And then he smiled. And the one statement he made that gave me the most indication that he liked what was going on, because he hadn’t said anything yet, nothing complimentary, nothing. At the studio, we walked in there, and Teo Macero, who was the producer, came in to the booth, the recording booth, and Miles said, “Hey Teo, listen to this.” And I could tell by Miles’ face he was just champing at the bit to show Teo his new band. And so we kicked off one of the tunes. I think it was “Seven Steps to Heaven.” And Teo almost fell off his chair, he couldn’t believe it. Because it was a very exciting group you know, and Tony at the time was seventeen years old. So he was — talking about a prodigy, that’s the prodigy. And he was a real phenomenon. And we played there, and then we recorded the album “Seven Steps to Heaven,” and the following week we played our first gig. I played Bowdoin College in Maine. And I was there for five and a half years after that.

275788.proposed: piano duet partner; two duo tours ('76 and '78) and a South America tour
275788.evidence: We — Chick and I — I should say about when we first got together to do the first tour, you know, when we first got together to rehearse, neither one of us had done anything quite like that before.
275788.subject: Herbie Hancock
275788.audit: {"change": "Performing duo tours together is 'played with', not 'collaborated with'; old evidence spliced.", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "piano duet partners, toured together in 1976 and 1978"}}

sources.speaker: HH
sources.text: We — Chick and I — I should say about when we first got together to do the first tour, you know, when we first got together to rehearse, neither one of us had done anything quite like that before. He had done some duets I guess with his, well his then-girlfriend, now wife, Gayle Moran, who was working in his band and she’s also a singer. But there was sort of a different story because she hadn’t had the same kinds of experiences. She wasn’t like a heavyweight piano player per se, that wasn’t what she was about. Anyway Chick had two pianos in his house and — two big Steinways I guess they were or maybe a Bosendorfer and a Steinway concert grands — which was fortunate. That way we didn’t have to pay for a rehearsal studio and we didn’t have to rent pianos. It was great. And then we could just take our time and still really relax. But I was a little nervous about it and Chick was a little nervous about it too because we both really respected each other. You know we’re both contemporaries. And so we decided to take a tune, I don’t remember which tune it was, but we were both so cautious in the beginning. But it was funny to notice that that became easy. So then we would each start to take a few more chances. And that became easy. And then we started being less and less polite you know. Because at first we were so polite. You know I would play something and then I would wait to hear what Chick was going to play and really try to follow him you know, and leave him a lot of space. And he’d leave me space. It got to the point where we didn’t have to leave each other any space. We could both just play simultaneously and it didn’t even conflict. So we said, “Well, it looks like this is going to be a lot easier than we © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

sources.speaker: HH
sources.text: thought.” It just happens that Chick and I just really fit each other. Somehow it just works. It’s amazing, you know, really amazing. I’ve had the great fortune also to play five concerts opposite Oscar Peterson but we played a couple of things together. So I mean that was a great opportunity for me. He’s one of the people that was a major influence on me when I was coming up. That’s a little more difficult, playing with Oscar. Maybe because he has been his own man for so long that he’s used to doing certain kinds of things and this is pretty far removed from what he’s accustomed to. But still, we were able to find a common ground and get something going. But with Chick it’s effortless. I don’t even have to think about him being, about providing a space for him you know. So it was really fantastic. And you’re right, we would feed each other constantly. I’ve got some stories I could tell you about some funny concerts. One time during the tour it became so easy to play together that we started trying to find other devices to use to kind of just a combination of either, like throwing a monkey wrench into the works just to give us something to deal with.

sources.speaker: HH
sources.text: Yeah. Exactly. So we started getting into playing inside the piano you know, and doing things like that, a combination of the two, and different effects, and then hitting, then we started hitting the sounding board and hitting the metal part, the harp of the piano, using that for rhythm. And I remember one concert, I think it was in Hamburg. We played the concert and the next morning the newspaper comes out and there’s a picture of Chick and I. Chick was in the piano, knees and everything. I mean he had crawled into the piano, I was under the piano on my back, banging on the sounding board, and we were actually, things had just gone that far. We were making music with rhythm using other parts of the piano. I mean it was amazing. We would use physical gestures sometimes. We’d get into where we were playing things and I’d do this, and then he would do this, or then he would do this. And then there were eye movements, you know. Up and down and you know, and that became part of it, and different things. And then you know he would do, but we would make it as though it were music. We’d make some kind of pattern, organized patterns out of it. And integrate that, those kind of body movements, with the notes that we were playing. And it made some sense. Once we played at the Montreaux Jazz Festival and this was incredible. We got so many standing ovations it was amazing. It got to the point where by the third or fourth or fifth standing ovation, we decided not to even go to the pianos. So I took a chair, set it down in the middle of the stage, Chick sat in the chair and I sat next to him, and we, for the last final encore, we never even touched the pianos. We were making sounds with our mouth, and doing things with gestures, and all kinds of things. And the people went crazy. They loved it. And because we had kind of gotten them to that. They were along for the trip. And it really worked. It was a great, © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

sources.speaker: HH
sources.text: great thing to experience for me. And we wound up actually doing two tours. One was in ‘76 and I think the other one was in 1978. So we had a great time together. And then we did a, we actually did a short tour in Brazil, and I’ve forgotten what year that was, Brazil and some other parts of South America, in the ‘80s.

And he really showed me the ropes in New York and he really encouraged me in so many ways and taught me a lot of things. And was the person responsible for me doing my very first record as a leader. He is responsible for me getting my own publishing company so that my first tunes were published in my own company, and not in the record company’s company. Thank goodness for that because one of the first tunes I wrote was “Watermelon Man.”

sources.speaker: HH

But when I saw this guy improvising and it sounded organized to me. I didn’t know what he was doing but it sounded like he knew what he was doing. Then I became fascinated. ‘Cause he was doing it on my instrument and he was my age. I thought you had to be much older to play jazz you know, like nineteen or something. But he was doing it. And so I started hanging out with this guy and asking him what is he listening to, how does he learn that, how do you do these things. And so at the time, his favorite pianist and the person he tried to emulate was George Shearing. 275788.proposed: second piano teacher; introduced him to dynamics and Chopin
275788.evidence: And then I got a new teacher, Mrs. Jordan.
275788.subject: Herbie Hancock
275788.audit: {"change": "Relation right; evidence spliced, made verbatim.", "previous": {"relation": "mentor of", "direction": "target", "proposed": "piano teacher"}}

sources.speaker: HH
sources.text: That’s a funny word. I’m starting to hear people use that more and more now in reference to me and my early life in music. But I never, I mean I think that way about some other people but never about myself, you know? I just did what I do. I started when I was seven, but you know I think that’s, I don’t know if that’s an average age, it may be an average age, it’s probably close to average for starting to learn to play an instrument. I’ve heard of people starting to play instruments as early as three. Now I guess with the Suzuki Method and some other methods, they start at one. When they come out of the womb they’re starting. But anyway, I seemed to be able to able to catch on to reading fairly quickly when I was young. My first teacher, which her name was Mrs. Whalen, and she taught me for two and a half years. She was the church organist for the Baptist church and I took lessons in the second floor of the Baptist church you know. And that was the church I belonged to at that time. Anyway, she didn’t teach me very much about dynamics. So I could only play at one volume level, and that was fairly loud. I didn’t know anything about playing soft, nothing about touch, nothing about nuances, and nothing about the history of music. I just learned to read what the notes were. And then I got a new teacher, Mrs. Jordan. And I remember sort of, it’s not exactly auditioning for her, but she wanted to hear, you know, hear me play something so she could tell what level I was at. And she said, “Ah, yes, you read very well.” And she said, “But did she © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

sources.speaker: HH
sources.text: Well that was during the time that I was with Mrs. Jordan, the second teacher. By that time I was playing Bach inventions, some fugues and preludes and some Chopin. I had gotten into etudes and I think maybe Chopin’s “Fantasie Impromptu,” some things like that. So in 1950 — actually 1950, is that right? No — 1951 I auditioned for this — basically it was a concert. The Young People’s Concert Series in Chicago. And what would happen is that you would audition for who was then the Assistant Conductor of the Chicago Symphony. And that was George Schick, who became President of Manhattan School of Music later on by the way. Anyway, so they would select one person from each instrument of the orchestra who would be a winner, and I happened to win for the piano. And the prize would be to play a concerto with the Chicago Symphony. Anyway, I won. And then, well the way I found out that I won was that I received a post card in the mail about two months later, that said, “Congratulations, you’ve been selected as the piano winner of the Young People’s Concert Series, however,” — oh by the way, the date you are to perform is February 5, 1952 I think it was. Or 1951, I’ve forgotten. And maybe I auditioned in ‘50 and played in ‘51. But anyway, so anyway it said, “However the concerto that you auditioned with, somehow we haven’t been able to locate the orchestral parts, so you’ll either have to learn a new concerto or forfeit the performance just so you know you are a winner but you won’t be able to play with the Chicago Symphony.” So I had to learn a new concerto you know? And that other one I knew cold. The new one I had to learn in about three months so I didn’t have nearly as much time. And so I made the performance, and as a matter of fact after the performance I signed the first autograph that I ever signed, you know. But the next week — oh I should say that the performance was at the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. And the next week my teacher had gotten herself and me tickets to see Myra Hess, who was a very famous classical pianist at the time, who was performing with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. So we went that week to see Myra Hess, guess what she played? The concerto that I auditioned with. So all of that nonsense that they said about not being able to find the parts was a bunch of bologna.

No — 1951 I auditioned for this — basically it was a concert. The Young People’s Concert Series in Chicago. And what would happen is that you would audition for who was then the Assistant Conductor of the Chicago Symphony. And that was George Schick, who became President of Manhattan School of Music later on by the way. Anyway, so they would select one person from each instrument of the orchestra who would be a winner, and I happened to win for the piano. Or 1951, I’ve forgotten. And maybe I auditioned in ‘50 and played in ‘51. But anyway, so anyway it said, “However the concerto that you auditioned with, somehow we haven’t been able to locate the orchestral parts, so you’ll either have to learn a new concerto or forfeit the performance just so you know you are a winner but you won’t be able to play with the Chicago Symphony.” So I had to learn a new concerto you know? And that other one I knew cold. The new one I had to learn in about three months so I didn’t have nearly as much time. And so I made the performance, and as a matter of fact after the performance I signed the first autograph that I ever signed, you know. But the next week — oh I should say that the performance was at the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. And the next week my teacher had gotten herself and me tickets to see Myra Hess, who was a very famous classical pianist at the time, who was performing with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. So we went that week to see Myra Hess, guess what she played? The concerto that I auditioned with. So all of that nonsense that they said about not being able to find the parts was a bunch of bologna.

And what would happen is that you would audition for who was then the Assistant Conductor of the Chicago Symphony. And that was George Schick, who became President of Manhattan School of Music later on by the way. Anyway, so they would select one person from each instrument of the orchestra who would be a winner, and I happened to win for the piano. And the prize would be to play a concerto with the Chicago Symphony. Anyway, I won. And then, well the way I found out that I won was that I received a post card in the mail about two months later, that said, “Congratulations, you’ve been selected as the piano winner of the Young People’s Concert Series, however,” — oh by the way, the date you are to perform is February 5, 1952 I think it was. Or 1951, I’ve forgotten. And maybe I auditioned in ‘50 and played in ‘51. But anyway, so anyway it said, “However the concerto that you auditioned with, somehow we haven’t been able to locate the orchestral parts, so you’ll either have to learn a new concerto or forfeit the performance just so you know you are a winner but you won’t be able to play with the Chicago Symphony.” So I had to learn a new concerto you know? And that other one I knew cold. The new one I had to learn in about three months so I didn’t have nearly as much time. And so I made the performance, and as a matter of fact after the performance I signed the first autograph that I ever signed, you know. But the next week — oh I should say that the performance was at the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. And the next week my teacher had gotten herself and me tickets to see Myra Hess, who was a very famous classical pianist at the time, who was performing with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. So we went that week to see Myra Hess, guess what she played? The concerto that I auditioned with. So all of that nonsense that they said about not being able to find the parts was a bunch of bologna.

And my wife is looking at me like, “I know you’re going to get us in front of shaking hands with the President,” and you know something, when they got about three steps from the President, I ran out of film. And I could see the rays coming from my wife. sources.text: I got on this Pullman, and there was all these great musicians on there, Doc Cheatham, Keg Johnson, Foots Thomas and all these guys. And I said Keg Johnson got me the gig, he recommended me, and I said to Keg, I say, “Keg, I didn’t ask Cab about no money or nothing,” I say, “He just told me to be here at nine o’clock.” He say, “Everybody in this band makes $100 a week.” I almost fainted. I almost fainted. I said I’ll be a millionaire in two months.

sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: piece of paper, and he’d reach in his pocket and pull out a sheet of stamps, and tear one off, and put it on his autograph. And I said, “Wow, man. If I get ever so — one day I will do that.” I haven’t made it yet, but — give me a sheet of stamps. But he was wonderful. And how I got the gig was they went to California to do this movie with Al Jolson, “The Singing Kid.” And Al Jolson was so great, I mean Al Morgan was so great and he had such photogenic features and things, that Cab looked around and the camera was on Al Morgan, it wasn’t on him. Well that didn’t sit too cool. And the director of the movie told Al Morgan, said, “Look, you’ve got a lot of style. If you’re out in here in California any time we do a movie with music in it, you have the job.” So Al Morgan quit. He stayed with Les Hite’s band, with Lionel and all those guys. And Cab Calloway had to come back east without a bass player, and Budd Johnson’s brother, Keg Johnson was in Cab’s band, and he say, “Well look, check out Milt Hinton if you’re going through Chicago. He’s down to the Three Deuces with Zutty Singleton and Art Tatum and Lee Childs.” I’m down there with them guys, $35 a week, best job in town.

275794.audit: {"change": "one-off concert group, not 'collaborated with'; who led is not stated", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "played together in a group for a concert in California organized by Carl Jefferson"}}

sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: He couldn’t get away from that. I got a funny one. There’s a million Benny Goodman stories. You know Carl Jefferson, he just passed from Concord Records, Carl Jefferson was out there in California, and he was having a big jazz party out there, and he called me up and he says, “Milt, I’d like for you to bring a group of major musicians from New York out, so get some guys.” And I say, “Okay, I’ll get them together.” So I got Jo Jones, Claude Hopkins, Budd Johnson, Benny Morton, Roy Eldridge, and I mentioned Jo Jones and myself. You couldn’t get a more senior group than that. So we were going to go to California to do this concert. So Benny Goodman’s going to be out there. So Carl Jefferson told says, told Benny, says, “Well Milt is going to come out and bring some guys,” and he says, “Oh he is?” Well maybe I can get them to play with me. He says, “Call him up and tell him that.” So Carl Jefferson says, “No, you call him and tell him that.” Now Carl Jefferson is giving me $6,000, a thousand dollars apiece for each one of us to come out there. And Benny Goodman called me up and say, “Hey, Milt, I see where you’re going to be out here in California at the concert.” I say, “Yeah.” He says, “I’m closing, do you want to play with me?” I say, “yeah Benny, I don’t mind playing with you,” I said, “what’s the bread like?” He says, “Will $185 be okay?” I say, “Oh, wait a minute, Benny, wait a minute” I say. He say, “Okay, what do you want?” So I figured out, I got greedy. I say, well I’m getting $1000 already, I’ll just ask him for $500 more. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: He couldn’t get away from that. I got a funny one. There’s a million Benny Goodman stories. You know Carl Jefferson, he just passed from Concord Records, Carl Jefferson was out there in California, and he was having a big jazz party out there, and he called me up and he says, “Milt, I’d like for you to bring a group of major musicians from New York out, so get some guys.” And I say, “Okay, I’ll get them together.” So I got Jo Jones, Claude Hopkins, Budd Johnson, Benny Morton, Roy Eldridge, and I mentioned Jo Jones and myself. You couldn’t get a more senior group than that. So we were going to go to California to do this concert. So Benny Goodman’s going to be out there. So Carl Jefferson told says, told Benny, says, “Well Milt is going to come out and bring some guys,” and he says, “Oh he is?” Well maybe I can get them to play with me. He says, “Call him up and tell him that.” So Carl Jefferson says, “No, you call him and tell him that.” Now Carl Jefferson is giving me $6,000, a thousand dollars apiece for each one of us to come out there. And Benny Goodman called me up and say, “Hey, Milt, I see where you’re going to be out here in California at the concert.” I say, “Yeah.” He says, “I’m closing, do you want to play with me?” I say, “yeah Benny, I don’t mind playing with you,” I said, “what’s the bread like?” He says, “Will $185 be okay?” I say, “Oh, wait a minute, Benny, wait a minute” I say. He say, “Okay, what do you want?” So I figured out, I got greedy. I say, well I’m getting $1000 already, I’ll just ask him for $500 more. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

And we were over in the corner playing and everybody’s congratulating Benny Goodman because his daughter’s getting married, and his foot is going like this, tapping his foot. And next thing we know he’s got his clarinet and he’s right over there with us. He was an insatiable musician.

So we get to the White House and now Benny wants a rehearsal. And you know Buddy Rich ain’t going to make no rehearsal. But of course I was there at the rehearsal, Bucky was there, and Hank Jones and I were there, up in Benny’s apartment and we come up there and sit around for a half hour, and Benny comes up, “Hello fellas.” He picks up his horn. sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: Yeah. But Milton thrives on it, and as I said we’ve been together over, well at least fifty- five years and it’s very important for him to do this. See Milton believes he’s never going to die. He says that he’s going to live forever. And I believe him, that’s been his basic philosophy, that he, as long as he shares his talents and his knowledge with young people, and those young people continue to carry it on, in that way, he says he’ll never die. And he has really spent his lifetime trying to, not really be a role model, he’s just being Milton. But in the end I mean that’s eventually what he is, I mean to show these young people that you can work with your church, with the Boy Scouts, you can be the best musician in the world, and you can make it. And I’m very fortunate I mean to have been able to work with Milton. We’ve been able to work together and Milt never wanted to be a band leader, he never wanted to have a lot of money, he believes that money is to be spent, to be used for the good, for somebody’s good. And I go along with him on that along those lines. So there’s many youngsters that have come through the years that have in later years I mean they have really shown us their appreciation for some of the things © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: Oh, I think he got that always. In the Calloway band, and then — I’ll tell you what happened — he came to New York after he left Calloway’s band, and he was walking down the street one day and he ran into Jackie Gleason and his manager Bull. So Jackie, well Milton knew Jackie when he was, when only the musicians were laughing at his jokes, when they used to buy him a drink, so but he, as I said the day he ran into Milton he said to Milton said, “well what are you doing.” And Milton says, “well I’m looking for a job.” I mean Milt was just freelancing a little bit around because he’d just come off the road. And so Jackie says to Bull he says, “you know we have a record date tomorrow with Bobby Hackett,” so he says, you know, “let’s get Milt.” So Bull says, “you already have a bass player.” He said, “Well now we’ve got two.” And he hired Milton to do that record date. Well consequently there were no black musicians were recording in those days like that. And but when he went in, the A&R man and the conductor and everyone saw that Milton was qualified, and this was, a contractor came over and got his name and the address and said well how can I contact you if I need you, and that’s how he became involved, because he was qualified. You see it didn’t make any difference whenever a contractor would call, it could be, he never asked who it was for. He would call and say, “is Mr. Hinton free at ten o’clock on Tuesday” or whatever it is, and I had an appointment book, and, “yes he’s free.” “Well have him at RCA Victor or Capitol or Columbia Studio at such and such a time. Now when he left home he didn’t know whether it was a rock ‘n roll, whether it was with Stravinsky, whether it was with Barbra Streisand, he didn’t, or with a — he didn’t know who it was for. Guy Lombardo, you know, it could be anybody. And these were the people that he just went there, they put the music up there, and he had to be on time, he says that, not looking for a place to park or not adjusting your strings, when that conductor’s baton came down across his nose you were there to get that first note. 275795.audit: {"change": "not a band member; travelled with the band", "previous": {"relation": "in music group with", "direction": "target", "proposed": "wife of Milton Hinton, traveling with Cab Calloway's band in the early 1950s"}}

sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: a lot of little things that you should know when you start out on the road. Fortunately, in the early 50’s I used to work in Chicago and they had this famous hotel there, the DuSable Hotel, and I worked there and it gave me an opportunity to meet a lot of the musicians. So I go back a long way. As I say it’s just been beautiful. I mean I’ve had a chance to meet all the musicians, and all the years that I was traveling with Milton with Cab Calloway’s band, I was the only female who traveled all the time, and I was like the den mother. I used to save their money — those who would drink and couldn’t handle it, I’d take their money away from them at night, and then when they got sober the next morning I’d return it to them. And I was just considered the den mother, and down through the years I’ve had this great opportunity to meet many, many, many, many families and I have extended families all over the world. As a result, I mean, I’ve just been Milton Hinton’s wife. So I don’t know what else you want me to —

sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: dressed and go out. Because that way it alleviated the necessity of having to try to find places to stay and we would go to California using the Pullman. And coming back — oh and I must say Cab had his big automobile on the car, on the Pullman, it was really nice. And then coming back we would hire, he would hire a Greyhound bus, a very nice bus. We were fortunate that we never had to travel in cars like most of the other musicians in those days. They had to pile in automobiles. But Calloway was first class all the way. He was always first class. And coming back we would have a bus and we used to keep the same driver, the same bus, and work our way back down through the south and back to New York. And it’s kinda funny that we had this one bus driver for quite a long time, and instead of sleeping when he was supposed to be sleeping while the band was playing, he would be partying. So it was my job, I had to sit up in the seat right behind him and keep him awake until daybreak, and then Mr. Wright, who was the road manager, then he’d come and he would sit up there, sit up there with him and then I could go take a nap. But it was fun. It was really fun as I say, and I was always the only female traveling with the band all the time. So I was the den mother.

sources.text: Mona Hinton is half of the jazz world’s most beloved couple. She has helped direct the marvelous career of her husband Milt Hinton, and acted as a business advisor to Count Basie as well as music contractor for Lena Horne, Quincy Jones and Sammy Davis. sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: Milton just loved to take pictures. On the road he and Keg Johnson, his dear friend, used to set up a darkroom in the bathroom in the theater or maybe the hotel where we were, and he took hundreds and hundreds of pictures. 275795.evidence: The minute you hear Teddy Wilson, something, that’s Teddy Wilson, you know what I mean?
275795.subject: Mona Hinton

sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: Oh sure, well that’s true. But you know that’s the secret of being, that’s the secret that most musicians should have. Because the minute that I hear Milton playing — we’ll get back to Louis — but I have to tell you this. The minute that I hear something, I can almost tell you that’s Milton Hinton playing, you know why? Because if you notice, see Milton pushed that 16 piece to 17 piece band all those years with Calloway with nothing but a little microphone, you know. So when you hear, you notice it, when you hear him you hear that solid beat, you know what I mean? Whereas you don’t hear it in any other musicians, even the bass players along that time, as I say. So that’s like your signature. The minute you hear Teddy Wilson, something, that’s Teddy Wilson, you know what I mean? But if somebody who is mimicking Teddy, you don’t know who in the devil they are. And that’s the way it was with Louis. I mean he had this quality of his tone or whatever you — I don’t know the exact or precise word to use for it, but the minute you heard it you knew that that was Louis Armstrong. As I say and that’s really what all musicians are striving for.

275795.evidence: So but the Basies and us we were friends and we were neighbors

sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: Well you see I never traveled with the Basie band. See Milton was with Calloway for about 15 or 16 years. So I was always with the Cab Calloway band. So but the Basies and us we were friends and we were neighbors, and I frequently, well Catherine loved, they had a beautiful backyard with an Olympic-sized swimming pool and whatnot. And she loved to give parties for a lot of charitable organizations. And I do remember on one occasion that Milton, and Bill, I call him Bill, but Basie would come over to our house, and he and Milton would sit in the basement and yak and we had this old piano, and he’d play like they used to do in the silent movies and whatnot. And so they were sitting down there one day and the band didn’t show up at Catherine’s party. So she came and she says “Bill you have to come, you have to come, you and Hinton” (she always called him Hinton). “You and Hinton have to come.” And so well they weren’t too happy about that. But there they are down there playing all these old, what do you call that music, like for the background for the silent movies? And he had to drop everything and go running back home, to play some music for her garden party. But as I say so I really don’t know too much about what happened there. 275795.evidence: he ran into Jackie Gleason and his manager Bull
275795.subject: Mona Hinton
275795.audit: {"change": "Gleason's manager in Milt's story", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: Oh, I think he got that always. In the Calloway band, and then — I’ll tell you what happened — he came to New York after he left Calloway’s band, and he was walking down the street one day and he ran into Jackie Gleason and his manager Bull. So Jackie, well Milton knew Jackie when he was, when only the musicians were laughing at his jokes, when they used to buy him a drink, so but he, as I said the day he ran into Milton he said to Milton said, “well what are you doing.” And Milton says, “well I’m looking for a job.” I mean Milt was just freelancing a little bit around because he’d just come off the road. And so Jackie says to Bull he says, “you know we have a record date tomorrow with Bobby Hackett,” so he says, you know, “let’s get Milt.” So Bull says, “you already have a bass player.” He said, “Well now we’ve got two.” And he hired Milton to do that record date. Well consequently there were no black musicians were recording in those days like that. And but when he went in, the A&R man and the conductor and everyone saw that Milton was qualified, and this was, a contractor came over and got his name and the address and said well how can I contact you if I need you, and that’s how he became involved, because he was qualified. You see it didn’t make any difference whenever a contractor would call, it could be, he never asked who it was for. He would call and say, “is Mr. Hinton free at ten o’clock on Tuesday” or whatever it is, and I had an appointment book, and, “yes he’s free.” “Well have him at RCA Victor or Capitol or Columbia Studio at such and such a time. Now when he left home he didn’t know whether it was a rock ‘n roll, whether it was with Stravinsky, whether it was with Barbra Streisand, he didn’t, or with a — he didn’t know who it was for. Guy Lombardo, you know, it could be anybody. And these were the people that he just went there, they put the music up there, and he had to be on time, he says that, not looking for a place to park or not adjusting your strings, when that conductor’s baton came down across his nose you were there to get that first note. And so Milton believes in punctuality. But these are the © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

275795.subject: Mona Hinton
275795.audit: {"change": "source block corrected", "previous": {"relation": "acquaintance of", "direction": "na", "proposed": "road manager in Cab Calloway's band"}}

sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: dressed and go out. Because that way it alleviated the necessity of having to try to find places to stay and we would go to California using the Pullman. And coming back — oh and I must say Cab had his big automobile on the car, on the Pullman, it was really nice. And then coming back we would hire, he would hire a Greyhound bus, a very nice bus. We were fortunate that we never had to travel in cars like most of the other musicians in those days. They had to pile in automobiles. But Calloway was first class all the way. He was always first class. And coming back we would have a bus and we used to keep the same driver, the same bus, and work our way back down through the south and back to New York. And it’s kinda funny that we had this one bus driver for quite a long time, and instead of sleeping when he was supposed to be sleeping while the band was playing, he would be partying. So it was my job, I had to sit up in the seat right behind him and keep him awake until daybreak, and then Mr. Wright, who was the road manager, then he’d come and he would sit up there, sit up there with him and then I could go take a nap. But it was fun. It was really fun as I say, and I was always the only female traveling with the band all the time. So I was the den mother.

275795.evidence: frequently we would run into Glenn Miller’s band
275795.subject: Mona Hinton

sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: Well, unfortunately, due to the climate of our society, you know that we had, the blacks and the whites were segregated. And it made it very difficult, especially when we were traveling in the south. Because frequently we would run into Glenn Miller’s band or Tommy Dorsey’s band, or some of the well known white bands. They were staying in nice hotels. And unfortunately the black musician would have to stay on the other side of the tracks, usually in someone’s home, or in a hotel that was not very good. And as I say unfortunately, frequently the owners of the hotels, they would take advantage I mean of the black musicians. They knew that we could not stay in places, and we’d run into places with rats and with the roaches and with the bed bugs and whatnot. So under those circumstances it was not good. Frequently we would go in towns and I would have to go out in the black community and try to help find rooms for the musicians in Calloway’s band, and sometimes it was very, very, the places where we had to eat were just intolerable. And as I say, we made it.

275795.evidence: He just did the soundtrack for Spike’s new movie called “Clockers”
275795.subject: Mona Hinton
275795.audit: {"change": "Milt recorded the Clockers soundtrack", "previous": null}

sources.speaker: MH
sources.text: Spike. He just did the soundtrack for Spike’s new movie called “Clockers” I think is the name of it. So since 1930, he has worked with every musician. And I must tell you an interesting story about Quincy. For Milton’s 80th birthday I think it was, he sent a home made video, a homemade videotape to the house, and he had someone take it. And he’s standing there with his envelope and piece of paper, and he says, “Bring the camera up I want you to be sure and see this, that Milt can see that this is his handwriting and this is his torn check.” And he tells a story on this tape saying that on his first recording date that any company allowed him to do under his own name, I don’t know whether the copyist messed up or whatever but anyway the date had to go into overtime. The company held him responsible for the overtime, and here is a young kid, his first recording date under his own name, didn’t have a dime. And so anyway, he borrowed and stole and got ahold of the money, and he paid every musician the money that was due them. And he says you know every musician took that money except you, Milton, and here’s, he reads the letter and he shows Milton the letter that Milton returned to him, and Milton evidently had torn the check and put it in the letter. sources.text: In November of 1995, the American Federation of Jazz Societies honored Jane Jarvis with a jazz festival celebrating her 80th birthday and distinguished career in music. Her diverse achievements include record producing for the Muzak Corporation, official organist for the Milwaukee Braves and New York Mets, jazz performing, recording, arranging and an ever-increasing role as a lecturer and spokesperson for jazz education. She is a founding member and pianist for the Statesmen of Jazz, a group of veteran musicians whose goals include presenting jazz to young audiences across the country. She records frequently and can be found in the company of such stellar bassists as Milt Hinton and Jay Leonhart.

sources.text: Well I’m pleased that you said that, but I was a drummer, and there’s a difference. And so for some reason when they took me to rehearsal to watch her, I would watch the drummer in the pit. And you never know why, Monk, you just don’t know why. I can’t tell you why, and you try to emulate what he did. You take your hands and — whether it’s good or bad you don’t know at the time at all. But all of a sudden you get kind of hooked on it when it comes in here and it comes in here. That’s what you want to do. And I’m very happy that I did get to do it. And then what happened, I’d go home and listen to Chick Webb and Jimmie Lunceford and Duke Ellington and Count Basie and Woody, stay up and listen to the remote broadcasts at night you know. “From the Park Central Hotel and now the King of the Drums, Chick Webb.” And he’d do a thing called “Let’s Get Together.” So I knew all the theme songs you know. And then, older, Benny Goodman’s band, Gene Krupa was the innovator. And I listened to him and I said, “boy that’s the greatest.” And it’s not that my sister said he wasn’t. sources.text: No. What it was, see it’s a fallacy. People write what they think. They think that I drove the bus, which I never did because I couldn’t ride a bicycle. I didn’t drive any bus. I could drive a car. What it was is I was his assistant so to speak. In other words they said that I went and played the charts and he sat when we got a new chart, that he sat in front listening to me play. That’s not true. Because when he was with Tommy, Harry James, Artie Shaw, there was no assistant drummer. He could play it the first time he heard it. So all I did was if he wanted to sing, I played. And when we did a dance if he felt like doing that, he did it. When we played the Paramount Theater or the Strand or all those theaters we played all over, the Apollo and the Howard in Washington and the Regal in Chicago, I played the acts when he wanted me to do it. But then it was interesting because playing with your idol, like if he would compliment me, if he would say, “boy you really sounded good,” I didn’t want to hear that because I didn’t believe it. See? So I’d say, “oh the bus is leaving at four o’clock.” I didn’t want to hear I play good. I don’t want to hear that. Because you know, you’re playing with your idol. It was better for me when I joined like Frankie Laine for six years and Patti Page and Josephine Baker. But we toured with Josephine. It was Sweets Edison, Buddy and myself. sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: called — well it was called Buddy’s Place but the restaurant was Sam’s Jazz Upstairs. Then the one on 33rd Street was a 400 seat club. And my first attraction was Buddy’s big band, Carmen McRae and Nipsy Russell. Because I wanted to bring the Paramount Theater days in there. And unfortunately the guy that owned the place was a thief. You know he did tricks. But we had Joe Williams in there with the Thad Jones band, we had Woody’s band in there. You know we had good stuff going on there. But the problem with me owning or even managing a club, if you talk in the club while they’re playing, you’re gone. I’d put you right out. I wouldn’t allow it. Well the reason is if you’re in Carnegie Hall and Mr. Rubenstein is playing or Mr. Horowitz, you’re not talking. I mean if you want to whisper, but when you get loud, in a small club— Stan Getz was playing in there and some people at the table were talking and I’d go over. I’d say, “see this sign here” I mean this little card, the tent card. “What does it say? Refrain from talking.” And you’d better pay attention there because if I come back again—” And they didn’t want to listen. So, “see I’m in a good mood tonight, that’s twice. The third time you’re gone. Now I’m telling you.” So they calmed down. And I went over to them, younger people, I said, “why did you come in here tonight?” You know, why did you come in here? “Well we’re fans of Stan Getz.” I said, “well see you’re not doing yourself justice. You could have saved all this money, stay home, play his records, and yell, scream, do whatever you want.” I said, “let me ask you something.” They would understand that. I said, “what business are you in, if I may ask?” “The furniture business.” I says, “is Saturday a big day for you? You make big sales on Saturday, don’t you?” I said, “if I came over while you’re taking a two thousand, three thousand dollar order and yell and scream and make noise, if it’s going to distract you, you couldn’t make the sale, right? It’s the same thing. That’s how they make their living. That’s rude.” You see? So therefore, with me, I mean if they talk when the band’s playing, I’m a little — who am I going to hurt? But I go tell them, don’t do that. Don’t get up and dance, we’re not a dance band. Go in the back. Go play records and do “Mama Loves Papa” or something. Go there and do it. Don’t do it in here. But that’s my honesty. And it’s not that I — I don’t try to offend anybody, I don’t try to be rude, I say please, this is not what we do. We don’t do this.

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: roll and the rap and then there’s whatever country, and that’s fine. But we get more respect, or most of the jazz players will tell you, in Europe and Japan. And I don’t understand that. I don’t understand that. Because it’s a great art to play jazz. I don’t know, you know, playing drums. And I love melodic things, and lyrical things, but doing this, I can’t play “Stardust” on the drum I don’t think. If I could I’d make a lot of money. But anyway you know what they do is they don’t respect it. They don’t respect. Oh I know what I was going to say, like I don’t know how these people play jazz. I don’t know how you can improvise. I don’t know how you can do that, like play anything you want to play and it becomes a melodic, and it becomes a composition. Oh there’s riffs, there’s standard riffs that we play. But like Lester Young played that thing behind Billie Holiday on the CBS special, that’s like one of the greatest melodic things I’ve ever heard. And it’s gorgeous to do that. But how do you do that you see? You got a lot of lead trumpet players that couldn’t play jazz. They could play great lead, like Conrad Gozzo and Bernie Glow and some of those guys, and I really think, we play enough high schools and colleges where they make a mistake. Because you go in and there’s the young players, the high school player. “Who is your favorite saxophone?” They’ll say John Coltrane. Right? Okay. Now they don’t know John Coltrane played with Earl Bostic’s band, played the blues, but he wanted to progress. “You know Johnny Hodges?” “No.” “You know Ben Webster?” “No.” “You know Sweets Edison?” “No.” Well if you don’t listen, how are you going to get to — if you don’t go to kindergarten and high school, how are you going to get to there? But the teachers don’t tell them. Sherrie will go in and say, “we’re going to play the blues.” “What’s the blues?” And they’ll read the chart, of course they play it every day. After four bars of improvisation they’re done. They can’t play one — after the fourth, the fifth bar, over. And you’re looking at, where is this all going to come from, what we’re trying to keep and preserve. I’m not a campaigner, but I’m just talking about honest truth. There’s a truth to what we do, there’s this truth to our music. I mean I love a marching band if it’s good in the street, I mean I go to the symphony and watch the symphonies play. But why? Why? I mean outside of Basie’s band, that’s not talking the dance band, not Glenn Miller. Buddy Morrow’s got an intact band. The rest of them, the Jimmy Dorsey band, the guys got the library to “Tangerine” and “Amapola,” he comes and gets twelve guys. They don’t know the difference. They say, “Tangerine,” oh, it’s the Jimmy Dorsey band. The Guy Lombardo band or whatever. The Harry James band. One guy, they come with the book, you know, “Sleepy Lagoon,” “You Made Me Love You” and they play. We out there, we buy these things. Maybe, I don’t know, Sherrie could correct me, twenty, thirty thousand dollars worth of arrangements. And we’re always trying to play new. And we’re always thinking of new things to do. Because we don’t want the band to get bored. It’s exciting. Let’s try this © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: act and I played. They see the big sling. Clark Terry told me, he said he was there and the word went out that Buddy’s arm is not broken, he wants to show he can play with one hand. But it was broken. So we played there a week, then we go into the Paramount Theater downtown and the managing director of the Paramount, Bob Whiteman, came up. And he said, “the rumor is that your arm is not broken but there’s a sensation — keep it in the sling.” If it’s not broken we could play the Paramount. See and he never liked two bass drums. He said, “Louie’s jive with it. It’s tough enough to play one.” But they were good friends, don’t get me wrong. He said, “call Ludwig. Send for two bass drums.” So he could get anything he wants. So two bass drums come in. Never practiced it, sat on a stool, no other drums around him, and just played the two bass drums like a tap dancer. With the arm broken and everything. But here’s the uncanny part of this whole thing. Now if you’re an athlete, and your arm is, you know a pitcher or — but your arm is sprained, you don’t throw the ball fast like the 90 mile an hour fast ball, right? You work it in. The next day he took the thing off he played like it was never broken. And I just said I don’t know where that’s coming from. And that’s what he did. That’s what he did. And another story, see he always felt the guys were putting him down because he couldn’t read music. I mean he didn’t know a note. He was like Erroll Garner. Wherever the hands went was the key. So they wrote a book for him, The Drum Book, Henry Aller. And it sold like a hundred thousand copies, but everybody wanted the dexterity that Buddy had. So he decides to want to read. And he gets the drum pad. And his band boy was a drummer. You know, an amateur but he could read some. So Buddy opens the book and it’s page one, and he’s got to play four quarter notes and — two bars of four quarter and two bars of eighth notes. He could play the four quarter notes, he’s going right, left, right, left, right. But he can’t play one and two and, see he doesn’t understand that. And he was impatient. So after four or five minutes he took the book and threw it up against the wall, he said the book is wrong. That was him. And then the other part, a kid comes, he did a one day theater. He was very quick, quick humor. He was walking out on stage. Buddy was in a good mood, and the kid comes with a book like this, and he’s on page 110. Difficult. Not page one, page 110. And he goes, “Mr. Rich,” he says, “I’m a big fan of yours.” He says, “excuse me,” he says, “I’m having trouble with this passage.” And he goes “can you tell me how to play that?” He says, “just like it’s written, kid, just like it’s written” and walked away from him. So that was the humor.

sources.text: Well when the band thing was over, you know, I caught some of the good part of it. When the business changed they went into vocalists, which was great, because the vocalist still accompanied the bands. And I took the gig, I had three days off, because I loved the way Buddy played trombone and I wanted to hear her sing. So I played for three days. The business changed I think, and due respect, when the rock & roll, whatever the name of those groups, the Chandeliers, the Lamps the Trees, the I don’t know the Beds. When they came in, that did it. You know they had this new thing. Because what they do, they don’t really — they listen — in my opinion, and I don’t argue with success or whoever you like. sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Shorty Sherock was a great trumpet player. He played with Horace Heidt. But Nat Pierce, I got Nat Pierce the job in the band. All right? But after that Buddy called me. And the way I joined the band, I get into town and I go to his suite and he said the first set was seven o’clock, because you played for dancing then. And I remember all the guys that were in the band I could tell you their names. So he said, “go down and play the first set.” He didn’t take me down. So I walked up to the bandstand, and the guys are saying, “where are you going, kid?” And listen to this statement, “I’m the new drummer in the band.” No, “I’m the drummer in the band.” “What are you here to steal the drums?” Buddy didn’t tell them he was hiring an assistant. That’s how I started. They said, “well who are you? What are you doing here?” I said, “well I’m the drummer.” “Something wrong with you? What does he do?” But he didn’t tell them. So that’s how we really started.

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Yeah well that’s where you learned. I mean I’d get in the bed, at one o’clock, I’d put my little radio on, of course they were doing remotes from all over the place. You know, “high on the top of the Astor roof we’re presenting Tommy Dorsey.” Or, “Horace Heidt and his Musical Knights.” Whatever they did. So, no, I loved it, and I love it today. I talk with the same enthusiasm as I did back then. Because music is, I’m very grateful for it. It has been very good for me, I’ve gotten to go all over the world because of music. I mean I know people that haven’t been over to Jersey yet and have been in New York. I’ve been all over the place. So I’m happy.

And then a month later he was doing, his wife was doing, right here in Tampa, Florida, he was doing something, that’s the home office, for a hospital. And he said, “who could I get for the benefit” for like one of the Catholic hospitals. I said, “well I’ll get you the Buddy Rich band for nothing.” ‘Cause I still managed them. But pay their way from California here to New Orleans, no money, and I’ll get you Mel Torme. But Mel gets paid. So Mel got five thousand, and it was very successful. And from then on there he trusted me. And I’ve been doing it for him for fifteen years. And he’ll say, like he gets nervous. If we’re going to do something he’ll say, “you screw this up one more time.” And now I know him so I just call him George, you know, but in front of people Mr. Steinbrenner. I says, “George, listen. I screwed it up fourteen times, another time doesn’t matter. Fifteen. It’s good. That’s my record. Fifteen screw ups you got me, the head screw up of your world here that I produce shows for.” And it’s been very good. He’s been — you know he’s got his things too but when I had a slight stroke he came to see me in the hospital three times, paid all my hospital bills, sent me to Florida to rehabilitate with the ball team, stayed at his hotel in a suite. And at that time, and Sherrie, really took care of me. She nursed me and took care of me, back to good health. I still have a little limp. Because I idolized Peg Leg Bates. I want to dance like him one day. But anyway I come with the rocker, and I’m going in where all the young guys are training, at the complex, all the young ball players. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well I’m pleased that you said that, but I was a drummer, and there’s a difference. I was very pleased and fortunate to have been able to fulfill my dreams and hopes because I started to play when I was about five years old, banging on pots and pans like most of us did. And the reason I got to do that was my sister was a very fine singer. She was like a child star. And she worked with Buddy Rich when he was Traps the Drum Wonder. And so for some reason when they took me to rehearsal to watch her, I would watch the drummer in the pit. And you never know why, Monk, you just don’t know why. I can’t tell you why, and you try to emulate what he did. You take your hands and — whether it’s good or bad you don’t know at the time at all. But all of a sudden you get kind of hooked on it when it comes in here and it comes in here. That’s what you want to do. And I’m very happy that I did get to do it. And then what happened, I’d go home and listen to Chick Webb and Jimmie Lunceford and Duke Ellington and Count Basie and Woody, stay up and listen to the remote broadcasts at night you know. “From the Park Central Hotel and now the King of the Drums, Chick Webb.” And he’d do a thing called “Let’s Get Together.” So I knew all the theme songs you know. And then, older, Benny Goodman’s band, Gene Krupa was the innovator. And I listened to him and I said, “boy that’s the greatest.” And it’s not that my sister said he wasn’t. She said, “well I know somebody that’s better than that.” And I said, “who’s better than Gene Krupa?” and I said, “and who is it?” “Buddy Rich.” She said, “well he’s playing at the Hickory House with a little band named Joe Marsala.” That was his first band after he left vaudeville. Vaudeville was over when he was about 17 years old. He was a vaudeville star. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

275809.proposed: played the club Kay ran

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: called — well it was called Buddy’s Place but the restaurant was Sam’s Jazz Upstairs. Then the one on 33rd Street was a 400 seat club. And my first attraction was Buddy’s big band, Carmen McRae and Nipsy Russell. Because I wanted to bring the Paramount Theater days in there. And unfortunately the guy that owned the place was a thief. You know he did tricks. But we had Joe Williams in there with the Thad Jones band, we had Woody’s band in there. You know we had good stuff going on there. But the problem with me owning or even managing a club, if you talk in the club while they’re playing, you’re gone. I’d put you right out. I wouldn’t allow it. Well the reason is if you’re in Carnegie Hall and Mr. Rubenstein is playing or Mr. Horowitz, you’re not talking. I mean if you want to whisper, but when you get loud, in a small club— Stan Getz was playing in there and some people at the table were talking and I’d go over. I’d say, “see this sign here” I mean this little card, the tent card. “What does it say? Refrain from talking.” And you’d better pay attention there because if I come back again—” And they didn’t want to listen. So, “see I’m in a good mood tonight, that’s twice. The third time you’re gone. Now I’m telling you.” So they calmed down. And I went over to them, younger people, I said, “why did you come in here tonight?” You know, why did you come in here? “Well we’re fans of Stan Getz.” I said, “well see you’re not doing yourself justice. You could have saved all this money, stay home, play his records, and yell, scream, do whatever you want.” I said, “let me ask you something.” They would understand that. I said, “what business are you in, if I may ask?” “The furniture business.” I says, “is Saturday a big day for you? You make big sales on Saturday, don’t you?” I said, “if I came over while you’re taking a two thousand, three thousand dollar order and yell and scream and make noise, if it’s going to distract you, you couldn’t make the sale, right? It’s the same thing. That’s how they make their living. That’s rude.” You see? So therefore, with me, I mean if they talk when the band’s playing, I’m a little — who am I going to hurt? But I go tell them, don’t do that. Don’t get up and dance, we’re not a dance band. Go in the back. Go play records and do “Mama Loves Papa” or something. Go there and do it. Don’t do it in here. But that’s my honesty. And it’s not that I — I don’t try to offend anybody, I don’t try to be rude, I say please, this is not what we do. We don’t do this.

sources.text: ’38, yeah. And in fact he did the Old Gold Show from CBS with Artie Shaw. And Robert Benchley was the host. And I’d stand there, it was like a seven o’clock or six o’clock broadcast And Robert Benchley was the host and they’d open up with, they’d say, “would somebody wake up Benchley?
