275809.evidence: Artie Shapiro played bass and Nat Jaffe played piano.
275809.subject: Stanley Kay
275809.audit: {"change": "Kay introduced himself to Buddy Rich, not to Jaffe", "previous": {"relation": "has met", "direction": "na", "proposed": "met at a jam session at the Hickory House in 1938"}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: He tap danced. Yeah. He was known as Traps the Drum Wonder. And he was the second highest paid child star to Jackie Coogan. He was making about $1,500 a week. But when the decline of vaudeville, he had no job. And he worked on the WPA when they had the WPA. And putting on a wig and dancing and stuff like that see? And well anyway she told me Buddy Rich. So on Sunday afternoon on 52nd Street was a place called the Hickory House. And it was a round bar, it was a steak house. It was owned by a guy named Popkin. And my sister called Buddy and she paid the way for me. And I’m 14 years old. You could eat there, so at 14 you’re okay you could go in. And jam sessions were about from three to six on Sunday in this big round circular bar. And it was Joe Marsala, his wife played harp, Adele Girard, his brother Marty Marsala played trumpet, Artie Shapiro played bass and Nat Jaffe played piano. And I walk in and I introduced myself. And he’s 19 now, he was five years older than me. And I was 14. So he greeted me, but all the guys used to sit in from all the bands on this jam session. Like bands like Tiny Bradshaw and Andy Kirk’s band, O’Neil Spencer was a wonderful drummer played with the John Kirby band. And he didn’t play. And it was now getting towards like 5:30 and I’m like what am I doing here, because I have to come to have a steak or, you know, I wanted to hear this guy play. Supposed to be this genius, see? And he sat down and played the last thing. It was what we call a flag waver, it was called “Jim Jamp’s Stump.” And when I heard “Jim Jamp”— and I heard him play, I said that’s it. My sister was right. That’s the greatest thing I ever heard. And I just idolized him. And I followed him. Bunny Berigan, when he went, and before that he came down to my house to hear me play. And he didn’t tell me but he told my sister, he said, “he can’t play.” And I cried. I really cried. I mean, whatever.

275809.proposed: his manager for 30 years (Hines Brothers); Kay also wrote and conducted their act
275809.evidence: I mean I managed the Hines Brothers for a long time, I did a show on Broadway. Maurice and I have been together 30 years.
275809.subject: Stanley Kay
275809.audit: {"change": "re-judged from the text", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "long-term professional association (30 years)"}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well and I always will be a musician. I will always be — I mean I managed the Hines Brothers for a long time, I did a show on Broadway. Maurice and I have been together 30 years. But if I could produce the biggest show on Broadway I’m a sideman. I will always be a musician. I would rather talk to guys and hear the story than talk to David Merrick. He doesn’t interest me. I like to talk to the guys. And sometimes they can’t drag me away because I’m laughing, talking the stories. That’s where I come from, that’s where I’ll always come from. It doesn’t matter about money or anything. That is my love. That’s what I want to do and I am so proud here, what Sherrie, the reaction to Sherrie and Nicki and Karolina and Anat. Because they are fine musicians. And they are as good as any of the guys playing. There’s no difference. There’s no difference. And they can prove it. They go out and do it. See? And maybe ten years from now when the women come in, they went, “well it’s a woman, I don’t know how she’s playing.” She can play. And that’s what we’re trying to accomplish and keep this thing together. And have you heard our big band?

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: And Snooky and I — he played for us when I managed the Hines Brothers. And I wrote their act and conducted. And I’m standing with Snooky and I said, “hey Snook,” I said, “you know I can’t believe I know you and you are my friend.” He said, “what are you saying?” He said, “you were my boss with the Hines Brothers.” Because I managed them. And I said, “no I was never your boss,” I said, “we worked together. But you are Snooky Young. And I saw you play in the Lunceford band and I know you.” He couldn’t understand that.

275809.evidence: we honored all the greats, like Clora Bryant who played with the International Sweethearts
275809.subject: Stanley Kay
275809.audit: {"change": "evidence not verbatim / source block id off by a page", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well I congratulate my band, our band. Sometimes I say my — it’s not mine it’s our band, it’s Sherrie’s and my band. I congratulate them because without the product I could maneuver all day long, but without the product I would have nothing. We’ve got a good product. We’ve got a great product. And I’m just hoping that people realize it, and give us a chance. You know the thing is that I went to the former president and vice president of Lippit, Harvey Schiller, through the Yankees. This is Yankee Nets now they bought the band. And I called Harvey up and I said, “you know, you know all the sponsors, you know all the people,” and I said, “you know you were with the Olympics. You’ve had women baseball teams, soccer teams, tennis team, golf team, archery, whatever. We’re no different.” See you’ve got to be careful how you say it, but Sherrie pointed it out to me, it’s a good band or a great band. But then you have to say but they all happen to be women. You see? And you don’t categorize it. But we can play up to anybody and prove it. There’s no thing in music. And I would say if you can play you can play. If you can’t play you can’t play. And I know a lot of guys that can’t play in my opinion you see. And also a lot of women. So that’s the key. So we’re — as American Express — I’m not hawking anything, I’m just telling you. And we’re an educational group. We play high schools and colleges. And we can save four people a year, or three, from making drugs or get them interested in playing, and look up and see — see the women of our band only had the men to look up to, whether it was Buddy, Woody, Lester Young, you know. But wouldn’t it be great to say I want to play drums like Sherrie. I want to play tenor like Anat Cohen. Who’s your idol playing drums? Sherrie. Who’s your idol? Anat Cohen. Who’s yours? Karolina. You see? There’s a whole world out there to try to get. And the reason I talk about the sponsorship, it’s not that we’re looking for their money, we’re looking for them to put us on a tour where we are beneficial to what they do. How do we help your product? At the same time, how do you help us you see. So that’s, and you mentioned John Levy. Well we just did a thing for Dress for Success. It’s about women who are — you know the organization. Well when I first heard about it, I heard it on my machine, I thought they said dress for stress. So I said how do you do a benefit for stressful people? Is it clothes that stressful people wear? I didn’t know what they were doing. So what we did, we honored all the greats, like Clora Bryant who played with the International Sweethearts, and Jane Jarvis, Carline Ray. And we honored Nancy Wilson. © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

275809.proposed: brought charts to and conducted Diva at Pace University
275809.evidence: And Bill Holman came in with music that could reach from here down – we’re on the eighth floor. And he conducted.
275809.subject: Stanley Kay
275809.audit: {"change": "re-judged from the text", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well she’s a joy. Sherrie makes me proud. She is dedicated, she cares. And like I say she’s the backbone of the band. She keeps it going. Her musicianship is superb, she’s a fine arranger and a wonderful composer. And we’re proud. It’s difficult at times because like with the male band, if you lose a bass player you can get 20 guys to play. Our book is very difficult. And the ladies come out of North Texas State, Berklee, like little Karolina, and Anat Cohen, they’re all musicians, studied. And it’s difficult because you can’t get, with due respect, we’re not playing “In the Mood” in this band. I mean you know. I don’t want to because you’re not going to play it as good as Glenn Miller and you’re not going to play “Sing Sing Sing” as good as Benny Goodman. And of course they’re going to compare you to that. If you want to do it, that’s fine. Whoever wants to do that, that’s the way they do it. This is not the way we do it. In fact before we got her we played at Pace University. And Bill Holman came in with music that could reach from here down – we’re on the eighth floor. And he conducted. But he came in with them killers. And the band just played it, and you’d beam. And Slide Hampton came in, a great trombone player, with things from space I think. They are first playing it up there. And then Tommy came in normal. Tommy Newsom. He came in “Close Your Eyes, George.” You know, nice, easy. But they played it, and they played it well, and they played it with dedication. And you sit there and you kind of go wow, look at that.

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Yeah. Well you know Neal brought in, Hefti, you know the story, “L’il Darlin.’” He went [scats]. And Basie said wait a minute, no, no, let’s do it that way. And it worked you see. sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well I’m pleased that you said that, but I was a drummer, and there’s a difference. I was very pleased and fortunate to have been able to fulfill my dreams and hopes because I started to play when I was about five years old, banging on pots and pans like most of us did. And the reason I got to do that was my sister was a very fine singer. She was like a child star. And she worked with Buddy Rich when he was Traps the Drum Wonder. And so for some reason when they took me to rehearsal to watch her, I would watch the drummer in the pit. And you never know why, Monk, you just don’t know why. I can’t tell you why, and you try to emulate what he did. You take your hands and — whether it’s good or bad you don’t know at the time at all. But all of a sudden you get kind of hooked on it when it comes in here and it comes in here. That’s what you want to do. And I’m very happy that I did get to do it. And then what happened, I’d go home and listen to Chick Webb and Jimmie Lunceford and Duke Ellington and Count Basie and Woody, stay up and listen to the remote broadcasts at night you know. “From the Park Central Hotel and now the King of the Drums, Chick Webb.” And he’d do a thing called “Let’s Get Together.” So I knew all the theme songs you know. And then, older, Benny Goodman’s band, Gene Krupa was the innovator. And I listened to him and I said, “boy that’s the greatest.” And it’s not that my sister said he wasn’t. She said, “well I know somebody that’s better than that.” And I said, “who’s better than Gene Krupa?” and I said, “and who is it?” “Buddy Rich.” She said, “well he’s playing at the Hickory House with a little band named Joe Marsala.” That was his first band after he left vaudeville. Vaudeville was over when he was about 17 years old. He was a vaudeville star. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

275809.audit: {"change": "re-judged from the text", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "na", "proposed": "performers at Buddy's Place club"}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: called — well it was called Buddy’s Place but the restaurant was Sam’s Jazz Upstairs. Then the one on 33rd Street was a 400 seat club. And my first attraction was Buddy’s big band, Carmen McRae and Nipsy Russell. Because I wanted to bring the Paramount Theater days in there. And unfortunately the guy that owned the place was a thief. You know he did tricks. But we had Joe Williams in there with the Thad Jones band, we had Woody’s band in there. You know we had good stuff going on there. But the problem with me owning or even managing a club, if you talk in the club while they’re playing, you’re gone. I’d put you right out. I wouldn’t allow it. Well the reason is if you’re in Carnegie Hall and Mr. Rubenstein is playing or Mr. Horowitz, you’re not talking. I mean if you want to whisper, but when you get loud, in a small club— Stan Getz was playing in there and some people at the table were talking and I’d go over. I’d say, “see this sign here” I mean this little card, the tent card. “What does it say? Refrain from talking.” And you’d better pay attention there because if I come back again—” And they didn’t want to listen. So, “see I’m in a good mood tonight, that’s twice. The third time you’re gone. Now I’m telling you.” So they calmed down. And I went over to them, younger people, I said, “why did you come in here tonight?” You know, why did you come in here? “Well we’re fans of Stan Getz.” I said, “well see you’re not doing yourself justice. You could have saved all this money, stay home, play his records, and yell, scream, do whatever you want.” I said, “let me ask you something.” They would understand that. I said, “what business are you in, if I may ask?” “The furniture business.” I says, “is Saturday a big day for you? You make big sales on Saturday, don’t you?” I said, “if I came over while you’re taking a two thousand, three thousand dollar order and yell and scream and make noise, if it’s going to distract you, you couldn’t make the sale, right? It’s the same thing. That’s how they make their living. That’s rude.” You see? So therefore, with me, I mean if they talk when the band’s playing, I’m a little — who am I going to hurt? But I go tell them, don’t do that. Don’t get up and dance, we’re not a dance band. Go in the back. Go play records and do “Mama Loves Papa” or something. Go there and do it. Don’t do it in here. But that’s my honesty. And it’s not that I — I don’t try to offend anybody, I don’t try to be rude, I say please, this is not what we do. We don’t do this.

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: He tap danced. Yeah. He was known as Traps the Drum Wonder. And he was the second highest paid child star to Jackie Coogan. He was making about $1,500 a week. But when the decline of vaudeville, he had no job. And he worked on the WPA when they had the WPA. And putting on a wig and dancing and stuff like that see? And well anyway she told me Buddy Rich. So on Sunday afternoon on 52nd Street was a place called the Hickory House. And it was a round bar, it was a steak house. It was owned by a guy named Popkin. And my sister called Buddy and she paid the way for me. And I’m 14 years old. You could eat there, so at 14 you’re okay you could go in. And jam sessions were about from three to six on Sunday in this big round circular bar. And it was Joe Marsala, his wife played harp, Adele Girard, his brother Marty Marsala played trumpet, Artie Shapiro played bass and Nat Jaffe played piano. And I walk in and I introduced myself. And he’s 19 now, he was five years older than me. And I was 14. So he greeted me, but all the guys used to sit in from all the bands on this jam session. Like bands like Tiny Bradshaw and Andy Kirk’s band, O’Neil Spencer was a wonderful drummer played with the John Kirby band. And he didn’t play. And it was now getting towards like 5:30 and I’m like what am I doing here, because I have to come to have a steak or, you know, I wanted to hear this guy play. Supposed to be this genius, see? And he sat down and played the last thing. It was what we call a flag waver, it was called “Jim Jamp’s Stump.” And when I heard “Jim Jamp”— and I heard him play, I said that’s it. My sister was right. That’s the greatest thing I ever heard. And I just idolized him. And I followed him. Bunny Berigan, when he went, and before that he came down to my house to hear me play. And he didn’t tell me but he told my sister, he said, “he can’t play.” And I cried. I really cried. I mean, whatever.

275809.evidence: we honored all the greats, like Clora Bryant who played with the International Sweethearts, and Jane Jarvis, Carline Ray.
275809.subject: Stanley Kay
275809.audit: {"change": "evidence not verbatim / source block id off by a page", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well I congratulate my band, our band. Sometimes I say my — it’s not mine it’s our band, it’s Sherrie’s and my band. I congratulate them because without the product I could maneuver all day long, but without the product I would have nothing. We’ve got a good product. We’ve got a great product. And I’m just hoping that people realize it, and give us a chance. You know the thing is that I went to the former president and vice president of Lippit, Harvey Schiller, through the Yankees. This is Yankee Nets now they bought the band. And I called Harvey up and I said, “you know, you know all the sponsors, you know all the people,” and I said, “you know you were with the Olympics. You’ve had women baseball teams, soccer teams, tennis team, golf team, archery, whatever. We’re no different.” See you’ve got to be careful how you say it, but Sherrie pointed it out to me, it’s a good band or a great band. But then you have to say but they all happen to be women. You see? And you don’t categorize it. But we can play up to anybody and prove it. There’s no thing in music. And I would say if you can play you can play. If you can’t play you can’t play. And I know a lot of guys that can’t play in my opinion you see. And also a lot of women. So that’s the key. So we’re — as American Express — I’m not hawking anything, I’m just telling you. And we’re an educational group. We play high schools and colleges. And we can save four people a year, or three, from making drugs or get them interested in playing, and look up and see — see the women of our band only had the men to look up to, whether it was Buddy, Woody, Lester Young, you know. But wouldn’t it be great to say I want to play drums like Sherrie. I want to play tenor like Anat Cohen. Who’s your idol playing drums? Sherrie. Who’s your idol? Anat Cohen. Who’s yours? Karolina. You see? There’s a whole world out there to try to get. And the reason I talk about the sponsorship, it’s not that we’re looking for their money, we’re looking for them to put us on a tour where we are beneficial to what they do. How do we help your product? At the same time, how do you help us you see. So that’s, and you mentioned John Levy. Well we just did a thing for Dress for Success. It’s about women who are — you know the organization. Well when I first heard about it, I heard it on my machine, I thought they said dress for stress. So I said how do you do a benefit for stressful people? Is it clothes that stressful people wear? I didn’t know what they were doing. So what we did, we honored all the greats, like Clora Bryant who played with the International Sweethearts, and Jane Jarvis, Carline Ray. And we honored Nancy Wilson. © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

And that’s what we’re trying to accomplish and keep this thing together. And have you heard our big band?

275809.audit: {"change": "evidence not verbatim / source block id off by a page", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: roll and the rap and then there’s whatever country, and that’s fine. But we get more respect, or most of the jazz players will tell you, in Europe and Japan. And I don’t understand that. I don’t understand that. Because it’s a great art to play jazz. I don’t know, you know, playing drums. And I love melodic things, and lyrical things, but doing this, I can’t play “Stardust” on the drum I don’t think. If I could I’d make a lot of money. But anyway you know what they do is they don’t respect it. They don’t respect. Oh I know what I was going to say, like I don’t know how these people play jazz. I don’t know how you can improvise. I don’t know how you can do that, like play anything you want to play and it becomes a melodic, and it becomes a composition. Oh there’s riffs, there’s standard riffs that we play. But like Lester Young played that thing behind Billie Holiday on the CBS special, that’s like one of the greatest melodic things I’ve ever heard. And it’s gorgeous to do that. But how do you do that you see? You got a lot of lead trumpet players that couldn’t play jazz. They could play great lead, like Conrad Gozzo and Bernie Glow and some of those guys, and I really think, we play enough high schools and colleges where they make a mistake. Because you go in and there’s the young players, the high school player. “Who is your favorite saxophone?” They’ll say John Coltrane. Right? Okay. Now they don’t know John Coltrane played with Earl Bostic’s band, played the blues, but he wanted to progress. “You know Johnny Hodges?” “No.” “You know Ben Webster?” “No.” “You know Sweets Edison?” “No.” Well if you don’t listen, how are you going to get to — if you don’t go to kindergarten and high school, how are you going to get to there? But the teachers don’t tell them. Sherrie will go in and say, “we’re going to play the blues.” “What’s the blues?” And they’ll read the chart, of course they play it every day. After four bars of improvisation they’re done. They can’t play one — after the fourth, the fifth bar, over. And you’re looking at, where is this all going to come from, what we’re trying to keep and preserve. I’m not a campaigner, but I’m just talking about honest truth. There’s a truth to what we do, there’s this truth to our music. I mean I love a marching band if it’s good in the street, I mean I go to the symphony and watch the symphonies play. But why? Why? I mean outside of Basie’s band, that’s not talking the dance band, not Glenn Miller. Buddy Morrow’s got an intact band. The rest of them, the Jimmy Dorsey band, the guys got the library to “Tangerine” and “Amapola,” he comes and gets twelve guys. They don’t know the difference. They say, “Tangerine,” oh, it’s the Jimmy Dorsey band. The Guy Lombardo band or whatever. The Harry James band. One guy, they come with the book, you know, “Sleepy Lagoon,” “You Made Me Love You” and they play. We out there, we buy these things. Maybe, I don’t know, Sherrie could correct me, twenty, thirty thousand dollars worth of arrangements. And we’re always trying to play new. And we’re always thinking of new things to do. Because we don’t want the band to get bored. It’s exciting. Let’s try this © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

sources.text: called — well it was called Buddy’s Place but the restaurant was Sam’s Jazz Upstairs. Then the one on 33rd Street was a 400 seat club. And my first attraction was Buddy’s big band, Carmen McRae and Nipsy Russell. Because I wanted to bring the Paramount Theater days in there. And unfortunately the guy that owned the place was a thief. You know he did tricks. But we had Joe Williams in there with the Thad Jones band, we had Woody’s band in there. You know we had good stuff going on there. But the problem with me owning or even managing a club, if you talk in the club while they’re playing, you’re gone. I’d put you right out. I wouldn’t allow it. Well the reason is if you’re in Carnegie Hall and Mr. Rubenstein is playing or Mr. Horowitz, you’re not talking. I mean if you want to whisper, but when you get loud, in a small club— Stan Getz was playing in there and some people at the table were talking and I’d go over. I’d say, “see this sign here” I mean this little card, the tent card. “What does it say? Refrain from talking.” And you’d better pay attention there because if I come back again—” And they didn’t want to listen. So, “see I’m in a good mood tonight, that’s twice. The third time you’re gone. Now I’m telling you.” So they calmed down. And I went over to them, younger people, I said, “why did you come in here tonight?” You know, why did you come in here? “Well we’re fans of Stan Getz.” I said, “well see you’re not doing yourself justice. You could have saved all this money, stay home, play his records, and yell, scream, do whatever you want.” I said, “let me ask you something.” They would understand that. I said, “what business are you in, if I may ask?” “The furniture business.” I says, “is Saturday a big day for you? You make big sales on Saturday, don’t you?” I said, “if I came over while you’re taking a two thousand, three thousand dollar order and yell and scream and make noise, if it’s going to distract you, you couldn’t make the sale, right? It’s the same thing. That’s how they make their living. That’s rude.” You see? So therefore, with me, I mean if they talk when the band’s playing, I’m a little — who am I going to hurt? But I go tell them, don’t do that. Don’t get up and dance, we’re not a dance band. Go in the back. Go play records and do “Mama Loves Papa” or something. Go there and do it. Don’t do it in here. But that’s my honesty. And it’s not that I — I don’t try to offend anybody, I don’t try to be rude, I say please, this is not what we do. We don’t do this.

sources.text: Well she’s a joy. Sherrie makes me proud. She is dedicated, she cares. And like I say she’s the backbone of the band. She keeps it going. And it’s difficult because you can’t get, with due respect, we’re not playing “In the Mood” in this band. I mean you know. I don’t want to because you’re not going to play it as good as Glenn Miller and you’re not going to play “Sing Sing Sing” as good as Benny Goodman. And of course they’re going to compare you to that. If you want to do it, that’s fine. Whoever wants to do that, that’s the way they do it. This is not the way we do it. In fact before we got her we played at Pace University. And Bill Holman came in with music that could reach from here down – we’re on the eighth floor. And he conducted. But he came in with them killers. And the band just played it, and you’d beam. 275809.evidence: the managing director of the Paramount, Bob Whiteman, came up. And he said, “the rumor is that your arm is not broken but there’s a sensation — keep it in the sling.”
275809.subject: Stanley Kay
275809.audit: {"change": "re-judged from the text", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: act and I played. They see the big sling. Clark Terry told me, he said he was there and the word went out that Buddy’s arm is not broken, he wants to show he can play with one hand. But it was broken. So we played there a week, then we go into the Paramount Theater downtown and the managing director of the Paramount, Bob Whiteman, came up. And he said, “the rumor is that your arm is not broken but there’s a sensation — keep it in the sling.” If it’s not broken we could play the Paramount. See and he never liked two bass drums. He said, “Louie’s jive with it. It’s tough enough to play one.” But they were good friends, don’t get me wrong. He said, “call Ludwig. Send for two bass drums.” So he could get anything he wants. So two bass drums come in. Never practiced it, sat on a stool, no other drums around him, and just played the two bass drums like a tap dancer. With the arm broken and everything. But here’s the uncanny part of this whole thing. Now if you’re an athlete, and your arm is, you know a pitcher or — but your arm is sprained, you don’t throw the ball fast like the 90 mile an hour fast ball, right? You work it in. The next day he took the thing off he played like it was never broken. And I just said I don’t know where that’s coming from. And that’s what he did. That’s what he did. And another story, see he always felt the guys were putting him down because he couldn’t read music. I mean he didn’t know a note. He was like Erroll Garner. Wherever the hands went was the key. So they wrote a book for him, The Drum Book, Henry Aller. And it sold like a hundred thousand copies, but everybody wanted the dexterity that Buddy had. So he decides to want to read. And he gets the drum pad. And his band boy was a drummer. You know, an amateur but he could read some. So Buddy opens the book and it’s page one, and he’s got to play four quarter notes and — two bars of four quarter and two bars of eighth notes. He could play the four quarter notes, he’s going right, left, right, left, right. But he can’t play one and two and, see he doesn’t understand that. And he was impatient. So after four or five minutes he took the book and threw it up against the wall, he said the book is wrong. That was him. And then the other part, a kid comes, he did a one day theater. He was very quick, quick humor. He was walking out on stage. Buddy was in a good mood, and the kid comes with a book like this, and he’s on page 110. Difficult. Not page one, page 110. And he goes, “Mr. Rich,” he says, “I’m a big fan of yours.” He says, “excuse me,” he says, “I’m having trouble with this passage.” And he goes “can you tell me how to play that?” He says, “just like it’s written, kid, just like it’s written” and walked away from him. So that was the humor.

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: roll and the rap and then there’s whatever country, and that’s fine. But we get more respect, or most of the jazz players will tell you, in Europe and Japan. And I don’t understand that. I don’t understand that. Because it’s a great art to play jazz. I don’t know, you know, playing drums. And I love melodic things, and lyrical things, but doing this, I can’t play “Stardust” on the drum I don’t think. If I could I’d make a lot of money. But anyway you know what they do is they don’t respect it. They don’t respect. Oh I know what I was going to say, like I don’t know how these people play jazz. I don’t know how you can improvise. I don’t know how you can do that, like play anything you want to play and it becomes a melodic, and it becomes a composition. Oh there’s riffs, there’s standard riffs that we play. But like Lester Young played that thing behind Billie Holiday on the CBS special, that’s like one of the greatest melodic things I’ve ever heard. And it’s gorgeous to do that. But how do you do that you see? You got a lot of lead trumpet players that couldn’t play jazz. They could play great lead, like Conrad Gozzo and Bernie Glow and some of those guys, and I really think, we play enough high schools and colleges where they make a mistake. Because you go in and there’s the young players, the high school player. “Who is your favorite saxophone?” They’ll say John Coltrane. Right? Okay. Now they don’t know John Coltrane played with Earl Bostic’s band, played the blues, but he wanted to progress. “You know Johnny Hodges?” “No.” “You know Ben Webster?” “No.” “You know Sweets Edison?” “No.” Well if you don’t listen, how are you going to get to — if you don’t go to kindergarten and high school, how are you going to get to there? But the teachers don’t tell them. Sherrie will go in and say, “we’re going to play the blues.” “What’s the blues?” And they’ll read the chart, of course they play it every day. After four bars of improvisation they’re done. They can’t play one — after the fourth, the fifth bar, over. And you’re looking at, where is this all going to come from, what we’re trying to keep and preserve. I’m not a campaigner, but I’m just talking about honest truth. There’s a truth to what we do, there’s this truth to our music. I mean I love a marching band if it’s good in the street, I mean I go to the symphony and watch the symphonies play. But why? Why? I mean outside of Basie’s band, that’s not talking the dance band, not Glenn Miller. Buddy Morrow’s got an intact band. The rest of them, the Jimmy Dorsey band, the guys got the library to “Tangerine” and “Amapola,” he comes and gets twelve guys. They don’t know the difference. They say, “Tangerine,” oh, it’s the Jimmy Dorsey band. The Guy Lombardo band or whatever. The Harry James band. One guy, they come with the book, you know, “Sleepy Lagoon,” “You Made Me Love You” and they play. We out there, we buy these things. Maybe, I don’t know, Sherrie could correct me, twenty, thirty thousand dollars worth of arrangements. And we’re always trying to play new. And we’re always thinking of new things to do. Because we don’t want the band to get bored. It’s exciting. Let’s try this © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

So we get into a town at eight in the morning, in Ohio. Columbus, Ohio. He said, “come on, let’s go to a movie.” He loved movies. Cowboy movies, D movies, E movies, Z’s, whatever they were. I said, “I’m not going to the movies today.” I said, “I’m going to the gym instead and I’m playing handball.” “I’m coming too,” he said. And his brother came, Nicky. We’re playing four wall handball. I don’t want to be the handball champ, I just want to hit the ball against the wall. But he’s got to be the best and he’s smashing it. But he ran into the wall like that. And he went ahh. So I said, “ah what? What are you singing?” So he said, “I think — my arm.” I said well go down and get a steam” they had a steam room there, a sauna, “and your brother and I will finish the game.” He comes back up. “My arm doesn’t feel good.” So I take him to the doctor. They put one of these slings on it, right? And we’re rooming together. And ah, at four in the morning, “my arm,” like a hypochondriac. So I says, “hey B listen,” I was straw boss of the band. “I got to get things going at seven in the morning. I can’t hear this all night.” But I said, “I’ll tell you something, if you die, I promise you I’ll make you a nice funeral. Let me get a little rest here.” I said, “I mess things up and then you’re going to get on me, ‘you don’t know what you’re doing,’ and I’m not going for that.” So anyway, we got three days left then we’re going to New York. We’ve got two days and we open at the Apollo Theater. He gets to New York and the arm was broken in three places. And he had like a brown suit, a brown sling, a gray suit, a gray –. He liked all that coordination. We opened the Apollo Theater — we were one of the favorites, and one of the few white bands that could do it. They liked Charlie Barnet and us. And he was a big favorite. So Tiny Kahn wrote a chart for us on the “Carioca.” I remember. See but he sits very high, and the layman don’t know if he’s playing with one hand or two hands. But [scats] but they don’t see it. They saw it when he came down to announce the © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

275809.proposed: booked as opening attraction at Buddy's Place, the club Kay ran
275809.evidence: And my first attraction was Buddy’s big band, Carmen McRae and Nipsy Russell.
275809.subject: Stanley Kay
275809.audit: {"change": "re-judged from the text", "previous": {"relation": "in music group with", "direction": "na", "proposed": "performers at Buddy's Place"}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: called — well it was called Buddy’s Place but the restaurant was Sam’s Jazz Upstairs. Then the one on 33rd Street was a 400 seat club. And my first attraction was Buddy’s big band, Carmen McRae and Nipsy Russell. Because I wanted to bring the Paramount Theater days in there. And unfortunately the guy that owned the place was a thief. You know he did tricks. But we had Joe Williams in there with the Thad Jones band, we had Woody’s band in there. You know we had good stuff going on there. But the problem with me owning or even managing a club, if you talk in the club while they’re playing, you’re gone. I’d put you right out. I wouldn’t allow it. Well the reason is if you’re in Carnegie Hall and Mr. Rubenstein is playing or Mr. Horowitz, you’re not talking. I mean if you want to whisper, but when you get loud, in a small club— Stan Getz was playing in there and some people at the table were talking and I’d go over. I’d say, “see this sign here” I mean this little card, the tent card. “What does it say? Refrain from talking.” And you’d better pay attention there because if I come back again—” And they didn’t want to listen. So, “see I’m in a good mood tonight, that’s twice. The third time you’re gone. Now I’m telling you.” So they calmed down. And I went over to them, younger people, I said, “why did you come in here tonight?” You know, why did you come in here? “Well we’re fans of Stan Getz.” I said, “well see you’re not doing yourself justice. You could have saved all this money, stay home, play his records, and yell, scream, do whatever you want.” I said, “let me ask you something.” They would understand that. I said, “what business are you in, if I may ask?” “The furniture business.” I says, “is Saturday a big day for you? You make big sales on Saturday, don’t you?” I said, “if I came over while you’re taking a two thousand, three thousand dollar order and yell and scream and make noise, if it’s going to distract you, you couldn’t make the sale, right? It’s the same thing. That’s how they make their living. That’s rude.” You see? So therefore, with me, I mean if they talk when the band’s playing, I’m a little — who am I going to hurt? But I go tell them, don’t do that. Don’t get up and dance, we’re not a dance band. Go in the back. Go play records and do “Mama Loves Papa” or something. Go there and do it. Don’t do it in here. But that’s my honesty. And it’s not that I — I don’t try to offend anybody, I don’t try to be rude, I say please, this is not what we do. We don’t do this.

275809.evidence: But like Lester Young played that thing behind Billie Holiday on the CBS special
275809.subject: Stanley Kay

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: roll and the rap and then there’s whatever country, and that’s fine. But we get more respect, or most of the jazz players will tell you, in Europe and Japan. And I don’t understand that. I don’t understand that. Because it’s a great art to play jazz. I don’t know, you know, playing drums. And I love melodic things, and lyrical things, but doing this, I can’t play “Stardust” on the drum I don’t think. If I could I’d make a lot of money. But anyway you know what they do is they don’t respect it. They don’t respect. Oh I know what I was going to say, like I don’t know how these people play jazz. I don’t know how you can improvise. I don’t know how you can do that, like play anything you want to play and it becomes a melodic, and it becomes a composition. Oh there’s riffs, there’s standard riffs that we play. But like Lester Young played that thing behind Billie Holiday on the CBS special, that’s like one of the greatest melodic things I’ve ever heard. And it’s gorgeous to do that. But how do you do that you see? You got a lot of lead trumpet players that couldn’t play jazz. They could play great lead, like Conrad Gozzo and Bernie Glow and some of those guys, and I really think, we play enough high schools and colleges where they make a mistake. Because you go in and there’s the young players, the high school player. “Who is your favorite saxophone?” They’ll say John Coltrane. Right? Okay. Now they don’t know John Coltrane played with Earl Bostic’s band, played the blues, but he wanted to progress. “You know Johnny Hodges?” “No.” “You know Ben Webster?” “No.” “You know Sweets Edison?” “No.” Well if you don’t listen, how are you going to get to — if you don’t go to kindergarten and high school, how are you going to get to there? But the teachers don’t tell them. Sherrie will go in and say, “we’re going to play the blues.” “What’s the blues?” And they’ll read the chart, of course they play it every day. After four bars of improvisation they’re done. They can’t play one — after the fourth, the fifth bar, over. And you’re looking at, where is this all going to come from, what we’re trying to keep and preserve. I’m not a campaigner, but I’m just talking about honest truth. There’s a truth to what we do, there’s this truth to our music. I mean I love a marching band if it’s good in the street, I mean I go to the symphony and watch the symphonies play. But why? Why? I mean outside of Basie’s band, that’s not talking the dance band, not Glenn Miller. Buddy Morrow’s got an intact band. The rest of them, the Jimmy Dorsey band, the guys got the library to “Tangerine” and “Amapola,” he comes and gets twelve guys. They don’t know the difference. They say, “Tangerine,” oh, it’s the Jimmy Dorsey band. The Guy Lombardo band or whatever. The Harry James band. One guy, they come with the book, you know, “Sleepy Lagoon,” “You Made Me Love You” and they play. We out there, we buy these things. Maybe, I don’t know, Sherrie could correct me, twenty, thirty thousand dollars worth of arrangements. And we’re always trying to play new. And we’re always thinking of new things to do. Because we don’t want the band to get bored. It’s exciting. Let’s try this © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

275809.proposed: drummer of Blood, Sweat & Tears whom Kay knew
275809.evidence: But I knew Bobby Colomby, the drummer. And I said I’ll call Bobby myself, I’ll beg him.
275809.subject: Stanley Kay
275809.audit: {"change": "re-judged from the text", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Steinbrenner,” I said, “somebody saw you coming.” You know they charge you money, they don’t make that kind of money. So who can you get? So I liked Blood, Sweat & Tears. They were on the way out, but you know, were still there. So I said I’ll call the William Morris Agency, which I did, talked to the agent, and he says they’re available. So I tell Mr. Steinbrenner. I said they’re available. And he checks things out to see who likes them, you know, if his daughter accepts it. So I called the agent and says they don’t want to do it. So I have to go back. He says, “you told me they’re available.” I says, “available doesn’t mean they’re going to do it.” But I knew Bobby Colomby, the drummer. And I said I’ll call Bobby myself, I’ll beg him. So now the agent says okay. Same money, ten thousand. I bring the rider back. I never saw this kind of rider and I’m looking at the rider. Dom Perignon, Cristal, steaks, orange juice, fresh eggs, what. And I’m looking at it and I’m reading and I’m going — he says, “what’s the matter with you?” I said, “I wouldn’t do this. This is not professional.” “Well you’re going to give it to them anyway.” You know. I said, “I don’t like it.” He said, “yeah I don’t like it. Get me someone else.” So I called the agent and I said no deal. “Well you gave me a verbal.” I said, “how do you ask for all this, steaks and chicken and chicken under glass, in glass, whatever, what is that? I don’t understand.” I said, “Frank Sinatra doesn’t ask for that.” You know, what is it? Anyway we canceled them out. And then a month later he was doing, his wife was doing, right here in Tampa, Florida, he was doing something, that’s the home office, for a hospital. And he said, “who could I get for the benefit” for like one of the Catholic hospitals. I said, “well I’ll get you the Buddy Rich band for nothing.” ‘Cause I still managed them. But pay their way from California here to New Orleans, no money, and I’ll get you Mel Torme. But Mel gets paid. So Mel got five thousand, and it was very successful. And from then on there he trusted me. And I’ve been doing it for him for fifteen years. And he’ll say, like he gets nervous. If we’re going to do something he’ll say, “you screw this up one more time.” And now I know him so I just call him George, you know, but in front of people Mr. Steinbrenner. I says, “George, listen. I screwed it up fourteen times, another time doesn’t matter. Fifteen. It’s good. That’s my record. Fifteen screw ups you got me, the head screw up of your world here that I produce shows for.” And it’s been very good. He’s been — you know he’s got his things too but when I had a slight stroke he came to see me in the hospital three times, paid all my hospital bills, sent me to Florida to rehabilitate with the ball team, stayed at his hotel in a suite. And at that time, and Sherrie, really took care of me. She nursed me and took care of me, back to good health. I still have a little limp. Because I idolized Peg Leg Bates. I want to dance like him one day. But anyway I come with the rocker, and I’m going in where all the young guys are training, at the complex, all the young ball players. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

275809.evidence: It was owned by a guy named Popkin.
275809.subject: Stanley Kay

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: He tap danced. Yeah. He was known as Traps the Drum Wonder. And he was the second highest paid child star to Jackie Coogan. He was making about $1,500 a week. But when the decline of vaudeville, he had no job. And he worked on the WPA when they had the WPA. And putting on a wig and dancing and stuff like that see? And well anyway she told me Buddy Rich. So on Sunday afternoon on 52nd Street was a place called the Hickory House. And it was a round bar, it was a steak house. It was owned by a guy named Popkin. And my sister called Buddy and she paid the way for me. And I’m 14 years old. You could eat there, so at 14 you’re okay you could go in. And jam sessions were about from three to six on Sunday in this big round circular bar. And it was Joe Marsala, his wife played harp, Adele Girard, his brother Marty Marsala played trumpet, Artie Shapiro played bass and Nat Jaffe played piano. And I walk in and I introduced myself. And he’s 19 now, he was five years older than me. And I was 14. So he greeted me, but all the guys used to sit in from all the bands on this jam session. Like bands like Tiny Bradshaw and Andy Kirk’s band, O’Neil Spencer was a wonderful drummer played with the John Kirby band. And he didn’t play. And it was now getting towards like 5:30 and I’m like what am I doing here, because I have to come to have a steak or, you know, I wanted to hear this guy play. Supposed to be this genius, see? And he sat down and played the last thing. It was what we call a flag waver, it was called “Jim Jamp’s Stump.” And when I heard “Jim Jamp”— and I heard him play, I said that’s it. My sister was right. That’s the greatest thing I ever heard. And I just idolized him. And I followed him. Bunny Berigan, when he went, and before that he came down to my house to hear me play. And he didn’t tell me but he told my sister, he said, “he can’t play.” And I cried. I really cried. I mean, whatever.

275809.proposed: sports executive Kay approached about sponsoring Diva
275809.evidence: Harvey Schiller, through the Yankees. This is Yankee Nets now they bought the band. And I called Harvey up
275809.subject: Stanley Kay
275809.audit: {"change": "phone contact, no meeting shown", "previous": {"relation": "has met", "direction": "na", "proposed": "former president/vice president of Lippit, contacted for sponsorship"}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well I congratulate my band, our band. Sometimes I say my — it’s not mine it’s our band, it’s Sherrie’s and my band. I congratulate them because without the product I could maneuver all day long, but without the product I would have nothing. We’ve got a good product. We’ve got a great product. And I’m just hoping that people realize it, and give us a chance. You know the thing is that I went to the former president and vice president of Lippit, Harvey Schiller, through the Yankees. This is Yankee Nets now they bought the band. And I called Harvey up and I said, “you know, you know all the sponsors, you know all the people,” and I said, “you know you were with the Olympics. You’ve had women baseball teams, soccer teams, tennis team, golf team, archery, whatever. We’re no different.” See you’ve got to be careful how you say it, but Sherrie pointed it out to me, it’s a good band or a great band. But then you have to say but they all happen to be women. You see? And you don’t categorize it. But we can play up to anybody and prove it. There’s no thing in music. And I would say if you can play you can play. If you can’t play you can’t play. And I know a lot of guys that can’t play in my opinion you see. And also a lot of women. So that’s the key. So we’re — as American Express — I’m not hawking anything, I’m just telling you. And we’re an educational group. We play high schools and colleges. And we can save four people a year, or three, from making drugs or get them interested in playing, and look up and see — see the women of our band only had the men to look up to, whether it was Buddy, Woody, Lester Young, you know. But wouldn’t it be great to say I want to play drums like Sherrie. I want to play tenor like Anat Cohen. Who’s your idol playing drums? Sherrie. Who’s your idol? Anat Cohen. Who’s yours? Karolina. You see? There’s a whole world out there to try to get. And the reason I talk about the sponsorship, it’s not that we’re looking for their money, we’re looking for them to put us on a tour where we are beneficial to what they do. How do we help your product? At the same time, how do you help us you see. So that’s, and you mentioned John Levy. Well we just did a thing for Dress for Success. It’s about women who are — you know the organization. Well when I first heard about it, I heard it on my machine, I thought they said dress for stress. So I said how do you do a benefit for stressful people? Is it clothes that stressful people wear? I didn’t know what they were doing. So what we did, we honored all the greats, like Clora Bryant who played with the International Sweethearts, and Jane Jarvis, Carline Ray. And we honored Nancy Wilson. © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

275809.evidence: I’d go home and listen to Chick Webb and Jimmie Lunceford and Duke Ellington and Count Basie and Woody, stay up and listen to the remote broadcasts at night you know.
275809.subject: Stanley Kay

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: Well I’m pleased that you said that, but I was a drummer, and there’s a difference. I was very pleased and fortunate to have been able to fulfill my dreams and hopes because I started to play when I was about five years old, banging on pots and pans like most of us did. And the reason I got to do that was my sister was a very fine singer. She was like a child star. And she worked with Buddy Rich when he was Traps the Drum Wonder. And so for some reason when they took me to rehearsal to watch her, I would watch the drummer in the pit. And you never know why, Monk, you just don’t know why. I can’t tell you why, and you try to emulate what he did. You take your hands and — whether it’s good or bad you don’t know at the time at all. But all of a sudden you get kind of hooked on it when it comes in here and it comes in here. That’s what you want to do. And I’m very happy that I did get to do it. And then what happened, I’d go home and listen to Chick Webb and Jimmie Lunceford and Duke Ellington and Count Basie and Woody, stay up and listen to the remote broadcasts at night you know. “From the Park Central Hotel and now the King of the Drums, Chick Webb.” And he’d do a thing called “Let’s Get Together.” So I knew all the theme songs you know. And then, older, Benny Goodman’s band, Gene Krupa was the innovator. And I listened to him and I said, “boy that’s the greatest.” And it’s not that my sister said he wasn’t. She said, “well I know somebody that’s better than that.” And I said, “who’s better than Gene Krupa?” and I said, “and who is it?” “Buddy Rich.” She said, “well he’s playing at the Hickory House with a little band named Joe Marsala.” That was his first band after he left vaudeville. Vaudeville was over when he was about 17 years old. He was a vaudeville star. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

275809.evidence: He said, “Louie’s jive with it. It’s tough enough to play one.” But they were good friends, don’t get me wrong.
275809.subject: Stanley Kay
275809.audit: {"change": "re-judged from the text", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "bandmates in a touring big band (Stanley Kay was straw boss, Louie Bellson was drummer)"}}

sources.speaker: SK
sources.text: act and I played. They see the big sling. Clark Terry told me, he said he was there and the word went out that Buddy’s arm is not broken, he wants to show he can play with one hand. But it was broken. So we played there a week, then we go into the Paramount Theater downtown and the managing director of the Paramount, Bob Whiteman, came up. And he said, “the rumor is that your arm is not broken but there’s a sensation — keep it in the sling.” If it’s not broken we could play the Paramount. See and he never liked two bass drums. He said, “Louie’s jive with it. It’s tough enough to play one.” But they were good friends, don’t get me wrong. He said, “call Ludwig. Send for two bass drums.” So he could get anything he wants. So two bass drums come in. Never practiced it, sat on a stool, no other drums around him, and just played the two bass drums like a tap dancer. With the arm broken and everything. But here’s the uncanny part of this whole thing. Now if you’re an athlete, and your arm is, you know a pitcher or — but your arm is sprained, you don’t throw the ball fast like the 90 mile an hour fast ball, right? You work it in. The next day he took the thing off he played like it was never broken. And I just said I don’t know where that’s coming from. And that’s what he did. That’s what he did. And another story, see he always felt the guys were putting him down because he couldn’t read music. I mean he didn’t know a note. He was like Erroll Garner. Wherever the hands went was the key. So they wrote a book for him, The Drum Book, Henry Aller. And it sold like a hundred thousand copies, but everybody wanted the dexterity that Buddy had. So he decides to want to read. And he gets the drum pad. And his band boy was a drummer. You know, an amateur but he could read some. sources.text: He tap danced. Yeah. He was known as Traps the Drum Wonder. And he was the second highest paid child star to Jackie Coogan. He was making about $1,500 a week. But when the decline of vaudeville, he had no job. And he worked on the WPA when they had the WPA. And putting on a wig and dancing and stuff like that see? And well anyway she told me Buddy Rich. So on Sunday afternoon on 52nd Street was a place called the Hickory House. And it was a round bar, it was a steak house. It was owned by a guy named Popkin. And my sister called Buddy and she paid the way for me. And I’m 14 years old. You could eat there, so at 14 you’re okay you could go in. And jam sessions were about from three to six on Sunday in this big round circular bar. And it was Joe Marsala, his wife played harp, Adele Girard, his brother Marty Marsala played trumpet, Artie Shapiro played bass and Nat Jaffe played piano. And I walk in and I introduced myself. And he’s 19 now, he was five years older than me. And I was 14. So he greeted me, but all the guys used to sit in from all the bands on this jam session. Like bands like Tiny Bradshaw and Andy Kirk’s band, O’Neil Spencer was a wonderful drummer played with the John Kirby band. And he didn’t play. And it was now getting towards like 5:30 and I’m like what am I doing here, because I have to come to have a steak or, you know, I wanted to hear this guy play. Supposed to be this genius, see? And he sat down and played the last thing. It was what we call a flag waver, it was called “Jim Jamp’s Stump.” And when I heard “Jim Jamp”— and I heard him play, I said that’s it. My sister was right. That’s the greatest thing I ever heard. And I just idolized him. And I followed him. Bunny Berigan, when he went, and before that he came down to my house to hear me play. And he didn’t tell me but he told my sister, he said, “he can’t play.” And I cried. I really cried. I mean, whatever.

sources.text: Steinbrenner,” I said, “somebody saw you coming.” You know they charge you money, they don’t make that kind of money. So who can you get? So I liked Blood, Sweat & Tears. They were on the way out, but you know, were still there. So I said I’ll call the William Morris Agency, which I did, talked to the agent, and he says they’re available. So I tell Mr. Steinbrenner. I said they’re available. And he checks things out to see who likes them, you know, if his daughter accepts it. So I called the agent and says they don’t want to do it. So I have to go back. He says, “you told me they’re available.” I says, “available doesn’t mean they’re going to do it.” But I knew Bobby Colomby, the drummer. And I said I’ll call Bobby myself, I’ll beg him. So now the agent says okay. Same money, ten thousand. I bring the rider back. I never saw this kind of rider and I’m looking at the rider. Dom Perignon, Cristal, steaks, orange juice, fresh eggs, what. And I’m looking at it and I’m reading and I’m going — he says, “what’s the matter with you?” I said, “I wouldn’t do this. This is not professional.” “Well you’re going to give it to them anyway.” You know. I said, “I don’t like it.” He said, “yeah I don’t like it. Get me someone else.” So I called the agent and I said no deal. “Well you gave me a verbal.” I said, “how do you ask for all this, steaks and chicken and chicken under glass, in glass, whatever, what is that? I don’t understand.” I said, “Frank Sinatra doesn’t ask for that.” You know, what is it? Anyway we canceled them out. And then a month later he was doing, his wife was doing, right here in Tampa, Florida, he was doing something, that’s the home office, for a hospital. And he said, “who could I get for the benefit” for like one of the Catholic hospitals. I said, “well I’ll get you the Buddy Rich band for nothing.” ‘Cause I still managed them. But pay their way from California here to New Orleans, no money, and I’ll get you Mel Torme. But Mel gets paid. So Mel got five thousand, and it was very successful. And from then on there he trusted me. And I’ve been doing it for him for fifteen years. And he’ll say, like he gets nervous. If we’re going to do something he’ll say, “you screw this up one more time.” And now I know him so I just call him George, you know, but in front of people Mr. Steinbrenner. I says, “George, listen. I screwed it up fourteen times, another time doesn’t matter. Fifteen. It’s good. That’s my record. Fifteen screw ups you got me, the head screw up of your world here that I produce shows for.” And it’s been very good. He’s been — you know he’s got his things too but when I had a slight stroke he came to see me in the hospital three times, paid all my hospital bills, sent me to Florida to rehabilitate with the ball team, stayed at his hotel in a suite. And at that time, and Sherrie, really took care of me. She nursed me and took care of me, back to good health. I still have a little limp. Because I idolized Peg Leg Bates. I want to dance like him one day. But anyway I come with the rocker, and I’m going in where all the young guys are training, at the complex, all the young ball players. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

It’s the same thing. That’s how they make their living. That’s rude.” You see? So therefore, with me, I mean if they talk when the band’s playing, I’m a little — who am I going to hurt? But that’s my honesty. And it’s not that I — I don’t try to offend anybody, I don’t try to be rude, I say please, this is not what we do. We don’t do this.

So on Sunday afternoon on 52nd Street was a place called the Hickory House. And it was a round bar, it was a steak house. It was owned by a guy named Popkin. And jam sessions were about from three to six on Sunday in this big round circular bar. And it was Joe Marsala, his wife played harp, Adele Girard, his brother Marty Marsala played trumpet, Artie Shapiro played bass and Nat Jaffe played piano. And I walk in and I introduced myself. And he’s 19 now, he was five years older than me. And I was 14. So he greeted me, but all the guys used to sit in from all the bands on this jam session. Like bands like Tiny Bradshaw and Andy Kirk’s band, O’Neil Spencer was a wonderful drummer played with the John Kirby band. And he didn’t play. And it was now getting towards like 5:30 and I’m like what am I doing here, because I have to come to have a steak or, you know, I wanted to hear this guy play. Supposed to be this genius, see? My sister was right. That’s the greatest thing I ever heard. And I just idolized him. And I followed him. Bunny Berigan, when he went, and before that he came down to my house to hear me play. And he didn’t tell me but he told my sister, he said, “he can’t play.” And I cried. I really cried. I mean, whatever.

275821.subject: Jimmy Lewis
275821.audit: {"change": "Basie hired him and he played in Basie's small group and big band; evidence was spliced", "previous": {"relation": "played under", "direction": "target", "proposed": "bassist in Count Basie's band, early 1950s"}}

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: the clubs and they said, “well what you do, go with Basie, you’ll get more experience.” They said, “we’re going to miss you but I think it’d be a good deal for you.” So I went with Basie. I met him in Chicago. I go to Chicago and I go to a place called the Southway Hotel, and I was sitting in the lobby waiting all day for Basie to show up. I didn’t think about getting a room or anything, I waited in case I was in the wrong place. I was right from Nashville, you know, down south. So I sat there, until about, oh it must have been about 9:00 at night. And in walks Clark Terry. Clark Terry, he looked at me, I see Clark Terry with his big old flugelhorn you know. The big wide shoulders, the overcoat, and these draped pants that they used to wear at that time, and a hat. I looked and I said, now wait a minute. I’m going to get in some other kind of company. And he said, “man get your room. You get a room. We don’t know when Basie’ll show up.” I said, “I thought we were going to start work.” And he said, “no, no, we’ll wait for Basie.” So I go and get a room. I think we waited about three days before Basie showed up. Basie showed up, and he came in boy looking like he’d been partying for days.

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Yeah, at that time I was fast on the bass you know. And I had a different sound from most of the guys, because I never learned to put the strings where they’re really supposed to be. Anyway you don’t have to play as hard or anything.” So I did it and I got used to it after a few weeks. And Joe Williams used to come in and he was very shy at that time. You know he’d come walking on the bandstand and he used to sing these little love songs you know, just real sweet and then he’d walk off the stand. And I said I wonder why Basie likes him so well. And so I asked Basie one day. I said, “Basie, what do you see in Joe Williams?” He say, “You just wait.” He said, “I see something that maybe nobody else sees.” But he said, “that man can sing.” I said okay. So I stayed with Basie and we worked the Brass Rail down at the Loop. We opened up one night and all the people were sitting at the tables you know, and so Basie started off real soft. We started playing soft you know. I thought I was playing louder than anybody, I mean I’m © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

275821.proposed: drummer and bassist in Count Basie's small group at the Brass Rail

275821.subject: Jimmy Lewis
275821.audit: {"change": "evidence was spliced from two blocks", "previous": {"relation": "in music group with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "drummer and bassist in Count Basie's small group at the Brass Rail"}}

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Yes, the small group. We had Wardell Gray, Clark Terry, Gus Johnson on drums, Freddie Green on guitar, me on bass and like we used Bud DeFranco playing tenor.

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: just playing it. Basie says, “Don’t play so loud.” He said, “they’ll hear ya.” So I cut down on the bass. And Basie set a tempo and then he’d watch the people’s feet. He said, “Okay, everybody’s starting to feel you over the conversation.” He said, “Now Gus, pick up your sticks.” Gus was playing with brushes. He said, “Pick up your sticks.” He said, “We’ve got ‘em now.” And by the time we opened up, everybody turned you know and looked and you couldn’t believe it. Buddy DeFranco walked out to the stand, and man, everybody would start to play. He and Clark Terry started doing tricks. Clark would take his horn, take the mouthpiece off and just put it in the end of a glass and blow you know, and make all kinds of funny sounds you know. And Gus Johnson, then here comes Wardell Gray. He’d walk up and he’d just play something like Lester Young you know. And we started playing anything he had. Neal Hefti was making arrangements for the band. And Neal wrote all these beautiful things. And we’d make the thing sound like a 16 piece band. And Freddie Green boy, he was like a metronome sitting there. And you couldn’t get away from him. The tempo might move up a little bit, I’d get excited, and Freddie would say, “come back here. Right here.” And boy that thing would take off. And Basie, he’d sit there and give signs. He had all kinds of signs. He’d do his face, you know when he’d want you to play louder or softer you know. And when he’d get ready to close a number he’d double his fists you know. And like if he wanted some excitement, he’d stand up from the piano and look at you you know. And boy, and Gus was sitting on the drums and you’d hear this thing, it sounded like it was coming up out of the floor. And boy the people just went crazy. We went there for two weeks. And they kept us six weeks in there. And after we left there, we went to another club called the Capitol Lounge. And we went there for two weeks. By that time we had added another horn. We had Marshall Royal. Marshall Royal came in the band and when we went to the Capitol Lounge, man, whew, people just couldn’t believe it, you know. People would stand there and look and they would applaud for the same tune over and over. And we’d play and play and play, the man would say, Basie’d say, “Well I guess our two weeks are up here.” And the man said, “No,” he said, “You’ve got eight more weeks here.” The man at the theater gave us ten weeks. And then we went out to California to a place called the Oasis. And we went in the Oasis and the same thing happened there, you know, just over and over. And then we got a call from one of these agents that said we had to do a movie with Sugar Chile Robinson, he was a little piano player, looked like he was a little midget. And so he went and did the movie, and we did the movie out there on the lot. I think until around 4:30 or 5:00 in the morning. But we’d get paid for that time, being there. Bing Crosby, he’d come through in his car you know. And Frank Sinatra, we went out to his house, went out to Esther Williams’ house. She had it all set up for all that swimming stuff. I think she must have made a picture back there. And we went to Rochester’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

275821.proposed: bassist in King Curtis's band for seven years
275821.evidence: I worked with King Curtis for seven years. Formed a solid band, everything.
275821.subject: Jimmy Lewis
275821.audit: {"change": "worked in King Curtis's band and later 'gave King Curtis my notice' - Curtis was the leader", "previous": {"relation": "played with", "direction": "na", "proposed": "bassist in King Curtis's band for seven years"}}

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Yeah. I worked with King Curtis for seven years. Formed a solid band, everything. But then I would go downtown and they’d call me for a record date and all. So I had to start playing the Fender bass. I had a different style from all the guys on the Fender bass — my own creation. But it worked out nice for me. So the first week I went down I think I made about three sessions, and I got seven hundred and something dollars. So I said now wait a minute — there’s money in this thing. I wonder if I can keep it going. So then I gave King Curtis my notice. Because he kept calling me you know. And this guy named Ray Burns, he saw me down there. And he says, “Jimmy, I heard you on one of these records down here, you’re playing the Fender.” I says, “yeah.” He said, “well you got a pencil and paper?” I said, “yeah.” I kept a little book, you know. He said “I’ve got 17 dates for you,” 17 recording dates. I put that down, and I made those dates, and you know you had to go to the union to pick up your check. I’m standing at the window picking up my check and one of the guys turned over and looked mad, I was picking up so many. And so after that I started — there was this play on Broadway called “Hair.” They came along. So there was a guy named Galt McDermott, he had a lot of music that he had been trying to get people to listen to, but he didn’t know what to do with it. He told me, “I don’t know what to do with this.” He said, “I can’t think of no bass lines,” he said, “I thought of a melody, but I can’t think of no lines.” I said, “I’ll tell you, play it. I’ll put some lines to it.” So I put some lines to the music and I think he put it on a record called, a company called Kilimanjaro I think he said it was, out of somewhere in Canada. And the thing, he called me two weeks later and he said, “Jimmy.” He said, “the thing is selling. People are listening to my music.” I said, “Yeah?” He said, “Could you come down to do one more date?” So I went down and when I got there that’s when he told me about “Hair.” He said, “Will you try to do that?” He said, “they got a lot of music.” I said, “well we’ll give it a try, I don’t know.” I went down there and went to the Shakespeare House down on, I forgot, anyway, we got down there and that’s where we rehearsed you know. Put the music down. I started, so he had a lot of chords down. So I took it and built bass lines from the chords you know. So I kept doing that and they had about thirty-some tunes. And so I looked at the guys and looked at the actors act out there, and I said now this kind of line would fit what they’re doing. You know so I’d look at that and then I put the thing together, and so we had a piano player named Neal Tate. Neal Tate said, “I’m going to write these things down for you.” So he wrote a whole book about this thick, of © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Yes, the small group. We had Wardell Gray, Clark Terry, Gus Johnson on drums, Freddie Green on guitar, me on bass and like we used Bud DeFranco playing tenor.

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: band. Now all these guys, when they got together it sounded like they’d been playing for years together. So he said, “this is what I want, I can do something with this.” So we had a rehearsal. Let’s see, Nat Pierce brought some arrangements down, Nat Pierce from Boston. And Neal Hefti brought some, and somebody else brought some and put them down in front of him. Clark Terry and Wardell Grey used to pick up the music like this and never seen it before, and sing it, just like they were reading it with the horns, then put it down and play it. So I look at these guys, and I wondered if I could take this, you know it was difficult. And so he said, “No, don’t worry about it.” He said, “I’m going to feature you.” He said, “I never featured a bass before but I’m going to feature you.” I said, “when?” He said, “wait until we get this movie called ‘Conversations.’” I don’t know if you saw it or not. And through the whole movie, they couldn’t think of a tune, but he told me he said “What do you want to do? Do what you want to do and we’ll follow you.” So I said, “Well I’ve got a tune I’d like to do.” He said, “okay, we’ll call it ‘Conversations.’ So you play as if you’re asking a question, and then Clark Terry will come up and take a solo, and then you answer him with your bass, and then Wardell will come up and Buddy” and like that. And so they named the tune “Conversations.” And the thing went over well, man. And for a long time it played. And every once in a while now you see it on T.V. And he said, “It’s the first time I’ve ever featured a bass you know.” And then I got out and we went to the Million Dollar Theater. We played the Million Dollar Theater and they had an all-girl band there too came in once and we played, and as we left the theater, I think we went to Las Vegas. A club — a big club out there called the Trochedera or something like that at that time. I don’t know what it is now. But anyway, we walked in that club and we had the Norman Miller dancers, we had a girl singer, and I think we had Pearl Bailey’s brother, a dancer, and somebody else. But anyway we put on a show. That night we get on the big stage, they put those lights on, and everything looked different. I said, “this must be Hollywood.” So it was so beautiful when they put the lights on, and we played everything right down here until the show come on. People dancing all out there, and when it was time for the show to come on, Basie said, “all right that’s it, ‘One O’Clock Jump.’” We did “One O’Clock Jump,” man, everybody knew it, people would recognize it, they started applauding. We played that then the man announced the show and the show came on. We played that show, and when we got through, people just kept applauding. They wouldn’t stop. And so he had to play another tune you know. I think the tune — oh I can’t think of it now. But anyway we left there and we had to go back to California to the Oasis. And then we left and went on tour, with Billy Eckstine and let’s see some-body else. But anyway, Billy Eckstine was a big headline. And oh yeah, George Shearing, Billy Eckstine, and somebody else, there was three different, oh, the Nicholas Brothers. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: band. Now all these guys, when they got together it sounded like they’d been playing for years together. So he said, “this is what I want, I can do something with this.” So we had a rehearsal. Let’s see, Nat Pierce brought some arrangements down, Nat Pierce from Boston. And Neal Hefti brought some, and somebody else brought some and put them down in front of him. Clark Terry and Wardell Grey used to pick up the music like this and never seen it before, and sing it, just like they were reading it with the horns, then put it down and play it. So I look at these guys, and I wondered if I could take this, you know it was difficult. And so he said, “No, don’t worry about it.” He said, “I’m going to feature you.” He said, “I never featured a bass before but I’m going to feature you.” I said, “when?” He said, “wait until we get this movie called ‘Conversations.’” I don’t know if you saw it or not. And through the whole movie, they couldn’t think of a tune, but he told me he said “What do you want to do? Do what you want to do and we’ll follow you.” So I said, “Well I’ve got a tune I’d like to do.” He said, “okay, we’ll call it ‘Conversations.’ So you play as if you’re asking a question, and then Clark Terry will come up and take a solo, and then you answer him with your bass, and then Wardell will come up and Buddy” and like that. And so they named the tune “Conversations.” And the thing went over well, man. And for a long time it played. And every once in a while now you see it on T.V. And he said, “It’s the first time I’ve ever featured a bass you know.” And then I got out and we went to the Million Dollar Theater. We played the Million Dollar Theater and they had an all-girl band there too came in once and we played, and as we left the theater, I think we went to Las Vegas. A club — a big club out there called the Trochedera or something like that at that time. I don’t know what it is now. But anyway, we walked in that club and we had the Norman Miller dancers, we had a girl singer, and I think we had Pearl Bailey’s brother, a dancer, and somebody else. But anyway we put on a show. That night we get on the big stage, they put those lights on, and everything looked different. I said, “this must be Hollywood.” So it was so beautiful when they put the lights on, and we played everything right down here until the show come on. People dancing all out there, and when it was time for the show to come on, Basie said, “all right that’s it, ‘One O’Clock Jump.’” We did “One O’Clock Jump,” man, everybody knew it, people would recognize it, they started applauding. We played that then the man announced the show and the show came on. We played that show, and when we got through, people just kept applauding. They wouldn’t stop. And so he had to play another tune you know. I think the tune — oh I can’t think of it now. But anyway we left there and we had to go back to California to the Oasis. And then we left and went on tour, with Billy Eckstine and let’s see some-body else. But anyway, Billy Eckstine was a big headline. And oh yeah, George Shearing, Billy Eckstine, and somebody else, there was three different, oh, the Nicholas Brothers. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Yeah, you know we had some Army camps to do. We had to ride in the Army planes, you know the ones with two tails you know, and that big thing in the middle. So we got, one day we got on this thing going to one of the camps, and it was noisy, this thing was so noisy you couldn’t hear. Now Billy Eckstine and all those guys were used to riding. But me, I was scared to death. We all had parachutes. Basie had on a parachute over by the door you know. So we were going to Texas, Corpus Christi, Texas. So the plane took off, but before we got there, something happened just before we got ready to land. They couldn’t get the landing gear down. So the guy kept punching it in back, there was some long pole they couldn’t get it down. So the man said, “we’re going to have to circle around and go further, and come back around again.” So they went around, and started back to see if we could land, and still couldn’t get it open. So one of the guys, the one who was right by the back door here, pulled that big door open. Now we were flying. So I said, “what’s this — what are you doing?” The guy said, “well see, we’re trying to get a little more air in the plane.” I said, “air in the plane!” I said, “man, we don’t need no more air.” So he said, “well, I’ll tell you, we’re having a problem with the landing gear.” And he said, “ you might have to bail out.” And Basie looked at me. He said “what do you mean bail out?” And so he asked the pilot, he said, “look, are you going to bail out too?” The pilot said, “no, I’ve got to stay with the plane.” He said, “well I’m going to stay with you,” he said, “I’m going on with you.” “Because,” he said, “if I jump out and I pull this string and the ‘chute don’t open up,” he said, “man, I can’t fly — I don’t have no wings.” Well everybody was laughing. And so Billy teased me, he said, “man” he said, “we’re going to crash.” — oh baby, I don’t know what to do. And I’m running back and forth. It’s funny, you know I’d never been in a plane before anyway.
