sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Yeah. I worked with King Curtis for seven years. Formed a solid band, everything. But then I would go downtown and they’d call me for a record date and all. So I had to start playing the Fender bass. I had a different style from all the guys on the Fender bass — my own creation. But it worked out nice for me. So the first week I went down I think I made about three sessions, and I got seven hundred and something dollars. So I said now wait a minute — there’s money in this thing. I wonder if I can keep it going. So then I gave King Curtis my notice. Because he kept calling me you know. And this guy named Ray Burns, he saw me down there. And he says, “Jimmy, I heard you on one of these records down here, you’re playing the Fender.” I says, “yeah.” He said, “well you got a pencil and paper?” I said, “yeah.” I kept a little book, you know. He said “I’ve got 17 dates for you,” 17 recording dates. I put that down, and I made those dates, and you know you had to go to the union to pick up your check. I’m standing at the window picking up my check and one of the guys turned over and looked mad, I was picking up so many. And so after that I started — there was this play on Broadway called “Hair.” They came along. So there was a guy named Galt McDermott, he had a lot of music that he had been trying to get people to listen to, but he didn’t know what to do with it. He told me, “I don’t know what to do with this.” He said, “I can’t think of no bass lines,” he said, “I thought of a melody, but I can’t think of no lines.” I said, “I’ll tell you, play it. I’ll put some lines to it.” So I put some lines to the music and I think he put it on a record called, a company called Kilimanjaro I think he said it was, out of somewhere in Canada. And the thing, he called me two weeks later and he said, “Jimmy.” He said, “the thing is selling. People are listening to my music.” I said, “Yeah?” He said, “Could you come down to do one more date?” So I went down and when I got there that’s when he told me about “Hair.” He said, “Will you try to do that?” He said, “they got a lot of music.” I said, “well we’ll give it a try, I don’t know.” I went down there and went to the Shakespeare House down on, I forgot, anyway, we got down there and that’s where we rehearsed you know. Put the music down. I started, so he had a lot of chords down. So I took it and built bass lines from the chords you know. So I kept doing that and they had about thirty-some tunes. And so I looked at the guys and looked at the actors act out there, and I said now this kind of line would fit what they’re doing. You know so I’d look at that and then I put the thing together, and so we had a piano player named Neal Tate. Neal Tate said, “I’m going to write these things down for you.” So he wrote a whole book about this thick, of © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Oh, yeah, yeah. I spent a lot of time trying to get the sound. Like they had a Zane Paul, and Don Leight. Zane Paul, he played bass clarinet and tenor and alto. Don Leight trumpet. Eddy Williams trumpet. And Neal Tate piano, Idris Muhammed on drums, and Charlie Brown acoustic guitar and let’s see who else did we have? Oh, Alan Fontaine, he played guitar, electric guitar. So now what I did, I said now I’ve got to voice this stuff to make it sound different from anything. Because the show is different from anything you ever heard of. It looked like it wasn’t anything. I figured it’d last about two weeks. So we got the thing together and did it. Then the critics came in and they listened, and they watched the show, and they liked it so well, man, doggone it was a hit. All right now. The thing was a hit and we had to already record the music. But I wasn’t satisfied with the sound. So I took it and polished it up. So Galt said, “look, I got to do another show,” and they said, “you just take care of the music part, you know, and hold the band together.” So I changed the whole style of the band. Not really, the music was the same except I updated it a little bit. And the kids went crazy on the floor man, oh, they were so glad to do the show. But they had in the opening of the show where they’d sit there and talk on the floor. And so I said well they need something in this act. So I created a tune called “Happy Feet.” And they played it very softly. You’ve got to really listen to hear it you know, but it was just the rhythm section you know, two guitars, electric bass and piano. We’d play that thing man, and it was almost like a jazz tune in parts you know. So boy we played that thing and the people in the audience, you could see them moving to the music you know. All right, but we never really put it in the show you know. I just wanted to fill it there. And when we got ready to close, this is what got me. We got in there one day, and Michael Butler, he was the guy that had all the money. And I think he said he had three hundred million dollars, and when he came to back the show you know, his father had some money he inherited. And so he was a young guy. He didn’t know what to do with it, so he said well I’ll do this. He used to give us big parties. We’d ride up and down Fifth Avenue in those double decker things and it was nice. The Four Seasons — we’d go to the Four Seasons and all this. So Michael one night, after about, let’s see we was there five years. Four years later, the people said, “well I think the show should go on two-fers” you know what I mean — they had to cut the price, see it wasn’t doing so good, that’s what they told Michael. The house packed like that. So Michael came in one day and he said, he went to the box office and he said, “I heard the show wasn’t doing so © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

275821.proposed: fellow member of Count Basie's small group (named 'Bud DeFranco playing tenor')
275821.evidence: me on bass and like we used Bud DeFranco playing tenor.
275821.subject: Jimmy Lewis
275821.audit: {"change": "old evidence was the interviewer reading Joe Williams; use the interviewee's own line (merged with Bud DeFranco)", "previous": {"relation": "in music group with", "direction": "na", "proposed": "bandmates at the Brass Rail under Count Basie"}}

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Yes, the small group. We had Wardell Gray, Clark Terry, Gus Johnson on drums, Freddie Green on guitar, me on bass and like we used Bud DeFranco playing tenor.

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: just playing it. Basie says, “Don’t play so loud.” He said, “they’ll hear ya.” So I cut down on the bass. And Basie set a tempo and then he’d watch the people’s feet. He said, “Okay, everybody’s starting to feel you over the conversation.” He said, “Now Gus, pick up your sticks.” Gus was playing with brushes. He said, “Pick up your sticks.” He said, “We’ve got ‘em now.” And by the time we opened up, everybody turned you know and looked and you couldn’t believe it. Buddy DeFranco walked out to the stand, and man, everybody would start to play. He and Clark Terry started doing tricks. Clark would take his horn, take the mouthpiece off and just put it in the end of a glass and blow you know, and make all kinds of funny sounds you know. And Gus Johnson, then here comes Wardell Gray. He’d walk up and he’d just play something like Lester Young you know. And we started playing anything he had. Neal Hefti was making arrangements for the band. And Neal wrote all these beautiful things. And we’d make the thing sound like a 16 piece band. And Freddie Green boy, he was like a metronome sitting there. And you couldn’t get away from him. The tempo might move up a little bit, I’d get excited, and Freddie would say, “come back here. Right here.” And boy that thing would take off. And Basie, he’d sit there and give signs. He had all kinds of signs. He’d do his face, you know when he’d want you to play louder or softer you know. And when he’d get ready to close a number he’d double his fists you know. And like if he wanted some excitement, he’d stand up from the piano and look at you you know. And boy, and Gus was sitting on the drums and you’d hear this thing, it sounded like it was coming up out of the floor. And boy the people just went crazy. We went there for two weeks. And they kept us six weeks in there. And after we left there, we went to another club called the Capitol Lounge. And we went there for two weeks. By that time we had added another horn. We had Marshall Royal. Marshall Royal came in the band and when we went to the Capitol Lounge, man, whew, people just couldn’t believe it, you know. People would stand there and look and they would applaud for the same tune over and over. And we’d play and play and play, the man would say, Basie’d say, “Well I guess our two weeks are up here.” And the man said, “No,” he said, “You’ve got eight more weeks here.” The man at the theater gave us ten weeks. And then we went out to California to a place called the Oasis. And we went in the Oasis and the same thing happened there, you know, just over and over. And then we got a call from one of these agents that said we had to do a movie with Sugar Chile Robinson, he was a little piano player, looked like he was a little midget. And so he went and did the movie, and we did the movie out there on the lot. I think until around 4:30 or 5:00 in the morning. But we’d get paid for that time, being there. Bing Crosby, he’d come through in his car you know. And Frank Sinatra, we went out to his house, went out to Esther Williams’ house. She had it all set up for all that swimming stuff. I think she must have made a picture back there. And we went to Rochester’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: Yeah, at that time I was fast on the bass you know. And I had a different sound from most of the guys, because I never learned to put the strings where they’re really supposed to be. But being around Ray Brown and Oscar Pettiford, all these guys, they got me out of that. They said, “look, put the strings down.” They said, “the bass don’t have the sound it’s supposed to have. Anyway you don’t have to play as hard or anything.” So I did it and I got used to it after a few weeks. And Joe Williams used to come in and he was very shy at that time. You know he’d come walking on the bandstand and he used to sing these little love songs you know, just real sweet and then he’d walk off the stand. And I said I wonder why Basie likes him so well. And so I asked Basie one day. I said, “Basie, what do you see in Joe Williams?” He say, “You just wait.” He said, “I see something that maybe nobody else sees.” But he said, “that man can sing.” I said okay. So I stayed with Basie and we worked the Brass Rail down at the Loop. We opened up one night and all the people were sitting at the tables you know, and so Basie started off real soft. We started playing soft you know. I thought I was playing louder than anybody, I mean I’m © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

sources.text: Bassist Jimmy Lewis was born in Nashville in 1918. He first played ukulele in bands, later picking up the bass to anchor some inspired jazz rhythm sections, including the Count Basie small group in the early 1950s. Jimmy has worked with Billie Holiday, Horace Silver and the Modern Jazz Quartet. His experience includes work in rhythm & blues as well, and he can be heard on albums with King Curtis, Ivory Joe Hunter and numerous soul organists. His musical contribution to the Broadway hit “Hair” helped ensure its wide success and he was a featured figure in the documentary “Count Basie, Swingin’ the Blues.”

275821.evidence: So me and Wendell Cully, we walked out to the plane and looked in, and we see all these parachutes on the seats
275821.subject: Jimmy Lewis
275821.audit: {"change": "fellow Basie bandsman on the army-camp tour; evidence was paraphrased", "previous": {"relation": "in music group with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "members of Count Basie's band"}}

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: So we get to Corpus Christi, Texas. Now, so finally we land. Everybody set there about 15 minutes before they got out of the plane. It was quiet — boy you could hear a mouse — quiet you know. So everybody started getting out one by one, taking off the parachute, taking their instruments and go outside. We got outside, and we had to play under some trees. We get out there, and set up under these trees out there, in the hot summertime. Oh, man, it looked like a big field. And people, as far as you could see. And they had all these big speakers about like that. So they set the band stand up, all the band stands, they put the music, you know the fella he’d take care of all that. And so then Basie went up to test the piano to see if it was in tune you know. So then he called us, his band. We got up there and Basie was telling about this trip, how much trouble we had with the plane and all that. So the people settled down you know. They settled down and he said, “Listen, we haven’t opened yet.” We started playing. As soon as we started playing, all these little scorpions come out of the tree and started falling on the bandstand. And it’s falling in the bell of the horn, and the guy’d dump it out and keep playing. I got me some string, tying it all around my pants legs you know, in case they would crawl up my leg. And so when we finished the job, now we’ve got to take this same plane and go to California. So me and Wendell Cully, we walked out to the plane and looked in, and we see all these parachutes on the seats, and Cully said, “They look like dead people, man.” He said, “We can’t take this thing again, can we?” I said, “No.” So I said well let’s go tell Basie we don’t think we’re going to go on this. So we went and told Basie and he said, “I don’t blame you, but,” he said, “I’ve got to stay with the band and so you go ahead and see if you can get a train out, and meet us in California.” So we did. We got a train. We got to California three days later. And I think we missed one gig. But we got to the gig and we played and everything. So we asked Basie, “How was the trip?” He said, “Man that was the worst trip I ever had,” he said. “Good thing you didn’t come, because somebody would have died.”

sources.text: well so I came to see what was happening.” So they said, “we don’t know nothing about that.” They said, “it’s been packed every day and night.” He said, “okay,” so he went up in the big office and talked to some of the people, and told them, “the show is closed as of this minute.” So he closed the show out. Man, but four days before he closed it, somebody stole my bass book. All the other books were there, but my bass book was gone. And so I went down to one of the record companies we were doing business with, and I happened to see all these books on the floor piled up, you know all these books. Music, Galt’s music. So I said look at this. So I peeked in and I looked at it, and I seen my bass lines there, among all the music you know. So I went back and told Gordon. Gordon didn’t know anything about it either you know. But I tried to get some money back. So then that’s when we had a little lawyer, he shaked them and found out how much they’ve sat on. And he told me he said, “you know how much money you’ve got coming?” I said, “no.” He said, “you should have about a quarter of a million dollars.” I said, “what!” He said, “it’s over eight million in records, two years ago.” I said, “oh man.” So well you know that’s part of business. And so I tried and I couldn’t get anything to happen with that. So then “Hair” closed. It closed and I decided I’d form me up a little group, a jazz group called Three Sparks and a Flame. Well she was the flame, and so over there, I had wrote about, oh over a hundred tunes at that time. I’ve got more now. But we decided we were going to do all our tunes. But we ended up doing a lot of Basie and Duke and all these different arrangements you know. I would arrange all the stuff, and set it to the style I wanted. And we could make a trio sound like an eight piece band. No horns. We could do that. And so we got pretty popular. We started getting all these big jobs you know around town. And they called us, in a place called Cafe Society. It was down on 22nd Street and Broadway I think. And we went down there and stayed there a while, and left there and went to another place on 54th Street. So we went in there for a while. And people liked it, they kept calling us back. So I took the group and so we decided we’d do our own booking. So I learned the business end of it. And we were getting a lot of good gigs you know, all these places way out in the suburbs, some places on Long Island, way out on Long Island. And the big golf clubs and all that. And so we did that for a long time, then I decided to do a video. I did a video but it didn’t turn out like I wanted. Now I’m working on a Broadway musical. But it’s going to be a different kind of musical from all these other musicals you’ve seen. It’s going to be like a play, it’s a love story. It’s going to be a play, and I wrote all the music for it, and I’m just kind of putting it together now.

Do what you want to do and we’ll follow you.” So I said, “Well I’ve got a tune I’d like to do.” He said, “okay, we’ll call it ‘Conversations.’ So you play as if you’re asking a question, and then Clark Terry will come up and take a solo, and then you answer him with your bass, and then Wardell will come up and Buddy” and like that. And so they named the tune “Conversations.” And the thing went over well, man. And for a long time it played. And every once in a while now you see it on T.V. And he said, “It’s the first time I’ve ever featured a bass you know.” And then I got out and we went to the Million Dollar Theater. We played the Million Dollar Theater and they had an all-girl band there too came in once and we played, and as we left the theater, I think we went to Las Vegas. A club — a big club out there called the Trochedera or something like that at that time. I don’t know what it is now. But anyway, we walked in that club and we had the Norman Miller dancers, we had a girl singer, and I think we had Pearl Bailey’s brother, a dancer, and somebody else. But anyway we put on a show. That night we get on the big stage, they put those lights on, and everything looked different. I said, “this must be Hollywood.” So it was so beautiful when they put the lights on, and we played everything right down here until the show come on. People dancing all out there, and when it was time for the show to come on, Basie said, “all right that’s it, ‘One O’Clock Jump.’” We did “One O’Clock Jump,” man, everybody knew it, people would recognize it, they started applauding. We played that then the man announced the show and the show came on. We played that show, and when we got through, people just kept applauding. They wouldn’t stop. And so he had to play another tune you know. I think the tune — oh I can’t think of it now. But anyway we left there and we had to go back to California to the Oasis. And then we left and went on tour, with Billy Eckstine and let’s see some-body else. But anyway, Billy Eckstine was a big headline. And oh yeah, George Shearing, Billy Eckstine, and somebody else, there was three different, oh, the Nicholas Brothers. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

275821.subject: Jimmy Lewis
275821.audit: {"change": "named as Wardell Gray's stylistic model", "previous": null}

sources.speaker: JL
sources.text: just playing it. Basie says, “Don’t play so loud.” He said, “they’ll hear ya.” So I cut down on the bass. And Basie set a tempo and then he’d watch the people’s feet. He said, “Okay, everybody’s starting to feel you over the conversation.” He said, “Now Gus, pick up your sticks.” Gus was playing with brushes. He said, “Pick up your sticks.” He said, “We’ve got ‘em now.” And by the time we opened up, everybody turned you know and looked and you couldn’t believe it. Buddy DeFranco walked out to the stand, and man, everybody would start to play. He and Clark Terry started doing tricks. Clark would take his horn, take the mouthpiece off and just put it in the end of a glass and blow you know, and make all kinds of funny sounds you know. And Gus Johnson, then here comes Wardell Gray. He’d walk up and he’d just play something like Lester Young you know. And we started playing anything he had. Neal Hefti was making arrangements for the band. And Neal wrote all these beautiful things. And we’d make the thing sound like a 16 piece band. And Freddie Green boy, he was like a metronome sitting there. And you couldn’t get away from him. The tempo might move up a little bit, I’d get excited, and Freddie would say, “come back here. Right here.” And boy that thing would take off. And Basie, he’d sit there and give signs. He had all kinds of signs. He’d do his face, you know when he’d want you to play louder or softer you know. And when he’d get ready to close a number he’d double his fists you know. And like if he wanted some excitement, he’d stand up from the piano and look at you you know. And boy, and Gus was sitting on the drums and you’d hear this thing, it sounded like it was coming up out of the floor. And boy the people just went crazy. We went there for two weeks. And they kept us six weeks in there. And after we left there, we went to another club called the Capitol Lounge. And we went there for two weeks. By that time we had added another horn. We had Marshall Royal. Marshall Royal came in the band and when we went to the Capitol Lounge, man, whew, people just couldn’t believe it, you know. People would stand there and look and they would applaud for the same tune over and over. And we’d play and play and play, the man would say, Basie’d say, “Well I guess our two weeks are up here.” And the man said, “No,” he said, “You’ve got eight more weeks here.” The man at the theater gave us ten weeks. And then we went out to California to a place called the Oasis. And we went in the Oasis and the same thing happened there, you know, just over and over. And then we got a call from one of these agents that said we had to do a movie with Sugar Chile Robinson, he was a little piano player, looked like he was a little midget. And so he went and did the movie, and we did the movie out there on the lot. I think until around 4:30 or 5:00 in the morning. But we’d get paid for that time, being there. Bing Crosby, he’d come through in his car you know. And Frank Sinatra, we went out to his house, went out to Esther Williams’ house. She had it all set up for all that swimming stuff. I think she must have made a picture back there. And we went to Rochester’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

So the trio would play the same way. So the people liked what we did and the place started getting crowded, because like I say every night — seven nights we came in. So I stayed there I think about three years. And then I left and went to another club right down the street, called the Herod Club, upstairs, so we got a night club and we played a few tunes just with the trio then we added a horn you know. We added a horn and one night a guy came in and says, a guy came in with his guitar in his arm, old raincoat you know, and hat all crumpled up. He says, “Could I sit in with you guys?” So we looked the guy and I said, “I don’t know.” One of the guys said, “You think you can play?” I said, “All right, come up.” He got up and he tuned up his guitar all open strings you know, and so he said, “What do you want to play?” So we started calling jazz tunes like “How High the Moon” and stuff like that. He said, “Okay.” And he played, and the guy played so well that he got through it. I said, “What’s your name?” He said, “Bill Jennings.” You know Bill used to play with Dogett?

275831.proposed: husband (married in Aachen); cornetist she played gigs with
275831.evidence: when Jimmy and I used to play a gig at The Dinkler Hotel in Syracuse
275831.subject: Marian McPartland
275831.audit: {"change": "wrongly skipped for sharing surname; he is her husband and they played gigs together; leadership of their gigs not stated, so 'played with'", "previous": {"skipped": "self_or_host"}}

sources.speaker: MM
sources.text: Well but in this particular area of where we are right now, when Jimmy and I used to play a gig at The Dinkler Hotel in Syracuse, the infamous Dinkler we called it. And people loved to dance. They were a bit loud actually, but I remember really enjoying that. Because we had Frank Tate on bass and we had a George — oh God isn’t this awful, I mean he’s a local drummer, a very good drummer, and we just played tune after tune after tune. That was when I was able to call on my extensive repertoire of tunes. And it was really a good experience, seeing how people loved us. And now things have changed so, I guess playing in a concert hall is a whole other thing and people do seem to like it. But I would never feel bad if I had to play for dancing.

sources.speaker: MM
sources.text: Unfortunately no. If I’d known what I was going to get into — I didn’t take pictures. Oh there are some, yeah there are some, but yeah there are some now that I think of it. But I should have kept a diary. And anyway we went through all of these miserably bombed and strafed towns that were just a mass of rubble, and we finally arrived in Belgium in a rest area, and it was called Eupen, and they had a big band and they had all kinds of stuff going on and the area shows would come there to rest, and they had an Officer’s Club, and that’s where I met Jimmy, one of the people in the USO show — Willy Shaw, was a comedian from Chicago, knew Jimmy, and said, “we can’t have this man out there being in combat, we’ve got to get him into Special Service,” so that’s what they did. So that’s how I met Jimmy, because he then became a member of this little band. But first they had a big party for him, all the band members and people are saying, “Jimmy McPartland’s coming, Jimmy McPartland’s coming,” and I’m going, “who?” I’d heard of Bud Freeman and Sidney Bechet, but I hadn’t heard of Jimmy yet. And they had a party in this tent and they were going to have a jam session, and Jimmy always told me afterwards, “oh I saw you across the tent and I knew you wanted to play and I said to myself ‘oh a woman musician, she wants to play and I know she’s going to be terrible,’ and you were,” he says. But I really wasn’t terrible I think I just didn’t know how to play with a big band at that point, I assume anyway.

sources.speaker: MM
sources.text: I don’t think it was ever an uphill struggle for me, because I sort of had my indoctrination in working with Jimmy and boy Jimmy was so supportive and proud of me. And so when I started at The Embers as a trio and Ed and Don, they couldn’t be nicer. I mean very seldom did I have a bad experience. I did have one guy at The Embers for a short time, I can’t think of his name — just as well — and I had to fire him and boy having to fire somebody that just really, you know I could probably do it now with great aplomb but luckily I haven’t had to. But I never had a real problem there. The only problems, or not problem, but things would be like I remember the first review I had from Leonard Feather was, “she has three strikes against her: she’s English, white and a woman.” And I don’t know it didn’t bother me that much. I don’t remember being too upset about that. And if there were things it’d probably be from the audience like, “oh you play good for a girl,” or, “you sound just like a man.” I mean you don’t hear those things anymore. And I mean there were a lot of women on the scene: Mary Lou Williams, Barbara Carroll, people I’d heard before I got there — Hazel Scott, Lil Armstrong. I never felt that the women were in such bad shape I guess. They went ahead and they had consciousness raising and I remember talking to Barbara about this, and she said, “well I didn’t know it was a thing, we’ve just been playing and doing our thing right along.” And I never had to feel that things were tough. I never did.

275831.evidence: Mary Lou Williams played it and I played it
275831.subject: Marian McPartland
275831.audit: {"change": "same festival bill is not playing together", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "performed together at the Kansas City women's festival and Billy Taylor's tribute event"}}

sources.speaker: MM
sources.text: Well we always said this, like when they had the Kansas City women’s festival, that was a long time ago, I think you were probably a real young boy then — I can’t remember how long ago, gee maybe it’s 15 or 20 years — and this was the, like the biggest jazz festival ever. Mary Lou Williams played it and I played it and Toshiko Akiyoshi had her big band, and I mean it was a large event. And they carried that on for three or four years and then they ran out of money. So actually, what Billy Taylor is doing, it’s the same kind of thing. They had it last year but they called it “A Tribute to Mary Lou Williams,” which was fine. And I was in it and the Maria Schneider big band and Joanne Brackeen. And I mean they certainly didn’t have to wont for good women players. Jane Ira Bloom, a wonderful sax player, so I don’t exactly know the cast of characters for this year but some of them — Trudy Pitts, a good piano player, I can’t remember, they had Maria Schneider’s big band again and there’s another woman’s big band called Diva, very, very good. But it’s true, I mean you don’t ever have to say Woody Herman and his all-male band, but yet you do have to say Diva is an all-girl band. It’s still a novelty and maybe it always will be I don’t know.

sources.text: Well but in this particular area of where we are right now, when Jimmy and I used to play a gig at The Dinkler Hotel in Syracuse, the infamous Dinkler we called it. sources.speaker: MM
sources.text: the public schools with just this thing in mind, to teach kids to play jazz. And I used all the local musicians and one of the best tunes I thought to get the kids started to play would be a blues, and then we picked “C Jam Blues” because it’s so repetitive, and the kids had these little instruments like a vibraharp, with two octaves they all had to play on. And we did in fact get kids to not only play this tune but to improvise on it. And we culminated with a concert with Duke, he came down and played with a small group for the kids in the school And it was one of the great experiences of my life. So at that time I thought that they really had done some good things and it was a shame that they couldn’t follow through, like after we left the program just fell apart. I mean it broke my heart because we really had kids improvising with the Navy band, which was, what an experience that was, I’ll never forget. Anyway, I guess I basically think that you can, if somebody is interested, you can point them in the right direction. I think kids have to be motivated. And I think if they really want to do it that’s half the battle. And then they will investigate and listen and that’s a part of it. But I have seen and done workshops and stage band clinics and things where you hear some of these kids and you think oh these kids will never play. Next year the kid comes back, having listened to Bill Evans or somebody, and is playing away, and I’ll never say never to anybody, because I think it takes wanting to do it, and motivation, and that’s about it really.

275831.evidence: Next year the kid comes back, having listened to Bill Evans or somebody, and is playing away

275831.audit: {"change": "source corrected to 14.0", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: MM
sources.text: the public schools with just this thing in mind, to teach kids to play jazz. And I used all the local musicians and one of the best tunes I thought to get the kids started to play would be a blues, and then we picked “C Jam Blues” because it’s so repetitive, and the kids had these little instruments like a vibraharp, with two octaves they all had to play on. And we did in fact get kids to not only play this tune but to improvise on it. And we culminated with a concert with Duke, he came down and played with a small group for the kids in the school And it was one of the great experiences of my life. So at that time I thought that they really had done some good things and it was a shame that they couldn’t follow through, like after we left the program just fell apart. I mean it broke my heart because we really had kids improvising with the Navy band, which was, what an experience that was, I’ll never forget. Anyway, I guess I basically think that you can, if somebody is interested, you can point them in the right direction. I think kids have to be motivated. And I think if they really want to do it that’s half the battle. And then they will investigate and listen and that’s a part of it. But I have seen and done workshops and stage band clinics and things where you hear some of these kids and you think oh these kids will never play. Next year the kid comes back, having listened to Bill Evans or somebody, and is playing away, and I’ll never say never to anybody, because I think it takes wanting to do it, and motivation, and that’s about it really.

sources.speaker: MM
sources.text: Oh, wonderful. I loved Chicago, I still love it. And we sort of broke in with working with different clubs. I mean that might have been maybe the thinnest part financially — was kind of for Jimmy to break back into things. And we did do a lot of interesting gigs however, and then and I don’t know, you probably don’t remember, you’re too young, Dave Garroway, who was — before he ever came to New York to be on “The Today Show” he had a coast-to-coast radio show and Jimmy was the soloist on that and he sounded wonderful. I still have that recording of that. And anyway Jimmy kept saying, “oh you should have your own group, you should have your own group.” And so we came to New York in 1950 I guess and we stopped on the way and played a club in Philadelphia that was very famous at the time it was called The Rendezvous Club, and I met people like Sidney DeParis, Wilbur DeParis played with the band. And so then we went on to New York and that’s when I started at The Embers. And Jimmy really arranged so many things for me. But it was tough because I was so green and callow and this was a top club and I had great sidemen — Ed Safranski from Kenton’s band and Don Lamond from Woody’s band, Woody Herman’s band, who were trying to break into the jingle scene in New York and so, I mean that was my first trio group. And at that same engagement, the owner brought in Roy Eldridge and Coleman Hawkins as guests so you can imagine, I got to play for them too. I do have pictures to prove that because that’s something I was very thrilled about. And they were very nice. Nobody ever said, “don’t play that change” or, “don’t do that.” So I guess I got by anyway.

But I never had a real problem there. The only problems, or not problem, but things would be like I remember the first review I had from Leonard Feather was, “she has three strikes against her: she’s English, white and a woman.” And I don’t know it didn’t bother me that much. They went ahead and they had consciousness raising and I remember talking to Barbara about this, and she said, “well I didn’t know it was a thing, we’ve just been playing and doing our thing right along.” And I never had to feel that things were tough. I never did.

sources.text: I don’t know quite how to answer that but I do remember of course all these wonderful bands that people did dance to, and going to The Statler Hotel in New York with Jimmy night after night to hear Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey’s band with Jimmy, Newt and Tommy and then all the other bands, the Benny Goodman band and I mean I listened to big bands in England, I guess that’s where I learned tunes, and to quote Wynton again, he has always said that jazz should be danced to. 275831.evidence: You know I felt like MacArthur wading ashore onto Omaha Beach
275831.subject: Marian McPartland
275831.audit: {"change": "figure of speech; sources corrected to 5.0", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: MM
sources.text: naturally I decided I would do that immediately, I didn’t have to think about it at all. So the pay was pretty decent, and we played all over the country. Accommodations and travel were not always the best because you know there was a war on. And we would get — there would be bombs dropping once in a while. But then I switched and went with regular American USO. Somebody said, “oh you ought to join USO, the pay is better and you’ll meet all these wonderful American guys” stuff like that, and I though oooh. So that’s what I did. And then we worked, it would be a regular show, like with a comedian or a singer or dancer, they had a guitar player and then I was the piano player played for the whole show. And it was the same kind of thing but on a higher level and we stayed at wonderful hotels. So then it got to be when they were going to have the invasion and after the invasion, they were sounding people who wanted to go over to France and of course I wanted to go and did go with the first group which was about a month after the invasion. And we went over in a boat and we had helmets and combat boots and everything the GIs had except the guns. You know I felt like MacArthur wading ashore onto Omaha Beach and straggling up the beach and we knew how to put up pup tents. But we never had to because somebody always did that for us.

sources.text: very nice to us, because he’s an old friend of Jimmy’s, they’d worked together of course. And we visited some clubs. I was hot to see everybody I’d read about or heard about or heard on records. We met Louis Armstrong and he was working in a club, and a whole bunch of people. We went to Nick’s. And anyway, Jimmy didn’t want to stay, he wanted to go back to Chicago and see the family. And it was sort of a turning point because Eddie Condon offered him a job with a band I think Wild Bill Davidson was taking a leave of absence or something. And I said, “oh, Jimmy, oh you really should take it.” And he refused, “oh I want to relax and see my family.” God knows what would have happened if he would have stayed there, but I guess it was not meant to be. sources.speaker: MM
sources.text: Oh, wonderful. I loved Chicago, I still love it. And we sort of broke in with working with different clubs. And so then we went on to New York and that’s when I started at The Embers. And Jimmy really arranged so many things for me. But it was tough because I was so green and callow and this was a top club and I had great sidemen — Ed Safranski from Kenton’s band and Don Lamond from Woody’s band, Woody Herman’s band, who were trying to break into the jingle scene in New York and so, I mean that was my first trio group. 275839.proposed: inspired interviewee to play tenor saxophone after seeing him perform
275839.evidence: When I seen Sonny Rollins play a solo saxophone at the Berkeley Jazz Festival when I was about 11, the next day I had to go get a tenor.
275839.subject: David Murray

sources.speaker: DM
sources.text: Well as long as I was playing the church music and improvising it wasn’t considered jazz. Like I mean I was getting into John Coltrane and Sonny Rollins and all these people, and I was putting that into the church. They didn’t know I was really getting into that. All they knew was that as long as I could play the church melodies fine, whatever else I played, they didn’t care. They didn’t even know if it was jazz or not. They didn’t care. But they knew that it was good. But they knew that when it came to playing that melody that I could play it strong. That was the point. So I got away with that I guess you could say. But that’s where I learned to improvise, in the church. It’s true.

sources.speaker: DM
sources.text: I had already, before I got in my teens, I had already determined that. That was already decided. When I seen Sonny Rollins play a solo saxophone at the Berkeley Jazz Festival when I was about 11, the next day I had to go get a tenor. I guess that would have been the moment. But I wanted to be a musician before that. But I wanted to be a tenor saxophone player after that. So that much I knew. So I asked my dad, I said, “I’ve got to get a tenor.” So he took me to his credit union and we worked it out and I got a job and I paid for it, and I worked gigs to pay for it. And over a year’s time I had a Mark VI. You know, that was my first tenor, a Mark VI. And I had the greatest horn in the world. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

sources.speaker: DM
sources.text: Well I would say that there’s so much information out here right now that I think the kids are bombarded with so much information. They have so much at their fingertips that sometimes they just don’t know where to start. It used to be that you’d hear something come out, you’d immediately go to your record player, slow it down to 16-1/2, to be an octave down, and you’d transcribe it, then you’ve got a Trane solo. There it is. Or you’ve got a Sonny Rollins solo you know. And Bobby Bradford, when he told me, when Bird came out, those guys, and Fats Navarro, those cats. They would go, in Texas, they would go and do the same thing. Oh man we heard Bird did a solo man, everybody ran out, got the record and transcribed it, and so by the time Bird came their way all the cats knew his solo. They were singing his solo you know. They had it. I don’t hear that kind of enthusiasm now, even though all those solos are already transcribed for everybody. So like sometimes when I do a class I say okay I want you guys to learn this solo up to this point. Give me six choruses. And it was like ahhhhh, do we got to? I say well you know, the fact is if we were back in those times, overnight this cat would have the solo. We’d have a solo. We might stay up all night to get that solo. And the whole thing was about memorizing the solo, not just playing the solo but memorizing the solo. These kids, they look in the book and play it, and then I say okay now play it without the book. Oh really? You want me to do that? Yeah. When I say play the solo, I mean play it by memory. Like it’s a head. Because it’s written so it should be a head to you, it’s just longer. That’s all it © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

275839.proposed: uses Coleman's concept in his own work
275839.evidence: I could take that and use Ornette Coleman’s concept and James Blood Ulmer
275839.subject: David Murray
275839.audit: {"change": "says he draws on Coleman's concept", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: DM
sources.text: Well my expertise — whatever expertise that I’ve developed in jazz, me personally, I could take that and use Ornette Coleman’s concept and James Blood Ulmer, they say jazz is the teacher and Funk is the preacher. So in other words when you say “funk” you mean, I think they mean that you have to include the young, and that’s the way to bring in the young, because the guy whose got the vocal box is the one — it’s like rap. You know eventually jazz and rap have to get a little closer together than it is even now, because that’s what the kids are listening to. And if people want an audience in the next hundred years, you’re going to have to do something besides play with your quartet to bring that on. So I feel like I’m doing that now. I’m trying to bring other people in. Because jazz is such a free music that it includes everybody. And everybody seems like they could put their two cents in. So I’m putting mine in too. But jazz is a teacher, and every other music is the preacher to whoever their constituents are.

sources.speaker: DM
sources.text: through, like I’ll do a piece like “Morning Song” or something like that, or any song. And next thing I do an octet arrangement, the next thing I do a big band arrangement of the same song. And so in that I’m learning about music through my song, through my own song. I suggest to most kids that they should write their own music and then put it through a couple of different keys and really start to understand what their music can teach them about themselves. Then they’re getting closer to finding out who they are. And in this process, playing your own stuff on the horn, playing for hours and hours of your own ideas, that’s when you start to get up there when the Ornette Colemans and the Birds and the Sonny Rollinses and the Clifford Jordans and all these people, that kind of time that you spend just working out your own personal ideas. That’s how you get a sound, by working like that. I mean like for instance I don’t know if a lot of people know it but Ben Webster you know, I met an old girlfriend of Ben Webster and she used to always tell me she’d say you know when Ben was living up here in Sccandinavia he used to only practice on baritone. He wouldn’t play the tenor until he came to the gig. There’s ways. That would get you a sound.

sources.speaker: DM
sources.text: Oh well, you know, God, first of all Bob Weir is really a good friend of mine. And the way we met was through Michael Nash and Carrie Williams. They asked me to be part of this — of writing the music for a musical about Satchel Paige. And so we began to collaborate, Taj Mahal, Bob Weir and myself, Michael Nash and Carrie were writing the libretto. And it’s been a process now that’s been going on for seven years you know. And I think — we’ve had several workshops, we had Avery Brooks come in and direct us, we’ve had several directors coming in to do workshops. And I think maybe approaching ten years, it’s going to eventually be out there on Broadway. We have 35 songs, and what we’ve realized ourselves, it’s pretty good songwriting. I think the music is far ahead of the script. And they’re doing revisions of the script. And this brought me into the idea of like them saying well hey David, we’re playing at Madison Square Garden, why don’t you come and sit in. Well all right, I’ll sit in, I’ll be down. So I come and sit in. Bamm it’s like twenty thousand people there. And I’d never seen such an attentive audience. I mean I play, I’ve played the Vanguard and this jazz club and that, the Blue Note and all this, there’s always somebody talking at the bar that I can hear, usually a musician you know. And I play, I say waaa on my sax and I see all the heads. Wow. They’re with me the whole time. What a wonderful audience these guys have developed. And I was just thinking man, I wish we had such a dedicated crew, especially twenty thousand of them you know. So then I go sit in with them out in San Francisco. Same thing. And then I played one other time with them. And I played with Jerry Garcia’s band, I sat in with him at the Madison Square Garden and that was a gas too, because this guy was fantastic. © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

275839.evidence: I remember coming home and putting it next to Coleman Hawkins, putting it next to, bar by bar, next to Coleman Hawkins’ solo and playing through mine, playing through his
275839.subject: David Murray

sources.speaker: DM
sources.text: Happy accidents. That’s a good way to put it. Well let’s put it like this. I remember when they came out with my first transcription of — I had recorded “Body and Soul.” And I remember coming home and putting it next to Coleman Hawkins, putting it next to, bar by bar, next to Coleman Hawkins’ solo and playing through mine, playing through his, playing through mine, playing through his. And then I realized that what I was doing, I mean on a solo like that you could, because in that particular solo I was pretty much playing in a more traditional kind of way. It would depend on which solo you transcribe. If it was a song where I just took off, then I’m not sure that the chord changes, at one point, sometimes when I’m playing sometimes the chord changes becomes more like, not necessarily that I’m not following the chord changes because I am, but I’m playing across the chord changes through the harmonic series. That would probably be very difficult to transcribe and be accurate as far as what I’m thinking when I’m playing. Now a happy accident — mmm — I’m not sure an accident would describe it. Because I always know where I am now. Maybe other people might not think I know where I am, but I’m always — when I’m playing with songs that have chords I’m very aware of the chord structure. I’m challenging that structure is what I’m trying to do. I’m trying to defy it. I’m trying very hard to defy it and dispel it at the same time that I’m playing it. Perhaps it sounds like an accident because I’m covering some new ground on it. And usually I would have probably played that song so many times before it got to that recording that I’m playing across that song like I own that song. That song, and it probably is mine anyway. So I feel like well I can do anything with my own song that I want to. And this is how I want the final result to sound like. So be it somebody else’s idea of an accident or a train wreck or whatever, fine, if you want to call it that, that’s cool. But that’s exactly what I was trying to get to, otherwise I wouldn’t have let it out. I mean I wouldn’t have let that version come out. So that’s pretty much the way I see it. I feel like what I’m trying to do as a soloist is to stretch the boundaries. Because to me everybody that comes to New York, each person that comes in, each soloist comes in, they set the bar a little higher and they challenge people to think a different way. And that’s kind of what I’m trying to do. I’m trying to let people think a different way about how they could approach even playing chord changes.

275839.proposed: co-writer (libretto) of the Satchel Paige musical Murray wrote music for
275839.evidence: And so we began to collaborate, Taj Mahal, Bob Weir and myself, Michael Nash and Carrie were writing the libretto.
275839.subject: David Murray
275839.audit: {"change": "writing collaboration on a musical", "previous": {"relation": "has met", "direction": "na", "proposed": "met through Michael Nash and Carrie Williams"}}

sources.speaker: DM
sources.text: Oh well, you know, God, first of all Bob Weir is really a good friend of mine. And the way we met was through Michael Nash and Carrie Williams. They asked me to be part of this — of writing the music for a musical about Satchel Paige. And so we began to collaborate, Taj Mahal, Bob Weir and myself, Michael Nash and Carrie were writing the libretto. And it’s been a process now that’s been going on for seven years you know. And I think — we’ve had several workshops, we had Avery Brooks come in and direct us, we’ve had several directors coming in to do workshops. And I think maybe approaching ten years, it’s going to eventually be out there on Broadway. We have 35 songs, and what we’ve realized ourselves, it’s pretty good songwriting. I think the music is far ahead of the script. And they’re doing revisions of the script. And this brought me into the idea of like them saying well hey David, we’re playing at Madison Square Garden, why don’t you come and sit in. Well all right, I’ll sit in, I’ll be down. So I come and sit in. Bamm it’s like twenty thousand people there. And I’d never seen such an attentive audience. I mean I play, I’ve played the Vanguard and this jazz club and that, the Blue Note and all this, there’s always somebody talking at the bar that I can hear, usually a musician you know. And I play, I say waaa on my sax and I see all the heads. Wow. They’re with me the whole time. What a wonderful audience these guys have developed. And I was just thinking man, I wish we had such a dedicated crew, especially twenty thousand of them you know. So then I go sit in with them out in San Francisco. Same thing. And then I played one other time with them. And I played with Jerry Garcia’s band, I sat in with him at the Madison Square Garden and that was a gas too, because this guy was fantastic. © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

sources.speaker: DM
sources.text: Well my expertise — whatever expertise that I’ve developed in jazz, me personally, I could take that and use Ornette Coleman’s concept and James Blood Ulmer, they say jazz is the teacher and Funk is the preacher. So in other words when you say “funk” you mean, I think they mean that you have to include the young, and that’s the way to bring in the young, because the guy whose got the vocal box is the one — it’s like rap. You know eventually jazz and rap have to get a little closer together than it is even now, because that’s what the kids are listening to. And if people want an audience in the next hundred years, you’re going to have to do something besides play with your quartet to bring that on. So I feel like I’m doing that now. I’m trying to bring other people in. Because jazz is such a free music that it includes everybody. And everybody seems like they could put their two cents in. So I’m putting mine in too. But jazz is a teacher, and every other music is the preacher to whoever their constituents are.

275839.subject: David Murray
275839.audit: {"change": "school music teacher figure who started him on sax; teaching relationship implied rather than detailed", "previous": {"relation": "mentor of", "direction": "target", "proposed": "gave interviewee his first saxophone and introduced him to jazz in the school system"}}

sources.speaker: DM
sources.text: Yeah. Certainly. When I was younger I started out in Gospel music. I remember the day I got my saxophone of Phil Hardymon, he came into the system, at the Berkeley, California school system. He is the one that handed me my alto. And he passed away a few years ago. A great trumpet player, Phil Hardymon. He is the one who is really responsible for bringing jazz into the Berkeley school system. And so that night I played the saxophone at church. I’m sure I was squeaking and sounding very strange, very much like I sound now but I had no idea what I was doing. My mother was playing piano, my brother on clarinet, my cousin playing trumpet, my father was playing guitar. I knew the songs but I didn’t know the fingerings, but I was working on it. A few weeks later I blended right in. I had been playing bongos with them for like a couple of years already, but at nine, that was where I was. And I had taken piano lessons for two years already with a stride piano player that my mother put me with. And with me it was always, wherever I was, I felt comfortable there, but I also yearned to play other things. Like I strived to get out of church music in fact. Because we were the church band, we played every night, well three nights a week at least and all day Sunday. And after a while, you know, I’m a young man, I’m a teenager, I wanted to get out, I wanted to play gigs, I wanted to do different, I wanted to play blues gigs, so I’m starting to go out and do these kinds of things. I grew up in a very strict Church of God and Christ environment, where playing or practicing jazz in our house was forbidden. So I had to go out to my friends’ places to practice and play that kind of music. After my mother passed away, when I was 13, things became a little looser because all of sudden this was three boys and a father, © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

And next thing I do an octet arrangement, the next thing I do a big band arrangement of the same song. And so in that I’m learning about music through my song, through my own song. That’s how you get a sound, by working like that. I mean like for instance I don’t know if a lot of people know it but Ben Webster you know, I met an old girlfriend of Ben Webster and she used to always tell me she’d say you know when Ben was living up here in Sccandinavia he used to only practice on baritone. There’s something about strings that can make you go into it. But the whole thing is to do it without being maudlin. It can be contrived. You know strings, you can be cornball city with strings too, especially if you approach it from the ballad thing. Anyway, and that’s the whole thing about melody and song form, there’s a battle in the society right now because everybody’s more conditioned to hear beats. And the song form is getting a licking right now. When a guy like Stevie Wonder can’t come up with a hit, you know he’s a real songwriter. I mean I’m speaking in the black community particularly right now. When the community is like hoodwinked into thinking that this is only music. These beats, and this rap. This is what we call music now and this other stuff is maudlin and contrived because it is a melody. It sounds like, to them, somebody’s in a theater and then all of a sudden they break into song. And it’s corny. No it’s not corny. It’s a song. Songs will always be back. But it’s not here right now. And I think, I’m waiting for the time when the songwriter in the community will raise his head again.

sources.text: Well my father is from the school of — civil rights was very high on his list. Even being a staunch church man, we believed in Martin Luther King, and that was the same year that Martin Luther King was killed. I mean the fact that he moved to Berkeley and put us in a better neighborhood than our cousins who lived in Oakland — I remember one of the most angry times that I’ve ever seen him was when my brother moved into a ghetto in Oakland. He went over there and made him move out because he said you don’t know how many sacrifices I had to make, being a garbageman and working extra jobs and doing this and that, for you to live in a city like Berkeley. So why in the hell would you go and live in a ghetto and put yourself at risk and now going to put my other brother at risk because he wants to live with you. I’ve never seen him so angry. So in his own way he was an activist. But not one that would join up with the Black Panthers or anything like that. But you know, just through the church you can express your anger. I think the church has been probably the strongest, I mean if you put it down for the year and years that they persevered, the church has been the strongest political animal in the black community, regardless of one speaker may raise up and be a communist or this or that, but the church has always been the overriding — it was always the place, even for them to hide if they needed sanctuary. The church would always take everybody back. And the church accepts everyone. The church, as far as acceptance, it’s ecumenical, churches. It takes everyone. Our church, The Church of God and Christ accepts everyone. There’s no lock in our churches. If a white man comes into our church we’re going to take him. If he’s down and out, come on in here and let’s get you together. And if you want to go on your way, fine. If you want to stay you’re welcome. That’s what church is. And to me that’s some activism right there, to me.

sources.speaker: DM
sources.text: Oh well, you know, God, first of all Bob Weir is really a good friend of mine. And the way we met was through Michael Nash and Carrie Williams. They asked me to be part of this — of writing the music for a musical about Satchel Paige. And I think — we’ve had several workshops, we had Avery Brooks come in and direct us, we’ve had several directors coming in to do workshops. And I think maybe approaching ten years, it’s going to eventually be out there on Broadway. We have 35 songs, and what we’ve realized ourselves, it’s pretty good songwriting. I think the music is far ahead of the script. And they’re doing revisions of the script. And this brought me into the idea of like them saying well hey David, we’re playing at Madison Square Garden, why don’t you come and sit in. Well all right, I’ll sit in, I’ll be down. So I come and sit in. Bamm it’s like twenty thousand people there. And I’d never seen such an attentive audience. I mean I play, I’ve played the Vanguard and this jazz club and that, the Blue Note and all this, there’s always somebody talking at the bar that I can hear, usually a musician you know. And I play, I say waaa on my sax and I see all the heads. Wow. They’re with me the whole time. What a wonderful audience these guys have developed. 275839.subject: David Murray

sources.speaker: DM
sources.text: Well I would say that there’s so much information out here right now that I think the kids are bombarded with so much information. They have so much at their fingertips that sometimes they just don’t know where to start. It used to be that you’d hear something come out, you’d immediately go to your record player, slow it down to 16-1/2, to be an octave down, and you’d transcribe it, then you’ve got a Trane solo. There it is. Or you’ve got a Sonny Rollins solo you know. And Bobby Bradford, when he told me, when Bird came out, those guys, and Fats Navarro, those cats. They would go, in Texas, they would go and do the same thing. Oh man we heard Bird did a solo man, everybody ran out, got the record and transcribed it, and so by the time Bird came their way all the cats knew his solo. They were singing his solo you know. They had it. I don’t hear that kind of enthusiasm now, even though all those solos are already transcribed for everybody. So like sometimes when I do a class I say okay I want you guys to learn this solo up to this point. Give me six choruses. And it was like ahhhhh, do we got to? I say well you know, the fact is if we were back in those times, overnight this cat would have the solo. We’d have a solo. We might stay up all night to get that solo. And the whole thing was about memorizing the solo, not just playing the solo but memorizing the solo. These kids, they look in the book and play it, and then I say okay now play it without the book. Oh really? You want me to do that? Yeah. When I say play the solo, I mean play it by memory. Like it’s a head. Because it’s written so it should be a head to you, it’s just longer. That’s all it © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

sources.text: through, like I’ll do a piece like “Morning Song” or something like that, or any song. And next thing I do an octet arrangement, the next thing I do a big band arrangement of the same song. And so in that I’m learning about music through my song, through my own song. I suggest to most kids that they should write their own music and then put it through a couple of different keys and really start to understand what their music can teach them about themselves. Then they’re getting closer to finding out who they are. And in this process, playing your own stuff on the horn, playing for hours and hours of your own ideas, that’s when you start to get up there when the Ornette Colemans and the Birds and the Sonny Rollinses and the Clifford Jordans and all these people, that kind of time that you spend just working out your own personal ideas. sources.text: Well you know my first musical role models and heroes were Gene Ammons and Lester Young, and of course Coleman Hawkins and Charlie Parker as the years went on. Blues,” because at the time Lester Young had a song out called “D.B. Blues,” so I learned the solo to “D.B. Blues.” Plus you could get girls —

sources.text: You know, yeah. So that was one of the things. Because you broaden your own scope and it gives you a lot to draw upon and a lot to appreciate. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-

275842.proposed: role model; later saw him at Beefsteak Charlie's
275842.evidence: my first musical role models and heroes were Gene Ammons and Lester Young, and of course Coleman Hawkins and Charlie Parker as the years went on

sources.speaker: HO
sources.text: Well you know my first musical role models and heroes were Gene Ammons and Lester Young, and of course Coleman Hawkins and Charlie Parker as the years went on. But the first people I guess that I really began to relate to was Gene Ammons because he was there in Chicago. And then of course Lester Young was very popular at the time and there was a lot of records out. And so I used to, I think I bought, I think Lester was playing a Conn at the time, and I bought a Conn. And then Gene Ammons was playing, I think he was playing a Brillhart mouthpiece, so I bought a Brillhart mouthpiece, thinking I was going to get the sound. I found out it wasn’t the mouthpiece at all. But I used to get a chance to go hear him a lot. So it was a lot of inspiration there. And “D.B. Blues,” because at the time Lester Young had a song out called “D.B. Blues,” so I learned the solo to “D.B. Blues.” Plus you could get girls —

sources.speaker: HO
sources.text: pay as much as record dates, but a lot of times you might be able to do five or six demo dates in a day so that was, you know, good money. So you would go in from one bar to another and see who you could find. It was like a networking, like here you just went around to see, you know, no telling who you might run into. But everybody used to go to The Turf or either there was Beefsteak Charlie’s. Now Beefsteak Charlie’s was the place where Milt Hinton and a lot of the musicians who were playing a lot of the better gigs, you know at Jim and Andy’s, who were on the record dates. So if you wanted to get into that, you know to meet someone, then you would go there. And at Beefsteak Charlie’s, Hawk — I used to see Coleman Hawkins, a lot of musicians, like a lot of the older musicians as well as the younger musicians would come in there, because you’d see these musicians and then you’d get gigs and demos and whatever was happening. But it was always a good place, and Papa Jo would be there. And so you know that was a great time during this time. And I lived at — the hotel they had told me about was The Flanders. And that was, they had two entrances, between 48th Street, they had a 48th Street entrance, and 47th Street. And all the musicians, whoever’s band you were in would stay there because the rent was economical. At that time I think you could get a room for $15, room and bath for $18. And plus you were right there at Times Square, the automat was open and you could go to the automat and you could get a meal for 50 cents, a dollar, a dollar and a quarter. And then you could sit up front in the window and you’re looking out on Broadway. And then you’d go three blocks up and that’s where The Turf was. And you’d go to 51st Street around to where Beefsteak Charlie’s was, and you’d go down to 52nd Street, there’s where Jim and Andy’s was. So people would be going back and forth. And then they had, like in the Brill Building and a couple of other buildings centered in that area, they would have the little small studios. That’s where you would go and do the demos. And the purpose of the demo was say for an artist who might not have had money to go in the studio, but he could go and do a demo date, and like if he had an agent, the agent would get a demo done on him. And they’d get the musician, and everybody saving money, but at the same time they’re making money but the artist gets a chance maybe to take his demo now to the record label. So it was a lot of activity like that going on.

sources.text: Well sometimes during this time a demo date might be 20, 25 dollars, it might even be 15 dollars. But if you — your hotel rent is due, you know what I mean, and you’re not working, that’s 15 dollars you’ve got to work with. You know what I mean? And sometimes the musicians had to deliver sandwiches during the day or if you’d find another — you know where there’s a will there’s a way. But the main thing you’re here in New York. And as long as you are out there, you got a chance to, there’s an opportunity of being in the right place at the right time. And then you’re constantly woodshedding. And at that time they used to have sessions at Small’s Paradise up in Harlem. And there was a little place called Connie’s. And I would take the subway train up to Small’s and the jam sessions usually started around ten, ten to two, and maybe I could go up there for two hours. And then they had jam sessions in Brooklyn. And at the time, well they had the Baby Grand, but there was a club, The Continental, it was a club in Brooklyn where Bud Powell used to play. So I had, when I got in New York naturally I sought out where all the places were. So I’d get on the subway train and sometimes people would drive in the car and by the time they’d get to The Continental, I’m there already. You’d look up, you know, but at that time that’s what you had — you tried to be everywhere necessary. And then down at the Village they had the Five Spot and they had the Club Bohemia, you know and I would go down there at the time Randy Weston was down there and he worked, in fact they had music seven nights a week, I think Randy worked six and on Monday nights they had off night groups. And there was just a lot of great music playing. And so you’d get a chance to hear a lot of music, plus you got exposed. And during that time record companies, if they heard somebody new was in town from somebody they knew like maybe somebody playing for the label would say oh so-and-so is a great trumpet player, you ought to hear him. They came out the clubs to listen to see who was in town and a lot of times that’s how musicians got on the recordings. You know that doesn’t happen like that now, it’s on another level. But at that time you know you might be sitting in at a club and in the audience was somebody from a record company was there and you got a date. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-

sources.speaker: HO
sources.text: for that particular show would come out and he’d let the people know what they’re going to see. Well as soon as that show let out, if your tent was next then you had to be there to catch those people. And you’d bring them to your site. And of course when they got to us the barker would tell them — and then he would say a lot of things that was not true, like we got the girl that does the dance of the seven veils and she’d drop these veils one by one. Then the girl that does the dance with the balloons or bubbles and you punch — and they were never on the show. And so the carnival is a place usually where the entertainers there are either entertainers that have been in the business a long time but are no longer at the top of the business, they’re not working as much, so the carnival offers work, or they’re young entertainers like myself trying to get started. So you don’t make no money on a still date. The only time you make money is doing the fair dates. That’s when you go to the cities where the farmers are selling their livestock and they have auto races, and the carnival is there. So they have a lot of people. And you work pretty hard. Like we would get on the midway at nine o’clock in the morning, and our last show would be at one o’clock in the morning. And so we would end up doing about 25 shows. But the carnival, it was a lot of fun, there was some hardship and a lot of times with no money but there’s still a certain something about it. You know like they say the sawdust in your vein kind of thing. There are things about it that you enjoy. But in the case of the carnival that we were at, I guess after I was on there a month, about two months, I said well I’m going to have to get back towards — the money was very short sometimes. So I said well the next time I get train fare, I’m going, I’m leaving. So that’s what happened a lot of times. I think I left in Muskogee, Oklahoma. But I traveled around, I saw a lot of things. In fact we had a trumpet player on there named Frank, he played two trumpets at one time. And he used to drink a lot. And so sometimes he’d throw the trumpet up, and a few times he missed it, and his trumpet was all bent up. You know, but it was a lot of fun, there was a lot of love there, and hard times, but it was a mixture of a lot of things. It was a good experience.

sources.text: No, Birdland was still open then. Like I said clubs in the Village were open. And Seventh Avenue at that time, they had four or five clubs. You could, you know — because Sugar Ray’s, well he was at 21st Street and a place called Red Randolph’s which was right across the street from there, and then 125th Street, they had something, then you go onto 135th Street you know. And then at that time you could just walk around, you know you could walk from 21st Street all the way up to 25th and 35th Street. And people would be hanging out and they would go by Wells — there was a place called Wells — it was right next to the Count Basie’s, and they had the greatest waffles and chicken. And everybody would come from downtown and after they leave the club go for chicken and waffles. And they’d meet in the morning and talk you know. But that — and then there were different after hour clubs if you knew where they were, and people would go and play. Then of course Birdland was open. And everybody would go down to Birdland, especially on Monday night. Because they had a section in Birdland, you could come in and you didn’t have to drink, you could just sit in that section and listen to the music, or you could go to the bar, or you could sit in a booth. 275842.proposed: worked together at Le Chat qui Peche, Paris
275842.evidence: he came to work at the Chat qui Peche. And he and I worked together.
275842.subject: Harold Ousley

sources.speaker: HO
sources.text: me a chance to get to Paris. So I left, well the show ended there and I stayed in Paris and I lived over in Montmarte. And I used to take the — well they call it the metro there. So I learned how to use the metro and you’d get all over Paris. And the great thing about the metro, if you knew where you were going you could find it very easily. And so I would go over to the Left Bank. In fact the club I worked in was a club called oh, Le Chat qui Peche, which means a cat with fishes. And the lady who owned the club was Madame Ricard. She used to smoke a cigar all the time. And she was one of the freedom fighters during the war. And where we played was down in the basement. And I think maybe at that time during the war there was maybe like a secret place that they utilized. But this was a cave where the music was. And because when I first came to Paris I heard about, they told me about the Chat qui Peche. And I went over there, a friend of mine, J.T. Hogan, a drummer, was working there. He had a band. And so I sat in and played, and he hired me. And at that time Alice Coltrane, who was not Coltrane then, she was married to a singer, Poncho [Kenny] Hagood, who used to work with Diz. And she was, they were living in Paris. She was a piano player there, and then when Clark Terry came over with Duke to join Free and Easy, which was a show that Quincy Jones had written, and that was a band full of stars man, everybody you can think of was in there. So it was like old home week. Because everybody used to meet. There was a place called Gabby and Haynes. And I forget — Gabby, I think that was a woman, and Haynes was a man. But he was a cook and he was from the United States. And it was a mixed couple. But their cooking, you could get greens, you could get all the home cooking. So everybody used to come there and meet and eat and drink. But it was just great. It was a good time to be there. When Clark joined Free and Easy and left the show, he came to work at the Chat qui Peche. And he and I worked together. And so it was a very good — when I came back, that’s when I did the Bethlehem recording. Because on the cover I had on a French tam and they had the setting like in France. Because over there they had, with the advertisements, they have a sort of cylindrical thing that they put the advertisement on.

But everybody used to go to The Turf or either there was Beefsteak Charlie’s. Now Beefsteak Charlie’s was the place where Milt Hinton and a lot of the musicians who were playing a lot of the better gigs, you know at Jim and Andy’s, who were on the record dates. So if you wanted to get into that, you know to meet someone, then you would go there. And at Beefsteak Charlie’s, Hawk — I used to see Coleman Hawkins, a lot of musicians, like a lot of the older musicians as well as the younger musicians would come in there, because you’d see these musicians and then you’d get gigs and demos and whatever was happening. But it was always a good place, and Papa Jo would be there. And so you know that was a great time during this time. And I lived at — the hotel they had told me about was The Flanders. And that was, they had two entrances, between 48th Street, they had a 48th Street entrance, and 47th Street. And all the musicians, whoever’s band you were in would stay there because the rent was economical. At that time I think you could get a room for $15, room and bath for $18. And plus you were right there at Times Square, the automat was open and you could go to the automat and you could get a meal for 50 cents, a dollar, a dollar and a quarter. And then you could sit up front in the window and you’re looking out on Broadway. And then you’d go three blocks up and that’s where The Turf was. And you’d go to 51st Street around to where Beefsteak Charlie’s was, and you’d go down to 52nd Street, there’s where Jim and Andy’s was. So people would be going back and forth. And then they had, like in the Brill Building and a couple of other buildings centered in that area, they would have the little small studios. That’s where you would go and do the demos. And the purpose of the demo was say for an artist who might not have had money to go in the studio, but he could go and do a demo date, and like if he had an agent, the agent would get a demo done on him. And they’d get the musician, and everybody saving money, but at the same time they’re making money but the artist gets a chance maybe to take his demo now to the record label. So it was a lot of activity like that going on.
