It’s all been done, it’s all been done. But to be able to say something in that, to keep that identity, like people like Trane or Dolphy and Ornette did, now that’s art. That we need more of. I’d like to hear more of that. John Zorn fits this category. He’s got a band called Masada, and they’ve got — it’s funny — they’ll go to the theme from “Batman” then they’ll go to a tune then they’ll go somewhere else. Just what we were talking about. Big wide pallet and spacey, funny, exciting and he also writes. He writes for the philharmonic, he writes string quartets, he writes movie music, I mean he does it all. This is my kind of guy. I’d like to hear more of that. I’m really not so interested in what Buddy Bolden sounded like. I couldn’t care less. Let the man rest. And I hear from people that were there say the cat couldn’t blow his nose anyway, so we’re not going to hear him. Okay, let’s get on with it.

sources.text: Record companies? I’ve never had a problem. I was with Prestige, nobody told us what to play. In those days, in the days of the independents, they were quite willing to rip you off modestly. No I mean you always had to give your tunes away in those days, I mean that was part of the deal. It was okay. At the time I didn’t understand it but I was really never asked to compromise the music. Never asked to compete with the majors. Whereas today, some of the big record companies — now you’re talking about a big rip. Some of these kids with the limos and stuff, they think the record company is paying for the limos. No, kids, check the fine print. I mean it’s megabucks now. They want jazz to compete with all the other musics and it’s messing it up a bit I think. Instead of just being an art music, we are not ready to accept just an art music. And maybe we shouldn’t, maybe it should be a mass music, or at least more distribution. I don’t know, I’m not a businessman, I don’t know, but I do know that it’s going to change, and I think the Internet’s going to change that. The whole technology is going to change that. The way we buy records is going to be completely different. I mean for years and years and years I heard about it’s distribution, I can’t get distribution. Well it all started with 78s. Then you got into LPs and you’ve still got bulk, you know what I mean? You still need kind of a specialty store. You’re not going to find them in every K-Mart and all that. I think that in the future, you’re going to be able to tap in through your computer and your hi-fi set. If you want to get a Phil Woods record or a Johnny Coates record or whatever, you just find it, put a blank CD in there and it’ll burn it and you’ve got it. You make up your own. sources.speaker: PW
sources.text: The show was a remake of “St. Louis Woman,” all the Harold Arlen songs. And we rehearsed at the American Pavilion in Brussels to put the show together. We’re talking here 1959. So we rehearsed at the American Pavilion. And we had to memorize all the charts — it was one of the great moments of my life — we’d show up at the theater for the morning’s work, and the dancers were blocking out and the singers were working with the accompanist and all that, saxophones would go here, trombones would go here, trumpets would go there, rhythm would go about their business. And we’d see how much music we could memorize. And then we’d put it together after lunch, and see how far — what section could get to the furthest letter in the chart you know. And you’d be surprised, you do that for a couple of weeks and the memory chops start to kick in and we were chewing up music. The hardest part of it, and no conductor, I mean Martha Flowers would drop her pinkie and the woodwinds would hit man, I mean you had to be a musician. We were behind the stairs — in that picture you might notice the staircase, that’s where the reeds were and the trumpets were over here, so it was impossible. I mean we had to work out — when she does that we come in, you know. But it was great fun. The hardest part was when they got to do a re-write you’d have to forget what you just memorized and memorize a new one. That, you would scramble. But it was great fun.

sources.text: Everybody got a hammer. Not the — you know they do that in Maryland but it’s to break crab claws. This is just to beat the heck out of the table. Now let me just preface this, at this period I didn’t know if my mouthpiece was right, I didn’t like the reed, I don’t like this horn, it’s not happening, I need new stuff, you know. So I got up my nerve and said, “Mr. Parker, perhaps you’d like to play my alto?” And he said, “that would be very nice, son.” Man I ran across Seventh Avenue and I got my horn, and I’m sitting — Bird was there and I was sitting there and the piano was there, just a drummer, just a snare drum and a piano and Bird. And I’m sitting there. I hand him the horn. He played “Long Ago and Far Away,” Jerome Kern. And I’m listening to this guy and it seems to me there’s nothing wrong with my saxophone. The saxophone sounds pretty darn good, you know what I mean? And he says, “now you play.” And I says oh Jesus. When kids talk about being awestruck, I know about awestruck. I did my feeble imitation of the master. He said, “sounds real good, son.” Oh man, this time I flew over Seventh Avenue, and I played the Bejesus out of “Harlem Nocturne” that night. sources.speaker: PW
sources.text: Record companies? I’ve never had a problem. I was with Prestige, nobody told us what to play. In those days, in the days of the independents, they were quite willing to rip you off modestly. No I mean you always had to give your tunes away in those days, I mean that was part of the deal. It was okay. At the time I didn’t understand it but I was really never asked to compromise the music. Never asked to compete with the majors. Whereas today, some of the big record companies — now you’re talking about a big rip. Some of these kids with the limos and stuff, they think the record company is paying for the limos. No, kids, check the fine print. I mean it’s megabucks now. They want jazz to compete with all the other musics and it’s messing it up a bit I think. Instead of just being an art music, we are not ready to accept just an art music. And maybe we shouldn’t, maybe it should be a mass music, or at least more distribution. I don’t know, I’m not a businessman, I don’t know, but I do know that it’s going to change, and I think the Internet’s going to change that. The whole technology is going to change that. The way we buy records is going to be completely different. I mean for years and years and years I heard about it’s distribution, I can’t get distribution. Well it all started with 78s. They’re pretty heavy. So there’s only a few limited stores that had jazz. You had to go to New York to get them. I mean I couldn’t find jazz records in my hometown. Then you got into LPs and you’ve still got bulk, you know what I mean? You still need kind of a specialty store. You’re not going to find them in every K-Mart and all that. I think that in the future, you’re going to be able to tap in through your computer and your hi-fi set. If you want to get a Phil Woods record or a Johnny Coates record or whatever, you just find it, put a blank CD in there and it’ll burn it and you’ve got it. You make up your own. It’s happening already. So there’s no more problem about distribution. It’ll solve that. I mean all they need is one copy in a bank somewhere. In other words, my music won’t take up any more room than Sting’s. But if you think about it though, you don’t have to compete for space, for shelf space. And I’m also hopeful, I don’t know if I’ll live to see this, but the equipment is getting so sophisticated. The reproduction with the DAT tapes and the CDs and all that. I don’t mean to negate the import of a kid picking up an instrument because if he’s got an instrument in his mouth he’s probably less liable to buy an assault rifle. I mean I think music is good. But the idea of jazz being alive and well, every campus has a jazz program, every school has a jazz program. But I don’t hear it. I think it’s going to be more — a typical set might be a tango, an Astor Piazzolla, a bossa nova, some pygmy music from Africa, a little Charlie Parker, a little free Archie Shepp. I mean it’s kind of become so collated and codified that everybody now has the same Real Book the same fake books. This is good but it should be more aggravating, it should stick in the craw. It’s too acceptable. It’s lacking color and it’s lacking a bit of humor. It doesn’t quite have the humor. Where are the Zoot Sims’ and the Al Cohn, like that. In Copenhagen they said, “Al, have you tried the elephant beer” and Al came back and said, “I drink to forget, man.” I mean I don’t hear that. sources.speaker: SH
sources.text: Well I’ll tell you, we have to look at that. Because I joined Dizzy’s band in either the late fifties or the early sixties. And the band that I joined was the band with Lee Morgan, Benny Golson, Wynton Kelly, Melba Liston was the musical director, and they were playing so much music man, my head was just — they had my head spinning. I never wrote anything for the band. Because the music that they were playing, the arrangements were so good that I just didn’t feel like I wanted to try to write something coming up to that level of arranging that they were doing. So actually I was just learning. I wasn’t able to contribute much or anything. They had all the great soloists there, they had the great arrangers there and everything. Dizzy was even writing himself, and Dizzy was playing fantastic himself. His chops were strong. And they were playing all these great arrangements. So I didn’t contribute that much to him until later when I joined the United Nations band. I started doing some writing for that. But it was always still very intimidating to be writing for him, because he was such a great arranger himself. Standards were very high.

So when you improvise you also use resolutions as a big part of the way that you make an improvisation.

275930.proposed: members of Dizzy Gillespie's band in the late 1950s/early 1960s

sources.speaker: SH
sources.text: Well I’ll tell you, we have to look at that. Because I joined Dizzy’s band in either the late fifties or the early sixties. And the band that I joined was the band with Lee Morgan, Benny Golson, Wynton Kelly, Melba Liston was the musical director, and they were playing so much music man, my head was just — they had my head spinning. I never wrote anything for the band. Because the music that they were playing, the arrangements were so good that I just didn’t feel like I wanted to try to write something coming up to that level of arranging that they were doing. So actually I was just learning. I wasn’t able to contribute much or anything. They had all the great soloists there, they had the great arrangers there and everything. Dizzy was even writing himself, and Dizzy was playing fantastic himself. His chops were strong. And they were playing all these great arrangements. So I didn’t contribute that much to him until later when I joined the United Nations band. I started doing some writing for that. But it was always still very intimidating to be writing for him, because he was such a great arranger himself. Standards were very high.

275930.proposed: trombonist in Woody Herman's band (England tour)
275930.evidence: he came to me and said, “Slide, I’m paying you more money than anybody in the band.
275930.subject: Slide Hampton
275930.audit: {"change": "Herman led the band and paid him: played under, not in music group with", "previous": {"relation": "in music group with", "direction": "na", "proposed": "member of Woody Herman's band"}}

sources.speaker: SH
sources.text: It was spontaneous. It wasn’t planned. Impromptu. I was playing with Woody Herman. And at that time when you joined a band you didn’t have any rehearsals or anything like that. You joined the band and you went right on the concert stage and played right there and you had to sight read everything and all of that. But we were always into that. Sight reading and all of that was a part of what we did for fun. When I was with Woody we played England for two weeks. And I have a very funny story with Woody because I was new in the band so his conducting I wasn’t familiar with. You know? So I’m just trying to follow the conductor. Because I feel when you give a downbeat I’m playing. But I was playing alone when he gave it out. So every time he would give a downbeat I would play, bamm. And then the band would play after me. So I’m wondering what’s going on, you know I said am I not seeing this right or what? So after the first week he came to me and said, “Slide, I’m paying you more money than anybody in the band. You’re the only one that’s playing wrong.” I said, “I know it. I just can’t figure out where your downbeat is.” And I says, “Is it here, is it here?” And the guys told me later they said, “We don’t play on his downbeat. He gives the downbeat and then we play when we think we should play.” So I said I’d wait for them. And after I played with him for two weeks some people found out that I was in England. They said while you’re over there come over on the continent of Europe and play some concerts over here. And I had never done this. And I didn’t know the condition. I didn’t know what the conditions would be. But they offered me such wonderful conditions. First class transportation, first class hotel, great money for the group and the concerts and everything. So I went over and played a few concerts and it was so unusual for me to be treated like that. I stayed for eight years.

275930.evidence: like Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie and Benny Goodman, Stan Getz, they all were raised in the big band period.
275930.subject: Slide Hampton

sources.speaker: SH
sources.text: You know you’re thinking — of course I’ve been asked that question many times and most musicians are. But see the thing is that we actually were raised in the big band period. And all the musicians that you hear playing the small groups that we aspired to, like Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie and Benny Goodman, Stan Getz, they all were raised in the big band period. sources.text: Well see when we played the Apollo Theater we had such success that the booking agents wanted us to stay in New York. And we would have had a good success in New York. But my sisters wanted to go back to Indianapolis. You know how ladies are. And so we didn’t stay. And after I was in New York the first time I remember when I was there I went to Birdland to hear Bud Powell play. That was it for me. I had to come to New York after that. And that’s all I talked about from that time until I got to New York is I have to go to New York. And I just had this great feeling for New York. And all I could think about was how can I get to New York. So I finally left Indianapolis on my way to New York, fifteen dollars in my pocket. So I only got as far as Cincinnati, Ohio. 275930.proposed: commissioned to write for Joe Henderson's big band CD
275930.evidence: I’ve had situations where I’ve been commissioned to do things for the Joe Henderson big band CD
275930.subject: Slide Hampton
275930.audit: {"change": "speaker added", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "composed for Joe Henderson's big band CD"}}

sources.speaker: SH
sources.text: Well I’ve been asked the question many times how do you start to approach either a composition or an arrangement. You have to start actually just be getting an idea of what it is that whoever you’re going to do it for, wants. And then to let it develop in a natural way. And the feeling for it, and the idea of it in your mind, let it develop in a natural way. So if you say you want a composition and you have a certain instrumentation, that instrumentation alone can inspire you a place to start. Once you get a place to start then the rest of it is natural development after that. I’ve had situations where I’ve been commissioned to do things for the Joe Henderson big band CD and when they gave me the composition, the first thing I try to do is find a melody. If you find a good melody — see because a good melody stands by itself. That’s an arrangement, that’s the composition, that’s everything, the theory and everything. If you find a good melody then the rest of the things are going to fall into place see. So if you’re going to arrange something for instance, you find a song that inspires you to arrange. And actually I feel like, except for people that write just to make a living, the only way that a person should approach an arrangement is by inspiration. So that whatever they’re inspired to do will leave some kind of long lasting musical standard that inspires the next person to write something that’s valuable. So I would start probably with finding a melody. And from that melody I would find the introduction later, the interludes, the way it’s going to resolve into other melodies, the way that it’s finally going to develop.

sources.speaker: RH
sources.text: Uh, I don’t remember making one with no drummer, but we did do some peculiar things. I remember many times when I first joined him, I said, “Well when we gonna rehearse?” “Oh I don’t have rehearsals.” I said, “What? You don’t have no rehearsals?” I said, “What am I going to play?” “Oh you’ll find something.” I asked Blue Mitchell, I say, “Man, what am I gonna play?” “Oh don’t worry about it, you’ll find something.” He says the reason he doesn’t rehearse is because he likes for it to be spontaneous. Your ideas, he say, he don’t want you to rehearse your ideas to put on the song. He wants you to be able to when you hear it play it. That’s the way he likes it. I said, “Fine with me.” So I just played whatever I felt I wanted to play. “Perfect, perfect!” I said, “That wasn’t shit.” But you know like I noticed that the audience, they went wild. I said, “I can’t believe this, man. What is this?” But it worked, so I said who am I to tell another person how to make his omelet? So, but I must say I enjoyed working with him. I made more money with John Mayall than any big band I ever worked with. And like when we would finish a 15- week tour, in Europe or wherever, he’d say, “Well fellas,” like if we were in Europe, he’d say, “Well I’m going to Spain for two weeks, anybody want to go? Come on, everything is free. You want your ladies sent for, I’ll pay for it.” And he’d maybe give you a couple of grand or a bonus at the end of the tour, stuff like that. I mean of course John Mayall was a millionaire, and he was making 50 or 60 thousand a night. So he could afford to do that, you know? And he like he couldn’t tell you a note big as this room, but he know chords and he could write out the chords to his song but they would be just basic chords, wouldn’t be no flat this and raise that.

And I joined his band, like at 3:00 that day and we rehearsed from 3 until about 6 the stuff that he was going to do. sources.text: Well there were a few people who could execute and express themselves beautifully and make it sound very melodic and convincing and with feeling. Then you’ve got some who play four million notes and you don’t feel nothing and you haven’t heard anything, you know. Now Bird was one who could play, I mean, fast and he could play a whole lot of stuff, and Sonny Stitt, Diz, and I mean with feeling, like when Bird played with Jay McShann. Man that cat when he got through playing some of them solos he played a million notes but they were important, they were not wasted, they were not just some notes. I mean it wasn’t a whole song, but it was just between certain phrases. He’d play maybe some cadenzas there inside those different phrases, and you’d say God damn, how did he do that? And then he’d lean on some of those blue notes, and boy I mean like it’s just something when you hear it, you know you can’t forget it. In fact, if you are a musician, if you hear it at night you go home and want to practice. Of course now Coltrane could do that too, because he had a very wonderful background with blues and stuff. And of course after a while you start teaching yourself, when you get the basics then you can venture out on your own and do whatever you want to do, you know. And I must say most of your stuff that he did, it made sense, it made sense, it made great sense. A lot of people don’t think so. There are some things during the experimental time that didn’t make too much sense, but after he really got into the groove of what was happening and finally got his — and what was that thing he said? He said sometimes he have so many ideas at one time he’d just play them all. He say he just play them all. So but that’s great, cause sometimes some people can’t do that. Some people can only play a certain select few ideas and I think the real goal of any musician is to be able to play all of their ideas, not necessarily all together, nevertheless, I think they should be able to © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

sources.speaker: RH
sources.text: I think my most famous record is I did an LP, the title of it was “No Tears Over You” and all of these songs I wrote myself except for one which was Art Hillary, he wrote one song on it. Then we went in the studio and we cut it in about 3-1/2 hours, this album, cause I was paying, you see, myself. So we ain’t going to be wasting no time here fellas. If you got anything on your mind, speak now. I think that was my best album. Because then there was a song titled “Music for Making Love.” I wrote this song for a pornography film, but then I took the music for my own album because I liked it so much. But I think, now there was one Clark Terry and I did called “Locksmith Blues.” My baby told me my key won’t fit her lock no more. But I’m a master locksmith, momma, I got a key that will fit any door. You know. Now that was one I wrote, and Clark really surprised me on that because he, the broad’s name was “Hey Magnolia” and Clark was supposed to say something, but he answered in a woman’s voice, he say, “What.” I say, “Huh?” Because I didn’t know he was going to do that, you know. And I think that was my best album because I did something I wanted to do, and between “Locksmith Blues” and “No Tears Over You,” I think those are my two best.

He just died in February. So just so many people are dying, friends that we know who really had something to say, and like I think about Clark all the time because he’s one of the last of the real heavyweights.

275937.proposed: his hero on the saxophone
275937.evidence: when I heard Lester Young and the Whirleys, man, I don’t want no parts on the clarinet. I wanted to play saxophone.
275937.subject: Red Holloway
275937.audit: {"change": "named as his hero; made him switch to saxophone", "previous": {"relation": "influenced by", "direction": "target", "proposed": "musical inspiration and hero"}}

sources.speaker: RH
sources.text: Oh, yeah, Lester Young, you know. Really the first thing I started was with a clarinet because Benny Goodman and Lionel Hampton and they were working with Benny Goodman and I wanted to play clarinet which I did for a while in school, but when I heard Lester Young and the Whirleys, man, I don’t want no parts on the clarinet. I wanted to play saxophone. So basically that’s when I went — There was a school teacher, a music teacher just out of high school called Captain Walter Dyett and like Johnny Griffin went, well we were in the same band together at the time, when he graduated in ‘45 and went with Hamp. And then there was Benny Green the trombone player and even Gene Ammons took a few courses from him. So he was a very, very important person in my life and a lot of other musicians’ lives. So that’s basically how I started really playing music for a living.

sources.speaker: RH
sources.text: If it ain’t got that swing. You know. And I don’t say every song has to be soulful, but it should have a feeling. Music is supposed to be something that’s beautiful and something that people can feel. And when it loses its feeling and beauty, that was one of the things that really kind of inspired me from Coleman Hawkins and Lester Young because of the fact that they just had so much feeling. And then when I heard Ben Webster, I said, “Oh, sure.” You know like this dude was just like a big gorilla, but when he picked up that saxophone, he was just like — some women used to call him their “prince.” But he was, you know it’s funny how they always say, which is true, you can’t judge a book by its cover because like you look at a person and you say, “Man this sucker here, what the hell can he play? I mean he look like he could be pouring iron.” You know, and then when they start to playing or something —. I’ll give you a good example, like Oscar Peterson, he’s such a big man, you would say, “What kind of music could he play?” But when he sits down at the piano, you say, “Wow.” You can tell that there’s been a lot of study going on there and there has been a lot of thinking, you know? And see now today, when I was growing up you couldn’t, there were no jazz studies. I went to the Chicago Conservatory, but everything was classical. But now they got schools where you can go and learn to play jazz. Now I don’t mean that you necessarily can be a great jazz player, but you will know all of the necessary things that you should know.

sources.text: That is so ridiculous. That is just really stupid. And I don’t care who hears it that’s stupid. That’s just a waste of time and money. The way we used to do, and the way I still do myself, is what I’ll do is like when I was working with Brother Jack McDuff, even John Mayall, now he’s a British, father of the British blues, I worked with him. We would rehearse the stuff at his house, all the changes that had to be made, then we would play it on some jobs. We’d play it maybe for a month. And I still do that, and McDuff. We’ll play our stuff for maybe 2-3 months and there would be, in fact, when I worked and made the first record for McDuff, him and George Benson and Joe Dukes had been playing together for oh a couple of years. And I had joined him like his saxophone player had to go down south because somebody had died in the family. And I joined his band, like at 3:00 that day and we rehearsed from 3 until about 6 the stuff that he was going to do. And we went to the studio and they had an audience and the audience had been drinking from 6 until 8, that’s when the session was starting. And basically everyone knew the music except myself, you know, but I went and rehearsed with him that day and I wrote down what I was playing, more or less the melodic lines, so it made it rather easy. Whereas George and McDuff was playing the harmony. So when we went to the session that night, it was perfect. The people, they had been, they got high and they had been drinking and eating barbecue ribs and just having a good time. So they were high and loose, and that was the album “Live at the Front Room.” And when it came out it was a hit. And that’s really what started the whole thing off. So like, even when I worked with John Mayall, we would practice the stuff and we’d play it on gigs, then we’d go in the studio and they’d take maybe 5 hours to do an album. But I mean this is stupid, going in, well they don’t, one of the thing is they don’t have anything prepared. That’s usually what it is. Most of the groups of today that tie up a studio for two and three months, cost $150,000-$200,000. That is stupid. And because usually most of them don’t really know anything about the instruments. sources.text: Well there were a few people who could execute and express themselves beautifully and make it sound very melodic and convincing and with feeling. Then you’ve got some who play four million notes and you don’t feel nothing and you haven’t heard anything, you know. Now Bird was one who could play, I mean, fast and he could play a whole lot of stuff, and Sonny Stitt, Diz, and I mean with feeling, like when Bird played with Jay McShann. Man that cat when he got through playing some of them solos he played a million notes but they were important, they were not wasted, they were not just some notes. I mean it wasn’t a whole song, but it was just between certain phrases. He’d play maybe some cadenzas there inside those different phrases, and you’d say God damn, how did he do that? And then he’d lean on some of those blue notes, and boy I mean like it’s just something when you hear it, you know you can’t forget it. In fact, if you are a musician, if you hear it at night you go home and want to practice. Of course now Coltrane could do that too, because he had a very wonderful background with blues and stuff. And of course after a while you start teaching yourself, when you get the basics then you can venture out on your own and do whatever you want to do, you know. And I must say most of your stuff that he did, it made sense, it made sense, it made great sense. A lot of people don’t think so. There are some things during the experimental time that didn’t make too much sense, but after he really got into the groove of what was happening and finally got his — and what was that thing he said? He said sometimes he have so many ideas at one time he’d just play them all. He say he just play them all. So but that’s great, cause sometimes some people can’t do that. Some people can only play a certain select few ideas and I think the real goal of any musician is to be able to play all of their ideas, not necessarily all together, nevertheless, I think they should be able to © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

275937.proposed: bandmates in John Mayall's band (incl. 1973 Australia trip)
275937.evidence: I asked Blue Mitchell, I say, “Man, what am I gonna play?” “Oh don’t worry about it, you’ll find something.”
275937.subject: Red Holloway
275937.audit: {"change": "fellow sideman Red consulted on joining Mayall's band", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "worked together in a band, early in interviewee's career"}}

sources.speaker: RH
sources.text: Uh, I don’t remember making one with no drummer, but we did do some peculiar things. I remember many times when I first joined him, I said, “Well when we gonna rehearse?” “Oh I don’t have rehearsals.” I said, “What? You don’t have no rehearsals?” I said, “What am I going to play?” “Oh you’ll find something.” I asked Blue Mitchell, I say, “Man, what am I gonna play?” “Oh don’t worry about it, you’ll find something.” He says the reason he doesn’t rehearse is because he likes for it to be spontaneous. Your ideas, he say, he don’t want you to rehearse your ideas to put on the song. He wants you to be able to when you hear it play it. That’s the way he likes it. I said, “Fine with me.” So I just played whatever I felt I wanted to play. “Perfect, perfect!” I said, “That wasn’t shit.” But you know like I noticed that the audience, they went wild. I said, “I can’t believe this, man. What is this?” But it worked, so I said who am I to tell another person how to make his omelet? So, but I must say I enjoyed working with him. I made more money with John Mayall than any big band I ever worked with. And like when we would finish a 15- week tour, in Europe or wherever, he’d say, “Well fellas,” like if we were in Europe, he’d say, “Well I’m going to Spain for two weeks, anybody want to go? Come on, everything is free. You want your ladies sent for, I’ll pay for it.” And he’d maybe give you a couple of grand or a bonus at the end of the tour, stuff like that. I mean of course John Mayall was a millionaire, and he was making 50 or 60 thousand a night. So he could afford to do that, you know? And he like he couldn’t tell you a note big as this room, but he know chords and he could write out the chords to his song but they would be just basic chords, wouldn’t be no flat this and raise that.

sources.speaker: RH
sources.text: Yeah, well my first trip to Australia was in 1973 with John Mayall. And in fact Blue Mitchell and Freddy Robinson, I don’t know if you’re familiar with these names—

275937.evidence: Errol Garner is a good one, you know, he didn’t really have the training
275937.subject: Red Holloway
275937.audit: {"change": "cited as a natural; heard on 52nd Street", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: RH
sources.text: Yes sir you’re right. You have got to sit and figure it out. Now some people have a great knack for that. Some people are just what you call naturals. I mean you know they have, well, Errol Garner is a good one, you know, he didn’t really have the training but he set down at that piano enough and studied and taught himself enough that he knew what to, what to put where and when, so that’s why I say you’ve got some people that are just naturally musically inclined, and they are able to do certain things like that. Then you got some, I had a cousin, because I was taking piano lessons, he went and took piano lessons for five years, and today he can’t play anything. In fact, he could only play what he read, and now he can’t do that. So I’m just saying, some people do not have that particular type, that knack that you need, that certain talent that you need to do certain things. And then you have some that really don’t, well Benny Green. Benny Green, he would only study when he had to. Great trombone player. He may not play for 4-5 months; pick up his trombone like he just played it an hour ago. You know some people are just like that. Gene Ammons, he’s another one, but Gene studied. But one of the things, I mean he had just — his sound was really one of the great things about his playing, as well as his articulation and stuff. Nevertheless his sound was really, that’s one of the things I was taught, says, one of the things you get first for identification is a sound. Your own sound. Now if you’re going to copy somebody else, if you’re going to copy how they play, at least get your own sound. Don’t copy their tone also, you know, because if everyone sounds alike then it’s just like making photocopies, everything looks and sounds alike. So that was one of the things that I always thought about and always tried to practice so that I wouldn’t sound like anyone else. Of course now I always liked Ben Webster, and I always liked those, you know those beautiful sounds, but I would try and do it but I would try to do it with my own sound. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

sources.speaker: RH
sources.text: you, I almost stopped playing. You heard music, and I mean this is when Bird and Diz and Errol Garner and everybody was on the street, and you heard real music. And I was still honking at that time. I was doing — I was playing Arnett Cobb and that type of saxophone. So and I heard all these changes and things I say, “I’ll never be able to play like that.” So I almost quit. But you know there’s something, if you love music, you just say well I’m going to have to learn how to do this regardless, because I certainly don’t want to be working in no foundry. Yeah, I remember when I got out of the service, I went to work in the Pullman Manufacturing Company. This was where they build the Vistadome, you know like when you take Amtrak, you can look out the observation car, you know, well I worked on the first one of those. And boy after about a month of that, I said, no I think I’m going to stick with this music. Yeah, so that really kind of put me on the straight and narrow.

275937.proposed: in Captain Walter Dyett's school band together; Red says they sound close
275937.evidence: like Johnny Griffin went, well we were in the same band together at the time, when he graduated in ‘45 and went with Hamp.
275937.subject: Red Holloway
275937.audit: {"change": "same school band under Dyett", "previous": {"relation": "friend of", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "peer and musical collaborator who exchanged licks and ideas"}}

sources.speaker: RH
sources.text: Oh, yeah, Lester Young, you know. Really the first thing I started was with a clarinet because Benny Goodman and Lionel Hampton and they were working with Benny Goodman and I wanted to play clarinet which I did for a while in school, but when I heard Lester Young and the Whirleys, man, I don’t want no parts on the clarinet. I wanted to play saxophone. So basically that’s when I went — There was a school teacher, a music teacher just out of high school called Captain Walter Dyett and like Johnny Griffin went, well we were in the same band together at the time, when he graduated in ‘45 and went with Hamp. And then there was Benny Green the trombone player and even Gene Ammons took a few courses from him. So he was a very, very important person in my life and a lot of other musicians’ lives. So that’s basically how I started really playing music for a living.

sources.speaker: RH
sources.text: Ahhh, listen, you know what? I don’t know. There was a friend of mine — in Los Angeles there’s is a young fellow, he says, “He sounds like you.” I said, “Well no, he doesn’t have the sound.” He said, “No, but the stuff that he plays and the phrasing,” he said Ricky Woodard. I can’t see it, but I listen to Ricky and there is this saxophone player, what’s his name — Wilbur Brown. Now Wilbur Brown is a hell of a saxophone player. He lives in L.A. sources.text: Well there were a few people who could execute and express themselves beautifully and make it sound very melodic and convincing and with feeling. And then he’d lean on some of those blue notes, and boy I mean like it’s just something when you hear it, you know you can’t forget it. 275937.evidence: Ella Fitzgerald, there’s just something

sources.text: If it ain’t got that swing. You know. And I don’t say every song has to be soulful, but it should have a feeling. I’ll give you a good example, like Oscar Peterson, he’s such a big man, you would say, “What kind of music could he play?” But when he sits down at the piano, you say, “Wow.” You can tell that there’s been a lot of study going on there and there has been a lot of thinking, you know? But like you had tap dancers, you had comedians, you had novelty acts, Butter Beans and Suzie, and Peg Leg Bates, you had a real collection of people to make up a show. The show would run maybe an hour and a half you know. 275937.evidence: like when Bird played with Jay McShann

275937.audit: {"change": "narrated tie", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: RH
sources.text: Well there were a few people who could execute and express themselves beautifully and make it sound very melodic and convincing and with feeling. Then you’ve got some who play four million notes and you don’t feel nothing and you haven’t heard anything, you know. Now Bird was one who could play, I mean, fast and he could play a whole lot of stuff, and Sonny Stitt, Diz, and I mean with feeling, like when Bird played with Jay McShann. Man that cat when he got through playing some of them solos he played a million notes but they were important, they were not wasted, they were not just some notes. I mean it wasn’t a whole song, but it was just between certain phrases. He’d play maybe some cadenzas there inside those different phrases, and you’d say God damn, how did he do that? And then he’d lean on some of those blue notes, and boy I mean like it’s just something when you hear it, you know you can’t forget it. In fact, if you are a musician, if you hear it at night you go home and want to practice. Of course now Coltrane could do that too, because he had a very wonderful background with blues and stuff. And of course after a while you start teaching yourself, when you get the basics then you can venture out on your own and do whatever you want to do, you know. And I must say most of your stuff that he did, it made sense, it made sense, it made great sense. A lot of people don’t think so. There are some things during the experimental time that didn’t make too much sense, but after he really got into the groove of what was happening and finally got his — and what was that thing he said? He said sometimes he have so many ideas at one time he’d just play them all. He say he just play them all. So but that’s great, cause sometimes some people can’t do that. Some people can only play a certain select few ideas and I think the real goal of any musician is to be able to play all of their ideas, not necessarily all together, nevertheless, I think they should be able to © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

sources.speaker: RH
sources.text: I think my most famous record is I did an LP, the title of it was “No Tears Over You” and all of these songs I wrote myself except for one which was Art Hillary, he wrote one song on it. And the song “No Tears” and then there was another one called “Hittin’ the Road Again.” Now I went in the studio and we rehearsed and played it on the job. Then we went in the studio and we cut it in about 3-1/2 hours, this album, cause I was paying, you see, myself. So we ain’t going to be wasting no time here fellas. If you got anything on your mind, speak now. I think that was my best album. Because then there was a song titled “Music for Making Love.” I wrote this song for a pornography film, but then I took the music for my own album because I liked it so much. But I think, now there was one Clark Terry and I did called “Locksmith Blues.” My baby told me my key won’t fit her lock no more. But I’m a master locksmith, momma, I got a key that will fit any door. You know. Now that was one I wrote, and Clark really surprised me on that because he, the broad’s name was “Hey Magnolia” and Clark was supposed to say something, but he answered in a woman’s voice, he say, “What.” I say, “Huh?” Because I didn’t know he was going to do that, you know. 275942.evidence: Why wouldn’t you hire Vince?
275942.subject: Leslie Johnson
275942.audit: {"change": "she names Vince Giordano as a local player IAJE should have hired; no personal tie shown", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: LJ
sources.text: I was astonished that there wasn’t anything at all. And Vince would be — I mean here he is local. Why wouldn’t you hire Vince? And Dan Levinson is here. I mean there are some extremely good classic jazz players in town. Dave Oscault is another one and Dave is very knowledgeable about Louis Armstrong in particular and is part of the Satchmo Summerfest in New Orleans. He does seminars and lectures down there and he’s a local musician here. He could have been part of this.

sources.speaker: LJ
sources.text: And I think that what you have with the traditional players is a lot of them are just scraping by financially. And it’s similar to my position with The Rag where now my husband now is a very accomplished publicist and has a career with that and he gets frustrated because I don’t promote The Rag. But what happens is there is so much effort going into the product you simply have no brain left. After I produce the paper all I want to do is sleep. I mean your energy is with the product. In Vince’s case for instance, or with a lot of the musicians, they’re trying to come up with the charts, they’re trying to get the right musicians, they’re trying to find the time to rehearse to get to the gig, which doesn’t pay very much money and just the whole process of performing takes so much energy, and they don’t have the money to do the promotion. So if you don’t start out with big money you’re really stuck. And when I started The Rag I started with two hundred dollars. I mean who in their right mind starts a publication with two hundred dollars, which was borrowed from my insurance company. So it’s a cash flow problem really. And if you’re going to get a good publicist you’ve got to pay him decent money. And if you’re going to even get flyers printed up that look professional, it costs money. And you say well okay, go out and borrow the money, well if you’re a musician who’s going to loan you money?

275942.proposed: fellow participants in the Milwaukee Jazz Experience education project
275942.evidence: And I participated in it and Butch Thompson participated in it
275942.subject: Leslie Johnson
275942.audit: {"change": "both took part as clinicians in John Bartles's Milwaukee Jazz Experience education project; thin", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "participants in the Milwaukee Jazz Experience"}}

sources.speaker: LJ
sources.text: It was something that was started by a guy named John Bartles in Milwaukee. And it was — I want to say it was the late seventies, maybe ’78 or so, ’79. And John really had a vision that was exactly what you’re talking about. And he put on two — I believe it was two events — called the Milwaukee Jazz Experience. And I participated in it and Butch Thompson participated in it, a guy named Reggie Buckner who was the head of jazz © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

sources.speaker: LJ
sources.text: studies at the University of Minnesota was part of it, and what John accomplished is he got the superintendent of schools in Milwaukee to cooperate with him and they — and the Milwaukee Journal — for a whole year they prepared kids for the Milwaukee Jazz Experience which happened — it was still during the school year, the end of the school year. And the Milwaukee Journal published tabloids, not real thick, but tabloids about — it had a timeline, a historical timeline of jazz, and it had capsule histories of the important people in jazz. They also published flash cards of jazz personalities, just like a baseball card, that were used in classes, and they built a curriculum, John and the teachers built a curriculum where it was part of English, it was part of art, it was part of the music class, it was part of the social studies class, and it covered K through 12. Then for the Milwaukee Jazz Experience they bussed kids in from the local schools to — I believe it was Viterbo College, was that the one? I can’t remember what the college was, it was a Catholic College and it had agreed to participate. And they turned over the whole campus to this Milwaukee Jazz Experience and it was very much of a budgeted sort of thing and people paid their own way to come there to participate in it. The clinicians didn’t get paid or anything. But they came in and they gave seminars. But the thing was the kids came to the concerts and they already knew something about the music because they’d been prepared or a whole year with these written materials and with the classroom curriculum. So for instance Butch Thompson did a whole section, he did a very good concert on the blues. And he just talked to the kids. And he mentioned how the blues came about, and played a little bit and talked about the different musicians and how they differed. But the kids could ask intelligent questions. It was a wonderful project. John did it for two years and then he unfortunately died of a heart attack and things just kind of fell apart. The superintendent moved on, the Milwaukee Journal people who were there, I believe Kevin Whitehead was at the Milwaukee Journal at that time and he’d be a good person to ask about this. Because he was very much involved in preparing some of the written materials and covering the Milwaukee Jazz Experience. It was a very ambitious project and it was head and shoulders and way ahead of the curve as far as any of this jazz curriculum thing is concerned. I’m so excited about what Dave Robinson is doing because that’s actually the sort of thing that John was trying to accomplish, to bring it into the schools for kids much younger. Because if you can get the kids who are young, they really respond to the music, to the early music. They’re very enthused about it. But if they get to be in high school you really have pretty much lost them.

275942.evidence: Bob Milne is a very good ragtime player and he improvises all over the place
275942.subject: Leslie Johnson
275942.audit: {"change": "describes him as an example; no personal tie", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: LJ
sources.text: You have to define it and you have to respect the various genres too. That’s the other part of it. I think I agree with Mat when he says it’s all good music. But you don’t sell it based on it’s all good music. In the same, Wycliffe saying can’t it all be considered jazz, but it really can’t because people have their favorites and they have their favorite genre and they’re so different. They all fall under the umbrella of improvisation up to a point until you get into the really arranged materials that you get in college. But the earlier jazz, it’s improvisation. In Ragtime there’s a big deal, there’s classic rag and there’s folk rag, that there’s a real division of if you play folk rag, if you play classic ragtime, tell me if you play classic ragtime and you’re playing just the notes exactly as the composer wrote it, there’s no improvisation whatsoever. Folk ragtime is far more lilting. It has more of a rolling quality to the music and it’s more improvisational. People who — I’ll give you an example of Bob Milne is a very good ragtime player and he improvises all over the place and he wrote a book called The Journeyman Piano Player about what it was like, and he still does this, traveling all over —

275942.proposed: writer for The Mississippi Rag; she edited his interviews and helped him find book publishers

275942.subject: Leslie Johnson
275942.audit: {"change": "she edited and published his interviews in The Rag and helped him find publishers", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "Interviewee edited Chip Deffaa's interviews for The Mississippi Rag and helped him find publishers for his books"}}

sources.speaker: LJ
sources.text: the challenge is trying to bring in new people. There is no interest on the part of the press. The general press has no interest in traditional jazz. And the rare times that they’re kind of forced into doing an article, the articles are rife with errors. And it’s almost more frustrating to have an article published with the errors than it is to not have an article at all. It just makes you want to tear out your hair, really. That’s one of the problems. Because you’re serving a small audience it’s expensive to publish a paper like mine. From the very first issue I paid my writers, which most traditional jazz publications never did. I paid them a pittance. But on the other hand because The Rag is respected they can build a reputation because I will work with writers to refine their writing skills, to help them make contacts, to give them access to musicians that they wouldn’t have access to. Chip Deffaa, you probably know Chip, he — every book that he writes, he writes something and he says you gave me my start, which is very sweet but it’s also very true. Because he’s written, put together, I believe it’s four books based on interviews that were first published in The Mississippi Rag. And they’re expanded interviews. I edited them down and, quite honestly, I think the edited versions are stronger, but he naturally had more material that he wanted to include. You know, he wanted to include the full interview. And the books are, I’m very glad that he had the books published, but I helped him to find the publishers. I could say you’re not going to like this publisher, they won’t work with you or they’re going to expect you to do more work or you’re going to end up putting out money and, you know, try this person instead. And so he’s done that and it’s worked out quite nicely for him. And he’s built up a good reputation. I think he got his job at the New York Post based largely on the access that he had to the musicians where we ran interviews in The Rag.

275942.audit: {"change": "wrongly skipped for sharing her surname; named as an object of purists' devotion", "previous": {"skipped": "self_or_host"}}

sources.speaker: LJ
sources.text: Well that’s right. And really the challenge was, when I started the paper, was okay folks, you have to cooperate if you want to have your own publication. Because there had been other publications that had started and the purists said well unless you only do it about George Lewis I’m not buying that publication. Unless you only do it about Bunk Johnson, I don’t have any time for it. Because they were so passionate about their particular musician. But nobody could exist as a publication. So my very first editorial said you’re going to have to trust me that I will try and cover whomever it is that you’re interested in, but you’re going to have to wait and you’re going to have to read other stuff. And to their credit they did, and they have remained — I can’t tell you how many subscribers I have who have every single issue of The Rag. Every single issue, which astounded me when that first started happening, you know, after the first year and I discovered that, you know it’s a tabloid in newsprint and I thought well they’ll read it and throw it away. No. They’ve kept them. Now as they’ve gotten older they’re having to downsize and they call up and they say, “I have 33 years worth of ‘Rags,’ I can’t bear to throw them out or recycle them, what can I do with them?” And I’ll say donate them to a music library or take them to a nursing home or give them to a music school. Because they just cannot stand to part with them. It’s really very, very sweet. But they did pay attention to that first editorial and honestly, that was like a mission statement and I really have not ever deviated from that over all this time. sources.speaker: LJ

275942.evidence: Kid Thomas I believe, he had a band that he called the Dixieland band
275942.subject: Leslie Johnson
275942.audit: {"change": "historical example", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: LJ
sources.text: Yeah. The tricky part of this is Dixieland was actually a fine term way back when both black and white bands used that term. It wasn’t just a white band that used the term Dixieland, a lot of the black bands did use it. Kid Thomas I believe, he had a band that he called the Dixieland band, the Kid Thomas Dixieland Band. That was not a bad word. What happened was it became more of associated with the novelty music or ice cream © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

275942.evidence: you’d never use that word around Wild Bill Davison for instance
275942.subject: Leslie Johnson
275942.audit: {"change": "anecdote about his dislike of the Dixieland label; no meeting shown", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: LJ
sources.text: social type music rather than serious improvisational jazz. It became a music where the solo was passed around rather than ensembling. And that, you just change the whole meaning of that word. And what you have, quite frankly, were people that formed a Dixieland band who could only play a little, not a lot. And so it took on a bad connotation where there were some musicians who didn’t want to be associated with that word at all, you’d never use that word around Wild Bill Davison for instance. Oh my goodness. He did not want to be considered a Dixieland player. So, but the tricky thing is there are some very good festivals who incorporate that word into their title. There are also some bands who are very good who use that word, or say they play Dixieland, and you don’t want to insult them and say, mmm, not a good word, because they’re actually good musicians. But if people ask me, oh do you cover Dixieland music I say well we like to call it classic jazz or early jazz or traditional jazz because it covers more than what would be considered Dixieland. Because I think that’s a very — people have a very closed idea of what that music is. If they think that’s all traditional jazz is that’s a mistake.

275942.evidence: I’m so excited about what Dave Robinson is doing
275942.subject: Leslie Johnson
275942.audit: {"change": "admires his education work", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: LJ
sources.text: studies at the University of Minnesota was part of it, and what John accomplished is he got the superintendent of schools in Milwaukee to cooperate with him and they — and the Milwaukee Journal — for a whole year they prepared kids for the Milwaukee Jazz Experience which happened — it was still during the school year, the end of the school year. And the Milwaukee Journal published tabloids, not real thick, but tabloids about — it had a timeline, a historical timeline of jazz, and it had capsule histories of the important people in jazz. They also published flash cards of jazz personalities, just like a baseball card, that were used in classes, and they built a curriculum, John and the teachers built a curriculum where it was part of English, it was part of art, it was part of the music class, it was part of the social studies class, and it covered K through 12. Then for the Milwaukee Jazz Experience they bussed kids in from the local schools to — I believe it was Viterbo College, was that the one? I can’t remember what the college was, it was a Catholic College and it had agreed to participate. And they turned over the whole campus to this Milwaukee Jazz Experience and it was very much of a budgeted sort of thing and people paid their own way to come there to participate in it. The clinicians didn’t get paid or anything. But they came in and they gave seminars. But the thing was the kids came to the concerts and they already knew something about the music because they’d been prepared or a whole year with these written materials and with the classroom curriculum. So for instance Butch Thompson did a whole section, he did a very good concert on the blues. And he just talked to the kids. And he mentioned how the blues came about, and played a little bit and talked about the different musicians and how they differed. But the kids could ask intelligent questions. It was a wonderful project. John did it for two years and then he unfortunately died of a heart attack and things just kind of fell apart. The superintendent moved on, the Milwaukee Journal people who were there, I believe Kevin Whitehead was at the Milwaukee Journal at that time and he’d be a good person to ask about this. Because he was very much involved in preparing some of the written materials and covering the Milwaukee Jazz Experience. It was a very ambitious project and it was head and shoulders and way ahead of the curve as far as any of this jazz curriculum thing is concerned. I’m so excited about what Dave Robinson is doing because that’s actually the sort of thing that John was trying to accomplish, to bring it into the schools for kids much younger. Because if you can get the kids who are young, they really respond to the music, to the early music. They’re very enthused about it. But if they get to be in high school you really have pretty much lost them.

And they turned over the whole campus to this Milwaukee Jazz Experience and it was very much of a budgeted sort of thing and people paid their own way to come there to participate in it. The clinicians didn’t get paid or anything. But they came in and they gave seminars. But the thing was the kids came to the concerts and they already knew something about the music because they’d been prepared or a whole year with these written materials and with the classroom curriculum. I’m so excited about what Dave Robinson is doing because that’s actually the sort of thing that John was trying to accomplish, to bring it into the schools for kids much younger. They’re always looking for something different rather than going back and playing the music that’s been played before. I think they tend to be innovators. And so I think that they’re always looking ahead rather than looking back. I feel badly that they don’t appreciate the tremendous history and in some cases they thought of it as Uncle Tom music because it was black bands playing for white audiences but having to come in the back door. I think he’s been very good for the music in that sense and helping the black community realize that there’s value in that history. So I really give him credit for that.

sources.text: At this time, during the 50s, this was like early — mid 50s, jazz, you didn’t have jazz in the schools. There were no jazz programs, no North Texas State, Berklee or any other. So that was unheard of in those days. So we just played the regular school type things. We played marches and played for football games and for auditorium, morning auditorium and all that. We didn’t play any — we had no charts or jazz charts or any of that. But that was fun, I mean that’s all we had and it was fun doing that. It was fun playing. And I really liked it, I mean this is what I wanted to do. And I remember there were some jazz records around my house, but not a lot. It wasn’t that my people were really jazz fans per se, but there were some things around the house and I liked that. And I did get interested in jazz and a little student at school told me about Charlie Parker. I’d never heard of him you know. And he said, “You should really check this Charlie Parker out.” And I did. I went to a little candy shop in my neighborhood and on the juke box there was a Charlie Parker record, a little 45. And I think he was playing “Tico Tico,” which is just a Brazilian samba type song. And it just blew me away. I knew immediately that this is what I wanted to do. It made perfect sense to me. I didn’t need to be nurtured or taught how to listen to this music. I mean it made perfect sense. And I remember, I was about 14, that to me, when I heard that, and I had no history of hearing a lot of jazz records, I had no concept of what’s considered bebop and modern jazz or any of that. Whatever that difference is, it has to be heard often enough by enough people, musicians, whatever, to be able to discern the little bit of difference. Because no two people are exactly alike. And the differences have to be discerned. 275957.evidence: Author Stanley Crouch sums up the deep sense of purpose he brings to his music in the liner notes to “First Flight Out.”
275957.subject: Charles McPherson

sources.text: Charles McPherson has been one of the top alto saxophonists in jazz since the 1960s. He was born in Joplin, Missouri on July 24, 1939 and moved to New York City at the age of 20. One of his first gigs was with bassist Charles Mingus, and this fruitful relationship lasted until 1974. While his playing reflects the influences of Johnny Hodges and Charlie Parker, he has developed a distinctive character on the alto that has in turn influenced numerous younger saxophone artists. Charles has recorded frequently throughout his career, often with pianist Barry Harris. He has led his own ensembles since 1972 and can be heard with his son Chuck on drums. Author Stanley Crouch sums up the deep sense of purpose he brings to his music in the liner notes to “First Flight Out.”
Crouch states, “McPherson never lets us forget the actual greatness of the art he represents.”

sources.speaker: CM
sources.text: Well I knew him as Noel. Oh, okay. All right. Now he was just a folk singer singing, playing his guitar, and then we had this jam session in the afternoon, and Bill Cosby or people like that or even Bob Dylan would be at some coffee house across the street, and everybody was just like struggling nonentities basically, really. And so in the afternoon we’d have these sessions. And Mingus came by one afternoon because he was in need of an alto player and a trumpet player. And we were recommended by Yusef, who worked with Mingus sometimes, and Eric Dolphy and a guy named Ted Curson, trumpet player, both respectively were going to quit Mingus and get their own groups. And so Mingus needed a saxophone player in there. And he was really mad at Eric and both of those guys. But anyway he came to the session in the afternoon and heard us and he hired us. He told us, “Well come to the club tonight and bring your horns and we’ll see what happens.” And Eric Dolphy was still there, because they had two weeks notice. So for about two weeks there were two altos and two trumpets in Mingus’ band. And Mingus, every night, tried to get Eric not to quit. Because Eric really played Mingus’ music well. And he had been working with Mingus a long time. And Mingus’ music was extremely difficult. It takes a long time to teach people these songs and then here Eric is going to quit. But anyway, the memorable thing that happened is Lonnie and I were in this club, owned by a gangster, definitely that scene. And we were in the club and it was at the end of the evening. And these people owed Mingus about two thousand dollars. That was the first time Lonnie and I had been in the company of Mingus like this. And so Mingus — the money was not there — and Mingus at this time weighed about three hundred pounds, probably 40 years old or so. He just tore the piano up. It was a Steinway grand, probably seven feet. He went inside the piano and took his fingers and plucked the strings, all that tension. You know piano wires hold locomotives. You know you can dangle a locomotive, that’s their claim to fame of how strong the tension is. He goes in there and © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

sources.speaker: CM
sources.text: make a record with Yusef Lateef, he might have been involved with James Moody on a record or something like that, but he never, he was kind of a tragic figure. And he just died in 1985, a young man. He was about 45. It was just one of those things. We went to New York together, as far as working with Mingus, yes. Yeah, we worked, let’s see this was around 1959 or ‘60. And there used to be a little coffee shop in the Village called the Cafe Wha?. And there were people I can remember folk singing was very popular at this time, as well as the jazz. And quite often they would have folk singing and jazz in the same club. 275957.evidence: because he had respect for Igor Stravinsky

275957.audit: {"change": "evidence made verbatim; narrated Parker's regard", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: CM
sources.text: Yeah, the best, you know, pantomime. A lot of things they were able to retrieve and use from Charlie Parker. Some things they were not able to do either because of the technology of it, or because of contractual situations like money or whatever. And in those instances I was involved. And then there were incidental scenes during the movie where certain background things needed to be, and of course Bird’s not there, and well they didn’t use him for things like that. There was one scene in the movie involving Charlie Parker riding in Beverly Hills with this woman, and she was showing him all the houses and things, you know, Humphrey Bogart’s mansion and then they rode farther and here’s Melvin Douglas’ or whatever. And this is supposedly true. And Bird really expressed really no heck of an interest, other than, “Oh yeah, really great, wonderful house.” Whatever. Until she got to Igor Stravinsky’s house. And of course this impressed him. He wanted to get, according to her he did get out of the car and just went up to this huge and massive gate and just kind of stared at the house, I mean, because he had respect for Igor Stravinsky. And Clint Eastwood suggested for this scene that I play a Kansas City style blues, and that would be superimposed on Stravinsky’s “Firebird Suite.” So and that was his suggestion, and I thought that was a nice arty thing to do, and it worked great because he had “Firebird Suite” going on and then this Kansas City blues on top of that.

275957.evidence: While his playing reflects the influences of Johnny Hodges and Charlie Parker
275957.subject: Charles McPherson
275957.audit: {"change": "only the archive's editorial note states it; CM never mentions Hodges", "previous": {"relation": "influenced by", "direction": "target", "proposed": "musical influence on alto saxophone style"}}

sources.text: Charles McPherson has been one of the top alto saxophonists in jazz since the 1960s. He was born in Joplin, Missouri on July 24, 1939 and moved to New York City at the age of 20. One of his first gigs was with bassist Charles Mingus, and this fruitful relationship lasted until 1974. While his playing reflects the influences of Johnny Hodges and Charlie Parker, he has developed a distinctive character on the alto that has in turn influenced numerous younger saxophone artists. Charles has recorded frequently throughout his career, often with pianist Barry Harris. He has led his own ensembles since 1972 and can be heard with his son Chuck on drums. Author Stanley Crouch sums up the deep sense of purpose he brings to his music in the liner notes to “First Flight Out.”

275957.evidence: if a martian came down to earth and listened to say Dizzy Gillespie, and say listened to Pete Candoli
275957.subject: Charles McPherson
275957.audit: {"change": "missed person; stylistic example", "previous": null}

sources.speaker: CM
sources.text: Yeah, right. And you know the differences that manifest itself in a particular person, has to be heard in the public consciousness long enough for the difference to be solidified in other people’s minds. You know what I mean? For them to say oh, this is a different style, this is Roy Eldridge. You know what I mean? Whatever that difference is, it has to be heard often enough by enough people, musicians, whatever, to be able to discern the little bit of difference. Because no two people are exactly alike. And the differences have to be discerned. Once they are discerned by enough people, industry people, other musicians, critics, writers, whomever is visible enough or heard enough for the people to know the difference between this and say Charlie Parker or Louis Armstrong, then that difference is no longer like this anymore, it’s like this, because it’s known. You see what I mean? And that’s what happened to some people. You know if a martian came down to earth and listened to say Dizzy Gillespie, and say listened to Pete Candoli, to him it would sound the same. You know what I’m saying? But not to us, because if you know Pete and you know his style kind of sounds sort of like that, and Dizzy is this and that. But to a martian well it’s like well it’s the same one. What’s the difference? And these little bit of difference only becomes bigger when you have isolated that difference.

sources.speaker: BT
sources.text: mean I was, I had the local, like at Virginia State we had a band that was the school band. It was an extracurricular activity. It wasn’t something the school sanctioned, but it was a dance band and a bunch of kids, and we had a faculty advisor, and it was a very fine musician, a guy named Solomon Phillips, who taught me to arrange and do some other things. But the Count Basie’s band was playing one nighters in Virginia. And they came through town. Well I mean we had all the Basie arrangements and we had, you know because in those days you could buy “One O’clock Jump” and “Jumpin’ at the Woodside” and all those things for a dollar. I mean it was a stock arrangement, transcribed from the record, by some, whoever the company was. And it was a good transcription because they had the right, they had the Basie solo and it had everybody’s solo in them. And so and we knew the arrangements. And so when the band came obviously everybody in the band wanted to go to hear these great musicians. And so we went, this was in Petersburg, Virginia. And so we went to the place where they were playing and we were standing around close to the band, nobody’s dancing, everybody’s listening to the — none of our group is dancing, we were listening to the music. And so a couple of the guys in my band met Jo Jones, who was a very accessible musician and said, “hey we’ve got a great piano player in our band, why don’t you get Basie to let him sit in?” Well I was embarrassed, I mean, because, hey, sit in with this rhythm section? With Count Basie? Lots of luck, you know. I mean I was just happy to be there. Anyway, Jo said “oh yeah, let me check him out.” And so he got Basie to let me sit in. So here I am with Freddie Green, Jo Jones and Walter Page. I mean a dream rhythm section you know? And that was my first meeting. I had seen them on stage and I had never been able to get backstage to meet them. It was my first person-to-person encounter with them. And from that point on, Jo was one of my mentors. So I mean he had a profound influence on my career.

sources.speaker: BT
sources.text: Not only did it make us play together, what happened is that the Duke Ellingtons, the Count Basies and the every strata of the music was available because they had nowhere else to go. We were all pressed into the black community. So everyone was accessible. I mean a man of Duke Ellington’s stature, a man of Count Basie’s stature, today would live, perhaps, in an area that I as a young musician couldn’t afford. So therefore he would not be as accessible as if he lived upstairs in the apartment above me you know, as many of them did.

sources.speaker: BT
sources.text: what we should do is have jazz as a first project. And I couldn’t find a way to make them do that. And a woman named Daphne Onstein went out to the World’s Fair and said, you know, with all these millions of dollars of buildings and all these things that people spent money on, here are people following a mobile bandstand all through the fairgrounds. And they’re listening to this live music. The city serviced our orchestra and they got Ray Nance in there, they got some jazz musicians in there and everything, but basically they were just playing nice music. And I said well why can’t we do something like that? And so, “you opened your big mouth, you got the project.” So I get the — we, Daphne and several other members of the Council and I went over to Ballantine Beer and got them to give us a parade float, and we put an electric piano on there, and went around the city. The idea was to update the New Orleans tradition. So we paraded — we took this float and went in a circle from say 137th Street between Lenox and Seventh Avenue, in a ten block radius. And we started there in a ten block radius and we came back playing as we went. And so we drew a second line. I mean kids were coming along and they were running along behind the parade. 275983.proposed: both spoke at the 1958 Music Educators National Conference; knew each other
275983.evidence: we knew each other but we didn’t confer before we went to the conference
275983.subject: Billy Taylor
275983.audit: {"change": "'we knew each other' = acquaintance, more than has met", "previous": {"relation": "has met", "direction": "na", "proposed": "met at the Music Educators’ National Conference in 1958"}}

sources.speaker: BT
sources.text: The Jazzmobile came about in 1958, well, in the early 50’s I had done a lot of lectures and I’d written some articles about jazz. I was very — Jo Jones had — when I first came to New York, immediately when I got here said, “Billy you’ve got to write a book.” And he said, “you’ve got a college education and you know you’re always spouting off about jazz this and jazz this, and you make a lot of sense so you ought to write it down.” I says, “right.” And I forgot all about that and I went on to try to learn how to play the piano. And ultimately in 1948, I did write a book — I wrote a little pamphlet — how to play bebop. And the reason I wrote it was because everyone had asked Dizzy and Bird to write it and they didn’t, they didn’t write anything at that point. So I felt that, hey, you’re not giving away any secrets. Everybody is, as soon as you put it on records, everybody can take it off, I mean so why not write down what indeed is going on in terms of the harmonic, rhythmic and melodic expansions of this music. How Dizzy and Bird took what Basie and Ellington and their predecessors had done and how they expanded, what some of the differences were and what the similarities were. So I began to write articles about this and do things. In 1958 I was invited to the Music Educators’ National Conference to give a speech and so was Stan Kenton that same year. And we both, not knowing — we knew each other but we didn’t confer before we went to the conference — and we both said the same thing: you as music educators should be including jazz in your educational process. It is being done on an informal basis, but it needs to be codified, it needs to be put into the general aspects of music teaching. They pat us both on the head, thanks a lot, don’t call us we’ll call you. And I was furious. I said you knew I was a jazz musician, why did you waste my time coming out here all the way from New York to California. I mean I come out to California to visit my friends. I don’t need to come out and be insulted you know. I was furious. And so was he. So we both came back and began to put in some kind of operation some of the things to say, you know, to thumb our nose at these people that we had very little respect for at that time. And what he did was to use his band as a workshop band. And what I did was a few years later — it took me a while to find a vehicle to do it — but a few years later I was a member of the Harlem Culture Council and they were looking for our first project. And I said okay, © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

275983.subject: Billy Taylor

sources.speaker: BT
sources.text: you one example. The thing that has frustrated me for many years, when I first came to New York, I had no idea of writing anything, I just wanted to know about the music. And I worked, my first job was on 52nd Street. So Jo Jones took me around and introduced me to many musicians. I was working with a friend of his, Sid Catlett. So I was working with it was Ben Webster’s quartet. And so 52nd Street, in 1946, was a history of jazz. I mean you had everything from every kind of jazz that existed up until that period was represented on that one, actually in that one block, right down the street between Fifth and Sixth Avenue on 52nd Street just a few blocks over. These were all speakeasys, formerly. They were now legitimate night clubs. But there were ten on either side of that one block. There were four or five down in the block between Sixth and Seventh. But the main conglomeration of clubs was in that one block. So I, you know, naturally these are all super-stars to me. I mean these are the guys whose records I had heard and people who I had not heard of whose names I’d heard and never heard them play and all that, and it was a great opportunity to hear in person what Sidney Bechet sounded like or what Jimmy McPartland or some of the guys from Chicago who I’d read about and heard on radio but never seen you know.
