275983.evidence: they got Ray Nance in there
275983.subject: Billy Taylor
275983.audit: {"change": "sources fixed", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: BT
sources.text: what we should do is have jazz as a first project. And I couldn’t find a way to make them do that. And a woman named Daphne Onstein went out to the World’s Fair and said, you know, with all these millions of dollars of buildings and all these things that people spent money on, here are people following a mobile bandstand all through the fairgrounds. And they’re listening to this live music. The city serviced our orchestra and they got Ray Nance in there, they got some jazz musicians in there and everything, but basically they were just playing nice music. And I said well why can’t we do something like that? And so, “you opened your big mouth, you got the project.” So I get the — we, Daphne and several other members of the Council and I went over to Ballantine Beer and got them to give us a parade float, and we put an electric piano on there, and went around the city. The idea was to update the New Orleans tradition. So we paraded — we took this float and went in a circle from say 137th Street between Lenox and Seventh Avenue, in a ten block radius. And we started there in a ten block radius and we came back playing as we went. And so we drew a second line. I mean kids were coming along and they were running along behind the parade. We had two police cars as buffers so they were safe, and it was like a little parade. We did this for a couple of years. Then the program began to grow. We started an educational part of it where we did workshops, where we did school concerts, and so forth. But it really was a way to bring the Count Basies, the Duke Ellingtons, the Dizzy Gillespies, the Lionel Hamptons, all of whom were very supportive, in coming out and having the people this close to them. Because even by the 60’s, the music, there were very few big bands — being Basie, Ellington and Thad Jones and one or two others were really the basic big bands. I don’t think Thad had actually started his when we started Jazzmobile. I think — what was the guy’s name — Duke Pearson had a big band and there was always some kind of workshop band that had the fine musicians that were doing studio and stuff like that and wanted to play jazz. But Basie had a touring band, Ellington had a touring band and those were really the mainstays for us.

275983.proposed: sat in with the Basie rhythm section (Freddie Green, Jo Jones, Walter Page) in college

sources.speaker: BT
sources.text: mean I was, I had the local, like at Virginia State we had a band that was the school band. It was an extracurricular activity. It wasn’t something the school sanctioned, but it was a dance band and a bunch of kids, and we had a faculty advisor, and it was a very fine musician, a guy named Solomon Phillips, who taught me to arrange and do some other things. But the Count Basie’s band was playing one nighters in Virginia. And they came through town. Well I mean we had all the Basie arrangements and we had, you know because in those days you could buy “One O’clock Jump” and “Jumpin’ at the Woodside” and all those things for a dollar. I mean it was a stock arrangement, transcribed from the record, by some, whoever the company was. And it was a good transcription because they had the right, they had the Basie solo and it had everybody’s solo in them. And so and we knew the arrangements. And so when the band came obviously everybody in the band wanted to go to hear these great musicians. And so we went, this was in Petersburg, Virginia. And so we went to the place where they were playing and we were standing around close to the band, nobody’s dancing, everybody’s listening to the — none of our group is dancing, we were listening to the music. And so a couple of the guys in my band met Jo Jones, who was a very accessible musician and said, “hey we’ve got a great piano player in our band, why don’t you get Basie to let him sit in?” Well I was embarrassed, I mean, because, hey, sit in with this rhythm section? With Count Basie? Lots of luck, you know. I mean I was just happy to be there. Anyway, Jo said “oh yeah, let me check him out.” And so he got Basie to let me sit in. So here I am with Freddie Green, Jo Jones and Walter Page. I mean a dream rhythm section you know? And that was my first meeting. I had seen them on stage and I had never been able to get backstage to meet them. It was my first person-to-person encounter with them. And from that point on, Jo was one of my mentors. So I mean he had a profound influence on my career.

And usually when the band played, Birdland was a small club, and the band took up the entire stage and part of the band was really down on the floor almost. And Basie was sitting at the piano and the piano was on the floor. And so the exciting thing was to hear Joe Williams get up and sing to — it wasn’t a predominantly white audience in those days. Because it was the, at Birdland, it was a very hip contingent of people who came downtown consistently. So you had 60/40 one night — white/black; and 60/40 the next night — black/white. So it really was a very interesting balance in that particular club. And so it was interesting to me regardless of which way the balance was in terms of the ethnic background, Joe would reach out and grab those folks with the classic things that he was doing with Basie in those days, and it didn’t make any difference, it was just a straight arrow to that audience you know. And it was really a very hip audience. I mean this is the audience that was so hip that normally the piano was on the stage and I would be seated here and I could hear, they didn’t realize it, they didn’t realize it, but the people sitting right behind me I could hear their conversations. Sometimes I didn’t want to. But I mean I could, you know, it was audible. And I’d be sitting there and the guy would be sitting behind me talking to his buddy. sources.speaker: BT
sources.text: The Jazzmobile came about in 1958, well, in the early 50’s I had done a lot of lectures and I’d written some articles about jazz. I was very — Jo Jones had — when I first came to New York, immediately when I got here said, “Billy you’ve got to write a book.” And he said, “you’ve got a college education and you know you’re always spouting off about jazz this and jazz this, and you make a lot of sense so you ought to write it down.” I says, “right.” And I forgot all about that and I went on to try to learn how to play the piano. And ultimately in 1948, I did write a book — I wrote a little pamphlet — how to play bebop. And the reason I wrote it was because everyone had asked Dizzy and Bird to write it and they didn’t, they didn’t write anything at that point. So I felt that, hey, you’re not giving away any secrets. Everybody is, as soon as you put it on records, everybody can take it off, I mean so why not write down what indeed is going on in terms of the harmonic, rhythmic and melodic expansions of this music. sources.text: Actually I wrote this in a book which was edited by Dave Baker. I was asked to make some suggestions as to where jazz could go. In education, where I’d like to see jazz go, I would like for people to recognize the intrinsic value of the music and to use it. Because it is like an ostrich to have your head in the sand and not realize that jazz has been the most pervasive music of this century. I mean the kinds of things that have come, that have been most popular, much of this music and the concepts that created the music, have come out of jazz. To take these things and to put them into their proper perspective, tells us who we are and what we’re about. So it’s beyond just music. It’s beyond culture. What’s going on as we speak with Congress getting rid of the NEA and trying to find ways to de-fund the arts makes it more mandatory to belabor a point, makes it really mandatory to put, to enhance, the 35,000 jazz ensembles that are in place already in schools around this country, to improve the instruction, to improve the visiting artist programs, to bring in to personal contact not just students who are interested in music, but students who are just ordinary people who when exposed to good music of any style will respond. You need to, jazz needs to be on television. It needs to be on video. It needs to, those of us who have the ability to project it, should do more. And they’re listening to this live music. I don’t think Thad had actually started his when we started Jazzmobile. sources.text: Well I was recruited, to be honest with you. I had no intention of going back to school. I had studied privately and I was doing some private study here in New York. But I just felt that the educational system as it related to music was terrible. And it was not only ineffectual, it was doing a disservice to musicians in this country. I still believe that to a great extent, for other reasons. I think that we have all of these resources we have all of this history, we have all of this and we only look at a very small part of it. Roland Williams was, people don’t know him, but he was a brilliant — he’s still around but he’s not in that position — he had a brilliant idea. He identified about ten to twenty people that he said, these are people who are teachers and don’t know they’re teachers. But they, if you look at what they do professionally, in everything they do there is some educational element. They are educating as they do their comedy or as they do their music or as they do their social work, or whatever it is. So he said maybe we can get all of these people up to the School of Education at U Mass and study them, and find some common denominator and put that into the hopper and make education a little more palatable. It was really like they were singing — the closest thing I can relate it to is if you listen to the Georgia Sea Islands records — those kinds of things — that’s the kind of music basically that we heard in this context. And I don’t know it just moved me in a different way. It didn’t, that was the part, I didn’t usually care for whatever the brother was preaching, but the music was, something was going on. And I couldn’t figure it out. It had to do with touching you, with music touching you. I mean I have felt the same way later with European music and with Indian music and with other kinds of music. And I didn’t have to know what that was. It was just that that piece of music in that particular context reached out and I said, oh man, wow, it just did something for me. And so this was that kind of association. For me it is an important part of everything I do. I mean the most used piece of music I have ever written is a piece called “I Wish I Knew How it Would Feel to be Free.” And that is in hymnals. I wrote it for my daughter because I was just trying to show her about her traditions. She was growing up in the 50s and 60s and really coming up with Motown and a lot of other things. And I’m saying, “Well that’s all right, but you have a tradition that goes beyond what I play and Motown and all of that. And you should know about that.” And she wasn’t getting that. We’re Catholic. And so she wasn’t getting that in church as I did. And so I figured as a father I should do that. And she was saying, “right, sure, thanks Dad.” Now she is grown and much more aware, having gone through experiences of her own and gone back and looked and listened to things out of her own tradition, so she’s much more aware than she was, you know, than I tried to make her. She did that on her own. But I wrote this trying to show her, I said you know this is something I can make up. It’s so important in your tradition. So I wrote the piece in about 15 minutes. I played it and I said that’s good and I liked it so I wrote it down. And it’s only about a 16-bar piece. But since then, so many other artists have done it. Nina Simone had the classic record on it in terms of like most of the singers who sang it sang the version based, their versions are based on her version. And her version is based on my instrumental version, which I did at the piano. But spiritual, I’ve written in recent years, something based on the concept that Ellington called “Sacred Music.” Where you use your best shot as far as what you do as a composer. And you try to say, using all the information at hand, something that has a religious context. And this was based on the Psalms that say “Make a Joyful Noise To the Lord.” As a matter of fact that’s the title of the piece. It’s a seven movement work, and it’s “Make a Joyful Noise.”

sources.text: Well he was a little more accepting of it than my mother was. My mother said, “Oh my goodness, another musician.” And then when I started traveling it was like she said to me one day she says, “If I knew that this is what I had to expect when I first let you go out on your first gig I would never have done it.” And I started traveling all over the world and stuff. I mean it’s a hard life on those who love you you know? It’s a hard life anyway but you don’t look at it that way. I mean to this day I still love to travel. And my happiest time is on the bandstand. I don’t want too much time between one gig and the next. But my father, now you know the first time I went out on the road was with Gene Ammons and Sonny Stitt. And the gig started on a Friday night. Nelson Boyd, remember the bass player Nelson Boyd? Dizzy Gillespie wrote the tune “Half Nelson” for him — no I mean Charlie Parker. I think Bird wrote the song “Half Nelson.” He wrote that for Nelson Boyd. Nelson Boyd was a good friend of the family’s. Me and my father were close buddies. Nelson was working at The Showboat in Philadelphia with Gene Ammons and Sonny Stitt. The gig got started on Tuesday. He couldn’t make the gig Friday and Saturday. And so he asked my father to do it. And my father was working so my father sent me. And that was my first really big gig. I guess I was 16. I was close to 17 because I was almost ready to graduate from high school. In fact, I was 17 because I think school © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: My concept of a sound came from my father. Because my father told me early on that that was what I had to go for. And see in the days when I came up sound was everything. You listened to Coleman Hawkins and you knew Coleman Hawkins as soon as he played one note. And you knew it wasn’t Ben Webster because nobody else sounded like Ben Webster and nobody sounded like Coleman Hawkins and nobody sounded like Prez and nobody sounded like Bird and nobody sounded like Miles. Miles was wise enough to early on realize that going after playing like Diz wasn’t going to be his claim to fame. Everybody had their own sound. Even piano players had their own sound. Horace Silver sounded totally different from Oscar Peterson, who sounded totally different from Art Tatum, who sounded totally different from Fats Waller, who sounded totally different from Phineas Newborn. All these guys — sound was the thing. To the day nobody has ever been able to copy the sound of Art Blakey on the drums. The way Art Blakey plays the drums, the way Elvin Jones played the drums, the way Philly Jo Jones played the drums, the way Art Taylor played the drums. Everybody had their own sound. Sound was the thing. Nowadays, this is the age of mediocrity. So many people are going after the wrong thing. Drummers are trying to learn a bunch of stuff on a snare drum rather than how to get a sound on the ride cymbal. They don’t realize the great value of a Ben Riley, how to ride, how to make a gig with nothing but the ride cymbal. Billy Higgins. Billy Higgins made a gig one time, the drums showed up late, so he took a chair — he had his cymbals so he took a chair and he played the chair and his cymbals. And when the drums came he was swinging so hard nobody wanted him to set up the drums. He played the whole gig with a wooden chair and a ride cymbal. Papa Jo Jones used to come to Bradley’s. Remember Bradley’s? Bradley’s was the infamous after hours place for New York, for duos. Piano and bass. Papa Jones used to come to Bradley’s with his brushes and his newspaper under his arm and he’d sit at the bar in front of the piano player and drummer and take his newspaper and fold it up, you know a folded up New York Times, and take his brushes and sit there and play brushes on the newspaper, and swing until the cows come home. I mean that was a climate, you came from the place of creativity in the days when I was learning how to play this music. So when you talk about my sound, it’s not — I worked on it, that’s what I went after. My father told me when I started working with all of these different singers and one night I was talking to my father, complaining © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: Yeah. You know a friend of mine, we were just talking about that the other day. One of the things that Herbie Hancock and Wayne Shorter and Ron Carter, since when you’re talking about Herbie and Wayne and Ron, you know you don’t have to use their last names, everybody knows who you’re talking about. One of the things that perpetrated their music was the fact that they played each other’s music. And that’s sort of the kind of thing that Bird and Monk and Miles and Dizzy, they did also. They played each other’s music, which is what we need to do more of. We need to play more of our contemporaries’ music. And that helps make the music standards. A lot of the standards that we call standards now came from plays, or came from movies, but a standard is never a standard if it’s only played once. It’s got to be played over and over again in different kind of situations. And that’s what makes it a standard. And I mean I’d like to see more of our music, meaning the jazz compositions, becoming standard material. I guess what helps is the kind of genres that it’s played in, the kind of situations that the music is used for.

And then he passed away, this was in 1960 when I went out on the road. Then in 1965 he passed away. But by that time I had been with Gene Ammons and Sonny Stitt, I was with Sarah Vaughan, I’d been with Dakota Staton and I was with Nancy Wilson. And he had seen things start to happen for me. 275990.evidence: Now I never heard Louis Armstrong do a tribute to anybody. His great tribute was to carry the music on.
275990.subject: Buster Williams

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: Yeah, the music of. Now I never heard Louis Armstrong do a tribute to anybody. His great tribute was to carry the music on. When you listen to Louis Armstrong you heard those who preceded him. He didn’t turn his back on the future and face the past to give validity to music. This music is only validified and further advanced in its credibility by those who look forward and constantly advance the music, you know, and build on top of what has already happened. And that idea is being totally lost. Those who want to do that are having a hard time. Those who are willing to turn their back on the future and look in the past and do a tribute to this and a tribute to that, you know, and just step back in time, they are being accepted a lot more than those who have a vision. So in many ways the Jazz at Lincoln Center has been a great deterrent to the development of this music. And then taking the young people now, look I love the fact that we have young people who want to play the music. When I started playing the music I was a young person. I was 14 years old. And you look at Kenny Dorham in his prime and Clifford Brown and all of the great heroes, they all were young. But what was happening then was a master-disciple relationship that is as essential now as it was then, maybe even more so now, because we’ve got to fight for it. You’ve got to learn from those who preceded you. And what better way than to be amongst them? You know the days when kings walked the earth, you know you wanted to come to New York because — and you wanted to stand out on 52nd and Broadway in hopes that one of your heroes would walk by, and they did. And then you went running behind. You’d find out where they were playing and you went and you crawled through the window or whatever you had to do to get in and listen to them. So in many ways the music — you know and you can’t even say that it’s more popular now. Okay it’s being used. Jazz sells everything. And there’s always those who want to be in the in. So it’s hip to have some kind of knowledge or some kind of understanding of jazz now.

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: You know? Now what does that say? We’ve got thousands — we’ve got many great musicians out here who need somebody to buy their records. But the top selling records in jazz in 2001 were Duke Ellington and Louis Armstrong. So now what did Ken Burns do for the music?

275990.evidence: nobody sounded like Bird and nobody sounded like Miles. Miles was wise enough to early on realize that going after playing like Diz wasn’t going to be his claim to fame.
275990.subject: Buster Williams
275990.audit: {"change": "source fixed", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: My concept of a sound came from my father. Because my father told me early on that that was what I had to go for. And see in the days when I came up sound was everything. You listened to Coleman Hawkins and you knew Coleman Hawkins as soon as he played one note. And you knew it wasn’t Ben Webster because nobody else sounded like Ben Webster and nobody sounded like Coleman Hawkins and nobody sounded like Prez and nobody sounded like Bird and nobody sounded like Miles. Miles was wise enough to early on realize that going after playing like Diz wasn’t going to be his claim to fame. Everybody had their own sound. Even piano players had their own sound. Horace Silver sounded totally different from Oscar Peterson, who sounded totally different from Art Tatum, who sounded totally different from Fats Waller, who sounded totally different from Phineas Newborn. All these guys — sound was the thing. To the day nobody has ever been able to copy the sound of Art Blakey on the drums. The way Art Blakey plays the drums, the way Elvin Jones played the drums, the way Philly Jo Jones played the drums, the way Art Taylor played the drums. Everybody had their own sound. Sound was the thing. Nowadays, this is the age of mediocrity. So many people are going after the wrong thing. Drummers are trying to learn a bunch of stuff on a snare drum rather than how to get a sound on the ride cymbal. They don’t realize the great value of a Ben Riley, how to ride, how to make a gig with nothing but the ride cymbal. Billy Higgins. Billy Higgins made a gig one time, the drums showed up late, so he took a chair — he had his cymbals so he took a chair and he played the chair and his cymbals. And when the drums came he was swinging so hard nobody wanted him to set up the drums. He played the whole gig with a wooden chair and a ride cymbal. Papa Jo Jones used to come to Bradley’s. Remember Bradley’s? Bradley’s was the infamous after hours place for New York, for duos. Piano and bass. Papa Jones used to come to Bradley’s with his brushes and his newspaper under his arm and he’d sit at the bar in front of the piano player and drummer and take his newspaper and fold it up, you know a folded up New York Times, and take his brushes and sit there and play brushes on the newspaper, and swing until the cows come home. I mean that was a climate, you came from the place of creativity in the days when I was learning how to play this music. So when you talk about my sound, it’s not — I worked on it, that’s what I went after. My father told me when I started working with all of these different singers and one night I was talking to my father, complaining © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: My earliest recollection of my father playing the bass is when I was a little boy. He used to sit on the sofa and put the bass between his legs and bow. One of his favorites was Slam Stewart. And my father — and Slam Stewart always had this, he developed this great bowing style, singing, the same phrases that he would play. And my father used to emulate that. And he was a great musician. He played piano and he also played drums. And so he was always playing music around the house. There was records, his musicians would come over to the house and they’d rehearse. Once he had a duo, he and a piano player, they were working together as a duo. They’d play all these different gigs. They were called The Rollers. Kenny Andrews was his name. Kenny Andrews would come over and he and my father would practice and I’d sit there and I’d listen to them, and they used to sing, play and sing. And then when I was about 16 or 17, my father used to start taking me out on gigs with him. And he would play drums and I would play the bass. So that was my earliest recollection of — well of course when I was a kid I’d see him leaving out on gigs, I used to run behind his car sometimes. He’s leaving out on the road, you know — “Daddy, Daddy, Daddy.” I remember one time running behind his car and my father was heartbroken because he had to go away. So very early on.

sources.text: My concept of a sound came from my father. Because my father told me early on that that was what I had to go for. And see in the days when I came up sound was everything. You listened to Coleman Hawkins and you knew Coleman Hawkins as soon as he played one note. And you knew it wasn’t Ben Webster because nobody else sounded like Ben Webster and nobody sounded like Coleman Hawkins and nobody sounded like Prez and nobody sounded like Bird and nobody sounded like Miles. Miles was wise enough to early on realize that going after playing like Diz wasn’t going to be his claim to fame. Everybody had their own sound. Even piano players had their own sound. Horace Silver sounded totally different from Oscar Peterson, who sounded totally different from Art Tatum, who sounded totally different from Fats Waller, who sounded totally different from Phineas Newborn. All these guys — sound was the thing. To the day nobody has ever been able to copy the sound of Art Blakey on the drums. The way Art Blakey plays the drums, the way Elvin Jones played the drums, the way Philly Jo Jones played the drums, the way Art Taylor played the drums. Everybody had their own sound. Sound was the thing. Nowadays, this is the age of mediocrity. So many people are going after the wrong thing. Drummers are trying to learn a bunch of stuff on a snare drum rather than how to get a sound on the ride cymbal. They don’t realize the great value of a Ben Riley, how to ride, how to make a gig with nothing but the ride cymbal. Billy Higgins. Billy Higgins made a gig one time, the drums showed up late, so he took a chair — he had his cymbals so he took a chair and he played the chair and his cymbals. And when the drums came he was swinging so hard nobody wanted him to set up the drums. He played the whole gig with a wooden chair and a ride cymbal. Papa Jo Jones used to come to Bradley’s. Remember Bradley’s? Bradley’s was the infamous after hours place for New York, for duos. Piano and bass. Papa Jones used to come to Bradley’s with his brushes and his newspaper under his arm and he’d sit at the bar in front of the piano player and drummer and take his newspaper and fold it up, you know a folded up New York Times, and take his brushes and sit there and play brushes on the newspaper, and swing until the cows come home. I mean that was a climate, you came from the place of creativity in the days when I was learning how to play this music. So when you talk about my sound, it’s not — I worked on it, that’s what I went after. My father told me when I started working with all of these different singers and one night I was talking to my father, complaining © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: Time is money. When I first moved out to California and then Ray Brown left Oscar Peterson and he came to California, then Ray Brown and I became very close and I became his number one sub. And he would send me on anything and everything. One time I had to go out to Universal Studios to do “McKenna’s Gold” with Gregory Peck. And I was the principal bassist. We had eight basses. All right? So Ray couldn’t make it and he was the principal bassist, so now I’m the principal bassist. I said “Ray, what do you want me to do?” He said “go on now and take charge.” You know? Any doubt that I had he never had. So I’m the one determining when it’s down bow, when it’s up bow. But you learn how to adapt real quick. And on these dates here, if it’s not done today it won’t be done. You don’t have two or three days, much less two or three months, to do © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

275990.subject: Buster Williams
275990.audit: {"change": "sideman on the interviewee's own album", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "co-appeared on Buster Williams' 1987 album for In and Out Records"}}

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: Yeah. You know I’ve been trying to be really busy with that band since 1990. I did an album for a label, In and Out Records, a label out of Germany. I did it in 1987. And it was released in Europe and Asia until 1995 when it was released here. But I did that album and I wrote out a majority of the music for it, Herbie Hancock was on it, Wayne Shorter, Al Foster, trumpet player named Shunzo Ohno. And after doing the album, six months later I still liked it. You know? I mean you know how when you’re working on something, you live with it so long and when it’s done it’s done, it’s like a release and a relief, and if you never hear it again that’s fine. But I liked it and I said well maybe it’s time now for me to put my own band together, contrary to the way things are these days. You get a brand new shiny horn and the first thing you think about is making a CD and putting a band together. I mean because the powers that be tell you that’s what you’re supposed to do. Now when I came up it was all about apprenticeship, which is a valuable commodity that’s being lost these days. But anyway that was the inspiration for me to put the band together, the fact that I still liked the music and maybe I would enjoy a night’s performance of playing my own music. I sure did have my own, what I consider to be my concept of what an integral working unit should sound like. Also, as Duke Ellington said, one of the greatest reasons to have a band is so that you can hear your stuff.

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: There hasn’t been too much. There hasn’t been a replacement. In fact I teach at the New School. I’ve been there about six or seven years I guess. Maybe seven or eight years. And it’s very interesting to see what happens semester after semester. The great thing about the New School at first, and probably still is, was the fact that young musicians from all over the world could focus on coming to New York where the music thrives, where the music is born, where the music is being developed constantly. And study at a university with these musicians who are active and constantly re-developing the music. But where do they go after school? Nowadays you bring your students together and you find out that what they’re doing after school is this guy over here, he and his friend have a studio where they’ve got all of the latest Pro Tools and whatever, and they’re actively involved in becoming producers of new hip hoppers. And then this person over here is carrying on a day job or a part time job at a bakery or something and is looking for somewhere to go out and play his instrument. And this person here has his own band and he’s working at night at the Knitting Factory or these little unknown clubs. But none of them have anywhere to go where they can sit for an evening but just paying five dollars such as you used to be able to do at Birdland, the real Birdland, and sit there all evening and sip a glass of beer in the peanut gallery, and nobody bothered you. And you could listen to two bands — Miles Davis’ band and as soon as he finishes, here comes Sonny Rollins’ band. Or you go down to the Jazz Gallery and you listen and there is John Coltrane with his famous band with Elvin Jones and Jimmy Garrison. And when they get off the bandstand then there’s Horace Silver. Those kind of things don’t exist anymore. So what you try and do is make sure that all of your students have an opportunity to come hear your band, my band. Like next week I’m at the Vanguard. So all my students are going to come down to the Vanguard and they can hear the band. There was a little club for a while called Small’s. I don’t know if it still exists. But night after night all of the young guys and girls would crowd down there and hope to have a chance to play. There’s a few places around the city, but it’s not like it used to be. And now I’m not crying for it to be like it used to be. Nothing is like it used to be. That’s the nature of things. Everything changes. Everything is in a constant state of flux, as it should be. But there should be some wisdom that’s garnished, an accumulation of understanding how things go and how to make things better as we continue on. For something as alive as this music, it’s like a © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

sources.text: She’s a very good singer. And she wants me to write music that fits her in. And a couple of years back I did a project for a Japanese singer and I wrote these songs and I wrote lyrics. sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: had been out for about a week and I went over to The Showboat. And after the first set Gene Ammons and Sonny Stitt took me aside and started calling me Junior. They were like my two daddies. And asked me to stay with the band. So this was Friday. Saturday night after the gig I went back to Camden to pack my bag and come back over to Philadelphia to meet everybody. We were leaving out for Chicago about four in the morning. And my father and my mother helped me pack my bag. My father gave me one of his suitcases. It looked like a checkerboard, one of those checkerboard suitcases with the strap that went around the center of it you know? And my father told me all of the things to look out for on the road. How to act like I was smoking reefer and not really be smoking reefer. How to always keep my bus fare home. All of these things he told me about. Everything he told me about I ran into. And he was like that. He was prepared for me to become a musician and he prepared me to become a musician. My mother, I know her heart was pounding, you know just her little baby getting ready to go out, I had never been away from home for any length of time. So he was more prepared for it than she was. And then he passed away, this was in 1960 when I went out on the road. Then in 1965 he passed away. But by that time I had been with Gene Ammons and Sonny Stitt, I was with Sarah Vaughan, I’d been with Dakota Staton and I was with Nancy Wilson. And he had seen things start to happen for me. I had made many records by that time. And he was proud.

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: Well he was a little more accepting of it than my mother was. My mother said, “Oh my goodness, another musician.” And then when I started traveling it was like she said to me one day she says, “If I knew that this is what I had to expect when I first let you go out on your first gig I would never have done it.” And I started traveling all over the world and stuff. I mean it’s a hard life on those who love you you know? It’s a hard life anyway but you don’t look at it that way. I mean to this day I still love to travel. And my happiest time is on the bandstand. I don’t want too much time between one gig and the next. But my father, now you know the first time I went out on the road was with Gene Ammons and Sonny Stitt. And the gig started on a Friday night. Nelson Boyd, remember the bass player Nelson Boyd? Dizzy Gillespie wrote the tune “Half Nelson” for him — no I mean Charlie Parker. I think Bird wrote the song “Half Nelson.” He wrote that for Nelson Boyd. Nelson Boyd was a good friend of the family’s. Me and my father were close buddies. Nelson was working at The Showboat in Philadelphia with Gene Ammons and Sonny Stitt. The gig got started on Tuesday. He couldn’t make the gig Friday and Saturday. And so he asked my father to do it. And my father was working so my father sent me. And that was my first really big gig. I guess I was 16. I was close to 17 because I was almost ready to graduate from high school. And he was like that. He was prepared for me to become a musician and he prepared me to become a musician. My mother, I know her heart was pounding, you know just her little baby getting ready to go out, I had never been away from home for any length of time. So he was more prepared for it than she was. And then he passed away, this was in 1960 when I went out on the road. Then in 1965 he passed away. 275990.evidence: nobody else sounded like Ben Webster
275990.subject: Buster Williams

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: My concept of a sound came from my father. Because my father told me early on that that was what I had to go for. And see in the days when I came up sound was everything. You listened to Coleman Hawkins and you knew Coleman Hawkins as soon as he played one note. And you knew it wasn’t Ben Webster because nobody else sounded like Ben Webster and nobody sounded like Coleman Hawkins and nobody sounded like Prez and nobody sounded like Bird and nobody sounded like Miles. Miles was wise enough to early on realize that going after playing like Diz wasn’t going to be his claim to fame. Everybody had their own sound. Even piano players had their own sound. Horace Silver sounded totally different from Oscar Peterson, who sounded totally different from Art Tatum, who sounded totally different from Fats Waller, who sounded totally different from Phineas Newborn. All these guys — sound was the thing. To the day nobody has ever been able to copy the sound of Art Blakey on the drums. The way Art Blakey plays the drums, the way Elvin Jones played the drums, the way Philly Jo Jones played the drums, the way Art Taylor played the drums. Everybody had their own sound. Sound was the thing. Nowadays, this is the age of mediocrity. So many people are going after the wrong thing. Drummers are trying to learn a bunch of stuff on a snare drum rather than how to get a sound on the ride cymbal. They don’t realize the great value of a Ben Riley, how to ride, how to make a gig with nothing but the ride cymbal. Billy Higgins. Billy Higgins made a gig one time, the drums showed up late, so he took a chair — he had his cymbals so he took a chair and he played the chair and his cymbals. And when the drums came he was swinging so hard nobody wanted him to set up the drums. He played the whole gig with a wooden chair and a ride cymbal. Papa Jo Jones used to come to Bradley’s. Remember Bradley’s? Bradley’s was the infamous after hours place for New York, for duos. Piano and bass. Papa Jones used to come to Bradley’s with his brushes and his newspaper under his arm and he’d sit at the bar in front of the piano player and drummer and take his newspaper and fold it up, you know a folded up New York Times, and take his brushes and sit there and play brushes on the newspaper, and swing until the cows come home. I mean that was a climate, you came from the place of creativity in the days when I was learning how to play this music. So when you talk about my sound, it’s not — I worked on it, that’s what I went after. My father told me when I started working with all of these different singers and one night I was talking to my father, complaining © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

275990.evidence: One of the things that Herbie Hancock and Wayne Shorter and Ron Carter, since when you’re talking about Herbie and Wayne and Ron, you know you don’t have to use their last names, everybody knows who you’re talking about.
275990.subject: Buster Williams
275990.audit: {"change": "only discussed as a composer whose music Herbie/Wayne played; no personal tie shown (was collaborated with)", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "member of the Herbie Hancock Quartet"}}

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: Yeah. You know a friend of mine, we were just talking about that the other day. One of the things that Herbie Hancock and Wayne Shorter and Ron Carter, since when you’re talking about Herbie and Wayne and Ron, you know you don’t have to use their last names, everybody knows who you’re talking about. One of the things that perpetrated their music was the fact that they played each other’s music. And that’s sort of the kind of thing that Bird and Monk and Miles and Dizzy, they did also. They played each other’s music, which is what we need to do more of. We need to play more of our contemporaries’ music. And that helps make the music standards. A lot of the standards that we call standards now came from plays, or came from movies, but a standard is never a standard if it’s only played once. It’s got to be played over and over again in different kind of situations. And that’s what makes it a standard. And I mean I’d like to see more of our music, meaning the jazz compositions, becoming standard material. I guess what helps is the kind of genres that it’s played in, the kind of situations that the music is used for.

275990.evidence: And you look at Kenny Dorham in his prime and Clifford Brown and all of the great heroes, they all were young.
275990.subject: Buster Williams

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: Yeah, the music of. Now I never heard Louis Armstrong do a tribute to anybody. His great tribute was to carry the music on. When you listen to Louis Armstrong you heard those who preceded him. He didn’t turn his back on the future and face the past to give validity to music. This music is only validified and further advanced in its credibility by those who look forward and constantly advance the music, you know, and build on top of what has already happened. And that idea is being totally lost. Those who want to do that are having a hard time. Those who are willing to turn their back on the future and look in the past and do a tribute to this and a tribute to that, you know, and just step back in time, they are being accepted a lot more than those who have a vision. So in many ways the Jazz at Lincoln Center has been a great deterrent to the development of this music. And then taking the young people now, look I love the fact that we have young people who want to play the music. When I started playing the music I was a young person. I was 14 years old. And you look at Kenny Dorham in his prime and Clifford Brown and all of the great heroes, they all were young. But what was happening then was a master-disciple relationship that is as essential now as it was then, maybe even more so now, because we’ve got to fight for it. You’ve got to learn from those who preceded you. And what better way than to be amongst them? You know the days when kings walked the earth, you know you wanted to come to New York because — and you wanted to stand out on 52nd and Broadway in hopes that one of your heroes would walk by, and they did. And then you went running behind. You’d find out where they were playing and you went and you crawled through the window or whatever you had to do to get in and listen to them. So in many ways the music — you know and you can’t even say that it’s more popular now. Okay it’s being used. Jazz sells everything. And there’s always those who want to be in the in. So it’s hip to have some kind of knowledge or some kind of understanding of jazz now.

275990.proposed: drummer on Williams's own 1987 album for In and Out Records (Williams leader, wrote most of the music)
275990.evidence: I did that album and I wrote out a majority of the music for it, Herbie Hancock was on it, Wayne Shorter, Al Foster, trumpet player named Shunzo Ohno.
275990.subject: Buster Williams
275990.audit: {"change": "sideman on the interviewee's own album", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "drummer on Buster Williams' 1987 album for In and Out Records"}}

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: Yeah. You know I’ve been trying to be really busy with that band since 1990. I did an album for a label, In and Out Records, a label out of Germany. I did it in 1987. And it was released in Europe and Asia until 1995 when it was released here. But I did that album and I wrote out a majority of the music for it, Herbie Hancock was on it, Wayne Shorter, Al Foster, trumpet player named Shunzo Ohno. And after doing the album, six months later I still liked it. You know? I mean you know how when you’re working on something, you live with it so long and when it’s done it’s done, it’s like a release and a relief, and if you never hear it again that’s fine. But I liked it and I said well maybe it’s time now for me to put my own band together, contrary to the way things are these days. You get a brand new shiny horn and the first thing you think about is making a CD and putting a band together. I mean because the powers that be tell you that’s what you’re supposed to do. Now when I came up it was all about apprenticeship, which is a valuable commodity that’s being lost these days. But anyway that was the inspiration for me to put the band together, the fact that I still liked the music and maybe I would enjoy a night’s performance of playing my own music. I sure did have my own, what I consider to be my concept of what an integral working unit should sound like. Also, as Duke Ellington said, one of the greatest reasons to have a band is so that you can hear your stuff.

275990.proposed: pianist in his father's duo The Rollers; rehearsed at the family home
275990.evidence: Kenny Andrews would come over and he and my father would practice and I’d sit there and I’d listen to them
275990.third_party: {"subject": "Kenny Andrews", "relation": "in music group with", "object": "Buster Williams's father"}
275990.subject: Buster Williams
275990.audit: {"change": "visited the house while he listened", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: My earliest recollection of my father playing the bass is when I was a little boy. He used to sit on the sofa and put the bass between his legs and bow. One of his favorites was Slam Stewart. And my father — and Slam Stewart always had this, he developed this great bowing style, singing, the same phrases that he would play. And my father used to emulate that. And he was a great musician. He played piano and he also played drums. And so he was always playing music around the house. There was records, his musicians would come over to the house and they’d rehearse. Once he had a duo, he and a piano player, they were working together as a duo. They’d play all these different gigs. They were called The Rollers. Kenny Andrews was his name. Kenny Andrews would come over and he and my father would practice and I’d sit there and I’d listen to them, and they used to sing, play and sing. And then when I was about 16 or 17, my father used to start taking me out on gigs with him. And he would play drums and I would play the bass. So that was my earliest recollection of — well of course when I was a kid I’d see him leaving out on gigs, I used to run behind his car sometimes. He’s leaving out on the road, you know — “Daddy, Daddy, Daddy.” I remember one time running behind his car and my father was heartbroken because he had to go away. So very early on.

275990.evidence: And you look at Kenny Dorham in his prime and Clifford Brown and all of the great heroes, they all were young.
275990.subject: Buster Williams
275990.audit: {"change": "old evidence did not name him", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: Yeah, the music of. Now I never heard Louis Armstrong do a tribute to anybody. His great tribute was to carry the music on. When you listen to Louis Armstrong you heard those who preceded him. He didn’t turn his back on the future and face the past to give validity to music. This music is only validified and further advanced in its credibility by those who look forward and constantly advance the music, you know, and build on top of what has already happened. And that idea is being totally lost. Those who want to do that are having a hard time. Those who are willing to turn their back on the future and look in the past and do a tribute to this and a tribute to that, you know, and just step back in time, they are being accepted a lot more than those who have a vision. So in many ways the Jazz at Lincoln Center has been a great deterrent to the development of this music. And then taking the young people now, look I love the fact that we have young people who want to play the music. When I started playing the music I was a young person. I was 14 years old. And you look at Kenny Dorham in his prime and Clifford Brown and all of the great heroes, they all were young. But what was happening then was a master-disciple relationship that is as essential now as it was then, maybe even more so now, because we’ve got to fight for it. sources.text: There hasn’t been too much. There hasn’t been a replacement. In fact I teach at the New School. I’ve been there about six or seven years I guess. Maybe seven or eight years. The great thing about the New School at first, and probably still is, was the fact that young musicians from all over the world could focus on coming to New York where the music thrives, where the music is born, where the music is being developed constantly. And study at a university with these musicians who are active and constantly re-developing the music. But where do they go after school? Nowadays you bring your students together and you find out that what they’re doing after school is this guy over here, he and his friend have a studio where they’ve got all of the latest Pro Tools and whatever, and they’re actively involved in becoming producers of new hip hoppers. And then this person over here is carrying on a day job or a part time job at a bakery or something and is looking for somewhere to go out and play his instrument. And this person here has his own band and he’s working at night at the Knitting Factory or these little unknown clubs. But none of them have anywhere to go where they can sit for an evening but just paying five dollars such as you used to be able to do at Birdland, the real Birdland, and sit there all evening and sip a glass of beer in the peanut gallery, and nobody bothered you. And you could listen to two bands — Miles Davis’ band and as soon as he finishes, here comes Sonny Rollins’ band. Or you go down to the Jazz Gallery and you listen and there is John Coltrane with his famous band with Elvin Jones and Jimmy Garrison. And when they get off the bandstand then there’s Horace Silver. Those kind of things don’t exist anymore. So what you try and do is make sure that all of your students have an opportunity to come hear your band, my band. Like next week I’m at the Vanguard. So all my students are going to come down to the Vanguard and they can hear the band. There was a little club for a while called Small’s. I don’t know if it still exists. 275990.subject: Buster Williams
275990.audit: {"change": "sideman on the interviewee's own album", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "na", "proposed": "trumpet player on the interviewee's 1987 album for In and Out Records"}}

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: Yeah. You know I’ve been trying to be really busy with that band since 1990. I did an album for a label, In and Out Records, a label out of Germany. I did it in 1987. And it was released in Europe and Asia until 1995 when it was released here. But I did that album and I wrote out a majority of the music for it, Herbie Hancock was on it, Wayne Shorter, Al Foster, trumpet player named Shunzo Ohno. And after doing the album, six months later I still liked it. You know? I mean you know how when you’re working on something, you live with it so long and when it’s done it’s done, it’s like a release and a relief, and if you never hear it again that’s fine. But I liked it and I said well maybe it’s time now for me to put my own band together, contrary to the way things are these days. You get a brand new shiny horn and the first thing you think about is making a CD and putting a band together. I mean because the powers that be tell you that’s what you’re supposed to do. Now when I came up it was all about apprenticeship, which is a valuable commodity that’s being lost these days. But anyway that was the inspiration for me to put the band together, the fact that I still liked the music and maybe I would enjoy a night’s performance of playing my own music. I sure did have my own, what I consider to be my concept of what an integral working unit should sound like. Also, as Duke Ellington said, one of the greatest reasons to have a band is so that you can hear your stuff.

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: Well a one bass family. I mean well I’m the second bass. My father was a bass player and he was my teacher.

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: My earliest recollection of my father playing the bass is when I was a little boy. He used to sit on the sofa and put the bass between his legs and bow. One of his favorites was Slam Stewart. And my father — and Slam Stewart always had this, he developed this great bowing style, singing, the same phrases that he would play. And my father used to emulate that. And he was a great musician. He played piano and he also played drums. And so he was always playing music around the house. There was records, his musicians would come over to the house and they’d rehearse. Once he had a duo, he and a piano player, they were working together as a duo. They’d play all these different gigs. They were called The Rollers. Kenny Andrews was his name. Kenny Andrews would come over and he and my father would practice and I’d sit there and I’d listen to them, and they used to sing, play and sing. And then when I was about 16 or 17, my father used to start taking me out on gigs with him. And he would play drums and I would play the bass. So that was my earliest recollection of — well of course when I was a kid I’d see him leaving out on gigs, I used to run behind his car sometimes. He’s leaving out on the road, you know — “Daddy, Daddy, Daddy.” I remember one time running behind his car and my father was heartbroken because he had to go away. So very early on.

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: My concept of a sound came from my father. Because my father told me early on that that was what I had to go for. And see in the days when I came up sound was everything. You listened to Coleman Hawkins and you knew Coleman Hawkins as soon as he played one note. And you knew it wasn’t Ben Webster because nobody else sounded like Ben Webster and nobody sounded like Coleman Hawkins and nobody sounded like Prez and nobody sounded like Bird and nobody sounded like Miles. Miles was wise enough to early on realize that going after playing like Diz wasn’t going to be his claim to fame. Everybody had their own sound. Even piano players had their own sound. Horace Silver sounded totally different from Oscar Peterson, who sounded totally different from Art Tatum, who sounded totally different from Fats Waller, who sounded totally different from Phineas Newborn. All these guys — sound was the thing. To the day nobody has ever been able to copy the sound of Art Blakey on the drums. The way Art Blakey plays the drums, the way Elvin Jones played the drums, the way Philly Jo Jones played the drums, the way Art Taylor played the drums. Everybody had their own sound. Sound was the thing. Nowadays, this is the age of mediocrity. So many people are going after the wrong thing. Drummers are trying to learn a bunch of stuff on a snare drum rather than how to get a sound on the ride cymbal. They don’t realize the great value of a Ben Riley, how to ride, how to make a gig with nothing but the ride cymbal. Billy Higgins. Billy Higgins made a gig one time, the drums showed up late, so he took a chair — he had his cymbals so he took a chair and he played the chair and his cymbals. And when the drums came he was swinging so hard nobody wanted him to set up the drums. He played the whole gig with a wooden chair and a ride cymbal. Papa Jo Jones used to come to Bradley’s. Remember Bradley’s? Bradley’s was the infamous after hours place for New York, for duos. Piano and bass. Papa Jones used to come to Bradley’s with his brushes and his newspaper under his arm and he’d sit at the bar in front of the piano player and drummer and take his newspaper and fold it up, you know a folded up New York Times, and take his brushes and sit there and play brushes on the newspaper, and swing until the cows come home. I mean that was a climate, you came from the place of creativity in the days when I was learning how to play this music. So when you talk about my sound, it’s not — I worked on it, that’s what I went after. My father told me when I started working with all of these different singers and one night I was talking to my father, complaining © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

sources.speaker: BW
sources.text: about the fact that the singers, you know you’re playing the same thing over and over again. He said, “Anytime that you’re able to have your instrument in your hand is a moment of reverie.” And he said, “If your responsibility tonight is to do nothing but play one whole note C, play it better tonight than you played it last night, with the resolve that you’ll play it better tomorrow than you play it tonight.” And he used to make me — he would allow no slack in my left hand. When my hands would hurt, my fingers would be sore, and the muscles in here just feel like they’re going to pop, he told me that the sound was coming from my left hand, and he was very strict about my left hand being correct at all times. Never relaxing. So when you talk about my sound, that’s something that has been my predominant goal.

And I might as well — I mean really what Barry was saying and I understand — I kind of understood it then — that this kind of excellence you have this kind of attitude about it no matter what you’re doing and so when you’re starting, when you’re playing music then that same level of willing to invest is still there so it’s not like — you use this for everything including music. sources.text: beats — so the harmony is moving at a quick pace. It’s not there for four bars, eight bars. But it’s moving every two bars. And the tempo is at a good clip. So there is a way that you have to look at all of that harmonic minutiae and there’s a way that you have to look at a broader arc over that, which means you really do have to have your ears on and think melodically at the same time that you’re adhering to time and space. So here again you’re really walking and chewing gum at the same time. And see here’s where all of this perception and how you’re looking at things come in. Now everybody’s different and there’s a lot of ways to look at music. You can look at music rhythmically only, harmonically only, or melodically only. But the real deal is amalgamating all of that into one homogeneous behavior and then so therefore having the output be whatever it is. But see there again lies this different — different ways to think. And everybody’s different. Yeah. So this is what Barry meant by you can’t be a C student with some of this stuff here. You know? This is some stuff you’ve got to deal with. Now having said that there’s also this part of the equation. The subconscious mind, who we are as human beings and people. Already here is every note that we’ve — we’ve heard every note it is. Because this big piece of meat is the greatest computer in the world. There’s only twelve notes. We’ve heard every one of them since we came out of — since we pop out of the womb. We’ve heard them. Okay we’ve heard rhythms, we’ve heard chords — whether we know what to think about them, how to think of them, it’s already there. So a lot of times success is based on what part of the mind, or what kind of mentation should I put in play to get the best results, and therein goes the four dimensional chess again and how people think you know, and you’ve got the variety of personality and then I can only say how I approach it. I’m sure other people approach it another way. But see yet again, I’ll look at all of that and realize say a tune like “Countdown” where the harmony is moving very quickly, but I will still — part of my way of thinking is what are some of the common notes with all of that harmonic movement. Because they can be moving quickly and changing quickly but there are certain common notes that’s connecting all of them or at least some of them. So your melodic ear has to be on. And see your cognitive mind, your analytical mind has to understand the form and structure of what’s actually going on. But how you artistically behave is a whole ‘nother game. That’s another part of the mind. The analytical part will just say oh, you know it’s “Countdown” so it’s going up a minor third and then it’s going to the fourth and then another minor third. You can get into all of that technical stuff and musical harmony and theory and all that. But how do you behave with that. Spend time — with time and space in real time and be creative. And that’s really something. But the way I look at things, I try to look for what I call as best as possible a “unified field theory.” Kind of what Einstein was looking for, a “unified field theory.” What is the equation that really kind of nails the whole shebang? 53571.proposed: sat in with her group at the 52nd St/8th Ave club (1952); friend who asked her opinion of his writing and strings; first heard in Kansas City

53571.subject: Mary Lou Williams
53571.audit: {"change": "relcheck: he sat in and played with her group one night (120.1) - a one-off performance, so played with outranks friend of", "previous": {"relation": "has met", "direction": "na", "proposed": "met while working at Wehnwood Beach"}}

sources.speaker: W:
sources.text: I said, "No, man, not the condition you're in." He said, "I'll do it, Mary. Anything you tell me I'll do." He said, "You know I'm not allowed to play in Birdland or any of the clubs." You know, that's during that period. So I told him, "Get up on the stand and let the people see how great you are." The place was really packed because see a lot of the people had followed me from the East Side. Some of these people had been to a ballet or something this night and they came in. They were all up in the balcony; it was Sunday night. Charlie Parker got up on the stand... he said, "Play the Kansas City Blues." Listen, I've never heard Coltrane play what that boy did! No! I talk about it often. When he finished the people in the place stood up and applauded. During the time that he played I don't know what carried us along with him because there were sounds that we'd never played before, Oscar and the bass and piano. To start out a blues - I think one of the guys had played one chorus...Charlie Parker kept going to keys and he kept going through changes... The one on the bass said, "Mary, where is he now?" I said, "Man, don't talk to me now," because Oscar said if anybody came up on the stand they were going to help him, so when Charlie stepped up there he said, "Lou, let's blow." So we were listening to his changes during it. I've never heard him play like that before in my life, the way he played.

sources.speaker: W:
sources.text: Well, you can, but you can't shift overnight; you have to rehearse with them. We went in there and started blowing. Oscar was great to play with because we composed at least 3 tunes a night or more. He'd start a bass figure and I would play, and that is really my schtick, my whole way of doing. I like to compose while I'm playing. We had a great session going except then he was crazy about his "Moscow Mule". He'd go around the corner on Eighth Avenue and I'd have to go to get him. So one night I got a stick and I hit him on his knee and I said, "Listen, you had too much Moscow Mule." He laughed about it, you know, and I decided to put him on cello. So I called in Percy Heath, for bass, a terrific bass player also. So one night I was blowing like mad. Oscar was on the cello, he turned around and said, "You don't blow like that with me." I said, "Yes, because you high off of Moscow Mule." So I did put the musicians back to work there in this particular club. Charlie Parker came in one night and he said to me, "Lou, let's get a band or something together. You know all the cats always want me to get a band with you."

sources.speaker: W
sources.text: Oh, yes. Charlie Parker would always call and ask me if I liked some things he had written and when he did the strings he asked me to come down to Birdland. He said, "I want you to tell me really what you think of it, Lou." I went down. Charlie was a wonderful guy. I was at Birdland one day - you know that bar was terrible.

53571.evidence: Father Woods was my confessor.

sources.speaker: W:
sources.text: Father Woods was my confessor. Professor Barry Ulanov got a hold of him to give me instructions.

sources.speaker: W:
sources.text: Father Anthony Woods, S. J., Jesuit. I'm telling you he was something else. When he passed away about 6 or 8 years ago I thought I was going to die myself. I didn't know I was leaning so hard. He did everything in his power to help me back to music and things that were still happening with me in a strange way, all this ESP working. He told me to call him any time and sometimes I called him 4 o'clock in the morning. He and Lorraine Gillespie, they had a ball on the phone when they talked about me. It was so funny, some of the things I'd call them about. He was so very kind to me. He went along with me and he finally got me back to jazz. When I went in the Hickory House about 7 years ago, he was there practically every night.

sources.speaker: W
sources.text: lyric to Father Woods and he said, no, they didn't capture the spirit of St. Martin. So I told him, "Well, you do it." He said, "I never wrote anything in poetry in my life, Mary, and can't do it." I said, "I'll tap it out for you." I did and he wrote a very beautiful lyric, he did, he wrote it. He had never written one before. So I asked him, "Let's do a blues." He said, "O.K." I said, "I'll get some slang words from Babs Gonzales." He said, "O.K." I said, "I'll call you tomorrow night." When I called back with all this slang I said "coat"; he said "rug"; "car"; he said "short" "chorus". He knew all the words. That's how he was, you see.

sources.speaker: W:
sources.text: Seymour and Jeanette. A strange thing happened. We came to New York - I think it was New York we had gone, either New York or Rochester, some place. So we were getting ready to rehearse. I'd always stand at the piano and look at it before I tackled it. I was just sitting there. So Seymour came out and they introduced - I don't think they introduced him to everybody. He just came out, because he was sitting there and was irritable all the time. He said, "What's that girl doing, sitting at the piano?" Nobody would say anything. He said, "Well, get her off the stage so we can play." Nobody would say anything. So I didn't move so he said, "Let's start the rehearsal." So I started playing and both of them had a fit. They didn't know that John had a woman with them. They had a fit because during this period because a woman was not really allowed to be in with a group of men or anything. They were so surprised. So he said, "We can't take her. We can't let not Keith but the manager see her because she's a black woman and we've got to put pants on her." They were wondering what they were going to do. They said, "She's good, she's good!" So John said, "Forget it; listen to her play." So we went on with that and everything was fine. About 6 months or a year later Seymour died and John Williams and the combo and I worked with Jeanette for a while till we were stranded in New York.

sources.speaker: W:
sources.text: One of the greatest acts on - I'll tell you, during that period you know how prejudiced they were. They wouldn't dare have a black person on Keith, Pantages, that. But Seymour and Jeanette were the only black team on Keith circuit, Pantages, and all - and Bill Bojangles. They only booked those two people. So John Williams received a wire that they needed a combo because Seymour did a strutting act and what not. He was very good at it but he had a bad heart, so he thought that if he got a small combo that would help him along. So he wired John and said he'd be making $75. Woo, that was like making a thousand dollars a week, you know! So we joined -

sources.speaker: W
sources.text: Yes. Florence Mills was a very good friend of Jeanette's. Jeanette used to take me everywhere with her. See I was very young and she wouldn't dare to leave me alone.

sources.speaker: W:

53571.evidence: Count Basie and I had about 30 pupils between us, that we were teaching to play jazz.

53571.audit: {"change": "under-claim: joint teaching in Kansas City", "previous": {"relation": "knows of", "direction": "na", "proposed": null}}

sources.speaker: W:
sources.text: Yes, whites came everywhere; that's the reason why the guys got into trouble. They were always in the black district. Count Basie and I had about 30 pupils between us, that we were teaching to play jazz.

sources.speaker: W
sources.text: During the period when the bands used to come to Pittsburgh I met Buck. He was a great pianist but I don't think many musicians knew it because he had that comedy act going with Bubbles. He'd come to Pittsburgh and he'd say, "Now I'm going to teach you some of my things." Buck was a great teacher for me. We'd be in the Subway jamming and he'd say, "Hey, look, girl, you like me. Come over here. I'm going to teach you something." He showed me runs. Later on after I met Count Basie and Art Tatum, Buck showed me a run that Art Tatum - it was his famous run. He made it from top to bottom and Buck had taught me that run. He said, "Now when you get in front of Count Basie and Art Tatum, you make it like this," and he turned it around. One night I was jamming with Art. Art played and I was playing so I played this run that Buck had taught me and Art Tatum said, "Hey, what's that? Play it again." For about 3 or 4 years he and Count Basie were making this run the wrong way. That's the type of musician Buck was. He'd show me something but he didn't want me to play it when they were around, 'cause he didn't want them to learn it. They came around and would hear me turn it around and make it some other way.

53571.proposed: owner of Cafe Society (Downtown and Uptown) where she was featured c. 1941-47; got her a WNEW radio show and put on her Town Hall concert
53571.evidence: Barney Josephson was very nice. I wrote the "Zodiac Suite" during that period and he put on a concert at Town Hall.
53571.subject: Mary Lou Williams
53571.audit: {"change": "proposed 'commissioned Zodiac Suite' not in text; evidence spliced", "previous": {"relation": "collaborated with", "direction": "mutual", "proposed": "owner of Cafe Society who booked her and commissioned her 'Zodiac Suite'"}}

sources.speaker: W:
sources.text: Well, I didn't leave. It kind of petered out a little, you know what I mean, after years and years of being there. There was a kind of a lull and so I just drifted away, went back to GLASER Glen and he booked me out of the city. You know to stay in the city for 5 years straight you have to keep presenting people with something new. Barney Josephson was very nice. I wrote the "Zodiac Suite" during that period and he put on a concert at Town Hall.

sources.speaker: W
sources.text: I did solo. I worked with - Edmond Hall's group was there and they later moved to the Cafe uptown. They had various groups while I was there - Josh White. It was such a beautiful thing to work in the Cafe. I remember times when one act wasn't going well, Josh White and Johnny Garrett would come out and boost us. I never smiled when I was playing and Barney Josephson, the owner of the club, did everything he could to try to get me to smile. He came down, he had me acting like Hazel and all that. Eddie Hayward said, "Leave her alone. She'll get to it."

sources.speaker: W:
sources.text: Well, I had started on the "Zodiac Suite" while I was in Cafe Society and I never finished it. I wrote, I think, three. Barney Josephson got me a radio show on WNEW, my own show and I was supposed to introduce one sign a week -Aries, Taurus, and whatnot. I wrote 3 of the signs in the beginning and discovered I was just without ideas. I couldn't write any more, like my inspiration had left me. So what I did to finish them, I went on WNEW and I had Nola Studios to record the program as I played it. So I wrote the rest - I just played them off like that.

sources.text: No, but I like Miles. When I began praying Miles called me Reverend Williams and I gave him prayers and I sent him a lot of things. I played a concert with him in Europe about 3 years ago and he was all love and kisses and whatnot. I think he's very fond of me. I don't know what happened; I really don't know if all these things are as bad as some people say, but I think he became discouraged. I wasn't there but I heard during that period that I used to see him in Birdland, that Miles was abused by a policeman or something and he's been through several things like that. That can discourage one, you know what I mean, because if a man's outside catching the air and

sources.speaker: W
sources.text: No indeed. The only person I helped, Miles happened to be with me one day and Milton Oreny, the composer - he had so many masters in music till he couldn't play or write. Some people study too much. Milton and I were just saying a combination of things and I mentioned about a tuba and I think that that thing, that sound that Miles got on a record, was an idea of me just thinking of instruments, and he called me back and thanked me.

sources.speaker: W:
sources.text: Benny Goodman things. We were sitting in the car and he started whistling a tune. I said, "Gee, that would be good. I'm going upstairs and write it," you know. He always flushed me with ideas. There was never a lull; there was always something new happening. The first sound that Miles got with the tuba and all that - well, Miles was here and he said, "I'd like a tuba." Somebody said, "I'd like this instrument," and so forth and so on. Miles went out and he called back and said, "Thank you, Lou," and that's how he got his sound going. See, because we were really happy in creating and doing things and helping one another. Milton was really terrific. I have some arrangements and things here that he wrote when I was still out.

53571.proposed: East Liberty nightclub owner ('Black Prince of East Liberty'), one of three important people in her youth; rescued her when stranded, taught her to drive, race and fix cars
53571.evidence: He played a very important part in my career.
53571.subject: Mary Lou Williams
53571.audit: {"change": "under-claim: patron/guide she calls a very important influence", "previous": {"relation": "acquaintance of", "direction": "na", "proposed": "man who picked her up when stranded at age 12"}}

sources.speaker: W
sources.text: He was what you call a sportsman; he had a nightclub and he became very wealthy among the people there in East Liberty and he was called the Black Prince of East Liberty. I met him when I was 12 years old. He taught me to drive a car. In fact there was about 6 young girls where we went to school. They could all drive but they had to ask me if they could drive the car. He played a very important part in my career.

sources.speaker: W
sources.text: Yes. Roland Mayfield later on - there were 3 important people in my life, including the pianist that I spoke about -

sources.speaker: W
sources.text: Oh, I did. I changed the tires and I'd fix them up. Roland Mayfield, you know, the man who used to pick me up in Pittsburgh, taught me how to drive and how to fix cars and everything. My brother-in-law helped and if anything was wrong with any of those cars I could fix it myself. His mother was with me. It was like being on a desert, all the turtle-back roads, sand, dirt roads, you know. So we finally made it there and got in all right. See Roland taught me how to - I used to race when I was 10 or 12 years old. He taught me how to race and all that, do tricks in the car.

sources.text: John Williams. There was Louis Armstrong, Bennie Carter, Johnny Hodges, Fats Waller, Willie the Lion, and Bennie Carter's cousin that played trumpet. He was just wonderful - I'm trying to think - Cuban Bennett. He was really sensational. He played somewhat like Sweets but all these modern changes and everything. He was just beautiful. He says, 'You'd better play.' So I sat down and played with them and I guess they liked it

sources.speaker: W:
sources.text: Yes. We had a date in the Lincoln Theatre - I imagine you've heard of the Lincoln Theatre in Harlem? Duke Ellington had just come into New York with his combo, the Washingtonians they were. They were playing the Lincoln with us because Seymour and Jeanette were the top black act. So he played on stage with the band and they had me in the pit playing with the band. Still couldn't read. I played in the band with Tricky Sam, Bubber Miley, and Sonny Greer, and then I'd go up on stage with the act. I met Fats Waller then and I can tell you he was just a sensation in New York, when they'd turn the light on people would scream, when he sat down, people would scream. I never saw such a thing. When he finished, that was the end; they had to let it cool off.

sources.speaker: W
sources.text: He said, "All right, Fats, we're ready for the music after you give the girl some routines." I'd say, "O.K." He'd bring out his jug and what-not and he'd say, "What's the title? What you doing?" Leonard would tell him the story. And the man would play it straight off, lyric and everything, a whole 32-bar song... So I was sitting over in the corner. This man had moved there because he was going to put them on, like a bet. He'd say, "This girl can play everything she heard you compose." "She can't!" "I bet you!" So I sat down and played. ( ) and all these other things. Fats took me and threw me up in the air. He grabbed me and threw me up in the air and he bit me and everything. I wished I wasn't even there after all that went on. I thought he was the most amazing woman's pianist, I'm going to do the same thing. What's the/name I told you my brother-in-law used to take me to hear in Pittsburgh? Lovey Austin used to write music and play with her left hand. I used to do that with Andy Kirk.

53571.subject: Mary Lou Williams
