Benny Waters

Benny Waters lays claim to be the oldest working jazzman in the country, probably in the world. Born in Maryland in 1902, Benny showed an early musical aptitude, giving piano recitals by age seven, and soon after learning the reed instruments from his older brother. He played in dance bands while still in high school and attended the Boston Conservatory of Music where he studied piano and theory while teaching clarinet. After leaving Boston, Benny found work with Charlie Johnson’s Paradise Orchestra, leading to gigs at Small’s Paradise in Harlem where he associated with great artists like Louis Armstrong. Starting in 1933, Benny played for ten years in the bands of Fletcher Henderson, Jimmie Lunceford and Hot Lips Page. A visit to Europe with Jimmy Archey led to a stay of almost 40 years and he became a senior member of Europe’s American jazz community. Benny worked with various groups in Paris until he struck out on his own at the age of 67 and toured Europe with the occasional visit to the U.S. These visits became more frequent and eventually led to Benny’s settling back in the homeland in 1992. His is a frequent performer on numerous jazz radio programs and a member of the newly-formed Statesmen of Jazz.
Benny was interviewed in Los Angeles, on September 1, 1995 by Michael Woods.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Hamilton College Jazz Archive are filming interviews with America’s greatest jazz musicians. We have here the elderstatesman of jazz, Benny Waters. Pleased to have you, Benny.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well thank you. I’m happy to be here.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: How did you get started in music?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: In music? Well I’m a protégé, I was, that’s maybe not the right word in English because I’ve been in France so long. Anyway, I was born playing, like a gift from God, see, at three years old. So I was playing the piano then, so then after I stopped playing the piano, I went to the trumpet. But my lips got so sore that I gave it up right quick. Then I went to clarinet — E flat clarinet — and I did band music and concert music. Then from the E flat clarinet to the B flat clarinet. And then on to the saxophone, on like that.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Everyone in your family was musical, weren’t they?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well no, all the brothers were. My brother, my oldest brother was quite a virtuoso. He played all of the wind instruments, rather all of the brass instruments like the tuba and the trombone and the trumpet. He majored on the trumpet, but he could play all the brass instruments and could play clarinet also. And he played a little flute and oboe. He was quite a virtuoso. And the other brother played trombone, and the other one played the, I © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: guess they called it a mellophone or something, I forget what the name of that thing is in the military band, see. But the sisters didn’t, they didn’t play anything, my sisters.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Yeah. You learned to hear music first, and play it by ear, and then you learned to read. Is that right?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Yeah. I started by ear, see at three years old I just —if I have time I can give you a little short story just how I started playing.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Okay.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: My mother was very religious, and she used to like to sing hymns. She didn’t have no voice, but she liked to still sing all day. She had an organ, an old organ, a country organ, I forget the, it has a particular name but I forget it now. Anyway it was one of those little country organs, and she would always have the key locked up because she was afraid I may break it, you know a young kid see. So she would hide the key. So I looked and looked and looked many months for that key. So finally I found it. I looked underneath the wall and I saw something shining under the molding, in the country house that my father bought, built, you know? And I saw something shining in a little crack of the molding. So I went well here’s the key. So I took the key and started playing. I unlocked the thing. And she came home from her work and heard me playing, and she broke down in tears, and kissed me and hugged me, and from then on the organ was never, never locked.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Oh, that’s great.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Yeah. I was quite unhappy about it too, because there’s a little joke there. Because my mother used to like to sing, sing these hymns from the church, and I had to play them. And sometimes I didn’t happen to feel like playing, I didn’t feel like playing all this stuff, you know? But I learned to play the organ, so she had me playing a little bit too often.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Well that’s another type of education in itself.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Yeah.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Tell us how you were trained formally, where you studied formally.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Not formally, formally, I was three years old, see? I studied later, when I was 18. That’s when I went to the New England Conservatory and took up theory, harmony and solfeggio. That’s what I studied, see.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Uh huh. Tell us about solfeggio.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well solfeggio is the sound, mostly. You make chords. The way we did, we, my teacher would make a C, then I would have to hum the third, the E and the fifth and so forth. That’s the principle see. Then you learn, solfeggio also contains notes — Do Re Me Fa So — I can sing those notes [sings]. So that is an advantage in playing jazz. That really is. Solfeggio I think is — well harmony naturally, we know we have to have harmony that’s the principle and theory — but after that solfeggio actually gave you the sound of © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: what’s going on, so that you can hear a chord across the street and if you studied a little bit, you can name that chord. You can tell just what it is, you know? So the solfeggio is quite important for jazz. You know some people have absolute pitch. I don’t have it. I have relative pitch. Some people have, some people are born just, you don’t have to be a musician to have absolute pitch, you know a lot of people are not musicians who still have relative pitch. But if you’re a musician and you have relative pitch, that helps more also in distinguishing chords and so forth. And in your playing, improvising I’m thinking of now. That’s where jazz is, improvising see.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Yes. Tell us some of the early band leaders that you worked with.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Band what?

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Some of the early band leaders that you worked with.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Oh. Like the first, well the very first band when I was 14 I was working with a group named Charlie Miller. And we wasn’t playing Dixieland or New Orleans as you may call it, we were swinging. We had a similar Dixieland combination. We had trombone, trumpet, and I was playing saxophone. But actually it was a Dixieland combination. But we didn’t play Dixieland music. We played just swing songs and popular songs at that period, you know? Like at that period we had songs like maybe “Margie” was back there, you know see? So we had a good band then. And I was only 14 then. I was working. I was really a kid in the band see?

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Tell us how you, some of the people that you played with after that. Kind of give us a little chronology.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: What do you mean, later?

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Uh huh.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well see I came up to New York, see I came up to New York in 1926 and stayed until way into the late 40’s. And the band that I worked with see had very, very, very top musicians in it. We had Edgar Sampson, the composer of “Stomping at the Savoy,” well he was a friend of mine, see. And we had the young Benny Carter. We had the great Jimmy Harrison. We had Sidney DeParis on trumpet. We had Jabbo Smith, the young Jabbo Smith, in his teens, and we had one of the greatest bass horn players that I’ve ever worked with, Billy Taylor. He finally later really, he joined Duke Ellington, but he was one of the greatest jazz bass, bass, and I hear a lot of that bass around here, you know, bass solos, you know, the bass horn I mean that big thing. But this guy Billy Taylor was the greatest I ever heard in my life. We had him on it see and we had arrangements galore. Benny Carter made arrangements on “Rhapsody in Blue” and we had a wilder arrangements, we had two arrangements on “Rhapsody in Blue” and things like that you know? And we worked at Small’s Paradise and it was easily considered the second biggest cabaret in America at that period that was say next to the Cotton Club. Because in © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: my interviews that I did in Paris on the Herald Tribune I said that it was better than the Cotton Club. But that was my own idea see. If I have time I’d give you a summation. We had twelve girls dancing at Small’s Paradise, and so the Cotton Club had twelve girls. So I made the statement that the Cotton Club had some of the most beautiful girls in Harlem, but they couldn’t dance. That was true. Because we had girls that could dance. They wasn’t so pretty, but they could dance, you know?

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: How long did, how long were you with the band there?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Ten years.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: When it comes to a band playing a specific job at a like you say a residency, how did that help you? Did it like just give you a forum where you could continually perfect your skills?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Not particularly in big bands you can’t. But I would say, this is my own opinion, as far as a jazz man, a soloist is concerned, you don’t get a chance to perfect much in a big band, see, because you have to read music first thing. Because the big band plays arrangements. It is not like a Dixieland band just playing whatever, you know. You have to know the notes down and when you do make your chorus you’re limited. You may take 16 bars and then finish and things like that or 8 bars you know. So it don’t develop that, not for that, the small combinations is where you develop to be a jazz artist. In small combos, you know? But not in big bands. To tell you the truth, big bands is hard. It’s hard work. Particularly if you can play solos because you’re reading and playing the solo too. While the other guys that can’t play solos just read, and you’re playing the solos and reading and doing everything, see?

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: When did those opportunities begin to come for you with the small combo work, where you got the solo space that you needed?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well the small combo came in with my own band in New York, yeah, I formed my own little group. Then I could play any way I felt, you know. And experiment also.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: What was your instrumentation with your small group?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well my instrumentation, I had my wife on piano, and I had a trumpet player, and a guitar player that played not vibraharp, vibraphone I think they called it. It’s something like a Hawaiian guitar, you know? He played them both, they’re two different instruments. And the drums, we had no bass, and it was quite unique because it was a little different from the other combinations. And we played popular songs, you know? Show songs, because we worked in a cabaret where it’s necessary to play pop songs for the public, the type of public that came to our place. So we had a good combination. I stayed there three years.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Now you made your first recording in 1924? © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: No, I made my first recording in Philadelphia way before that. But I, myself have never heard it. I made it for a guy named Perry, Perry Bradford I think or something like that. I can’t, I forget his name a little bit. He was a kind of pioneer in recording in those days. He recorded the famous Mamie Smith, see that’s what I’m talking about, in that period.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Black Swan Records? He was with Black Swan?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: No, I don’t know if it was Black — I don’t know the name of the record right now, see. I don’t know if it was Okeh, Black Swan or Emerson or what. In that category, yes. But that was my first record. But the next record I made it was with this band that I worked so long at Small’s Paradise. That was on Victor Records. And at that session we had Benny Carter, we had Jimmy Harrison, we had Jabbo Smith, we had Sidney DeParis and this bass player I’m telling you about. And at that session I made all the arrangements except three. Benny Carter made two, and a white arranger named Ken McComa made one, and all the rest I made. And that can be bought now, see it’s on Victor Records and it’s been at least five or six times it’s been revived.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Reissued.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Reissued, that’s the word.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Marvelous, marvelous.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: And I have a number on there of mine that I feel kind of proud of it because with the other arrangements I had to arrange it exactly the way he asked me to. If it wasn’t to my liking, I got paid, see, so I had to arrange it the way he said. But this number of mine called “Harlem Drag” is my own number and though he gave me the privilege of making it the way I want. So that’s on this Victor recording.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Marvelous.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: It’s called the “Charlie Johnson’s Paradise Ten.” That’s the name of the band, see? Charlie Johnson’s Paradise Ten.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: You are one of the musicians that decided to live in Europe for a while.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Forty years, yeah.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Tell us about some of your experiences there.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well I had quite a lot. You know what I mean?

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Well I mean compare it to the United States.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well I had a very good deal in Europe. I, the first thing, I made money, and I guess that’s what every musician wants to do you know? So I made more money in Europe than I did in America. Well everybody did but the times were different, see? I guess when I was working at Small’s I guess the money was about, well everything was cheaper, I guess it was maybe about the same thing. But I started doing solo work. And solo work is where you make money, see? It’s hard work because you play with everybody — good musicians, bad musicians, all types. But you can make more money, see? © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Compare the audiences in the United States to Europe. How are the audiences? Do they respond differently?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well I don’t know. That’s really a good question. That has been asked me so often. If you want to know where I think are the greatest audiences that I’ve ever played for, it was not in Europe and not in America either, it was in the what do you call it, Czechoslovakia and Poland. That’s where the greatest audiences. They came, the first thing, they would be lined up outside to get into the hall, and they all would be dressed up in tuxedos, just like a classic concert, you know? In tuxedos. And when you played, you didn’t hear a sound. And when you finished playing, just applause. Never no hollering or whistling or anything like that. Just applause, applause, applause, applause. They took it as an art, you know? You know I’m speaking of Czechoslovakia mostly now. But in France, why actually in France, I mean I was there, I owned a little house there in France, so I was living there, but working all over Europe. They didn’t dress up much, maybe a few bands have a uniform but we didn’t have much uniforms there.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: You know you are known as a person who continually updates your skills and your sounds, always listening to new artists and picking up new ideas. And can you tell us about that? Just the process of hearing new things and bringing them into your repertoire of sounds.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well this can be explained, I’ll tell you why, because I don’t never get tired of listening, you know? And I listen to everybody, everything. I listen to free jazz. I listen to bebop. I listen to fusion. And I find I get something from everything. Dixieland. I worked in a Dixieland band three years at Jimmy Ryan’s. So, I worked in a blues band, see for a year and a half. So I didn’t like the band so well, see but the guy liked me so I stayed there see until I got tired and I left. But if it seems that I play fresh, I think that’s what you are trying to say see, it’s because I listen, well the first thing is I studied. I know harmony. I know what I’m doing see? I know the chords. I may not play all that I know but I know the harmonies you know. See I played the piano you know see? And everything I play on saxophone I can play on the piano. I don’t care how hard it may be, oh songs such as “I Remember April” and things like that. I remember when “Laura” first got popular in France, I didn’t know it on my saxophone, but I could play it on the piano, see, so I transferred the chords from that, from the piano to the saxophone, see? Then I listen to the other guy. I think that’s one of the great things, listen to everybody. You don’t have to play like everybody, or copy it, but you can get so much from everybody. I was telling, I tell, when it comes to alto saxophone, I have three idols that I’ve admired, three people who I’ve admired, see and I was inspired, influenced I will say, huh? That was first Johnny Hart at 13 years of age in Boston; second I worked and arranged for Earl Bostic, that’s when he had a small band there. I worked in the band and also arranged for Earl. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Not exclusive, but I made several arrangements for him, see? And then the next was Benny Carter, the young Benny Carter. That’s on alto. And on tenor, there was no one in that period but Coleman Hawkins. Because he was the greatest of all at that period, see? Then you listen to everybody else, see, so you can get something from everybody.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: In fact, listening —

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: And then practice makes perfect is the old saying you know? You practice, you know? You can’t just stay in — age hasn’t really much to do with it. I mean that’s, I’ve had that argument so much in Europe, you know. A lot of people think when you get old you can’t play this or you can’t play that. Age has nothing to do with it whatever. But education has a lot to do with it. You know? Education. Knowing what you’re doing and the next thing important is to know what the other fellow is doing, because you can’t copy if you don’t know what the other fellow is doing also. So that’s the way I keep up. And you have to practice too you know see? Then another thing I think is important, don’t never get to the point that you think you sound so great, you know? You know? Always think there’s more room for improvement. See because in music it’s a science. There’s no such thing as finished. You can always get a better tone. You can always get better ideas. You can always get new harmonies. So many things you can always —as long as you live see? So that, I think that clears your question.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: That’s a beautiful answer. Do you have a regular practice routine today?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Yeah, I practice every day around — more so than ever. I’ve been practicing now more so than I ever did in my life. On account of I’m not working as much as I did before. I have time, see, so the spare time that I have I just use the horn to work little things out, you know. Because you can always work them out you know.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Tell us about how it felt to get the phone call to be one of the “Statesmen of Jazz.”

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Huh?

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Tell us about how it felt when you were called to be one of the members of the “Statesmen of Jazz” — the senior member.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well I thought it was a great thing, see? And I still think it’s a great thing in the regards that if I’m playing in it or who, I think the idea is great and I wish it a big success. But I think, I think that if we’re going to record, I think we could have made more stress on getting a perfect record, and to do that you have to have rehearsals. See that’s my only complaint, see? But the idea is great. Because you have thousands and thousands of guys 65 and over that play well. You may not have many 93 year olds, because they’re not living. See but 65 and 70, you know, oh between 65 to 80 for instance, there’s thousands of guys that, I’ll tell you the truth, for my part, some of the best musicians who are playing jazz are over 65. The type of jazz I like, you know? © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: You know you are a living historian. Every time you play, you know, you’re the oldest internationally touring musician active in jazz. So every time you play, you are history. What does that feel like?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well I don’t know. That’s what people say, you know they say, not mine. I’m just doing the best I can you know, see? I’m not — how the people feel, their reaction it’s up to the people you know? I haven’t been playing so much in the States, but in Europe, the reaction has been great, you know. Stand up ovations and so forth, every place I play. Crowded places, you know? And I was telling some friend of mine, I said jazz don’t owe me anything because what I didn’t make financially in the States, I made up for it in Europe. See so it’s been good to me you know?

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: That’s a wonderful story too. The fact that you have this positive relationship with the art form itself.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Yes well I’ve been in it a long time, see? I was playing as a soloist organ in the church and in concerts when I was three years old. I had my sister pumping the thing. I forget the name of that organ in that little church, the country organ. I couldn’t reach the pedals, you know, you play like that. I couldn’t reach it. I was too short. And my sister used to pump while I’d play. And I was doing concerts. It was booked as a boy wonder you know, one of those things. So I’ve been playing as a soloist a long time.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Yeah. Ninety years, wow. Have you have occasion during your many years of experience, to work with either Count Basie or Joe Williams?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: No I haven’t. No I haven’t. I wish I did. But I tell you I did work with a band that, well I may be saying something that people will agree, you know, but I had a pleasure working with Jimmie Lunceford and I thought it was a greater band than Count Basie. Not musically. Not musically. Exclusive musically. But for all around entertaining and music combined, I think it was a better band than Count Basie. So I had the pleasure of working with Jimmie a couple of years, I mean Jimmie Lunceford see. And I worked with Fletcher Henderson three years. Fletcher was the king of swing at that time. It wasn’t nobody, that was way before Basie or Duke and all those, Charlie Johnson or any of those bands. Fletcher pioneered. See that’s why Benny Carter got, I mean Benny Goodman got him to make the arrangements. That’s when I was working with Fletcher at the same time that he was arranging for Benny Goodman. And Fletcher was really something else there, as far as a swing group. There was nobody that could excel Fletcher, particularly after he made his change and got such guys as Coleman Hawkins, well Coleman was there first. But when he had Benny Carter in the band and he also got the great Louis Armstrong. And when he got the great Louis Armstrong, that, they did just like Ella Fitzgerald did with Chick Webb, you know, lifted them right on up higher and higher, you know?

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Oh that’s marvelous. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: But the bands that I think were great were Jimmie Lunceford. Not that his band was any greater musically than Count, or Duke, or Fletcher, but we had more entertaining than all those bands. See we had five singers, individual singers in the band; we had a quartet; we had a trio; and we all did group singing. And we had five singers. Joe Thomas used to sing well, the little saxophone player, Willie Smith sang well, that’s two. He had Dan Grissom as a soloist that sang all the time. We had Trummy Young back there singing and he had another trumpet player I forget his name, and Sy Oliver, you know. They all did well. So that was, for me, it was a little bit better than Count or Duke. I mean in my opinion you know.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: As a alto sax player, can you relate to anything, relate for us anything that the innovations that came on the scene when Charlie Parker came on the scene?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well explain that again.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: How did he change the way that alto sax players played?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well Charlie gets credit for that see? Of pioneering in a new style. Firstly, I’ve heard Benny Carter play so much when he was young, see? And I always thought Benny was a pioneer also. He started at, particularly at that period. But I give Charlie the credit of changing the scene in alto playing. But you know he did most of that when he arrived in New York. I heard him in Kansas City with Jay McShann. He wasn’t playing exactly the same way. He was still, you could hear edges of his style coming out, but it wasn’t perfected until he got associated in New York City with Dizzy. That’s when it came out see?

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: If you, after all your many years of experience, if you could leave today’s music scene in our young and upcoming students —

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well say that again I didn’t understand you.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: If you could leave our young students coming up with a word of wisdom about how this music is put together or why jazz is such a beautiful art form, or, could you just give us a word of wisdom?

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Yeah I could say that right quick, I mean study. That’s all. Study. You know what I mean? Remember that joke about the guy in the street on Seventh Avenue and another guy asked him, “how can I get to Carnegie Hall?” He says, “practice, man, practice.”

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Oh, that is great. That is great.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: So study that’s all. Other people, I know jazz musicians that try to tell some of the young guys they tell them nonsense I call it, they say, “oh man when you study too much it takes away from playing.” That’s the biggest lie that they ever heard of. There’s no such thing as study taking away from anything. I don’t care — I know there are guys that are gifted. Johnny Hodges is one of them. And so many I know that’s one of them, that are gifted and play. See but it’s nothing better than study. Know what you’re doing. And the © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: more you study the better you get. To prove it, some of the greatest musicians that we have in jazz are guys who have studied also. We have some that didn’t okay. But that’s my idea, I say study, you know, that’s what I would say. Study harmonies, you know so you know what you’re doing, see? The more harmonies you know the more you can place them, you know?

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: The more variation you can bring to the music.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: That’s right. And then, by studying you can play one way today and another way the next day, you know? I can, that’s why I have so much trouble with the mic sometimes. I can’t express myself the way I want to because I don’t play entirely stereotype, you know? I play whatever comes to my mind but I can’t do it if the mic don’t work so I can hear myself. That’s why I have so much trouble with the mic. So, and but you still can’t play it unless, you must know it on your horn. You can’t go beyond your knowledge, see? And if a person is playing and another person is playing, the other guy has more knowledge, it’s going to sound better. It’s going to sound better. If two guys have the same talent and the same, even a guy was playing a song called “Gut Bucket” saxophone, the guy was playing “Gut Bucket” saxophone and they’re both playing the same. The one that has the most knowledge is the one who will sound better because he can take more advantages. So it goes back to the same thing, just study that’s all, see? But the young kids are studying now. It’s not like it used to be, see? So I took it up when I was 18 and it was rare. It was not many jazz musicians in this school where I went, the New England Conservatory. I took advantage of it only ‘cause my mother, it was in her will for me to study music, not to study jazz, it was to study classics.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Tell us about that will. Tell us what was in that.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: She wanted to tell my aunt to see that I went to the Conservatory, which I did. But I didn’t do like she wanted — she wanted me to be a concert pianist. When I got to Boston I got to drinking whiskey and smoking and little tricks you know? But I still went three days a week as an irregular student for about five years. So I got a lot you know?

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Yes.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: I got a lot, see? It’s always more you can learn, but I got quite a lot of musical knowledge from that.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: A time of formal study seems —

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: I just stayed — in Europe I mean I was working with a piano player that also went to Berklee. But he didn’t know how to play an introduction for a singer. So I got to the piano and played the introduction, the singer came in just as easy. But for what reason? Because at the end of the phrase where you’re supposed to use a seventh chord, a dominant chord rather you can say more so, a dominant chord of a common song, to © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: bring a singer in, because you can hear the note. He wasn’t doing that. And I did. And that’s from knowledge. It’s not a gift, it’s from knowledge.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Marvelous.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Now I’m not a piano player, see I’m a saxophone player. But this guy was a good piano player. But he just didn’t know how to play for a singer, because he didn’t have the experience you know? And the knowledge.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Well, this concludes our interview with the great Benny Waters, one of the most fabulous alto sax players in these United States.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Them’s big words partner.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: But you live up to it in every way. You live up to it in every way.

275887.speaker: BW
275887.text: Well I thank you so much, but I don’t feel that way myself. I just feel that I play quite well for my age and so forth, and I play quite well, but so many guys play so well, you know.

275887.speaker: MW
275887.text: Thank you, thank you. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

Gerald Wiggins

Pianist Gerald Wiggins has been a fixture in the West Coast jazz scene for many years. Originally from New York, born in 1922, Gerald first made his mark with Les Hite, Louis Armstrong and Benny Carter. His West Coast work included stints in the film and recording studios and he accompanied numerous jazz vocalists, including Lena Horne and Kay Starr. Gerald can be heard at festivals and concerts across the country and still records with such artists as Red Holloway and Clark Terry.
Gerald was interviewed in Los Angeles on September 2, 1995 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: My name is Monk Rowe and we’re filming today on behalf of Hamilton College Jazz Archive. We are attending the L.A. Classic Jazz Festival and are really pleased today to be with a fine pianist and well-known jazz figure Gerald Wiggins.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Hi.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Pleased to meet you, and glad to finally find an hour — I know you are a busy man. It’s a pleasure to talk to you. You’re an East Coast man transplanted to the west?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: That’s about it, yes.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: How did that come about?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well I was working with an old time comedian, Stepin Fetchit.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Stepin Fetchit.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Remember him?

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: I like the name.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Anyhow, we were working at the Brooklyn Strand and there was a west coast band backing the show by the name of Les Hite. Well the Army took Les Hite’s piano player, and Step had a little problem he had to talk to the police about so he disappeared. So Les said to me, “You don’t have a boss and I don’t have a piano player. How would you like to go to California?” So I was young and crazy I said, “Great.”

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: And how old were you then?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: I must have been just about 18 then. I was just out of high school.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Yeah. It’s so interesting to hear the ages that a lot of folks we’ve talked to have started at. What kind of, just to step back once, what kind of piano playing did you do for Stepin?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well I was mostly part of his act. I had played some things and I had to help him with a few little things he did like he said, “Help me with this coat” and I put it up to his shoulder and he said, “the hand down there” and I had to drop it down and put it on his hand. It was really, you know, cornball stuff, but it made him a millionaire so what can I say? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Then you traveled around doing little shows?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: We didn’t do too—I didn’t stay with him that long. I think we played maybe about four or five weeks. We went as far as Anderson, Indiana and came right back. At that time everything was weekend shows, you know, little towns. Friday and Saturday night was it.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: And this was after you went to, was there a high school in New York?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: The High School of Music and Art, yeah. Well I graduated in 1940.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Was that a good experience there? Was that at that time—

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Music and art?

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Yeah.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Fantastic. Oh it was something new, and we’ve got Mayor LaGuardia to thank for that. The only hang-up was that most of the students that went there were piano players. So we all had to take another instrument. I picked up the bass violin. Stupid me. I used to carry it home every night and bring it back the next morning. I got tired of that too.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: I’ll bet.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: But that was a great education. We had, you know, regular school subjects, history and math and all the rest of it, but you had to keep up your grades in that too or out you go. But I got a chance to actually play in the symphony orchestra, and some great music. Things I never would have had a chance to play. So, and Benny Goodman used to come up with the trio every Friday. That was nice.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: At the — he’d play at the school?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Yeah. That was a big treat, when you could get in, because it would be packed. Yeah it was quite a school.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Great. And there was a certain amount — you learned at that point to read music but you must have developed your ear very quickly—

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh, no, my mother had me taking lessons when I was four years old. And I played classical music until I was 16 or 17 and found out I couldn’t make a dime doing it, so it just was the wrong time. So I just gravitated to jazz. And it’s been good to me. I can’t complain at all.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Right. What kind of experience did you have during the war years?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh lovely. I was in Fort Lewis, Washington from 1944 to 46, and I was with a Special Service Unit. And we didn’t have to do too much except play for the parades on a Saturday. The rest of the time I was in Seattle.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: What did you play for the parades?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Beg pardon?

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: What did you play for the parades?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh I played glockenspiel sometimes, or I’d take a clarinet out, or a trombone. I had a working knowledge of them you know. I wasn’t good at it but I could fake it pretty good. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: And in Seattle, when you were still in the service, what was going on there?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well I had a job then, yeah, I had a steady job. I worked with a saxophone player by the name of Tooty Boyd who has passed on since then, but we used to drive down to Portland for a job and I had some jobs in Seattle on Jackson Street, which was a hot street in Seattle at that time. So I made more outside of the Army than I made in the Army.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Yeah? Today we think of a gig as usually nine to one, ten to two, sometimes less than that. What was a typical night like back then?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well when I was working, I had a gig in Greenwich Village and that was eight at night until four in the morning.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Lord.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: And then I started working uptown and Monroe’s Uptown House and we’d go to work about eleven thirty and get off at daylight. But that was all I needed because all I’d do is go up the hill and go to school. My first class was 7:30 so I was in business. I’d play all night and sleep in school all day.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: I was going to say, how can you handle that?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well now my history teacher moved out here, and she pulled the cover off me. She told my wife she says, “Yeah I often wondered why Gerry was so sleepy in class — I found out.”

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: He was a working man already. That’s great. And the atmosphere in New York at that time was pretty happening, right?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh, New York was great because especially for a youngster trying to learn the music business. Because the older guys would show you everything, you know, whatever you asked, you couldn’t do it but they’d show you. I know I asked Tatum several times to show me certain things, he’d say, “Oh, Gerry,” [scats]. I’d say thanks.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Slow motion please?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: But Art got me the gig with Stepin Fetchit.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Yeah?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Yeah he got me my first gig.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Was the average piano player intimidated by Art Tatum?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: No, they just wished he’d go away, you know. One guy told me he says, “Wig, don’t worry about Art Tatum” he says, “much as he plays, he can only be in one place at one time, and he can’t work all the gigs all at once so you’re safe.” Which makes sense.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Right.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Art was really a sweetheart. He was a nice man, except he didn’t want to talk music, he wanted to talk baseball. You know he could tell you the average of Ty Cobb or anybody years before, you know? And how much they batted and what they did and all that. He was a good pinochle player too. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Interesting. You have accompanied along the way some great singers, too.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Yeah, I’ve been with Lena Horne, Dinah Washington, Kay Starr, I even was with Dinah Shore one night. And let’s see who else. So many I forget most of them, yeah.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Did you ever cross paths with Joe Williams?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh, I see Joe all the time. Every time he comes to L.A. he usually hired my trio, yeah. His piano player doesn’t want to make the trip out here so I get the job, which is great for me.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: What’s it like working with Joe?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Easiest job on earth. But I don’t have to play his regular stuff. You know when he works with his piano player, they have all this stuff set up. But when he comes out here he says, “Wig, don’t worry about it.” The blues. We do the blues in any — all kind of keys. We do a ballad now and then, but it’s very easy working for him.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: That’s interesting. You know the non-jazz musician always finds it fascinating when if you watch someone and they say B flat, and that’s all the band needs. You know, that’s one great thing about —

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well you’re supposed to know the tunes, you know?

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: That’s another thing — for this type of festival, too, when you watch the bands up there, and you’ve really got to have a repertory in your head of tunes. Because some of them aren’t groups that work together all the time, so someone turns around and says, you know, this particular tune—

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: You better know it.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: In E flat, and you better know it.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Yeah. Any key they call you’re supposed to be able to play it.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Yeah. When did you start doing, you did some vocal coaching in the studios out here?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: I did a little of it yeah.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: How did you get into that?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well people would call me since I’d worked with Lena and all the different people they figured I knew something about singers. I started believing them too.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: And you would do that for the studios?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh, no, the only person I really coached in the studio was Marilyn Monroe. I got that job through Jackie Mills who used to be a drummer with Tommy Dorsey, and he had an in with Jack Cole, the choreographer. So he took me out of the studio one day and Jack Cole liked what I did so every time Marilyn did a musical, I was there.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: I read that it took her a lot of takes to get, in films sometimes. Is that true?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well she wasn’t a singer per se you know, but she worked hard at it. And Jack Cole changed her style so much. He gave her things to do that she could half talk and half sing. So it came off pretty good for her. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Did you, were you involved with “Some Like It Hot?”

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well yeah, but that was mostly, what was it Jack Lemmon? Who was in that?

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Jack Lemmon and Tony Curtis.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: And Tony Curtis, yeah. And I didn’t have too much to do with that but I was in “Les Girls,” what is it “Let’s Make Love,” about five or six of them.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: I think I read you worked with Spike Jones?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Yeah well, that happened, that’s right. I was working with Spike’s wife, Helen Grayco. And Spike’s piano player Arnold Ross became ill, so Spike asked Helen could he borrow me for a while. So I went on the road with the Spike Jones band. And that was a trip. I said this crazy music, this ought to be fun to play. I think the first tune was “Poet and Peasant” for real. You know so if you couldn’t read you were in a whole lot of trouble. Fortunately I could read. That was tough music.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Yeah, you had to be good to play in that.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: And everything was timed to the second. And there was no goofing on that gig, believe me. Spike was a funny man but he was a taskmaster too, you know, you had to do it. I remember the first time I went to his home I walked in and there was a picture of the Blue Boy with Spike’s head on top of it, which cracked me up. But then the next picture was Whistler’s Mother with a racing form in her lap. And that was Spike all the way. He used to go to all the dog kennels when we were traveling, and tape the dogs barking and everything, and they put a record together of “Memories are Made of Things Like This” or something. He put all those dogs barking and this tune was fantastic.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: What an imagination.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh he was something else, he was fantastic, yeah, I really loved him.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: And we listen to that stuff now and we remember that it was done without any studio tricks, just live.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh yeah, that was just him editing and putting it together.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: That’s interesting. They had some hot players though, to pull that stuff off.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh, yeah. He had George Rock who was a fantastic trumpet player. And the tenor player Gil Bernal, he’s still around. He called me a couple of years ago, he’s been on the same job out here for about 30 years. I’d wondered what happened to him, you know. And there was Mousey, and oh what was the little midget’s name?

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Oh, I remember from the T.V. shows they did, that guy running out on stage, the real small one.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Yeah. Billy Barty. Yeah he was there. Yeah, Spike had quite a show.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: In what kind of venue — where would you play with him? In what kind of setting?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh we did all the college gyms.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: College gyms. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Yeah. In the middle of winter. And it was something else. It wasn’t bad. I had a lot of fun.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: You’ve had some nice albums on your own. Who are the guys that you like to play with? Anybody special nowadays?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh, now I use Paul Humphrey on drums and Andy Simpkins on bass. But on occasion I use Sherman Ferguson and other guys, you know. This town is full of good drummers and good bass players so you’re never at a loss for a good rhythm section.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: What kind of traveling in other parts of the world have you been able to do.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh, when I was with singers I did quite a bit of travel, especially with Helen Humes, we used to go to Europe every year for George Wein. But she passed away in I guess it was ‘81. So I don’t go out too much now. If I go out it’s for a couple of days or so. You know, I don’t want anything steady. I had enough of steady work.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Yeah? I’m glad to hear that you can take what you want.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well it’s not so much that, I just, I’m an old man. I can’t stand that anymore.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: And you’ve been in L.A. for how long? A long time?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well like I said I first got out here in 1940, but I didn’t stay then. But the weather got to me. It was Christmas Day and a hundred degrees here, and in New York is was like ice, snow, and everything else. I immediately called my mother and said I found God’s country, don’t look for me in New York anymore. I went back naturally but when I got a chance to settle here I did.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: What do you think of the state of jazz today?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: It’s the same as it’s always been with youngsters coming up with new ideas. I know when — I’m from more or less the bop era, and the older guys didn’t understand what we were doing and we didn’t know what we were doing either, but we were doing something you know? It evolved into bop. Well the kids are doing the same thing now. They want their own voice and their own sound and that’s what they’re doing. Now you can either like it or not like it, but it’s here, and it’s not going away.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Yeah. And if you don’t like it you don’t have to listen to it.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: So well yeah, but I found out you have to listen to find out what they’re doing. And it’s new so it’s strange, so you have to get used to — give it a good listen and find out what they’re doing. I know the first time I heard bop well I’d been around Dizzy quite a bit, so he was just getting it together, you know with the flat fives and raised ninths. And nobody knew what he was doing. He used to drive little trumpet players crazy. I was working in a place called Monroe’s Uptown House and we had two trumpet players: Vic Coulson and Joe Treadwell who later married Sarah Vaughan. They bought themselves a couple of cornets and it was terrible to hear them try to play like Diz, I mean they were in bad shape. But they tried. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Wasn’t that the place where Thelonious Monk was doing some of that early —

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: No that was downtown. That was, oh what was the name of that joint? But Monroe’s Uptown House was in Harlem, about 134th or 135th Street. But the place you’re talking about, how can I forget it?

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Minton’s?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Minton’s. Minton’s Playhouse, yeah. That’s where Monk was.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Did you notice when jazz moved from the Swing Era I guess into the bop, when bop became real popular, was there a loss of audience? Or did that affect your career at all? I mean the music changed drastically after World War II.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well I joined Benny Carter about that time. And I was kidding him I says, “Are we going to start playing bop?” And he says, “Well you’re playing it already.” I said, “Oh, good.” Benny Carter had a big influence on my career because he’s a superhuman guy. That guy is unbelievable. He can write, he can play, and he’s a nice man which helps a lot you know.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: What’s in your future? Do you do these festivals quite often?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Yeah, I do them. I do Sarasota, New Jersey, you name it. This is easy. You do a couple of days, three days at the most, and come home. This time I’m home so it doesn’t matter. But it’s fun, and they pay the bills. It’s not like sitting on a steady job working from nine to one or nine to two every night. That I couldn’t do anymore. For no amount of money. It’s just—

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: It’s a long gig.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: I’m just not geared that way I can’t even stay in a club a week. I get antsy after one or two days and I want out.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Did you ever get in a position, either in the studio or someone ask you to play any electronics? Electronic pianos or anything like that?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Not really. I remember my first rhythm & blues record date the guy said, “Okay, Wig, now we’re going to do this tune.” And I’m all set you know, I’m full of it and I’m going to show him what I know. And he said, “Okay, now, right here I want you to play a bad chord.” So I reached out, and I said, I’m gonna shock him with this. And I played this chord. He said, “No. I want you to play it like you don’t know anything about the piano and you’ve got gloves on. I mean a bad chord.” That was my first and last rock & roll date.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Wow. Whose session was that do you remember?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: I forget. It’s been so long ago. But I said, you know, he really wanted me to play like I didn’t know how to play the piano. I felt insulted.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Well, seeing as how you put all that time into learning how to—

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Yeah. They never called me again, believe me. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: What was your definition when you went to play that bad chord? Do you remember what kind of thing you might have played?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh I was trying to play a polytonal type thing, you know.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Yeah? One in one hand and one in the other. Yeah.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: But he wasn’t having any of that. He wanted me to play like I didn’t know what the piano was for. And I was really crushed.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: We’ve had a couple of people talk about reacting to what producers wanted.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Yeah well they’re looking for something, they’re looking for something to sell you know. As he said, “I want you to act like you don’t know what the piano is for, just hit something.”

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Do you have any road stories that you can share with us?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: I can’t tell them, no. I can’t even write a book about them.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: They don’t translate on to film, huh?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well, my lips are sealed, believe me.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: How about the best road experience you had, either with Les Hite or anybody from—

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well I had fun with all the gigs I had, with the singers and the bands, you know. There were good times and bad times. I think the worst time I had was when I joined Louis Armstrong. I joined Louis out here, and we made 50 one nighters, all through the south. And at that time the south was pretty bad. So two weeks before we got to New York, I put in my notice. I loved the band and everything but I just couldn’t stand what we were going through. It wasn’t very nice. Anyhow we got to New York and I was home about three or four days and Benny Carter called me. He says, “Wig, you want to go take a trip to the west coast?” I said, “Yeah.” I said, “You’re not going south are you?” He said, “Oh, no, don’t even think about that.” I got on the train with Bumps Myers and I went to sleep and I woke up and I was in Macon, Georgia. I’d like to die. I gave him my notice right then and there. And he said, “Okay.” And that was the end of it. And J.J. Johnson and Max Roach they say, “Oh Wig, come on” you know. So a couple of days later I went to Benny and I said, “About that notice I gave you I’d like to take it back.” He said, “What notice?” I said, “Oh, okay.”

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Was there a difference in that tour than with Louis?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well we didn’t stay there. Benny wasn’t about to stay down there.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Just passing through.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Pass through, yeah.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Louis went down in the south quite a bit, didn’t he?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well that was his territory. It sure wasn’t mine.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: What was it like musically working with him? © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well I never knew because with Louis we just played a gig and get out of town. We really didn’t have a chance to meet anybody. By the time you got there it was time to play. When you finished you packed up and on to the next town. We were making like 500 mile jumps every night. So it was a little rough.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Any chances to go overseas with some of the singers?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh yeah. My first time overseas was with Lena Horne. That was 1950. That was a ball because I got a chance to play the London Palladium, you know, and that was, to me, really something. And we traveled all over Europe. We went to Spain, Sweden, [inaudible] wherever that is, Belgium I guess. It was a ball. And then when I joined Helen Humes we used to go over every year with George Wein’s jazz thing. So I spent a lot of time in Europe. I made a lot of friends over there.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Helen Humes. She was with Basie for a while wasn’t she?

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Yeah. She was with Basie. Now she could have told you some things about Basie and the band. You would have loved to talk to her. Too bad she’s gone.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Was the Basie band something that you listened to off and on? We’ve talked with some people about the sound of their rhythm section. Was that something that —

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Oh, they had a tight rhythm section, yeah. They were together. You don’t find that anymore. Yeah with Papa Jo Jones and whoever the bass player was, and Basie, and Freddie on guitar. Jesus.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Can’t do any better than that.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Couldn’t beat that. Yeah they had a thing going. But bands are not like that today. They’re not, well to have a band like that, the piano player’s got to be the leader, to keep a rhythm section together. And most days now, it’s a trumpet player or a saxophone player, and they don’t stress that as much.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Well we’ve enjoyed talking with you very much. If you have any last things you’d like to say that I haven’t thought of —

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Well, if you see my friend Allen Tinney, tell him hello. I think he’s in Buffalo now.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Umm — that’s not far from us.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: Yeah, now he’s a guy who would have some good stories for you about New York, with Tinney, and Bud Powell and myself. That’s another thing. We won’t go into that. You get that from him.

275892.speaker: MR
275892.text: Okay. Well on behalf of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive, we’d like to thank Gerald Wiggins for this time together, and hope that your next festival is a lot of fun, and thanks for your time.

275892.speaker: GW
275892.text: All right. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
