296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Have you got it? I guess I should try and push that.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: I’m good, I think you’re probably —

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: There’s a little thing for me to poke. I don’t need to do it?

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: I don’t think so, but — if you’ve got something telling you —

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: It looks like I’m supposed to say “Got it”. Okay just a minute.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Yeah, you can say got it, or okay. All right guys.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: All right. Thank you very much.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Okay.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius — I’m going to start again.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah don’t talk when he’s talking. Okay? Lee Ann? Okay go ahead.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: All right. My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive and I’m very pleased to be speaking with Charles McPherson after 26-some years before — our first interview. Thank you for joining me.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Well thank you, thank you for having me.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: You know the first time around we got to shake hands, now we’re sort of zooming hands.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yup.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: This is a sort of a tough question but you’ve been involved in jazz for a long time. We spoke about your time with Charles Mingus and having your own bands all these years. And then you just spoke about playing a jazz festival like three weeks ago in Upstate New York. Can you think about the biggest changes you’ve noticed in jazz and the business of jazz between that time back in the sixties and now?

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Well yeah, that’s — I think there — you know I think there might be more genres of jazz maybe now than before. In the sixties you had the influence of Charlie Mingus, people like John Coltrane, the avante garde was happening you know, Ornette was there. You had you know Art Blakey and of course Thelonious Monk, Max Roach, you had these great musicians that were still here and everybody had their own style but I think now the difference is there just might be more different offshoots of jazz. Or people that play or record companies that promote and they’ll use the term jazz you know, and there are just more variations I would say. Maybe a little more variations. In terms of the aesthetic of it, © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: I mean the actual quality and level of musicianship and artistry, you know the sixties and even before that had very high levels of musicianship and artistry you know. That didn’t start with the sixties, that’s always been around. And now you — I’ll tell you what is different, academia is different. There are more schools — high schools, colleges — that have jazz programs. That wasn’t quite like that in the sixties and of course earlier. So that’s different, so therefore it’s producing younger players, you know there’s a lot of young people that are enamored of jazz, some kind of jazz, and it’s in the schools and so it’s more available in a way, at least by way of academia. And so that’s a little different, and it produces, you know, a slew of young players that are being, you know that are getting out of schools, that are starting careers. So there might be, maybe more people playing jazz and yeah — so things have changed but to answer your question the best way I can I would say that there’s more genres now maybe, and a lot more players you know.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Interesting you say that because on my way home last night I had an NPR show on and they were playing this music and I couldn’t quite place it but then the person came on and they were doing a show about Indian music — music from India — and its effect on jazz and how some people embrace that. So you’re correct, there’s Celtic influences, in fact bands sometimes like to promote themselves as embracing world music so you have jazz and all these other influences coming in. When you mention about the number of players coming into the music, have you had people come to you, young players seeking advice about how to make a living in jazz?

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Oh yeah, I do. I am, you know a lot of young players will call me up and talk, which I like, I like that. And they will ask for advice — musical advice — more often than not that kind of advice or saxophone advice. And then now and then business advice. And I will, you know, I will tell them the little I know and give them the best advice I can. And you know that’s a hard — I’m much better at giving musical advice or saxophone advice. Business advice, I need some advice myself on that. I’ve done things my way, I’ve gone my way, my particular way, and so each player of these young people, it’s very important to figure out what demographic they want to cater to in terms of the public, and these are the things I tell them about. You know jazz is — we talked earlier — is a pretty under the name of so-called jazz is a pretty big umbrella you know, and a variety of style and musical behavior by people and groups that will say “jazz.” So okay, so be it. So with that in mind I will tell — I give the advice to young people since it is that way then figure out who do you want to reach you know? Because there’s an audience for all of these different nuances and these different genres. There’s a straight-ahead bebop audience, or neo-bebop that leans towards that. I’m a member of that club. There are people that are more into more popular forms that have jazz as part of their DNA and then you have © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: rock, you have rhythm & blues, you have funk, you know you have all of these different takes on jazz music. And you’ve got people from all over the world that are playing that are bringing nuances of their culture to the music and amalgamating it with some of the part of the DNA of what I would say jazz is. So you have all that. So there’s a big audience and who do you want to reach. And then think about that deeply, because whatever — you want to do something that makes you happy, you want to do something that you do need to take care of yourself, you need shelter, you need — you know you’ve got to pay your rent, you’ve got to live and it takes money to live. Think about just the basic mundane problems of trying to play art in this society and music in particular, and jazz is really a pretty difficult sell. So you have to think about that and then think about what kind of music are you able to be honest about and play, and then think about the business aspect. I definitely tell them to learn all of the new ways that music is being used these days. So you’ve got all the digital, all of that, and then you know you’ve got cell phone, you’ve got streaming, you’ve got — there’s millions of dollars being made with music and so I will tell them to understand every aspect of the music business, not just playing in some bar you know, “I Got Rhythm” in some club, or “Countdown” in some joint, which is fine, I love that, but think about the ways that music generates money, and make sure that you get paid. Because there’s a lot of people that really make a lot of money off of music and by way of music and music is being played by people. Make sure that you get your just due. So that means you have to have some business awareness and understanding, and you’ve got to take part of your consciousness and your energy and really kind of look at these things. Now I will say this: a lot of the young players of today are a lot more on that page than I was as a younger person in my early twenties. You know I didn’t really think deeply about money, business, or anything. I just really wanted to learn how to play, and really play really well you know play as fast as possible.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Yeah you take me back to you had told a story about hearing Charlie Parker play “Tico Tico” and that it made sense to you.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Well yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: That was so interesting that it just made sense to you. And you said, “I knew immediately that this is what I wanted to do.”

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yes. Right. That’s true. Yeah. And I think a lot of people felt that when they first heard Charlie Parker. I’m not the only one. But when I first heard Bird, yeah, that was overwhelming because it made perfect sense to me. And there was something about the way — because he played a lot of notes, but a lot of people played a lot of notes but I could hear the linear logic with Charlie Parker. I could tell — and I couldn’t — I would never use terms like that — “linear logic” or — I wouldn’t use that term. I wouldn’t even know what that was when I’m 15, 14 years old. But I could understand it, let’s put it that © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: way. It made sense to me. And so that was what got me. It was compelling. And I got it. I couldn’t say what it was, I couldn’t use the right verbiage or the right semantics to describe — I knew nothing about harmony or theory or any of that. I did know major scales. I could play the major scales but I didn’t know anything about the cycle of fifths or any of that you know. But I could tell that he connected these long sentences and they were like perfectly, seamlessly connected. And then the logic of it was apparent to me, and that’s what got me.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: I have a quote here I want to read from the late Jimmy Heath. It says, “I think Charles McPherson is the number one saxophonist who has incorporated the Charlie Parker language. He has this quality of eruption in his lines, he has that Charlie Parker language and he’s still himself. He’s so far inside of the part nobody else gets, that you would have to say it’s amazing.”

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Oh well I didn’t know he said that, that is really a nice compliment.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: It is indeed.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah that is a very nice — in fact yeah, that’s a nice one.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: I think I’ll send that to you.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Thank you, Jimmy, thank you.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Put it on your resume.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah, that is beautiful. I mean it’s self-serving that I say that, but coming from a great musician like him, and a wonderful, wonderful saxophonist and wonderful composer, that was around during the really golden age. You know his age really was privy to all of the great musicians before Charlie Parker. These people were still around and still living, and he’s heard these people in person. It’s not abstract for his — what was he born, 19 what 29 or 28? I don’t know somewhere probably 1926, 27, whatever it is. But that age of those people, that generation, were privy to all these great saxophone players, trumpets, big bands, you know just all — everybody was still living pretty much. So he’s a great musician and his playing and his writing reflects his natural talent but it also reflects all of this great music that he absorbed. So that’s — a compliment from him is very special.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: You were indicating finding your audience for young musicians and reaching them. I want you to see if you can name this tune. Are you ready?

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: It starts with a rest. [scats]

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Okay. Well I know what it is already but go ahead. I think it’s mine — I think it’s an intro.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: It is indeed.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: to a tune I wrote for my last CD and last record project, and it’s entitled “Dynamic Duo.”

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: “Dynamic Duo.” © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah. And it features David Wong, bassist and Jeb Patton, pianist. And both of whom were with my group.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: I want to ask you about the, not just the writing of it but the arrangement. Way back in ’98 when we spoke you said, “The writing process is the loneliest, most miserable thing.”

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Oh for me — I’m sure it is not with everybody but, yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: But beyond the initial tune I found that the arrangement of it was compelling because you had that very memorable little lick and then it went into this unison piano and bass complex, followed by a bass solo, and it wasn’t until over like 3-1/2 minutes that we heard anything as far as a sax or trumpet solo.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Was this a conscious decision to —

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah. It was. Yeah. Because most of the time you’re going to get the trumpet or the saxophone or the horns play first. So just for the sake of variation and, you know, to add a different flavor, you know I like to have the bass or piano player play first, not only in clubs but on records as well. And it was written to be their feature you know. It was written to be their feature. And it was basically inspired by my involvement with Paul Chambers, Barry Harris, Billy Higgins, and Lonnie Hillyer, a trumpet player, and myself. We had a gig and you know the great Barry Harris and also Paul Chambers both Detroit people, and of course I’m from Detroit and Lonnie Hillyer, the trumpet player was from Detroit as well. So Billy Higgins who is I think from California or Texas or something like that. But that was the rhythm section of a gig many years ago, in the late sixties. And so I was kind of inspired by the way Paul Chambers and Barry Harris played with each other. So fast forward to now, when we decided to do a record, a live record date with Smoke Records in New York, I wanted — that CD and record project is dedicated, it’s a tribute to Barry Harris, a great pianist and my mentor as a kid. And so I really wanted to just my tipping of the hat to Paul Chambers and Barry Harris. Because during that gig these two people, and Billy Higgins, I mean these people were really playing really well with each — really good with each other you know. And it was inspiring to hear that. And I just said let me write something for this great bass player of today, which is David Wong, and great young pianist Jeb Patton, and just write a really interesting tune, or figure for bass and piano.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Indeed. And I’m picturing you, were you sitting at the piano laboriously writing out this [scats]-type line?

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Is that how you did it?

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah. Basically yeah. I actually basically it’s really kind of like a solo I would do. And of course I have a way of — what would you say — framing it a certain way so that there © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: are certain nuances being adhered to that will make it not just a solo but a tune, and there’s a way that you can — I use the term “box it” or conceptualize certain phrasing and melodic nuance and a way that you maybe recapitulate to some degree here or there that makes it not just a rambling solo but actually a little tune. And so I’ve tried to do the best I could trying to do that. Yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: You did good.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: I bet they were happy to see it. I’m just picturing —

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: No they weren’t that happy. I don’t know if they were happy to see it because they had to really — they had to — I mean it’s pretty notey, you know there’s a lot of notes there and so, and it’s in unison and the rhythm is kind of tricky a little bit. It’s just based on “I Got Rhythm” but you know the line is not real easy. Now I’ve seen other people look at that and not want to deal with it so — yeah but these two guys are so talented, David Wong and Jeb Patton, that they — I mean for them it’s a challenge and they ate it up. They nailed it for sure.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: They did. It sounds perfect.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: And I just want to compliment you on the idea of the formatting of it, even up to the end where it’s sort of a surprise ending.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Um hum. Yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: [scats]

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah. Abrupt. Yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Excellent.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Thank you.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: You mentioned of course Barry Harris, and I just did a review on this book with Pepper Adams.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yes.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: And you are quoted a number of times. I wanted to read one thing here I found fascinating.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Okay.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: When you got together with this group of young men around Barry and you said, “‘Man these people are really different.’ Harris was a taskmaster and at one point asked McPherson to show him his high school report card. He had a C average and Harris was unimpressed. ‘Oh you’re an average kind of guy,’ the pianist said. It won’t work because this music is complicated and you’re not going to be able to play it if you’re a C kind of guy.’”

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah. That’s true. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: “This is not a skinny bubble here.”

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah, yup, no that’s true. That change — that made an impression on me. I never had thought of it like that and when he said that I under — it made it me understand because I’m learning how to play this music and I’m understanding and seeing the complexity of it. I’m learning that oh, this is some higher math here. This is not arithmetic. This is trigonometry. So I could tell that yeah — and then when he made that statement and equated it to music and the complexity of the music, then I knew that I’m going to have to deal with — dealing with complexity no matter where it’s coming from or what the medium is, is going to be something to deal with. And so I immediately knew that there is a level of — what would you say — deliberate yeah, a level of really deliberate effort to try to do anything at a certain level whether it’s getting a better report card or playing music or playing basketball — it didn’t make any difference. It’s a level of seriousness and dedication that you’re going to have to actually be willing to invest. And I might as well — I mean really what Barry was saying and I understand — I kind of understood it then — that this kind of excellence you have this kind of attitude about it no matter what you’re doing and so when you’re starting, when you’re playing music then that same level of willing to invest is still there so it’s not like — you use this for everything including music. So get accustomed to pushing yourself, no matter what it is. And then I don’t care if it’s getting your schoolwork, homework, understanding something in class, be willing to invest your mind toward making that better or nailing it, completely understanding it and doing it at a high level and just building your chops in that way will make anything you do the same, because it’s all the same, really. And what makes it all the same is you’re the one behaving at a certain point in time with whatever the situation is, and so just get yourself to having a high level of attainment no matter what it is, so when you get ready to play then your chops are there because you’re already thinking that way. I understood what he meant you know.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Yeah. I was involved in an aesthetic education program for some years and you’re making me think of how we used to connect the different art forms and that observing an abstract painting or watching a dance performance — especially a modern dance performance — and being able to make some cognitive sense about it applies certainly to your playing as well.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah I think it applies to everything. So what I mean by that is — I was reading something about Beethoven, like a kind of biographical thing. And he made a statement that was curious. And he said, “If you know the secret of correspondence you can do anything.” And I think I understood what that meant, and that’s kind of what Barry meant. And I see what it means now. And basically when you say looking at dance, looking at art, if you’re able to look at anything and see how it corresponds to any other © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: thing, no matter what the construct is, no matter what the medium through which a particular behavior is being — it doesn’t make any difference. You see the — you see the correspondence between the two supposedly different constructs. But the behavior — you can see it. So then you become — you understand the DNA of metaphor and the DNA of analogy — analogists. You can see the thing. And the only difference is the mediums through which particular things are being expressed, but it’s still being expressed by human behavior and everything that’s dealing with that. So it applies to anything. So I can look at a basketball player, say like a guy like Michael Jordan for instance, and him going down the basketball court, and the way he pivots and zigzags I can make that be accents, rhythmic accents. Instead of a drumstick on a drum doing an accent, it’s a human body doing an accent. So an accent, if you see the correspondence and you’re able to see that, then you start seeing the bigger picture of things and the little minutiae starts making sense because you see the macro and the micro starts making sense. Because you already are looking at the bigger picture. And the micro and the macro are the same. The only difference is the viewpoint. So, and then if you can look at the bigger picture, that gives birth to metaphor. That gives birth to the secret of correspondence, that gives birth to that, so that makes probably anything you do, whether it’s playing a horn, whether it’s playing golf, it doesn’t make any difference what the medium — it’s like if you can understand that then that’s like an epiphany in a way. There’s a dimension of mind and conscious cognitive awareness that happens right there you know.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Marvelous. I wonder if you’ve ever had a circumstance where you were the elder musician with wisdom and, much like Barry Harris, and you tried to pass that on to younger musicians who might have been on a very narrow path?

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah, well I do, I mean because I teach so I don’t teach it in a school, but I teach privately. And I teach, you know kids and, adults as well. And that is one of the things that I kind of learned about teaching is like the art of — you’ve got the craft of teaching and then you have the art of teaching. And really to me art is the higher level of what craft is. Because yeah, but anyway to make a long story short, I think this is when you start having a bunch of students you start developing — first of all you have to be a wordsmith of some sort because you’ve got people, some of these people are young and their attention span is what it is. You’ve got to be able to nail maybe difficult abstract thought with ten words or less in order to cause the epiphany. To cause the door to open. To cause the Aha! moments, and you don’t have much time quite often. So you will develop metaphor, you start developing/using analogy, and all of this that we were talking about is being able to explain abstract thought to someone who knows less and have the door open. And that, a lot of times you have to have the Will Rogers approach, it’s this really simple language, knowing how to use metaphor, ten words or less to cause © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: the door to open. The Aha! moment for the student. And that becomes like I think that’s a part of the DNA of a teacher. Because it’s not like you’re just dispensing data and information, you’ve got to do it in a way that it’s being absorbed and then that’s where you have to — there’s a little four dimensional chess being played there because you’ve got to understand how the mind works, how the subconscious mind, the conscious mind — you kind of have to understand the difference between craft, between art. And you’ve got to be able to nail it and you’ve got to use words that’s understandable and then so therefore this is what I mean. You have to be a little bit of a wordsmith.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Well I watched an Aha! moment, one of your lessons with a saxophone player is on a video, and I just got a kick out of this because he played something and then you said something that’s so basic that most people wouldn’t bother. And you told him to put both his feet on the floor.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Like —

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: What was he playing? Was he playing saxophone?

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Playing a tenor.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Okay.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: And he had one of the iRealPro things on the screen I think. But I think he was sitting but your point was you’re not rooted to the ground here.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah, right, yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: You know and it’s a very basic thing and I was pleased to hear you just point that out and the look on his face was like oh, okay.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Well yeah, so there again there’s — for me there’s a reason for that and it had nothing to do with how it looks. It’s got something to do with — because there’s a lot of unconscious — oh what would you say — a lot of unconscious things going on with how you — what you do with your body. Your body language. And then you know it’s not just that but it’s also just basic physics you know. Your feet on the ground on an unconscious level, your two feet flat and in a certain position is telling a part of your mind to be in a state of readiness. Okay so that means it’s a different level of alert, of being alert. The other thing, just the physics of it, you have the earth under your feet and for your feet to be a certain way it’s the security of it. There’s a security there of it, and a state of readiness. And all that. So you’ve got the psychological minutiae involved with that. And then you’ve got just basic physics. You’ve got better leverage. So and I always use this as an example in terms of state of readiness. If you look at two great tennis players just before they start to volley, look at how their feet are and then look at what they’re doing. They’re actually moving left and right with both feet because they’re getting in a state of readiness for the ball to be over in this corner, the corner to © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: the right, and anywhere on the court. Because the guy, the person, is going to hit the ball anywhere. So his state of readiness is not for him to stand up with his feet any kind of way. It’s ready to volley, which means the ball might do anything. Well when you’re playing and you’re improvising in the stream of time, that same state of readiness psychologically, physically, and what that does mentally in terms of subconsciously making you be in a state of readiness is what kind of state you need to be in when you’re improvising. Because you’re taking time, space, and — rhythm, time, and space, twelve tones at least in the Western scale, and you’re behaving in an improvisational way in real time. That — you’ve got — it’s a state of readiness on a high level of alertness on all levels — left brain, right brain, consciously, physically. So there you go. So it’s a way of — so that’s what I meant by that. Now I’m not going to say all of that to a student, it’s too many words. But I’m just saying that behind it is not just the empty being concerned about visuals. I’m thinking about leverage, I’m thinking about state of readiness, which occurs here. I’m thinking about the whole body, mind-body. So I’m thinking about the psychology of it on all levels. And that’s because the one thing that I do do for myself is when I think — I will think in as many dimensions as possible. I’ll try to look at any particular whatever, as many different ways as possible. And that’s still subjective, because it’s still me looking. And it’s my concept of dimension and all that. So it’s in the world of subjectivity. But I will give it a — what would you call it — a conscious effort to look at it more than one angle. And this is where I will, when I do that, even if I don’t cover everything at least I’m using my will — volition — to know that maybe I should. And I will, I’ll try you know.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Let me ask you about —

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Now this is that part — I’m talking about the cognitive, deliberate analytical aspect up here. So I always make a point of really sort of segmenting the activity of who we are here, because we’ve got all these different ways of taking information and parsing it a certain way. So I’m aware of that also, and then I’ll use terms and words to — I’ll use it to what I want to do, and what I want to explain, and how I want to explain it to them and to myself.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Is there a difference in your thinking process if you’re playing on a tune like “So What” you’ve got two chords that last fairly long,

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: or if you’re playing on something like “Giant Steps.” Is there a difference that’s going on up here?

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Oh yeah. There’s a difference. Let’s see, now see this is complicated because one tune has got two chords, another tune has a million chords. So here again is the psychology stuff. There’s a certain — when you’re dealing with harmonic movement that’s only two © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: beats — so the harmony is moving at a quick pace. It’s not there for four bars, eight bars. But it’s moving every two bars. And the tempo is at a good clip. So there is a way that you have to look at all of that harmonic minutiae and there’s a way that you have to look at a broader arc over that, which means you really do have to have your ears on and think melodically at the same time that you’re adhering to time and space. So here again you’re really walking and chewing gum at the same time. And see here’s where all of this perception and how you’re looking at things come in. Now everybody’s different and there’s a lot of ways to look at music. You can look at music rhythmically only, harmonically only, or melodically only. But the real deal is amalgamating all of that into one homogeneous behavior and then so therefore having the output be whatever it is. But see there again lies this different — different ways to think. And everybody’s different. Yeah. So this is what Barry meant by you can’t be a C student with some of this stuff here. You know? This is some stuff you’ve got to deal with. Now having said that there’s also this part of the equation. The subconscious mind, who we are as human beings and people. Already here is every note that we’ve — we’ve heard every note it is. Because this big piece of meat is the greatest computer in the world. There’s only twelve notes. We’ve heard every one of them since we came out of — since we pop out of the womb. We’ve heard them. Okay we’ve heard rhythms, we’ve heard chords — whether we know what to think about them, how to think of them, it’s already there. So a lot of times success is based on what part of the mind, or what kind of mentation should I put in play to get the best results, and therein goes the four dimensional chess again and how people think you know, and you’ve got the variety of personality and then I can only say how I approach it. I’m sure other people approach it another way. But see yet again, I’ll look at all of that and realize say a tune like “Countdown” where the harmony is moving very quickly, but I will still — part of my way of thinking is what are some of the common notes with all of that harmonic movement. Because they can be moving quickly and changing quickly but there are certain common notes that’s connecting all of them or at least some of them. So your melodic ear has to be on. And see your cognitive mind, your analytical mind has to understand the form and structure of what’s actually going on. But how you artistically behave is a whole ‘nother game. That’s another part of the mind. The analytical part will just say oh, you know it’s “Countdown” so it’s going up a minor third and then it’s going to the fourth and then another minor third. You can get into all of that technical stuff and musical harmony and theory and all that. But how do you behave with that. Spend time — with time and space in real time and be creative. And that’s really something. But the way I look at things, I try to look for what I call as best as possible a “unified field theory.” Kind of what Einstein was looking for, a “unified field theory.” What is the equation that really kind of nails the whole shebang? And maybe there’s no © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: such thing, maybe there is. But I always try to look at what is the one thing that I can maybe — the form of mentation that might give me the best results. Is there one thing, of all of the many things and ways to think of things, what is the one thing that will amalgamate all these moving parts and all these brain departments and functionality. And then for me it’s rhythm. Rhythm. Phrasing. That’s for me. And my melodic ear is on. It’s on, I have it on. There are certain things that I would say is static. They’re always on. These ears are always open. They’re never off. They shouldn’t be. They should be always on. And then the rest is like phrasing it and the rhythmic aspect, rhythmic configurations. How do you phrase what you hear? And see rhythm has almost the last thing to say about it because you can hear anything. You might be — people who have perfect pitch, they can identify what they’re hearing. Say well this is A, this is D or this is a A minor or this is a G seventh. They can tell you that without even thinking about it because they’ve got perfect pitch, whatever that means. They can tell you that. But how do you behave with that? How do you phrase that? There is a whole different thing right there, see? So this is like — what is the one thing that I could bring all these different mental functionalities together so that I could behave in a way that I’m musically successful. And then for me I — for me it’s almost like the phrasing and the rhythm. Because I can hear what’s going on. Fine. But how do I phrase it? And what is the rhythmic configuration of what I’m hearing? I can play a whole note, I can play a half note, I can play sixteenth notes. I can play any configuration I want. But what am I? Or how am I going to slice this hearing into parts? And what’s the boss? What’s telling me what note when? What’s telling me? So I have a way of looking at music like what, where, when. So I’ll use language as a metaphor. What, where, when. What is whatever the note is. Whatever the chord is. Whatever the sound is. Is it a diminished? Is it half-diminished? Is it major? Is it this, is it that. When and where is how do you sequence and geographically distribute what into these smaller pieces. And when is the rhythmic, the time and space aspect. When. You know when, what, where. You know when, what, where. So it’s all three in it. All three. Now which one is more important/less important? And guess what? They’re all equally important. Because what is meaningless. Where you put what is meaningless. And everything is time and space, according to some point of reference. Everything.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: If the when is working well for you, does that help to — I’m going to use the word “justify” pitches that maybe you didn’t mean to play but if rhythmically they fit into your phrasing, does that sort of —

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Well I think — here’s what I think — I think there’s something magic about concerning yourself with the phrasing and the rhythmic aspect. And what I mean by that I think once you start thinking that way there is something very compelling about that because you’ve trained your mind to actually think that way, and that has a way of setting up a part of © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: your mind for it to actually be freed up and I think you start playing the right notes. Yeah. Because there’s something compelling and hypnotic about that. For me. I can see — there’s a high tendency of the note being right because some kind of way because the phrase rhythmically is the right configuration for the moment. It is so much the truth that the truth of the note will be there with that, it’s a package deal.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: I like that. It’s a package deal.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Are there more right notes these days, in 2024, than there were back in the late sixties?

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: You know I’m going to have to take a bathroom break right quick.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Sure.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yup, 30 seconds.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Okay.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: I think I was trying to talk about —

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Are there wrong notes? More wrong notes now?

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: The harmonic language that’s acceptable nowadays as opposed to what might have raised eyebrows decades ago.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Well I mean you know, so you used the magic word “acceptable.” That depends. Because it’s the same — at least in Western music it’s the same twelve tones. It’s still the same twelve tones. But what you could do with them is a lot different than it was hundreds of years ago of course. So nothing has changed, the only thing that has changed is people doing what they want to do. So really when you say “wrong” note or “right” note, it’s almost according to what? You know according to what? So if you say a system of harmony, twelve tones allows for so many notes to be wrong or right, depending on how you’re framing these notes. You know what I mean? So there again, I mean, because if you just play chromatics for instance, that’s all twelve notes. You know, now, and let’s say we can, you know like, you know people who play Indian music like sitar or some of those instruments, they’re playing semi-tones. They’re all between — everybody doesn’t have the same system that Europe has. There are scales that there are tones between the tones. And it’s even American composers that have dealt with semi-tones and all this stuff. So it all exists. But just dealing with the twelve tones mathematically boy, that’s so many combinations of things. And what makes it right or wrong depends on what else — compared to what note. A wrong note is wrong only if the rest of it has been set up a certain way, the rest of the notes set up a certain way in order to make that. And then you could say well it’s just dissonant. There’s no such thing as a wrong note. So I mean you can always get intellectual about it. It’s just like this: if you take art for instance, and you take a person who has a canvas and takes a bucket of paint and just throws it on the canvas and then whatever happens happens. So you know people could sit down and say, © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: “Well that doesn’t look like Rembrandt,” or “It doesn’t look like Monet,” it looks like — and then another person says, “Yeah but look how this yellow drips down, it mixes with this red and I did it with no kind of egoic intent at all, I just did it in gravity and do it, and who said art isn’t that? And what it looks like and whatever you think it is is what’s still art. So you can get into all these banter, these intellectual arguments, but for me at this point, a wrong note, I don’t know if there is such a thing as that. But I do know there is such a thing as right ones. If that makes any —

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Well I’ve struggled to find a better word than “wrong.” And most people answer well what’s your intent or what did you do to justify, and I just want to insert something about what you were talking about with the bucket of paint, that in 1998 you said to me, “Almost anything that human beings that alter God or nature can be art.”

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Okay. Yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: I like that.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: I didn’t know that. That’s pretty good. Yeah.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: I should send you the transcript of what you said back then because, like today, you’re very quotable, Charles. So I want to wrap up just a little bit of talk, I rarely do this but —

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Okay.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Talk about saxophones.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Okay.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Because when I saw the video from Smoke I thought your saxophone, your alto was quite experienced-looking.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Oh that’s true. It’s an old Selmer.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: It was a beautiful thing. Can you just hold it up there?

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Now wait a minute because was it the record date because I played at Smokes twice, the record date it was on a Selmer VI and then I appeared at Smoke, maybe a year later, and it was a King Super 20.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Well I’m not sure which horn it was.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: If I see the picture I’ll know which one it was.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Yes, but which one do you have with you now?

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: I have the Selmer. Want me to play a couple of notes on it?

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Well I’d love to compare the —

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Oh okay, now let me see your horn, let me see your neck.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: This is a Buffet.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Oh that’s a Buffet?

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Yes. And —

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Wow. © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: The reason I was doing this is because I noticed something in your horn, whichever it was, and that was you know for years people have looked at this horn and go, “Wow, that’s old.”

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Yeah. It’s an old —

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Finally somebody said, “Oh what a nice patina.” Patina. So that’s the word I’ve latched on to, to make me feel good about my horn.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Patina. Yeah. Well you know when I saw the neck I thought it was a Selmer Balance Action.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Okay.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Well yeah. But those — I did have a Buffet at one time but I had a newer one. Yours is older than mine and I bet money that the sound is beautiful on that.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Yeah. I’ve had it since 1966.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: You want to play it for me?

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: No not really.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: All right. Okay.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Well this has been fascinating, Charles, you’re a very deep thinker. And you can come up with better adjectives than I can.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Oh I don’t know about that.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: I feel you are. But you also, you know you said this about yourself, there’s a great promo that’s out about “Reverence,” your latest recording, and one of the things you said about yourself, “I really like the language of bebop which allows for a broad range of expression, but I’m not a civilized bebopper, I’m a wild bebopper and I might go anywhere from that jumping off spot.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Oh well yeah, yup, yup, yup. Yeah. I try, and I will if I hear it.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: What’s up next for you?

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Well I’m traveling a lot. Let me see, I’ve got a record date that I’m going to do with Brian Lynch coming up in November. You know Brian Lynch, really wonderful trumpet player, a good friend. And let me see, I’ll probably do Smoke again at some point next year. Oh and I got a boat — a jazz cruise coming up in January. And I’m working quite a bit, I’m in Los Angeles in a couple of weeks from now, so I’ve been traveling quite a bit you know. So it’s been good. Since Covid kind of calmed down a bit I have been working a lot.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Well I really appreciate your time today, once again, and I wish I could shake hands but we’ll just you know —

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Okay. We’ll do it. All right. Thank you. I had a good time.

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Good. And thank Lynn for me for her assistance here.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: Okay. And send the link or whatever you can. © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

296790.speaker: MR
296790.text: Definitely will. Safe travels to you.

296790.speaker: CM
296790.text: All right thank you so much. Good seeing you. Take care. Bye-bye. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
INTERVIEWS WITH JAZZ MUSICIANS
MARY LOU WILLIAMS
Jazz Oral History Project
Interviewed by John S. Wilson
on 6/26/1973

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Let's start from the beginning. When were you born and where?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I was born in Atlanta, Georgia, 1910, 8th of May.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: 8th of May, 1910. What was your name when you were born?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Mary Louise Scruggs. That was my father's name. I was born out of wedlock.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did you know your father?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I met my father. Before I went to Europe I had to go to Atlanta, Georgia, to find out my birth date, because it seems that during the period when I was born they had these - what do they call the women that delivered babies?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Midwives.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Midwives, and my mother didn't really remember my birth date. I couldn't get it in Pittsburgh so I had to go back to Atlanta, Georgia, to try to get it.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: And you met your father there?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No. I met him in 1952.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How did you run into him then?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I have a half-brother in Atlanta, Georgia. He's a school teacher -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What's his name?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Willis Scruggs. He was just a little boy when I was about 2 or 3 years old. He just loved music arou
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: the house and he played and he's always had an admiration for my playing, to note that I had started so early. When I went to Atlanta, Georgia to try to get a birth certificate he took me out to meet my Dad.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: You met him?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, I met him.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How did you get along?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Well, the one thing that was a drag to me, he says, "You know who I am?" I said, "No." He said, "I'm your father. What'd you bring me?" I said, "Of all things, you've never done anything for me." So that ruined my day almost.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: That was the end of your father as far as you were concerned. Did you know anything about his background at all?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No. I'm from a family that never talked much about backgrounds and what-not, except for a few things that I learned from them at an early age. I used to, as a young kid, I'd sneak under the bed and listen to their conversation and I learned a great deal about the past through that. They never allowed the kids to sit in on conversations when they had company or anything like that.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: But this was not in relation to your father?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, I never knew about him at all. I never knew that I was born out of wedlock until I was 10 or 12 years
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: old and a relative of mine got angry with me and said, 'You grew up like a weed. You don't even belong to the family,' or something like that. Then I discovered it.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How did you feel?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I felt very discouraged but I've always been a strong person. I've never allowed anything to linger long with me to make me feel unhappy. I'd turn it off and go out and play or do something.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Now your mother. What was her name?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Virginia Burley, B-u-r-l-e-y. She was born in Atlanta, Georgia, and she played piano for the church, danced for the church to raise money. She said that they'd pull a curtain down across the pulpit and she'd dance to raise money for the church and she also played for the church. When I was around between 2 and 3 she said I was always getting into things as a child, was a nervous baby. She was nervous all the time she was practicing the organ so she decided to put me on her lap while she was practicing. She said one day while she had me on her lap I started picking out melodies. It must have been unusual because she dropped me and ran out to call the neighbors to come in and hear it. From that day on she had professional musicians around me like Jack Howard. He was a terrific boogie-woogie pianist you see, who played rag-time. This was in Atlanta, Georgia. I was still there. I didn't leave Atlanta until I was
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: around 4, 5, or 6. You lose track of the dates and age but I know that I was at least 4 or 5. So she had Jack Howard and professional musicians to come in. I like Jack Howard because he played such a strong piano he could break up all the pianos and as a baby I started playing like that. I think I got the masculine quality from him, of playing.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: At that early age did you have any professional teachers?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, my mother wouldn't allow anyone to teach me because she took one lesson and after that she couldn't improvise any more. So she allowed no one to teach me and I'm very happy that she didn't because later on I discovered that I had a strong pitch, perfect pitch. In Pittsburgh I found out. I happened to be sitting in a class and the teacher had lost her harp. She couldn't give the class the tone to start their singing, so I told her I could do that, and she was surprised when I did it. She went out in the hall where the piano was and I had given her the right tone, and I discovered that I had perfect pitch.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Are there dangers in having perfect pitch or is it just a help?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: It's a great help. It's a danger in studying early because you may lose it. I know some, great musicians that never lost it, like Dizzy Gillespie, but it's a danger in losing it through studying music, you know.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Why does studying make you lose it?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, because everything's on paper and you don't get any more sounds or anything. I think it's best, especially in jazz, for a musician to learn to feel everything and teach himself. If he's going to play the classics - like one summer I went to a teacher for about 2 weeks and I knew what to do, you see, but there's a danger in losing the feeling in jazz because it's a self-taught music and since I was going to play nothing but jazz I benefited by not studying...

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How did you know you were going to play nothing but jazz?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, I never really knew but my guidance in life - I never really knew what I was going to do. I think God was working me towards doing greater things - I have a feeling about God using certain people to help others and they're - they really don't know what they're going to do but it works out that they're doing a terrific job for Him, and that has been my whole life. I never knew that I was going to play jazz or the classics but I knew that I loved jazz.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: We'll get to that as we get along. But getting back to Atlanta, did you have any brothers or sisters then?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Oh, many, maybe nine or eleven. Twins - I have two twins that were born on the same day I was born but a different year, the 8th of May.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Let's start from the beginning. When were you born and where?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I was born in Atlanta, Georgia, 1910, 8th of May.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: 8th of May, 1910. What was your name when you were born?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Mary Louise Scruggs. That was my father's name. I was born out of wedlock.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did you know your father?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I met my father. Before I went to Europe I had to go to Atlanta, Georgia, to find out my birth date, because it seems that during the period when I was born they had these - what do they call the women that delivered babies?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Midwives.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Midwives, and my mother didn't really remember my birth date. I couldn't get it in Pittsburgh so I had to go back to Atlanta, Georgia, to try to get it.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: And you met your father there?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No. I met him in 1952.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How did you run into him then?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I have a half-brother in Atlanta, Georgia. He's a school teacher -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What's his name?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Willis Scruggs. He was just a little boy when I was about 2 or 3 years old. He just loved music arou
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It was because I had taken the neighborhood on.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: This was after, um in Pittsburgh, in East Liberty.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Down in Atlanta, you stayed there until what - 3 or 4?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Until I was, I think, 3 or 4. It's difficult, it's been so long, to remember how old I was because I never heard them tell me how old I was when we left Atlanta. I think I was between 3 and 4.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Do you know how old your mother was when you left Atlanta?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No. I know one time in Pittsburgh we had one of the youngest generations in America, it was listed as that in Pittsburgh.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: You and your mother?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: See, my great-grandmother was living when I was born and my sister got married before she died and had a little baby. I think my mother must have married when she was 16.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: You mentioned your great-grandmother. This was on your mother's side?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: My mother's side.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did they all come from Atlanta?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: They all came from Atlanta.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: And had been there for several generations?
WILLIAMS 8

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, Atlanta.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Aside from your mother, were they musical particularly?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, I think only my mother and myself. My brother, the twin brother - you know, the two twins I mentioned - he was musical but he didn't work at it. He could dance and play a little piano.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When you started picking out those tunes on your mother's lap, do you know now what you were doing?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, that's the strange thing, I didn't know what I was doing.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: I mean do you know the tunes now? Did your mother tell you?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, when I played the History of Jazz I played the same tune that she taught me... it was a rag-time. we called it 'Fandango' And "Mother Pin a Rose on Me", my stepfather taught me that when I was - I used to play that.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: This was, when you talk of your stepfather, Fletcher Burley?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Fletcher Burley.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: So that gets us up into Pittsburgh. Why did your mother leave Atlanta?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Well, I don't know. I think they just moved away because they had a yearning to go. My grandmother's sister, all her sisters, had moved I guess years previously
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: and so they decided to go and move to Philadelphia, also her mother, my grandmother Mrs.(Rouser)- Anna Jane(Rouser) rather - and her mother was also there, the Parkers, and her father, in Pittsburgh, so I think they decided to go there to be with the family.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: So you're maybe roughly 4 years old when you get to Pittsburgh?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What was the family life like then? Your mother was not married at this point?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, I think she married Fletcher Burley about a year later.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: And she was living with her sister?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: She was living with her aunt, my grandmother's sister.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: I see. When she married Fletcher Burley did she still live there or did you all move somewhere else?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: We lived there for a while. I started to school there and then we moved to Euclid Avenue in East Liberty; later on Wilmington Avenue and Hamilton Avenue after that. We moved about 3 different places before the family really became settled.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Once you got to Pittsburgh do you remember early years of playing piano?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I never stopped playing piano. I had a cousin
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: that used to dance and we'd make a little money dancing. At one time when I was about 6 or 7 years old I made more money than my stepfather by this. The teachers used to take me home with them and give me a little handkerchief pocket full of money. I'd play for the (musician?), they'd give a little afternoon tea. I'd have to sit on someone's lap, I was so small. I'd play for the little teas and for the neighborhood. I'd charge a dollar an hour.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What did you play mostly?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: All requests. I couldn't read piano and - well, this is getting a little ahead of it, but I'll talk about it now while it's on my mind. When I was 10 or 12 I played with a union band there and tunes like "The Doll Dance" I couldn't read it but I had such a terrific ear that after they played the first chorus, I knew it. They'd have the music up in front of me and I never even told them I couldn't read it. But it must have been all right and no complaints because I was hired from year to year to play with them.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Were you a member of the union?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No. The strangest thing happened after the musicians found out that I was playing with them. They used to come by the house, when I was between the ages of 8 and 10 or 12, when I was in grade school, and take me out. and pick me up mother, a I had a family that didn't mind. In the beginning they had an older member to go with me and after a while some
WILLIANS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: musician would get her confid_ence, gain her confidence and then she'd allow me to go with them.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: At this stage were you just playing what people wanted you to play or were there certain kinds of things that you liked to play?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, I played anything they asked me to play. There were certain things that I played, like Fats Waller - I'd get his records. My stepfather bought me a piano but it was a what-do-you-call-it - set player? - style where you had rolls - player piano. I learned the classics from that.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How? By watching the keys?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: The keys, my fingers would go down on the keys, yes... I had 3 people in the family - my grandfather, my uncle, and my stepfather, that would give me a weekly allowance to play their favorite tunes. My uncle liked Irish songs. My grandfather liked the classics and my stepfather liked boogie-woogie, so he'd give me more money than my - my uncle or grandfather would give me 50¢ a week and he'd give me 15 or 20.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: You mean, if the one that liked classics had given you $25 -

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: 50¢ a week.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: A little more you might have ended up playing classical music?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I don't think so because I liked jazz.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When did you start playing with any regularity anywhere? Was it during this period?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: From the age of 6 until I was 14 I was all over the city playing. I played for the Mellons. I became the little piano girl of East Liberty and anytime anybody was having a party or anything they'd say, "Well, let's get the little piano girl." So by this time I was among nothing but the wealthy people of Pittsburgh, playing for their parties. The chauffeur would pick me up or my stepfather, Fletcher Burley, would take me. He would take me to parties like for the Mellons and my brother-in-law, Hugh Floyd, would take me to theatres to keep my ears open and listen to musicians. Sometimes I would go to sleep and he'd throw me over his shoulder and bring me home.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: So you were getting real training?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes. Roland Mayfield later on - there were 3 important people in my life, including the pianist that I spoke about -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Jack Howard.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Jack Howard. There was Roland Mayfield, when I was stranded at the age of 12 - I'd go out by myself a lot and he'd get in his car and pick me up and bring me home.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Who was Roland Mayfield?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Roland Mayfield was a very important man.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: He was what you call a sportsman; he had a nightclub and he became very wealthy among the people there in East Liberty and he was called the Black Prince of East Liberty. I met him when I was 12 years old. He taught me to drive a car. In fact there was about 6 young girls where we went to school. They could all drive but they had to ask me if they could drive the car. He played a very important part in my career.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: In what ways?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: He would always pick me up or give me anything that I needed. I would never write home and ask anybody for anything when I was out on the road. He would ask, "How's the kid?... She don't look and sound too good." He'd jump in his car, I don't care what was happening, even at work in his place of business, and pick me up and bring me home.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How about Jack Howard?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Jack Howard was an influence as far as giving me strength on the piano. He told me always to play the left hand louder than the right because that's where the beat and the feeling was. It's just like a drum keeping a steady beat. He taught me a lot of professional things it would have taken me years and years to learn.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: You first met him in Atlanta?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes. The first date that I began to play my mother got him to come in...

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: And then he was in Pittsburgh later?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, he came to Pittsburgh. In fact all my mother's
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: friends came to Pittsburgh.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Who was the third influence?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Fletcher Burley, my stepfather.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What sort of a man was he?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: He was the kind of a man that he loved me so much he would almost put his own kids aside for me, if I needed anything. Well, he was very charitable. Sometimes I'd bring kids in that didn't have shoes and he'd give them money to buy shoes or to buy clothing. Fletcher had a big coat - this is funny - he had a big oversized coat made and he took me in gambling joints and everywhere and he'd put me under this coat because.... (NOT CLEAR) He was considered a very good, bad man, not overbearing but he was treacherous if you made him angry. Everybody in Pittsburgh knew about this and nobody even tried to harm me. But he was a very sweet man. He'd say, "Stop the game. I want you to hear my little girl play." He'd put a dollar in the hat and then they'd pass the hat around after I had finished and he'd take me outside and he'd say, "Give me my dollar back."... My mother didn't know what he was doing until three years ago. I was talking to her and she said 'My Goodness, you didn't tell me!'

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Who else was an influence?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Just a few. They were big influences people of course in music.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was Fletcher Burley....?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, he was, but he was a strange man. He would
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: not gamble. He worked every day; he would not gamble with that money. He'd take the money home and give it to my mother for her bills and what-not and he'd go up the street and have a friend throw him in the game. That's what they called it - that is, give him a stake in the game. He was a terrific gambler.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Now you talked about Roland Mayfield coming out and getting you when you were stranded. Were you touring the whole time -

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I was with home talent shows and things like that. I was talking to him one time, "Roland, do you remember when you picked me up in New York when I was stranded?" He said, "New York, Buffalo, Cincinnati, Chicago, Cleveland, Steubenville."

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When did you start playing at something more than parties?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Do you remember the Cotton Pickers?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: McKinney's Cotton Pickers?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes. When I was in around 5th or 6th grade they used to come to Pittsburgh and they'd drive this big bus on our street, all these musicians, Chu Berry and all of them would take me out on gigs with them.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Because you were that well known?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes. I was well known by musicians. When they'd come to Pittsburgh they'd come by and pick me up and take me out with them. I went out with the home
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: talent show then. The first time I left really professionally is when a show came to Pittsburgh and the pianist, something happened to him so the Western Union boy hdd delivered a wire to the owner of the show. The owner told him, "My goodness, I need a pianist. I've got to go out..." He said, "I know who you should get, the little piano girl." He said, "What?" He said, "Come and go with me, I'll take you to East Liberty to her house." So he brought this man all the way - about 8 miles from downtown to East Liberty. When the manager drove up I was on the sidewalk playing Hop Scotch with the kids. He was so angry and upset because he didn't have much time before the show that night. He said, "Why would you take up so much of my time bringing me out here?" He said, "Wait till you hear her play." So he went in and out, and he asked me if I could memorize and I said yes. He hummed the entire show to me and I memorized it. That night I played it.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was any of it material you had heard before?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Nothing I had heard before - Bandanna Days and all that kind of thing, I had never heard them before. You know during that period they were all tunes like that, like old-fashioned, like, I don't know what you'd call them, but they were like minstrel show tunes, you know? So I went up - he had to go to a notary with my mother so that I'd be able to go out. It was during the summer vacation
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: and school was out, so my mother signed papers for me to go out with a lady. I worked with him about two months until school opened in September.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Whereabouts did you go?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I went to all these little cities like Springfield, Ohio, Springfield something, Indianapolis -

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: One-nighters?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, weekly shows.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What kind of a show was this?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Vaudeville, the worst...T.O.B.A, you've heard of that. Tough On Black Actors.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was this Brodson Harris? 'Buzzin'

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Brodson Harris. Buzzin'

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What did he do?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: He was the owner of the show.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: He didn't perform?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, he was a comedian, a very good one, a black-face comedian.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: So when you got back from your summer's tour, what became of your career then?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well I was still in school, in school for a long time, but see I'd go out in summer vacations. One time I ran away and my mother came and got me.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Where did you go? Why did you run away?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, because I had that blood in me like a gypsy. I wanted to go out and play, be with musicians.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How old were you?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I really don't know. I was under 16 because you know, because when I played with Duke Ellington's Washingtonians I was between 16 and 17. I just found a date I went to Pittsburgh... I have some stockings, my first stockings that I wore with Seymour and Jeanette; I'll show them to you later. I just washed them last night. Peter brought all these things out in a trunk and so I found the date. It was in about '25 or '26 when I was with Seymour and Jeanette.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: You mean you washed them and they didn't fall apart?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No. I'll show them to you; they're wonderful. I have all the first things that I wore with them, except the shoes and the dress. You were asking me about -

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: About your touring after that summer with Buzzin' Fredeson Harris. The home talent show - you were going to tell me about the home talent show.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, in Washington, Pennsylvania - I went there and she didn't know where I was so she found out where I was through a friend.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was this your mother?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, my mother, so she came there and picked me up. I was kind of glad because the owner of the show - they had these young kids, 12 and 14, 15 years old, and this
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: man was not too good. One person I appreciate very much and she was a very good friend, she was 18. She watched over these kids. This man had taken 3 of us into a room and I never had a drink in my life except once when I was a little baby.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How did you get in contact with this man?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: He knew about me. By this time everybody knew about me, even musicians from New York. I was playing a style of piano that must have been amazing to them but it was nothing to me. You know, I never had a needle or anything, I was just playing, that's all, but it reached musicians in New York and everywhere knew about my playing.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Well, did the man come to your house?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: For the home talent, yes. They usually called - we didn't have a phone then - they got in touch. It seemed that everybody knew about me all over East Liberty and downtown.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Do you remember this man's name?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, I don't remember his name and happy I forgot it, because he was not too nice with these kids.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: He got you and the other girls in a room?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: In a room and he was giving us whiskey and Coca-Cola, and Margaret came in. He was just about to do his act, you know, and she came into the room. I was so sick.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: He put it in Cola-Cola and we thought we were drinking Coca-Cola. None of us knew the taste of whiskey. She came in and she took a stick and she was beating all over his head. Margaret Warren, she was beautiful. She was watching over us and we didn't even know it.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What became of the home talent show?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: He was the one that got this home talent, the manager of the home talent.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was this the beginning of it or the break-up of it?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, the beginning of it was, we rehearsed and we did the home talent show in Pittsburgh. Then we ventured out to Washington, Pennsylvania, to a theatre there, to do the same show and he had all these young kids with him.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: So was that as far as you got, just to Washington?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes. Margaret pulled out and took 3 of us home with her.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did you work with her again?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, with the Buzzin' Harris show, and I always had that same protection from her.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: So this is another person that -?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, Margaret Warren. She was such a beautiful person. She would walk over and you wouldn't even know it. She was so quiet and easy going, just a beautiful person.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What became of her, do you know?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: She's still in Pittsburgh; I just saw her when I did the Mass there. She was dancing with the chorus, you see. She was teaching the girls. She was 18 herself but we were 14, 15 years old.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Earlier you mentioned about your listening to Fats Waller records. What else were you listening to?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Jelly Roll Morton and Willie the Lion. I didn't get many of his records. I had copies of Jelly Roll's records. I happened to go to New York one time and I was playing his 'Pearls' and he, you know how he was, a little irritable and he said, "You don't play it like that! You play it like this!" And then he showed me how he wanted me to play it.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: But back in an earlier stage in Pittsburgh you were listening to Waller and to Jelly Roll and to Willie the Lion?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Jelly Johnson's rolls for the set player.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: After the home talent show what happened next?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: John Williams - I later married him, you know, my first husband - joined up with the Harris Buzzin' Harris show in Cleveland.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: You went out twice with that show?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I went out twice. The second time John Williams and his combo joined it.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: But the first time was just summer vacation?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: And then in about a year or so, was this a summer vacation?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I really don't know whether it was summer vacation but I decided to go out and stay out, which I didn't. I had to come back and go to school again. I went to Cleveland and several other places and by that time John Williams had joined with a small combo and he won my mother's confidence. He was very smart. He really should have been a psychiatrist because the things he did to help Andy Kirk in the band, keeping him down dissenting and all that and making a guy play and do his instrument was really terrific.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How old was he when you first met him?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: He must have been around 19 or 20. I think he's about 5 or 6 years older than I am, something like that.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: You were 14?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, I was... He had a small combo, it was the most terrific thing you've ever heard in your life. See, John was the first musician that ever played a baritone and he was really in demand all over the country, everybody heard about him. But he chose to work with other people, you know, and he had his own little combo. We had a trombone player there that played more trombone with his foot than I hear today.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What was his name?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Sylvester Briscoe. His music was just terrific.
WILLIAMS
Buzzin

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When you went out with the Harris show were you just part of the band or did you have a special spot of your own?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, no special, all I did was I played for the show and when they were short a chorus girl I'd go up on the stage and dance. I never did a solo but we did a combo. You know that was during the era in the 20's of the jazz band, you know, small combos and all they did was clown. A lot of music was coming out of the horns but there was a lot of clowning. That was the jazz band era...

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What sort of clowning?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, I'd play music and I'd turn around on the stool... I used to put a sheet over the keys and play with my elbows...

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How did you do that?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Just did it. You know I used to sit at the piano, my brother-in-law said, when I was nothing but a baby, crawl out, I wouldn't eat, I wouldn't do anything, and I'd just drink a glass of water. My brother-in-law, Hugh Floyd, he tried to play alto and for a long time I never liked altos because he used to get on my nerves, but that sound, that tone he was getting, made my flesh crawl. One day I hit him with a lamp on his head. He went out and bought a gold saxophone; still couldn't play it. So we'd get into such arguments that - even as a kid
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: because these sounds would get into me. I'd sit at that piano, getting sounds myself, all day, and just rehearse and play. This was during the period, I guess just before I went out with anybody. It was during the time I was playing for parties. The police on their way - the police station was on the corner - they'd stop on the porch and I'd have to play a concert for them. If I was out late at night by myself, coming from a gig, they'd stop and bring me down in the patrol car to the house. They'd wait at the streetcar for me. I played concerts for them and the Hamilton Packing Company - these big trucks, you know, they'd always stop Saturdays...

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: In those days when you were coming home late at night, did you ever have any trouble?

53571.speaker: W:
