53571.text: None. There was always that strange protection like Margaret Warren, the police. I had a close shave a couple of times playing for parties, young boys, their parents had gone to Europe, and I just left. They were upstairs getting drunk and I ran out and left. I wouldn't tell my stepfather because he would have gone back and killed everybody, because he was very mean about things like that.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Well, we left you where you had just met John Williams. Did he join the Buzzin Harris show by himself...?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: With a combo, about 6 of us including myself.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: You joined his group then?...

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I don't remember if I just played piano and that's all for the show. I don't remember having a drummer or anybody then.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: So you were the whole thing?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I may have been. I don't remember drums or bass or tuba. See they used tubas then.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: When John Williams brought his group in and you became a part of it, what was your early reaction to John? Did you like him or not like him, or what?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Not enough to (ask him) but I did it to get away from home. I admired him because he was such a giant in bringing love among musicians and bringing them together. He was such a giant in picking out problems right away and I admired him for his ability, but as far as marrying I don't think I loved him enough.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: This time how long did the whole show stay together?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: For a long time. We just went right to the end there, till there was nothing else more to do. They stuck together for a long time.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How wide an area did you tour?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Let's see, Indiana, Ohio - we never did hit the major cities. We were in Oklahoma, small places. It was impossible to really make a living...

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How long did this go on, a couple years?
WILLIAMS
I cant remember.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It may have.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What do you remember next?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: During this period we played for circuses and carnivals and that is the worst life that anybody could ever - oh, my goodness. I thought about that and I just shivered in bed once because these roustabouts - you call them that? - they are terrible... Doc Cheatham, good trumpeter, did you ever hear of him? He sounded like an [ ]. He was sensational. He was with us during that period and we played some really rough places. That's a terrible life.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When you worked a carnival what did you do for a piano?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, they had a piano, there was always a piano there.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did the carnival provide it or did you have to carry it with you?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I really don't know. No, we didn't have enough money to carry anything with us. We were just barely making it.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Speaking of Doc Cheatham, who else was in your group?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Doc Cheatham, Briscoe, and Joe Williams, a terrific guitarist. He made a banjo sound like a guitar and I loved it, because banjos - I used to hate the sound of them. He was very good. Briscoe and a drummer - I have forgotten his name completely. Later on with Seymour and Jeanette
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: we had Abey somebody. I can't remember his last name.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Well then eventually the Buz Harris show, the tour just came to an end?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, I tell you, John Williams got an offer to go with Seymour and Jeanette.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: While you were still working with Buz?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, and it had really petered out.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Who were Seymour and Jeanette?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: One of the greatest acts on - I'll tell you, during that period you know how prejudiced they were. They wouldn't dare have a black person on Keith, Pantages, that. But Seymour and Jeanette were the only black team on Keith circuit, Pantages, and all - and Bill Bojangles. They only booked those two people. So John Williams received a wire that they needed a combo because Seymour did a strutting act and what not. He was very good at it but he had a bad heart, so he thought that if he got a small combo that would help him along. So he wired John and said he'd be making $75. Woo, that was like making a thousand dollars a week, you know! So we joined -

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: A week.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: For how many people?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: $75 each, so that was like a thousand dollars a week because we had been making $25 or $30. So we joined
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Seymour and Jeanette. A strange thing happened. We came to New York - I think it was New York we had gone, either New York or Rochester, some place. So we were getting ready to rehearse. I'd always stand at the piano and look at it before I tackled it. I was just sitting there. So Seymour came out and they introduced - I don't think they introduced him to everybody. He just came out, because he was sitting there and was irritable all the time. He said, "What's that girl doing, sitting at the piano?" Nobody would say anything. He said, "Well, get her off the stage so we can play." Nobody would say anything. So I didn't move so he said, "Let's start the rehearsal." So I started playing and both of them had a fit. They didn't know that John had a woman with them. They had a fit because during this period because a woman was not really allowed to be in with a group of men or anything. They were so surprised. So he said, "We can't take her. We can't let not Keith but the manager see her because she's a black woman and we've got to put pants on her." They were wondering what they were going to do. They said, "She's good, she's good!" So John said, "Forget it; listen to her play." So we went on with that and everything was fine. About 6 months or a year later Seymour died and John Williams and the combo and I worked with Jeanette for a while till we were stranded in New York.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Stranded in New York?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yep. We got stranded in New York and so we went back to Pittsburgh, Joe Williams, John, and I, then later on to Memphis with John. During this period is when I met Fats Waller.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: When you were in New York with Seymour and Jeanette?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes. We had a date in the Lincoln Theatre - I imagine you've heard of the Lincoln Theatre in Harlem? Duke Ellington had just come into New York with his combo, the Washingtonians they were. They were playing the Lincoln with us because Seymour and Jeanette were the top black act. So he played on stage with the band and they had me in the pit playing with the band. Still couldn't read. I played in the band with Tricky Sam, Bubber Miley, and Sonny Greer, and then I'd go up on stage with the act. I met Fats Waller then and I can tell you he was just a sensation in New York, when they'd turn the light on people would scream, when he sat down, people would scream. I never saw such a thing. When he finished, that was the end; they had to let it cool off.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was he playing the organ just as a solo specialty?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No.... He probably was playing for the movie but this week he did a tune before the show.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: I remember someone telling me he used to play for the news reel. Nobody was watching the news reel and he did all kind of things.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, he was terrific. Later on in Scranton he
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: was working in the Cotton Club, Connie's Inn. one Which/was in Harlem?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: The Cotton Club was too.
(THIS SECTION IS NOT CLEAR)

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Connie's Inn. A friend of his took me there and ...He said, "I have a little girl who can play everything you composed." Now this man was a giant. Leonard, the producer, I've forgotten his name -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Leonard Harper.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: He said, "All right, Fats, we're ready for the music after you give the girl some routines." I'd say, "O.K." He'd bring out his jug and what-not and he'd say, "What's the title? What you doing?" Leonard would tell him the story. And the man would play it straight off, lyric and everything, a whole 32-bar song... So I was sitting over in the corner. This man had moved there because he was going to put them on, like a bet. He'd say, "This girl can play everything she heard you compose." "She can't!" "I bet you!" So I sat down and played. ( ) and all these other things. Fats took me and threw me up in the air. He grabbed me and threw me up in the air and he bit me and everything. I wished I wasn't even there after all that went on. I thought he was the most amazing woman's pianist, I'm going to do the same thing. What's the/name I told you my brother-in-law used to take me to hear in Pittsburgh? Lovey Austin used to write music and play with her left hand. I used to do that with Andy Kirk.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Where did you run into Lovey Austin?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I ran into Lovey Austin when I was about 8 or 9 or 10 years old. I must have been pretty small because my brother-in-law used to throw me on his shoulder if I went to sleep in the theatre, and bring me home like that. He took me up there to see her, what she was doing. She had her legs crossed, with a cigarette in her mouth, playing and writing music for the next act. When the next act came on, the music was ready. She'd pass it out to the musicians who were going to play it. So I thought, I'm going to do that one day, and I did. That's how I used to work out my arrangements with Benny Goodman, when I was with Kirk.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Why did you want to do it?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Because it was amazing, that someone could concentrate like that - play, smoke a cigarette, with her legs crossed, and playing that music... And it comes easy after once you get on to it. I always wanted to do that... because it's so creative... I think there were two people inspired me because I wanted to do what they were doing.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: We're coming to the end of this reel so why don't we sort of break here.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Mary, let's get back to when you were born in Atlanta. Tell me about the circumstances of the place where you were born.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Well, I used to hear my parents speak of the land where the house was built. It seems that it was a sunken cemetery of soldiers of the Civil War and then at the time I was born - there was a midwife brought me into the world - I was born like with a veil. I guess this was a superstition but we were living in a neighborhood of a lot of superstitious people down South. This midwife told my mother that I was born with a veil over my eyes and for her to save this veil and dry it out and she could tell when I was sick and all that. I used to hear so many stories about spooks and ghosts and everything. Seemed like I picked up on that when I was about two or three years old because my mother was afraid to take me out anywhere with us. She said that one day we were walking in the field and I saw a little white dog and the white dog grew into a cow. I said, 'Come on down, Mother,' but she ran and left me but she came back. Everybody was afraid to be around me because I was seeing so many weird things.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When you saw the little white dog grow into a cow, did it?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It certainly did. I remember that. My Mother said it's amazing some of the things I used to see and some of the things I remember when I was two years old. It seems that I was playing with this little white dog
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: and she didn't pay any attention to it. I reached up and said, 'Oh, it's a cow,' or something like that. She ran but she said she came back and picked me up and took me home.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What did they do with the cow?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I guess it disappeared. But she said at an early age I was seeing spirits. I often wondered about a lot of other kids, you know, with their imagination. They are probably able to see them also. Because I've gone through life like that, seeing various things, except when I became Catholic - now I feel them more or less. I don't see them any more.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: We'll get to that part later. But when you were saying you were seeing things and now you feel them, was this extrasensory perception?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It's a little bit of everything I guess in that direction because when I was with the Andy Kirk band my husband used to have to tie me in bed because in a hotel, a very bad hotel, I remember walking up the steps going into the hotel and I saw a man standing up at the top... with his head hanging off. I'd run or something, you know what I mean, and they'd say, there she goes again.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: For example, they had to tie you in bed because otherwise what would happen?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It's like a nightmare. Whatever happened in that room, maybe a suicide or I don't know what it is, I'd see strange things from it, you know.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: This kind of sense that you had, entirely aside from seeing that sort of thing and reconstructing something that happened some place, how did it affect your music?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I think that when anybody has anything like that, ESP, if you're an artist it should be put into your music, because at one time I could hear a musician playing and could hear the note he was going to make next. It was just that fast. It was just like seeing spiritual or telling someone's fortune, I knew exactly what he was going to do.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: This is why you could listen to Fats Waller improvise a whole score and then you sit down and play it?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, I don't know, but it may have something to do with the fastness of the mind and hearing. See, when you develop a thing like that it can be good for you or it can be very bad. You can use it in a bad way, 'cause there's nothing we can do about what's happening to us. Some people lose their minds. But I think it's useful in your work.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Is this something you can control?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, you can't control it... You see these things when you're not even expecting them. I may be walking down the street with somebody - there was a little incident when my brother-in-law was bringing me home from
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: a party and he carried me on his shoulder, because I had gone to sleep. That's what the men did in the family. I I was a little tired they'd just put me on their shoulder and take me home. I woke up and I said, "Don't walk into that man." He started running with me because it's a frightening thing, you know. I could see a man on the street but he couldn't see him. Once with Andy Kirk's band I grabbed the wheel because I saw an old couple on the road, passing, and the old man was crippled and passed in front of the car and /I/ grabbed the wheel... and they weren't there. I was the only person that saw it.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What would have happened, do you suppose, if you hadn't grabbed the wheel and gone right straight through what you say wasn't really there. Would there have been something there?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: It could be an accident but I'm in control of that now. I've seen things while I was driving but I just kept straight through it. That happened to me not too long ago, I guess about 20 years ago, or 15. I saw a little kid run in front of the car. He was not there. Seemed like all of a sudden I thought, gosh, it's after one o'clock. There's no kid out here this size... Perhaps some little kid had got killed there.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Another thing, back in Atlanta, your mother married. Was she married before you were born or after?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: She was married - I think she had left him shortly after I was born, when I was born, I'm sure, because I never met him. I only saw a picture of him.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What was his first name?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Mose Winn, W-i-n-n.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: When you were younger were you Mary Lou Winn for a while?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I used Winn and I used Burley for the last name. I was Mary Louise Winn and I used Burley.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Did you use them interchangeably...?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I just mixed them up. Often when someone was interviewing me I said Mary Lou Winn and I'd say Mary Lou Burley. One time I said Mary Louise Winn Burley, until Jack Kapp with the Decca, changed my name to Mary Lou Williams. Well, I had married John Williams, so he changed my name to Mary Lou Williams.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Up until that point had you ever called yourself professionally Mary Lou Williams?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, never. Jack Kapp did this.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: We'll get to the Andy Kirk part. You never, when you sat in with the Andy Kirk band, you were never Mary Lou Williams then?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Were you anything consistent...?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Burley. In some of the old write-ups you'd see Mary Lou Winn Burley, or Mary Lou Winn.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: But there wasn't a period in which you stopped being Mary Lou Winn and became Mary Lou Burley?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, before I was named Williams, before I got married. I stuck to the Burley because I was very fond of my stepfather, Fletcher Burley.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: That's when you dropped the Winn?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: O.K., now, we left you in New York and that's Jelly Roll Morton? when you met Fats Waller. Was that when you met John Williams?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I met John Williams while I was with the Buzzy Harris show.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: No, I said Jelly Roll Morton.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Before I joined the Buzzin' Harris show somebody brought me to New York for a visit, some musical person. I was playing so much of Jelly Roll Morton until somebody took me to his office... I was not with the band or anything.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: And that was when you played the Pearls' for him?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: I see, and you were told that was not the way to play it?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: In a very rough way.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Did you play some of your own things for him then too?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, I was only interested in him. I don't think I was writing too much then. I was just playing things that I heard or people were teaching me new tunes or things like that. I didn't start to write until I was with Andy Kirk.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Now, after New York you went back to Pittsburgh and then you went to Memphis?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I went to Memphis after Seymour died. We went with Seymour and Jeanette, his wife, for a while and we were stranded, as I said, and finally made it to Pittsburgh. Joe Williams - I left him there with my people, the guitar and banjo player.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Had you married John Williams at that time?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, we got married in Memphis.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was Joe related to John?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, but they went to school together. Joe Williams was from Kansas City, Kansas; and John was from Memphis, Tennessee, but he went to school in Kansas City. That's where he met Joe. When we went to Memphis, Tennessee, that's where John Williams my husband - who later became my husband - was born and so we got in the band together. He was such a terrific man. The union musicians there - they had no union when I was there - he got a union going for them. The musicians would work like from 8 o'clock till 3 or 4 in the morning and they'd get
WILLIAMS 39

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: paid $2, so John, when he left Memphis they were making over $20-25 and the leader $30, because I remember once - they were very, very prejudiced in Memphis - he had such a terrific band and Jimmy Lunceford was teaching at a high school there. He and Jimmy Lunceford were very good friends (John Williams and Jimmy Lunceford). So everything that John did Jimmy would try to do something better. So he said to John, "I'm going to get a band better than that combo you have." Jimmy got himself a girl piano player and he taught kids - high school pupils, he was teaching in a high school - he taught them music. All these young kids being brought up in Memphis, he taught them music. He and John used to play checkers and John would beat him playing checkers and he'd say, "That's all right; I'm going to get a band better than you."

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: So I worked there for a while. Being in the North so long I was pretty mean to get along with because I wasn't used to what was happening. Before John got his combo I got a little job out on the outskirts of Memphis and these people were ringing a bell and saying, "I want this," and telling me, "You're from the North and if you don't do what we want you to do... yeah, we'll lynch you" and this guy took me home every night, he was talking all this talk and I waited till I got in front of the house and started screaming and so... (LAUGHTER)

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Were you playing solo?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, by myself. I worked for Mrs. Singleton and it was a bad night club, you know, where they gambled and everything. Mrs. Singleton owned this club.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was she related to Zutty?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, no relation. This was in Memphis. One night I went to sleep on the street car. Usually when you sat in the front and it began to get crowded with whites you had to move to the back. I was sleeping so when we got out to the end of the street car line the conductor said, "You're going to be hurt, little girl, because you're supposed to move in the back." I said, "I went to sleep." When the car made the last stop I started screaming on him and scratching him. I didn't understand this, you know. I worked for Mrs. Singleton about a year and a half till I had to leave because a farmer came in from Mississippi and had paid the black cook $50 to kidnap me and take me down to Mississippi. You wouldn't have heard from me any more because that had happened to many, many younger people in Memphis. They'd take them to in Mississippi, man and you'd have to go through each town to get back to Memphis and they'd stop you on the way. So Mrs. Singleton had me go home and wait till this guy left. He stayed around Memphis for 2 weeks trying to get me down to Mississippi.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was Mrs. Singleton black?
WILLIAMS 41

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: She was white. She was very nice and kind. She also had a little young kid that it seemed that the family had died out or something and left her with a little young boy and he was about 15 years old. She was as nice as she could be to him. She was very kind but I didn't like some of the other people that was there.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: You worked there for about a year?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Well, just about 6 months or so because/She I had to leave - wouldn't trust me - I mean wouldn't... because of conditions that existed like that in Tennessee. So what happened, John got this terrific combo going out at the White Rose or something like that. in Memphis. We were just doing real great and all of a sudden wo decided to join Andy Kirk's band. So I had to get someone to play with me to take his place so I hired Jimmy Lunceford. He worked /with me for about 6 months and this was while we were in Memphis.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What became of Jimmy's band...?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Jimmy didn't have his band. It wasn't organized. He didn't organize it until maybe about 6 months or a year after I left Memphis.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: It wasn't Andy Kirk that John was going to join?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No. J. Holder

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It seemed that was kind of a reckless guy with money and he'd done this so many times so that the entire band called a meeting and they decided to have Andy as the leader of the band...
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: This happened after you had joined?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: After I had joined. Jimmy Lunceford worked for me for about, I guess, 6 months, I don't know how long it was...

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Why did you stay that long in Memphis after John left?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Because he had built up such a big clientele with all the gigs and jobs and things that he had worked for - I guess we were there 2 or 3 years. They still wanted some parts of the band - he was missing and I was a big part of it, being so tiny and whatnot, and then we had some dates that we had to play. We had to finish these dates. We got some more dates then to play.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: I see. So you led the band and finished those up? Then was that when you went to Oklahoma City?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, drove to Oklahoma City, changed tires and everything. His mother was with me. A little old car that John had, a Chevrolet, looked like a bathtub. I have a picture of it now and I laugh about it. I drove from Memphis to Oklahoma.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How far is that?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I guess about 600 miles.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How long did it take you, do you know?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I don't remember. I know we had flat tires and everything on the way.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Who changed the tires?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, I did. I changed the tires and I'd fix them up. Roland Mayfield, you know, the man who used to pick me up in Pittsburgh, taught me how to drive and how to fix cars and everything. My brother-in-law helped and if anything was wrong with any of those cars I could fix it myself. His mother was with me. It was like being on a desert, all the turtle-back roads, sand, dirt roads, you know. So we finally made it there and got in all right. See Roland taught me how to - I used to race when I was 10 or 12 years old. He taught me how to race and all that, do tricks in the car.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: So we got into Oklahoma City. After I arrived, the boys were dissatisfied about T. Holder and they called a meeting -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did you join the band to play?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, I was there as John's wife but he was very shrewd about it. He had his way of working me in. The pianist was very, very great but not as exciting. He was more of a - how shall I say it? - legit pianist, very beautiful chords and very wonderful pianist. So what I did was to go out on trips with them and when they were stuck - I'd sit in the instrumental truck, I'd drive a car or the instrumental truck or something - and if they got stuck and weren't going over big they'd call me in to do "Froggy Bottom" or something.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Were you doing "Froggy Bottom" by then?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, there were other tunes similar to that, but "Froggy Bottom" later, about a year later it was written. Before we even recorded it, you know. So we did this for quite a while and I traveled with the band and I'd sit in and play with him. After we played Oklahoma City, played one-nighters and all down through the Indian Territory. This was very exciting for me. We decided to leave. One thing I wanted to tell you - there was the most handsome - the boys were the most handsome guys and the most wonderful gentlemen that I've ever met. I don't think any one of them was over 25 or 26 years old but they were so well trained. Most of them were college graduates or something and they dressed very fine and they were so respectful of people. I've never been around a group like that, of musicians.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How had T. Holder managed to get this group together, especially...?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I really don't know. I never did find out but it was something really special. Claude Williams had played the violin and he was terrific. This was the most wonderful thing how they rehearsed. They'd call a rehearsal and nobody would prepare an arrangement. They'd do it while they were there. In one corner somebody would be playing cards or talking or something and Andy would say, "O.K.,
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: rhythm section first." And after that the trumpets and the saxophones. In this particular band they had a guy that played - they called him like a clown. He did all the acrobatics and everything on his back with this tenor and all that. They had other musicians that were real true musicians and what I did when I began writing, I'd teach this guy how to phrase with them because he was a little corny - the one that was doing all the tricks while he was playing. They did little acts and they did everything. They could play like Guy Lombardo and they could swing like Count Basie. It was the most amazing band I've ever been with in my life. They could play so many different styles and this put them in the category of Guy Lombardo. They could play for proms and everything and then go to an all black dance and be just as good, you know, swinging.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: They worked a lot of white dates?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, they did more white dates than anything else. Then when we first began to hit in the 30's everyone thought Andy was white because they had never seen a picture of him, because the band sounded like it on some things that we played. He believed in phrasing ballads in a very beautiful way, like violins. This band, they had a way of getting arrangements and things on the spot. During that era we didn't have great readers among black musicians and these guys could read anything. Like the first trumpet had such a sound, Big Jim Lawson, he was terrific.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Maybe the other two trumpets or one trumpet sound wasn't as big and he just covered the entire band sometimes when we didn't have everybody with a good sound. It was a most enjoyable thing after I joined them. It was exciting and I think they are really the reasons that I began to arrange.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How long after you and John went to Oklahoma City did Andy take over the band?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I think it was a matter of about 3 months because I remember going to their first rehearsal and the next 2 or 3 was a meeting when they decided to get rid of Teholder because he had gambled away their salary for that week and he had been doing that all along.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Once Andy took over the band did you play more? Was there any difference in - ?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I didn't play with that band - now that must have been around 1928, '27 or '28. I didn't join the band until '31 and all this time I was traveling and on one-nighters and everything with them.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Driving a bus?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Driving everything.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What else did they have besides a bus?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: They didn't have a bus. We had a fleet of cars. The boys had bought the instrumental truck that carried the instruments.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: You drove that too?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Once or twice. I'd drive John's car, the Chevrolet.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How wide an area did the band cover then?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: All through Oklahoma, even to Mississippi, Arkansas, and Colorado. Let's see; they went even to as far as - we didn't go all the way to California then, but we went some peculiar places that I never dreamed of being: Peoria, Illinois - just little small towns, you know.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: At this time where was your home base, in Oklahoma City?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It was in Oklahoma.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Do you mean the state or the city?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, the city, the city of Oklahoma. We worked in Tulsa maybe 3 or 4 months during the summer season and then we'd go back to Oklahoma.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When did the band get into Kansas City?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: The band got into Kansas City I think about 2 years after John Williams joined it. There was an opening at the Playmore there in Kansas, I think it was the Playmore, and Andy decided to go there. After that Kansas City became the headquarters for the band.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Once the band got to Kansas City, was that when you started to write.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, write. Andy knew that I had ideas - I was writing all along but I couldn't write it down. I'd give them
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: ideas during the rehearsal. Maybe they wanted to play a song like "Singing in the Rain" and I'd say, "Well, listen to this." Andy would take it down real fast but sometimes they didn't at all. In Kansas City he'd come to the house like 10 o'clock in the morning and sit there till 12. I said, I can't go through this, so after about 2 weeks or a week or so he came down and I had an arrangement ready for him. The only thing that wasn't really balanced right was the tenor and the trombones and he showed me that. From that day on I began writing.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Were you just doing this from instinct then, the writing?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I watched him. I can learn a lot through watching. That was my bag, see, watching people and doing what they do.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: All this period, this two years when you're traveling with the band and just occasionally getting to play, how did you feel? Did you feel that you were going anywhere?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, it wasn't that; I thought I was helping. There's a peculiar thing about me in life. You know if you want to really hear me play or write something, give me somebody to help. If I think that I'm helping a situation, somebody say, Mary come out to the church and do something and help us and do this - it's amazing the work that I can
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: do and I'm very happy with my work. That's been my bag since I've been born. If I think I'm helping someone I get great things going and I was helping them in a way. I discovered chords and Andy used to say to me, "You can't do that. It's against the rules of writing music." I said, "But I hear a sixth in this chord." He said, "But you can't do it." I said, "I'm going to do it." I did the arrangement of, before I did "Walkin'", trumpet and 3 saxophones. We only had 3 saxophones and one trumpet and trombone, something like that. So what I did, I put a trumpet in and I had 3 saxophones to play 4-part harmony. He kept telling me it was against the rules of the chord. In that year I guess it was but I was hearing - I found these things on the piano and I said, this will sound good - it sounds good here. After a while I started arranging it.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How did you happen to become a regular member of the band?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Well, we scuffled. Let's see, we went to the Savoy in New York. By this time we were playing "Froggy Bottom" and things like that. They called me in to sing because Chick Webb was really blasting town with all bands and they were getting rid of all bands that came in there. I guess you heard about that era; it was sensational. When he came in you just prayed that you'd go over.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: So they called for me and I'd be out in the car, I'd be downstairs playing miniature golf, and I'd go up and break it up, 'cause I was so tiny.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Mary, if you all these years have been breaking it up on this basis of being called in specially, why did they never put you on a regular basis?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, because they had this pianist. They respected him. Jack was a nice guy. Number one, Jack - I don't know his name - Jack Somebody. He was a good man and everything. It may have been that they didn't want a woman in the band because women during that era was not playing with men. That was another thing that made people scream and carry on, because they saw a woman and one that weighed 90 pounds. My feet was just barely touching the floor. That was a good point about it, but to hear me play so heavy like a man, that was something else. I don't know why John wasn't pushing it but he was through. He was putting me like, you know, in position. He had me on the scene. But I tell you what happened. We worked with Blanche Calloway in Philadelphia. This was before I joined the band. Whenever they went on tours I was with them. We went to Philadelphia; we worked for the Steeple there. You've heard about that. They were Ethel Waters, Bill Bailey -

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: This is the Pearl Theatre?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Pearl Theatre, we were working at the Pearl Theatre
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: in Philadelphia. Andy decided to use me for that theatre date, so he put me on a little miniature piano and had Jack on a big Steinway. So I was on the left of it, a left-handed stage, and he was over to the right. One afternoon Jack got sick or something happened to him. Steeple used to bring people in - he said, "Call the kid." He had the people sitting in the theatre just listening to me play and all that but they wouldn't do anything about Jack. So this particular time when Jack got sick, or whatever happened to him, I jumped on the big piano and started playing. That ended his career. Steeple said, "You don't need him. Keep her - great!"

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When you worked at Pearl Theatre were you there with Andy Kirk's band or ...

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: With Andy Kirk's band.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: But were you with Blanche Calloway?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I think that's when they had changed it to Blanche Calloway. Victor had recorded her like that also, Blanche Calloway and her band.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Were you in the band?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, I was just still sitting there -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: But it was Andy Kirk's band?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, but they wouldn't record Jack; they recorded me. Decca told them to send for me from Kansas City, said they wouldn't record them if they didn't send for me.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It was Brunswick then. I received a wire. I was there, you know. They had left me in Kansas City.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was this before the Pearl Theatre?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: This was after the Pearl, I think.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Well, let's stick with the Pearl Theatre a minute. During the engagement at the Pearl Theatre it was Andy Kirk's band with you on piano, but actually it was called Blanche Calloway. And it was during that engagement that Blanche Calloway recorded for Victor? Were you in the same position?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Before we went into Pearl Blanche Calloway recorded for Victor, with the band, with her heading the bill.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: 'I Need Loving', was that one of the things you did?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, that was that date.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did you just do one session with Blanche?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I think so; we may have done two, for the tunes that you heard. We may have.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: I see. Well, then, when did the Brunswick recording date come up?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: That was later.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was this the first recording you had ever done?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, when I recorded with Blanche. That was before we went to the Pearl; I remember now because later on
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I went back to Kansas City with the band and then Andy Kirk received a wire for them to come to Chicago. They went without me. They left me in Kansas City and what I did was join them because Jack Capp wouldn't record them without me.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Had you made any records by yourself at that time?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No. I think Jack Capp heard about me so I went there for him to hear me and while I was playing, thinking it was an audition, he recorded me, and that was 'Night Life'. I never got paid for it or anything. They put it out, 'Night Life' and the other thing, that was my first record.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: And that was made at the same time as the Kirk records for Brunswick?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: The very first records, yes.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Now this I gather was all before you got to the Savoy and became a regular part of the -

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, we had been to the Savoy.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: And you still weren't a regular part of the band?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, the first time we went to the Savoy I wasn't a regular part of the band.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: You told me about the time they called you to come in and take over -

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: We hadn't gone to the Pearl Theatre or recorded for Brunswick then.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: I see, this all comes later.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes... When we went to Chicago to record for Jack Kapp, that was the beginning of the success of the band and then later on Jack Kapp moved to New York and became Decca. I guess that was less than a year and Joe Glaser came out of Chicago. Then when they had those hits, that was in '33 or '34.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: So it was, in other words, more or less from the time of the Brunswick recordings in Chicago that this was the time the band began to rise?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Right.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Then after that you did the Pearl and then after that you did the Savoy, is that right?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: We did the Pearl - now I'm confused. We did the Pearl Theatre before I was called to Chicago to record for Brunswick.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: ...It was after that that you played at the Savoy...

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I played the Savoy again, but the next time they played I was with the band.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was it the first time at the Savoy that you actually became a regular member of the band?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, the first time I became a regular member was in the Pearl Theatre when they had the double piano. See they used me on the show with them.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: And then they kept - Jack was dropped after that?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: They were dropped after that afternoon and then it was maybe a month before we went to Kansas City.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: I see, O.K., it's confusing.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I'm sure it is. 'Cause if you get those dates wrong.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Kansas City became more or less home territory for you, right?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes. After that.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Going back again, when the band first went to Kansas City and you settled down there and you weren't playing with the band, what did you do?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: After the Pearl Theatre and the Brunswick recordings we went back to Kansas City with me - I mean I was with them then, after the Pearl Theatre. So we went into the Wehnwood Beach there for that summer, I guess about 3 or 4 months or so. Then after that we came back to New York to record for Decca. I think we went in two Wehnwood Beach around '31 or '32, I'm sure. During that period before we came back to New York to record for Decca we played Fairyland - Wehnwood Beach, Fairyland, and places like that. The band began to rise after that, because we came back to New York to record for Decca and we recorded every day for 2 or 3 weeks. They just kept me in a hotel, somebody'd bring me sandwiches. I wrote 20 things in one week. They were all hits.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What did you write? What were some of the things?
WILLIAMS 56

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I did another thing on "Froggy Bottom" and I rearranged "Messa Stomp". That was my first arrangement. I think we recorded that once before when we recorded with Blanche, "Messa Stomp". That was my first composition. I got the title - my grandfather used to call me "Messy" and 'Messa', something like that, so I called it "Messa Stomp". Let's see, "Froggy Bottom" "Messa" 'Lotta', "A Lot of Sax Appeal" - oh, let's see, what else. Oh, there's 20 things. "Mary's Idea". "Cloudy". That was quite late.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: This was all part of the first session for Decca?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes. We did all this in one week almost.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Up until then, before you sat down and wrote 20 things...right off the bat like that, about how much had you written for the band? Had you been writing for quite some time?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, I guess I had given them almost a complete book because I was the only one writing at the time till Earl Thompson came in and then later on we picked up on other people, you know, on the outside. But I was doing most of the arranging, Andy and I.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Now was this part of the period when you were playing mostly in Kansas City, you had a chance to live there? I mean, you were part of the musical life in Kansas City?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, yes, a great part of it. Without me - oh, that was terrific, especially when we were in the park.
WILLIAMS
Pinet

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: We worked every night from 9 till 12 and during the summer Tiny Brown's place was open. That's where Joe - the blues singer - Joe Turner and Pete Johnson were working. John would drive by and drop the boys off there and I'd go home and change from my sweaty outfit, take a bath. Oh, one thing I want to tell you. When we passed the place we'd hear "Georgia Brown". I'd go home, take a bath and dress and put on something cool and come back and they were still playing "Georgia Brown". But Hot Lips Page and about 15 musicians would come in and there was such a terrific arrangement that you'd just pull your hair out. Martha Raye was on her way - she was around 18 years old, I think they said - was on her way to make a movie in Hollywood. It cost them, they said, a million dollars or more wiring and sending for her and she don't want to leave. She had such a ball. She just stayed there. She used to come up and sing every night. I'm telling you, those sessions were something else!
(sweat)
Raye

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Who were some of the people? You mentioned Hot Lips Page. Do you want to stop a minute and think?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: The Sunset Cafe, and when Martha came through?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was she already famous at that point?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No. I think they said she was 18 years old.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Someone told me her age while she was there, but she was getting well known among musicians because she could really sing and she got herself a movie. The strange thing about it, with all the great pianists around including Sleepy - you know he's the type of pianist that played like Art Tatum in B natural and A natural, exactly like him.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: But only in B natural and A natural?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: That's right, in all the hard keys.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did Sleepy have any other name?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, I don't remember it. That's all we ever called him. I met him in Kansas City 2 or 3 weeks ago; he's still around.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Yes? Playing?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, yes. There was another pianist that had a terrific beat. His name was Lincoln and I'm telling you he could really swing. That's the only pianist that Martha would sing with. She'd grab Lincoln and they'd start singing and then Joe Turner would sing and they had some great sessions there.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: This was the time when Martha was supposed to go to Hollywood and she wouldn't leave?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, she wouldn't leave. She stayed about 2 weeks. She was supposed to just drop off and change trains in Kansas City but she heard about Piney Brown's place and she wanted to see it.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Oh, I see, this was the first time she had ever been there?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It was the first time she'd ever been to Kansas City.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did she ever come back?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I don't know, because I left maybe 3 or 4 years after that. But what a time she had.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Who were some of the other musicians who were around in Kansas City?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: The great names like Lester, Jo Jones, Walter -(Page)

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When did you first run into Lester Young?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: When Ben Webster left (the) Andy Kirk to join Cab Calloway, Lester Young joined us in Kansas City, but he didn't stay with us very long because shortly after that he went to Count Basie's band.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When Lester followed someone like Ben Webster wasn't there a problem of the difference of sound?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, we missed Ben Webster on account of sound but Lester was more free and whatnot in solos to play a hundred solos and never repeat. Ben Webster was the type of guy that could put so much in one bar. If you played with him he could do so much with one bar than any other man could do. Lester would play 12 or 15 choruses and each one of them would sound different. But with a man in the band like Ben, you'd miss him.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was Lester appreciated in Kansas City?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, yes. In other words, that was the era of the well-trained musician, that was the last of the well-trained musicians. Out of that era came Charlie Parker, Dizzy, and the bop era. These musicians, we never went out against each other, say, I'm going to outplay another pianist. We had some terrific women around. We'd just exchange ideas and play and have a ball and drink and eat together, but we never had that thing that someone's going to cut you completely out or make a fool out of you.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: You mentioned other women. Who were some of the other women?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Don't ask me about names.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: O.K.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Julia Lee was a great pianist - oh, goodness, I can't remember. It's been so long. But they played like men.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: But in other words, you were not particularly unique in Kansas City?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, just unique being with the band, all male band.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: The others were playing by themselves?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Wasn't Julia Lee playing with her brother's band?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, yes, but I was somebody that started that. After I did that several bands got girls in St. Louis.
WILLIAMS 61

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It was just like Count Basie started the beat that he had, then everybody else came in with the idea.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Do you remember when you first met Charlie Parker?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: When we were working at Wehnwood Beach we'd go by where he was playing with Andy Kirk's wife, Mary, who was a very good pianist, but she had the old style... and Charlie Parker was playing just the way he did when he was in New York and it sounded funny to the boys. They'd say, "I don't know what that alto player's playing." "He sounds good but I don't know what he's doing." The two combinations together were really funny.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: I asked you this before, but did the people in general in Kansas City understand what Charlie was doing?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I don't think so... because Kansas City even to now is a little back on the modern era, and to really go over big in Kansas City you have to swing. It was kind of like a slapstick thing. Therefore a small audience of modern jazz lovers but not as big as would like the Count Basie style of playing.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Of course back in the days that you're talking about which was the late 20's or early 30's approximately, what Charlie Parker was doing was so utterly outlandish, compared to -

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: He leave had to in Kansas City, because everything you had to have a strong beat, like Fats Waller swinging thing.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: As I recall, the bands that had a very solid beat like, for example, the Bennie Moten band, some of the earlier records of the Bennie Moten band, are very... but once Basie and Walter Page and some of those people came in about 1930, the sound changed decidedly. It was lighter.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It was lighter but it was that same thing. You see, Bennie Moten used a slapstick drummer... but the approach of Count Basie was without slapstick...ching-a-ching-a-ching, four. you know

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: We're coming to the end of this tape.
....out of sequence - go to p. 83!

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: ...Deering's Farm and we had a very successful run there. We went in in August and stayed there till October or September. Everything was going great. We had on our bill a great blues singer, Joe Williams who I thought was fabulous. I had never heard anyone sing like him before - and a stage show there. Everything was going fine until Duke Ellington's band came to town and they happened to hear about us being there. Ben Webster and all the cats including Duke Ellington came out to the farm... I had such fabulous musicians. I didn't know how great they were until the night that Duke Ellington and these guys came in there. They had played an engagement in Cleveland. We did our show and we had a jam session and I think Baby Lee Laurence the great tap dancer was with them, so we really
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: had a ball that night. Ben Webster took out his horn, he came up and jammed with us and I discovered that Orlando Wright whose name is now Musa Kalim was just about one of the greatest tenor men going. He was around 17 or 18 years old. So Ben got up on the stand and he was blowing "Body and Soul" so when it came time for Orlando to take his solo he said, he stuttered, "Miss-miss-miss Williams, E natural." I said, "Oh, my goodness." He played it in E natural and before he finished he said, "B natural." He played in all these keys and Ben Webster looked at him with his big eyes and said, "Well, man, that's too much for me!" Art Blakey's time wasn't too good. Hal and I used to have to sit on the stand with him with his foot marking time, but he was really blowing. He could swing like mad. We trained him, the both of us. We were just almost in between him, like the piano was here and Art Blakey was there and Hal Baker was next to him. So at the end of about 2 or 3 weeks he was really good. His time didn't vary, it wasn't noticeable rather. But what happened, when I went home that night I discovered - no, it was the next morning when I woke up - I got ahead of myself. Hal Baker and I had married, you know. We got married before he left the band, before they came through Pittsburgh on their way to another city. I discovered that Hal was nowhere around the next morning when I got up.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I didn't see him. They had a meeting of the musicians and I didn't know about it. All I did was take care of the music and play. So I waited for him. We had a couple more days to go. We didn't have no trumpet player. I was really disgusted to discover that he had left with Duke Ellington's band. Now, I'm the leader of the band and I don't even know what was going on. So later on when I heard from him I discovered that the boys got in great arguments and whatnot when he wasn't home with me. He was trying to break up their arguments. They were jealous and some of them wanted all Pittsburghers in the band and didn't want anyone from St. Louis, and a lot of foolish things were happening that I didn't know about. So when Duke Ellington heard Hal Baker he hired him right on the spot and he left the next day.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Leaving you -

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: With the group and after that these kids that wanted all Pittsburghers - Art Blakey said to me, "Well, it's good he's gone because there's a guy in Pittsburgh that's the greatest." I said, "O.K., we'll go by and pick him up." We had another engagement, I think through John Hammond, Kelly's Stable in New York with Thelma Carpenter, a great singer. What happened, they brought in a guy from Pittsburgh and the boy couldn't even play the parts. See, Hal Baker was so terrific and he'd take about 10 choruses.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: He'd jump back on the ensembles with the group. I just never could find another trumpet player to play as good as Harold did. We tried out several musicians. We tried out everybody but Dizzy Gillespie and he wasn't around then, you know. So when we came to New York I decided to dis-band and not even bother because the other kid wasn't good enough for the group. So I didn't hear from Harold for quite a while and I stayed in Kelly's Stable I think for about 4 weeks and I decided to come out. I don't know where Art Blakey went and his group but I heard later that Fletcher Henderson went to Pittsburgh and hired all Pittsburghers with Art Blakey and they got angry with him when he was on his way to Chicago and when he reached the job where he was going, he had no band! So I was kind of glad to get out of that.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: What I did - I was here practically stranded in New York except I wouldn't tell anyone. I got myself a room at the hotel, Dewey Square Hotel, and I stayed inside that hotel. I ate and slept for about 2 weeks. I called John Hammond; he got me in touch with Louise Crane - you know the Crane paper, C-r-a-n-e? I think they - stationery or something. John Hammond booked me into the Cafe Society downtown. I just slept and thought over things and meditated as to which way I was going.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What did Louise Crane do for you?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I think through John Hammond she booked us into acts. Kelly's Stable. She was trying to book/ She had a couple of people like Baby Laurence or something like that, or some other dancer.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: She had nothing to do with the paper business?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, she was quite rich. She was trying her hand at booking musicians and things like that. I was with her a while and it didn't work out because I'm more or less at home around men. So what I did was, as I said before, I stayed in the Dewey Square Hotel trying to think things out, so John Hammond says, "Well, I have a place for you, Cafe Society." So I went downtown. This was between '41 and '42, 1941 and 1942 that I went into the Cafe. I stayed in the Cafe off and on for 5 years.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: There you had a group, right?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I did solo. I worked with - Edmond Hall's group was there and they later moved to the Cafe uptown. They had various groups while I was there - Josh White. It was such a beautiful thing to work in the Cafe. I remember times when one act wasn't going well, Josh White and Johnny Garrett would come out and boost us. I never smiled when I was playing and Barney Josephson, the owner of the club, did everything he could to try to get me to smile. He came down, he had me acting like Hazel and all that. Eddie Hayward said, "Leave her alone. She'll get to it."
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: So one night I was playing and Johnny Garrett used to walk in back of me to make me smile. He'd do the Bronx cheer and I'd laugh. Barney happened to be there and he said, "What do you mean doing that and that's my star act." Johnny said, "You wanted her to smile, didn't you? Look at her now." And so he gave Johnny a raise.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Who was Johnny?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Johnny Garrett came to the Cafe as a valet for us, where he pushed the piano on and off. He learned a great deal while he was there and he went out with Sarah and helped make her Vaughan/great. He's a terrific man. He just watched and he learned through watching and he became a great manager. Through him and Sarah Vaughan's husband and the pianist, they really brought her out in good style to the public.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: You know Johnny's the maitre de at a restaurant around here now? Rust Brown?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, he's terrific. He knows the lighting and he knows everything. Imogene Coca was with us there and she was the type that was always nervous about going on. She walked through the club and when she got to the ladies' dressing room - we all dressed in the same room - she'd say, "Oh, we're not going to go over. I know it; I can feel it." And Johnny would hype her real good, make her do a real good show. He was very good at that.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: During those years that you were at Cafe Society were you recording too?
WILLIAMS
Asch

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, for Moe Asch. I did a lot of records for him during that period. I did a couple of sessions for Victor. That was "Waltz Boogie". That was the first time, you know, that 3/4 was ever recorded, I mean, composed into 3/4.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: That was an all-girl trio too, wasn't it?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I did that later on the session, but they wanted all boogies so I gave them about 4 boogies - "Hesitation Boogie", "Waltz Boogie", and a couple more.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What kind of writing were you doing, or were you writing then?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, I stopped writing after I left the band and the only kind of things I'd do were arrangements for myself and the only way I did them - you see, then musicians could really hear fast. On my way down the sound of the subway would bring me inspiration and I'd write an arrangement in my head before I got to the club and I'd tell J. C. Heard (he was our drummer during this period), "I'd like to do 'Limehouse Blues'. Follow me." And he did. If the musician was just great enough, anything you did they could follow. You wouldn't have to rehearse.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did you have a bass and drums with you?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, bass and drums, no band at all.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: This was what? - the early 40's?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, it was after the 40's. It was between '41 and '42.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: And then 5 years from then on into '46 and '47?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, '46 and '47.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: This was when bop was beginning to happen.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Bop happened a little later than that, about 2 years later, because Hazel went out and I went uptown. I began to follow -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: You mean Cafe Society uptown?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Cafe Society uptown. He had both Cafe Society uptown, Barney Josephson did, and Cafe Society downtown. So I began hanging out on 52nd Street with the cats and they knew that I always helped musicians and so they'd - we'd come uptown around 4 o'clock or 4:30 in the morning and stay up all day, playing. There was Tadd Dameron, Bud Powell, Erroll Garner, Mel (Torme D'Armaine), and Miles Davis. Let's see, another trumpet player - Fats Navarro. A tenor man that was with Benny Goodman when he came out East - Wardell Gray, and sometimes Leonard Feather. I had a white rug on the floor and we'd sit on the floor and each one would take turns playing.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Oh, you played at your place, you mean?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Here at this apartment, yes.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: But it wasn't jamming in the club or anything like that?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, we jammed here. Thelonius Monk - I remember once one morning I got sleepy so I said, "I'm going to bed."
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: When the guys left the door was open and Monk rang the doorbell and he came inside. He discovered that I was asleep - it was around 8 o'clock in the morning. I had a big, big twin bed, so when I woke up I saw something on the other bed and I screamed. He yelled too and ran out the door and ran in to the closet and the clothes fell on him. I said, "What are you doing here?" He said, "Well, I wanted to write something or play something and you were sleeping and I didn't want to disturb you," and he was lying on his back with this tam on. That was the funniest thing. I told him about that when I saw him in California and he laughed about it. That was so funny. Monk would write a tune and he'd come here and play it for 2 or 3 months. I'd say, "Why do you keep playing the same thing over and over?" He'd say, "I'm trying to see if it's a hit. It'll stay with you if it's a hit."

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Why did you leave Cafe Society?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, I didn't leave. It kind of petered out a little, you know what I mean, after years and years of being there. There was a kind of a lull and so I just drifted away, went back to GLASER Glen and he booked me out of the city. You know to stay in the city for 5 years straight you have to keep presenting people with something new. Barney Josephson was very nice. I wrote the "Zodiac Suite" during that period and he put on a concert at Town Hall.
WILLIAMS 71

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Then later Norman Granz came through with this new Jazz at the Philharmonic and he asked me if I'd play with them. I was very popular then, you know, drawing big crowds so I told him yes, if you will get permission for me to play with the New York Symphony, and I'll play for you for nothing. So he did. Mr. Ripp was the manager then. (movements) What I did was to arrange three of the Zodiac Suite. I had Brent Milton Aranda who was way out, way ahead of Coltrane or anybody. I don't know if you ever heard of him.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: I remember his name.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: He was coming here -

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What did he play?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: He played - not a very good musician but he was more or less a writer, composer, and he had studied all these weird sounds. Often when we had the jazz musicians up here like Sarah Vaughan and all of them, they couldn't stand to hear these chords and things that he was playing. They sounded like discords and whatnot. They'd leave. Milton taught me a great deal. That's the reason I kept up with the times and what was happening. During that period we both wrote "In the Land of Oo-Bla-Dee". He started it and I helped him a little with it.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: When you say you helped a little bit - ?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I didn't do a heck of a lot but I did enough to get the name on. He'd always start things like, we set
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Benny Goodman things. We were sitting in the car and he started whistling a tune. I said, "Gee, that would be good. I'm going upstairs and write it," you know. He always flushed me with ideas. There was never a lull; there was always something new happening. The first sound that Miles got with the tuba and all that - well, Miles was here and he said, "I'd like a tuba." Somebody said, "I'd like this instrument," and so forth and so on. Miles went out and he called back and said, "Thank you, Lou," and that's how he got his sound going. See, because we were really happy in creating and doing things and helping one another. Milton was really terrific. I have some arrangements and things here that he wrote when I was still out.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How did you happen to write the "Zodiac Suite"?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, I had started on the "Zodiac Suite" while I was in Cafe Society and I never finished it. I wrote, I think, three. Barney Josephson got me a radio show on WNEW, my own show and I was supposed to introduce one sign a week -Aries, Taurus, and whatnot. I wrote 3 of the signs in the beginning and discovered I was just without ideas. I couldn't write any more, like my inspiration had left me. So what I did to finish them, I went on WNEW and I had Nola Studios to record the program as I played it. So I wrote the rest - I just played them off like that.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What was your radio program like? What kind of a program was it?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, I don't know how to describe it but it was just a radio program of not much talk but talk explaining each sign of the zodiac.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: The whole thing built around the zodiac?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, and I'd have one guest star. Canada Lee was on one Sunday, and other people. I've forgotten just who they were.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How big a group did you have with you?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Bass, drums, and piano.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: When Norman Granz arranged the concert with the- was it the New York Philharmonic?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, the Philharmonic, I didn't finish that. Milton Great Arendt was helping me with the arrangements. There was four of the "Zodiac Suite". So he had a gig coming up Saturday that he had forgotten about. It was an important gig, like he was the leader, and he had to go up in the country to play bass. So he said, "Pussy Cat" - that was my nickname then - "I can't finish the arrangements." I said, "Oh, goodness, I'll finish them myself." I did "Scorpio". He was so surprised. I had never written for a symphony in my life. About 7 o'clock in the evening after I had finished, David Stone Martin - you remember him? - he came here and I said, "David, I can't write for
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: a symphony. I don't know what I'm going to do. I need another tune." He said, "Oh, darling, you can do it. Go ahead, darling," and he kept saying that until I got on the floor and I started writing and I finished off "Scorpio". All of a sudden I decided I wanted them to play a blues. So I sat there and I made up a blues. I heard a record - I didn't copy all of Charlie Parker's solo but I said I better give them a bop thing because I'm going to give it to 36 violins. It was 100 pieces. So I wrote this blues and David said, "How you doing?" He sat with me all night. I sat there - it took me from 7 o'clock till 11 o'clock and my rehearsal was at 12, because I copied all the parts on the blues. So when I took all my arrangements in, Mr. Ripp was there, the manager of the Carnegie, and I was afraid to pass the blues out. So I had the girl to rehearse just the "Zodiac Suite". When someone called Mr. Ripp to the phone I said, "Wait a minute, wait a minute. I gave you the wrong arrangement. Here, this one." So I passed it out fast while he was away and they played it and the musicians went wild. They never played anything like that before. I've seen them in the last two or three years and they say, "When are you going to write something else like that for the Symphony?" I had them doing a boogie thing and they'd play a blues on it. I had no difficulty in teaching them how to phrase it or do it. Yeh, 36 violins, they stood up and played this kind of a boppish chorus.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: When was the concert?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: The concert was either that night or a couple of days later.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What year was this, do you remember?

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: 1946. At Carnegie Hall?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: At Carnegie Hall.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: And what reaction was there to 'Zodiac Suite'?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Terrific. I don't remember the public but the musicians applauded more than anybody. They stood up and applauded.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was there any interest in recording it then?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, but somebody stole it. Someone stole that recording and somebody stole the recording of the concert that Barney did for me at Town Hall.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Barney's concert at Town Hall was a separate thing, is that right?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Before or after this?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: That was before this.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What did you do then?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I did the 'Zodiac Suite' in Rome with a combo of about 18 men including oboe, flute, and all that, violins.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: So that meant all new arrangements for that too?
WILLIAMS 76

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, yes. Milton helped me. I gave him the ideas and he wrote some down and he helped me when I'd get stuck.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: I have some notes here about the days of Cafe Society. You mentioned Canada Lee; and were there some fights?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, the fights. That was the most exciting thing. It was during the war. We had quite a few biased people to come up like from the South. They didn't understand a lot of things, like mixing and all that. Sundays you couldn't get in the club. They were outside standing and waiting to come in and like every other night there was a big fight. At this particular time I done a request of 'Roll 'Em' and it went over big. Some bright guy in the audience said, "Play it again!" He ran up and grabbed me and was holding me like this, so Eddie Heywood said, "Turn her loose! Man, man, man, turn her loose so she can take her encore!" You know, he stuttered. This guy wouldn't turn me loose so the fight started. Canada Lee happened to be in there and he cooled it off. In about 2 minutes we didn't have anybody there, not even the bartenders. So when Barney came back (Barney Josephson was away on vacation), "I heard you had another fight here. And you, Doc Cheatham, you were skating across my bar." Doc Cheatham said, "Man, I was trying to get to the door."

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Josh White was there too, wasn't he?
X 'Roll 'Em'
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, yes, he was there.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How did you get along with Josh White?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, Josh White was just beautiful. You know when Barney Josephson booked new singers in his idea was to create a new star within the star that was there. He'd bring a known talent in and show them off. A big star would draw the people in and he'd show somebody unknown off and make a star out of him. Josh White was just terrific to work with, as I said before. We rode uptown together every night; he'd take me home and then he'd go home. He was such a beautiful person to work with. I used to do three or four benefits with him a night.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Really?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I did so many benefits at the Cafe that I just don't feel like doing any now.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Recording for Moe Asch, was that different from recording for other people?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, it was different because Moe Ash had more love and he had more respect for jazz artists. Often he would take us to dinner, the nicest dinners, steak dinners, the nicest places and it was his idea that an artist should be heard if they're talented. He'd turn the tape on and go away, let you record anything you wanted to record and it always worked out great. He wanted to record Erroll Garner, you know. Erroll Garner was in Pittsburgh. I went there
WILLIAMS 78

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: on a vacation. By the way, we're both from Pittsburgh. He had been to New York and was a little discouraged. I said, "Come on back." So he came back later on, his girl friend or someone brought him here. Moe Ash heard Erroll Garner and he said, "Mary, try to get Errd1 Garner and Art Tatum to record." I knew Errd1 Garner needed money. I said, "I think it will cost you about $1500 for Art Tatum; $750 for Errd1." He said, "I don't care; I'll pay them. Get them." Moe Ash was so great that when I talked with Art Tatum, Art Tatum charged him $750. I said, "Why, he was willing to pay you more money?" He said, "As great as that man is, I record for him for nothing." Erroll Garner asked him for $250. That's how great he is. I guess that's the reason why he has no money. Like, Victor sued him once and he said he didn't care because he was going to put the records out because he had sold them some tapes and they didn't put the tapes out. He said, "Because a real artist should be heard." At one time he had all the great records, like of Indians and something unusual and folk singers and everything, and the major companies had to buy the tapes from him. Because if you're talented he doesn't bother you about what you should do and whatnot. He'd just tell you to go ahead and record what you wanted to record.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: But after you made the records for Moe did they get out much? Was there much circulation?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, they did, they got out quite a bit. He did business with somebody else. I forget the name of that company. He did all kinds of things trying to get the artists heard. That was his main thing. I've done recordings with Josh White and a lot of artists there. I'd get a lot of recording artists for him and then he allowed me to go to Pittsburgh to record some musicians. I went there.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: After you finished in Cafe Society, where did you go then?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I had been in that one place so long till I went in and out of the city. Glaser booked me. We never could get along but I love Glaser. He's somebody that I always cared for and I think he was very fond of me. I went to him and he booked me on a lot of things. I worked for him for quite a while and then Moe Gale decided that they wanted to break a ban in Europe, a ban of 30 years, so they said the best person to send over there is Mary Lou because the musicians like her. That meant that if I played with all the musicians in England, that the ban would be automatically broken. It seems that 30 years previously to that, English musicians came here to America. Something happened they weren't allowed to play, so that when any American musicians went to England they did the same thing. It was some kind of a battle between the unions.
