So Moe Gale got together and they sent me to England to break this ban of 30 years. So I played with Ted Heath
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: and all the big bands there, every musician in England. That automatically broke the ban. The next person that came over was - the Jazz at the Philharmonic, what was his name - ?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Norman Granz.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Norman Granz.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When you played with Heath were you playing concerts?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, I played at the Palladium with Heath and all bands there, Johnny Dankworth - just all the musicians I worked with there.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How long did you stay in England?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Well, I went there for 9 days and I was held over 6 months. I stayed in England 11 months. I didn't have any clothes or anything. I had to send back to the store and have my saleslady send me a couple of dresses, but they fitted; she knew what I liked. From there I went to Paris.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Just before you get to Paris, Mary - England was the first time you had ever been out of the country?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How did you like living some place other than the United States?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I really don't know what people like about foreign countries. I don't know, maybe I'm corny. I don't
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: like it; I like America. The English were very nice to me and all that and also Paris, but I just like Americans. I wouldn't want to live there. I like to go for a short visit. I stayed in England and the food during that time was very bad, you know, people still didn't have food. The guys on the S. S. United, they used to bring me 20 and 25 steaks and the cook would cook me something special. So one day I had a birthday there and they wanted to give a party for me on the ship. They were coming in. The newspaper people are the people that held me over, so they were holding me over for the third time. I decided I didn't want any more of England so I packed all my bags and closed them up and left the door open. They brought the cake in and steaks and everything but I had left. I went to Paris.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What did you do in Paris?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I played there a while. I made probably more money than I've ever made in my life.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Where did you play?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I played all the concert halls there including an engagement with about 10 classical pianists. I can't remember the names of those places. I played the Boeuf sur le Tait, a night club.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: All as a solo act?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, but what really happened that got me on to
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: praying was before I left England the Queen's cousin Lascelles follows jazz and he gave a party. I must have looked disturbed because there was one other black person, a GI. He says, "You seem like you're disturbed. My grandmother always said to read the 91st Psalm." I've never been able to drink at one time over two drinks without really getting high, so I thought he said read all the Psalms so I went home and started reading them all. Seemed like that just turned me around and started me to praying.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Just coming out of you now. Was this before you left England?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Before I left England.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Then when you got to Paris, how did this develop?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I worked there for a while, for about I guess a month. Garland Wilson was there and he passed away, he died, you know. It's a place where the customers that really frequent this place didn't like women, but I got in because I was a friend of his. Mr. Orion that owned this place liked me also because he was crazy about Garland. So I got a job there for about 2 months. I was doubling at the theatre, making money. All the Americans had gone back to America and they had so many things for you to do because they had only one left and that was me. All of a sudden I just put everything down and walked off and left

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: my salary and that's the worst thing you can do in Paris because you'll never get it. But I ran into a wonderful drummer, Gerard Pochonet. He used to play for all the Americans when they came over. He was on a newspaper and everything so he got my money and everything else, you know, for me. He took me out to his house in the country to stay with he and his grandmother.
We're at the end of your tape, so I: This is beginning to imitate you; I'm going to stop. End tape 3

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When did you first meet Thelonious Monk?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I think it was the year of 1930 in Kansas City. He was traveling with a show somewhat like a medicine show. The music was so great in Kansas City so he stopped off there. They had opened up a new night club called the Subway or something like that in Kansas City and I met Monk there and he was playing the same way he plays now. No one understood it. I used to hang out with him and we became great friends then. During that period Lester Young, Herschel Evans, and Count Basie and all the musicians used to go down to the Subway to hear Monk play.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What happened to music in Kansas City because of Monk?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I don't think the music changed too much as far as Monk was concerned. Everybody in Kansas City you must remember were playing different sounds, you know. They were playing in their own individual styles.
WILLIAMS 84

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Like we had one pianist - I think I mentioned that to you once before - his name was Sleepy. His eyes were half closed and he played exactly like Art Tatum in all the difficult keys like F sharp, B natural, A natural. What was great as far as the scene of Kansas City was, that all these various styles and everybody was so original.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was this true of all the musicians or are you speaking primarily -

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Practically all the musicians. No one ever copied anybody else. That was really unique, you know, as far as Kansas City. We had the Cherry Blossom where we used to go and jam.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Where was the Cherry Blossom?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Oh goodness, I've forgotten the street. I think 18th and Vine. This was where they had a floor show and everything but after the floor show everybody would jam I guess from 1 o'clock till maybe 12 the next day. We had a wonderful friend that used to help out the musicians. He and Piney Brown were really friends of the musicians. He was known by the name of Country and he worked for a judge there, Judge Gershon. We used to laugh about the two of them together. Country was the chauffeur and Judge Gershon's right-hand man. Whenever anybody got into trouble Country would - these two were the most comical act you've ever seen, whether in the movies or anything. Whenever one of the musicians had gotten into trouble his case
WILLIAMS 85

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: would come up in court and Gershon would say, "So-and-so blabla," whatever his name was and Country would sneak out the door. He'd say, "Come back here, Country. I know what you've done." See the musician didn't appear and Country had gone out to where he was jailed and told that Judge Gershon said to turn him loose. It was a big political town anyway and he did things like that and the Judge would come down 18th Street - I saw him myself. It happened to be around 3 o'clock and he'd look in all the pool halls and all the restaurants and everything, asking for Country and Country was hiding underneath the pool table. Country was a fabulous and fine-looking tall black man. He was just handsome. He was hiding under this pool table and Gershon was walking up and down 18th Street looking for him. He'd say, "Don't tell him where I am." He'd gotten drunk all night and had lost his voice and everything, so Gershon said, "I'm looking for Country. Do you know what he did?" Country had pawned two tires on his Cadillac. He'd carry on with the musicians and buy drinks and do things for them so this particular night he pawned these two tires and the car was hiked up on one side without any tires on it. That was really funny, what happened with him. Let's see, something else happened.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Did musicians in Kansas City get in trouble a lot? Were they -

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, no, not in trouble. I'll tell you what happened a couple of times. Kansas City was really prejudiced
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: when I first went there, about the streetcar, the blacks sitting in the back but in a matter of a year that was cleared up. What really happened was that they'd probably be in the house drinking with white and black. This was during Prohibition and I remember 3 or 4 of our boys got picked up like that. They were sitting drinking with - there was two white girls and the others were the boys in the band. About 3 of the boys out of the band was just sitting there drinking. We used to jam and do things like that and the girls would come around to hear it. It so happened that one of the girls was married or was a girl friend to a big detective there and he'd been peeping under the curtain all the time they were in the house. So he went away and brought the wagon back and arrested all of them but it didn't stand up at all because some of them was released before Country even came into the picture because the law is that black and white could be in the same house drinking and there was no need to arrest them if no one had taken their coats off. That was a peculiar law. They had just arrived in the house and this detective happened to follow his girl friend and saw her. He was peeping under the curtain and Salty Dog, somebody like that, ran in the house. A guy by the name of Salty Dog told the guys that this detective was outside but it was too late then. He called the police and picked them up.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Just little things like that. They didn't get into big trouble and whatever they did it was just like they hadn't because Country would release them.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: You say after about a year though the white and black thing got straightened out?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Oh, yes, it wasn't very long because I think I arrived in Kansas City, to really live there, in '29 or '30 and I was too busy with music to pay much attention to anything but it disappeared quite fast.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Did whites come down to the black clubs?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, whites came everywhere; that's the reason why the guys got into trouble. They were always in the black district. Count Basie and I had about 30 pupils between us, that we were teaching to play jazz.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: And they were white?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, they were white.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Did you have black pupils too?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Oh sure, we had both, but we had more whites than anything else.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was there any jazz in the white sections of town in Kansas City?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: There was jazz clubs. My attention was focused where the giants were and that was 18th and Vine or 12th Street. We had many white musicians that came there, mostly out of the city, like Ben Pollack and those people like that.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: When they were traveling through?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Where did they usually play?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Oh, the Muhlenbach Hotel was a popular place for them there. I think that was the only one that they played.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How about Stumpy Buddy

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Stumpy Buddy was a terrific trombonist...

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: About Lucille and Louise?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: They put them in the music scene because they followed all the musicians. They were crazy about musicians but they were two beautiful girls and I think their father was a big political leader and a wonderful Italian man off of Fifth Avenue. Fifth Avenue was a pretty rough street; after jam sessions certain nights we'd all go there. Lucille and Louise were not allowed out, not unless their mother asked me if I was going along with them. I don't know why she thought I could protect them. They were both older than what I was by 2 years. There was another friend of mine - Louise, Lucille, and Rosita (Shewing,) I'm telling you they was something else. I didn't have one chance to sit in on a jam session after we went out together because the whole town practically was destroyed. These two little girls (I think they were between 18 and 20 years old), they'd go in a night club and if they took a couple of drinks or so, they'd just take the pictures off the wall. Sammy Price happened to be playing in the club one night and he was a
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: terrific boogie-woogie pianist and they always liked to go to see him. The minute he saw us coming up the stairs he said, 'Well, I guess I better go home,' because he was expecting the piano to disappear. They had such a ball. We'd go down to Fifth Avenue where their Dad was. It was pretty rough down there.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Rough in what way, Mary Lou?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It was during the Prohibition and a little bit of everything was happening in Kansas City. Certain people did exactly what they wanted to do. It was during the time when all the gangsters was really a big thing. I've heard people speak of gangsters in New York. Well, they were kids to the ones I've worked for. Count Basie and our band worked for some gangsters in Kansas City. Before I joined the band they made Count Basie work without pay for one or two weeks. Andy Kirk came in next.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Why did they make him work without pay?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: If you angered them their temper was terrible. If you angered them in any way.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What was the pay like then in Kansas City?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I don't think it was very much. I hadn't joined the band then. I heard that Count Basie had to work either one or two weeks without pay. Andy Kirk's band went in next and we had a singer with us and he got in a dispute with one of the gangsters there. The gangster looked at
WILLIAMS 90

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: him and he says, "Andy, if it wasn't for you I'd kill him!"

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: And he meant it?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Oh, sure he meant it, sure. We worked for the Gershwin brothers.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was this the judge?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, that isn't the - I've forgotten their name. The Luscoe brothers. They were pretty well to the point to, had to be careful. I remember once after playing they told the boys, "Let's go out and play softball." Whoever wins had to go back to the club and get a keg of beer. Naturally the boys won and the Luscoe brothers looked for them and they had gone home, because they were afraid to go back and pick up the beer.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: While you were in Kansas City, musically did anything rub off on you? Did you have something that you were never doing before?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, nothing rubbed off on me. I think music was such a great thing that you could hit me on top of the head and I wouldn't know. All I did was just stay up nights, days and nights, playing. Joe Smith that married Louise Mann - you remember Joe Smith the trumpet player that was with McKinney's Cotton Pickers?

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Right. I think he was with Henderson too.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Right.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Do you want to jump to Florence Mills?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Oh, yes. I met Florence Mills when I was about 14. By the way, I went home to look for some things and I
WILLIAMS 91

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: had some stockings that I wore during that period. I brought my dates up to where I knew what was happening if I had to tell the story. I found a picture of Jeanette -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Oh really? Of Seymour and Jeanette?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes. Florence Mills was a very good friend of Jeanette's. Jeanette used to take me everywhere with her. See I was very young and she wouldn't dare to leave me alone.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How old were you?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Between 14 and 16. I met Ziegfeld. Oh, a wonderful thing about Ziegfeld, I heard them talking in the dressing room that whenever he found a good singer like Sarah or Ella he'd really make a singer by introducing this singer to a very handsome, tall, handsome good-looking guy and the minute he felt that she was in love with this man, he'd snatch the man away from her. He'd say, "Now go out and sing!" She'd never see the man again. He'd say, "Now you'll sing with more feeling." He had his way of dealing with people to make them dance and sing. Florence Mills was the most beautiful little delicate-looking person and very sweet. I was wondering why there isn't more said or done about her because she was a great star. I met her. Met Gertrude Saunders, the girl that - I think they had difficulties out of Gertrude Saunders, so Ziegfeld found Florence Mills to take her place.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When you knew Florence Mills, what was she doing then?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: She was in a show on - I think it was Seventh Avenue. You know the night clubs and theatres were a big thing. There was no Broadway then; it was Seventh Avenue and Harlem. Everything existed there, you know.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Tell me a little bit about Florence Mills. In performance, what was she like?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Just beautiful. She reminded me of - what was the girl from Paris? Josephine Baker, that type.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: They were contemporaries, were'nt they, just about the same time?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I think Josephine was younger. During that time I met, in fact I played for Moms Mabley. Her name was Jackie Mabley then. And John Mason - oh, they were the most fabulous comedians. They were the same on the street. John Mason had a little baby just could barely talk. He'd stand on the street and everybody would be laughing. They'd go around the Tree of Hope and he had taught this kid every curse word in the book. If you walked up and said, 'Hello, how are you, little -' he'd call you rotten and then John Mason, his father, would break down and laugh. That was his kicks during the time he wasn't working, to teach his own son these words. The Tree of Hope, that's where most of the performers used to hang out. During that period I met also Bojangles.
WILLIAMS 93

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: The guys were so fascinated - in the band, you know, John Williams and the group that I worked with - so fascinated with him that they used to hang out where he was. He was a great pool player. He'd bet like $500 on a game. He was very good at it and most times he'd win and also he used to bet some of the guys on the street that he could run backwards as fast as anyone running forward. He'd win that. I saw him running backwards. That's the funniest thing I've ever seen in my life. He was really great at doing things like that.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: That was part of his dancing ability, wasn't it, the fact that he could run backwards?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I don't know but he could really run fast backwards.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was Florence Mills a dancer too?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, she was a dancer and a singer.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: She went to Europe, didn't she?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I don't know because see I saw her a couple of times, I met her, I went back stage with Jeanette. They were good friends, the team of Seymour and Jeanette, the lady I worked with. I wasn't in her company too much.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: But what sort of an impression did she make?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: A very good one. I was very unhappy when I found out she had passed away because she was so sweet you just had to fall in love with her.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: But she was in the Ziegfeld show when - ?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, 'Poor Little Blackbird' or something like that show, that's when I met her.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Do you want to go on with this particular period?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, about the Rhythm Club. I was just talking to Bennie Carter -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Where was the Rhythm Club?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I think it was at 132nd and Seventh Avenue in New York.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Roughly around what time?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, maybe '28 or '29. No, '26 or '27. I've forgotten, it was during that time. My husband - he later became my husband - took me in the Rhythm Club, I remember, one night.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was this John Williams?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: John Williams. There was Louis Armstrong, Bennie Carter, Johnny Hodges, Fats Waller, Willie the Lion, and Bennie Carter's cousin that played trumpet. He was just wonderful - I'm trying to think - Cuban Bennett. He was really sensational. He played somewhat like Sweets but all these modern changes and everything. He was just beautiful. Louis Armstrong I mentioned, and J. P. Johnson, and they had this great jam session going. I was hiding practically. My husband says, 'Get up and play.' I said, Oh no,' and I started crying. He says, 'You'd better play.' So I sat down and played with them and I guess they liked it
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: because they, everybody began hugging and kissing and whatnot. But the thing that impressed me about Louis, I hadn't met him before or heard him play; I had heard about him. He was just like a god among them. When he took his chorus - he had a thing of hitting high notes - they'd say, "Ta-ta, 'yeah,' and the cats in the place, "Ta-ta, 'yeah,' and when he hit the top note everybody would fall out on the floor and scream. It was one of the greatest jam sessions. John Williams used to take me around every night. He'd make me play with all of them.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: They had jam sessions like that every night?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, every night, during the day sometimes but the best sessions were at night, where all the greats were. All the great musicians came there.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Did you get used to playing then?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Oh, after while. No, I think each time he had to threaten to hit me or something if I didn't play. I was scared each time.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: O.K., do you want to stop a minute? Now then, that time when Fats Waller threw you up in the air, what happened then?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I got a job in - it wasn't the Cotton Club, it was Connie's Inn and they had me there for one week and the people didn't dance or eat because I was so short, my feet was about 6 inches from the floor and everybody was
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: looking at my feet. I'd get on the tip end of the piano stool. My foot would start bouncing up so high, they'd watch that. Nobody ate and they'd dance right in front of the piano and stop. So I got a job, paying good money too. Well, $75 a week was like $1200 then.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: (NOT CLEAR) But it was just a week?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, and it also helped. We were practically stranded and we were out of work. It was during the period after Seymour died and we didn't have any work coming in. Nobody was working so that helped me to give the boys some money. So when I played and worked I gave them some of the money.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: I'd like to go back to Thelonious Monk. You first saw him in Kansas City? When was the next time you saw him?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I saw him in New York during the 30's. We became very, very good friends. In fact, Bud Powell, Monk, and I were inseparable. During the 40's that was every day, every night, all the time.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: During the 30's what did you do?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Really I got close with him when he was working at Minton's. That was before anybody ever heard of bop. I was living at the Dewey Square Hotel, 118th and Seventh Avenue and I used to go around to Minton's every night to the jam sessions and Monk was playing there.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How did Monk happen to be at Minton's?
WILLIAMS 97

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: All the bop musicians were jamming or playing there every night because there was no work for them on 52nd Street. Nobody understood what they were playing.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was this the time that Monk had tried to start a big band?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: He did start it, because everybody used to pitch in 50¢ or do arrangements and often I gave them money. They used to rehearse in the basement of some place, but the whole idea was, you know, like our black people never get credit, receive credit for anything they do or create. So what they were doing, they created a new music as far as Monk is concerned in order to get some kind of recognition for us, so they stayed in this cellar - basement - and rehearsed as long as they could and then they'd come out and try to get jobs. Then everybody copied it; they lost again.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: The real beginnings of bebop then were in this big band that Monk had organized?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes. Well, I'll say Dizzy was the real beginning. It happened to be an era of music that everybody played, like boogie-woogie. Every kid born playing something played boogie-woogie. I heard Monk play but he wasn't actually playing the real bebop. It was Dizzy that created the real bebop.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was Dizzy in Monk's big band?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, Monk always worked for Dizzy. He's always
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: been a leaner. Before I forget it, when I ran off from the Kirk band I came here to New York - I had brought Art Blakey in from Pittsburgh - he was about 18 - I told you that story. I was out of work so Dizzy and the modern musicians always cared for me. They liked me and they liked being around me. We used to always pal together and all that. So Dizzy discovered I was out of work so he gave me a job on 149th Street. It was a big, big ball room. This particular night when I went there they advertised my name, that I hadn't been playing in New York as a single since I was with the band. So I played and this particular night - it was Saturday night. Dizzy had to go to another gig and he made me the leader of the group. Illinois Jacquet and I think Art Blakey on drums... (NOISE) Oscar Pettiford on bass and one more person - a trumpet player. I can't remember his name.
(NOISE)

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: When you were subbing for Dizzy?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes. We were playing and I went to the manager to find out - I forgot to ask how much we were making. He said, 'Six dollars.' I said, 'Oh, no.' So I waited till intermission. Intermission was around 11:30 so I refused to play. The place was jammed and packed. I refused to play at all. I said, 'No, I'm not going to play any more. You'll have to give us more money. You'll have to at least
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: give me $20 and the boys $15." So they had to do it. We didn't know that the delegate from the union was there. So after the gig was over they had us up, you know, the Board. Out of town musicians was working below scale; they had been doing it for a long time, but they thought that I should become a member, a special kind of member because I stopped the dance... That's the only thing that saved me. So they had all of us at a Board meeting and they were going to fine us for working this gig. So that's the only thing that saved all of us, was that I stopped and I told them. Whoever was there told them, "This woman is somebody great to have in the union because she stopped them at 11:30. She told them, you have to give us a raise or we aren't going to play any more." That raised the salary of that particular place. So that's how I became a union member.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Then to get back to Monk and his big band, they were rehearsing in the cellar and then they had to get out and get some jobs?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, Monk and Bud Powell were together. I don't know how they were doing it, but Bud idolized Monk. He always did. Monk would write great compositions and Bud would actually play them very well.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: So when you say they were together, you mean they were both involved with the big band.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, they were involved.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Who else was in the big band?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I don't remember because they were musicians -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did they ever get out of the cellar?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, they had to. They got very hungry.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: I mean as a band.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, I think it disbanded. All the guys used to hang out at Minton's and play.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: So that was how Monk got playing at Minton's, because -

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, that was how all the new era of music started up at Minton's, you know they named it the House that Built Bop. Well, they did, because I happen to know that.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What drew all this particular group of musicians to Minton's?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: There was no other place to go except Minton's. They had been all over town. When I was with Andy Kirk I used to come to New York. Dick Wilson, Lester Young, some of the Count Basie musicians, and I - we'd go all over town opening up new places and the minute the business was going well they'd throw us out, wouldn't allow us to come in any more.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: That doesn't seem to make sense. Man!

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: That's what happened. One time we were jamming in a club at 110th Street and a delegate was walking outside
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: saying that this is a non-union place. They said, "If you don't come out in a half hour I'm going to report you to the union." Dick Wilson stuck his head out and said, "Man, go ahead now because we're going to jam." We stayed there and went back the next day. We didn't care what he did because during that era everybody was just thirsting to play. You just had to play someplace. There was another club, private club, we opened up when Don Byas was with us on the jam session. It was a private club and there was about 3 people in this club when we first started jamming there. The place became packed and jammed. One night we went to jam and they wouldn't let us in.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Where was that club?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: At 118th and Seventh Avenue?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did it have a name?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, I don't know the name of it.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Were you at Minton's quite a bit too?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Every night.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How did it work out if Monk - did everybody take turns on the piano or -

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, they had the same idea that Kansas City had, you know. Several pianists were there and they'd take turns.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: I heard stories about musicians coming up from downtown and trying to find out what was happening.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: They did and they would write music on their cuffs, on toilet paper, and everything.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did they try to sit in?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, they didn't try to sit in. They were trying to get the phrasing of it so Monk and the cats said, "What's the use? We just have to try to get on out downtown and try to get a job."

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How about some of the older black musicians? Did they sit in too?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Well, I only saw Dizzy there and I think Roy Eldridge and, who else?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: I heard stories of Fats Waller.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I never saw Fats there but I wasn't there all the time. I was there maybe about a year, six months, I don't remember just how long, but I've never seen any of the older musicians. In fact I lost the friendship of a lot of older musicians by hanging out with the young musicians.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Why?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It created a jealousy. When bop came along they felt that it was so strange that it wasn't right, that it wasn't good. You know, you always have that dissension.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was it that they didn't understand it?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: They didn't understand it and it was so far out. I understand that a lot of musicians were in the Army. When they came out and heard that, they put their instruments
WILLIAMS 103

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: down and got a job working. They thought maybe the music was too tough to play.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Why did you have no trouble going along with it?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Because most of them needed inspiration and they wrote the music up here at the house. I had a white carpet here on the floor. We used to sit on this carpet. I kept it clean, you know. We ate on it and did everything. Tadd Dameron and all the cats used to come. Monk used to come here and write his music. I have some music he left here now - and Bud. If they wrote at home they'd bring it here for me to hear it and see how I liked it.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How long have you had this carpet?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Since '41, 32 years. Very famous house. Mel Torme used to come here, Sarah Vaughan, even Leonard Feather, Benny Goodman. Seemed like it was more inspiration for them than I had out of the house. I had to go down to Nola's and get my inspiration. Dizzy, Miles - oh, just all the musicians came here. Seemed like I was inspiration or something for them.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: As you came into the period when bop was happening, were you dissatisfied with the older music or did you happen to like it?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I was dissatisfied completely with the older music. I was working at the Cafe downtown and I was late so many times that Barney fired me when I went uptown. I was so happy when he fired me. I said to John Castle,
WILLIAMS 104

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: "Oo, I got fired!" I was talking to Thelma Carpenter and somebody /said, "Where are you working?" "I don't know, I got fired." Thelma said, "You shouldn't do that." in New York. You wouldn't get another job." I said, "I'd rather be out." I was up there playing real commercial music and skipping notes on classical - the worse you played it the better you'd go over - and the worst commercial music. I was hanging out on 52nd Street where Billie Holiday was. I heard this music and it was terrific. Barney did hire me back. He wanted me back and I stayed a short time, but the music was so beautiful it just gave you a sight of a new picture happening in the jazz. It had such a beautiful feeling. It didn't take me very long to get on to it or create in my own way from it, for certain things that had happened.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When you say you seem to have been an inspiration to all these people that came up here, in what way were you an inspiration. Was it that you gave them ideas?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Well, sometimes I did Tadd Dameron when he'd get stuck in his arrangement like me or any other arranger. He'd come up and I'd say, "Get out of it this way." I'd play it on the piano or if he didn't like that I'd play a record. I get my inspiration from modern classical things. I get in a mood, you know, to write. I always have used that as inspiration for writing.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Play records of modern classical things?
WILLIAMS
stack of them.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Delius or Schönberg. I have a lot of don't ask me to name it all - in the closet. After a while a musician knew what I was doing and he stole them. I've got for about 5 copies of Schönberg, you know, when he did - well, I can't remember names, but it was very inspiring to write music. I'd either do that or play something or help him with the arrangement.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: But in order to get yourself in the mood, you played records, is that right?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Sometimes. Often if I was feeling good I'd just sit on down and play some things and see if he liked it.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Even when you were writing new things, did you sometimes reach into your own past to get ideas?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No. I tell you what it happensa. It would just come right out. You may be walking down the street and it comes out of the sky. But there's other times when you don't feel like writing or you're just dry. I would never take a job as an arranger or creative artist because you can run dry and you just have to leave it alone for 6 months, 4 to 6 months. Sometimes riding on the subway would inspire me, the clicking of the wheels, to write something. But there are times when everything is completely gone as if you've never written anything and nothing happens at all.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: A dry spell. You say you wouldn't take a job as a creative artist, what are you doing - ?
WILLIAMS 106

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I mean as an arranger or writer, that's what I mean, because I'm too creative. I have to wait for an inspiration.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: But every time you sit down to play you've been creative.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, it's better for me that way. I can create much better if the bass player's with me, if he doesn't interfere.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Now, want to stop a minute?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Let's go back to Pittsburgh where you were brought up.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, I was in grade school. I can tell you about this wonderful principal we had, Miss Milholland. It was a white school and all white teachers. She had a deep something for black kids and black people. She was the most beautiful woman I've ever seen. I think she was about 6 feet something - she was very tall. If she discovered a talented black person she'd do everything in her power to help them. I think I was supposed to be in school - I was only in the third grade now. I was supposed to be in school at 9 o'clock. She'd give me until 9:30 or 10 to get in. She was booking me on gigs over at Tech University. She'd take me home with her and have me play for everybody in the place where she lived. She just was so beautiful.
WILLIAMS 107

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: What really happened - I used to hide under the bed. I don't know if I told you about this and I think it's a terrible thing that anybody would indoctrinate a black kid against what happened to them when they were in slavery, what happened to their parents when they were in slavery, because it affected me so when I was quite young. I was in the third grade, I remember. I usedto hide under the bed and listen to my great-grandparents talk about slaves and things. It infuriated me so that when I went to school I hit my teacher, Miss Itzel, with a stick. I just walked in school and hit her with a stick.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Why?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I said, "You hate black people and I hate white people," something like that. So Miss Itzel said, "This poor child," and she bought me dolls and candy and everything and Miss Milholland heard about it. They discovered I had perfect pitch and she did everything about instruments and a lot of things - she's so talented she can play all the instruments. She had a music store to send all the instruments out to me and I played violin and the teacher got rid of me fast. He says to them, "You better not bother her because already she's playing "The Sheik" on one string." You just leave her alone and let her find out her own music and find out what she's going to do." As I said before, Miss Milholland would book me over for afternoon teas at
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: the Tech University and other little gigs. That's the reason why I think it's very bad in telling a child about anything that has happened in the past against any race of people.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: In your case it wasn't the school that was telling you this, this was overheard in your home?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: This was overheard. You see, my great-grandparents were born I guess about a year after the slaves were freed. They were both very fair, my grandmother especially. My grandfather had blonde hair. She used to tell how they used to put them out in the sun and try to parch them black because they were very, very fair and my grandmother is too. I'd hear them tell all these tales and about the slaves and what had happened. It really angered me and I can understand what's happened to the young black kids of today, because they really shouldn't - they should find out the history but they shouldn't hear too many things because they start thinking wrong. But eventually

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When you say they shouldn't hear about the history, you mean they should get the whole -

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: The whole history.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: The whole and not just pieces of it.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: And especially they should get the history of black Americans. I think that's really what they need now.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: You say the school was a white school that you went to?
WILLIAMS 109

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, it was an all white school.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: All white except you?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, they had Italians and black people and Irish and everybody going to the school. I think they had more Italians and blacks than any other race. This particular school, when I was going, I guess I was about 12 years old when I met Roland Mayfield - you know he's a big part of my life in music because he did everything to help. He used to buy cars and things and he allowed the girls - he taught all of us how to drive and how to race and how to do a lot of things.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How to race?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes. I used to race cars but it was in the city, on the Bigelow Boulevard.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What kind of races were they?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Just racing. Somebody would come up and bump the back of your car and it meant they wanted to race. When I was 12 years old he taught me how to fix a car. I was a mechanic; I could fix cars. There was a man on his way to meet my aunt in Philadelphia and he took us to Philadelphia. Margaret Warren, the girl I told you about that protected us when we were out with the show - she was a dancer - was riding along with us and he walked back about a mile to the garage and I drove the car in. The men there laughed because I had fixed the car. Roland taught me how
WILLIAMS 110

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: to do that. When Earl Hines gave his little dances in Pittsburgh - I think he was about 6 or 7 years older than any of us - they had a tough gang from downtown come out and try to break up the dances, fight, and they did a little bit of everything - Soho gang. When Roland stepped out, the street car wasn't going fast enough for them to jump on the street car and try to get away because he'd break up the gangs and everything. He was a terrific man.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Do you want to get into the Buck and Bubbles?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: The bands, when they came to Pittsburgh they'd drive in to my little street on (Wehnwood) street and pick me up and take me out on gigs with them, during the period when the bands used to come to Pittsburgh. By this time I was known as the little piano girl. Everybody called me that and Roland Mayfield had gotten a special made (Ford?) Chrysler with a 4-gear shift on it and he'd given me this car. My mother said, 'Roland is crazy.' I was going to school. He'd come to school, park the car, walk back and get in one of these other cars. He had about 3 or 4 cars. I'd drive down to a night club - I think that was also called the Subway - on Wiley Avenue. My mother never knew I was going down there because Wiley Avenue was so rough. It was so tough that they said one night a guy got on the street car and took over and threw the motorman off. During this period Buck and Bubbles - Buck was a terrific pianist
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: and nobody knew that. He came to town -

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Didn't he play piano in the act, though?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, he played piano and was terrific, a style that you never heard before. The swing part of it equaled Fats Waller. It was terrific.
WILLIAMS 112

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: During the period when the bands used to come to Pittsburgh I met Buck. He was a great pianist but I don't think many musicians knew it because he had that comedy act going with Bubbles. He'd come to Pittsburgh and he'd say, "Now I'm going to teach you some of my things." Buck was a great teacher for me. We'd be in the Subway jamming and he'd say, "Hey, look, girl, you like me. Come over here. I'm going to teach you something." He showed me runs. Later on after I met Count Basie and Art Tatum, Buck showed me a run that Art Tatum - it was his famous run. He made it from top to bottom and Buck had taught me that run. He said, "Now when you get in front of Count Basie and Art Tatum, you make it like this," and he turned it around. One night I was jamming with Art. Art played and I was playing so I played this run that Buck had taught me and Art Tatum said, "Hey, what's that? Play it again." For about 3 or 4 years he and Count Basie were making this run the wrong way. That's the type of musician Buck was. He'd show me something but he didn't want me to play it when they were around, 'cause he didn't want them to learn it. They came around and would hear me turn it around and make it some other way.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was there a lot of jealousy around then?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: There was jealousy all during all my period. It was mostly around women. I remember once when I was with
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Buzzin the Buzz and Harris show. We were traveling and it seems I was so tiny that - I said to you once before that one of the musicians grabbed me and threw me up in the air, just grabbed me and kissed me and kissed me. The reason I'm afraid of a knife, someone pulls a knife out I'll faint almost, because our trumpet player's wife happened to be around and when he did that, she pulled a razor out on me. I was nothing but a little girl. I became so frightened. Then her husband put me down and she hit me. I accidentally knocked her out because I was warding off her blows. That frightened me and I fainted.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: One other time that I ran into something like that, my husband was very tall, handsome ladies' man and he was always teasing. He had one girl in Tulsa, Oklahoma, thinking that he was going to marry her, but his wife wouldn't allow it. I knew nothing about it and the wives were protecting me in the Andy Kirk band and I didn't know it. Bessie Lawson and Ophie Harrington and Mabel Durham and a couple of the girls, they lived across the street from me and when I got out to go to the store or anything I noticed they'd come out of the house and go to the store with me. He'd met one of the natives down there and she was very, very jealous of him. He was kidding around with her and she was trying to kill me. She was thinking that maybe I wouldn't give him a divorce to marry her. She was more in love with him than he was with her.
WILLIAMS 114

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Did you ever run into her?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, I never saw her. They said she was a blonde girl, something, I don't know. They described her to me but I never even went looking for her. I was so dumb, so full of music till they called me "Dummy". I never paid attention to any danger or anything else. There was always music around, but later on I discovered that the wives were protecting me and they often would protect me. There was quite a bit of jealousy around. With this Buz ZIN Harris thing, his wife was very jealous of me and one day he hit her in the eye. We happened to be out in the country and he walked around a cow all day because he said something like that if you put it on the eye it's like a raw steak. He was walking to get something to heal her eye.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Anything else you can tell us?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I guess plenty of things. I can't think of anything right now... Ben Webster in Kansas City, I met him. Did I tell you about him? He came from a very wealthy wonderful family of doctors and lawyers and teachers, but he lived right around the corner from 12th Street, a pretty rough street where all the night clubs were. They said when Ben Webster was 15 or 16 years old his parents were putting $75, $100, $50 suits on him then. He was called little Peck's Bad Boy because they couldn't keep him in college. He'd been sent to several colleges. One day Ben was telling
WILLIAMS 115

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: us a story. He said the girls were dressing in the dormitory and he was peeping through the window and fell through the window. He had a cut on his arm. But he was a terrific tenor man and Ben Webster was really my first love. We used to be together all the time. I loved him. Things that he did in the band would shame the boys and after he was with us about a year he was just as nice and calm, because the guys were so nice in the band and they always helped wild musicians like Ben and he was really a wild one.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: But he was your first love and nothing ever came of it?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, no, no. He was really a wild man and he was really too wild for me.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Do you want to stop and check your notes again?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Mildred Bailey.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, I recorded with her. She was a great favorite of John Hammond's, you know. Mildred asked me to do an engagement with her at the 18th Hole on 52nd Street, so that's where we were in the summer of '52 with George Auld's band. It was a terrific engagement except Mildred used to become disturbed. There was a girl that used to be in New York - Stella Brooks, did you ever hear of her? Stella Brooks was a very good singer and very good actress.
WILLIAMS 116

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I loved her and she's a very good friend of mine, but Stella had something going in her that used to disturb all the singers including Sarah and Billie Holiday. Once they asked Billie Holiday, "Do you like Stella Brooks' singing?" Billie Holiday said, "She can't even blow her nose." Because Stella with her bad ways had angered so many singers at things until they disliked her. This one engagement Mildred just couldn't sing one night and I asked her what was wrong. She said, "Mary, get her out, get her out. She came here to see you. Get her out. I can't sing. She's out there making faces..." Stella was so funny when she came around.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Why did she bother singers? What did she do to singers?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I don't know, something happened with singers. No, she didn't bother me because I played piano, but there was something - Stella was a very beautiful person, you could have a ball with her, but she didn't like anybody much, you know what I mean, when they were playing or anything. I guess she didn't bother me because she thought one day I'd be accompanying her on piano but I would be afraid to work for her. I loved Stella; Stella was very nice. I used to hang out with Mildred. I'd go down to her house and this particular morning she was just sick about the whole thing because I couldn't get Stella to leave. She sat there and made catcalls and everything
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: while Mildred was singing. She used to do the same thing to Billie but not for long.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was Mildred a rather unhappy person when you knew her?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: She didn't seem to be unhappy when I was around her but I heard she was, because I'd go to her place and we'd get into music. She was always so jolly. I also heard she was difficult to get along with but I got along with her.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was this when she split up with Red Norvo?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, this was when she split up with him. She was with him when I first met her and they had had a dispute or something. It happened one morning when I went to see her. But we'd go all up in Harlem and everything. Andy Kirk had a barbecue place and she ordered barbecued chili and so many different things and got sick that night and said the food was no good. The next time she went up there Andy said to her, 'Well, if you eat as much as you eat, you will get sick.'

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: She had to do something to keep her figure.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Right. A little later on I went into another club on 52nd Street. I think (Mavis Irvin) Levy owned this place, you know, it was part of Birdland. What had really happened, Birdland brought all the bop modern musicians out - Charlie Parker and all of them. Max Roach, Bud Powell, and some
WILLIAMS 118

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: of them would come to me and ask my advice about things.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Why were you doing this?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I don't know what happened because see I was working on the East Side and various places out of the city, but when I got this job I was alternating with Billy Taylor. I can't remember the name of this place, at 52nd and Eighth Avenue. So I had a way of always helping musicians. At one time I was recording for Moe Asch and what happened, he was expecting a pianist and I had taken Bill Coleman and Al Hail with me and he got a little peeved about it but he recorded it, because they were out of work and I put them back to work by doing that. So they wanted me in this particular place with a piano, bass, and drums - trio. So Klook and Oscar and all of them told me that they were barred out of Birdland. So I said come on and work with me. So with me when I went in this place I had Oscar Pettiford, Kenny Clarke on drums, Kenny Durham on trumpet, and Kai Winding on trombone. There was a terrific little thing happened. One night I felt that I wasn't accompanying the boys right so Bags - you know, with the Modern - came in and I said, "I have to go up to the ladies' rest-room. Will you sit and play a set for me?" He said, "Yes, Lou." So he sat down and while I was up there I was using toilet paper to write down the notes the way he was pushing. and When I came down it was much better. Because I had dropped
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: in from the East Side playing all that corn and with the cats. My whole thing is to needle the band to play their best for anybody who is soloing because if they play a good solo then I have inspiration to play.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: But you just can't shift from the East Side -

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, you can, but you can't shift overnight; you have to rehearse with them. We went in there and started blowing. Oscar was great to play with because we composed at least 3 tunes a night or more. He'd start a bass figure and I would play, and that is really my schtick, my whole way of doing. I like to compose while I'm playing. We had a great session going except then he was crazy about his "Moscow Mule". He'd go around the corner on Eighth Avenue and I'd have to go to get him. So one night I got a stick and I hit him on his knee and I said, "Listen, you had too much Moscow Mule." He laughed about it, you know, and I decided to put him on cello. So I called in Percy Heath, for bass, a terrific bass player also. So one night I was blowing like mad. Oscar was on the cello, he turned around and said, "You don't blow like that with me." I said, "Yes, because you high off of Moscow Mule." So I did put the musicians back to work there in this particular club. Charlie Parker came in one night and he said to me, "Lou, let's get a band or something together. You know all the cats always want me to get a band with you."
WILLIAMS 120

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I said, "No, man, not the condition you're in." He said, "I'll do it, Mary. Anything you tell me I'll do." He said, "You know I'm not allowed to play in Birdland or any of the clubs." You know, that's during that period. So I told him, "Get up on the stand and let the people see how great you are." The place was really packed because see a lot of the people had followed me from the East Side. Some of these people had been to a ballet or something this night and they came in. They were all up in the balcony; it was Sunday night. Charlie Parker got up on the stand... he said, "Play the Kansas City Blues." Listen, I've never heard Coltrane play what that boy did! No! I talk about it often. When he finished the people in the place stood up and applauded. During the time that he played I don't know what carried us along with him because there were sounds that we'd never played before, Oscar and the bass and piano. To start out a blues - I think one of the guys had played one chorus...Charlie Parker kept going to keys and he kept going through changes... The one on the bass said, "Mary, where is he now?" I said, "Man, don't talk to me now," because Oscar said if anybody came up on the stand they were going to help him, so when Charlie stepped up there he said, "Lou, let's blow." So we were listening to his changes during it. I've never heard him play like that before in my life, the way he played.
WILLIAMS 121

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: When he finished everybody just screamed. He said, "How was that?" I said, "Man, that was too great for me."

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: But you still didn't go with him, in the band?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I didn't see him any more after that because later on I went to Europe. This was in the year of '52.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was this when you worked with Woody Herman?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Ok yes. You know what really happened when I was on this engagement. My brother always comes around. He could really play drums but he never worked at it, piano - Jerry Burley, my brother. He's a dancer. He used to tap dance like Baby Laurence, the greatest dancer in the world, just never worked at anything like that. He happened to be in the club one night when I went in. No, it was later. I went to work one night and Glaser's always had an idea to put me with the Woody Herman group. I walked in and he didn't even tell me that he had fired all of my guys and had this band up here. I'm the only black person working in it. Well, that didn't bother me at all, but the idea that they didn't ask me if I wanted it. So Chick was standing against the wall and I said, "What happened, man?" He said, "They fired us." I said, "Like that, without a notice?" "Yes." He said, "You're going to be sorry because they ain't no other drummer you can play with." I said, "Oh, man, I don't want to hear that." But he told the truth because I haven't been able to play with anybody since
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: except Mickey Roker. I said, "This can't happen." So you know what - I'm kind of headstrong. I'll go your way or anybody's way with you for a while and if that stubborn streak hit me then you're in trouble. I'm not going to do any more. So my brother came in about 4 nights later to hear the group play. I was so mad sitting up there on the stand. Cat would tell you to play some of the tunes that they played with Woody Herman. They were trying to play some of the wrong changes according to the record. So I said, "They're wrong. You've given me the wrong changes on them and you're playing the wrong changes," what I'd figured out with my ear. All that kind of thing was going. I really missed my other guys anyway. So I told Billy Taylor, "Billy, came over and play this set. I got to go up to the ladies' restroom." He came over and I came down with my coat and hat on. I think it was in the winter. I think it was because in December I went to Europe. My brother happened to be there. He said, "Where you going?" He said, "You know you work for gangsters and they're tough. They'll do something." I said, "Listen, as mad as I am I'll take your head off. You better leave me alone." And I walked out. I left them up there and I walked out. So they tried to beg me, we'll give you $50 more, we'll give you this and that - because they were having crowds from the East Side. They followed me there. And I never went back.
WILLIAMS 123

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: That's when I had the offer to go to Europe. Gale's office called. They wanted to break a ban of 30 years, that had existed with the two unions, the English union and the American one. I don't even know what happened. It seems some English musicians came over here and they wouldn't allow them off the beat to play.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Jack Hilton's band?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I don't know. I heard something, so I got ready to leave to go to England. I had turned down offers before and I decided to go.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: That gets us over to - you discussed your going to England. We talked about your going to England before and we got you over to Paris..( )

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: During the period that I was on 52nd Street and 8th Avenue with Billy Taylor, the boppers then were Bud Powell, Max Roach, Charlie Parker, and Kenny Durham. Most of the cats made their little complaints about Birdland and what they were doing. One day Max Roach and Bud Powell ran up and said, "Lou, you should come down and see how they're treating us and what's happening." I said, "O.K., I'll come down," but I didn't tell them when I was coming down. So I went down there and I slipped in on Bud Powell. I didn't see Max. Bud Powell was really gone; he was out of his mind. Something happened - it wasn't his drinking or smoking or anything else. I think from my feelings and Bud being around
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: me I think he was over-sensitive, you know. He felt every-body, felt everything because he was so terrific in his music. Usually when he'd get into these things I'd take him home and make him take a hot bath and just put him in my front room and make him sleep. When he got up he'd play like mad and he'd go like mad. But if he had an engagement at Birdland or places like that, for about 3 days he was all right and the fourth day he was gone, he was out of sight, and nobody could do anything with him. At one time Birdland offered me $75 a week to take care of him and all that. I said no, I have to work myself. Then too you'd have to have a man around, with him. But this particular time I slipped in on Bud and he was so funny till everybody in the place was laughing. He'd sit there playing, Art Tatum..... Shearing Sherry...... and he'd sit there and he'd look at the audience like this and when he got up from the piano he went around to the cash register and just went "Bing!" (Gory?) and took out what he wanted. I think John Gara, you know, who was with Sarah Vaughan, he grabbed him and said, "Come back, Bud." So when they put him off the stand, when I saw him I said, "Oh, so you want me to come down and help you and talk for you, and look what you did tonight." He said, "Ah, Baby Doll," - he called me Baby Doll. I knew when he was going off because he was a good friend, musical friend and everything else, but when he was going out of his
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: mind, going to the other planet, he felt I was his girl friend. I couldn't even have a little baby around the house; he kicked at my little nephew. He let nobody come near me. I said to him, "All right, I'm going to tell Monk what you did." Then he'd straighten up. I don't care what he was doing, if I told him I was going to tell Monk, he'd straighten up.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Why did that have an effect on him?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I don't know, I don't know why. I don't know if he was afraid of Monk or he respected him so much. So that's how I controlled him, through telling him I was going to get in touch with Monk. One time I held him here in the house and my brother got angry with me. I said, "I'm going to cure you of every thing you're doing." I kept him in the house two days and wouldn't allow him out. My brother came and said, "You shouldn't do that, because anything could happen to you." I said, "Not with him; he won't even steal from me." A lot of times the guys that were jealous of the cats coming up said, "Mary, they'll steal. They'll do this and that 'cause they'll need it, you know, for their drinks and whatnot." I said, "Nobody'll steal from me." Then I started planting money around to see if they would, and they wouldn't. Bud needed 50¢ one day and he said, "Hey, Baby Doll, give me 50¢." I said, "I haven't got it." He said, "Yes, you have. You have two
WILLIAMS 126

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: dollars and a half on the kitchen table." They wouldn't take anything from me, no. Whatever they were doing they never allowed me to do it, because one time I said to them, "Give me some of that, that you're doing." I was kidding with him. "Oh, Baby Doll," he got on his knees, "don't you ever do that."

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Who were some of the other musicians you took care of?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Practically all of them.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Charlie Parker?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, yes. Charlie Parker would always call and ask me if I liked some things he had written and when he did the strings he asked me to come down to Birdland. He said, "I want you to tell me really what you think of it, Lou." I went down. Charlie was a wonderful guy. I was at Birdland one day - you know that bar was terrible.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Terrible in what sense?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: As I understand it, nice people never go to a bar. Well, not everybody's good, you know what I mean, but I'm talking about the character's you'll find mostly at bars, nice places, than you will sitting at a table. My schtick was hanging out at the bar with the guys, the musicians. So that's where you'd find me. He came up protecting me from a girl that had taken my pocketbook and he got it back for me and then drove me home that night.
WILLIAMS 127

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: He was a very nice person.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When you went down to hear the strings - you started to tell me about that. What happened then?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It was so great. I told him how great they were and he thanked me... I understand he recorded them later.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did you help him with the strings?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No indeed. The only person I helped, Miles happened to be with me one day and Milton Oreny, the composer - he had so many masters in music till he couldn't play or write. Some people study too much. Milton and I were just saying a combination of things and I mentioned about a tuba and I think that that thing, that sound that Miles got on a record, was an idea of me just thinking of instruments, and he called me back and thanked me.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was this when Miles had that 9-piece group?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, that beautiful sound. We were all just sitting here naming instruments that we'd like to do things with, you know. He thanked me.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How about- you saw quite a bit of Miles, didn't you, during that period?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, sure. We used to go to Birdland. It's the most peculiar thing to see him like he is now. I can't understand it. We'd be at Birdland and Miles had made some changes on Yesterday's. He'd say, "Look at this, Lou." You know, I'm a much better reader looking at music than I
WILLIAMS 128

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: am when I read it there, 'cause my mind starts wandering and I listen to the musicians and all that. It's a little confusing. He had brought in some changes on 'Yesterday.' I looked up at the stand and I looked at them. All of a sudden Fats Navarro, Charlie Parker, and all of them were so high until they had gone asleep. He said, "Look, look, Lou. I'd rather be something he is than to be in that condition." I understand a little later than that, maybe less than a year, Miles ran into Fats Navarro and Fats Navarro was out. Miles was so disgusted he said, "Man, give me that," and he went out with him. So that was the beginning of his drinking and whatnot. But he's a beautiful cat.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Do you see Miles at all these days?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, but I like Miles. When I began praying Miles called me Reverend Williams and I gave him prayers and I sent him a lot of things. I played a concert with him in Europe about 3 years ago and he was all love and kisses and whatnot. I think he's very fond of me. I don't know what happened; I really don't know if all these things are as bad as some people say, but I think he became discouraged. I wasn't there but I heard during that period that I used to see him in Birdland, that Miles was abused by a policeman or something and he's been through several things like that. That can discourage one, you know what I mean, because if a man's outside catching the air and
WILLIAMS 129

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: trying to rest or do something like that and someone come up and abuse them for no reason whatsoever, well - I think a series of things like that happened to him to discourage him. I really don't know if he's as bad as what I hear, because I still like him and my brother Jerry is really crazy about him. I've had people to tell me to go down and see him. I said, "I don't want to go down and see him if he's in a bad way. He may not remember me as a person that he liked."

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How was Max Roach in those days at Birdland that you're talking about? He had a period in which he was very upset and disturbed.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, we were talking about that in Kansas City the other day. Something happened to him to change him around and he was very disturbed and upset and used to get in a lot of things. Now he's a very nice guy. I used to talk to Max Roach and Bud Powell about certain things. See, Max doesn't understand about a cross or anything. Max perhaps thinks that everything should come easy after a certain period. What I talked to them about, certain crosses you carry till you die. Things can't be smooth all the time. The only time I have a discussion, the way he thinks politically his political scene I never went for and I tell him.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What's his political - ?
WILLIAMS 130

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: His idea about life in that direction, I don't particularly go for it, you know.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Which direction is he looking at?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Nonsense to me. It wasn't going to make it. I saw him over at the UN once and we got in a discussion. I said, 'Wait a minute, now stop, let me tell you something, bla-bla,' and I give it to him.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What's he advocating?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Well, the mistreatment of the black man, but after a while as far as I'm concerned, that's just a detraction to my music. I should stick to my music and maybe someday that will disappear, because I feel my music is like a prayer.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Have you ever been interested in politics at all?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, I got hung up in it through working in the Cafe, but I think all musicians or people like me would get mixed up in something, looking for some people to help them and help the race. But they can never be anything but a musician. Through doing benefits and a lot of other things, and you don't know how serious it is - but there's not one musician I think would be in any kind of political anything if they weren't disturbed about the race, as being abused and whatnot of the race, trying to help the poor. I've been in practically everything but I've come out of it. It doesn't take me a year to find out that it's wrong.
WILLIAMS 131

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Do you find most of them, most of the things you have been interested in, were wrong?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, I found out and discovered that in the end the best thing for me to do is stick with my music. If I believe in a political thing or something like that, I push other people. Believe it or not, I've never voted, but I think I can get more votes than anybody else. If I think there's a good man out there, if I have time to think about it, I usually try to get people to vote for him. Well, I'll tell you what happened in Kansas City. We were living there and Johnny Harrington and I, a clarinet player, he and his wife went downtown and voted. I don't think anybody else. Maybe Andy did or some of the boys thought about it or remembered to vote. About 3 months after the election they were charging him tax on somebody else's furniture. They found out where he was.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: It's dangerous.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: So I never voted after that.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Have you ever gotten interested at all in the idea of Africa as a home for blacks?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Never. I learned about Africa when I was 12, during that period. I learned all about the whole history of Africa because my great-grandparents used to talk about that, about Africans, how they were brought over. I think I probably know the whole scene on it - how they were sold
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: by the chiefs and all that. I would never be interested in Africa. I believe that I wouldn't be able to live in Africa because of their ways. I have quite a few friends from Africa and they just think different than I do, well me want to being a musician naturally. I wouldn't/Be over there nor would I want to see Americans go back because - what they don't understand there are so many black people, Americans, they put them in concentration camps because Africans and Indians Westerners are jealous of Americans. They think they're rich and they're a rich country. They're jealous of the jazz, the spiritual, that was created and made such a big hit at one time. I read articles in Europe when I went there that they don't want us there. They just want people that can help teach their kids or to help them. Whenever a black American buys property, he buys a house and not the land. A lot of things, they don't want them living there, except artists or somebody that can help them. I've had dealings with them to know that they're dangerous and the worst thing that could happen was the black magic that the black Americans went into because it's so strong it could destroy. They don't know how to deal with anything like that, especially musicians that are playing that type of music. They've got to bedestroyed in the end, because that's not our way of living and how we've been brought up. We've been brought up as Americans. What /We should do is
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: get something going in a love way to fight conditions here and get rid of conditions and be our freedom here, because if we have to go to another country to help us to be freed in America, we all should go somewhere away from here, because it's not going to happen that way. I never wanted to go even to Europe. I like America. If everybody was like me, all the money wouldn't be over there, 'cause when I make some I bring it back. I don't spend any of it, 'cause you can find everything they have over here. Because when you do go to Europe and talk with people, they're all jealous because they think we have the money. This is a young country. One day we're not going to have anything because we're so gullible over there. Africa really laid a bomb on the black Americans. That was one of the sweetest races and one of the purest races. I said to Peter and he laughed at me, "The Germans thought their race was pure. Suffering makes you pure. Who's got the purest race if you was going to go there and talk about nonsense like that? It would be the black man." At one time they were the sweetest. Now it is Uncle Tom-ish to see a man out on the street dancing and he has a dime in his pocket, but if you look at it in another way, that man was happy. If you look at it and say, how in the world could somebody do that and he has no money and don't know where he's going to eat. At one time they were just that happy. Somebody had
WILLIAMS 134

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: to disturb them so until they're out of their mind. You can't even tell them when they're going wrong and what they're doing and they've got 'em knocking the white man and yet they're still afraid of him. I think... those people like that, like the Jehovah's Witnesses, now, I'm not talking about religion and all that - they know when to strike, when to try to get you in. That's the reason why I went through all the religions, practically all of them, Muslims and everything, threw books out the window and asked God to keep me around the corner to the Catholic church. That's my way.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When did you start going through all the religions? When did that happen?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: During the period when most of the musicians were becoming Muslims.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Was that after the World War, during the World War?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: This was before I went to Europe.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Late 1940's?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: They'd bring the books up here and anything I don't understand and if the words aren't in the dictionary or some kind of language, I don't bother with it. I don't bother with it. I think I can understand practically everything. If I was reading French and couldn't understand the words I'd get the dictionary. But I don't understand what
WILLIAMS 135

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: their thoughts were. The Muslims, as I understand it, later on it's the devil, because the religion is really the Moslems. I just heard that; I don't know; I haven't gone into it deeply. It's apolitical thing that they introduced to America. Everything that comes from Europe and is introduced in America becomes an evil and I don't understand it. These other things in Europe - there's a lot of love among the Muslims, Moslems - there's a lot of love. I told some people: "Black people love white people and vice versa."
