So the last time I was there when I played the concert with Miles Davis. I saw this girl, she sneaked on the bus and she had a white baby in her arms, this black girl. She was a Muslim in America and she had a white husband. Now she divorced her husband and he divorced her. He married a white girl and she married a white man. I looked at her. She was trying to hide from me because before she was talking against white people. I looked at her and I said, "I told you!" That's all I said to her. She said, "Yes, Mary, I understand what you meant." I said when anything is introduced in America it becomes an evil. There's hatred in it and I don't know why.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How did you arrive at what you found was the right thing to do?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, because there was so much confusion in everything else and I couldn't understand it. I read the
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Jehovah's Witness things. When I was reading a little pamphlet I found out that there was a man - I don't know if this is true or not - one man receives all the money and he has everybody out on the street working for him. I think God is a little different than that. You work together and you share. Now if you're head of an organization or something you have to have money in escrow or save money to save it and pay for things and help the poor. Their only concern is pulling people in off the street and through my experience, you can become a fanatic when you deal with God. If I grab you and started pulling you into a religion, which I did, the reason I can tell you this - I'm a guinea pig. I can become a fanatic because when you start dealing with God you have to be very careful. Once that comes about, I'm telling you that's the end of it. You have to take it easy with people if you're going to win them over for God. You can't just be sticking material in the door and pulling them and talking and all that kind of stuff. You pray for them and you do it the easy way. Now I did that and Father Woods said to me, "You want to go to a psychiatrist? I'm going to send you to one." They remind me of fanatics.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How did you get into this whole thing, Mary?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: We left you over in Paris...

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: What I really, how I got into it, I left America
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: and of course you know I went to Europe when the ban was broken there. How I broke the ban was that I played with all the musicians in Europe, all the bands and all the musicians in England, London, and all over. I happened to be at a party that Lascelles, you know, he's the Queen's cousin, he gave a party for Garland Wilson and I. There happened to be a little GI there, black soldier. He said, "You look disturbed, upset." I said, "Yeah, I'm trying to get out of England." The newspapers and the people were if you beautiful but you see/were born in New York, a fast-thinking country, you're held back. Like the guy with the newspaper that says, "Why is it that Americans come over here and after a while they're going so fast until they meet themselves going and coming. Everybody's looking at them." It happens like that. I was held over. I was supposed to go there for 9 days or 11 days and I was held over 11 months. The newspaper did this. So at this party I was just anxious. I wanted to get out. He says, "My grandmother always told me to read the 91st Psalm." Well, you know I never could drink and I had had about 3 Scotches. I was drunk. So I misunderstood him; I thought he said read all the Psalms. It took me two days; however, it worked. Everybody was so nice like the S. S. United cooks and all the guys on the S. S. United. They knew that the food wasn't good and they used to bring me like 50 steaks. They were the most delicious steaks. They'd bring them to the house and I'd give them to
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: people, you know what I mean, because there were too many, they'd spoil. They knew I was going to have a birthday party and so the cook on the ship baked me a birthday cake. The guys were coming to enjoy themselves and I had the room and everything. All of a sudden I left the room open and locked all my bags and left them there and went to Paris, just like that. When they came they called all over Paris and everything. I went over there with Nicole Barclay, who owned the Blue Star Records, I think. I went to visit her. I never went back. So they had a party. I don't know what happened but -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: One thing I don't understand. Reading all the Psalms, what did that do to you?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: You know what that did? I discovered I was stuck and it uprooted me like it would a tree when a storm hit it and moved me on to things I was supposed to be doing. I wasn't supposed to be there because the last two months I hadn't worked at all. I was finished in England until a later date. You know, you can stay too long. In Europe if you go there, when you go in fresh you get maybe $100 a night but if you keep staying it gets smaller and smaller. I just couldn't get away.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: How did reading the Psalms unstick you?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Have you ever read the Psalms? Any of them?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Sure -

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: You're calling for help madly.
WILLIAMS 139

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: But I never read all of them.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Well, that's what I did.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What effect did it have on you. Did it make you get up and move, was that the idea?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: You're crying out so for God's help till you shed everything, everything that's holding you back. You see, sometimes we can get hung up in a situation and can't get out. You know, it's just like a magnet; it keeps holding you. Sometimes we can get out too soon. We don't let it worry us but some things can just drag and drag and drag. You feel, I'm finished here. Like, I've been in a night club. They'd want to held me over and I'd say no, I'm gone. Because until a later date, because you peter out, see, completely. So that's what I felt. But what this does - you have to do it to find out. But it's magic.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When you got to Paris what happened?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: All during my lifetime I made more money than I've ever made in my life. I was working in Bœuf sur le Toit. My best friend, Garland Wilson, great pianist, he knew he wasn't going to live long and he always loved me from the first day he met me and I loved him. He came to England. He said, "I came here because I heard you were here. The doctors give me 6 months to live and I'm going to die with you, where you are." I said, "I'm going so fast I don't know if you can keep up if you're sick."
WILLIAMS 140

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: He said, 'I'm not kidding.' I said, 'Oh, go on with you. You look so fat and healthy.' So when I left England he was right in back of me. So we had a suite of rooms together and Garland used to come and he'd just lay across the foot of my bed all night. we'd sleep like that. I was picking up his sickness. I was getting sick and he was getting well. The Baroness Koenigswarter came and brought me medicine and whatnot. She thought I had a cold but it was Garland. I had to sleep away from him. Shortly after that he passed away.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What did he have?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Complications of something, I don't know. He had told me but I forgot.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Did you actually pick it up from him?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, I was. He was getting stronger and I was getting weak, just going down, down, down. So he was working in the Boeuf sur le Toit and certain people they didn't allow to work in there, especially a woman. Not didn't allow but they just didn't go for women as much as they did men. So what I did was to take over his job and they loved me because they loved Garland, not because I was Mary but because they loved him. So I worked in there and I made good money and I doubled at the theatre. All the Americans had camp back to America and the theatre had to pay what I asked for. It was so successful with an American
WILLIAMS 141

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: musician there so they wanted me in. I doubled from the theatre back to the night club. So all of a sudden I just walked off from both gigs. It was a good thing that I knew Gerard Pochonet, a French drummer that played with all the Americans there, because he took me out to his grandmother's house in the country.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Stop here while we change tapes.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: You went with Gerard Pochonet to the country to live with his grandmother?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, I went to live with his grandmother. Gerard was a wonderful guy. Gerard was the type of drummer who played for most of the Americans, like Lena Horne, Hazel Scott, and all the great stars when they came in. He had such a terrific beat on drums, and feeling. He was a newspaper man; he was an all-around man and one good thing about him, when musicians were stranded or needed help or recording dates, he always helped them, especially the Americans. He favored them because he just loved their music. So he took me out in the country and I stayed there with him, I guess about 6, 7, or 8 months before coming back to America. I canceled everything. I wouldn't go out with anybody to work or anything. All I did was pray and eat and sleep.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What got you started praying?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: The incident in England when the guy told me to
WILLIAMS 142

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: read the 91st Psalm.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Had you prayed ever since then?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, I never stopped even up until now. You know really, John, what I think happened to me, I was going to tell you - I have been a very psychic person. I was born a psychic person. You know in the beginning of the story I told you, but what I did, I put that in my music. Like I told you once before that I could, if I was playing with any musician on earth - it could be Charlie Parker - I could almost hear, could hear most of the time, the next note they're going to play. All this was in my music to help me musically, because I've done some fantastic things, you know, and not studied as much as other musicians in the music field. So I think what happened to me after I stopped playing then my vision and everything went on the outside of music and I began to hear what was going to happen musically while I was praying. Like I saw Charlie Parker's death. I felt that a strange foreign sound would enter into the strains of jazz and would destroy the heritage, would destroy jazz completely. Jazz came out of the spirituals; ragtime, Kansas City swing - well, the 1929 year of jazz bands, Kansas City swing, boogie and the blues of that era. Well, the blues has always been there, that's a spiritual feeling. The next era was bop. Now we've waited I don't know how many
WILLIAMS 143

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: years for a new sound in jazz and it hasn't come forth as yet. I could see all this happening while I was in Paris. It kind of frightened me. It seemed like my feelings was altogether out on the street, or what was happening in the world. I was able to make several predictions maybe 20 years ahead. Some of the predictions that I had was, are black musicians losing our rich heritage, called jazz. The only bad thing about it is the name jazz and I think all the musicians in all eras of jazz have tried to change that name. My era was the swing era and we tried to change it. Also I saw Charlie Parker's death and also very, very bad disturbance among black people, as far as the riots. They've been so disturbed until they're going in the wrong direction and losing the beauty that they had gained through suffering.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: We're talking about basically a period when you were in France and you had gone out to Gerard Pochonet's grandmother's and were staying there. How did this affect you then? What followed the time that you were out at his grandmother's?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I wanted to come home very fast and see what help I could be, you know especially with Charlie Parker. When I did arrive my brother happened to see him coming out of the hospital with sneakers on. My brother Jerry called me from Harlem Hospital and said, 'Mary, I just saw Charlie

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: and it's below zero. Have you got any money or anything you can do to help him?" I said, well, tell him to come by the house. He had Charlie to talk with me and Charlie promised to come up the next day or so. That's the day that he was on the way to the Baroness. He went to her place instead. I thought maybe if I came home there was something I could do about talking or doing something with the musicians or helping.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: When you got back there, what happened? Had you planned to go on playing?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I don't know what I had in mind. My only thoughts were of helping my people, because I saw all these terrible things, like you would looking at TV. I saw these things happening and all these terrible riots and whatnot. Gerard used to say in Paris, he said I was crazy, but he learned later on after he came to America that I wasn't. Thank God for Father Woods because Father Woods got me out of it completely and back to music.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Who was Father Woods?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Father Woods was my confessor. Professor Barry Ulanov got a hold of him to give me instructions.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: We'll go back further. You came back to the United States from France. Were you going to church then or...

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I went to church a couple of times there with
WILLIAMS 145

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: a couple of friends. But I really started going to church when I came back to America.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Tell me about, just before we get into that, what was your religious background as a child, for example?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: It wasn't too much because I came out of the church. I was Baptist then. Most of my sisters and brothers were baptized Catholic and I saw so many things going down with the preacher and what was happening in the church, I felt that I shouldn't even be there. So I came out; I never went to church any more. As I said before this, I didn't know if I did in the first part of my story, I met an insurance man who used to follow me when I was with the Andy Kirk band. I was at the Apollo Theatre. He'd get a cab and hold the cab all during the time the show was on, all day. He was a very, very wealthy man. He'd come back stage and he'd have gifts for me. One thing that he gave me was a little white Bible and he told me, 'This is your wealth and your health and always keep it.' Well, I kept this Bible with me but I never read it. So what happened, I never even thought about praying or doing anything until after Europe in the 50's and I got a sound, that everybody should pray in the church every day because the world would change and you would encounter selfish people and a lot of selfishness in the world. So the only church I followed was the Catholic church and I used to go in and meditate and pray.
WILLIAMS 146

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Did you try other churches first?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, other religions. When I returned I went to several religions. I was working with a dancer who became a preacher at 125th Street and Seventh Avenue in a church there. He was snatching people off the street baptizing. You know what really happened during that period? A lot of musicians and dancers became preachers and they began to preach. They must have gotten the same thing. This dancer I worked with until I began - I think I got together the Bel Canto Foundation to help dope addicts and alcoholics, musicians.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: With this dancer or by yourself?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, no, no, by myself. I left him after I began praying in the Catholic church.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: But then you finally decided on the Catholic church because it was open, was that the reason?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, that was the only reason. Well, the other reason is that was the only church that I felt good in, that I could meditate without vibes hitting me in the head.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was this the period when you just went to the church every day and prayed?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, I prayed. I prayed for everybody but myself until Father Crowley says, 'Listen, you better pray for yourself too while you're praying for everybody.'
WILLIAMS 147

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Who's Father Crowley?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Father Crowley, he was concerned about, after he heard I had stopped playing, he was traveling around with the Newport Jazz Festival and Father O'Connor. They both were friends. So he began coming around to try to get me out to play. He came to the house and he told Dizzy and Elaine, "Mary is a saint." They said, "Why would you say this?" He said, "You should go to her house." I had people in here from the Welfare and everywhere and I was sleeping on the floor. I was feeding and clothing them and doing a lot of things with them, you know.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Now you weren't working at this point?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, I wasn't working.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Where did you get the money to feed and clothe them?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I had royalties coming in and friends helped, especially Dizzy Gillespie and Lorraine. I never asked them for anything in my life, but it seems like they were in tune with me. Days I thought I wouldn't have anything to eat - Dizzy's cousin (or a nephew), his name is Boo Frazier - he'd ring the doorbell and he'd have a basket full of food for me - hams, steaks, and a lot of things in there. Lorraine said, "I thought you were hungry so I sent you some food." They were really beautiful; they looked after me and they were so kind to me.
WILLIAMS 148

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Had you met Father Woods before Father Crowley?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, you see, what I was going to tell you, that Father Crowley told Barry what I was doing. He took me down to Barry Ulanov's house. He spoke to him about me, the things that I was doing. He said, "She should be Catholic. Get a priest for her. She wants to be Catholic." So Barry said, "I'll get one of the greatest priest's that's ever lived." He got hold of Father Woods and he was really something else. Dizzy loved him and all the musicians.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What is Father Woods' first name?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Father Anthony Woods, S. J., Jesuit. I'm telling you he was something else. When he passed away about 6 or 8 years ago I thought I was going to die myself. I didn't know I was leaning so hard. He did everything in his power to help me back to music and things that were still happening with me in a strange way, all this ESP working. He told me to call him any time and sometimes I called him 4 o'clock in the morning. He and Lorraine Gillespie, they had a ball on the phone when they talked about me. It was so funny, some of the things I'd call them about. He was so very kind to me. He went along with me and he finally got me back to jazz. When I went in the Hickory House about 7 years ago, he was there practically every night.
WILLIAMS 149

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Why did you stop playing?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, I didn't really stop on my own. Something carried me away; I began praying and I never thought about playing any more. I just thought about helping people other than - as I understand and have experienced that God was helping many souls through music, but I decided to help them in flesh instead of playing for them. I understand that you can offer it up every note you play to help some /souls and things like that but I was going on my own without the talent. The talent was much stronger for helping people.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How did Father Crowley convince you to go back to playing?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Father Crowley and Father O'Connor talked to me, several priests. They also asked me to write a Mass, but Father Woods is the only one that really stuck with me until I really began praying, and Dizzy. Dizzy would send Melba, "Go up there and see what Lou's doing. See how she's playing." Melba, I understand, would go back and say, "Man, Lou played some chords and you ought to hear them. They're really great." He said, "Well, get her out." Melba would come here and when he took me out to the Newport Jazz Festival, Melba arranged some things. He said, "Those arrangements were really good." She said, "I didn't do them. That was Lou's arrangement. I was in the room and I just sat
WILLIAMS 150

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: down and took the music down." He said, "What! Get her out here!" He finally got me out to Newport where they were all wheeling like mad, like most of the priests did, to get me to write a Mass. Father O'Connor said, "Well, I tell you, if you don't write a Mass just play it, play it on the piano, Mass." I guess I had gotten myself so holy fasting and doing so many things and suffering, till they thought perhaps the music would be good. Sometimes I'd fast 9 days and just drink water for 9 days. The first time I fasted I ate 9 apples a day and Father Crowley came to visit me. He said, "It's a wonder you didn't turn into applesauce."

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: The Hickory House is the first place that you played after what period? Seven years?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Let's see, '52 to '56. Four years, about three or four years. I think I stayed away for 3 years, 3 or 4 years.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: But when you went into the Hickory House, how did you feel getting back into that atmosphere?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Oh, just terrible. My first experience in getting back into the atmosphere was just awful. See, I had stayed in the house away from people so long and after I did the Newport Festival the next thing was - let's see, what's the name of that club, piano house on 56th and -

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: It's not there any more. I know, begins with a C.
WILLIAMS 151

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: The name of that room was the Composer Room. That was the most beautiful room and I loved it. But the craziest thing happened. We had two managers there and the crowds were tremendous. They just fought, fought, fought so much even with the big crowds there until finally people just stopped going, you know. But it was terrific. Now that was the first club date that I had. I worked there and then repeated a couple of times and then I went in again. Dizzy called and Melba and all the musicians were trying to get me out. Even Miles Davis called and said, 'Why don't you come out and record with me?' They were working like mad to get me to come out and play. Well, I was going to tell you what happened in the Composer Room. I hadn't been around people in a long time. When I came off the stand I'd run to the checkroom and hide behind the coats. People like Pops Whitaker from the New Yorker, Robert Sylvester, and a lot of newspaper men. At one time I used to pal around with them. I'd go to the News or something for dinner and all that. I think they thought I was a little bit wacky too. I'd get off the stand and run to the checkroom, so the checkroom girl called the owner and said, 'Listen, I can't hang up the clothes for that trio that you booked here! So she runs to the checkroom and two musicians are doing the same thing.' The bass player
WILLIAMS 152

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: and the drummer, Bill Clark and my bass player, they were running to the checkroom with me after a while. I guess they thought something bad was going to happen and I was trying to get to the checkroom. I did this for about 3 weeks and after a while Sy, Sy Baron, that was his name (he's a lovely cat) said to me, "Mary, you're going to have to come out of that checkroom." "I'm not, I'm not." So he finally coaxed me out and I sat with the people. I'd sit in the corner as if I was having a chill. It's just terrible to get away from people 6 months or a year and then go around them. You're shy and you're withdrawn. That was my first engagement and I went back again after that. I did a couple of dates and the next thing was the Hickory House. Father Woods was with me there.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: When you say he was with you there what do you mean?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: He used to go down and sit with me, see that I didn't walk out the door. I was upset, nervous I guess.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: You mentioned the fact that people were asking you to write a mass. Had you started working on that at this particular time?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, I wanted to write one but I didn't know just the type of music until St. Martin de Porres was canonized in '62 and I wrote this thing, St. Martin de Porres, dedicated to him. I tried to get a lyricist and all but I took the
WILLIAMS 153

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: lyric to Father Woods and he said, no, they didn't capture the spirit of St. Martin. So I told him, "Well, you do it." He said, "I never wrote anything in poetry in my life, Mary, and can't do it." I said, "I'll tap it out for you." I did and he wrote a very beautiful lyric, he did, he wrote it. He had never written one before. So I asked him, "Let's do a blues." He said, "O.K." I said, "I'll get some slang words from Babs Gonzales." He said, "O.K." I said, "I'll call you tomorrow night." When I called back with all this slang I said "coat"; he said "rug"; "car"; he said "short" "chorus". He knew all the words. That's how he was, you see.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: But getting back to Babs Gonzales, you know I haven't told you something about this terrific character that's so fantastic. He wrote some of the greatest books on the slang idiom. He became so abused and confused about people taking his compositions and things that he had written He used to live down the street from me and on his way to the subway he would pass here every day. He said, "Listen Mary, I've written a book." He took this book to a disc jockey... This guy used his entire book and had it published under his name, Fred Robinson. So Babs said, "Oh, that's all right," and he used to dance around. The next thing musicians were recording his compositions and what-not and he became so bitter about it till he began to go
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: around town fighting. I used to meet him and he'd say, "Lou, I'm really sick of what they're doing to me." He was so talented; he could create all these various things that he sang. I was trying to baby him. I said, "Oh, Babs, don't do that." One time he went down to the Roost - or Broadway I think it was the Roost, Rooster or something like that - and Erroll Garner was playing and he started some stuff there. They said Babs used to carry red pepper in his hands. He was under a fan and he was trying to throw this in the manager's eyes and the fan blew it back in his eyes. He was going all around town just in a bad way. So I said, "Babs, if I were you I wouldn't do that." He said "What let people take advantage of you and steal all your material and that everything?" And from that day on was the nicest guy that I've ever seen in my life. He used to get jobs for anybody that was out of work and do the craziest and nicest things for them and all of a sudden he changed, losing so much. One day I got kind of angry because somebody owed me some royalties and he met me downtown. I was puffing and blowing... and I was so mad. He said, "Oh, so you're the lady that told me to stop fighting!" But I've seen some of the material he's written and it's so different and so great. I've just heard here recently, and I've just said to myself, I'll be glad when he gets back the way he used to be.
WILLIAMS 155

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: I hope. Mary, once you went through this period of praying and being away from music and in the church, what was the reaction of the people aside from Dizzy that you knew in the jazz world, to what was happening?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Not immediately. I used to give prayers for musicians and Monk, Hal Baker, Bud Powell in the summer would meet me at the Lady of Lourdes. Mass went on at 6:30 then, I think, or 7. They'd meet me at 6 o'clock and they'd go in church with me. I'd keep them through three masses. The first time I took Monk to church, it wasn't during mass, it was in the afternoon. I said, 'Come on and meditate.' He told his wife, why don't you go with Mary? She said, 'Oh, go ahead, Monk,' so he finally made up his mind. He said, 'Why don't you go with her, Nelly?' Finally he made up his mind. He said, 'Wait a minute,' and I had a car and he stopped and went some place. I didn't watch where he had gone. He got himself a whole pint of wine or something and he drank all of it. So when we got to the church door Monk fell inside on the floor, fell out. I pulled him up and said, 'Get up, you big ape,' pulling on him and everything. See, during the afternoon there's nobody in church at all, you know, you can go and meditate. I said, 'What happened to you?' He wouldn't say anything and he sat down and he prayed and everything. But about a week later he said he thought he was going to die. (LAUGHTER)
WILLIAMS 156

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: The reason why he got the wine, he said he had never been in a church or anything like that before. He said he thought I was coming because I thought maybe he was going to die, so he went and got this wine and drank it. But I used to have a ball. I'd meet the musicians and like if anybody was hung up I'd take them into church and I'd teach them to pray, how to do the rosary beads. I used to sit in the Lady of Lourdes. I'd go to the mass in the morning, 7 o'clock mass, and sat through all the masses. I'd get out about 9 or 10. I'd come home and fix lunch for all the poor people I had in the house I was feeding. I'd go right back and meditate a couple hours and then I'd come home. I was from the house to the store to the church.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: That was your life then? When did you start the Bel Canto Foundation?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I don't know what year it was but it was during that period while I was praying.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How did it start?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I decided that I wanted to help the few - well, after comparing rock I said the few - few musicians that were using dope, jazz musicians that were using dope. I decided I'd like to help them and so I went on out on my own with a method of my own. I had success with two.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What was your method?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Prayers and music, either give them Psalms to
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: read or write something. Like I had a drummer that was on it and his wife timed him. It took him 5 minutes to go home. He'd come here 8 o'clock in the morning and I'd just keep him in the house. See, a dope addict, anyone on heroin, they're like a baby. So I'd keep them with me all day. If I had to go, I'd say, "Come on, we'll go to the Five and Ten." One time I took him to the Five and Ten and I forgot to give him breakfast. I said, oh, I hope he doesn't steal anything while we're in here. Sure enough, he told me this two or three years later. He said, "Remember when you took me to the Five and Ten. I was so hungry I was getting ready to steal some candy. I looked on the floor and saw a quarter." He bought the candy. I said, "Man, I was praying for you that you didn't steal anything." ... This guy, it must have been in his mind or something because he was cured so very fast, but later on I had to take him to someone for injections and whatnot to counteract what he was doing. The first night I had him here in the house he began to want a fix and so I said, "I just wrote a drum part." I wrote and I wrote and I said, "Dig this." He said, "Yeah." I said, "Well, play it." He had a pad, and ... He played it and he forgot. Everytime that happened I said, "Hey," and I'd write something else. That worked on him I noticed that night because it took his mind off completely... or else the staff. They gave him was so weak.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: night he didn't have anything from 8 o'clock till 12 o'clock at night. I usually sent him home around 11 or 12 and I'd call his wife and say, "Five minutes is up. Is he there?" She'd say yes. So that's how I did that.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: The other person was a dealer but they told me what they were and I kept them. Father Crowley said to me, "Listen, what you're doing is very dangerous." I said, "I don't care as long as I'm helping them, a poor person." This other one he got away from it completely.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What was the Bel Canto Foundation?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: It was a foundation to help dope addicts and alcoholics.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How did it function to do this?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Now that is something else. My lawyer said to me, "This is the strangest board I've ever seen. The president never has a board meeting or I don't know what she's doing. I think we all better leave her alone before we go to jail." The lawyer, Bill (Sousa(?)), terrific. Father Woods called him. He was a friend of Father Woods and he told him, "Please take care of Mary," and he has. He's done a lot of things he could charge me for and he's just never asked me for the money. He's gone to court and gotten me out of things, and some of my relatives. I'm sure I couldn't pay his price. I had a store front to raise money selling clothing.
WILLIAMS 159

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Where was that?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: East 29th Street was the first and I moved up here in Harlem to 1667 Amsterdam. When I'd go to the Welfare Section where you get permits to sell clothing, Mr. Rosenberg would say - they'd laugh when I'd come through the door - "Well, Bel Canto, we were down to the store and you weren't there." I said, "Business was bad and I took the clothes to Pittsburgh and sold them." He'd laugh, "Ha, ha, ha!" They'd just laugh like mad. He said, "Never in my life have I heard of any kind of a transaction with stuff like you.. When somebody comes to the store you're supposed to be there, especially from this department. I'll tell you what you do, please, before we lose our jobs here. Will you pleasego down to ( )Street and get a permit to sell second-hand clothing?" They laughed at me and that's how they got rid of me because for a whole two years they would expect me to be in the store.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Was the store just you?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: That's the only person in there.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: You collected the clothes and then you...

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I collected the clothes and then I had the store and everything. If I didn't move all these things - I had a thousand dollar dress. I had some very expensive things. Some people like John Hammond's wife had given me, and some
WILLIAMS 160

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: very wealthy people and if I got them I couldn't move them in the store. One girl, one of the cousins of the Mellons, was here - Peggy Hitchcock, she was very good to me. She gave me her trousseau. I couldn't move them. Some of the dresses were almost $700. I took them back to her. If everyone in Harlem knew what I had in the store when I moved up here they probably would have broken into it because I had $200 shoes, and oh, just things.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: How were you able to be in the store enough to sell anything?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I just stayed in the store all the time. See, I was alone, I was by myself then. I had gotten rid of all the people that I had in the house. If I picked up anything I'd go downtown and get them - Sak's Fifth Avenue or whatever, they'd send it direct to the store. Michael's, you know this rich place that sells second-hand things, they sent me boxes. Sometimes I'd pick them up somewhere. I'd do that early in the morning and then I'd stay in the store till 7 o'clock in the evening.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What finally became of the store?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I had to give it up because after I went in the Hickory House I saw no reason for me to pay $125 a month when I'm working nights. So I decided to go back to music but I didn't. I couldn't get started until the scene led up to the time when Father Peter O'Brien, a young Jesuit
WILLIAMS 161

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: priest, called me from California. He used to call me practically every week to find out what I was doing.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Where did you first meet him - the Hickory House? Where did you first meet Father O'Brien?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: It's a strange thing. Father Peter O'Brien was going to school down where Father Woods was, a young boy. See, I met him when he was 19 or 20. He was not really a friend of Father Woods' but he knew Father Woods. I happened to be playing in the Hickory House and this little young boy, happy and everything, walked in and sat at the bar. He'd come to see me often. He left and I discovered that he did know Father Woods. We became very close friends, Father Peter O'Brien and I. You know, a Jesuit priest never stops going to school. He was out in California and he called me and said, "What are you doing? You'd better get out here and do something about jazz. It's dying everywhere." I said, "I'm not going out there among those riots and burn myself up unless you come with me." He said, "I'll be back right away." So he came back and that's how we got together and I dropped the store. In the meantime I had decided to go into business. I had talked with Mr. Wells that owns the Wells Restaurant. He was always so nice to me, like he gave me money to do record dates and everything. I played in his place for him
WILLIAMS 162

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: in Harlem. I was trying to bring white patrons back to Harlem. A lot of them did come up while I was there. So I went back into his place until the same night, day, that the President was assassinated. I couldn't take it; I just came on out. I decided I wanted to go into business. He was talking to me about going into business. In the meantime he married a girl, the most beautiful girl I've ever seen in my life. She may have been a little upset because Mr. Wells was close to me and he'd always say to me, "Well, Madam Queen, what do you think about me doing so-and-so?" I guess she wanted me to not perhaps interfere with the business, so there was a disagreement there and I decided to drop it all. I lost about $12,000 of my own money in it because when I worked I'd put it right back in Bel Canto. So I just closed it off right away and let her have anything she wanted to do because it became very disagreeable, and sneaky about a lot of things and I couldn't be in that scene. I had a piano up there and I used to play in the evenings, you know, on the piano. So I took that out and I just left and just forgot about the whole thing.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: So this was what, about 1963 or '4 that you went to California with Peter?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, I've forgotten what year that was. It's been at least 8 or 9 years ago.
WILLIAMS 163

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: But in any event the first thing you did with him was when he told you to come to California?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, he came from California and he dropped everything. He was going to school out there. I said if you go out with me and he said, "I'll come back." So that's what he did. He came back here.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: And did you go to California then?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I didn't go to California with him, no. We've been out two years - that's been two years ago. He came back (?) we went down to Barney Josephson, the old night club owner of Cafe Society Uptown and Downtown. So he said he was down there feeling him out and couldn't get to him. He said, "Come on down town and talk to him." I said, "You're the one that's supposed to get the job, not me. I'm supposed to play after you get it." (LAUGHTER) I decided to go downtown with him. I was talking to Barney and I said, "Barney, put a piano over there," just like that. He said, "Oh, I have some customers here." He had some old customers that sat all day and read the paper and he said if they would hear music it would be terrible. I said, "Barney, put a piano over there." He thought about it and he said, "Go to the union and find out what kind of scale you can get." So I went to the union and I got a bigger scale for sidemen than I did for myself. That thing cost me about 3 or 4 thousand dollars. I had to save my
WILLIAMS 164

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: money for 4 weeks to pay my rent, electric light, and everything and I sat down there and played and Peter run around. For one thing all the rock places - you know that big place down there where Miles played - the Fillmore East - all the rock places closed and the kids used to come in and they were saying to their parents that they had found a new pianist and a new music. When someone came to the Cafe to tell me about it we just laughed like mad. A lot of times during that period they had a line. The kids they talked, talked, talked and when I got ready to leave, my land, they came to me and said, "Miss Williams, you're gonna really leave? Your music is so peaceful." I said, "I didn't think you were listening." So that was the beginning of our thing and we went through/and he borrowed a lot of strain money and he did a lot of things, from his parents and what-not. He's a real good friend to have.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: This was what - 2 or 3 years ago?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Two years ago.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: There's a sort of a gap between your talking about the night that the President was assassinated back in 1963. This was about 7 years later. What happened in between...?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well I was trying to record. That's when I did St. Martin de Porres when that great saint was canonized. That was '62 or '63. I would get gigs now and then.
WILLIAMS 165

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Dizzy would book me - not book me but he'd recommend me for various places. I don't guess I had over 3 or 4 jobs a year. But the strangest thing happened. I think I received more royalties than I ever received, I don't know why. I had no money coming in but it came in through friends, Lorraine, Dizzy, or royalties. Maybe somebody had sold - let's see, how much do you get, about 6 or 7 hundred dollars per (.) It goes up and down for things like that. I didn't have too much but I believe if you give away - during that period I was so stupid. I've always been like that; I'd give away my last penny and seemed like I'd find 4 times more, as much or something. I didn't have many jobs. I don't know how I existed but I did. I existed enough to help others.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: So when you weren't actually working on a job, you no longer had the Bel Canto store. What were you doing during the interim?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I decided to try to go out on my own. Really I haven't been successful in doing things except when Peter came and picked me up. I tried things and I did jobs now and then. It didn't pay enough even for me... because jazz was kind of going down then, you know, and rock was coming up. Priests and Father Woods - oh, Father Woods raised some money for me once. We were the first blacks in the Lincoln Hall Philharmonic. They were not going to have any black
WILLIAMS 166

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: opera singers in. The whole thing was prejudiced. The musicians were meeting up here in a little room in Harlem. So I called Father Woods and said, "...A lot of the musicians are having meetings up in Harlem and they're talking about Philharmonic." He said, "Break it up." I said, "I cannot break it up." He said, "Break it up! Let's try something else." So I went to the meeting. The only thing I could do was pretend I drank a little beer. I said, "I've been drinking. If you don't get out of this place we're going to fight." I tried everything else." She said, "What's wrong with you?" So she came up and she told the musicians, "Tell Lou I'm back with my music." I felt that we had a Communist in it because when the kids would speak or something, specifically to do with something that would help the thing along, there would be a big argument against it. I think he's the cat that tried to blow up pull the Statue of Liberty down. I'm not sure but I think he was. We found out later. He'd seeped in on this and everything was a big, big argument. So when she came out the whole thing broke up. I went to Father Woods and he said, "I think you ought to do something with Dizy." So Father Woods got together and he booked us in the Philharmonic himself and he'd never done anything like that before. So he got together and he did it. I told Dizy, "I think we have a thing in the Philharmonic." Dizy had a
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: 25-piece band and I did the History of Jazz, the ragtime. They said, "Why do we have to go back so far?" I said, "Well, I'm going to do the History of Jazz." He thought it was something else, you know. So we were the first in the Philharmonic as a jazz unit.
The Fundargle and
Ailey
Henry(?)
used to by a lot
MV
he just had a fit

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What brought you and Alvin Henry(?) together?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Peter, and Brother John. Peter went to all the ballets. He thinks everything I do is so great. I said, one day you're going to be disappointed. He said, you should do a ballet. He went to all the ballets trying to get me do something. After he found out that Katherine Dunham dance one of my things - I said, "Peter, I don't want to be with the ballet." He kept running around so after a while he met Brother John Sellers. John Sellers started pushing with him and the next thing I knew - well you see, Alvin Ailey is the type of person that you could tell him about a lot of things but he has to find it himself, so it seeped in and the minute it seeped in, oh my goodness, I couldn't get rid of him. "Oh, we've got to do this! Oh, I'm going to do this with you!" He went to, he just had a fit and started bragging and going on about the ballet. But Peter did that. He just kept going back because see, I had to train him. I said, "Now I've

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: been away a long time. It's just like me coming out fresh but you have a better chance because I did have a little name when I stopped." So I told him some things to do and he caught on fast on his own.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: To get back to Alvin Ailey and the mass, did you have to adapt things for that or how did you work that?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: He adapted his ballet to the mass. He's working on it now. He's going to do some of the things over. He's not satisfied. Neither am I because the best thing he has there is the "Our Father" prayer and the "People in Trouble". See, I explained the story to him. "People in Trouble" was written for these people that were rioting in Harlem. They weren't hurting anybody but the black people of Harlem in all the black districts, because when they bombed people out instead of getting them out in a different way, there were some older people in Harlem that had gone to the little stores for years and years and didn't know where to go and they were too sick to walk 5 or 6 blocks for things like that and then they began to rob us. That was written for people in trouble, children in pain, too mean to care, too weak to share, work so hard trying to find a brother, became impatient, now we hate each other. Trying to find a brother, if you walk down the street and somebody say, "Hi, sister! Hi, brother!", that would infuriate me because they come in here a couple of times and
part explaining. Now The
WILLIAMS 169

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: stole my things. I said, "Man, the least thing I would do if I was going to steal something and hated whites so bad, I'd go down there and get it." I said, "You could be stealing from people with money and they still haven't got enough money for you to do that." I told him the story of it and he did a good thing on that; and also "Lazarus" is really terrific. I like "Lazarus".

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: But the thing is in process of changing?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, they say it takes Alvin about a year to finish off one of his ballets.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: It's a finishing process?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: As a result of doing that, has anything come out of it for you?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: W: I'm telling you the truth. He said, "It's like you said, you've been away a long time. This is going to help ." I said, "I don't think so." It did circulate my name a great deal because all the write-ups were sensational. But it didn't get me to working night clubs. See, I'm a jazz pianist, a jazz arranger. It didn't work anything that way but it gave me recognition among people that didn't know anything about me, in another field, the ballet, see, that would never come to a night club. But as far as getting work, no. Peter had to work like a dog to get me work.
WILLIAMS 170

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: There are no commissions coming from other ballet companies?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No. No, see they had flops with other jazz things. I guess they were afraid to try. I mean they got bad write-ups. But the mass they say is really successful, even when they do it on the tape in other cities.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Do you consider yourself primarily a jazz pianist rather than a composer?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, by all means. Jazz is my thing - I mean, piano is the thing but.......I gained merit from graces to write.) I didn't /Start to write until Kansas City. I told you about the scene where Andy and I used to sit all night taking down ideas, came back and I had them arranged. That was like a hobby with me then because I used to do it for practically nothing. I never made any money doing that nor have I ever been hired just as an arranger except when I traveled with Duke, oh 6 months in Canada and all around, when Harold Baker joined. No, I don't consider myself a composer-arranger. That's part of it but the basic thing is the piano because I can do so many things on the piano, switching and changing and doing things. I may not have the greatest technique but I can do things on piano that arranging and writing is secondary. My Arranging and composing comes while I'm playing piano. All the records I recorded
WILLIAMS 171

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: with Andy Kirk and didn't get paid for, I lost them all because I didn't have them copyrighted. I just sat down and played and my arranging and composing flows from playing.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What do you do now to protect yourself against losing a..... ?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I think of a melody, don't tell anybody that it isn't copyrighted. I think of a melody similar to that but it's very bad for me to do that because if I have a bass player that can hear me and follow me, practically all night long, I'll start to compose. It's bad that I do things like that, but now what I do, I'll start a little thing, a little melody and get a copyright and then work from that. That blocks me a little bit. It doesn't really flow as freely as something, you know, like the "Zodiac Suite" when I did that, I wrote two of them and I couldn't write any more. The thing I was telling you about, that sometimes arrangers run dry. I was on WNEW introducing them in one week and Canada Lee was with me a couple of times. You know what happened? I couldn't write any more so I had to record my program and the rest of the suite I composed them while I was playing. I'm at my best composing that way.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: That's the end of this one.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Mary, when you began praying, what were some of the things that happened?
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Well, I don't know, I prayed so very hard. One thing I was very happy that I became Catholic because their liturgy and what they preach teach you about everyday life if you catch on to it. You're never unhappy if you pay attention to what you read and what's said in the Gospels. One thing that happened with me when I was praying, I remember reading little pamphlets - every thing in the church I'd sit and read it and I never studied so hard in all my life, as far as reading. I'd pray for the souls in purgatory. You know what actually happened with me, I prayed so hard for priests and later on a lot of them came up with me. I don't know why I was praying so hard for them but most of my prayers - and I used to light candles for them in the church, you know. I felt that lighting a candle was not the candle itself God was doing the work and I'd light candles just for the days that I was doing a Novena. I had a dream once that I was worried about lighting a candle. I had a dream that Buck Clayton and all of them were sitting up in the balcony and God showed me that it was just a light that was being shined down on them for their soul and all that and it wasn't superstition to fool around with candles. I used to pray so hard for the souls and if anybody died till when anyone died, they actually came to the house. I had an aunt that died and she was in chains. I spoke to her and asked her and she came back to me in a dream and said to me
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: that they chained her down like that in a house. Well, they did. People took her house from her and just had her in a bed and she wasn't being fed and a lot of things. Levy, the owner, one of the brothers of Birdland got killed and I called Father Woods and I said to him, "There's a man here from Birdland - " - I used to call him Father - the silliest thing - that's what he and Lorraine used to laugh about over the phone - and I picked up the News, somebody came to the house or something and brought the News in and Levy, they read where he'd gotten killed. He'd come to the house for a prayer. People like that, after a while I was so polluted with friends or things dying or getting killed that I began to go to church and get those brown candles for the dead. I became frightened here in the house, you know, and I'd get brown candles and burn them for the dead in the house. After a while I got rid of that completely, after I became Catholic. This was during the period when I was taking my instructions. Strange things like that were happening to me.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: There was another guy, a newspaper man. I can't remember his name, with King Features. He was a very good friend of mine. He used to come and take me out and Peter (ran up?) Rabbit - well, this hasn't been too long ago and he was telling me about his death or something. I said, "He was
WILLIAMS 174

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: here last night; he came to me in a dream." Even if that happens to me now and somebody dies, I'll go and have a Novena done on them. All that opened up since I was praying.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Once you got back into music and were not praying as constantly as you had been, was there a change in anything?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, there was a little change because you see, what I was trying to tell you, that ESP was in my music and the more music I played and the more jobs, it's not so much now, just a little. Maybe once or twice a year or three times a year. See, it's getting back into the music again, but it was on the outside. That's the reason why I told you that story so you'd know what had happened. See I had very good - I was better than Dixon, that woman in Washington, but I didn't know it; see, it was in my music.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Somehow it's going back in.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: It's going back in. I'm seeing less and less of these things but if anything important - I had a flash about 2 or 3 months ago. I've forgotten what it was. A strange thing used to happen to me too, say for instance I've never been to your house and all of a sudden maybe one day I could see you walking into your house, or I could see you. You know? That used to happen, things like that. They were just terrible for a while. I could hear people talking about me. Lorraine and Dizzy were saying something one day - this was before I began really playing.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: They were saying one day, "Has she given it to you/yet?" I was coming down the hall and I heard Lorraine say, "No." He said, "Well, I gave her some bla-bla..." I had a pocketbook that Hazel had brought back from Paris and it was worth, oh, $300, a beaded pocketbook. She gave it to me to raise money, Hazel Scott. Lorraine liked it but I didn't know whether I should give it - I wanted to give it to Lorraine. So that night I called Father and I said - and Father said, "Yes, they're your friends, Mary." Lorraine called me and she said, "Guess what? I was just talking to Dizzy about you. Dizzy asked if you still had the pocketbook. I said Mary's not going to give that pocketbook; Mary's honest and she knows she has to raise money with it and I don't have the money to buy it." So what I finally did, I returned it to Hazel because I couldn't - it was new, a beautiful pocketbook and I couldn't raise money.
and the Jazz Festival.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Tell me about Cardinal Wright in Pittsburgh.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes, that is something else. Father Woods got in touch with him. See, I went to Pittsburgh, I was back and forth to Pittsburgh for two years. Father called me one day and said, "Why don't you come back to New York to play your music. I'll tell you what to do. Get in touch with (he was a Bishop then) Bishop Wright." He wired Bishop Wright; A friend of mine, A.W. Stubble, wired him.
WILLIAMS 176

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: And so Father Woods had gotten in touch with me to help me. He saw me right away. So I had never been in front of a Bishop and I felt so strange. I just looked at him, you know, with all these colors on and everything. He said, "What can I do for you?" I said, "Jazz, jazz. There won't be any jazz after while." He looked at me and I told him about mother. He had confirmed them and all these people and he loved her, because he has - he does many, many favors for black people. He cleaned up Wiley Avenue where the dope addicts and all that was and he just does a lot of favors. I understood that he gave a man $12,000 for a project and the Ku Klux burned a cross on him before he went to Europe because he did that, you know, it was publicized. So he threw up his hands and he said, "We'll put on a festival for you." He must have gotten somebody least to put up at 50 to 75 thousand dollars because the musicians cast tossed $25,000 dollars to go in. So they did this festival every year. I got out of it because I got hold of George Weir to do it and I didn't think I should go down as a producer of a thing like that. I just let him take it all over himself, you know. I did two or three of the concerts, then I got out of it because I didn't want to wear myself out in Pittsburgh.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: What was wrong with Pittsburgh?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: It was a pretty tough town. The reason I went
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: was because that is not an artistic town. Sometimes you can be lucky enough to start something up that's never happened in an old rusty broken-down town like that.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: What's happened with the festival? Are they still going on with it?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: ... They failed in it so they got George Wein (Wing?) back over there again. The Gulf Oil was sponsoring one cat over there and it wasn't too good.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Then there was another period, wasn't there, Mary, in 1968 when you went to Copenhagen and Rome?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Oh, yes, that was wonderful. I went over to open a new club of Baron Timme Rosencranz, a real baron...

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: This was in Copenhagen?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Copenhagen, yes. Well, I asked her that I wanted to go. Things like that happened to me. I didn't know that he was sick and I just thought I was going over to help him. It was a nice engagement except that I didn't work for about 2 months. They were still building the club. It was a very nice engagement.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: And then you went to Rome after that?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I went through Rome but I had been to Rome - yes, I think that's when we put on the first jazz mass but it didn't really go through. They had newspapers out from everywhere, from all other countries and everywhere else,
WILLIAMS 178

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: because there had never been a jazz mass in Rome. What they did, what really stopped it, the Italians like to be told what they're going to do but everybody was afraid to tell them because it would have taken them another year to say yes. So they said, well, let's do it fast. It would have gone through but the girl at the Vatican radio caught us or played it smart. She came in one afternoon while we were rehearsing and said, "Guess what, I just broadcast the mass right on the lap of the Pope." The Pope listened to the radio at certain times. Everybody said, "Oh, my goodness, oh, oh." And so they told the Cardinal not to do it. Yes, because they didn't like people coming to their country like that, doing things. So it was done as a concert after the mass.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: As things are now, Mary, are you active in the church?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yes, I'm very active but I don't go to church every day. I go Sundays or Saturday mass. I used to go every day.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Why have you cut down?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Most of the thing is going into my work now and I didn't have anything to do then when I was doing that. Then that is too much anyway to go every day. It's all right. It's good if you can do it but then there's a chance
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: of you not going at all through going every day, you get sick of it. What I was doing, when it was time I guess for me to cut out on it, it happened.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: In other words, that period when you were going every day, you don't feel that you overdid it?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, because I needed the strength. The world can destroy me - not really, I'm a strong woman through being around men, but I could really be bent badly, you know, being in the company of people and things like that. I think what it does is to put an aura around me and to strengthen me to do further work for God.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: You mentioned being around men all the time. You spent your whole life really in a man's world.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: On his lap and in his world, yet I'm feminine. You know, some women they change their sex after they've been around men like that all the time, but being around men gave me, you know, like Monk said once when he was here at the house and Nelly, his wife was talking to him. He says, "I won't listen to silly women. Mary's the only woman I'll take any advice from." See, they taught me their trend of thought and their way of thinking. I'd rather gossip in front of a man because it really isn't gossip. You're talking to have fun, you know, it's something to laugh about. But if I did that with a woman
WILLIAMS 180

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: it would be all over the country and it would be gossip, they just sound different. Now I feel I'm out of place... I know some very good women musicians but I'm just out of place with them. If I had to do a battle or anything with them I wouldn't play nothing because I do have something like this happen, that they're not my equal, and that's very bad. That could be prejudice or something's the matter. I never want to be prejudiced or something like that, but there's something else, John, something like they're still thinking this way and I don't think that way. I withdraw. If I had a contest or had to do something with another woman, she'd win; I'd give it to her because she doesn't matter to me that much. I never thought about breaking that because it isn't important. I don't harm anybody through it.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Except you wouldn't give it to them on piano, would you?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I'd let them have anything they want. It doesn't matter because they're not my equal in thinking. They can be most intelligent or anything else, I have something that has been embedded in me through good strong men, and men that were real good men and you don't find them today.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Did you have trouble being accepted as a musician by another women?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Never, that's the thing about it, that's the
WILLIAMS 181

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: reason why I don't understand - never in my life. When Earl Hines had his little band and was playing for afternoon things in Pittsburgh, the boys after the session would come and get me. It's always been that. They'd come and get me and take me to play and anything, if I was playing wrong, they showed me. I was just like one of the boys.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: You have always worked with black music, right or not?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Well, what do you mean when you say that?

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: This is what you've been playing.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: That's what I like but I haven't always done that. I learned the classics through the set player. I had to get my other 50¢ a week.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Would you have liked to have played classical music?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: No, I don't think so. A concert pianist told me - Robert Harris been trying to get me to do that. He heard me when I was really in good form at the Hickory House. You know, the same reason I won't play commercial rock. Commercial rock makes you corny. Jazz pushes off, you know, like an eighth note tied/over to a quarter in the next bar. It pushes off, it goes easy, like this, but rock, 1-2-3-4-bop, like that... I don't want to get stiff like that. I had a drummer and a bass player to kind of stiffen me out a couple of times. I played with them a while and was kind
WILLIAMS 182

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: of happy I got away from them. But that's the reason why I'm afraid if I played the classics and went all the way with it I'd lose the feeling of the greatest (now I'm not putting the classics down) - the greatest music that I think has ever been -'cause I can write the classics and everything here. I can write that too you know, once I get into it. One day - my husband, he was kind of mean, said, "You better save your money 'cause you'll be old." Here I'm 22 - "and you won't be able to play." I said, "I'll be playing when I'm 100 years old." And I believe so. That's from here, you know, because I'll be playing because he made a dirty remark. I'm about 22 and he's going to tell me I'm not going to play, save your money, and all that. But I like classical music and as I told you before I get my inspirations from it. But I don't want to go into it. I had 5 Juilliard pianists that come here for lessons and I had to let them all go because they taught them with their hands up here. Jazz you hug the keys. Like when the phone rang Hilton called me, Hilton Ruiz, I helped him, piano. He was doing all this with his hands up too high. I said, "You better drop your hands down on those keys." But probably with his fingers like that, he was fast.
(PHONE RINGS)

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: About kids playing.
WILLIAMS 183

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Oh, about the position of the hands.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: You see, that's something else. Now, I'm going to play classical music, I'm sure, before I die, because ever since a little kid I wanted to do that. But I'm so involved with this and these other things that I like about jazz, see. I'm going to write some classical things and play them. The greatest concert pianist, Robert Harris - I don't think you met him but he's usually at my parties - he teaches over at Juilliard and if you ever want to know the piano and learn how to play the piano, get to him. I hurt my fingers and I went to him and he gave me exercises to do, just not on the keys but other things to do. His teacher was the teacher of Clyde - what's his name - that went to Europe, the young kid that went to Europe -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Van Cliburn.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Van Cliburn, yes, and so he is sensational in teaching.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Is it really possible to shift over to classical music after -

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Very possible. I had a pupil here and she was playing Bach and I had to teach her how to memorize and how to really play it. In about 5 minutes I was playing 4 bars. You understand? You know what classical music is - something that somebody's written and you do exercises on it in your woodshed and play it. But jazz is difficult. You think what
WILLIAMS 184

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: they've written and you have to play it then. So why should I want to play something somebody else has written? When I was a kid and my principal got all these teachers and all these things for me, I couldn't play Rachmaninoff and any of those things. I had to improvise in it. I couldn't play it the way the music was. I can't play music - when I'm reading, I have to improvise then. I hear it and see it, you know. I'm improvising then; I can't play it the way it's written. I never could play anything note for note so it wouldn't be good for me.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Playing classical music?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Yes.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: This I think would be your problem, because classical music is based on the fact that you play it as written; you interpret it but you play it as written.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Right, right.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Whereas you don't play that way.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: No, I don't play that way at all. But a lot of musicians can. Dizzy can; he can play note for note and things, but I can't. I have to improvise or add something.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: At this point what is it that you want to do that you're not doing, aside from playing classical music?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: I'm doing everything I want to do now except there are certain things I want to do, reach, go as high as I can now for the sake of others and not for Mary Lou (or to die, uh.)
WILLIAMS 185

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: Go as high as you can in what sense?

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: In the music field, I mean reach the pinnacle for public relations and get a lot of things going, because I cannot help the poor if I haven't got any strength in myself or any power to do so. I found that out. I can feed a lot of mouths if I got strength to go to somebody and ask for it. The world is still based on phony things and so what I'm trying to do is to do as many things like - such things as that street being named after me but I think I was cut down a little bit. It didn't leave Kansas City. (LAUGHTER) Isn't that something? The biggest thing that ever happened in the world of music and it was put up on a high level and everything and not one public relations man was there that could spread it all over the world. I've never heard of such a thing. If you were there and saw what went down - I don't think they knew what they were doing or they didn't exploit it right. That was a big deal. That was the biggest deal you ever heard of.

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: I think you should mention for the sake of the tape -

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: What?

53571.speaker: I:
53571.text: For the sake of the tape that we should mention what you're retalking about.

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: The Charlie Parker Foundation and the streets that were named after such artists as Ella Fitzgerald, Count Basie,
WILLIAMS 186

53571.speaker: W:
53571.text: Bennie Moten, Mary Lou Williams, and Dizzy Gillespie, five of us. But it was the way in which they did it. It was a big deal. I know they must have spent a fortune doing it, had a party and Gloria Vanderbilt, her husband, and the Hallmark people were sponsoring the Charlie Parker Foundation.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Were they the sponsors for it?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Yeah, they own practically Kansas City and this Hotel they built, it opened the same day that I got there. The governor, the mayor, and oh, just a big thing. Duke Ellington was there, Count Basie with his band, but no big exploitation on the outside of Kansas City. They raised a lot of money and they charged about $50 a plate. Had 2 or 3 nights of that.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: That was a big deal and what's it called, Charlie Parker Houses?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Charlie Parker Foundation.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: But it's a housing development, and these are the streets in the housing development and the housing development is named after Charlie Parker.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Right. /We were trying to get you to go there.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Oh, they were after me to go.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: None of the newspaper men - Leonard Feather had to do something and the guy with the New Yorker and all the newspaper men should have been there. Look at the Newport Jazz Festival. They all went there at one time or another.
WILLIAMS

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: But none of them came from out of the -

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: From a distance. I want to get the argument about how these things break. How do you feel now? You've lived your life -

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: But I don't feel that I have. I don't know if I'm old, white, or black.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: You haven't finished it. It's still going on, sure. But how do you feel about how it's worked out for you so far?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Beautiful. I'd live it again, go over the same things, one-nighters with Andy Kirk, starvation, and many, many things that happened. I'd go over it again.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: If you went over it again do you feel that you would do it any better than you did it this time?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: I think we all would if we experienced a lot of things. We'd know how to do them, but I think we'd do worse if we haven't experienced anything. But if I have experienced something and had to go over it again I think I'd do it better.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: Most of us would. Well, any thing more you want to say?

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: Not right now. I'll remember something when you get home.

53571.speaker: I
53571.text: We'll pick it up later then.

53571.speaker: W
53571.text: O.K.

ABBEY LINCOLN
NEA Jazz Master (2003)
INTERVIEWEE: ABBEY LINCOLN (AUGUST 6, 1930 – AUGUST 14, 2010)
INTERVIEWER: SALLY PLAXSON
REPOSITORY: ARCHIVES CENTER, NATIONAL MUSEUM OF AMERICAN HISTORY, SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION DESCRIPTION: TRANSCRIPT, 68 PAGES

Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.speaker: SALLY PLAXSON
Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.text: So, Abbey Lincoln, it's great to have yet another chance to talk with you about your life.

Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.speaker: ABBEY LINCOLN
Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.text: You, too, Sally.

Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.speaker: SALLY PLAXSON
Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.text: Because it's always -- even though it's our third interview, I always learn so much more when we talk. I'm always newly inspired.

Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.speaker: ABBEY LINCOLN
Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.text: Thank you.

Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.speaker: SALLY PLAXSON
Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.text: I thought we could start right from the beginning and just work our way through which is not terribly original, but I think it's the way we should do it. Let's start with Chicago, but I'd like to even look at something that we haven't talked about much before. Some of the prehistory of your family and background of your parents, and you were born in Chicago, but how far back can you trace the family history?

Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.speaker: ABBEY LINCOLN
Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.text: Mama was the storyteller at home and she told us about our grandparents and our great-grandparents and she told us about our fathers' grandparents, and in the autobiography that I'm writing, she wrote the first part of the book, 38 pages,

Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.speaker: ABBEY LINCOLN
Abbey-Lincoln-Transcription-2020.text: and she told everything about -- I mean, she told about the life that we lived before I was born. My grandfather was named Charles Coffey and he was a slave until he was 14 and his mother was named Ann Carter and she was a slave, I guess all her life, and she brought five or nine children. One time, mama said it was nine when she got a little older. I think it was five boys she had. Probably by an Irishman or a man who was like an octoroon. He was a slaver anyway, and when slavery was declared illegal, they sent her out of the house with a dime and a couple of blankets and they walked across Missouri and several of them had tent time and ragtime, like that. My mother lived in abandoned street cars with my father and my grandfather and my grandmother because my father -- my grandfather, mama used to complain about it a lot, had lost his zest for achieving anything. Also, I mean, there were awful things that she remembered that he did. He was a degraded man in some ways. I asked her if she thought it was because of slavery and she said some people are just born low, but I know better now, you know. My mother's mother was a child. She was -- there were 21 children. Her father was an African. Mama said he was never a slave. His name was Roberts, Henry Roberts, but he didn't have an African name, and his wife was named Katherine, and she said Katherine was probably an Indian. She had long hair and she was pale-skinned, she said, because they didn't let them have black women then, and they had 21 children, and my grandmother was a school teacher. She met my grandfather on a boat, one of those gambling boats. They were total opposites, and my father, she told us that his father was mostly Indian and he had some African, but his name was Wooldridge, which is an English name, right? And he went to jail for killing two men, and I think he served some time in Pittsburgh, and my grandmother's name was Nellie, Nellie Wooldridge, who gave birth to my father, Alexander, who was an only child and a genius. He probably would have been a singer, but he opted to be a family man, and they had the same problems that people have today in marriage.
