Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You were working through combinations of notes at the keyboard, trying to hear what sounded right to you, and you would bring those to the gig.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Exactly.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Tell me about the formation of the octet. How did that . . .?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Right there in Milhaud’s class.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: In terms of performing, my understand is that between 1947 and 1949, the octet had only three paying gigs.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: But did you also perform – did you get together informally to play and practice?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah. And once in a while, somebody will say, “Oh, but I heard you at University of California, Berkeley.” It’s a gig I forgot. So maybe there were four or five. But there weren’t many. At Mills College, Marines Memorial in San Francisco, College of Pacific in Stockton, University of California, Berkeley.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I’m told that your father, after hearing a concert by the octet, once told a newspaper writer, “That was the damndest bunch of notes I ever heard.” Is that true?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Noise.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: “Bunch of noise I ever heard.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah. He said that, and he meant it. I told him he was the best critic who ever heard me.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Did you have a sense at that time that the music you were doing had commercial potential? What were – did you have – here you are. You’re doing very experimental music. A few years later you’re famous. Did you anticipate that at all, or envision that happening?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah, to the point where I would justify the hardship I was putting my family through. I would in complete confidence sometimes question my wife whether this was correct or not, knowing that even if she said no, I was going to still do it, but I wanted to know if she were ready to give up. I’ve seen too many times where a love affair would break up over the musician devoting too much time to what he was doing, or the husband and wife – I’ve seen many [ ] “If you don’t give up your drive in music, I think we’ll have to get a divorce.” I’ve seen that close up, with guys that are working for me. “Either come home or divorce.” With Paul Desmond, it was with the understanding that Paul would become the greatest saxophonist and his wife would become the greatest actress. They split up, and they were going to come back together. It can work that way. It’s strange how you’ve got to have somebody that really understands and is willing to sacrifice almost everything – a roof over your head, even.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: In terms of timing – let me know Dave – my thought is that we can go another 15 minutes today. Is that all right?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Sure.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: March 1949 your octet performed at the Marines Memorial Auditorium. This is almost a very important historic event, I think, in the history of jazz and modern jazz and West Coast jazz. How did this come about? Were there other acts on the bill? How did you get this venue? What are your recollections of it?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Technically, the octet should have been called something like the workshop ensemble. It wasn’t under my name, because we were all equals as far as talent goes. Again, Iola will know the man’s name who wanted to produce us like the octet. We ran into him recently someplace. I should never forget him, but sometimes I forget people’s

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: names. I remember a lot about him. He came to my house and said he’d like to do a concert with the octet, but it had to have my name on it. So I told the guys in the group, we will have to use my name or we can’t have the concert. What do you want to do? They said, take the concert. After the concert . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Was that at the Marines Memorial Concert?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Okay. That was that engagement.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: But I want you to check this whole story with Iola. After the concert I think Jimmy Lyons went to the head of NBC. Maria Corbin – check these names – was the head of classical music at NBC. She went to the concert. They both went to the head of NBC and said, you should do a program with this group. One’s the head of jazz – Jimmy – and one’s the head of classical music for NBC. So the guy’s thinking it over, and said okay. Then he said, “But we can’t afford an octet. Can you do it with a trio?” That’s how the trio got born, from the octet.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: At this point in time, you are doing a type of modern jazz that sounds very different from what anyone else is doing. When I listen to those octet recordings, they just sound unique. They don’t sound like anything else. At the same time [ ] mostly back East with Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker, Bud Powell, [Thelonious] Monk, Lennie Tristano – how aware were you of this? How much did you listen to it? Did it influence you? It seems like there’s these two different styles of modern jazz.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I think you’re influenced by everything you’ve heard, and you can’t not hear Dizzy and Charlie Parker. After all, I toured with Charlie. When you play at Birdland, in those days, Dizzy’s there, and Charlie.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: When did you first hear that music, though? Probably when you got out of – after the war?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah. I sure didn’t hear it during the war. I was very removed. Then when I started hearing it, I thought it was great, but I wanted to do what I did, and it was fine if they did what they did. There was no law against each of us, or every guy, doing what he wants to do musically.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let me ask just one more question, and then we’ll wrap up today. At the time you began working with the octet and the trio, San Francisco was seen more as a dixieland type of town, Lu Watters and later Turk Murphy and all that. Were there other people doing really modern, adventurous jazz in San Francisco that influenced you, or were you

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: really – how did you relate to the rest of the jazz scene there? Did you have many interactions with these dixieland people?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I liked – one time we were in the car, driving down to play in Los Angeles. The kids were up behind the seat in the coupe. Two of them could lie down up there, Iola and I in the front. As we drove down the road – I think it was near Stanford University that I said – excuse me. We were talking about Lu Watters and the . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Lu Watters and the dixieland scene in San Francisco.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: And who was the other?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I mentioned Turk Murphy.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Turk Murphy. I said, “Turk Murphy. Look, there’s a sign in front of that nightclub. Turk Murphy plays there.” My little son, Darius, said, “Stop. We should hear Turk Murphy.” I said, “What do you know about Turk Murphy?” He goes, [Brubeck sings a melody popularized by Murphy]. I said, “How could you . . .?” He said, “You’ve got a Turk Murphy recording at home.” Do you remember that song?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Sure.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s the way he was. From the time he was little, he remembered everything.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Why don’t we stop it here. We’ve covered all the way up to the start of the trio. That will give us tomorrow. We can – we made it up to 1950, more or less.
[recording interrupted]

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: This is Ted Gioia. It’s August 7th, 2007. This is the second day of the oral history with Dave Brubeck conducted by the Smithsonian Institution as part of their program to conduct oral histories with NEA Jazz Masters. We are at Chris Brubeck’s house in Wilton, Connecticut. This will be the second and final day of our oral history. Dave, yesterday we finished talking about the octet. I now want to talk to you about some smaller combos you had at the time. I’d like to start with a group called the Three D’s, which I believe first played at a place called El Baracho and then at the Geary Cellar in San Francisco. Can you tell me how this group came about and what kind of music it played?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The Three D’s was composed of Darrell Cutler, who was from Stockton, California, and at the University – College of Pacific at the same time I was. We worked in Stockton as undergraduates. He went on into the Marines and was a Marine aviator and

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: squadron leader. Very sharp guy in every way. So he and I were friends before the war, and after the war we got together again. That’s one D. Don Rattle, also from University – College of Pacific, from Stockton, is the second D. He’s still alive, living in Santa Cruz. The third D is Dave Brubeck. That group grew out of the friends at Stockton.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There was a vocalist that sometimes joined the group, Francis Lynne. Is that correct?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Francis Lynne.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: This is unusual, for you to be in a group with a singer. Did you play differently to back up a singer? Or would this be the same kind of experimental stuff you were doing with the octet or trio?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: This would be all popular songs.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You were playing standards.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s it. Yeah. Francis just sent me her new recording, which is very good. She’s married to Johnny Coppola, the trumpet player who is still working in the San Francisco area, but he spent much of his life as either lead [trumpeter] or jazz [trumpet soloist] with Kenton or Woody Herman or – almost any group you can think of wanted him. He’s a San Francisco musician.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: One night Paul Desmond comes to see the Three D’s. He comes home that night. He tells his wife that he had heard a piano player who was a genius. So this was his first encounter with you. What is your first recollection of Paul? Can you tell me about your first meeting with him?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You really want to know the first?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yes I would.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I was on my way overseas in the infantry. Dave Van Kreidt, who had come to live in the bomb shelter at the College of Pacific – unannounced one day, I came back from school and there in the cellar was Dave Van Kreidt on one of the rusty old beds. He’d moved in without asking anybody. What he did was visit classes that he liked. He wouldn’t register. But Dr. Bodley lived across the street, and he’d take private lessons. [ ] He was close friends with Paul Desmond. During the war, Kreidt would write to me and say, you should be in this band. He’d describe the band at the Presidio in San Francisco. Pete Rugolo was in another part of the Presidio, and my old drummer, Joe Dodge, was there.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Anyway, when I’m on leave, knowing I’m going overseas, Kreidt set up an audition for me to get into that band. So I came and played. I was to play with some of the musicians. Paul Desmond had been picked to be one of the people that would play with me. There were a few others – Dave Van Kreidt. They would pass judgment on me. The first tune we played I think was a blues in G, and I started it out in G in the left hand and B-flat in the right hand, and Paul said, “Wigsville. Those nutty changes.” He called me – later on he called me Surly Sue and other words, and said I had a purple Army jacket on, which I don’t believe, but he swore that I was one of the most radical guys he’d ever seen. I didn’t get into that band. It would have been wonderful not to go overseas, because I was classified as a rifleman, and not the happiest future ahead. That’s my first encounter with Paul. He loved to elaborate on, “Who is this crazy man?”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let me ask you about another person that you met probably around this same time: Jimmy Lyons. He became a very important advocate for your music. How did that come about?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: When I was – the first place that the Three D’s played was right in Stockton . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Is that so?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . in a nightclub. From there we moved to San Francisco, to El Baracho.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: And then the Geary Cellar.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Then the Geary Cellar.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Okay. I didn’t know that.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The Geary Cellar was under the Geary Theater. NBC was around the block, in the same block, their main studios, and Jimmy was broadcasting every night. I can’t remember meeting at the Geary Cellar, but apparently he came in. Then when we played the Marines Memorial, he came to that concert. Ralph Gleason came to that concert and really gave us a bad review.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Ralph Gleason gave you a bad review.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Oh yeah. He was good at that, at giving me bad reviews, because he was moldy fig at that point. A highly intelligent guy. A good writer. He gradually changed his tune, because he was up against too many people that were approving of what I was doing. But what really changed him was The Real Ambassadors at the Monterey Jazz

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Festival. Everybody that was at that concert that night thinks it was a hallmark concert for Monterey, and highly emotional [ ] Louis Armstrong in a whole different light. But I got away from what you were asking me.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: About you meeting Jimmy Lyons. You said he came and heard you at the Geary Cellar and at the Marines Memorial.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There he decided to have us do a show, and eight people were too many for NBC, but they would do it as a trio. That’s where I think Jimmy Lyons and I started getting more friendly and knowing each other. I’d appear a lot on his show. In fact if you’ve got the old octet record, Jimmy Lyons is narrating How High the Moon. So you know that he was involved. Then the classical – Maria Corbin was very impressed with the writing of the octet, considering it classical. So we right away were crossing between the jazz and the classical, which we were trying to do. When we played a concert, we’d divide it into three sections: one would be classical pieces that we’re playing; two would be jazz pieces that we composed or arranged; and the third, a jazz session, which would be quite free. That’s our format for concerts. We would have done that at Marines Memorial. So you could see, if we were doing something like Dave Van Kreidt’s Fugue on Bop Themes, that crosses over between bop and classical, but it’s a serious fugue that Milhaud would have looked at and said – I remember him saying, “This is a very good fugue,” and that’s in our fugue class. So it grew right out of Milhaud’s class. There’s a whole great amount of music that was lost when Kreidt took the octet book to Australia, when he moved there. He had it in a garage that was flooded. I’ve tried and tried and tried – even if it’s got ink all running, we could put it together – but they won’t cooperate, the sons and relatives that could have done me a great favor and sent that back after Kreidt died. So we lost so many classical compositions and jazz compositions. If we hadn’t recorded, we’d have nothing. Bill Russo’s arranger-copyist – Bill wanted us to play in Chicago. We said we had no music. Russo talked with him. They said this man that works for Bill Russo will listen to the recording and write it all down.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: This was for the Chicago Jazz Festival. Neil Tesser was the one. Do you know Neil? The writer.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Jazz writer. Sure.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Neil called me up and said that the octet was the most quintessentially perfect group in jazz, it needed to be featured, and could we do it? I told him the story: we had no music, but we have a recording. He said, “But there’s a recording.” I said, “Yeah.” He said, “I know the perfect guy to transcribe it, Jeff Levinson.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Didn’t he work [ ]

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So I contacted Jeff. We sent him a tape. The music started to come to me a week before the festival. This was in August of 2001. I looked at this, and the very first thing I saw was a Bill Smith arrangement of What is This Thing Called Love? in E-major. Bill is a very creative person, but he’s also extremely practical and lazy when it comes to solos. He’s not going to write a solo for himself that he’s going to have to play in F-sharp. So I called him up. I said, “Bill, what did you write This Thing Called Love?? What key?” “E­ flat.” I looked at every other piece. Every piece was off by a half-step because of the tape speed, which Jeff never would have known. He’s transcribing. I am frantically now trying to fix everything. This is early stages of the computer. It’s taken us some a couple – there’s still some wrong notes in Dave’s arrangement of Just the Way You Look Tonight, which we just cannot find it. The performance was over the Labor Day weekend in August [sic: September] of 2001. Dave was incredible, because he set this whole thing up with the audience in terms of World War II, coming back, everything that took place. Our world all changed – because he brought Pearl Harbor in on it, and our world changed 12 days later.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So that’s the only music we have.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It’s a tragedy.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Why did I think Bill Russo?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It’s confusing because of cross-references, but this was Neil Tesser. We did it – we’ve done it at Avery Fisher, and we got the greatest single review we ever got in the New York Times. Lew Soloff was the trumpet player. Just before we went on stage, Wynton [Marsalis] came back stage. He’s looking around. He’s going, like, “Lew. You’ve got music in your hand. Have you been practicing?” Lew said, “Wynton, this is the hardest music I’ve ever played in here, in my life.” He said, “I’m going along. It’s all fine. It’s all easy. I turn a page, and suddenly I’m doing a solo in 12-tone.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I can believe that. I think to this day no-one has ever done music like the octet. I listen to something like Playland at the Beach or . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The other interesting thing on this composition is that – why is Cannery Row so incredibly effective? It’s because Dave uses minimalist writing which all came from the octet. The hardest damn thing in working on the octet music is there’s no place to hide. Just the Way You [inaudible], You’ve got this counterpoint between alto and trumpet.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Every note is important.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Every note.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Can you imagine these New York guys saying, “Where’d you get these musicians?” Bill Smith came and played live in New York. Their mouths dropped open. I heard one guy say, “Where’s he been all my life?” You remember that?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: These were top guys – number one guys.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Lew Soloff says it all, right? Rondo is the piece that he was talking about, which is, it’s very nice, it’s Dave’s piece, it’s just – then you turn the page and the next thing, you’ve got a solo in 12-tone.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I think I got you off the subject.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah, but it’s an interesting topic, because the octet music is very important, and I still don’t think it’s as widely heard as it should be, because it’s unique. It really is. I don’t think – people talk about what Miles was doing, but what you were doing is just worlds apart. I think it’s got these classical elements and these twists and turns in it. Miles’s music sounds very straightforward by comparison, I believe, not to detract from The Birth of the Cool.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: One of the greatest books of writing was lost in that flood. It’s just heartbreaking that I couldn’t get Kreidt’s family to [ ].

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I want to talk about some of the financial challenges you faced during this period. You had begun playing with Paul at the Band Box in Palo Alto, and that required you to take a cut in pay from the Geary Cellar. Soon you even lost that gig, when Paul took an engagement at Feather River. Around this time I understand you were struggling financially. You were trying to supplement your income by selling sandwiches in San Francisco and doing other things to make money. Tell me about this period of your life and how you survived through it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Quickly summing it up, I had a very good job at the Geary Cellar with the Three D’s: scale plus and a steady job. Paul hired away Francis Lynne, the vocalist, and Norman Bates, the bassist. He would be the leader and take a group where he had a job at a place near Stanford University called the Band Box. I just remembered why it was called the Band Box, because I remembered the song that Paul had us sing: “The Band Box is the joint for you. Get high when you’re happy and blind when you’re blue. The whiskey is old, but the music is new at the Band Box. If the state you arrive in

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: encourages jivin’, relax on a sofa with a chick you can go fa’. That’s why the proletariat make merry at the Band Box.” That’s the way we’d open the show every night. Then he gets a job at Russian River, where he worked other summers, and he says he’s going there. I said, “What happens here?” He said, “We just break up, and when I get back, maybe I’ll get everybody together.” The owner said, “Dave, why don’t you keep this job and get another horn player?” I would have gotten Bill Smith, because Bill and I worked a lot together. Paul flipped out, saying “It’s my job, and I won’t have you playing here.” So he goes to Feather River, and I’m trying to figure out, what’s the big attraction to Feather River, which I can never figure, because he loved playing with this group that he’s just destroying. He loved gambling more than he loved the group, and it was near Reno. He could drive over to Reno. He loved the slot machines. He was hooked. It’s like a guy that’s hooked on cigarettes, which he also was hooked on. That’s why he did that. So I had to take another job. This was at scale at a lake about 100 miles from San Francisco: Silver Log Tavern, it was called, on Clear Lake. You can see Clear Lake. The owner of that place had the same name as the owner of the Oakland Raiders.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Al Davis.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Al Davis. I never knew if it was a young Al Davis, the real McCoy, or not.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We’ll look into that.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We worked there. Lived in a corrugated iron tent – about the size of a big tent. No win[dows ] It got very hot every day. We’d take the kids to the lake every day and let them just float in the water. They were too young to swim or anything, but that cooled them off. I got a phone call from Jimmy Lyons saying, “Are you interested? I think I’ve got a trio job for you at the Burma Lounge in Oakland, right near Lake Merritt.” I said, “I’m very interested.” So we went there. Clint Eastwood came in there when he was 15. He recently told me he used to sneak in there, because he was tall, and it was dark at the entrance. They didn’t see he had a young face. Then Jimmy called me. He said, “I think I can have you play at the Blackhawk in San Francisco.” So the trio moved to San Francisco. We opened the Blackhawk as a jazz club. It was a store turned into a place with chairs and a small stage, which had to hold the Count Basie band or Duke Ellington, with half of them on the floor. That worked. I worked three months of the year, then three months off, then back for three months. It didn’t pay much more than scale, but it was steady. But I couldn’t make it. So I started trying to go to L.A. That’s where I met Gerry Mulligan with his quartet.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So in the time you were off from the Blackhawk, during those three months, you would do engagements in Los Angeles.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: If I could get them.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Where would you play in Los Angeles?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Where Gerry was playing, one night a week.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: At the Haig.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: At the Haig, yeah. They hired me six nights a week. Red Norvo was playing on the off nights, with Tal Farlow and Charlie Mingus and Red, which was one of my favorite groups. I had just started Fantasy Records, so I talked the Weiss brothers into recording Red Norvo’s trio, which I think is some of the greatest small combo recordings ever made. I talked them into recording Gerry. Gerry said I gave him his first steady job by moving him into the Blackhawk. Then Red Norvo came up there. But I still had to work. That’s when I started investigating going on the road more.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let me ask you about a couple of other things that happened around this time. Is it true that you taught an extension course on the history of jazz at U. C. Berkeley?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Absolutely.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Tell me about that.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Remember I couldn’t teach.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s right. You violated your promise there.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I knew we had no work at this time and that that would pay $15 a week. Maybe we could live on that. The way I figured out how to do that is Iola did the lecturing to the class, because she was a speech major in college, and acting. So it wasn’t a problem for her. At this point I couldn’t open my mouth in front of people, but I played. She’d ask me to play examples. In that class was a young Chinese student [ ] jazz than we could ever dream of knowing, so it was rather embarrassing when we were stuck with asking questions. Russell?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Herb Wong.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That was Herb Wong! I think Herb started writing for Down Beat when he was 13 years old or something.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He was just a kid.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah I know. I don’t think the editors there knew how young their San Francisco correspondent was.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So we got to know Herb really well, and of course we work with him all the time at Monterey now. We’re old friends. Then we moved over to San Francisco extension.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: For San Francisco State?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No. Where did we teach in San Francisco?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I was asking about teaching jazz at U. C. extension. Iola Brubeck: Yes, in Berkeley and in San Francisco.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: At San Francisco State?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No. They had an extension . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Oh, it was a Berkeley extension course but took place in San Francisco.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: In San Francisco.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Where are you going to sit? How you ever found this.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Actually, I knew that there was a file someplace that we’d thrown all this kind of stuff in, and George found it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Can you bring Iola a chair, Russell? You’d rather have a straight chair, wouldn’t you?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: A straight chair is fine.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There you go. Will she be able to be heard?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Should we get a microphone for her? Will the microphone pick her up? Kimery: It should be able to pick her up.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I’ll speak up.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Okay. Listen on the headphones. If we need to stop . . . If you look at the 1949 phone book for San Francisco and you look under Paul Desmond, you see that he’s listed as a music teacher. So it’s clear that Paul took students around this time. Did you do that as well? Did you take any piano students?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We all discovered that if we put down “jazz musician,” we’d never get a phone.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s true.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So we were months and months and months trying to call the company. They’d always make up some excuse. One of the Mills girls lived downstairs on 18th Street. Who was that?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That was Bert.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Bert Corvello, music major from Mills. Worked at the telephone company. She said, “They will never give a jazz musician, or even maybe a musician, a phone. You’ll be last on the list, and the list is long. Put down ‘teacher’.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: This was shortly after World War II, and there really was a priority list about who got a telephone.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: And jazz musicians were at the bottom of the list.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: At the bottom.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: At the bottom of the list.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: After drug dealers and everything else, you had jazz. Did you ever take piano students during this period? Did you ever teach piano?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: How did you approach that? Was that something that you found satisfying, or frustrating?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It was interesting. It’s all right. I am still in touch with one of my students. Do you think Earle would . . .?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Earle, are you talking about?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Do you think Earle would mind being . . . Earle Weatherwax is his name. He went on to be an entertainer in nightclubs as singer and pianist. We see him quite frequently. Chris see him, and Danny sees him a lot.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Where does he live? Do you know, Russell?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He lives in Arizona most of the time.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He’s involved with a young lady named Georgia Frontiere, who owns the St. Louis Rams . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I know who Georgia Frontiere, sure

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . and they have 36 homes.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Okay. [ ] from day to day.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Primarily they live in Sedona and St. Louis. She just bought a private rail car. They’re going to be in Malibu in . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: When we play at Pepperdine, we usually stay in their Malibu [home], if it’s offered to us. I don’t know if we should say she owns 36 homes.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It’s probably down to 34.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We will edit that out of the transcript. Things like this we will edit out. They don’t need to go into the Smithsonian.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: And that’s not counting the new railroad car.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: And you better not mention Georgie. But she’s really interested in helping the Institute too. Don’t you think?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: And he is too. They have become very close friends, and yet I always feel you have to protect her, and him, because . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: She’s a remarkable woman.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: She was an opera singer at one time.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Last time we were at dinner, she said to me, “Russell, life is so strange. I started off life singing in an opera chorus, and now I own an NFL team.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: 1947. Your first son is born. How did the responsibility of parenthood impact your life and career?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Oh . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No impact at all, I’m sure.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It was a good surprise. But when I think of Darius’s birth, there’s a lot that goes into that. Staying up all night with my closest friend, Bob Skinner, the pianist in San Francisco, and I taking Iola to the Children’s Hospital and nothing too much happening. For some reason we were dismissed, and you went to the birthing room, I think.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yes.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So we drove out to the beach – Playland at the Beach – area and just sat in the car. I’d known him from the day he was born in the house that joined the back of our house in Concord. He was born at home like I was. He’s six months later. We had to go back to the hospital, and Iola is not having the baby. It’s going on and on and on in the evening. Now, it’s getting close to time to go to the Geary Cellar and start playing with the trio. Still no baby, but finally she had the baby. I told her – now I knew I’m late for work – I told her “I’ve got to leave, but I don’t want to leave until I know you’re aware of what’s going on and what’s happening. Here’s a little bell.” It was shaped like a bell, a black bell. “If you need a nurse, because I’m leaving now, you just press this button.” She nods. “Now put it down.” She did. I went back and said, “What is that little black object there?” She said, “It’s an umbrella.” It kind of had an umbrella shape. So I thought, oh boy. Can I leave this woman? I finally just trusted that a nurse would come and she [ ]. So I got to the Geary Cellar and the owner, standing behind the bar, said, “Brubeck, you’re fired.” I said, “My wife just had a baby. That’s why I’m late.” He said, “Drinks on the house.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: [inaudible] a wonderful message from Darius, that he just wrote a note, “Welcome to this beautiful world.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s when I brought Darius home. I sat him on the grand piano – Howard’s. We were living with Howard – grand piano, and played Milhaud for him, so that that would be the first music he heard, I had that note, “Welcome to this beautiful world,” which it’s so amazing for a guy that’s in a wheelchair, in pain every day of his life, dependent on his wife to push into airplanes or into auditoriums. Nothing ever stopped them from seeing

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: plays and movies and going to restaurants. And she’s so small, and he was so big, but nothing stopped her. She’s still alive, 104, and living in their old apartment in Pigalle.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Tell me about how Fantasy Records came about and about your relationship and impressions of the Weiss brothers.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There was a teacher from Stanford University named – the trombonist from Stanford – had the first – recorded me.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Oh. You’re talking about Scobey, right?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We can fix this later, once again, the transcript.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I’m not sure where you’re heading, so I can’t . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He said the first recording.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: These were the masters that were made, and then the Weiss brothers acquired those masters, because he couldn’t pay the bills for the pressing.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s right.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: And who was that leader’s name?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I’ve got that in my own notes. I could go back. His name was Lloyd somebody? No? Maybe not.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It must have been that early dixieland trombonist around San Francisco.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We don’t need that.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He recorded me, and he did not pay for the record session: Cal Tjader, Ron Crotty, and myself. So when I asked him – I said, “My sidemen are complaining that they haven’t been paid and the records are out.” He said, “I can’t pay you, because they’re not selling at all.” So I went to the Weiss brothers, who produced those records – Jack Sheedy was his name.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s right. Jack Sheedy.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I said, “Jack said that they’re not selling.” The Weiss brothers said, “Your records are selling. His aren’t, but he’s keeping his company going by selling your records and keeping the money.” They said, “Why don’t you go to him and tell him that if he can’t pay for the record sessions that [ ] like to buy the recordings back and own them.” So I went to him. He was glad to sell them to me for cost. That would have been around three hundred dollars or four, maybe at the most.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I think it was less than that.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You do?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Um-hmm.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Then the Weiss brothers said, “We’ll just take those, we’ll keep manufacturing them, we’ll call it Fantasy Records, and we’ll be partners.” The records started really taking off. Jimmy Lyons was playing them every night on his broadcasts, so you heard them up and down the West Coast and out past the Hawaiian islands to the sailors at sea who would come into San Francisco for their leave and look me up. We had a lot of sailors at places like the Blackhawk because of Jimmy’s show. So we just kept making trio records. Everything was going pretty well. Then I went to Honolulu, where I got in a swimming accident. The accident was bad enough that the ambulance drivers I could hear talking said, “We’re bringing in a d.o.a.” They brought me to the Army hospital, because Queens Hospital – I didn’t have any insurance or any money – wouldn’t take me. They said, “Were you in the service?” I said, “Yes.” They said, “We’ll call the Army hospital.” They put me in a holding cellar under the hospital on a gurney. They said, “If you move, you’ll probably be paralyzed, or die.” So I lay very still all through lunch hour. The doctors were up eating lunch in the hospital. Then they brought me up and started working me in various ways, with weights over my head. Finally they called Iola. You take it from here.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It was quite late at night before I heard from anybody. Then a doctor from the Tripler? Army Hospital phoned me and said, “There seemed to be some life in his limbs. He’s going to survive, but now it’s a question of how much he’s going to have use of his limbs.” But the recovery started quite remarkably fast, because he had – how many pounds?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: 10 pounds.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: 10-pound weights at the chin strap, and the weights would go over the back of the bed in the hospital. So he just had to lie flat with this thing stretching you. Dave’s lower back was very much affected too, but what they were really working on was what was up here, because that was the crucial part.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: How long before you came back to California?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I was 21 days in traction. I’m trying to get out of the hospital. Finally the doctor said, “I’ve never talked to anybody that wanted to get out so bad. There’s one thing that maybe would work. If I let you go, you have to promise me to go back to Waikiki Beach, where you got hurt, and float [ ] hours a day, because what we’re doing here is pulling your neck off the nerve, and one other way that can help it is to float. Your body starts floating and the bones moving somewhat into the right place.” Can you believe that? So I go right back where I got hurt, and more than a month of floating, right?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: About a month, I think.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Then he said, “If you’ll do this every day of your life.” As soon as we finished yesterday, I went and floated. At home, I have a pool in the basement. I used to have the pulleys in the basement. I could work my neck that way. Some days I’d be better off than others. At the Blackhawk, I could not stand up when the set was over. By that time, nerves and bones had shifted into a different position, from sitting, but I could pull myself up by grabbing the top of the piano. Then there would be a blackout on the stand. I’d stand there until feeling came back in my limbs and arms, some nights better than others.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Is it true that while you were recovering, the Weiss brothers pressured Cal Tjader and Ron Crotty to find another piano player?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Very true. I felt very betrayed in some ways.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Actually it was Cal and Jack Weeks rather than Ron Crotty.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Okay. It was Jack Weeks. Thank you for clarifying that.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Jack, yeah. But maybe they didn’t want to do it. They had to work, though. I think they got Vince Guaraldi. No. [John] Marabuto. What’s strange is, we always were friends, even when I felt that the Weiss brothers and everything I had started, they should have waited until I recovered, because it was maybe three months or four months before I could play again. This arm and these hands weren’t working up to snuff at all.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We’ll talk in a second about the formation of the quartet and about Paul Desmond joining the band at that point, but I just want you to speculate. If you had not had that

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: swimming accident in Hawaii, do you think you would have kept with the trio? Is it possible your career could have gone off in some completely different direction if that hadn’t happened?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Probably, but Paul was not going to take no for an answer. He wanted to come to Honolulu. I had to talk him out of that. Free. He would just come, so he could play. If you read his book . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Doug Ramsey’s book.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . , you’ll see in the introduction, it was – a drive in his life, was to play with me.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So the quartet might have formed anyway, inevitably, because Paul was very focused on this.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I think that it might also – Dave, I think, always had in the back of his mind wanting to revive the octet, because there were times when you were playing with a trio that you would add Paul and Dick Collins when an opportunity arose. So I think in the back of his mind, you were thinking in terms of a quartet or quintet, but Paul was the one that was centered on it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: And you letting Paul in the house, when I said, “Never let him in the house.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Tell me about this.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He had really destroyed my life when he went to do Feather River. That was a real betrayal. So I told Iola, “Never let [ ]. If he’s coming around, I don’t want to see him.” So she let him in.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He came back from New York, knocking at the door and all enthusiastic, wanting to see Dave. It was pretty hard to say no.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I was hanging out diapers on the back porch on one of those old pulley wires. I turned around, and there’s Paul, standing on the landing and saying, “I’ll wash your dishes. I’ll wash your car.” What else was he going to do?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He’ll baby-sit, do the grocery shopping. He would do anything.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Before you leave Hawaii, mention your bank account.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: My bank account? Oh yeah. I was broke, and I didn’t know how I was going to get home. The doctor told me, “You cannot fly.” You see, to sit was murder. He said, “You cannot sit on an airplane.” I just turned down an hour ago going to England to play with

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: the LSO and the BBC, because the next day was in Humphrey’s, in San Diego. I said to Russell, “I can’t do it. I can’t sit.” When I have to sit, to this day, it is really hard. I have to do it, but I do it, but it’s not fun.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Anyway, the bank account was . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Shall we take a break? Are we running out of tape? Kimery: Yeah. Just hold that thought.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let him change the tape here.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah, I was thinking of that, because it was like a minor miracle.
[recording interrupted]

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We were talking about your bank account.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The bank account. How am I going to get home? I’d only worked two weeks in Honolulu before the accidents, and we had to pay rent and food for our family. So there was nothing left in the bank. Zero. Maybe a few dollars. So I went to the bank to close the account. They came back with the statement that I had – five hundred, wasn’t it?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I don’t remember the figure.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It was a lot of money in those days – to my credit. I said, “You’ve made a mistake. I never deposited any money.” They said, “It’s here, it’s yours, and you might as well take it.” I said, “That’s going to solve how I get home to San Francisco, but I still believe you’re going to want this money from me someday.” So I left my parents’ address, because I didn’t have an address. “Eventually I’ll pay you if you write and tell me.” They said, “All right.” So that way we bought tickets on the Lurline, which was a Maxim ship from San Francisco to Honolulu and sometimes on to . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Hong Kong.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: – Hong Kong was it? Or Sydney.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Mostly it was back and forth between the Hawaiian Islands and San Francisco.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So that’s the way we got home. I asked my dad, “Did you put money in my account?” He said, “No.” I asked Joe Glaser. Joe said no. I asked anybody – brothers. I never found out where the five hundred came from. But I’ll tell you, without saying – I just thought of something. [ ] this woman in the world who used to . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s the only person that I could think of.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . used to come into the club.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Doris Duke.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Doris Duke. So it might have been her.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah. She was very nice to me. I just thought of it now. Could it? Who would have money like that that I would know?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It’s a possibility, because she came into the club, and people who came into the club were aware of the accident and what happened. So it could have been her.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: A miraculous story there of the money when you needed that money showing up.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Now there’s a Doris Duke Foundation, and I hope it’s helping jazz musicians still.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It is. It does help jazz musicians.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let me ask you about the early quartet recordings. Those are quite extraordinary recordings, because they sound very spontaneous, but they also very well planned and conceived. I’m trying to understand, what kind of preparation or rehearsal? How planned were they? How did you get that kind of combination between the planned and the spontaneous?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Is this the quartet?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: How about the early quartet recordings.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: When people talk about “cool,” I recommend that they listen to an NBC broadcast from a club, live in Los Angeles, This Can’t Be Love and Look for the Silver Lining. To this day, I think that’s some of the most spontaneous, hard-swinging, far from West Coast “cool,” so to speak. How can they call us “cool”? That is wild. Have you heard that?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Absolutely.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Did that come from a head arrangement, and then just free after that? Silver Lining was a head arrangement, wasn’t it?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah, sure. Nothing written out. Then, at the end, Paul plays The Eyes and Ears of the World [Brubeck sings that melody]. That’s just crazy.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You were furious with him.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There’s one cymbal crash that everybody thinks is cymbal, and it’s me going “schewwwww,” telling the drummer to start filling. Herb Barman and Bull Ruther. What a wild rhythm section that was. So I always think, boy . . . Then we took that group to New York, didn’t we? To Birdland.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: What would have been their first – would that have been the first time you performed in New York?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Tell me about that, your reception there and how . . .? Did they know about you in New York? Because of the recordings, they must have.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I guess the word had gotten – we’d had a good review from John Hammond, a really good review. Then two other reviewers – the one married to the actress. A friend of Barbara’s . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The trio had had some good reviews, and the quartet was newer on the scene, but in some of the magazines at that time, there were good reviews of the trio recordings. Metronome. Oh, Barry Ulanov. Is that who you mean?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Barry. Who is he married to?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Barbara Bel Geddes.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There you go.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let me ask you about your own musical development at this time. When you had the quartet during these early years, did you have a practice regimen? Did you have rehearsals? Or did you do most of your music on the stage?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Most of the time, it would be something they developed on the job [ ]. There were real rehearsals in our house. I can’t remember too many other rehearsals. Can you?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Occasionally there would be rehearsals in preparation for a recording, if it was new material that you had not played in concert or in clubs. The [Jazz Impressions of] Eurasia album, I think there were a few rehearsals, because it was all new.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So if you were going to record standards, it was very straightforward, but if you were going to do Time Out or something that was different, then there would be rehearsals. Let me ask you about the transition from recording for a small label like Fantasy to moving to Columbia and how that was different for you. How did that change things, all of a sudden working for a major label?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: When you consider that we were using Ampex maybe for the first time. Our first session for Fantasy was with the trio. We went – we had a three-hour session. At about two and a half hours, we had to realize that the Ampex [tape recorder] was not running at a steady – it would go flat or sharp. Weiss brothers said, “We’ve got to go to acetate,” which was right there, “and do four tunes, and then we’ll be all right.” So we did four tunes. One tune, Russell says, we repeated. The others were just first take. Our first session was made in a half hour, four sides. The Weiss brothers usually referred to my music as “garbage.” Remember that? Which . . .?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: They made a lot of money off of it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: When you’d be in the studio, and somebody would say, “Okay. Let’s go over this garbage,” it’s no way to feel good about what you were about to do. Your mood in studios – you want to have a certain dignity. The word “garbage” always stuck in my mind.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I remember I met Max Weiss. I did a long interview with him. He told me, “I’m not a jazz guy. I’ve never been a jazz guy. My philosophy is, you can’t fall in love with the product. It’s just a product.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s a good description. Sol Weiss must have been an excellent recording engineer, because those old trio things are so well done. Sometimes I think with maybe one microphone. Now it takes us seven mics on the drums, balance, and all that.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Were the first recordings that you made for Columbia in the studio without as many mics and so-on as they do now? I wasn’t around for those.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No, but we had great, famous engineers. Columbia had the time guys: Clough. Fred?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Fred Clough.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Fred Clough often did our sessions. We had to do three albums a year. That was my contract, and I never missed, that I can remember, in 17 years at Columbia.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I think you did more. I think if you – I look at the discography. I’ve done a count. You did at least three a year, sometimes more.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Then one for Fantasy [ ] we all decided. Many years – that would be four – then there’d be special products, where I had very little to do with it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I remember I once went through your discography, and I did a count. It seemed every 12 to 14 weeks there would be a new Dave Brubeck recording on the market.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: And Paul Desmond’s remark: “This group can make a recording for a streetcar token and a ham sandwich.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let’s take a break now, because we’ve been going for a while. Keep every . . .
[recording interrupted]

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Dave, we were talking about your recordings for Columbia. You made so many of them, many of them based on various themes. You did West Side Story or Time Out or A Tribute to Cole Porter or Dave Does Disney. How were those projects decided upon? Was that you sitting down with the quartet? Or was it George Avakian? Or was it, in the middle of the night you would get an idea? How did you determine the various themes for these projects?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s a good question, because I remember somebody would say something like, you should start playing show tunes of some of the most well-known Broadway shows and just do a whole series of those. So we did Cole Porter and . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Richard Rogers.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . Richard Rogers. Then my favorite is . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Matt Dennis.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . Matt Dennis.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Who suggested that? Did that come from George Avakian?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That came from me. My friend in the Army taught me all the Matt Dennis tunes. He was Festus in “Gunsmoke.” Ken Curtis. He could sing with the big bands and often took the place of Frank Sinatra or somebody. He was that good.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let me talk about once again your relationship with Columbia. After Take Five, you have a huge hit single, unusual. It’s unusual for any jazz musician to have a hit single, but for an instrumental and in 5/4, these are unique events. After that, was there pressure on you from Columbia to become more of a hit-maker and do more commercial music? Or did they give you freedom to define what you wanted?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: They had to give me freedom. Once in a while I’d remind them that my contract allowed me freedom.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Is that so?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I think so. Don’t you?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yes.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: People find it hard to believe, because it’s so hard to put that in. But I made my first contract. I didn’t have an attorney. So I made a lot of mistakes. But artistic mistakes, I covered my territory very well, because that – I wasn’t thinking about money and residuals and that. Columbia could take advantage of young artists, claim all their compositions, and put it in their own publishing. I didn’t know about that. That’s when you need a music attorney that is going to protect you. I finally got that with Jim Bancroft from San Francisco and Richard Juler now. They started protecting me in the ways of commercial recordings that you want to protect yourself, because when they saw that Columbia had told me they weren’t going to put out Time Out unless I adjust the royalties for the rights.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Because they were all originals.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: They said, when it’s all originals. I think they gave me 12 cents for the whole album. When Jim Bancroft saw that, he got it up, because [ ]. Congress was approached by BMI and ASCAP and companies like that, so we got a protection of, if you did that, it had to be 36 cents, instead of 12. So that is how much I lost over the years, is two-thirds of – so getting a good attorney is very important.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: At Columbia – when I think of Columbia during that period, I know one of the influential people there is John Hammond. Hammond was an admirer of your music, but I don’t often hear his name in association with your time at Columbia. Did you have any dealings with John when you were at Columbia?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No, and I kept thinking I would have. But it was different artists represented the guys that – Cal Lampley. Do you remember that name? The first jazz that Teo [Macero]

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: ever did was, I believe, with me. So, in a way, I broke him into the business. He’s such a sharp guy. He caught on quite quickly.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: When I look at your various achievements, there’s so many of them. But there’s one I want to focus on that’s not often talked about. It seems to me that you were very key in moving jazz from nightclubs and onto college campuses. The whole idea – today you look at – so much jazz takes place on college campuses, but as I look at it, you were almost the first. Tell me how that came about.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It was through Iola, and even before Iola would be Darius Milhaud, telling us to play for the Mills College assembly. Then we went up to College of Pacific with the octet. Then Iola . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Then U. C. Berkeley. The octet played there.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You started writing to . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah. Just started out with a list of colleges within driving distance of San Francisco and offered. Sometimes worked out a deal with the student association, where if they guaranteed a certain low amount, that would cover the effort of getting there. Then you split the profits over so much. So the association made some money and had the incentive to try to bring people in, and the band got more money. This really worked, because – especially if there was a good music department and the students were really interested. Students couldn’t really afford to come into nightclubs, and some of them weren’t of age to go into a nightclub. So bringing the music to them seemed the logical step for new music and a new group.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: November 8th, 1954. Your picture’s on the cover of Time magazine. How did that impact your career? Did this – for good or for bad. Did it change your life?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There’s rumors that it’s not all gravy.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There was a backlash, I would imagine.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah, a backlash for sure. There’s stories abound that the bad luck that somebody had after being on the cover, or bad criticism. That did happen to a certain degree. But to balance it, the good that comes from it balances any – by far, the good is far better than then negative.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Is it true that you were on the road in the same city as Duke Ellington the day that [ ] story?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Touring with the Duke Ellington band. I believe we were in Denver at the time. There was a knock on my door, seven in the morning. There’s Duke Ellington with Time magazine, saying, “Dave, you’re on the cover.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: What a remarkable way to find out.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I was hoping – because I knew they were doing a story on both of us – that Duke would come first, as he should. There it was. There was no way. But soon Ellington was on the cover.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Tell me how The Real Ambassadors came about.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Through Iola, we would write about Louis Armstrong and cultural exchange and how we should do a show. I remember Iola and I were always busy driving the kids to lessons. When I was gone, she’d have to drive children to 20 lessons a week. We counted them up.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah, we counted them.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Six kids: ballet, horseback, saxophone, trumpet, piano, cello. We’d always take writing pads along, because you’ve got to sit in front of the house or the school where somebody’s in taking a lesson. We would have to take advantage of those times. We’d go right to work while they’re in taking a lesson. I remember working on the Ambassadors.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: A lot of it was written in the car.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Was there ever a thought of taking that to Broadway?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I did. I went away thinking I’m going to be recognized as a Broadway show writer, because one of the top guys that I took this to was so thrilled with the music I’d written. I remember he called his wife into the room and said, “Listen to this.” I played it for her and him again. That was Josh Logan. He sent one of his people in production up to Lenox School.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That was Leyland Hayward.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Oh. That was Leyland Hayward. So there’s two top names that were very interested. Then finally when it came time to not just interest, but putting up the money – I remember this session with them. They said, “Dave, the Broadway audience is not ready for a show on integration. You’ve got to remember that you’re lecturing to an audience that’s there to be entertained.” He made his point, that we were trying to – I wouldn’t call it lecture, but make people aware of the unfairness of segregation. They

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
