Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: came close to producing it, but said it wouldn’t work. Soon there was Raisin in the Sun, on Broadway.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Actually Raisin in the Sun predated that.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: [ ]. We went to a reading of it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yes, and also another play that did not get on, that she wrote – I can’t think of her name at the moment – that Nemeroff was trying to produce. Yeah, I think it was difficult. That was – The Raisin in the Sun was a drama, and I think people expect a little more . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Social issues.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yes. They’re willing to accept that, but in a musical – at that time, they expected a musical to be entertaining and not much else. It wasn’t until later that musicals started taking on a message, so to speak.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Then when we finally did - the only performance was Monterey Jazz Festival. Iola was on one stage, doing the narration. You couldn’t do the entire show, but we could – on the other stage with Louis Armstrong, Carmen McRae, Lambert, Hendricks, and Bavan, Louis’s band, and my band. She would read in between. Explain your part.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There was just a narration that tied the songs together into some kind of story – sequence could be followed. But it was primarily music, very few words, except what were in the lyrics. But the message got through. It was really an extraordinary night, because so many musicians came backstage afterwards that were so moved by it. Of course, with Louis Armstrong singing it, how could you miss?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Joe Glaser wasn’t anxious for it to be a success, because he’d have his top moneymaker and me, who was doing well, tied up for six shows and a matinee a week. He could probably send Louis out and make that much money in one night. So he wasn’t hot for this. But he did set it up, when I told him I wanted to do this show with Louis, that I could meet Louis in Chicago. His manager, Frenchie, when I went to the hotel, would not tell me Louis’s room number and really kept me away from Louis. So from one of the hall porters, I found out Louis’s room number and went up and sat on the floor in the hall between rooms until a waiter was bringing Louis’s dinner. When he said, “Room service,” Louis came to the door. When he opened the door, he saw me sitting on the floor. He said, “Dave, what are you doing?” I said, “I was waiting to see you.” “Come in. Why didn’t you come in?” I said, “I was told not to bother you, by Frenchie.” “Oh, Frenchie.” He said, “Don’t listen to him. Have you eaten anything?” I said, “No, I haven’t eaten yet.” He said, “Bring that boy the same thing you just brought me.” So I

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: went in. We ate. He said, “Dave, I hope you’ll sit in with me tonight.” I said, “Oh, Louis, I don’t think I want to do that.” “It would be nice if you did.” I said, “I did hope to come to your show.” He spotted me in the show and brought me on. There’s Billy Kyle at the piano. That’s the first jazz pianist I heard when I was a kid, was the Billy Kyle Trio. I’m thinking, “My goodness, [ ] taking Billy Kyle’s place!” But it all worked out. Real kind people, full of smiles. It was a wonderful experience. Even Ralph Gleason gave me a great review at Monterey, and Leonard Feather gave it a rave review. Other reviewers came from all over the country. Some, I think, from Europe were there. So it was very successful, and very successful with the real aware jazz audience, so why wouldn’t it have gone on Broadway, or even a musical film? It should have worked.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Also I think it’s important to say that it meant a lot to Louis Armstrong. I read an interview he had with Leonard Feather. Louis was in Stockholm someplace. He was talking about The Real Ambassadors and saying that that was one of the most important things that he had done, because I think he felt this was his opportunity to make a statement.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I look back at that period, Dave, and you yourself were something of a real ambassador. I think 1958 you go to Poland . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Turkey.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . through the State Department. Then you go behind the Eastern curtain, and then down into the Middle East, Turkey, places like that. What kind of reception did you find? Were people aware of your music? Were they responsive to it?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Poland was very responsive. Turkey – we played in movie houses in Istanbul. Ankara, we played in a nightclub. Was it Isfahan?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Izmir.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Izmir. So Turkey was good. Very good musicians in Turkey. In those days in Europe – and consider that Turkey’s almost part of Europe – there’s always big bands at the radio stations. Sometimes more than one. Really great jazz players. So those kind of people were very aware of American jazz players. In England and Germany, to this day they still have radio bands, and they’re great. They’re on call every day. That’s the kind of job that jazz musicians want to get. Get off the road. It pays well, and it’s steady work. Some of my friends have been in a band in Germany maybe 15 or 20 years.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah. I think Herb Geller just retired.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Herb and Paul Desmond were together in that band . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Jack Fina?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No. When Paul was in New York and came home.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I thought that was Jack Fina.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That guitar player. Jack?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Eddie Duran.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Alvino Rey.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Alvino Rey.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: On that Turkey date, I think it’s important to mention a group, Blue Rondo a la Turk.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I was on my way to a radio station to be interviewed in Turkey. I was walking through the streets. There were street musicians playing in 9/8. [Brubeck sings a 9/8 rhythmic pattern.] Like that. So when I got to the radio station, there was a wonderful musician named June [ ], a friend of Gunther Schuller. I said to June, “What is this rhythm? di-ya di-ya di-ya ta-ta-ta di-ya di-ya.” He turned and looked at the band and pointed, and the whole band started playing something in 9/8 with that rhythm. I thought to myself, boy, when I get home, I’m going to write a tune – or maybe tonight, I started using that rhythm. I’ll put harmony to it, and my own melody. That’s how I started Blue Rondo a la Turk. It’s too bad that I said “a la Turk.” I was trying to be amusing by using Mozart’s term. The reason that Columbia did not push it, they said Blue Rondo a la Turk is too long to be listed on a jukebox. Take Five is just perfect. I said, yeah, I did that to myself. I named Paul’s tune Take Five and mine Blue Rondo a la Turk. But Blue Rondo was played as much before Columbia started pushing. They said they had to have an A side and a B side. They though Take Five, being that title, should be the A side. If they had left it alone, they’d have had two monster hits. To this day, Blue Rondo is played all over the road. Take Five, played more. But they were equal for a while.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I can believe that.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: They should have split it up . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Two singles.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . so they could have two A sides. But that was the thinking in those days, that the B side just was along for the ride, and they pushed the one side.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Tell me about Joe Morello coming into the quartet. How did that change things? And is it true that Paul Desmond was unhappy with that change in the band?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Paul Desmond asked me to go hear Joe Morello. He was playing at the Hickory House with Marian McPartland. We were at the Blue Note. So we went over there in our intermission. This marvelous drummer. He was playing brushes. Paul just loved somebody that played brushes and didn’t interrupt with some hard licks with sticks and clashing cymbals. So he said, as long as Joe Dodge has to go home to San Francisco, maybe this is the guy. So I talked to Joe. Joe was going to be on a vacation, because Marian McPartland was going home to London. So he would be out of work until she returned, which was quite a while. So he said, “I’m interested in your group, but your drummer’s out to lunch. I want to be featured.” I said, “That’s interesting, Joe. What do you mean ‘featured’?” He said, “Doing solos and experimenting and really doing some things I’d like to do.” I said that would be fine with me. Our next and first job was Chicago at the Blue Note. In the first set, at the end of the first set, I gave Joe a solo. He tore the place up and got a standing ovation. Joe always says, “a little standing ovation.” How can you get a little standing ovation? Then we went [ ] room, and Paul came in and said, “He goes or I go.” I said, “Paul, he’s not going to go. I like very much the direction we can go. Things I’ve wanted to do clear back to the octet: different time signatures and things with the trio.” So he said he’s leaving, and the bass player, Norman [Bates] was going to go with him. The next day I had a session at Columbia in Chicago. Those guys stood out on the other side of the control booth and wouldn’t come in. So Joe and I played for about three hours. I don’t know what ever happened to it. Then we went to the job that night, thinking, it’s going to be a duet. Just when it was time to start, they came in, just on time, walking into the club. So I was able to save my group. I don’t know what I would have done, but I would have gone without them, because I could see where Joe and I were going to go. You know, Joe could play a different tempo with each hand and each foot at the same time. I’ve never seen anybody that had that much control. Now, there might be guys in this world at that time that had that much dexterity, but I hadn’t heard them. I knew this guy’s a phenomenon. So I was so happy, and Paul was so unhappy. That’s a terrible situation, when you’ve got two star players and they’re not getting along. It took years for them to come – like Joe said, he loved Paul. At the end of Paul’s life, it was one of Joe’s students that Joe asked to

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: go live with Paul, when he was dying. They became so close to each other. Everybody in the group was close to each other. Eugene Wright was so wonderful all those years.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The quartet disbands at the end of 1967. How’d that come about?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I wanted to be with my family. I gave the guys a year’s notice, which no-one believed. It was documented by NBC with . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Chet Huntley

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . Huntley and Brinkley Report. We were playing in Pittsburgh in a big hotel with a big ballroom. They announced – if Iola, you can remember – a national . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: An American institution.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: An American institution.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The end of an American institution.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So it was big news. That was the announcement on that news channel that almost everybody heard. Then going to the airport the next day in the car to go home, Joe said, “Dave, I know you’ll be calling me next week.” I said, “Joe, I don’t think so. This is it.” He said, “Aw, you’ll call me.” The guys could not accept [ ]. Paul, and at times Gene, did play with me. Right up to his death Paul was playing some concerts with me, even when he was so ill that he had to have transfusions all day long. He came to my concert at Lincoln Center so he could play his last concert. He played his first concert with me and his last concert with me. At the end he – we got an encore and Paul said, “I can’t go back, even one more.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Both of you are native Californians, but you’ve moved to Connecticut. How did that happen? When did that happen? Why?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We came for a year. I talked the wife, Iola, and the family into making a move, and we’d go back to our wonderful home in Montclair, outside of Oakland.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: What year would that have been that you moved out here?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Did you ever see our house in Oakland, Heartwood Drive?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It’s still there. It was very outstanding at the time that it was built. I guess people still drive by to look at it, because it was one of the first cantilevered houses.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It cost $27,000. I just closed in my sun porch, which cost $40,000.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There’s been a little bit of inflation. So you came out here for a year, and you decided to stay.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We were here, and the kids liked the school system. Everything seemed to work out here. At that time, some of the school situation in Oakland wasn’t going as well as it had been. Is that how to put it? It was better out here by far.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: In high school, yeah. The lower grades were fine, because that was more neighborhood, but once you got to a central high school, it was getting pretty tough in Oakland. But the main reason was that there were not that many places on the West Coast to play. So Dave was spending most of his time on an airplane going back and forth to the East Coast.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: And recording out here.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So the proximity to New York made this a good location. There were good schools. It’s a beautiful setting too.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: My A&R man from New York . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Irving Townsend.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . Irving Townsend said, “I am going to be head of Columbia on the West Coast, so I am leaving my house. It would be a great place for you to live while you’re out here for a year.” It was a great place, right here in Wilton. We found our property where we are and decided to build here and to live here. I can’t believe Iola, that’s fourth generation California, and I’m second at least, maybe more, California – and I wanted all of our kids born in California. If we were on tour, I’d say to Iola, “Go home.” So now - we had five children when we moved here, and then we had one more in Connecticut that isn’t a Californian, Matthew. But the school [ ], they were fantastic in this area.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let me focus on 1971. Columbia starts going through turmoil. They’re changing their roster. They’re moving away from a lot of the jazz acts, and your contract is terminated at that point. How did that happen? What were your reactions? Why did that happen?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It’s a strange thing. I didn’t know that I had been terminated. No-one told me. I forget how I finally found out.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I know.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Jim Bancroft came to negotiate a new deal. He called up the business [?].

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You tell them.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The attorneys came to negotiate, because it was time to renew the contract. Every year it had been renewed just sort of automatically. No-one even talked about it. It just renewed. So when they said that their business, the reason they had come, was to negotiate Dave’s next contract, then they said, “Oh, there’s nothing to negotiate. We’ve dropped him.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: “We dropped him six months ago.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No notification, even.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There was another artist they dropped at the same time too, which proved a very funny story.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Tony . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I will sell that story. There was a world meeting of – Columbia representatives from every part of the world were meeting in New York. They request who they’d like to hear of their artists. It’s usually someone that they’ve done business with for years and is doing well. That’s who would entertain at their gathering. So Goddard Lieberson, then president of Columbia, called me and said, “Could you come in and play for the Columbia meeting.” I said, “I’m no longer – I’ve been dropped from your company.” See, he’d been kicked upstairs and Clive Davis, I think, was moved in to be president. Goddard was running the Yankees – the baseball team – a children’s store . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: A conglomerate of industries. But Clive Davis was the head of the record.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So I got to the meeting. Everybody’s glad to see me, like they have been for years. I see Tony Bennett. I say hello. I said, “Tony, I don’t belong here.” He said, “Why?” I said, “They’ve dropped me, and yet Goddard has begged me to come and play.” He said, “They’ve dropped me too, and Goddard asked me to come.” So here are the guys that have dropped. I’ll tell you, we had done a good job for Columbia over the years.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: And still do. Those recordings still sell in huge numbers.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I remember seeing Tony go through a low period, and then, because of his son or something, to get back to Columbia and just go sky-high in sales. He’s still doing it. I could be doing it too, but there’s problems [ ]. I’m still with the label, but no agreements or anything. They’re mostly sending out my old records and repackaging them, instead of – they should be doing new things if they want to keep up to date with me. But I have three other companies now, Telarc, Concord, and old Fantasy, all under one big company. So I’m doing fine, but I’m not doing what I should be doing with SONY Legacy.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Around this same time . . . Let’s go on. My thought is another 15 minutes, take a break . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: All right.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . but if at any time you want to . . Around the same time, jazz musicians are starting to play synthesizers, wearing psychedelic clothes, trying to become rock stars. But it seems to me Dave – I look at your career and it seems like you never – I was talking to Ken about this last night. I can’t think of a single project you did that seemed really overtly commercial, or something that you did for the money. But there must have been pressure on you to try to do commercial things.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Can you talk about that?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Somebody told me recently that there’s 160 CDs where I’m the leader. I don’t know if there’s that many . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There could well be.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . but I can’t think of one that was done strictly as a commercial thing, except maybe Red, Hot, and Cool. That was done so quickly, without me really knowing about it. But it’s a good album.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I was going to say, Dave, the musical content had nothing to do with it. It was the promotional aspects of it . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It was very commercial, I’ll say, because the music is fine.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . that they connected, the lipstick and the cover and that sort of thing. But the musical content had nothing with it. You would put that out probably anyway, with a different cover, if they hadn’t made this commercial tie-in.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So I guess I haven’t done a real commercial idea on any of the recordings. If I have, it’s few and far between.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You played a little bit, I think, of Fender Rhodes electric piano. Never extensively, but dabbled with it. What was your reaction when these electric keyboards came into use?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It might have been early in this whole business. I had a Baldwin electric piano. I had written a piece that was recorded on Decca, where it needed a kind of organ sound for one sound. I brought along that one keyboard and pressed the “organ” button. Do you remember that?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Was that Truth is Fallen?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No, Gates of Justice.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: [The] Gates of Justice.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It’s on [inaudible].

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So that’s the only time. But my sons have used synthesizers and electric keyboards.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let’s talk about Two Generations of Brubeck. Does it make it easier to be a bandleader, or does it make it harder? Like when you collaborated on The Real Ambassadors. How does that change the dynamic? Or does it? Is it just like any other band?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Right now, my sons will tell me, “When are we going to play together again, Dad?” They want [ ]. So the important thing is at the end of your life, your sons really want to play with you. There were times when we were going out as a family group, where there would be disagreements from the wives of the sons. That puts the sons in a situation where they have a pull between, am I loyal to the old man or am I going to have divorce coming up? When that happened, fortunately I usually lost, because I didn’t want to be the reason that their marriage went to pieces. Then the marriage always went to pieces after I bowed out. That happened with my own sidemen that I had for years. “Come home, or I’m getting a divorce.” He goes home, and they get a divorce.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: My sons have been really wonderful to me, and they’ve been wonderful to Iola. I went through period where their wives were accusing me of things that my sons now wouldn’t dream. At the time they might go along, saying, “Oh, is that true?” to their wives. Saying, “Is that what he’s doing, taking advantage of me?” When I told my attorney, Jim Bancroft, he was saying that the salaries were a little different when I hired my sons. They seemed more than when I hired just regular guys that weren’t my sons. I said, “Yes, and my sons are all making more than me,” but I was being accused by their wives of taking advantage of them. This is the kind of thing you don’t want to have happen. As soon as those wives left, there was never a problem again.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Your children have had musical careers . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Am I in dangerous territory?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: What is it?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Am I in dangerous territory saying this?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No, no. It’s all right. But the thrust of the question was the dynamics within the group itself. My observation was that off the stand, it was father-sons and on the stand it seemed to me like it was with any other group, where the musical standards were that you had to live up to a certain standard. It was – that was business. That was my observation.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I give you credit, because I know in my own situation, trying to – when I’ve had opportunities to do things in a commercial setting with members of the family, I just shy away from it. I don’t want to complicate the family relationship. But you seem to do it. Your children have really flourished as musicians. Was that encouraged from an early age? Did you know at a very early age that your children were going to be musicians? Or was it something that you nurtured, or really came from them?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I think it came from them. I’d be rehearsing, say, at home with Gerry Mulligan and Jack Six. The kids would come home from school and go right to the rehearsal and sit there quietly. My son Danny eventually studied with my drummer. He’d been brought up watching Joe Morello. Joe even left his drum set for Danny [ ]. Michael loved – who’s stopped playing – he and Paul Desmond were so close. He loved Paul’s playing and loved to be with Uncle Paul. The kids all called him Uncle Paul. They thought he was my brother, for years. Very close. Eugene Wright – did Eugene leave a bass in our house? Where did that bass come from?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There was a small bass at our house, but I don’t know whose it was. Maybe it was Eugene’s.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Chris would come home from school when he was a little kid, and he’d go lie down under the piano where I was playing, where the bass was stored, so it wouldn’t be kicked when you walked through the living room. You don’t want to kick and knock the bass over. So if it’s under the piano – he’d be under the piano with the bass and be fingering the bass at my rehearsals. One day, we were doing a recording at our house for a piece called Don’t Spindle, Mutilate . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Don’t Fold, Spindle, or Mutilate.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You remember that recording?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah, for the Canadian Broadcasting Company.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There was a tough piece in a screwy time signature that whoever was on bass with my group at the time couldn’t get into it. He said, “Why don’t you have Chris play it?” You remember? So Chris came out, sight-read it on electric bass, and cut it perfectly. Danny was on cymbals. He was ten years old. So even hanging out at rehearsals, here’s a record session where the kids did something constructive.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I remember one time when Gerry Mulligan was at our house. The kids came home from school. I guess – I don’t know whether you invited them or what, but anyway, they – Chris and Dan started playing with you and Gerry. I remember when Gerry was packing up to go home, he said, “Boy, have you got it made. You have an in-house rhythm section.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let me ask you about Gerry Mulligan and then we will take a break. Tell me about that collaboration. How did you approach that? Would you approach playing with Gerry the same way you would with Paul? How did that come about? There was a lengthy period there where you often collaborated with Gerry.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah, and Paul often played with Gerry.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s right as well, yes.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He was a musician that couldn’t resist playing when he was around. He just had to sit in, and nobody would say, “Don’t sit in” to him, because it always seemed to add something that just propelled whatever group he sat in with. I remember at the Newport Jazz Festival George Wein saying, “That Gerry. He’s all over the place, sitting in with everybody.” Maybe some people didn’t like it, but I liked it. We first got to know each other in that period where I brought him to Fantasy. Then we often did concerts where his group would play and then my group, or my group and then

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: his group, depending on the situation. [ ] in Europe with both groups. Russell, would you remember the years?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It was in the ’90s.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Late ’90s.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We toured together all over Europe. He had a very strong group.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Ted Rosenthal was his pianist.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Ted and – the drummer?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I can’t think of his . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I don’t remember.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: They both married Mills [College] girls. You remember?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I had forgotten about that. Jerry had substituted for Paul a few times when Paul was unable to play. There just always was an easy musical relationship. You can tell him the story about how George Wein induced you to go Mexico. That’s really how it began.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: George had a festival in Mexico.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: 1968, for the Olympics.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The Olympic year.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I had just broken up the quartet. He called me, and he said, “Can you come and play?” I said, “I don’t have a group, George. I just disbanded my quartet.” “Just come and play.” I said, “I can’t do that.” He said, “I’ve got a lot of groups down there.” He named all the groups. A big festival. “There’s all these different rhythm sections. You could play with them. And I’ve got Gerry Mulligan. Would you play with Gerry?” I said, “Yeah, but I’m not playing with an unknown group and an unknown rhythm section where I’ve been so big, in Mexico. I think it would be terrible to come down there and not have a real firm group instead of a pick-up group.” So I told him I didn’t want to do it. He said, “Look. You’ve got Gerry. You know Gerry. All you need is a bass and a drummer.” I said, “I just used a wonderful bass,” because I was doing The Light in the Wilderness, and the symphony orchestra called a surprise concert, and I had hired their first-chair classical bassist. It’s the day of the concert, and I get all this. So I said to the drummer, who I also

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: – because I didn’t have a group – was highly recommended to me – I said, “Who do you know that can sight-read this without rehearsal and can improvise too?” He said, “Jack Six.” So I called Jack to mind. In my mind, I thought he’d be the guy I could take to Mexico, but I need a drummer. I didn’t want to take a strange drummer. So I told George Wein, “I’ve got to find a drummer, but I just don’t want a great drummer. I want a great man.” He said, “They’re out there. You’ll find somebody.” In a half hour [ ] his wife called and said, “Dave, I’ve got a great drummer that’s a great man. His name is Alan Dawson. You get him. You’ll have what you want.” So I called him. “Come to Wilton and rehearse,” and Jack Six to come to Wilton. I started playing one tune. They played it through. Jack put his bass down. Alan stood up. They came close to each other and embraced, without saying a word. I said, man, I’ve got the great drummers and the great bass players. Glyod: You’re also being a bit modest about why George Wein was so insistent.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I hate to tell you this, but it’s true. George said, “If you don’t come, all of your friends down here are going to lose their jobs, because the festival won’t go on unless you’re there.” So that really put some pressure on me to get down there. For some reason we were very big in Mexico.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You had just gone there the year before, and that’s where you did the Bravo Brubeck. You used Mexican musicians.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: What’d he say?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He says because Bravo Brubeck had come out.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Oh yeah.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yes. He’d been there before. I think the spillover from California, too, that the relationship with Mexico – there’s always been a big following.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s right. A lot of people come across that border into California for a year, go back.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We were playing in the big park. When you go to Mexico, you play in Bayes Artes, downtown, and it costs a lot. The next day, you’re in the park. It’s usually a Sunday afternoon, and it’s almost free. I think we added it up that it was 52 cents for a ticket. Maybe six to ten thousand people. We played there. How did I get the Mexican musicians?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That was the year before.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Year before. We just played tunes I’d known from California. No rehearsal. I tried to have a rehearsal, but the Mexicans never came on the right day.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That tour, that recording, is probably Paul’s greatest solo, which is [inaudible].

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s a beautiful recording. Let’s take a break here. We’re making good progress. We’re down to . . .
[recording interrupted]

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Dave, I want to return to the theme of you being a real ambassador during your career. You were part of the Reagan-Gorbachev summit, and you contributed to creating some lasting goodwill on that occasion. Could you tell me what your recollections are?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: With Gorbachev and Reagan. I had a few things come to mind: a room where Garbechev had just made life a lot easier for poets and musicians or political people that had been sent to Siberia. Sitting next to Iola was a general in the Russian Army. Here these people – I wish I could remember the scientist’s name. Or the wife. He was such an important scientist, but he’d been ostracized.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Sakharov?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Was that it Iola? Say that again.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Andrei Sakharov.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: [ ]. Wasn’t he there?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: She was there. I don’t remember meeting him, but maybe he was. Someplace I have a guest list for this.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Anyway, there’s starting to be a feeling of . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: This was the glasnost period.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . glasnost, and yet the United States, I’ve heard, had a list of people that they would send, and I was on the top of the list. They had a list in Russia of people they would accept, and I was on the top of the list. So it was natural that I would go.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Part of that, Dave – excuse me – was also because you’d been there the year before on a cultural exchange. So the Russian people really knew who he was. Then Nancy Reagan was the one, I think, who made a decision that for the state dinner, they would invite you to go.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: In this room where we were meeting, floor to ceiling thick curtains were on every window. There was no air in there to speak of, and how many hundred people?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There was a lot crowded into one room, and it was very hot, because it was in May and it was not an air-conditioned room. But obviously there were reasons for keeping that so curtained.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Security.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It was surrounded by apartment houses and a lot of sentries and everybody watching everything, but you still felt that there could be sniper, maybe up, and that’s why they had sealed this room off. So we’re going to play in this room. You just feel a little nervous tension. When we started playing – you wouldn’t think this is important, but I called a tune that had a lot of rhythm and a good strong beat. The unifying thing was the jazz beat. You could see enemies out there all going like this. This was the beginning of people responding. I’ve had this happen a couple times in my life, where it was very important that the people were responding with their foot-tapping. You wouldn’t think that’s important. The first time was at an Army camp in Los Angeles where almost everyone in a certain ward was a catatonic. They had not responded in any way. Sometimes they’d sit, for sure all day, or maybe through the night. They never look at anybody. They never show any expression. We were asked to play, and pretty quick the feet started tapping, and the doctors came to me and said, “This is the first response I’ve ever seen.” Pretty quick a guy jumped up and grabbed a trumpet from one of the musicians and started playing what you’d have to call free jazz, because he was not a trumpet player. But it was making some kind of sense. Those psychiatrics doctors just said, this is [ ]. We’re going to play the same tape tomorrow. With us there that day – help, Iola.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Gerald Herd and Aldus Huxley.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Herd and Huxley. Huxley’s wife. Some other very – who wrote, I Am a Camera?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Christopher Isherwood.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Thank you. So you see, this is the group that’s there. They said, tomorrow, we’re going to play this same tape with these same catatonics. Not a response. Not a foot movement. Now isn’t that strange? The union had allowed these musicians to come and play. It was called Sawtell. That was the name of that place. No response. But the head of the union came and said, “This is so

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: important, I’m going to ask for volunteers to come out and play one day a week and see if we can get a response from these people. Then I went to a different department, and I played. It was outdoor in the courtyard. A guy jumped up on the stand and started playing piano like Teddy Wilson. I was amazed with this guy who was so unwell in so many ways could play complicated jazz. Then again, you think, does he have a chance? Is there a piano where he can go and use it? There’s so much can be done. There was some follow-up there. I don’t know how many years it would have gone on, whether there was follow-up. But people realized that live music, not recorded music – that was enough. That’s what they wanted to find out. It took live musicians to get this response, this one on one situation.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Then in Russia it was funny to see, around the room, because, as Dave said, it was very, very edgy. People were kind of like this. I’m sure the way the people were seated – like I was between two Russians who didn’t speak English, and I didn’t speak Russian, but the music did loosen everybody up.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Universal language.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We had responded.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Then it came time for me play a duet with Eugene Wright, who wasn’t in my group. I had just said, “Eugene, you have to go to Russia. All the things you’ve done for me, all the things you’ve been through in situations where it was not easy, I want you to go to Russia.” He wasn’t on the stage, but he had to come in through a door that was over the first table. Who’s at the first table? Gorbechev. And Reagan is on the other side, at the first table. Gorbechev didn’t know there’s going to be a giant American with a bass over his head squeezing by him. As he looked up, he saw this bass and this huge man, African- American. His mouth dropped open. I wondered how many guards wondered, what is this? Gene went up, we played a duet, and Gorbechev loved it. Afterwards, through his interpreter, he said, “[ ] when you two played together.” He said, “Would you sign . . .” – his interpreter. The guy with the high forehead, that you always see with Gorbechev – “Would you sign your autograph for me.” I said, “Sure.” He said, “Wouldn’t this be the time I don’t have anything for you to sign. Here, sign this.” I looked at it. It was his pass to the Kremlin. I said, “You don’t want me to sign that.” “I don’t need that pass anymore. Sign it please.” But this thing about the beat – I hate to tell you something that’s so important to me – Russell. Come here a second. I need your help. And Chris, you could come.
[interview interrupted by phone call]
Who was in government that was important?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Shultz.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: What’s his first . . .? – George.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: George Shultz.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah. Well, I can tell you. Close the door.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The next day, we were going to the ballet.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Iola was in line to go to the ballet. I had to do interviews where there was just every – ABC, NBC, Fox – just lines of guys interviewing you from a balcony over Red Square. So I was stuck there. I said, “I won’t be able to get into the ballet. Look at that line.” “We’ll get you in.” So I’m the only guy that gets past the line. I’m in there in an empty lobby. Everybody else is outside. Pretty quick, a phalanx of guards come in. In this part of the phalanx is George Shultz. I’m shoved to the back end of that lobby. George went through the phalanx and came right over to me. He said, “Dave, you saved the meeting – the summit.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: “You saved the summit.” He said, “There was so much tension, but after last night, everything is so much more relaxed.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I hate not to tell you this, and I’d hate to see it in print and people think, what an ego. But this is what I’m talking about.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Sure, no. It’s an important story.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It is.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let me ask about other political situations you’ve been involved in. You’ve been involved playing at the White House or presidential events I think going back to the Kennedy administration.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Is that correct?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s right.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: How do you approach that? How do you play at the White House? Do you play a song? Do you play a set? How do you adapt to that?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: A little background to that: Pierre Salinger, whether you know it or not, could have had a career as a classical pianist. He used to come into the Geary Cellar in San Francisco when he was a writer for the [San Francisco] Chronicle. Didn’t he go with one of the girls downstairs?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah. Denise McCluggage.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Do you know who Denise McClugagge is?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: She’s the first top great woman race driver. She’s a Mills graduate. She was living [ ] little house downstairs on 18th Street. Pierre would know me. He was Kennedy’s press secretary. Kennedy – every Thursday afternoon he had invited college students and special students that were interested in Washington government to come and live for the summer. We’re finished.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: What was this?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: George Shultz.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Oh, at the Bolshoi.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Tell them what he said.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: This was the day after the summit. After the night of the summit we went from [?] to the Rossiya Hotel, because all the networks had set up. The balcony of the Rossiya overlooks Red Square and St. Basel’s. So it’s “the shot,” to do a live CNN. As Dave came through the corridor on the second floor, every single news organization in the world was set up there. They all came up and applauded Dave, because they’d all seen it. Who was the black anchor for CNN? Bernard . . . [Shaw].

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Bernard . . . wonderful guy.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He was the CNN anchor man. Bernard . . . Anyway, does the interview with Dave, finishes it up. He turns to Dave and he says, “Dave, I have to tell you something. Listening to you play Take the ‘A’ Train made me proud to be an American.” He said, “We all were just so emotional at what was taking place.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gloyd
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The next day, the Bolshoi. It was an all-star gala thing. We were ready to go in, and Shultz comes up. He’s all through the security. He sees Dave. He goes to Dave, through the security line, embraces him, and says, “Dave, you made the summit. Nothing was happening until last night, when everybody looked around and saw that they appreciated the same music.” So that was a pretty emotional evening.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Cultural exchange works.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You were taking about Pierre Salinger.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Thursday afternoon these – pages were a lot of them – . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Interns.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . interns were invited to the White House. They would not know why they were coming, except it was Kennedy’s afternoon to entertain them. Word got out that I was going to be the entertainment. The lawn at the White House was flooded, and they could not keep that date there, so they moved us to the Washington monument. I don’t remember whether Jack Kennedy came or not.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I don’t think he did.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Bobby was supposed to have been there.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I think there was talk. If he came, he came and went without our knowing it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Security and all that was changed now. They said, “Would you play a song for Tony Bennett to sing?” I said, “Sure. What’s he want to sing?” Tony, without rehearsals - was it Night and Day?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That Old Black Magic.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That Old Black Magic. It came off just great. It’s on one of my records with different artists. It sounds like we knew what each other was doing. There were thousands and thousands at that, out in the open air. Then the next year – who’d we go for?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Johnson.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Johnson. Oh yeah.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: King Hussein.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: King Hussein had requested this.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I guess King Hussein was a real jazz fan. So that was the first [ ] group that performed at a state dinner function. They had performed for dances and that sort of thing, but as the entertainer for a state function, it was the first time. From what we understand, it was King Hussein who requested it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I see. What’s the protocol for that? Do you play a whole set? Do you play just one or two numbers?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You play maybe three or four. The Ellington night, there’s so many jazz musicians that you just go up and play one tune. When I think of the Ellington night, I think of the night that I really liked Dick Nixon, who I hadn’t been a fan of. But he said – we’re at the dinner in a separate room. He gets up to make a speech of welcome. He said, “In this room there’s been welcome and entertainment for kings and queens and leaders of the world, but tonight we entertain our first Duke.” Then he said, “It’s come full circle. Duke’s father was the head” – did he call him . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Butler.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: “. . . butler in this room. Tonight we’re entertaining and honoring his son.” Isn’t that great? It was so wonderful. Iola was sitting with Mercer [Ellington] in a room full of musicians and great statesmen. I don’t know why I got on that, but I was thinking of how great that was, Duke being raised in Washington.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s right. His father catered meals at the White House.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: What’d you say?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: His father catered meals at the White House.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah, and wasn’t it wonderful of Nixon to bring that . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: For his birthday.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . full circle. Then [Gerald] Ford. He had a train going across the country. We went to the station.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: This was ’76, the Freedom Train.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Who else?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: There was a [Jimmy] Carter event. Were you at the Carter jazz . . .?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Yeah, in the Rose Garden, Carter.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s the night I played with Lionel [Hampton], wasn’t it? Lionel had told us what he’s going to play. He didn’t play one thing that he told us. That great bass player . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Ron Carter.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Ron said, “What the heck’s he playing? I don’t know this song.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s right. He played a tune that neither of you had ever played.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Neither of us knew.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: If you and Ron don’t know it, it’s got to be a pretty obscure song.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: We got through it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Let me ask about another world figure: Pope John Paul II. You performed Upon this Rock for his visit to San Francisco. You’ve also written a number of other widely performed liturgical works. Can you talk about that aspect of your career?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So many times, like today, I’ll get a phone call for something very important to do. Many times I can’t do it or wouldn’t think it’s appropriate. I can tell you a story about Johnson, President Johnson. I’m in my tomato garden at home, and I am called to come to the phone, saying, “It’s the White House.” I go to the phone. They say, “Dave, we need you to come to . . .”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Thailand.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: “. . . Thailand. Can you get on the next plane and come?”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The King of Thailand is a big jazz fan.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He had requested us. I said, “Why? Why do I have to come?” “We’re in big trouble. The President, when he’s seated, is taller than the King is standing. This is

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: causing such tremendous problems. On top of it, the President has crossed his legs and pointed his shoe at the President” [sic: the King].

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The bottom of his shoe.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The bottom of – “We are in big trouble, but we think because the King likes you so much, that if you came and played, it might save the situation.” So I said, “I can’t go. I have other concerts that I have to do during this period.” “Can you think of somebody else that the King would like?” I said, “How about Stan Getz?” “Oh, he’d like that.” I guess I’m talking to his social person.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Social secretary.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So, great. Send Stan. Stan goes all the way there. Didn’t like something that somebody said. Turns around and comes back. Then is talked into going back, and gets on the next plane and goes back. He finally saved the situation. Now we have a friend that’s in Thailand for the King, to teach his kids.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Life is funny, the circles, because one of the Mills girls . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That lived downstairs.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . that lived on 18th Street in San Francisco ended up being the music teacher for the King of Thailand’s children.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: She goes back every year. She might be there now.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Isn’t that crazy?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It’s like The King and I.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s funny. I’ve been considering trying to get an interview with the King of Thailand, because I hear he’s a great jazz fan. So I’ve sent these e-mails to the consulate and the ambassador. I tell my wife, “If someone calls and says they’re the King of Thailand on the phone, don’t hang up. It’s not a practical joke.” He hasn’t phoned me back. I’m still hopeful to get an interview at some point.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I kind of got off the track.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That is an interesting story. By all means. We’re moving on. We’re doing world figures now. We’re going to do Pope John Paul II and you writing a work for his visit to San Francisco.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I get a call when I’m in Los Angeles. They call Russell. Russell comes in my room, and said, “The Pope is coming to San Francisco – the diocese in San Francisco. He needs you to write nine minutes for his entrance into Candlestick Park. He will in the Popemobile coming in and circle the park. We don’t have any music ready for that. Could you write something?” I said, “Russell, what do they want me to write?” He said, “They’ve given me one sentence: ‘upon this rock, I will build my church, and the jaws of Hell cannot [ ]’.” I said, “Nine minutes on that? Turn it down.” So he calls back. “Mr. Brubeck thinks he cannot write nine minutes of music for the Pope on that one sentence.” So I go to bed – and this often happens to me. I will dream an answer, because I’m so pent up about this assignment. Bach would write a fugue and could use the words over and over again. I said, “Ask them if they could give me one more sentence? That would help give me more to work with.” So he called back. Everything was going fine. They’ll give me “what is loosed on earth shall be loosed in heaven,” which is . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It’s part of the same gospel.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It’s the next sentence. “Which is bound on earth will be bound in heaven.” So I got that sentence, and I started that chorale. I would meet the organist that was the choir director for that – is it called Glass Cathedral, that new cathedral in San Francisco? Not Glass. But it’s beautiful.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The Grace Cathedral.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Not the Grace. It’s a new one.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Because Grace is Episcopal.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It’s a Catholic.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You’re right. It’s not.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: So we’re on the way to Japan or Australia, and I said, “If I show the director of the choir, and he’s the person that’s going to be working with this – have him come to the airport in San Francisco and meet us. We’ll go to some room, and I’ll show him the music that I’ve started.” So he meets us there, and I said, “I think I’ve found the solution. I think I’ve written a fugue.” He said, “Let me see it.” He looks at it and sings perfectly the subject, then the counter-subject, then the stretto. “What do you mean, you think you’ve written a fugue? This is a fugue!”, which was good news to hear. So while we’re gone, the bishop, Quinn, is also an organist. He showed the bishop what I’d written. He said, “This is good music, but we’ve had two articles against using Dave, a jazz musician, to perform for the Pope,” very negative articles in both papers. But he

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: said, “I can defend this music. I’m a musician.” So we get to the part – now I’ve got the quartet. Russell has had one rehearsal with the choir and the musicians. I wrote it for 21 brass and percussion, because outdoors, in a baseball diamond – the altar is on second base, put up like a jigsaw puzzle, just perfectly, very expensive, because they’ve got to put it up and take it down, because there’s a ball game there that night. Can you imagine? It cost hundreds of thousands of dollars. I forget exactly. So [ ] The bishop said, “Dave, don’t use the quartet. The press will kill you. They’ll call it a jazz mass. You’ve written” – he said, “I love your quartet, but I know these guys. Just do the chorale and fugue.” So I brought the group. They were there. They didn’t play a note. You know, he was right, because it’s the narrowness of people that write about things like this to not know that this is America’s music, as Billy – Dr. Billy . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Taylor.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Taylor has said, “This is America’s classical music.” This we got to realize, that it’s the basic music of every Broadway show you go to, of rock, of movies – especially in a chase scene. It’s always jazz. Our classical composers that are world-wide known – and this is what Darius Milhaud told me – if you want to express, you have to use the jazz idiom, just as Bartok used the Hungarian folk music, and I’ve used French music, and Bach – Bach used drinking songs. O Sacred Head Now Wounded is a drinking song. Why don’t people realize that almost from the beginning of classical music, they were using folk music and comedy songs. Beethoven, I think, used dance songs that were popular at the time as a point of departure. Over and over. That’s why America has to realize that jazz is the basis of our music, and what’s going to live in our music – like Bernstein, Copland, Gershwin, and Charles Ives have used the jazz idiom. That’s what America should realize. That’s what our teachers, our government, should be thankful that we have such a great music that says in so many words “freedom” to the whole world. This is the expression of freedom, which is the expression of the United States.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Dave, I think I interviewed you back in 1988. At that time I had found an interview you had given in the 1950s in which you had told an interviewer that you would like to spend more time doing classical composition. I mentioned that to you in this 1988 interview, and you said, “I still feel the same way today. I wish I was spending more time doing classical composition.” It seems to me, though, that you have – in the last 20 years, you’ve devoted increasing amounts of time to these compositions. Is there a lot of your music, of compositions that have not been recorded? What is there out there?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The piece that I wrote for the Pope hasn’t been recorded – Upon this Rock – hasn’t been recorded, and I love that piece. It’s a good fugue. It is well-written, as far as I’m concerned. It should have been recorded. But it looks like it will. It’s going to be sung at the Catholic . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Notre Dame.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Notre Dame. Maybe someone will record it there. But I know who will record it, will be the Pacific Mozart Chorale, but they’ll record it probably without orchestra – do it a cappella. It would be great if they could record it with orchestra, but that costs a lot of money.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: How many works of yours are there that haven’t been recorded? A small number? A large number? What is there in your archives that we haven’t heard?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Have we recorded Chief Seattle?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Not a commercial recording.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Wonderful piece. Chief Seattle spoke to the President of the United States, to the Great Father in Washington. “How can you buy or sell the sky?” Because Washington wanted his land, all of Chief Seattle’s land. There was no way he could stop that from happening. But the speech is one of the greatest speeches on ecology. “Will you teach your children what we have taught our children if I sell you our land? Will you respect the trees, the water, the air, the animals, the fish?” Washington agreed to all of this. Put him on an island off of Seattle, where he could never return to Seattle, where he died. I’ve been to his grave there, with Iola. It was a little frightening to play for the Suquamish tribe Chief Seattle’s speech, because they do not like people to take their music or their texts. So at the first performance, a young chief came and read – what did he read? Part of Chief Seattle? He spoke himself.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He gave the prayer to the four winds, and there was a blessing of the concert.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Then he said, “I have to be gone tomorrow,” because there was a performance the next day, “But I’ll be back.” So he disappeared the next day and came back with an eagle feather that you could smell the smoke where it had been blessed. He gave that to me and said I must wave it when I go to the next world. [ ]

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: A great-great-great granddaughter of Chief Seattle came to the concert. They were thrilled with it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It was just the opposite. I was afraid to play my music, do this thing that Iola and I had written. Then we did it live with . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Russell Means.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: . . . Russell Means, who’s this magnificent man. He was in something you would think of as an American Indian costume, but it wasn’t. He just had the feathers.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: His hair was braided.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Braided. He read this with such passion. Do you know much about him?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Just a little.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Because he’s such a powerful force.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: He was the head of the AIM, the American Indian Movement. Remember that? They were pretty radical there for a while. Then I think he has done some acting in Hollywood. He is a man of great presence and a very intense, fierce [inaudible].

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: These are the kind of things that aren’t recorded. The Praise of Mary Canticles haven’t been recorded. These are 35-, 40 minute . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: These are major compositions of yours that most people haven’t had a chance to hear.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Then this bunch of new things will be recorded.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The Cannery Row work that you performed at Monterey – has that been recorded?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: No.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s another one that I’ve read reviews of, but haven’t had a chance to hear the music. A lot of people would like to hear this.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It could be . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The live performance was recorded, and actually, it’s well enough recorded . . .

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It could be commercially released.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I’d love to see that. Clint Eastwood had cameras there. He’s doing a documentary on me.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: My next question was going to be to ask you about that.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I keep saying, “Are you going to use Cannery Row?” – through the people in his staff – “Are you going to use Cannery Row in the documentary?” They said, “We’ll use it

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: as bookends.” I said, “It’s such a good first and only performance, that I would very much like you to do the whole thing.”

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That could be an extra feature on the DVD. Now that they have DVDs, they have an extra feature. They could just have the whole performance there.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: You just said the answer.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Oh, Is that so? Great minds think alike.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’s how they answered me. What’d they call it? A bonus.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: A bonus feature. That would be great.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: “We’ll put it on the end.” They said, “If it’s so important to you, we’d like you to know that we’ve thought of a way. We’ll put it as a complete piece as a bonus.” I don’t know how that works. Maybe you do.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: That’ll be great. That will get great visibility. A lot of people will see it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It will? I’m so anxious to see that.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Just a couple more questions. I’d like to ask you about your marriage. You’ve had – I think you’re going to celebrate your 65th anniversary this year. Is that correct? Is that right?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Isn’t it more?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It may seem like it.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
