Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I think it’s 66 coming up.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I just think that’s wonderful. In so many celebrities and musicians, they’re unable to have successful marriages. To see you with such a long, successful marriage and your kids to turn out well. How [ ]? What’s the secret to that success? That’s a great success in its own right, over and above the music.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The secret to everything is one word – love. If you haven’t got that, you’re in trouble. If you have it, you have a chance to be happy. There’s always unhappiness and suffering in this life, but this is what will help you through it all. We’ve had that as the saving of our situation.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Ask my wife.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Iola, do you have any comments on that?

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Within the family, it has its ups and downs. There’s strains and everything. But Dave is right, is that underneath there is something that binds you all together. You think of the other person, whether it’s a child or your husband or – but it is as important to you as your own life. If you have those priorities all straight, I think that things work themselves out, if you’re patient and have time and really want them to be resolved. I often quote Dave, because he says, “In music there is no mistake, as long as you can make the resolution.” So that’s kind of the way with life, right? It isn’t a mistake if there is a resolution to whatever the problem is.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I give both of you tremendous credit. I tell you, it’s very inspirational to see. Most people with the kind of fame and career that you’ve had, and to have a stable marriage and the kids turn out the way they have – I give you tremendous credit for that.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Thank you.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: I’ve got one last question. The NEA has asked us to do this. They want the people that have been named NEA Masters to give some comments on what it means to them to have been part of the NEA Master program. So any thoughts or observations you have on that would be greatly appreciated.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: Joining a group of people that you really respect and honor, then it’s an honor if you’re included in that. That’s the way I feel, that we’ve been very fortunate to be included.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: And I think that it has brought to the general public an awareness of the value of the jazz legends, like they did in Washington, D.C., last spring – this spring, wasn’t it? – that, just as in Japan, they have national treasures, that these are our national treasures, that this is our native music. I think that bringing that to the general public – I think the average person now, when they use the term “jazz,” have no idea what they’re talking about, because when you find out, “Oh, you love jazz? Who are some of your favorite players?”, and they all name people that you wouldn’t dream of putting under the classification of jazz. So, I think that’s helped. Then, another area that it’s helped – it has helped people who are trying to start or have a jazz series in a city. I know that it has worked in Arizona. They brought you and the sons in to open a jazz series. They’re selling subscriptions. That brought enough people in that it sustained the subscription. How they did this was calling upon the National Endowment for this backup that is being offered. I’m sure that that’s happened over and

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Iola
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: over again, where people who want to sponsor [ ] provide seed money that helps them get started and bring people in, so that they can afford to bring a headliner, and then some of the others they can afford to have on the series. So I think what your brother has done at the National Endowment is giving jazz more recognition than jazz has ever had from any official source.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Gioia
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: The Pulitzer Prize in music, for many years they would never give it to a jazz musician, which is a shame when you think of all the great jazz music, and every year they give a Pulitzer Prize in composition. For so many years no jazz musician ever got that. I know Dana wants to use the NEA Jazz Masters to have that kind of – something equivalent to what a Pulitzer Prize in jazz would be. Dave and Iola, I want to thank you. We ran long both days. We told you it would be three hours a day. We did more than four yesterday. We’ve been doing about four today, too. So, thank you very much.

Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.speaker: Brubeck
Dave-Brubeck-Transcription-2020.text: It’s been very pleasant, and I thank you.
(transcribed and edited by Barry Kernfeld)

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Funding for the Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Program NEA Jazz Master interview was provided by the National Endowment for the Arts.
ROY HAYNES
NEA Jazz Master (1995)
Interviewee: Roy Haynes (March 13, 1925 - )
Interviewer: Anthony Brown with recording engineer Ken Kimery Description: Transcript, 79 pp.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Can I swear on this?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You can say whatever you like.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Damn, they’ll bleep it out.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Today is May 15th, 1994. This is the Smithsonian Institution Jazz Oral History Program interview with Roy Haynes in his home in Roosevelt, Long Island, New York. Mr. Haynes, if we could start by you stating your full name, your birth date, and place of birth, please.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Roy Owen Haynes, Boston, Massachusetts, March 13th, 1925.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: If you could tell us your father’s full name, your mother’s full name.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: My father was Gus Haynes. My mother was – her maiden name was Payne – Edna Gertrude Payne.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: P-a-y-n-e?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: P-a-y-n-e.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Where were they from?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: They were from Barbados.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Were they married in Barbados?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: They were married in Barbados.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What city in Barbados were they from?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What city? I think Barbados is the city. I think they call them parish – I think St. John.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Your siblings, and their names?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Douglas Haynes. That was the oldest brother. Vincent Haynes. Douglas was born in Barbados. Vincent Haynes was born in Boston. Roy Haynes, Boston. Michael Haynes, Boston. He’s the youngest.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Four sons.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Four sons.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you were the second or third?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I was the third.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What neighborhood did you grow up in?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Roxbury, Massachusetts, which at that time, the street that we lived on was like the U.N. We had a little of everything there, all kind of people, which was great.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you basically grew up in an integrated neighborhood and had a variety of friends?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: A variety of friends, yes.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Do you remember any things that you used to do as a child, any childhood games?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Definitely. I used to like to build carts, four-wheel carts. That was my hobby, nails and hammers, building and driving the fast carts, with number 13 on them, which was my birthday.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Is that your lucky number?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I don’t know about that, but that’s when I was born. My mother often says it was her lucky number.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Do you remember any of the schools that you went to, the names of the schools that you went to?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yes. The first school was William Bacon. That was walking distance from my house. The next school was the Dudley school, James P. Timilty, and then Roxbury Memorial. They threw me out of there.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Uh-oh.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It was a high school.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Would you like to elaborate on that?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Do I care to? I was – I had a habit of drumming on the desk with my fingers. I would do it a lot, and I was good at doing it. I had the whole class in the palm of my hand. Naturally the teacher didn’t like that. He sent me to the principal with a letter. Then when I got to the principal, I think, they told me don’t come back until I brought my parent – one of my parents – with me. My mother went with me. The principal talked about me like I had constantly been in trouble. I’d never had no problem before. My mother was thinking that couldn’t possibly be her son Roy that he’s talking about. I don’t know if this guy was mixed up with somebody else, or what, or what the teacher had said in the note. But I don’t think I went back much after that. I was already playing gigs. I was a teenager. So I didn’t go to school much after that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you didn’t complete high school?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: If you want to say that. I did on the bandstand. I completed life, almost.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah, you got your doctorate in music, for sure.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Well, I just got that the last few years.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Officially.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Officially. Very good.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What were your favorite subjects in school?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Music, art, and recess.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You said music. Were you allowed to take music? Did you have music schools?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: We had music in those schools there, yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: From what age were you able to participate in music?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It was since I can remember. I remember at the Dudley school, West Indian parents, especially the mothers, always wanted their sons to play violin it seems like. Like I said, the street that we lived on, we had some other people from different parts of the West Indies there. They would have a boy and a girl. One summer day this man came through the neighborhood, stopping in different people’s homes, asking if they had children. He had this deal where they would take ten violin lessons and get a free violin. I think at that time the lessons were 50 cents, a quarter or 50 cents. We’d all be in the same class. My mother wanted me to take these violin lessons, so I got this free violin. I went from there. I was playing it all wrong. I had the wrong fingering.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Would you describe your neighborhood and your family’s income as middle class? It seems like you had some money to be able to afford . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Middle class. When I was about two years old, my father bought a house there. I don’t know whether that was middle class, or what it was. They were immigrants. I think maybe at that time he was working for the Standard Oil company.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: As – in what capacity?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I really wouldn’t know. I don’t know.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Did your mother work?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: She did domestic work periodically.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Raising those four boys.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. You say describe the neighborhood. Okay. On the right-hand side of us there were French-Canadian people. There was a man there that looked like Fred Astaire. He would have his derby on, and the whole thing. He wouldn’t say much. His moustache and his umbrella all the time. He would look like he was from England or something, but he was French-Canadian. One of his daughters – he had two daughters. They were much older than myself. They were probably the age of my mother, almost. One of the ladies, she used to play piano and sing opera. She knew all the Broadway shows. That’s where I heard a lot of the Gershwin songs and all the writers from that period. Across the street was a Jewish synagogue. On the left house was Miss Kelly, some Irish people. So I had – then there were some other families from the South, black families, lived a little further down the street – so I had it all there. It was really great growing up in the environment.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Do you remember any experiences with any kind of racial animosity in that neighborhood?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I imagine there may have been, but not too much, because we were all almost on the same level financially. I didn’t realize until many years later that a lot of the kids would say, Roy Haynes’s father, he lives in a private house. I didn’t know it was any big deal. But evidently it was different.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The schools that you went to, were they also integrated?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The schools were really, because the part of the street that we lived on – it was a small hill. When you lived at a certain part of the street, you would go to the school up there. You lived over there, you would go to the school down there. The school down there was predominantly black and the school up there was predominantly white. So there were maybe a few black kids in the class, one or two, at the Dudley school.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You mentioned the violin teacher. Could you describe him a little bit more? Do you remember his name?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No, I don’t remember his name, but he was a big fat white man. He had these coins in his pocket during the – when we’d be studying, he’d be shaking his – all I could hear is the money and all the kids playing out of tune. Got girls and boys. He says, “E, A, D.” He didn’t care if we hit the wrong notes. He just wanted those 50 cents, I imagine. So I do remember that about him.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How frequent were these lessons?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Once a week.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: He had them all in – everybody in the room?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yes.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: About how many students?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Maybe 10 – between 10 and 15, something like that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Were any of your other brothers taking lessons?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh, no. Just me.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Why you?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I have no idea. I guess I was very musical around the house, anyhow. But I wanted to play drums then.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Your parents knew this?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh yes. My father, he was into me playing drums. I guess my mother just wanted me to do that for a while. I still may have that violin around there somewhere. Not the same house, of course, but – because my folks are all gone, but my brother has a house up there.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So it was your mother’s idea to take violin lessons?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It was my mother’s idea, yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How long did you take lessons?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: For quite a while. I don’t remember how long. At least over a whole season. Then I tried playing in school, in the band in school.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What other musical activities did you do in school? Were you singing in school? Did you have singing lessons? Did you learn how to read or any of those kinds of things?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: We did all of that. I don’t remember none of it now. I don’t remember any of it.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When did you – since we know that you were playing on the tabletops, etc., did you study it formally? Did you take drum lessons?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I studied later – I studied maybe 1944, at Boston Conservatory, because it was fashionable. I remember the teacher’s name was Karl Ludwig. He was an old German teacher, very legitimate. I learned nothing there. I went because it sounded good, Boston Conservatory.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you were able to go to Boston Conservatory? You hadn’t finished high school.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: This was later.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I didn’t finish high school. I started working. I started making a few bucks and trying to behave myself, and it worked.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When did you get your first drum set, or first drum?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: First drum. Good idea. I never had a complete set when I started. I had bits. When I was still in high school, I was working, I think, five nights a week in the Italian section of Boston. We had to play shows there for tap dancers and play for singers. It was just a little trio. Each week I would buy either another cymbal or a tom-tom. I built the set like that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What did you start off with?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I started off with a snare drum that one of my teenage buddies had got someplace for me. I don’t know where he got it.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Playing at night?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Playing at night, yes.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Do you remember the hours, starting when, and how long you played?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It was probably from either 9 to 12, 8 to 12, something like that. I think I got off at 12 o’clock at night.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So here you are working professionally. What was your parents’ attitude about that fact that you were no longer going to school, but now you’re working?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I didn’t stop school immediately. I was still going to school, but sleeping in school. I couldn’t concentrate. But I would accomplish a lot financially, and I was trying

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: to behave myself. I wasn’t acting the fool outside, trying to respect my parents, my family in general, and myself. So they didn’t say anything. I was bringing money home. I would give my mother some money as well.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you were essentially encouraged to pursue a musical career.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. I would think. Yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Do you remember how much you were getting paid for those gigs? Were you getting paid by the week?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The last gig, yeah. I was making $12 a week. It was pretty cool, during that period.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you were buying your own instruments. You were probably – do you remember what year that was?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Maybe – I’m just guessing now – maybe 1942?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So that’s your first professional gig?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Not that particular one. I had played down the street at another place where I was making less money. I don’t think it was as many nights. That may have been just weekends. Then before that I had made a few one-nights gigs around Boston.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What type of music were you playing?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I was playing straight-ahead jazz, as far as I know.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You started off playing jazz.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s all it was, to play in nightclubs, I think. I wasn’t playing no Irish music or nothing like that, even though Boston was an Irish town.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What kind of music was played in your household? What kind of music did your family – your mother and father play?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: My mother was very religious. My father was loose. He wasn’t necessarily religious. He ended up coming to see me with Charlie Parker and all those people later. He came to New York once and came to the Five Spot. I think I was there with Monk, Thelonious Monk. The household was – my mother – I had a lot of records when I was

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: very young, the latest jazz records. She didn’t particularly like me to play them on Sunday. She was that kind of strict.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What did she say?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: She’d say no. She would tell me, no, don’t play that jazz music on Sunday.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What about the radio? Was the radio on in the house?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The radio was on a lot. I heard – I knew lyrics to all the songs, whatever was played, whether it’s Billie Holiday or Bing Crosby. They had good – Boston was hip for the music. I listened to a lot of Basie, Artie Shaw, Benny Goodman. I heard all that. Then my oldest brother Douglas, he spent a lot of time in New York when he was a teenager. So he would always come back and tell me everything. He knew Jo Jones. He was up on all the . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Was he also a musician?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: He went to New England.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Conservatory?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. But even before that, he studied. He went in the Army. The Army tore him up. When he came out of the Army, he was no good. He still went to school.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Did he serve in the war?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: He served in the war, yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Was he sent overseas?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yes.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Which, Europe or Asia?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: He was in Europe. That really tore him up. He come back, he was a nervous wreck.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Was he wounded?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Maybe psychologically, not physically.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Definitely. Yeah, definitely psychologically.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Do you remember where he served or what country he was in?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I’m not too sure on all that. Because I had another brother that went in also. Vin went in. But Vin was drafted. I think the situation with my oldest brother Douglas, they picked him up somewhere, to go in. I was very young then and into the music, so I wasn’t following that. But I think later on he told me. He had a hard time.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So how did you get out of the Army?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh, good question. I love that. I learned how to stay out and was proud of it. There was another musician – because I was getting pretty popular around Boston. A lot of bands would come from New York. If they needed a drummer, at one period I was usually the drummer that they would get. They had a lot – a lot of people that were in the service from other cities were in Boston. Boston was the hub for a lot of things, musically and otherwise. One of the older musicians, he was telling me how he got rejected from AUSA. If I didn’t get rejected, I was going to – the guys were going to get me in the band and the whole thing. But I had no eyes for the armed service. I was a Boy Scout, but that’s as far as I wanted to go. So I got rejected. I told them a story how I had ulcer. I was 17, 18. when I went down. They asked me what I took. I told them this medicine that this pianist had told me about, Amphagel or something like that. Then when I come to New York later on, not to jump ahead of you, when I was with Charlie Parker, they called me down again. I forget what war that was.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That was the Korean War.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Korean War. I still had my 4-F from Boston. I told them, I said, “You don’t want – you don’t really like black people anyway. What you want with me?” I got rejected then. Because the guys were planning – I had just bought that new – that car. 1950. I think that was the Korean War. I was in Birdland playing with Charlie Parker. There were a couple drummers planning on what they would do if Roy Haynes went in. One drummer said he would take his gig with Bird, and the other said, “I’ll take his car.” In the meantime, people like Symphony Sid, who was a very popular DJ, they knew I was going to be called by the draft board, so they started teasing me, even on the radio. They would say, “Corporal Roy Haynes.” Then they’d start saying, “Sergeant Roy Haynes.” On a radio broadcast. Evidently they sold the broadcast to Europe. When I got to Europe in 1954, some of the jazz fans were calling me “Sergeant Roy Haynes.” That’s

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: how I knew they were still into music, they were selling records all over the world. That’s when I found out, early. Break time.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Okay.
[recording interrupted]

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Disrupting the class. Let’s go back and talk about the records that you were collecting. You said you were collecting records.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Did I say that already?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yes, but you didn’t say which records.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I was collecting records. Are we rolling?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yes.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I had very good ears. I could hear like a monster. Jo Jones. Jonathan “Jo” Jones. That was the guy that I – I dug that sound or feeling he got. Chick Webb – I had the record Liza by Chick Webb. I was a youngster when I bought that. I had Cozy Cole’s Crescendo in Drums. I liked that. I could hear just a couple of beats by different drummers that really intrigued me: Shadow Wilson, Queer Street, with Basie. I think he had a four-bar break in there. I had met him anyhow. I met Shadow. I met Kenny Clarke, early, maybe 1942, ’43, somewhere in there. He was playing with Red Allen. I met Art Blakey with Fletcher Henderson, early ’40s. So I was up on all these guys.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Where were they playing, and how did you get a chance to meet these gentlemen?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Like I said, I was getting pretty popular around my area, in Boston then, and they would have Sunday sessions at different places.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Jam sessions.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah, and I was usually there, from the time I started to play, at the Sunday jam sessions.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Do you remember where any of these locations were?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yes. One place they used to have them was the Ken Club – K-e-n. That was a cellar place – basement, I should say. George Wein and I met there together, because he was trying to play piano. We were about the same age. We used to hang out there. There was this guitarist by the name of Tom Brown. That’s who I used to work with a lot. He used to try to play like Charlie Christian. He had all Charlie Christian’s records, so I used to listen to that. Jo Jones was on some of those. I knew all those little breaks he played. It just went on and on. I would listen to Louis Jordan.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The Tympany Five.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Right. Erskine Hawkins. We had – teenage guys, we used to hang out – we had all the records, After Hours. I was listening to everything.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So when you would go to see these other drummers, did you go up and ask them anything?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I imagine I did. I didn’t just go to see the drummers all the time. I would just be there, and they would come in with a band from New York. Like I met Kenny Clarke. He was playing with Red Allen then. They would play – the featured band would play. Then between that, they would have different guys jam. So that’s how I got to meet some of the – then there was another place called the Tic-Toc. That was where the big bands played. That’s where I saw Fats Waller, Louis Armstrong, Fletcher Henderson, when Art Blakey was playing with Fletcher Henderson, early ’40s. Naturally I would always meet the drummers. Art Blakey fell in love with Boston, and he stayed there. He left the band and stayed there. So we became very tight. I was like his son. He used to call me “son.” So it just went on and on. I finally met Jo Jones. I was still in high school when he was with Count Basie. It just grew. Then later on I went to New York. I got a one-way train ticket from Luis Russell. Somebody had told him about me.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: We’ll get to that. Back in those days, what was distinctive about these different drummers’ styles, like Art Blakey or Kenny Clarke or Papa Jo? What was it particularly that was so captivating for

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Papa Jo – he wasn’t known as Papa Jo then, but he was Papa Jo, whether he realized it or I realized it. He had such a happy feeling. Whatever he played, if it was just one beat, it knocked me out, the way he did it. I wasn’t into necessarily all that rudimental brrrrrrrrrr – all of that. This guy was flashy, and the way he said what he said, that was it. How I met Kenny Clarke: he was introduced by one of the deejays at the same Sunday session – one of the Sunday sessions at the Ken Club. He was the last one to be introduced to the audience, Kenny Clarke. The deejay said, “If you want to know anything about this guy, ask Jo Jones.” When he said that, I had to love him automatically.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What was distinctive about Kenny’s style? He was playing with Red Allen, so that was more of a New Orleans style, wasn’t it? Or a more traditional style?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Maybe traditional. I would think traditional. But the way – his taste on the cymbals, the way he was playing. Sid Catlett, I dug. I dug all that. I didn’t hear much of Kenny Clarke on records then, but I had met him in person. But I had heard Sid Catlett on records, and naturally Jo Jones, and seen him in person. Art Blakey hadn’t made many records with people, but then he went with Bill Eckstine’s big band, which would have been maybe – I don’t know – ’44 maybe. I forget exactly. So it went on and on. It just kept growing.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You were going to say something about that cymbal.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The cymbal, the way he danced on the cymbal. I was into the – I had a good feeling then. Swing. Klook had that thing, Sid Catlett, Jo Jones. I was into that. Art Blakey had a more of a driving – he reminded me more of Chick Webb.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You saw Chick Webb.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I didn’t see Chick Webb.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You never saw Chick Webb.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I just had Liza and another record. I didn’t see him at all. My brother would come back from the Savoy Ballroom when they would have the battle of the bands and tell me everything about him. So it was like seeing him.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When I said, Papa Jo, you said, he didn’t know it back then. Why . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: He wasn’t Papa Jo. They didn’t call him Papa Jo during that period.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Right.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That was the ’40s, ’50s.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Why do you say he was even Papa back then?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: He was – this guy – they used to tell me I look like him. Then later on, Dorothy Donegan said, “You really look like Jo Jones now.” I said, “Yes, I wear it well.” She said, “You have no choice.” That was my guy, man.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How about local drummers in the Boston area?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Very good. I love that. They had local drummers. There was a drummer named Joe Booker. He played with Sabby Lewis. Swing his butt off. Swing. Swing his butt off. Didn’t care much about solos. Swing the band to death. They had another drummer named Bob Elliott, could swing. Bob was a show drummer. He would play with a snare drum or cymbal maybe, and one tom-tom, and burn. I used to watch him all night.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: And no bass drum?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Pardon?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Bass drum, no?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: He had to have a bass drum, yeah. He was playing them shows. His hands were vrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrr, bam, but I mean here. I used to watch him play for dances. Boston was one of those towns. They had a lot of tap dancers and all that. That whole thing going. During that time, when you were young coming up, everything was very cliquish. Youngsters had a hard time. When you were young you had to – what’d they say? You had to keep the tempo. A drummer had to keep – you couldn’t vary. You had to keep the tempo. You couldn’t rush or go forward. When you’re young you may have a tendency to want to go ahead. So it’s very – it was hard coming up there. But it was good.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Do you remember any of the older musicians schooling you on some of the do’s and don’ts, other than how to stay out of the draft?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: There was only one guy that did that, that we were talking about. I was interested. I wanted to know that. Yeah. Like I said, they were very strict there. But I started breaking some of the rules in a nice way – I think in a nice way.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What were some of the first rules you remember breaking?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I don’t remember exactly. I was hearing some other stuff a lot of times.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Did you hear Dizzy Gillespie while you were still in Boston?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I heard the records. And another thing . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: But he didn’t come live.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I would come to New York on weekends when I wasn’t working, before I ever went to join the band. The first time I come to New York, my brother Vin was stationed in Jersey.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Fort Dix?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I think Fort Dix? Somewhere down in – it must have been. My father was going to come to New York to see him. He come and missed him. I think he didn’t have a furlough that weekend. They expected him to get shipped to Europe or somewhere. So my father missed him. My father and my brother’s wife, then they went back on the train the following week, and I went with them. It was my first time in New York. You know the first place I went at night: 52nd Street. When I got there, I couldn’t believe it. It was like a dream.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You can get – I guess you were old enough then to get in. You were 18? You could get into the clubs?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I guess I was. Something like that. I wasn’t drinking anyhow. I would drink Coca-Cola, which would cost 75 cents. I’m talking about 1944 – ’43 or ’44, I guess it was.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What’s the cover to get in those clubs?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: At the bar there was no cover, I don’t think.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh, you could just – so there’s no entrance fee. You just had to pay for drinks?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No, they didn’t have that then.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: They would have a minimum or something at the tables. And during that period you’d be dressed. You wouldn’t come in with no jeans or nothing like that. During that period, go to any of the places. That’s where I saw Dizzy for the first time. But my brother knew Dizzy too, even before that, when my brother was living in Harlem.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let’s take a break.
[recording interrupted]

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You grew up in an integrated neighborhood. You went to integrated schools. How about the working situation for musicians. What was that like? Was that still segregated, or was that integrated – the bands that you were performing with, the audiences?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: There were mixed bands. Oh yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: There were mixed bands? You started . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: There were mixed bands.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: . . . in the ’40s, the early ’40s?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: And playing for mixed audiences too?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So the clubs were integrated clubs?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. Sure. They had an organization called the Harvard Jazz Society.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Harvard Jazz Society.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. I think those were the people that started bring people like Sidney Bechet. They were there a lot. I met Bunk Johnson and – what was the bass player’s name that played with them? From New Orleans . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Pops Foster?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Pops Foster. I met all these guys. I even played with Bechet. You know who lives near me? What’s his name? Played bass with Louis Armstrong – Arvell Shaw. Arvell reminded me that we played together with – I’ve played so many gigs I forgot. You know I played with Louis Armstrong for one week in 1946.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Sure. Let’s talk about that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: During that period, Harlem was so very exciting. Many hotels in Harlem. The Teresa was the biggest hotel. The Braddock Hotel – that was 126th Street between 7th and 8th Avenue. A lot of musicians would stay there. There was a Braddock bar, where you could meet any musician. You could get a gig there. You could see any black musician there, from the greatest to not the greatest. Everybody was there. Bands would leave from there to go South or wherever they were going. At one point Louis Armstrong’s band was leaving there by bus to go down South in 1946. It happened that I was off that week, because I was with Luis Russell’s band. Their drummer was sick. I forget his name. His nickname was the name of one of the cities in Pennsylvania. That was his nickname. I can’t think of what that city is offhand.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: We won’t say Philly.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Well we know Philly. It’s something “-town,” I think. Anyhow, they needed a drummer, and I was there. I lived in Sugar Hill then. I took the bus back uptown to get my bag, came back on the bus, and got on the bus with the band. There was a first trumpet player named Fats Ford, who later changed his name to Merenghito. He was playing with a lot of Spanish bands up in the mountains later, and he was speaking Spanish and smoking his cigars. I don’t know if they have too much drum music, and you don’t have time to rehearse with bands in those days. Luis Russell, okay, we rehearsed when I first joined the band for a long time. The first trumpet player, he would tell me different cues that were coming up in the different arrangements. So it was like I had been there, and it worked out good.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It was how long? One week?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: One week. We went to cities like Raleigh, North Carolina.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Do you remember anybody else?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Played at tobacco warehouses, mostly dances.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: For primarily black audiences?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I would imagine it was, yes, if I remember correctly.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: And dances, or concerts?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: They were dances. People listen or dance. Mostly dancing.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Do you remember anybody else in the band?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: There was a younger pianist. They gave him a nickname. It was like one of the classical players, because I think he was into a little classic. I forget his name. I can’t remember too many.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How about your relationship with Pops? Did you . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Before you know it, time has gone by. It worked out great. The relationship was great. I used to love to hear him. I used to hear him on the radio all the time, when he would come to play the Tic-Toc in Boston. This was before I got to New York. If he didn’t sing Sleepy Time Down South, I’d get an attitude, because the band would play [Haynes sings “bap, doo, bah-bah, doo-buh” and snaps his fingers on the backbeat]. This was the tempo. The whole thing would knock me out. So when I got a chance to play with him, hey, buddy, I loved all of that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let’s go back to – before you left Boston for New York – let’s go back to Boston. You’re working professionally before you even completed high school, and you were working before you got to Luis Russell. Do you want to talk about some of the other bands that you worked with before you got to Luis Russell?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Sabby Lewis had a – he was the most popular one around Boston then, as a bandleader, because he played – one of his big breaks came when he played one of those big radio shows during the early ’40s, which may have been ’42 or ’41. I don’t remember exactly. It was the Bandwagon – something Bandwagon. It was a hookup that would go all over the country – maybe other countries as well. When he played there, he burned. Then he went to New York to play at Kelly’s Stable. Joe Booker was the drummer. That was the guy I was talking about that could swing so much. He had a steel plate in his arm, and he had to go to have something done, or replaced, or something, at one period, and I was to play with the band then. That was my first experience with a band of that size. It worked out pretty good, but one night I saw this brother come in the door – we’re playing the Savoy in Boston – and this brother came in. He came in smiling and looking right to the bandstand. Our eyes met, and I was wondering, who is this guy? He was Osie Johnson, coming to play with the band, and I didn’t know. Osie always says I was playing until he got there. Sabby didn’t let me know. I thought I was – I thought I had the gig there. When Osie came in, he was smiling from ear to ear, from the door, walking to

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: the bandstand. He came up, maybe not on the same set. The next set, he played. He was so fast – they didn’t have any drum music – Osie was so fast, he was reading the trumpet parts. This guy [?]. Then later on, that band, I tell you, they were used to a drummer swinging. He was so busy reading, they say, “Yeah, but he’s not swinging.” They would always complain. Those guys could complain their butt off in the band. This guy was doing that. This guy was that. That was one of things they would do in Boston. In fact it was always the guy that couldn’t play that much that would complain. He could read music, read his butt off . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Still today.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: . . . but as far as improvising and …, he didn’t have it. Those guys would complain. Anyhow, Osie went. That’s the first time meeting him. Then I played with another band, the band that Paul Gonsalves used to play with. That was Phil Edmond. They were all from the Cape area of Massachusetts. I think Paul was from Pawtucket, Rhode Island, somewhere around in there. They had a lot of hard music, like a Jimmie Lunceford-type band, a lot of broken-up, cut-up music. But it was a good band. I caught hell there, man. They used to call me the Kid, because I was the youngest in the band. They say, “Kid, Kid, come on.” The bandleader used to say, “Kid, where’s your memory? Where’s your memory?” I’d forget this and forget that. He said, “Where’s your memory?” But it was a beautiful period. Then I think Paul – I don’t know what happened to Paul, but they had another tenor player that came from Gary, Indiana, named Lester Shackleford. Lester’s the first one that told me about Charlie Parker.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Can we get some chronology here? Can we figure out how long you were with the Lewis band and then how long you – or when?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I joined Luis’s band 1945. That was after all these other bands.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I mean not – Sabby Lewis.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Sabby Lewis I only stayed with a matter of weeks before . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Osie showed up.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: . . . Osie came in and told me to get up. He didn’t tell me to get up, but he might as well have. I’m very young.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When I went to New York, Sabby had owed me some money. I’m big time now. I’m going to New York. I say, “Sabby.” The word was – I was very independent then, even. Just starting, I’m independent. You’re supposed to ask for some money, or more money than they’re paying. I started out doing that with Sabby. One time I sent him a letter from New York. He owed me some money. He said, “How much is it?” He said, “You know that’s more than what we pay.” But it worked.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let me get some spellings here. Sabby – S-a-b-b-y?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Right.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: L-e-w-i-s?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Right

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Okay. And the next band?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Phil Edmond.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Edmond – E-d-m-o-n-d?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Right.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Okay. How long were you with Phil’s band?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I was with that band for quite a while. I don’t know how long – maybe a year, maybe less than a year – because in that period Phil had a steady job at one of these clubs in Boston. Then it was called Little Dixie, owned by the Italians.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Playing what kind of charts? You had a big band. Were they original charts?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That one – that wasn’t – that was – what did he have? Two trumpets. He had maybe two saxophones, alto, tenor. They were doubling something. I don’t know if there was a baritone. Maybe there was. I think he was the only trumpet, I think at that time. I don’t know if we had a trombone. But he had a few horns. Maybe six or seven pieces, something like that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: And you were with that band for how long?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That was [?]. I was there for maybe a year or so, I figure. We also had to play shows sometimes in there. I remember we were playing for shake dances. I remember that was one of the first times I heard that song Black and Tan Fantasy. [Haynes sings a

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: phrase from the piece]. The girls would be shaking their butt off. [Haynes continues the phrase]. I loved all of that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Did you all rehearse when they had a band – when a show come in?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh yeah. We used to rehearse a lot.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you rehearsed during the day?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: We’d rehearse, yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So then you went from Sabby to Phil Edmond and then to Luis Russell?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Not immediately, because I went to Connecticut to play for a while. That’s where I met this alto saxophonist Charlie Holmes, whom had played with Louis Armstrong and Luis Russell. He told Luis Russell about me. Luis Russell had never heard me. He sent me a special delivery letter. We were playing at Martha’s Vineyard, part of Cape Cod there.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: With - when you say “we,” who was with you?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I was still with Phil Edmond. I did send him back a telegram. I told him I was interested in joining the band, but I couldn’t join until after Labor Day, because that was a summer gig that we had. Then I come to New York.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you started out making 12 bucks a week playing in a trio. Then how much were you making by the time you were getting ready to leave Phil Edmond?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I don’t know what it was then. It was much more though, but I don’t remember. I guess I remember that 12 because it was my first weekly salary playing drums.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I was just trying to get a feel for what the fees were like back in those days.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: A summer gig. I don’t know if it was 25 or what. Maybe.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: And traveling. Were you doing much?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: We would travel from Boston to New Hampshire and then drive back. If we had a couple of gigs we’d stay over somewhere.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Did you have band uniforms? Do you remember if you had . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Good question. I don’t remember. They must have. But a lot of those – in Boston, a lot of times naturally it would be black suit, black tie. That was traditional.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So now it’s after Labor Day. What year?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That was 1945.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you say, okay, I’m going to go head into this gig with Luis Russell. So what happened when you showed up for the gig?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The thing about it, I had a feeling to want to play with a big band right after, and that thing came right on time, to go to New York. I started at the Savoy Ballroom with him, and the Apollo Theater, and all those places.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Who else was in the band?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh boy. There were some older guys in the band. They always had a singer – a male singer. There was one saxophonist, played tenor, from Harlem: Ed [?] – he didn’t continue on. He was good. Then they started getting some younger players in the band. They got a younger trombone player from New Orleans, who’s still playing. His hair is white now. He’s younger than I am. Emery Thompson, his name is. He was with the band. He wasn’t there when I joined, but I think he come in while I was there. They had a singer by the name of Lee Richardson that was making – had hit records. I had stayed with the band one year, I quit, and then I went back when Lee had these records coming out. Once we played the Earl Theater in Philadelphia. Nat Cole was headlining, but Lee Richardson was kicking butt. All them little girls – all the girls would come. I had a feature drum thing with the band. So it was very exciting, playing all those theaters and dances.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let’s talk about that trip to New York. So here you’re going down to play with Luis Russell. What happens? You got to get a place to stay. You’re going to New York.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No, Luis Russell told me I could stay at his house until I got situated, until his wife practically told me, you’ve got to get your own room now, because I was going to 52nd Street the nights we weren’t working, coming back in at 5 o-clock in the morning, and I was living – staying in the living room. You know what I mean? Sleeping all day. So that didn’t look – this young boy from Boston.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So where did you finally end up living?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: One day, he says his wife had the a-s-s. So he says to me, “You better go to the Y, get you a room.” I was really not Y[MCA] material. I don’t know if I like the Y. So I

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: was walking from – he lived at 159th Street and Broadway, one of the slick, tall buildings. So I’m walking from there to the Y, which is 135th Street. En route there, I meet this piano player whom I had played with in Connecticut, where I met Charlie Holmes on that gig. He says, “My landlady has a room.” I went over there. It was a brownstone on 149th Street between Amsterdam and Broadway, which in those days was a very nice neighborhood. Still pretty good now. I had a door there for – it was about $5 a week. It had a fireplace and everything in it, really. It was wild. It was a wild period.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Who else lived in that neighborhood? Were there other musicians living there?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Good question. Bird had lived – not the same time, but on the same street, down there. Kansas Fields, a drummer, had lived in that same block. A trumpet player from Duke Ellington’s band, deceased – not Cat Anderson. One of the others had lived there. A lot of guys had lived there. A lot of musicians lived in that area. That was Sugar Hill. Miles [Davis] lived around the corner. I was 149th. He was 147th. He lived – some people from East St. Louis – in fact the record Sippin’ at Bells, they had a restaurant called Bells. It was Bob Bell and George Bell, two brothers. One was a musician and the other wasn’t. They owned a couple houses – buildings. So Miles lived there, around the corner. I stayed there until this West Indian guy bought the house. I was – what he did, he started chopping up the room when he bought the house. He made the room next to me bigger. So that would make my room smaller. In the meantime, I’m bringing these girls by my room. He was – he had the walls, they weren’t complete. I got an attitude. I’m going to have this room – I don’t want this guy next door to see what’s happening in my room. So I took her to a hotel. So I got attitude. I told this guy I wasn’t going to pay my rent. He told the landlord. The landlord come up there one morning, knocking on my door. He had these thick eyeglasses. He said, “If you don’t have your rent paid by 12 o’clock, you’ll be lock out.” 12 o’clock I moved out. Before 12. I had one of my buddies with his car. We moved out all my – so I started living in hotels after that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Coming down from Boston, you must have brought your own drum set.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I think I must have sent my drums early, before I arrived, to Luis Russell’s house. I got all these fiber cases. I was very big time.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you didn’t have drums in the apartment. You had them just at the clubs?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: But they were in Luis Russell’s apartment. He had a room in the back. He didn’t let me stay in that room in the back, though, because he told me I would have to go through his bedroom. He had this young wife. You know what I’m saying. That wouldn’t work.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you’re hitting it with Luis Russell. You’re getting to know all the musicians in New York.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I had known all them before, like Coleman Hawkins. I used to love Don Byas. I had met all of these guys before I got to New York. That’s why I was hanging on 52nd Street.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Are you starting to go to any jam sessions or anything once you hit New York?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Of course.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Where were you going?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Minton’s on Monday night was the thing.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Who was – do you have any recollections, any memories, from those early days in New York?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Of course. I can’t think of all the recollections at this point, but man, it was – first of all, let me say this. New York at that time was so beautiful. Harlem, oh, man. Sugar Ray Robinson’s bar. It was just very exciting. You could see anybody. Joe Louis – all the champions, they’d come to the clubs and listen to you play. It was an exciting period almost all over the world, but New York was the Mecca. The music.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: And Harlem.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Harlem. You didn’t have to – a lot of people – a lot of old people would say, they wouldn’t leave Harlem to go to heaven. That was the saying. It was everything there, everything, so much beauty, so much life, so much warmth, so much togetherness.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I’m not going to ask you what happened.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh please. All over the world the same thing has happened. No, all over our country, the same thing has happened, all the cities.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: But when you got there in ’45, it was still thriving? You had . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh man, it was thriving way after that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What about the consciousness of the people, particularly the black community? Was there the sense of pride that . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You said it. It was a lot of love. Naturally, getting back to the musicians, there were less of us, and we were closer together. I’ve been thinking about that a lot lately. It was like – you talk about family. You could drive with the top down if you had a convertible. Stop for the red lights. A woman could be driving. I heard some of the ladies say that. It’s such a great place. It was beautiful. I guess it was too beautiful. It had to be destroyed. It was destroyed. All of the cities, though. I go to Philly. I go to Detroit. D.C., Boston. I was in Boston last week. I couldn’t wait to get out.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: But Harlem in particular.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh boy.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Because during the ’20s, you had the Harlem Renaissance. You had this growing black consciousness, a sense of self, a sense of pride, that manifests itself in this cultural – you had poetry. You had Duke Ellington music. You had the arts. Then of course the ’30s with the Depression, but still the music was thriving. Then the ’40s there seemed to be a resurgence. I think you really are capturing that. I’m trying to figure out – because most jazz histories say bebop was a revolution, but they only talk about it as a revolution taking place in a vacuum. Nobody talks about the cultural environment of Harlem, and here you are talking about how it was a family.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It felt that way. Like the Savoy Ballroom, they had certain nights where – they were called kitchen mechanic nights. All the workers, the females – I don’t know if they got in free, but everyone would be there. Let me tell you this short story about the Apollo. I heard this many years later. Played Apollo Theater. There were a group of drummers that would be in the audience for the first show. During those days you did five, six, shows a day at the Apollo Theater.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Starting at what time?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: In the morning. A.M. I don’t remember exactly. But I mean, if it was a hot show, where the people were coming, they’d have lines, so they would do – they would add shows. It wouldn’t be a contract saying you had to do this amount. They would add. Every time you come off, you’d see what time the half was – the half hour before the show. So I’m this youngster, playing with Luis Russell’s band. Nervous, yeah. Playing a show. I learned one thing with Luis Russell. He says, “If you ever get lost, lose the meter, or you lose your place, playing for something,” he said, he told me to roll. If you roll, there’s no bap-bap-bap-bap-bap. There’s no time. It’s almost like playing free. That’s

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: how I learned to play free, because you don’t give no definite beat. You just let it flow. So I got that from Luis Russell, when you roll. Anyhow, many years later, after I became – I’m in my thirties or forties. I’m with Panama Francis. Panama was one of the hot drummers from that area. He played with Cab [Calloway]. He used to play with Lucky Millinder a lot. He told me that they would always wait in the front row – a group of drummers – so if the drummer couldn’t play the show, they would get the gig for the week. If a new drummer with a band or a young guy come in that couldn’t play the show, you wouldn’t work that week. You have to be off or something [?]. Panama told me this many years later. He said, “When you came, them guys looked at each other and said, we might as well go home.” That’s the whole … It was so great. But I managed to weather the storm. I did it, whatever it was to do. It looked a little stormy in there to me.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Was there – you talk about a family, not only just the community at large, maybe not only just the musician community. What about drummers?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. I thought of that when I said it.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Who was a member of that family?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It grew. Naturally Max, Klook, Art. Joe Harris came in. He was younger than me. Teddy – Teddy from Kansas City – Teddy Stewart, swing his butt off. He was with Dizzy’s big band. We were about the same age and we come around the same time, Teddy and myself. Art Blakey’s with Bill Eckstine’s big band. I’m excited about that. I remember there was a place in Harlem called the Club Sudan. Art – at that time I lived at 117th or 118th Street, the first-floor apartment. I would go to the Club Sudan and sit on the bandstand. Art would be playing. The whole bandstand would be shaking. He have – you could feel the vibe coming up through the wood. Rrrrrrrr. Roughing it off. Playing for dances. The whole thing. After we get off, I’d hang out with him, go by his house, hang around with him until daylight. Guy keep me out all night. Even the last days, before he – he had me at one of the clubs in New York. I think it was when the wake for – what was that writer’s name? He was living in France when he passed away.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: James Baldwin.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: James Baldwin, exactly. The wake. I run into him at Michael’s. I think they went to Michael’s after the wake. He was trying to get away from the people there. He was driving one car. I was driving my car. He says, “Follow me downtown.” He goes

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: through all these back streets. He’s driving his butt off. I said, this brother had a lot of energy. I used to hang out with him a lot in the early days. It was a lot of closeness, like I said. It was something that happened then that you don’t feel a lot of now, maybe because we were all younger then, or whatever, or we’ve all – the few of us who are left – become so sophisticated.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What did you guys talk about when you were all young? Here you guys are in your early twenties. You guys are all rising jazz stars. You’re at the top of the world.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When you’re around Art, Art does a lot of the talking.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What did he talk about?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: He talked about a lot of things. He would tell some fibs, too, tell you some stories. “Ain’t that right, bro? Ain’t that right?” You’ve been around Art. Then Max [Roach]. Max was very intellectual. He knew he was. I would have my say periodically, but I would do more listening than talking. I’ll tell you one thing today. Not to put any youngsters down, but they do all the – they know everything. They seem to me – I can’t say they know everything, but it seems like they know everything. It’s great. I can learn. But there’s always something missing, to know so much. Take a break.
[recording interrupted]

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Kimery
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Kimery: There’s nowhere to go. Did you turn that off or on?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I’ll turn it back on now.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No, I’m going to leave that alone.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You don’t have to worry. They can’t implicate you. That happened 50 years ago. There’s nothing they can say. And besides, it wasn’t true. What was that scene like though, the whole drug scene? A lot of people talk about it.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You mean back – way back then?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah, back then.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh, I don’t want to go too – that far with that, because all the drugs were better then. Now you got a lot of stuff that they make, that they’re trying to replace that with. They’re trying to make you crazy with what they make for you. It was designed for you. That I know.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Do you think that it was purposely or consciously being filtered into Harlem?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: To all the Harlems of our country, yes. Are you kidding me? All the Harlems.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: To what end?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: To the South end.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: For what purpose?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: For what purpose? To design us to be certain ways, especially the youngsters coming up. To put them in a certain mode. Next.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let’s continue on. You’re with Luis Russell. You’re in the center of jazz in the world. You’re playing with a hot band. You’re playing in all the major ballrooms, Savoy, Apollo. Then what?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: After – I stayed with the band a year, like I said. We would travel by bus. I was tired of that bus after the first year. And growing up in Boston, we’d get to places like Maryland. To see the attitude with some people with that race situation. That was my first time seeing it outright. It was probably – it could have been sneaky in other places. My father was more hip to it than me, but then he was – my father had a way of working all around that anyhow. So I watched the way he was, and I think some of that rubbed off on me. I didn’t let a lot of things bother me that they would think necessarily would have to bother me. I don’t know.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When you say you worked around it, you’re just talking about trying to get around the whole Jim Crow and having to be Steppin’ Fetchit.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I had ways of, I guess, of maneuvering. I remember – even in Boston – I was in the Boy Scouts, like I said earlier. They had – I was Troop Six. That was the Shaw House. It was black. One time, the Norfolk House was near me. It was probably as close to me as the Shaws. The Norfolk House was white. That was near where I went to school, almost across the street from the Dudley School. So one time I’m going to go put on my uniform and go up and check out their Scout. I forget what their troop number was. I went up there, and it was practically – I knew it. I said, “Okay, what’s up?” They said,

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: “No . . .” – they froze there. I was still at the same school across the street, but I couldn’t go to their scout meeting.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So that’s really your first experience with segregation?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s my first experience outright that I could really check out, see about that. They don’t want me here.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What about your mother’s church?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What about it?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: As far as integrated or segregated?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The church was in our section of town then. Probably you’d see some white people come to there. Very few. I know there was an Italian guy called Brother Tony. I used to see him. He used to come with this bald head. He used to come there. He was Sanctified, because my mother went to a Sanctified church, Pentecostal.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Did you go too?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Did I go too?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Did you go to church?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: My mother made me go to church.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
