Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Did you participate in music-making in church.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Very good question. My uncle had a church that we would go to sometime, my mother’s brother, Pentecost. He had a bass drum in there. You couldn’t keep me out of that church. But he used to want to play the bass drum. After he found out I could play it, it wasn’t too cool, because he wanted to play the bass drum. So I played it as much as I could. Then my mother had some cymbals. You’d play them together. I’d play all in my church. I used to get down. You know they had the beat there.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Sanctified Church.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The tambourine and everything. I went to church so much that I got tired of – I used to have to go to Sunday School. I got tired of that. So after I started working nights, I started dropping out a little.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Okay, so this was the digression from your experiences touring down South and having to confront racism.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No, I got really tired of . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The road.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Because I didn’t hardly get too much involved with the racism there, but I could see it when the bus would pull up, somebody would ask a question, and somebody in the street and that whole thing. I could see. It was a change. I’m from up North a little, where it’s there, but I didn’t always have to deal with it. I went back with the band, stayed another year, after I had quit. Then, after that, 1947, I joined Lester Young, at the Savoy Ballroom also. That was a little band. I wanted to get with a little band then anyhow. It was cool.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How did that come out? How did that work out?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It worked out good.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I mean, how did that come to – how did you – how did that work?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Dense Thornton – Sadik Hakim – was playing piano in there.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Argonne Thornton?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What did you call him?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Dense Thornton.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Dense

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: D-e-n-s-e. I think that was his first name, before Sadik Hakim. Dense. On some records it says Dense Thornton. I knew him around 52nd Street as Dense.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s Omar’s . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s what?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s Omar Hakim’s father.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Right – no, no, no. That’s another guy. The trombone player is Omar’s father, not . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Sadik Hakim, no? We’re worry about that later. We’ll clean that up.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Another Hakim is the father. It’s not the same guy. He plays trombone. Dense didn’t – I don’t think Dense had any kids. If he did . . .
[Omar Hakim is the son of the trombonist Hasaan Hakim.]

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I thought his name was Argonne Thornton.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah, Argonne. Maybe Dense was his nickname.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Okay.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Argonne was his real name. You got me on that one. But yeah, he didn’t have – if he did have kids, they wouldn’t be all black, because he loved blond ladies. Can you keep that in there?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Sure.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I think I might have a taste. Go ahead brother.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Are you married by this time?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Was I married at this time?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No. We’re talking about ’47. Let’s talk about how you hooked up. So Dense introduces you? How did he facilitate this?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No. He knew about me, because I think we probably had played gigs or something together, because he used to be around Miles. He was on that record with Bird and Miles anyhow. He played piano on those records.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. ’45 sessions on Savoy. Ko-Ko.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Like I say, once certain people in the music – it was almost like a family, so different people knew me. He told the manager, who was Charlie Carpenter. I started with them at the Savoy in that same week.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Of?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Of Lester Young.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Okay.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I think that’s who either come by to get me or something. I started with them right at the Savoy. In that same week they had to play at Town Hall one night and accompany Billie Holiday. So I was really into that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s well documented. That history with you, and the use of the word “slave.” He said – what did he say?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh yeah. He wouldn’t hear that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: If you want to tell me. Whatever you want to be on the official record.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: He thought I was swinging. He told me that after I played a couple tunes. He said, “You’re sure swinging Pres. If you have eyes, the slave is yours.” I stayed there two years. I hope that’s the last time I have to say that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Okay. That will be the only time you have to say it here.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: See, some people don’t know how he meant that, or they don’t know how he spoke. So when you start saying, or when it starts getting out, people say it, they say it wrong, say the wrong thing. A lot of the black musicians, they started a lot of the lingo that still is around now, that’s used on t.v. and all of these – a lot of the lingo came from the musicians. “Having eyes.” That was – a lot of the – what he meant is something you like. Say it to someone else, they don’t know what the hell you’re talking about. That’s why I hate to – I keep saying it over and over, and somebody gets this out of it. Then they say it. I say no, it wasn’t like that. It was like this. He meant, “You’re playing your ass off. You’re swinging. I like it. The job is yours.” We call – a job was a “slave.” I’m sure you know about that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you spent a time with Pres. Pres must have been – in ’47 Pres was – that was the cat. He created the languages. He had the dress. He . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: He was original all the way round, I thought. Monk reminded me a lot of Lester Young.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Who else was in the band?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Shorts McConnell, playing trumpet. On bass was – oh boy. I forget. I ccould see him. The bass player, he used to go to the Catholic Church, and Shorts McConnell. Shorts used to hit all the high notes with Bill Eckstine and Earl Hines. Then he had sort of lost his chops. It was there, but it wasn’t the same as it used to be. They used to go to church a lot, the bass player – Briscoe – Ted Briscoe, from Washington, D.C., and Lester Young nicknamed them the Religious Brothers. He had a nickname for everybody. He’d say, “You two are Religious Brothers.”

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What was the nickname he had for you?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Not too much. He used to call me the Royal of Haynes. I didn’t hear him have any other titles for me.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Were you composing any music by this time yourself?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No, I was just trying to compose the drums and the drum parts. No I wasn’t.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Who were your? – who were the drummers? – were you? – I know you were hanging out with Bu – Art Blakey – and Max, and Klook’s back on the set after the war now. Did you spend much time with Klook?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Every now and then. When he first come back out of the service, he did take me aside one time and tell me that he thought it was very different what I was trying to play.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What was he specifically – what was that in reference to?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What I was playing on the drums. I can’t say what it was. I don’t know. Whatever I was trying to do, he thought it was very different. That’s what he had told me.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Max – did Max say anything about what you were doing?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yes, yes. I do remember – maybe it was 1947 or ’48. We’re playing at a place called the Royal Roost. Max is there. In fact that’s where Klook had come in. I was playing with Lester Young then. After the gig was over that night, I think Max and I were going to the subway together. Max says, “That was a hell of a 16 bar you played on that tune.” I said, oh my God. I didn’t even realize it was a 16 bar. It was – the song was Lover Come Back to Me, which is long, and I played the bridge. I know the feeling of the bridge, the feeling of the amount of bars, but I never thought in terms of how many bars it was. When he threw that at me, “That was a hell of a 16-bar solo you played,” I said, oh, shit, because I wasn’t thinking of it in terms of 16 bars. I could feel 16 bars, 32 bars, naturally 8 bars, but I wasn’t necessarily counting it. I said, this guy is . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Nowadays most people, even though they may be playing with another band, also are taking up other gigs. During the time you were working with Pres, were you also working with other people too?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Not too often, because we were working pretty steady.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Were you doing tours, while you were with Norman Granz – no, not Norman Granz.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. We were traveling all over the country, a lot of different places. There was some time off. Maybe sometime in between I would do something with somebody else, with Babs Gonzales or somebody – something uptown.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Can we backtrack and go back to your first recording session?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: First recording session was with Luis Russell’s big band. Interesting thing about that, when I go to places like England, one of the older guys will tell me the record, the name of it, and tell me he has it. I think somebody give it to me on cassette, so it should be around here. I just got this past summer. Because a lot of the American people, they’re not aware of it, that I recorded it. Or a lot of other records that I made as a leader, they’re not even aware of it, like say, I did a few on Prestige. I did one called Cymbalism that I never hear, hardly hear anything about. There are a few. We know about We Three. I did one called Just Us. That was after We Three – never hear anything about, as a leader. There’s several more. My first record date as a leader was 1954 in Europe, in Denmark. It was then, I think, EmArcy – which was Bob Shad – had put it out. It was his last 10-inch. A lot of times I remember myself as being one of the last of certain things. It was the last 10-inch. Then they put it out on a 12-inch – that’s what came after the 10-inch – disc called Jazz Abroad, with Roy Haynes and Quincy Jones. Did I tell you that before? You’re smiling like crazy.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: They had it in that same order.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Top bill.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Jesus. If I look around here I may even find it somewhere.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let’s go back to that first recording session. Were you nervous? It was your first record.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: With Luis Russell?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Uh-hmm.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I was nervous all the time. Are you kidding me? I was nervous all the time. Somebody asked me – I was on Gil Noble t.v., when they put out that Charlie Parker story. Gil Noble asked me – see, now, here’s a guy. This is a brother, too, and Max is the one that invited me there, because I think he really just wanted Max. A.T. [Art Taylor] was on it too, and Jackie Mac [McLean] and Dizzy. I don’t know if he particularly wanted me, but Max had told me. Anyhow, when we did it in two sections, during the break between the two sections, I happened to be talking to Gil. I said, “Yes” I said, “I replaced Max with Charlie Parker.” Gil says, “Oh really?” So when we went back on the air, we’re taping again, he brings it up in a way as if it wasn’t so, whatever, and it puts me on the spot. So I talk about it. I say exactly what happened, what had happened. Max and Dizzy, they had to get together, because it’s bringing back the memories to them. I recall – I may be jumping a little – in 1949 Max and Miles were both with Bird. Miles leaves Bird to go to work at a place in Brooklyn.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Soldier’s?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Soldier[?], and I’m his drummer. Then, after that gig, we went to across the street from the Three Deuces. The name had changed from the Onyx Room to the Orchid Room. You know that. You got that already. It’s Bud Powell, Nelson Boyd, myself, Sonny Stitt, and I think maybe Miles. We’re burnin’. That’s where Max had come to ask me to replace him with Bird. I didn’t say yes or no. I didn’t say no “Yeah, man.” He came back. He said, “If you don’t want to make it, I’ll get Kansas Fields.” So I say that on t.v. And they both start laughing. Dizzy was saying, “Yeah, there was always Kansas Fields there.” There was another drummer named Jack the Bear – Jackie Parker. They would always get – if they needed a drummer, it was either Kansas or Jackie. They all could swing, these guys in Harlem, wherever. So they started laughing at that, because they knew it was true. Then Bird comes over himself, maybe the next night, and asks me himself to join his band, 1949, September or October.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you couldn’t refuse that offer.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I didn’t. But then something else – I’m going to talk about it later. I’m not going to talk about it here. I may talk about it tomorrow, if I remember.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Go ahead. We’re here now.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No, I can’t put everything here. I’ve got to save something.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh, okay.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You got to save something for whenever, whichever.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So before we went on this digression, we were still with Pres. You’re working with Pres.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. Up until ’49. So that’s almost – only reason I left Pres – I was at the Three Deuces with Kai Winding for that summer. I did that because Lester Young went with Norman Granz Jazz at the Philharmonic. That was the first time he had went since I had been with him. That was during the summer. I started getting more gigs and more record dates and getting a little more popular around on the scene. So I didn’t go back with Pres after that, when he started back in September, whenever it was.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How long was that group together, with you, Miles, Nelson Boyd, and Sonny Stitt?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: In those days you made that gig and then you probably made a couple other gigs after that, kept going different ways. The scene was a lot different then. There was a lot of naughtiness going on.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You were working with Bud. You’ve done a lot of different things with Bud. Was that . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Bud was fresh then. That was before he had went to that hospital for 18 months. That was before that. When he came out of there, which may have been ’50 or ’51, they had interjected him with a whole bunch of whatever. He was almost like a vegetable at some points.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Then you’re working with Bird. What was . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: We never rehearsed anything. Just went right in. It was beautiful.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Who was in the band, if Miles had already left?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Red Rodney. Red Rodney was there. Tommy Potter. Al Haig, I think.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Al Haig.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Then sometimes Kenny Dorham was with us. I’ll never the forget the summer of – I guess it was June or July of 1950, which would have been the following year. We go into Café Society in the Village for four weeks, which was a long gig in New York,

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: opposite Art Tatum. Imagine playing opposite Art Tatum, and you’re playing with Bird, for four weeks. Opening night you can’t get in the place, and Billie Holiday comes up and sings with us. Can you imagine all that? We’re wearing ties and suits. I don’t even know if they had it air conditioned in the club in those days. But it was such a beautiful period. That was a beautiful time. Jesus. I couldn’t wait to go to work at night. The feeling. Lovely. I’m glad I did the period when I did, even came along, because it was so much – things today – like people say, “How does it compare with today?” – a lot of things. This is such a very computerized button-pushing period. Quality is not too important today with a lot of things: with the food that you eat, the clothes that you wear, a lot of things, even automobiles. You can go and get an automobile like that. It’s a lot of plastic. A very synthetic period. So I’m glad I was here before to – not that I can’t adjust to it. I’m not particularly restless, but it’s such a difference with everything. A lot of people seem to be hungry, greedy. The true feeling of love with a lot of things seems to be very synthetic.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let’s talk about that first car you got – you’re so proud of in that picture. You’re talking about cars.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah, the hood was long.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you were making good . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Just that period, that time, that time period. I drive where I bought the car from. It’s now a high-rise building there. Used to be a car lot. Just that period of time when I did that seemed so important and so special. I see people older than myself talk about the period when they came along, but things have really changed. I guess really you know this. I’ll be 70 years old in 10 months.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Next March.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Jesus. I don’t think everybody that’s this age talks the same. But it’s been a great life. It been so great to be in this music and go all over and meet people. Sometimes you meet people who are real nice. You do. You get a chance to meet a lot of different people. There are some beautiful people on this earth. When you run into them, and you can feel it, I cherish it, because there’s so much other crap going on that’s, to me, a lot of it is unnecessary, but it’s – I don’t know – everybody seems to be – not everybody, but a lot of people fear, fear this, they fear that, instead of just letting your true self come out. Enjoy people. Enjoy life. Enjoy the music. I hear the word “jazz” and the word “bebop.” They turn me off, in a way, because the way they’re said. Like sometimes, if I’m introduced to somebody, say, “That’s Roy Haynes. He’s a jazz drummer” or “He’s a jazz musician.” Years ago, I didn’t hear that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I’d hear, “He’s a musician.” Everything is so categorized. All that’s by design. They categorize this, categorize – even for the records. Years ago, if you had a record, your record could be in the record shop in the window. Now to get a display, you either got to kiss butt or it cost you a lot of money or you’ve got to be number one on the chart or you’ve got – there’s so much … that wasn’t here then. I had a record on – I didn’t even know it was on the charts back when I did that Out of the Afternoon. We had a single out of Fly Me to the Moon. It wasn’t on the charts per se. But any record that would be number one on the charts, they would list the other versions of that record by other artists. That’s how – I remember I was sitting up in the Queen booking agent, which was owned by Dinah Washington. She said, “Roy Haynes is on the charts.” I looked at her. I say, “Oh …” I didn’t know the difference. It said, “Roy Haynes, Fly Me to the Moon.” Today – I was on some charts my last record, come to think of it. First time maybe since then. Are we rolling or we’re not?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah, we’re rolling. I want to talk about your car, because you’re making money to buy a car. Not everyone’s buying a car.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Then. Yeah, it was amazing then. It was then. You could count the drummers. Car. I had a convertible with the top down.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Describe it for us. What brand, etc.? And how much did you pay for it?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It was a 19 . . . – a late – what was it? I bought it in 1950. So it was a late ’49 98 convertible Oldsmobile, light gray. I remember having it parked in front of Café Society. The hood was as long as this room then. It was when they had the last of the rocket engines. The top was down. I was coming out of Café Society with Bird and Chan. Chan was young and beautiful then. Chan says to Bird, “Bird, is that a Cadillac?” And Bird says, “Yes.” It was an Oldsmobile. But oh man, it was so beautiful. Not only the car, but just – but I had money before I went with Bird. It wasn’t – people say, “How you playing with Bird and buying a new car?”

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Was the money okay when you were working with Bird? I mean, did he . . . he didn’t handle the money? Otherwise you might not have got paid.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When we would play Philadelphia – Bird never stayed in Philly, because he said if he did stay there, he would be arrested. He’d be busted. So he would commute. It would take money to commute. By the end of the week, sometimes there was no money there. The union would be there. The union man would be at a lot of the clubs when we played Philly. We’d be there until almost daylight, waiting to get whatever else was scrambled up. We didn’t make a lot of money in those days, but it was cool enough for me to do what I wanted to do. I made less money with Lester Young. With Lester Young

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I made $100 a week, and they took tax out of that. I made around 90 – taxes were very low, maybe 4 or 5 dollars – I made – I got around $96. That wasn’t considered too much, even then.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you worked with Bird pretty much – you had the Café Society gig.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That was the longest gig that we had.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Then following that?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I can’t remember everything. I do remember the four weeks there. I think we got the strings right after that. We may have went into Birdland. Yeah, that’s what happened, because that gig was advertised for strings, I think, Café Society, but then we did it at Birdland, which would have been maybe the last part of July, maybe something like that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You had rehearsals for that?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Every day.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Was Mitch Miller – was he . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That was only on the recording?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Tommy Mace was playing. Tommy Mace was playing oboe. I think he made some of the records. I think Mitch Miller may have done the initial record – LP, as they were called.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How was that, working with strings?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I enjoyed it, but naturally, being young, I wanted to get down. Sometimes we played a little – just with the quartet.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Your parents, by this time they’ve accepted the fact that . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: My parents were cool a long time. My father was cool. My mother got it, because I carried myself. I didn’t get in no trouble. I never caused no problems. I’d bring home a little money. I was buying things for the house.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Your father wanted you to be a jockey. What did your mother want you to be?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You remember that, huh? My father must have thought that we were in another country, huh? He wanted me to be a jockey back – what? – in the ’30s or ’40s. I was very little. He wasn’t much bigger.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: But your mom accepted . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: My mother, she never did preach what she wanted me to be.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Just as long as you was happy.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I guess as long as I was cool and doing – so to speak – doing the right thing.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So when did you get married?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I got married – hmm – good question – in the ’50s – late ’50s.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh, the late ’50s.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: And then I left Sarah Vaughan.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Okay. Let’s backtrack. So you’re already with Bird, doing Bird and strings. So, early ’50s. After you left Bird, or probably while you’re working with Bird, you’re working with some other folks then too.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: In between, because we didn’t work steady, steady during that period. Miles used to say then that Bird stole his drummer.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: But you ended up recording with Miles in the early ’50s.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: ’51, I think it was

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: ’51. You didn’t – your first trip to Europe wasn’t until ’54. Is that correct?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: ’54, right, with Sarah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you’re working mostly small ensemble jazz gigs at this time? You weren’t doing other things. You weren’t doing Broadway shows or any soundtracks, any of those kinds of things. Basically live groups.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No, but after Sarah that almost came about. There was some – a little interest there. The bassist Joe Benjamin, he started going that direction, and I was thinking about it. But I’m glad I didn’t go that direction.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How did you hook up with Sarah? How did that come about?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: George Treadwell was her manager. I think we had played – even when I was with Lester Young, we played Chicago for a few weeks. Sarah was there, so I had to accompany her there. He was always hoping from then on that I’d be Sarah’s drummer. And she liked me. I went and did that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Had you done much touring across other parts of the country? Had you gone to California yet? Or had you gone to the Midwest?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I went to California with Pres – Lester Young.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What’d you think?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let me tell you what I thought about California. Good question. That was the first time I had went to Cal – I think – I don’t know if we played Frisco. We went to Seattle first. We played Seattle for a couple of weeks, maybe a few weeks. It was the Washington Social Club. That was the name of the place. That was like a private after[­ hours] – we would go to work at midnight. Then we went to San Francisco. From San Francisco we went to L.A. Going to L.A. – I had never been to Europe at that point, but it felt like it was in another country, because drummers came out of the woodwork. I remember one drummer, Lawrence Marable. He was a kid then. Then I was staying – Lester Young had – he had this big house someplace. I think it was his first wife. I don’t know if it was his first wife, but his wife was there. All these drummers started coming by there after the – I’m this young guy, and I hadn’t made any records that they were aware of. All the drummers and musicians started coming by to hang out with me. Pres said, “Oh yeah, I know about it,” because he went through it too, when he was the Pres. It was so wild. They hadn’t heard anything like that. That was the feeling. So it was great.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Pres’s brother was probably in L.A.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Lee Young.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Lee Young.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I don’t remember if I met Lee that time or later. I remember meeting his sister. But I met Lee – we used to hang around later, when he was with Nat Cole we traveled a lot, when I was with Sarah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How were you received in Frisco and also in Seattle?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That was great. That was great. I met a lot of good people, nice ladies. I was enjoying it.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So then Sarah basically is where you got to go to Europe . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That was the first time I went to Europe, yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: . . . did extensive recording, lots of different contexts for your musical . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah, yeah. That was enjoyable too.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How about getting along with musical directors and having to put up with conductors? What was that relationship like?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: We didn’t have to deal with that, because the conductors would be out of the band. It wouldn’t be – it would either be Jimmy Jones, or John Malachi was the other at first. Jimmy had studied conducting. I was free to – we had a tight trio, because we would take the arrangements – the big-band arrangements – and make – they would just grow into arrangements. They got pretty intricate without somebody saying, “Here’s a part.” It was just loose enough to make your own part, and it really happened.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So you were composing your own parts in these arrangements.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s right. Just around the arrangement itself, adding to it and putting other things. It’s some very interesting stuff that was loose and then we could vary on it a little bit. You know what I mean?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: And the trio?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It was happy.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It was Joe Benjamin at first and John Malachi. Then Jimmy Jones had come back, because he was sick for a while. Then when he left, I think Ronnell Bright. Then Joe had an automobile accident. I think Richard Davis had come in. Then when Ronnell Bright came in, it started changing, going in another . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So that period, from basically – from ’54 to ’58 – is that? – it was late ’52? When did you . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Go with Sarah?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yes.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I think it was ’53 I joined.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah, that’s what I think so too. So you basically weren’t taking any other gigs. You were working with primarily . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Sometimes I did. I went with Sonny Rollins one time in the Vanguard in between – we would have four weeks off during the summer, so I would take things in between there. I think I did something with Bird in between there too. I think that’s when that famous picture was made, in ’54, down at the Open Door, with Monk, Mingus, Bird, and myself. So I was taking stuff in between, mostly the summer. I think she would take August off.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: There was an article published in ’52 where you were asked what musicians are not getting enough play. You mention Clifford Brown.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I don’t know – no, they thought – I don’t know if they said getting enough play, but they said something about newcomers coming.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Newcomers – well, unknown.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: He always thanked me for that. Who was the other musician? Do you remember?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Sonny.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Sonny Rollins. Yeah, so he started getting play then. That was ’52, huh? Okay. Got you. Sonny? Let me hear from you.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You guys don’t stay in touch?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Return my call, man. Please return my call, Sonny.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How did you meet Clifford Brown.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s – when somebody asks you a question like that – “How did you meet” so-and-so? – that’s hard for a guy in my position, because usually they know about me before I know about them. Usually there’s nothing formal when you say, “This is Roy Haynes.” Usually they come up to you, back in that period, and they start talking to you like they know you. I used to play Philly a lot. He used to come around us when I was with Bird. He used to come. In fact one time he did something. He played. I wish that was captured on some kind of record or something. He played with us a bit with Bird in Philly. Then he was playing with one of those bands. I think it may have been – early ’50s, when I was playing with Hank and Ella. So I think that may have been ’52. He was in New York playing.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You were playing with Hank Jones and Ella Fitzgerald? Is that what you said?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The whole summer, ’52. Nelson Boyd on bass again.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Based in New York. No, Philly. Where?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: We weren’t based. We were working out of New York. I guess we really was based. But we were playing Michigan, Boston, Providence. I did the whole summer with them, ’52. Let’s see. ’52 or ’51? ’52. Yeah, because I still would have been doing little hits with Bird in between there.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Why did you leave Sarah?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Why did I leave? I stayed too long at the fair. I enjoyed it. It was happening, and I was enjoying it. I liked the clubs. I wasn’t making a whole lot of money, but it was pretty steady. I got – I started having children, and I wanted to hang with my children.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Were you able to still maintain your presence on the scene, even through you’re doing . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: With Sarah?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Maintain my presence on the scene.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: As a member of the avant garde.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: To some extent, but not really in the same way for that period. Not really. Because we were playing Birdland, which is on the scene. I just didn’t have to wait long

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: for my money or nothing. Got my money right there. Got in my car and cut out with the fine little ladies.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I guess that leads us into getting married and having children.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: During that period, I was hanging. I was hanging heavy. Even when I was with Bird. There was a lot of fine ladies that were into the music, and nice.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Did you know the Baroness?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Sure I knew the Baroness? Why didn’t I? Yeah, I knew her, but I wasn’t thinking about going that direction.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So, Roy Haynes is now a family man. Roy Haynes is coming off from a five- year stint with Sarah Vaughan, raising a family. So you’re having to juggle now, family commitments and a professional career. Did you find that challenging?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yes, I guess it was challenging, but I made it.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So when . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I think one of the wise things that I did when I was – I bought a house. I bought a two-family house. That was before I was married.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Where was it?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: In Queens. In Hollis. It’s still there.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s where your daughter lives.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah, my daughter’s there.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Leslie.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Craig is there periodically.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Craig is the oldest?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Craig is the oldest.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When was he born?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Hayns: He was born – I forget their ages. He was born in the ’50s when I was with Sarah. He was born when I was with Sarah. I remember I got a – I was working in Washington, D.C., and his mother sent me a telegram.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Announcing his birth?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: His mother’s name?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Lee. I met her when I was with Miles, by the way. She was from Brownsville.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Brownsville?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. That’s Brooklyn. That’s where a lot of the fighters are coming from these days. Mike Tyson’s from there, and Willie Bo[?].

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Her maiden name.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Lee Nevilles.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Nevilles. Can you spell her first name?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: L-e-e.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Sometimes it’s spelled L-e-i-g-h.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Right, right.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Nevilles?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Her folks were from North Carolina. Her father’s still living. He’s maybe close to 100 now, close to it. He’s still in Brooklyn.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Then Leslie. Is she the middle child? Yeah, she has to be.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Leslie is in the middle. She was born the day that Billie Holiday died. That’s July 17th.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I forget. Then Graham – Graham and Craig, they’re both Virgos. August – no, September 16th and 17th.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What was Lee’s occupation, profession?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let’s see. She wanted to study to – she was studying acting for a while, but she never got into it professionally. So she would just work around. She was into the music. Like I say, I was working with Miles when first I’d seen her, not even knowing we’d get hooked up later on.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So in order to facilitate your family life, you would just take gigs here in the New York area? You would minimize your touring?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yes. I had been around a lot. Yeah. That’s when I started doing things with Kenny Burrell a little bit then. The Vanguard – I think we did a record down there. And the Monk thing . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: ’58. Let’s go back to that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: . . . which was a low-paying thing, too.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The Five Spot. But that’s starting to get . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It was a lot of fun, and it was a challenge.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Is that the first time you’d played with Monk? No, because you played with him in ’54, because the picture at the – the famous picture with you, Mingus, Monk, Bird.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Right. Well, he was a sideman then. We were playing . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Bird was the leader of that group?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That was Bird’s gig, yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Okay.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: If I remember correctly, because – what’s the guy? Bob Reisner. Yeah, that was Bird’s thing.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That must have been interesting to have Mingus and Monk and you and Bird in the group. What was the dynamic between Monk and Bird?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I don’t even remember that. I don’t remember. I think – I don’t know if we did a complete week there. We might have done a weekend. I don’t remember exactly. I don’t remember. But I also did some other things with Mingus and Bud [Powell] that was Bud’s gig, so it wasn’t the Mingus that we – even though Mingus went out a little bit while he was there. He went out.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: On Bud’s gig? Yeah, that’s the famous – Mingus storming out.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah, he didn’t go out necessary on. Backstage there was some scenes where – there was some scenes. He was going through different things backstage that ended up seeming like he was the one that was just let out of the hospital and that Bud was the cool one.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: But they now have released, first of all, the Five Spot with Johnny Griffin. That’s been released. That’s been available for a while.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. That was out legitimately, I think.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Now they’ve released one with Trane [John Coltrane].

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah, which I think has a lot of controversy about. He was saying – one writer would say, “I know Roy was with Sarah during that time, so it couldn’t have been him.” These – they think they know so much ... They knew I had time off when I could do others. Who knows when it was? Because I had forgotten about it. They were saying, “Are you sure it’s him?” Oh, man. These people think they know so damn much. They know everything, like them young people I was talking about. How can anybody know everything? Jesus Christ. Hey, I’m sorry.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Here’s to you, Mr. Know-it-all.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Was that the first time you worked with Trane?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Maybe. I don’t remember. Maybe so.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That must have been – how long was that engagement at Five Spot with Monk? How long was that?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That was more than once, too.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Okay.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It wasn’t just – I don’t think it was just one time. It was a whole 16, 18 weeks. I don’t know.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: In a spurt – with breaks.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I think, yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You like Monk’s music? I love the way you play on Evidence.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: On Evidence? I did the [?] of that. Oh, boy.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The way you . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Monk’s – it was really a challenge. He used to say, he says, “Drummers can only play at three tempos.” He know that his … was odd tempos and odd – sometime you didn’t know what to – you had to make something to play on it.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Was he like all the other great leaders you worked for, just let you do what you want to do? Or did he suggest anything?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Even if he didn’t suggest anything, he would come in – especially on one of my solos – any way he wanted to.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Listening to that, he laid out a lot too, whenever Johnny was playing. That’s very rare, because – he was laying out a lot in those sessions.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. Johnny would say, “I got it. I got it. I got it.” You can hear him saying that on record – say it to Monk and me.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let’s go back to ’54, your trip to Europe.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Please.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Did we want to ex- . . . no. Okay.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Explain that?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No, because then you started getting into laying out and you made me think – you see, that’s what I mean about – you start re-living certain things over again as you talk about them. Then sometimes it’s something that you don’t want to re-live over again. You know what I mean? So that’s why I said, “Please.” It’s not – we went back into . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s life, isn’t it?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s true.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: You’ve got the up and downs.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah, but when you have to deal with it in life, you deal with it, you cope with it. But then after that, if you finished cope with it and think that you’ve overcome it or you’re through with that obstacle, whatever it is, if it’s not an obstacle, or whatever it is. Like in school, when there was a test, I couldn’t wait to finish that … …, regardless if I thought I did it good or not. So now we say, “It’s life,” true, it’s life, but it’s behind you, and when you keep bringing it back – it’s like something in your stomach that’s irritating, you can bring it back in here, aaaaaaaaah, here it comes again. You understand what I’m trying to say?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Okay.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When I play I love to play. So that’s why I play less now, and I usually play – it’s usually my project. I do what I want to do. I seem to get to the audience. People, when they leave, they – some people that may have never heard that type of music before – they’re saying great compliments. So there must be something, the way I can do something my way, that can work, and works. When I’m in with somebody else’s thing, I’m trying to get in between. I’m trying to find a happy medium. But sometimes there’s a way – there’s something in me that hasn’t been out enough to let enough of the people that think they know everything, learn about me. It’s been happening. I’ve been noticing it. People – “wow.” One guy – a writer once said in Chicago when I was with Trane, “I didn’t know you could play like that.” I didn’t like it, the way he said it. The writer, I don’t think he’s living now. My reply to him – I said, “You should have asked Elvin.” I was saying that for a purpose, because Elvin knew. We would respect. But they were acting like they – then this guy went back and asked – called up Trane. That’s how those notes on that record that they use – The Beat of a Different Drummer – whatever – this new stuff they put out – that’s why that was written, because Trane was answering this guy, whoever that is. I can’t think of his name. Don’t really want to think of his name. But there are a lot of people like that. One time, I’m in – I’m jumping around, but that’s the way I live and that’s the way I talk – I’m in Texas for a festival there one time. I had been playing with Stan Getz then, whom you didn’t mention yet. I spent a lot of time

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: with Stan Getz. After we finished out performance – this is for George Wein, the guy that I said that I knew, and we almost grew up together. We’re the same age in Boston. It’s George Wein’s gig. He comes up. Meantime, Miles is there too with his band, standing at the end of the stage. He wants to put Coleman Hawkins on, and I’m getting an attitude, because I haven’t been able to play my little … with Stan yet. Now here come – I love Coleman Hawkins, but I’m part of the thing too. [?] to respect him. So George says, “Play some fast, Roy.” I say I don’t necessarily want to play something fast. I think he wanted to play Body and Soul. Anyhow, at the end I go and play something. Tony [Williams]’s there at the end of the stage. Miles’s at the end of the stage. Everyone. So when I come off, I’m talking to Miles about it. I say, “Here’s a guy, Miles, that knew me since I was a youngster, a teenager.” Miles said, “He don’t know you.” I’m talking again. I say, “Yeah, but he knew me since then.” “He don’t know you.” Miles knows – or knew. A lot of people – then so many other people – somebody sit back – they’ll put this guy here or something and say – so when I do my thing, and I don’t do it that often now. I go out and play. I pace my own way, and I try to put in it a lot of the little things I learned, a lot of important things that are going to mean something to me and listener and the musicians playing. It seems to work. That’s all I want to say.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It’s in Europe that you do your first record date as a leader. Is that correct?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How did that come about? Who had the foresight to know that – to recognize that you would be . . .?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I was also on the cover – I was accompanying Sarah then, accompanying – I was on the cover of the jazz magazine. I won a poll over there. That was 1954. I don’t know. I don’t remember what the name of the record company was now, but that’s the way it happened.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Who – how big a group did you have on there?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I had Shahib Shihab, Joe Benjamin. I had – I think a baritone. One of the guys from over there, and a tenor player from over there. We had – I had around seven pieces.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Who was the musical director?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: We all pitched in and did . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So a kind of a collective.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: We’re all directors. Adrian Acey [?], piano. Used to play with Jackie. Because Jackie’s band was there on a tour. It was some tour.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What was it like being in Europe?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What was it like? Then?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Yeah. How long was the tour?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The tour was maybe between four and six weeks. We had a week off in Paris. During that time Sarah Vaughan was managed by her husband, George Treadwell. When we had a week off in Paris, these French people had a record date lined up for me every day. I had no days off. One of the – a lot of the stuff, some of it was intricate, like with guitars and piano. I was in the studio all day. I didn’t particularly appreciate that, because there was this French – not a French lady – this English lady that I was hanging out with. She took the boat all the way from England to come over and just hang out with her. In the meantime I’m in the studio every day. I don’t have time for the lady. I got so much money. The older guys – Jimmy Jones was telling me, you can’t bring all that money back, because you can’t bring but so much money back, so I went on the Champs D’Elysses and bought all kind of silk scarfs and gold cigarette lighters, giving them to different girlfriends of mine. I was dumb.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When did you start to be very conscious and ultimately a trend-setter as far as your sartorial standards, as dress maximus?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I don’t know. I didn’t know I was a trend-setter, but I was – listen. When I was a youngster in Boston, a teenager, during those periods when I used to come to New York for weekends, I used to come to New York to go to 125th Street to buy shirts. They had some things up in Harlem at some of the stores that they didn’t have nowhere else in the world: a tie and handkerchief set with suspenders to match. I was doing all that then. So I don’t know if I was setting any pace, but I always was into some kind of style of dress. That’s why I like colors. I like painting in school. I like coordinating, even though sometimes it could be way off, but Miles used to say that’s one thing: Duke Ellington can put some colors together that you don’t think would fit. It’s the way he did his music. So we learned a lot from people like Duke. Kind of heavy, ain’t it?
[recording interrupted]
Hey man. Damn it. You got two hours already.
[recording interrupted]
Come on man. Damn.
[recording interrupted]

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Him personally?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Him personally, and then . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Then it’s the whole okiedoke about the business too, I presume. I have to assume.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: He was an opportunist. He did – you want me to talk about all that? He was definitely an opportunist. He knew how to do it. He did it good. He could be – one minute he could be a sweet guy and the next minute he’d be an asshole, complete. So I’d rather not spend much time. I brought his name up, because the name should be in it somewhere, but I don’t think I’m going to elaborate or get too involved in that …

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let’s talk about Trane, since that seems to be something that . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Now you’re talking about something.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let’s go.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What can you – Elvin probably will give you more about Trane than me. What can you say?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I want your experience with Trane. I’m even talking – I’m going to talk to Elvin about his experience with Trane too, but now I want to talk about your experience with Trane.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When you get to that number, huh?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When he gets to that magic number.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I said when you get to that number, meaning his number anyway.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Oh yeah, well – when he gets to . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So what am I going to do? What am I going to do? Talk about Trane. Lead me on. It’s a temptation. Hello. Give me a drink. I’ve got to get out. The weather’s good. I’ve

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: got to get out. I feel like – that’s what I’m trying to tell you. At some point I’m – it’s so beautiful now. Then I’m re-living this … all over. Even – regardless where I go, a lot of this … I’m talking about will be on my mind. See, you’re a little younger, so it’s a little different for you. A lot of this … I’m talking about will still be on my mind, and it will take a lot of time before, because I’m up there to it, almost re-living it. To get back down, it’s not that easy. There’s somebody who’s just going to make up some … or just … a lot as they’re going. A lot of people do that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It’s a very . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It’s hard.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: These are critical moments in the development of music, world music culture.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I realize that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What you were doing with Trane. What you were doing with everyone that you play [with]. It’s like you said. That’s a one-time thing. That will never occur in the history of humankind, never again.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: It’s hard for me to just jump right on to it.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: When someone says John Coltrane to you, playing with John Coltrane, what does that evoke in you?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s what it does. It evokes something in me. Oh boy, man. Oh man. Are we there now, to the ’60s? Are we to the Trane?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Let’s go with Trane, ’61.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: With John I could do a lot of things that [?] as far as playing the drums. The things that I would think about doing with other people, maybe I could do it with them, and it wouldn’t flow the same way. So I could really express myself. He had that type of – a lot of critics said at some times that he was playing scales. They didn’t realize that every time this guy would play a note, it would be right in the pocket, if it’s [Haynes sings]. Whatever. It was right there. When someone else plays a note, it’s either a little bit ahead, it’s rushing, it’s not in the pocket, and it’s hard to play with, for me, you understand? This guy, it was right there. It was so easy. It was like playing with Count Basie’s big band when Joe Newman, Thad Jones, the two Franks, and all those guys were there. That was one of the greatest thrills for a drummer. That’s the way Trane was. All you had to do was accompany this guy. You could decorate him. Some other people, you

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: got to carry, or they’re playing against – I don’t want to start calling names. I could. Other tenor players whom we like and whom I love.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: And don’t return your calls.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No. They were doing an experiment, going against it purposely to try to – but our natural way of breathing, our natural heartbeat. That’s what I found in Trane. He was a very spiritual guy. It was something. It’s almost like you couldn’t put it into words. You could put in a lot of words, but a lot of words don’t always mean, to me, don’t mean that much, but the feeling. There was a certain thing that was there that it’s hard to find.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Perhaps you hit on what is really fundamentally the key here, and that is that spiritual element.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That’s part of it. That’s not only it. It’s more than that. It’s something he knew. Something he knew. I know sometimes I’d be in Philly when he was playing out there. He’d just be around there – when I was with Bird, he’d just stay in the audience, not acting big or knowing too much. Listen. At one period he lived in Queens. I lived in Queens. He called me up. Or maybe – what was the guy used to be the road manager for Miles and him? I forget his name. He also lived in Queens. He called me probably first and said, “Trane’s going to call you. He wants you to go to Chicago.” Then Trane would call me, say, “I’ll be by to pick you up at 6 o’clock,” and he would drive to Chicago. Trane ended up getting to my house maybe midnight the same day, or maybe just a little bit before, maybe 11 o’clock. Then we’d drive to Brooklyn to get Jimmy Garrison. Pick up Garrison. Garrison would go in the back, go to sleep. I’m sitting up front. Trane would start to drive. Wouldn’t say nothing. He wasn’t a – he was not a man of a lot of words. He wouldn’t ya-ta-ta-ta. He wasn’t into ya-ta-ta ya-ta-ta, talking. He would say what he had to say. We went to Chicago. We were driving to Chicago. He hardly said nothing all the way, until he got tired. He’s in Ohio, stop in a gas station. I guess he wanted me to drive. I drove the rest of the way. When he woke up, he was in Chicago. That was the type of man he was. All I could smell was that funny cologne he had on. But he’d get on the bandstand – I know one time – I went to Montreal, Canada, with him. This is the same time I think we played at Newport, when we did that stuff. We’re playing at a place called La Tête de l’Art, which had stairs to walk up. I think it meant the top of the pig or something in French, La Tête de l’Art, whatever. Coltrane’s staying across the street at the Queen Elizabeth Hotel. He would come in after we had been playing with the trio, McCoy and Garrison. He’d have his horns out of the cases under his arms, soprano, tenor. It looked like he just got out of bed. His hair wasn’t necessarily combed. He wouldn’t even tune up. Maybe he had been playing in the hotel. I don’t know. He come and he get on the bandstand and just start to burn. I never had anything like this before. Just start to burn. He’d burn and take an intermission, then go up to the piano at some point. I don’t know if that was the cue to come back on, but after a while he would start

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: dingling on the piano. We go and play some more. He would close his eyes, and before he was finished, the waiters were taking the chairs, putting them on the tables. Half the people had left. I’d walk down the stairs. I had a taxi waiting for me, holding my insides like this after playing, but feeling like I’ve done something. That’s – I never had that experience with anybody. You want to know about John Coltrane. Getting back to Chicago, it’s time to go home now, Sunday night. He’s staying upstairs somewhere, over the place where we’re working. I’m staying at another hotel not too far from there. He said, “I’ll be by to pick you up at 4 o’clock.” 4 o’clock am. 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 – maybe 10 o’clock in the morning, I put a note on my drum and leave them, catch me a plane, go back to New York. Coltrane. Wonderful experience, warm person. Don’t show up when he says he’s going to though, but I can excuse him for that. But it was like a whole other world. He didn’t talk much. Even at record dates he wouldn’t explain. He would just say, okay, this is some of this or that. Maybe I can hear you on the cymbals here or maybe here with the mallets. He wouldn’t say much. Spare brother, through. Next.
[recording interrupted; it resumes in mid-sentence]

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: . . . I was talking about before even Eric [Dolphy].

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Go ahead.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Eric and I were very close, but I couldn’t get that feeling. I couldn’t get that kind of feeling with notes or anything. When I would get to California during the time I was with Sarah, Eric – we’d be together almost all the time. Then he was playing more like Bird. But after, when the change – when he went the other direction, some of the stuff I didn’t understand. I know he got interesting compositions. But what he was playing, it didn’t hit me here like that, like Trane. I didn’t feel that. And that was my buddy. He come to see me in my house before he went away and passed. So I can’t – there’s nothing much I could add there, because he’s one of the guys I was talking about to be – it wasn’t in the pocket to me, his playing. It was good. Ornette was a little more smoother than that. He was a good musician. I like maybe more on bass clarinet than the alto.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I’d just like to state this is tape number two, Jazz Oral History Program interview with Roy Haynes in his home in Long Island. This is May 15th, 1994.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Thank you sir.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: So the ’60s, that’s yet another period. You talked about the feeling of the ’40s, the ’50s. You had quite a varied career, but pretty much centered with your tenure with Sarah Vaughan. In the ’60s you seem to be now – you’re working with Trane . . .

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Go ahead.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Go ahead. Describe the ’60s.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The ’60s, it was a lot of weird, weird stuff happening in the ’60s, you know that.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: The civil rights movement and the war.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Not that. That was a wild period. I had some good bands in the ’60s. I had bands with Wayne at Slugs. Did you say Slugs a minute ago? Did I hear Slugs?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: No.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I had a band with Wayne Shorter, Albert Dailey, and Cecil McBee.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How did that band come about? Why Wayne Shorter in the band?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: At one point when I had left Sarah, I had called up Trane. We’re in the ’60s. I think we’re still in the ’60s. Or late ’58, ’59. I was doing stuff at the Five Spot on Tuesdays – Tuesday nights or something like that. I wanted to get Trane for something, and I had called Trane to get him to play with me. I think he was getting work done on his teeth or something then. He said, “I got a guy who’s badder than me.” I think those were his words. Said, “I’ll let you talk to him. His name is Wayne Shorter. He just got out of the service.” Wayne used to call me. I remember sitting on my steps – not these steps, but my other house in Queens – which lead to the basement, talking to Wayne on the phone. He was telling me about these compositions he had written. He wanted to play with me. If I was the type of guy – say maybe Bu [Art Blakey], for example, the way he’d grab up guys quick. That’s why I got Wayne. Because Wayne always then – before he went with Bu, before he went with Miles – he had talked to me on the phone, because Trane had told me about him. He was at Trane’s house. If I do remember correctly, that was it. Then he gave me his number. He lived in Jersey then. Then later on I got Wayne to make some stuff with me. I would just – we’re playing at Slugs – I would just go into a rhythm and Wayne

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: had one of his own compositions, or he used to do a lot of stuff from Black Orpheus there. He would put a song right in. It would sound like we had arranged or we had rehearsed. He was very melodic. That’s how that come about. He was there with me for a while. I had one time with Chick Corea there, Joe Henderson.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: How about Joe?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I had Joe down at Slugs with me. In fact, I got some – somewhere around here I got some reel-to-reel of a little of that, if one of my slick sons didn’t take it and do something with it. I was looking for that. I had some people interviewing me. I was looking for it. I couldn’t find it then. I got some reel-to-reel way upstairs on the fifth floor. I had some good bands. I had one band with Sonny Rollins, Kenny Dorham, at the Audubon Ballroom.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: What year would that have been about?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: That was late ’50s, in the ’50s, after Sarah.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: This seems to be a gradual progression, that now you are leading your own bands after leaving Sarah. Was that the impetus then, to lead your own bands and have your own?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: I had to – it was necessary not to lead my own bands, but just to make some gigs periodically and get the people you wanted to – I’m glad you noticed that thing. Sonny Rollins wasn’t big then when I mentioned him. I’m glad that you checked that out, because these all the time are the people I would reach for. But afterwards, he – he was one of the ones that we thought – we, some of the cats up on a hill – what he did, he didn’t never come back to us, so to speak, where some of the other guys would reach back, but as far as that was concerned, the only one that ever came back – reached back to me that ever did something that I could think of first was Chick Corea. If we’re in the ’60s. I’m still in the ’60s. There’s a guy. Of course, Trane had left, but Trane said nice things. He left. Bird had left before a lot of stuff was even documented. Sarah, I used to call her. She never even returned – when Sarah was dying – pardon me for saying it this way – I had called her up, because sometimes I used to ask her – I’d say, “Why don’t – is it possibly you could let my group open for you somewhere at some slick joint?” The last time I talked, she said, “Yes. I’ve got a new manager.” She could hardly talk then. She was under heavy medication. But then, it’s too late then. One time I asked her before about doing it. She said, “Who’s in your group?” I’m not going to have nobody going to be sad or some … like that. I said, here’s the lady I’ve been with the longest. We’ve got to reach back. One hand helps the other. How’s it go?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: One hand washes the other.

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Haynes
Haynes_Roy_Transcript.text: Okay, yeah, thank you. You said it. That’s right. That’s what I was looking for. So, getting back to Chick. Chick – okay, we did that record, Now He Sings, Now He Sobs. We didn’t get credit. “We” meaning the bass player and myself, Miroslav Vitous. I don’t really know what went down on that, but when the record come out, in magazines, a lot of people would say, that’s who it is. It’s Haynes. That’s the one. So that’s Vitous. There was a lot of guessing going on. Then I heard later – I saw the producer. He told me otherwise. He said, “I don’t know.” He says he tried to get Chick to put our names on. That’s what he told me. So I never did know what happened. At one point I had the flat ride cymbal, a Paiste, the one you were talking about. Chick was living in Queens, so he came over to my house to borrow a cymbal. This was maybe before he started Return to Forever. So I do know – I heard that band play when they – what’s his name? Airto?

Haynes_Roy_Transcript.speaker: Brown
