Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. I remember that phrase. She called it guinea-pigging.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, and she didn’t want that for my brother and I. She didn’t want us to be the guinea pigs.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Were you teased by other children? Did they tease you?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No, no. I never discussed it with other kids.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: You held it inside.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, and I went on and actually didn’t learn about until I was much older. Then when I got much older, I began to realize, something is different, because my brother – my older brother would go to the bathrooom, and I’d say, “I got to go, too.” I’d run to the bathroom. He’d shut the door. I wouldn’t say anything, but I thought, why did you shut the door? I learned that that was why he shut the door. He didn’t want to discuss it with me, about the syndrome or anything. All I wanted from him was for him to be my brother. Just be my brother. Hey, that’s all. I never discussed it. I let it go, lived with it. My mother encouraged that, as far as living with it. She encouraged that in a lot of ways.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: When you say she encouraged that, you mean she encouraged you to be hopeful and cope with what your reality was?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. Live with it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Live with it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Learn to live with it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Learn to live with it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Because it’s going to be there.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: There ain’t nothing you can do about it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Nothing. That’s right. But like I say, every girl has – if they had boys – they had that syndrome. The first boy or the second boy.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: The women in your family were the carriers.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Right. If they carried a baby, and if it was a boy, in the birth of that child, he had to live with the syndrome. But I feel that they’re wrong for what they do. They don’t teach them anything that will teach them anything that will help them understand what they’re living with. I think that’s so wrong, because it’s life.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And you have to be prepared . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: There you go. To live it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . and have help to be emotionally prepared. How old were you when your mom died, because didn’t the . . . ?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: How old? 13.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Didn’t the tragedy of her death coincide with your understanding that you also had this deficiency.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I knew that was the person who, if I needed something or needed to understand something . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That was mom.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . she was the one that would. My father would never talk to me. My father and I, we were distant.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: He just came and went whenever he wanted to.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So you lived with it. Mom would say, you live with it. That’s what I did.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Tell us about the circumstance of her death, how she died when you were 13.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I went to school that day. Something told me to skip school. I decided I was going to skip school that same day. If she had been living, she would have whipped my butt for skipping, and I’d say, oh Lord. But something kept nagging me to go home. I didn’t think of it as it was trying to tell me something was wrong or nothing like that. The whole problem was, I had an older sister that was very, very selfish. She was a selfish girl. My mother was taking her to school or going with her to school, because the teachers had asked her to come so they could talk with her about how my sister was acting in school. So she was doing something wrong. If you’re just sitting around in school, yeah, mom was coming. She’s coming to find out what you did and then whup your heine. You got a good whuppin’ if you did something wrong in school.
[interview interrupted]

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: You were saying your sister acted up in school, and mom had to go to school to hear about it from the teachers.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: She had to go. That was the day they asked her to come to school, so they could talk to her and tell her about what my sister was doing. On the way to school with my sister, they got to a point where they were crossing the street. This driver shot out from – wanted to get to the front of the cars, and there was space for it. But my sister stepped out in the street. My mother saw it, and she reached for my sister to save her. Pushed her back off the curb of the street. The car hit my mother instead of hitting my sister. My mother stepped in that, trying to save my sister – that’s how that happened – and got all tangled up. It tore her – when she got [?], they found out it tore her arm off. They were going to try to put it back, but couldn’t put it back together. That was it. It shocked me. Mama. Wait a minute. What are you doing to her?, I’m thinking. Kids. You know. You don’t know what’s on. You think anything. That was my buddy though life. I could depend on her. My father had no good. We never had a father and son conversation, never. It hurts, because you’ve seen others who shared things with their father. But I got that sharing with an older person from my brother-in­ law. He was mechanic and fixed cars. He was unique. All the neighbors, if their car broke down, here comes – here they come. They’re going to get Leon to fix their car.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So the death of your mother – where . . .? – tell us about how you learned about it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I went home.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Right, from the day . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Like I said, I skipped school. I went home at the noon break, when you’d just be going home for lunch or something like that. No, I just went home to stay. That was my intent, to go home and stay. When I got there, Nadine, one of my sisters, she tried to keep me from knowing that my older sister was upstairs, but my mother wasn’t. So I said, “What’s going on?” I was surprised to see her home too. “What’s going on?” “Shirley’s upstairs in the bathroom. Don’t go up there.” I said, “Okay,” knowing them and their attitudes about things. I just left it alone. But I kept thinking, something’s wrong. Then I got to thinking, where is Mom? Where’s Mom? If Shirley’s home, where is my mother? “Mom’s at the hospital.” “The hospital? For what?” Then I began to question things like that in my mind. Eventually I got it out of them that she had been hit by a car. That’s the way I got it. We were waiting all day that day for someone to tell us that she was going to be all right. That’s all we wanted to know. Was she going to be all right? We waited all day that Friday. Saturday, they got a hold of my grandmother, who was very distant to my mother in her growing up and in her – they’d never got along. So that was a problem there. But my grandmother was there. She broke the family up, because she put us in – they call it a detention home. The kids hadn’t done anything wrong. Why were we going to the detention home? The thing that got me the most mad was the games that they played with me about things concerning my mother’s death. Shirley and Nadine got together, and they schemed up an idea to keep me from going to the funeral home to see my mother. I said, “You better get out of here.” I was really upset. But this they had done other times, little – like I told you, I’m ready to give you the other side of the book. I said, wait a minute. Why aren’t they telling me something about my mother or what’s going on with the funeral home. The funeral home came and gave us the service with their cars to take the kids to the funeral home so they could see their mother the last time. I went. I saw her in her casket. Then they take us back home after that. Instead of home, we went back to the detention home. That I couldn’t figure.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So your dad was absent.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, he wasn’t around.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So he couldn’t take responsibility for keeping . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: To save . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . to save the family.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And there was no other. Your grandmother didn’t want to do it. So what had . . . ?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: She . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So what had . . . ?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Huh?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Go ahead.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: You dig? Listen. He didn’t care. My mom’s gone. That was it. That was the end of the family. That’s why I say they – a family life, they don’t know the importance of being a family with one another. No. No they don’t, because – I see why. I understand why – because it wasn’t presented to them in the right way. He wasn’t a father to us and wasn’t there at times we knew we needed him. So that was one of the problems that was involved in their life.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So here you are at age 13. Your mom’s gone. Your dad won’t step up to the plate and assume responsibility. Your siblings are at each other’s throats or scheming.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. Couldn’t get along with each other. You’re right.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Couldn’t get along with each other. So no-one’s really pulling together. You and your brother go off. How did you – describe to us what it must have been like to be a 13­ year-old Jimmy Scott or a 14-year-old . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Then, after that, leaving – what happened, they gave us a – they called it a worker or something.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Worker’s compensation?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No. They gave us a woman who . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Oh. A social worker.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Social worker.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Right.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: It was up to her to place us in foster homes. A brother and I, and my younger brother, who is now determined – he destroyed himself – he’s destroying himself, being a hoodlum. He’s just messed up, and it hurts, because my mother didn’t allow that. I know it, and they know my mother didn’t allow it. But, how can you tell him? He got a hold of that junk, and he started using it. This is my younger brother. He’s much younger. He’s

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: before the last kid. The last kid was a boy also: Justin, who’s named after my mother. However, that was what the situation was.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So after she died, there was this moral breakdown. There was a moral breakdown. There was nobody to take charge and tell them what is right and what is wrong and you can do this.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No, no, nobody.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Because she was such a strong person when she was alive. She held it all together. And when she died it all kind of . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: It will fall apart.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: It all fell apart. What do you think kept you from falling apart?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: My interest in music.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: All right, all right.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: My interest in music.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So music saved you.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: When I would sing or something after that . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: It was healing to you.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . I’d say, wait a minute. This is what mom was trying to tell me or something like that.
[interview interrupted]

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Jimmy, getting back to the thing with music, was there ever a point – I’m just trying to put myself in your shoes. Your mom dies. Your dad’s not taking responsibility. The kid’s are at each other’s throats. They’re scheming against you.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Like I say, that destroyed the family.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That destroyed the family. Was there ever a point that you feel as though you were going to fall apart. In other words, did you ever go in your mind, I can’t handle this. I can’t live without my mom. I can’t live with this situation.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: It’s too funky. It’s too crazy.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But then there were things that she had said to us before she died . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That kept you together.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: What were those things?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I said, listen, mom wouldn’t appreciate me falling. She’d whup my butt if I fell apart. I’m saying that to myself.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So in other words, even in her death, she remained a present source of strength for you.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Even in her death, she remained alive.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. I tell many people. I tell them, wait a minute. You know better than that. Mom – because, they were old enough. There were enough of them. They were old enough to hold the thing together. But those that were old enough, they all drifted apart. Now we go back to the foster homes. As I said, my brother and my youngest brother – two younger brothers – were put in a foster home together in Youngstown, Ohio. No, we were put in Miss Gray’s home first, in Cleveland. We didn’t get along there, so we were shifted to this home in Youngstown. This home in Youngstown, this lady was a beautiful, beautiful lady and did a beautiful job of caring for my brothers and myself. But the thing was, when I got 16, I could leave the home. I got 16. That’s just what I did: went back to Cleveland to try to find a home. I had to get a job and get a place to live. So I did. Went back and wasn’t welcomed back. People, when they don’t want to be bothered with you, they do a lot of funny things. You know this. I know that. Okay. That was what was being done. Nobody wanted to be bothered. I was their brother, but wait a minute. You don’t bother with me. Burnt. When I got paid, I saw you in my face, asking for money. To hell with you. And you don’t want to be bothered with me. Took a long time. When I moved here, that was another reason I moved here, is because they weren’t together.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: You mean moved here to Las Vegas?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Uh-huh.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Just to get away from Cleveland.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And the squabbling of family.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I was tired of it. I felt I knew something about family and what it should be. It wasn’t there, so I would rather be by myself than to be around them, knowing what my mother taught us, and it wasn’t in practice. Now that she’s gone, they didn’t practice it any more, living like that.
[recording interrupted]

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Jimmy, we were talking before about, in the aftermath of your mother’s death, where music was so important to your heart and helped to heal your heart. Was that music you were listening to on the radio? Music that you heard live? Singers like . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, and then there in Cleveland on Sunday mornings, all the gospel churches would be on the radio.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And you’d listen to that, and that would remind you of your mother.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, because my mother played piano for the church we went to. That was my comfort.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: How about artists like – when – how old were you when you heard artists like Paul Robeson?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I was just a young kid, 6, 7 years old, something like that.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: What was your impression of that music?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Wait a minute. This man is telling a story and singing it. The way he sang was very expressive. I said, uh-uh. I got – that’s the way I got to sing. It’s got to mean something. If you listen to him, it meant something, and you knew it meant something. Paul Robeson, you’d hear him on a record or something, it meant something.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So it was the dramatic way that he told the story in song.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, that’s right. That’s where I learned a lot of what I do as a singer, those things. Then I start looking for it in all of the singers.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: The story-telling.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. Dinah [Washington] was fabulous, and look how long she held the rein.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Look how long she held the rein.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: She reined for a long time as the champion.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I know your dad liked to go to clubs and hang out.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Oh yeah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Would you go to those clubs with him ever and hear music in those clubs?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Those clubs he went to? No.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: They were just drinking places?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: They were just drinking and talking menacingly to me. It didn’t mean anything to me, listening to them, because they wasn’t talking about nothing that was interesting enough to listen.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: When do you remember the first time – I can’t remember this – when do you remember the first time that you walked into a jazz club and heard jazz or any kind of music in a nightclub? How old were you or when do you remember – I remember as a kid. I remember walking into Birdland, hearing Count Basie. My heart starts to beat fast. How old were you – when do you remember hearing live music outside of church?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I’ll tell you what was happening. I don’t whether you’d remember. What was happening was that little theaters in my home town began to bring bands and people like Dinah Washington – different musicians with names – they started bringing them to Cleveland in the theaters that we had there. That’s my first time hearing the live music.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That’s a beautiful thing.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So, before the movie started.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Oh, listen. And I said, oh, looky here. We were getting live music every week for a period of time.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: You’re talking about hearing Jimmie Lunceford?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes, and Earl Hines.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: The great bands.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And Cab Calloway. He was one of them that was out there. Then Lionel. I had gotten to know him and was anxious to get a chance to work with him.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But tell us, before you got to Lionel, and you’re moved back to Cleveland and 16 years old after the homes and so forth.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I got jobs. Worked various places. I worked the hotel. I worked restaurants. Busboying and whatnot.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Before – so you’re going to all these live shows with the big bands, Earl Hines and Lunceford. Where did you begin to build up your chops? When did you start to sing in front of people before Lionel Hampton?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I was working with a couple of tap dancers. I remember the names: Lem Neal and Dickie Sims. They were a team. They picked me up at the theater in my home and asked me, did I want to valet for them? Oh yeah. Anxious to be around show business. This would give me a chance to hear all kind of music. I’m going around, meeting all these guys. I was working with them, and Lester was in the band that was playing on this gig they did.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Lester Young.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Lester Young. He was playing his tenor in the band. He was another one I had fallen in love with – music – it was like hearing birds or somebody. He was in the band. They played. One of the fellows that I worked for said, “Come on, man. They want you to sing.” I said, “What? Want me to sing?” I didn’t know anything about me. I felt like, hey, you know. Anyway, Talk of the Town was the song I sang. [Scott sings:] “I can’t show my face. Can’t go any place. People stop and stare. It’s so hard to bear. Everybody knows I love you. It’s the talk of the town. Friends and our relations send congratulations. I’m not setting our wedding day. Friends and our relations send congratulations. How can I face them? What can I say?” It stops there with me. Those are the last lyrics I remember. But that’s an old song. Talk of the Town.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So you went out and you sang.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I went out and sang that for them. Then they wanted another one. They kept applauding. “Bring him back here. Bring him back here. Give us another.” I could hear

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: the people say that. It was in Pennsylvania that this was happening. What was that town? I’m trying to think of the town. Not Meadville, but we were near Meadville. You could just cross the street almost and be in Meadville, but this sound started with an S.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Scranton?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Huh?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I forgot. Not Scranton?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So you’re in Pennsylvania . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: It was little. One of those little towns, little country towns.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So they asked you to do another song after Talk of the Town.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And I did Don’t take your love from me. That was the other one that I did. That and . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Talk of the Town.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, Talk of the Town. Those two I did. That spurred me on. I had done two. Okay, I’m going back home and be a singer. It was a couple of clubs that I knew wanted me to sing for them, but the guy was so cheap, a lot of artists wouldn’t work for it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So you wouldn’t work with the guy because he was too cheap.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Anyway, I went ahead – like I said, did those two nights with them. They had – this was a weekend – three-night gig that we were on. The dancers had – it was their date. Like I said, it opened my eyes that I could keep on singing.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. You got the bug. Let me ask you one thing before we leave the initial time you sang Don’t take your love from me and Talk of the Town. When Lester Young said, let him sing, and after you did sing, what was his remarks to you.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: He said, “Go back in the dressing room. You’re a valet. You don’t belong out here.” I felt so bad about what he had said to me. So I went back in the dressing room. I didn’t say anything. Just moseyed back in and sat down and thought about it. I said, I don’t have to be insulted like this. I told the fellows. I said, “I’m sorry. I’m going back

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: home” – the fellows I was working for. So they gave me my money and my fare back home, because I had to take a bus from there to Cleveland. I took the bus fare and got the bus.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Do you know what’s so interesting about that though – was Lester telling you, I don’t like the way you sing? - Scott: No.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Or was he just telling you, you shouldn’t be doing this. You’re a valet?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, that’s all. In other words, I really deciphered what he meant by it. “Now don’t get a big head, boy.” Because I had stopped the show. The people just kept raving.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So he was kind of jealous that you were getting all this attention.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I don’t think that it was jealousy more than trying to express, don’t get the big head, boy. When I thought about it – the longer I thought about it, the more that came to me, that uh-uh, he was just telling me, don’t get the big head. I was hurt, of course, because he said this, and in the way he said it, I was hurt, because that’s Lester speaking to me, telling me.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Did he tell that to you on stage? When did he actually make those remarks, Lester?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No. The band had stopped playing. The dancers had went into the dressing room. I was standing outside, watching them come back to the dressing rooms. I stood by the door that came out of the stage. I was standing there. Here come Lester, with his horn. He saw me over there and he looks. He says, “Go back in the dressing room. You belong in the dressing room.” Belong in the dressing room? Why would you say that?, I’m thinking. So I did. I went on back to the dressing room. I knew I was going to leave that place and he didn’t have to worry about insulting me any more.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Do you know, what’s so interesting to me about that, is that Lester Young, who had such an individual style, and obviously had an influence on you, because he was so relaxed. He was always behind the beat. He didn’t care about – he was his own man, the way you became your own man. It would seem like he would be one of the biggest appreciators.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Later it came. Oh yeah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Good. I’m happy to hear that. Later it came.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Later we were friends. It was, “Hey, there’s that boy.” Blah-blah-blah-blah-blah. “How you doing? Where you been singing?” and like that. No, later we became very great friends.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And he was an appreciator of yours and your style, because he probably heard his own style in your stuff. Jimmy, building up to where we began today, which was building back up to this Lionel Hampton, how did you . . .? – so these years, you’re singing the Cleveland clubs. Now you’re off the road with the dancing guys. How did you come to hear about Hampton’s band and get to sing for them?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: They had – I was singing in a club in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The fellows got him – two of the fellows got him. He liked going around to clubs. Especially when he had time, he would take time out and go. So, this night, before our show – I think it was the second show in Milwaukee – I looked up and they were sitting in the audience. I was a bit surprised.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So you look out in the audience, and there’s Hamp.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Huh?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: You look out in the audience, and there’s Hamp.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. But the fellow that had him and made him come with them to hear me. That’s what they had – this was some of the band. Then, after he did that, we all went to dinner – lunch – a little lunch, whatever. We got to talking. I met Gladys.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: His wife.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: His wife.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: The boss.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That’s right. The next thing I know, about a week or two weeks after that, I got a message telling me where to meet him. There’d be somebody to meet me, and I was to go with them. I said, what is this? Lionel Hampton? But I followed instructions. We went to this room where they were. It was like a hotel room. We went and sat there on the couch. Out comes Gladys. “Hi there. How are you?” “Fine.” Then, “How long will it take you to get your clothes?” I said, what are they saying, how long will it take me to get my clothes? Anyhow, she told me they were going to hire me for the band. I said, “Oh?” Then I thought to myself, well I will have to get my clothes.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Did they discuss what material you would sing?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No. I sang, “Why was I born? Why am I living?” [Why was I born]. That was one of the features that he wanted me to do. And a couple of things he had me doing. Don’t take your love was one, and Everybody’s Somebody’s Fool, after we recorded it. That was one of them that I did. When I left the band, he tried to get the singers that he had to do the song, because the song was getting popular.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Everybody’s Somebody’s Fool?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Everybody’s Somebody’s Fool. He couldn’t get anyone to do it, because they’re saying, no, that’s Jimmy’s song. We ain’t going to do that. Most of them were loyal in that sense. That was how it went.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: How long of a period of time were you out there with Hampton? Did you travel all over the country?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes. We traveled many places. That’s the first time I got to Hawaii, was with his band. It was an overnight thing. When I woke up, I’m laying on the ground, on the grass, and they’re telling me, “Come on. Get up.” “Get up? Where am I?” I must be in Heaven somewhere.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Must be in Heaven; turned out to be Hawaii.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. That’s right. It turned out to be Hawaii. They entertained us that evening. Then we slept. Then they entertained us that night, before we left. Then we got the bus and left there and crossed all that water. They had a ship that took us across.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Tell us a little bit about the different kinds of music, the different styles that the Hampton band played.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Many, many. He was a uniquely equipped musician, Hampton was. The beauty was in the vibraphones that he played. Sometimes he’d play them with a song I was singing, and I just thought I was in Heaven.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Just hearing him play the vibes behind you.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Uh-huh. It was beauty, it was truth, and music.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Beauty, truth, and music. Tell me – but there was also parts of that world that had like – they were still playing Illinois Jacquet’s Flyin’ Home and there was still the heavy . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Oh yeah. They’re still – all those songs that he specialized in.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: The big hits and the rock-and-roll-ish or rhythm-and-blues-ish honkin’ and shoutin’.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I’ll tell you. Winnie Brown came to one of our – was it in Chicago? yeah, in Chicago – Winnie Brown came and sang with the band as a guest singer.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Tell me what it was like singing with – singing on the same band as Betty Carter. What was she like in those days?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Betty was unique, different, in her style. It was – you could tell instantly different. Betty was a good showman.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: In her presentation, you mean.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Right.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: How she used her hands and sold the song to the audience.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: All the different little things, yeah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: In terms of you developing your style as a showperson . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Who?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: In terms of you developing – I’m just thinking about how you developed your style as a showperson on stage, delivering a song to the audience – how you used your hands, how . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. That . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That’s so unusual.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . came from a coach I had in school. He was the bandleader of our band at the school. Then he’d have music classes. Certain ones that he liked, he’d pick you out and have them, and we’d all meet up as a class for him. Mr. Todd. Both he and – Miss McGrath was her name. Miss McGrath was supposed to be our art teacher. She was an art teacher. Every time we’d turn around, she’d have us on stage, doing some kind of play or something. But that was interesting. There was another lesson, learning how to act on the stage.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: The use of the hands, your gestures, how you do when you’re on stage – that came out of acting class, you think? Or you came out of – or were you influenced by people like Judy Garland or Betty Carter? Or by then you had developed your own style?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Judy was one of the influences for me, Judy Garland. I forget the kid that was with her.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Mickey Rooney?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Mickey, yeah, but he didn’t do vocal. He did the movies and thing with her, but he wasn’t active in the music. No, but he was always behind her.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Donald O’Connor.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Oh yeah. That was the tap dancer – the young . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: You like to see his movies.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No, he was a tap dancer. He was a young man doing all that tap dancing. We used to go to see the movies just to see him tap dance.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: When you got on stage with Hampton, and you’re getting all this reaction – you cut Everybody’s Somebody’s Fool – did you surprise yourself by what an emotional vocalist you were, by how much feeling poured out of you? Was that a surprise for you, Jimmy? Did . . .?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: A surprise to me?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. Did you ever go, my God, I didn’t know I had this much feeling . . .?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: To give.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . to give.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: In a way, yes. But again Lester popped into my head. Don’t get the big head, boy.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Why did – tell us – first tell us the story of Everybody’s Somebody’s Fool.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: This young lady, Regina Adams – she used to come to the Apollo every time we were there. She would talk with me about this song she wanted me to sing. We never got to do it for her, but before we left New York, she brought a music sheet to me and said, “Here. Here’s the song.” So I looked at it. There were a few changes I had to make, but nothing big. We got it together and made our decisions about how we would express it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: One night – no, one day, here comes Hamp. “Jim Scott.” “Yes sir.” “Where’s that song that girl gave you?” I didn’t even know he knew the girl gave me a song, but I think someone in the band probably told him, because they would be – we were all back in the dressing rooms together. So, I just let it go. I said, ”Okay. I say, “Here. Just a minute. I’ll get it for you.” I went and got it, and he had somebody in the band write an arrangement for it. That was what you heard on the record.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But when it came out, it didn’t have your name on it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No. You know what?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: What?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: The only person he ever put their name on the record was Dinah Washington. Only person he put her on it. Nobody’s name – none of the others – and if you check it out, none of the other singers, their names weren’t on the records.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So when it came out, were you upset? Were you angry that your name wasn’t on it? Or you didn’t even expect anything?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No, no. I didn’t even think about it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: You didn’t have any expectations. So you didn’t have any expectations of having your name on it. You were okay that your name wasn’t on it. But how about when it began to be played on the air and everybody was listening to it and calling for it and screaming when you did it? Then did you – what was going through your mind then? I better quit this band?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No. I was just hoping that it would be successful. You’re anxious to do a good job, and you hope it’s successful.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But when it was successful, what was your reaction?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I wondered, wait a minute, because I had some doubts about the young lady’s lyric to the song, but I sang them as they were and put it together, and we went ahead and recorded it. Do you know, that’s a big request now, when I am on the stage. I get many requests for that song, Everybody’s Somebody’s Fool.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Why did you leave Lionel’s band?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: We had a little discrepancy, and I didn’t want to stay in the band and be fussing and all that. No, I don’t need this. I don’t need this. I’m here to do a job. I will do it, and

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: that’s the end of it. But I don’t need to be arguing with the man or his wife. That’s why I left the band.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So you were – the discrepancy was over not getting paid what you felt you needed to get paid.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes, in a way it was about not being paid. Not only that. We had done the record, and everybody said, “How much did you get?” The fellows in the band. I said, “What do you mean, how much did I get? I ain’t got nothing.” Oh man. Then them cats – the cats in the band started talking then, and it came out that he had did this to others. I said, if that’s the case, then I don’t have be with the band.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I see. So you didn’t get one penny.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Not one penny did I get out of the record.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No advance, no royalties.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No nothing.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: You just showed up and sang . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Not nothing. He . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . as part of your job as the band singer.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: He had the contract with Decca.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, the recording company.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: See? So he presented the song to Decca. Yes, yes, yeah. Somebody in Decca wanted to hear me sing. It must have been somebody pretty important, because if it was somebody important, Lionel Hampton is going to do what he’s supposed to – what he can to please that person. That’s the way Lionel was.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: What did you do after you left the band?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Went home to Cleveland. Got a job.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: What kind of job?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I worked in the drugstore that I grew up. He was on the corner. Curlander’s Drug Store. That was the name of the fellow who owned it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: How old were you at this point?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Huh?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: How old were you at this point?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: At that point, I guess I must have been like almost 30 years old, not quite.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: In your 20s.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I was in my 20s, late 20s.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Were you discouraged? Did you feel like, my voice is on this hit song, it’s being played all over the country, and here I am working at a drug store – what the hell’s happening?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No, no.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That was not your . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I didn’t even think about it. Keep going on.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Keep going on.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No turning back. I still had a job to do.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: At the drug store.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But were you also singing gigs in Cleveland?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I did do a couple of little places that used to know me. I’d go by and sing there. Then, when I was home, they’d ask me to do gigs for them and how much did I charge and like that. So I did. I went. One guy had the club – honey, you’d know. You don’t know the name of the club either, where Goo-Goo Eyes and myself – this was a blues singer . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: This period when you’re back in Cleveland, you’re regrouping your strength and determination . . .
[recording interrupted]

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I did that club. That’s where I did my first production. I produced a show . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: At the Cedar Gardens.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . at Cedar Gardens. It was like an old-time burlesque.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Oh yeah. You produced a whole show with dancers.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No, I don’t think it was a whole show. It was – Cedar Gardens was a nightclub, always a nightclub.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: The Cotton Club she’s talking about. Jeannie Scott: The Cotton Club [?]. Jimmy Scott: The Cotton Club, that was something else. That was downtown. That was downtown.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Let me ask you this: talking about the Cleveland jazz environment. When you were in Cleveland, you knew Tadd Dameron, right?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Tadd Dameron, we grew up sort of together, in schools and things. Tadd would say, “Come on and sit in” on the piano stool with him. I’d sit down. He’d say, “Sing – let’s get the key” for such and such a number that he’d want to play for me. If I knew it, he’d play it and I’d sing it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So what was happening in music . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: His brother played tenor – Caesar Dameron.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Right, Caesar Dameron.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Caesar Dameron

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: In Cleveland, before you went to New York and Newark and all that to kind of settle in, would the big name beboppers come through Cleveland? Would you see Dizzy [Gillespie] or Bird [Charlie Parker] or Dexter Gordon or whoever?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No, they hadn’t come through yet. No. They hadn’t come through yet, because I was away from home when they did come through.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But how about Tadd though? He must have introduced you to – because he was such an advanced musical mind.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Oh yeah. He was a bad piano player, baby.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But an arranger and composer as well.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Do you think he influenced your musical vision?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I think so. I think so in many ways, because he’d get after me about having my notes to the songs, like that. He’d sit down. He says, now this one, you sing in such and such. I said, whoa. He’d give me the information about the keys that I sang the songs in.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Right. So he was a teacher.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Let me ask you this about the other big-time jazz vocalists who were coming through in that era – Ella [Fitzgerald] and Billie and Sarah. I know they loved you to a degree, when they heard you.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: There was a club called [Café] Tia Juana in Cleveland. That’s where they would come, to the Tia Juana.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And you’d go hear them.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, because that was mostly jazz. It was one of the clubs that dedicated themselves to jazz only.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: To jazz only. But when you heard these tremendously individual styles, like Ella . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Or Billie Holiday.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . or Billie – Sarah Vaughan.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. Dinah was there.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Dinah, big individualist.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, all of them sang at the Tia Juana. When they came, they were exposed at the Tia Juana.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But did you feel, sitting in the audience, listening to Billie or Dinah or Sarah Vaughan, did you feel like, they’re great, they’re great, they’re great, but I have my own style already in place? Or did you feel that you . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I never thought of things like that. I just – truthfully, I never thought of things like that.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: You just heard them live and went on and sang.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: If I had to do a gig, I was prepared. My music was prepared. I knew what I was going to do and got with the piano player when they come to the club and said, okay, let’s get the keys to the songs, and I’d ask them, which songs do they know?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And that was it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That was it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: How did you first – because this is an important part of history – how did you first get a recording contract, with the name Jimmy Scott on the record?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Teddy Reig . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, we just – Teddy Reig.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And, what’s it? What’s his name? Jeannie Scott: Jack [Hook?] Jimmy Scott: Jack Hook.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. They had a label that they were trying to make go. I did a – I think I did two songs for them. They of course sold it back-to-back, the record. That was back-to-back, the two songs that I did for them. I’m trying to remember what they’re called, the record company.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But Teddy Reig, how had he heard you or how had you met him?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Teddy was always around.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: He was talking about the . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Roost. That’s right, baby.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, the Roost label.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That was the name of that record company: Roost Records.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So Teddy. You were talking about how you met Teddy. He was always around.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, he was always around Count Basie or the bands.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, I know he was a Basie guy.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So he started coming around us, hanging, and I’m wondering, who in the hell is this cat? Because he had to be somebody, if he could walk in the door and nobody’d say nothing. He’d just walk in. So I says, got to be somebody they know. The clubs knew him. Anyhow, he’d start coming around. He asked me to do some records, and they put Jimmy Scott on those records. That was one of the first records I did outside of doing the Hampton record.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: In terms of the musical input and how they wanted you to sing and the accompaniment, was that mainly up to you? Were you . . .?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No, see, that was the whole trouble.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I see. Okay.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I had no choice. They’d bring a song . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . that you’d have to sing.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And that was annoying, because there was many songs I wanted to sing that were great music. But no, they didn’t do it like that. So that was a problem.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So you didn’t have the artistic freedom that you needed.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: There you go. I didn’t have the choice to do what I wanted. That wasn’t – what they were all – all of them was looking for somebody to rock the place. Wait a minute. I didn’t come here – I come here as a singer, not . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And it wasn’t in your nature to say, wait a minute. I’m not going to sing this song, because it doesn’t suit me.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No, I wouldn’t do that. I wouldn’t do that. I’d say, okay. Then, with my voice, I’d figure out a way to do it, and do it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Let ask me something while it’s on my mind, Jimmy – jumping ahead a tiny bit – not too far. During this period, the 1950s, when you heard certain vocalists – remember Johnnie Ray?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: [sings:] “If your sweetheart sends a letter goodbye . .” – when you heard these – he was obviously modeled on you, and later he would tell that to everybody – but when you would hear Johnnie Ray on the radio sing Cry or The Little [White] Cloud that Cried, whatever those songs were, did you ever feel like, God, that’s me, that’s my style? Or that’s not in your nature either?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I never thought about it. But Johnnie Ray, every time I was in the Apollo, Johnnie Ray would be sitting there.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Listening and talking notes.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes. He’d be sitting there. Finally he came and introduced hisself. Say yeah, okay, this is the guy.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: This is the guy. So you never went through a period when you said, it ain’t fair. Why should he be getting his big old hit and get all the big old money, and I ain’t. That’s just not in your nature. You just kind of said, I’ll go on and do my thing. Let him do his thing.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: As you were recording in the early days for Roost, do you think what they were trying for, or what you thought they were trying for, was to get a pop hit on the radio? As opposed to, hey, we’re working with a great jazz vocalist and we’ll let him be a great jazz vocalist. Did – when you were making those recordings, did you feel as though they were striving for a hit song?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, they were striving for a hit song, but it was a hit song that they thought was going to be a hit.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Not that you thought.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No. My interest wasn’t important to them. All right. They’d get this song, and they’d bring it, and they’d say – I’m saying to myself, I don’t sing that kind of stuff. Then they’d have somebody sit down and play it for Howard Biggs. He played the piano for them.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, Howard.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No, it just didn’t work.
[recording interrupted]

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: My name is David Ritz, here in the home of Jeannie and Jimmy Scott, September 24th, 2008. I can’t believe it’s 2008. 2008.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: How about that.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: 2008, and you were born in 1925.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, how about that.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That’s beautiful. You lived a long and one of the most interesting lives of anyone I’ve ever met in my life.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: A long time.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I would have to say you have lived one of the most interesting lives of anyone I’ve ever met in my life.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: It’s been rough.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Been rough.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But I’ll overcome.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I will overcome, he says. Let’s get back to the timeline here. 1953 you do the things for Roost and this and that. Then, from the middle of the 1950s to the end of the 1950s, you’re in Newark and you’re getting hooked up with this guy named Herman Lubinsky. How did you meet Herman?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: He came to meet me at the club that I was at. I was at a club there. He came over and invited me to the store, because he did all this work right above one of the stores that he had.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: This is in Newark.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: In Newark. Then that’s when he told – what was his name? The one that worked . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Freddie Mendelsohn?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes. That’s when he told Freddie to arrange the studio. I think that was in Linden, that studio.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Where you began to record. You knew of his recording label, Savoy.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, but I didn’t know what he was doing to folks.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But you knew that on his label Charlie Parker recorded.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Right. I mean, then he had a big thing with Wynonie Harris. That was his biggest thing. He wanted that back again. But Wynonie Harris was dead and gone.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So he basically saw you as a guy who might be able to give him some hits the way Wynonie Harris had given him some r-and-b.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, but like I told you yesterday, everything was what he wanted. Nothing was what I wanted to do, which I felt good about doing. That wasn’t the case.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yet, in that period in the 1950s, you recorded a number of songs . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . that you’re proud of and that got through even though you weren’t in charge of the recording and you weren’t really asked what you wanted to record. But nonetheless, aren’t there a lot of those recordings that you love and that you like?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Some.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But not a lot.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Some, but I wasn’t big on them, because I couldn’t do my own selection of the tunes.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So you continue to be frustrated by your ability to choose the material . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. You go through it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . that was most close to your heart.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
