Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I’ve been what?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: True to your art form.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes, I do. I’ve given it all that I have and will continue to give it all that I have. That’s my sincere determination, is to give it all that I have, because it hasn’t done me bad. Others outside of the business, they did me bad, but the business itself hasn’t done me bad, I don’t think. It’s just that persons who didn’t mean right, they caused problems that weren’t necessary. That’s where my problems began. It was other people. My family was a big innovator of that, the problems I had in the business. So that’s why I say, the business didn’t treat me bad. It would have been much better if I had had the sincerity from the folks I was dealing with, sincerity in the sense of nobody wanted to learn how they could help me or what could they do that would help me. That wasn’t – but their biggest reasons were, “Man, you got the money?” I said, “No, I don’t have no money.” “You got paid last night, didn’t you?” That was family as well as so-called friends in the street. That was the attitude, which interfered in a lot of ways with my thinking. That was a part of life I had to deal with. When I decided to drop that part, okay, things changed. But the force that helped them change was this little girl right here, Jeannie.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: When you look, do you think you’ve been an unfor – do you think you’ve been a man who’s encountered a great deal of misfortune? Or a man who’s really been blessed?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: A great deal of misfortune, you can say. It has been a great deal of misfortune. But if I’d had someone in the business who was serious about being in the business and doing the right thing, I know there would have been success out of it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I know you’ve read deeply into Christian theology and also Eastern religion. So I know you’ve given a lot of thought to the meaning of God in our lives. Why do you think a guy like you – was a sweetheart and a loving disposition – has had this much misfortune imposed on you?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: People prey on that. There’s people out there that prey on that.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That’s exactly what I’m talking about.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I didn’t – I ignored that. Out of ignoring that, I fell into the hands of many people who didn’t care about my career. What the hell? That wasn’t their business, and it wasn’t important to them. It was only important to me. But like I say, I ignored a lot of it. Out of ignoring a lot of it, it became a damage to me.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And also, do you feel as though you took care of your own business?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: The best I could, yes. I also feel that I trusted too many people.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Ah, too trusting a heart.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I trusted too many people. It didn’t do me any good. It didn’t create success for me at all. But like I say, you give out, but you don’t give up. That was my attitude about the whole thing, and still is.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Because the truth is, you began to sing as a teenage, and at 82, you’re still singing, and there was no time when you didn’t sing. You had other jobs, but you always went back to the little club. So you have this tenacity, where you keep on coming back, keep on coming back, keep on coming back, keep on coming back. But when you look at the great stylists whose eras that you lived in – Lionel Hampton, Nat King Cole, Billy Eckstine, Ella, Dinah, Nancy Wilson, people whose styles have been so influenced by you, do you feel like you’ve been left out?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: In a way, yes, but they had reason for leaving me out. I wasn’t important to them. So there. I had to understand that. Because I looked around. People like James Brown, they were friends. All those kids. They were popular, but they were friends where I was concerned, and they treated me as a friend. So the artists in the business treated me with respect.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: As an equal.
[recording interrupted]

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I was there that night that you were awarded the NEH Jazz Master award. Remember, in the hotel in New York, with – Nancy Wilson gave you the award. What did that mean to you? What was that evening like?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: It meant a lot. It was like graduating at school or something. It’s like a graduation for me, to a better side of life.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Of course it must have been nice, the award was given by Nancy.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes, but I wondered why sometime. Why did they pick her to do that? Because it wasn’t necessary, and there was never any apologies for things that she did. So I just took it with a smile, kept on going.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: When you think back to the years in Cleveland or L.A. or in Newark or in New York, and you want to warm your heart when you might feel bad from a physical point of view or a little sad, what memories do you conjure forth, do you bring up, that warm your heart and make you happy?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I think of my mother.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, I knew you were going to say that. That’s so sweet.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: She would play the piano, and I’d hear this. Even since she’s been dead, I’ve heard the music. It’s always gospel. It’s always gospel, and it was a thrill listening to it and hearing it and singing it inside of myself.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: What other warm memories do you bring up to comfort your heart when you feel bad, when you hurt?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Now I have something to feel good about, seriously. I feel that I have something to feel good about. We’re going to make it, huh?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: When people – when you think of your concept of God, do you feel like – tell me just how you react to this phrase – do you feel like God has been good to you?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Oh my goodness, yes.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Good.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes sir. All the good that’s ever happened to me . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Comes from God.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I figure some people don’t stop and realize what it’s all about. They deny themselves of that trust and care that God gives.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So you’re grateful to God. You’ve . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Oh my Lord, yes.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I like to hear that. And you feel blessed.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Listen. How many times have I fell, and he picked me up. I look at it just like that. My trust [?] than it’s ever been before.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That’s a beautiful thing. When you think back over the large extent of your life, who are the great characters who stand out the most, the really most brilliant, the most charismatic, most colorful, most unforgettable characters? Were I to just ask you to name them, without giving it too much thought.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Bird.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Bird.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: One of them. Dinah is another, because before Dinah passed, every time she had to do an important gig, the gig she was on she had to leave, she would call me to take her place.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That’s quite a compliment.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Oh yes. Listen. This goes back to the Flame . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: In Detroit.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . in Detroit, and places like that. She’d always have a spot for me.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Had a spot for Jimmy.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I love her for it . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So we love Dinah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . because it kept me alive. Now there’s another point where you can’t help but thank God, because with friends like that . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Let me ask you something else, before we run out of tape here, which is a big concept in your life. You’ll always be remembered in a lot of ways, but one of the ways you’ll be most remembered is in your notion of time and rhythm and how you have your sense of it. Throughout your career, you’ve been criticized and also applauded. On one hand, people love you for having such an individualistic sense of time. On the other hand, you’ve had people criticize you and in certain instances, like Charlie Mingus, get up and leave when they’re recording and saying . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, we were recording . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: You go ahead and tell that story.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . and he threw the bass. He said, oh man, this cat he ain’t doing – can’t sing.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: This is the ’50s.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: The other cats had to go get him. They told him – they said, they can’t be there when you get there. That was the way they expressed it to him about me.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: To Mingus.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah. I’m saying, here is a cat who – time was no problem for him. No. So why did he pick me to say the things he said at the session.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: But were you ever challenged to the point where you went, maybe they’re right? Maybe my timing’s off? Maybe I have to pay more attention to the meter and be – keep a stricter sense of time? Did you ever have those doubts? Did you ever think . . .? You always knew that you were going to take your time.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, I knew that worked out well. I was going to sing the song that way.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: No matter what.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And it seemed to work. It works.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So you had enough people who appreciated . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . your individualism.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah, my audiences. It started out like that for me. They appreciate what I was doing . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So in other words . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . and I worked hard at it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So in other words, part of the reason you were able to stick to your individualism is because your early responses had been very positive.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: When you did Everybody’s Somebody’s Fool with the Hampton band, the audiences loved it and went crazy, and they didn’t care if you were behind the beat. They didn’t – they just . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: They didn’t know about that.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: They didn’t know about that. What they heard was your heart, and their hearts connected to your heart, so they went crazy.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And I figure, if people listen to the lyrics . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: They’d really get it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . they’d understand that the singer’s telling them a story.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: In his own way.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I guess what I was thinking was, in the case of Lester Young and Mingus, two of the most highly individual people in the history of jazz, getting kicked in the ass by them early on and still maintaining your integrity, I think is impressive, to me. The other thing I wanted to ask you was, the other challenges of your life – we’ve touched on the women. We’ve touched on the career – but the other challenges – I remember the story that went around about you, when Everybody’s Somebody’s Fool came out, and people were saying, “That’s not a man. That’s a lesbian in drag.” Jimmy, you must have heard those stories. Did you hear those stories? Or not?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yeah but, again, like I say, you ignore it . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So that didn’t hurt you.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . and move on. You have to move on. You can’t let those things stop you. You hear them, and you are disappointed that it’s being said, but that’s just a disappointment, and you ignore it. You learn to ignore it. The main thing is, you don’t want it a part of your life. You don’t want it a part of your life. So you learn how to ignore those things when they come about.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: So you don’t feel as though you had been taunted more than you could take. You felt as though you were equipped to handle the taunts and handle the teasing.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes. Exactly. I never had a confusion with a person about things like that.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: I see. So sexually, you always knew who you were . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Right.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . and were confident about it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: My mother was very strict with my brother and I about, “Get up boy. Stand up there.” You don’t drop down to other people’s things. No. You don’t do that. She was very strict about that. Yeah. And if I see her, she’s saying, “If I catch you ever, I’d tear your butt up.” And she would have.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Do you mean by that, catch you with a man? Or just catch you . . .?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Oh, anything derogative in life. “If I catch it, you going to get it.” That’s what that – that was her slogan. That’s her way. I didn’t want to get it, so I didn’t drop down to it.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: That should be the name of this interview. You look like you’re getting a little tired?

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: A little bit.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: All right. I think we should dedicate this interview to your mother . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Thank you.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . and to Jeannie . . .

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: And to Jeannie.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: . . . the two women, one of whom gave you life, and the other of whom continues to give you life.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Scott
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: Yes, yes. You got it just right.

Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.speaker: Ritz
Jimmy_Scott_SI-NEA_oral_history new logo.text: All right. On that happy note . . .
(transcribed and edited by Barry Kernfeld)

JOHN LEVY
NEA Jazz Master (2008)
Interviewer: John Mitchell with recording engineer Ken Kimery Institution Description: Transcript, 99 pp.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My name is John Mitchell. I’m a staff writer for the Los Angeles Times. Today is December 10th, 2006. We’re in the home of John Levy and his wife Devra Hall at 1827 Coolidge Avenue, Altadena, California. We’re here as part of the Smithsonian’s Jazz Oral History Project to record John Levy’s story. A former bass player, John has been managing the careers of music artists since 1951. In his musical prime he played the bass when jazz was at its heyday on New York’s 52nd Street. Duke Ellington wanted him in his orchestra. Billie Holiday hired him for her comeback concert at Carnegie Hall in 1948. Then John put away his upright to sit behind a desk and manage the careers of artists. He had a rich stable of clients: George Shearing, Dakota Staton, Betty Carter, Lou Donaldson, Herbie Mann, Les McCann, Ernie Andrews, Randy Crawford, Brook Benton, Ahmad Jamal, Freddie Hubbard, Cannonball Adderley, Wes Montgomery, Joe Williams, Shirley Horn, Ramsey Lewis, Roberta Flack, Donny Hathaway, Eddie Harris, Johnny Hartman, Stanley Turrentine, Diane Reeves, Sarah Vaughan, Nancy Wilson, and the list goes on. So much history. So many lives touched. We want to start at the beginning. So John, why don’t you start by giving us your full name and spelling it for us.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My name, John Levy. I’ve been called John or Levy, and John Levy, Jr., but the usual name that I go by is John Levy. John O. Levy. Note: There is no middle initial on his birth certificate. Here is the explanation from page 35 of “Men, Women, and Girl Singers” –

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: By the time Michael was born in March of 1943, I had a temporary job as a clerk at the Post Office. I filled out the forms for Social Security with my name, John Oscar Levy, Jr. I didn’t have a middle name when I was christened, but sometime during my childhood I had found a photograph of my mother and a man I didn’t know. “Name’s Oscar,” Grandma told me. “Your Mama was married to him, but then he died.” I didn’t know Mama had been married before. Why I wrote John Oscar Levy on that form I don’t really know. Maybe it gave me some sense of being a part of something that I wasn’t really a part of. The name Oscar stayed with me for a long time—it’s still on some old papers and a few reference books—but after a while I stopped using it and dropped the Jr. after my name. It was probably some insecurity in not being able to look at my father and say ‘well you know, this guy’s the most important male image in my life,’ because he really wasn’t. He had my respect and all that, but we just didn’t have anything in common.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Your birth date?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My birth date? I was born April the 11th, 1912, in New Orleans, Louisiana, and moved to Chicago when I was about five years old, then spent most of my life – my early life – in the Chicago area before moving to New York, which was much later in my life.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Let’s stay in New Orleans for a hot minute.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Okay.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What are your early recollections of New Orleans?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: The most things that stick closer to my mind is the music, because that was the era [of] dixieland music being played, the funeral parades, the church-going, and the social things that were happening in my family at that time, which really helped me to establish myself later on as a musician. The main thing was the music. I recall that more than anything else.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Let’s talk about family. Your mother and your father – give us their names and what they did for a living, and tell us about the home environment.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My mother was what was called a trained nurse and midwife. In those days, especially with the black community, they had midwives, which delivered the babies and did all of the health things for the communities at that time. This is what my mother was doing. My father was a stoker for the railroad. His job was to go into the roundhouse, which is where the engines at that time – the steam engines – were started up. They had to build a fire each day – each morning – for each engine – each fire engine – to start the crews – before the crews came on to move the trains around – the freight around from the yard – the freight-yards. That was his job. That’s what he did.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Give me his name.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My father’s name is John, so I was – that’s where the “Jr.” comes in for my name.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: And Levy – what’s the history of that name?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Levy, as far as I could discern – the periods that I traced it was through my father’s father, who was part of a slave thing. All of the people on the plantation had the name of Levy. In other words, all of the slaves had the name of Levy. So that’s where the name came from.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Was this in New Orleans? In Louisiana?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: This was in – it was outside of New Orleans. The plantation that these slaves worked on was called Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana. There was the slave owner – which a lot of time people said that the Jewish people never had any slaves, but these were Jewish – French Jews, and they did have slaves. This was from that slavery – from that plantation that the name Levy derived and followed through with my self . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Do you know what type of plantation it was? What was grown? What was on the plantation?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No. I don’t know what was grown on it, on a plantation.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What can you tell us about your mother – her name, her background?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My mother’s name is Laura. She was the oldest of the two girls in the family. There was another girl, which was my aunt. That was Ida. My mother’s name was Laura. There were, I think, four or five brothers. Let’s see. There was Josie, Tommy, Sherman, and – that’s it, I think. Yeah. Forgot two of the uncles: Johnny and Nathaniel (called Nat)

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Her maiden name?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My mother’s maiden name?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yes.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Laura.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Laura was her . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Laura. Laura Hagen.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Kagen?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Hagen. H-a-g-e-n.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Hagen.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Hagen, right.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Do you know when they were born, or what years, or any information about . . .?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No, I don’t have any information on it.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What about brothers or sisters?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I had no brothers or sisters.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Tell us about those early years in New Orleans and what it was like growing up as an only child.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I was spoiled. I was spoiled, and especially from my grandmother and grandfather. They – I could do no wrong with them. Being raised in a family where we all lived together – grandmother, grandfather, and even uncles and aunts all lived together – not everybody. Some lived in the same house, but the aunts and uncles, three or four of them lived in the same place that I was born in – the same house that I was born in.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Where was that house.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: That house is in the seventh ward in New Orleans. It was 1240 Touro Street in New Orleans. It was in the seventh ward.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Could you spell that. Touro?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Touro – T-o-u-r-o. Touro.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Okay. Touro Street.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah. It’s in the seventh ward, and the house still stands.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Even with [Hurricane] Katrina?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Even with Katrina. I’ve been back there a couple of times. It’s still standing, still there. It wasn’t completely destroyed, but I can see – along the side of the house, I noticed the water mark – how high the water came up to it. I was never able to find anybody home there for me to go inside. Each time I went back to New Orleans I wanted to try to go in and see what the insides

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: looked like and see if I could recall anything from it. I know there was an upstairs – a staircase on the inside of the house that led up to an upstairs bedroom. But I was never able to go back in and check it out.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: So you’ve even been back since the hurricane.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yes, I’ve been back since the hurricane.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Do you go back because of the hurricane?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No. I went back – Nancy Wilson did a benefit concert for the university there, and we went back for that affair. That’s when I – the most recent time that I went back. Note: Nancy’s performance was for Dillard University, June 30, 2006

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: You go by the house whenever you visit?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yes. The other thing was the Heritage jazz festival. I was back there for that, and I also went – checked the house out.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: That’s usually in April? Am I correct?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I can’t recall the exact . . . (April 29, 2005)

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I believe it is.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: . . . date of the Heritage festival. But there was two incidents. One was I went back for the Heritage festival, and the other one was for the university (Dillard).

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Can you tell us about the feeling – what kind of emotions come up when you see the house, or the feeling that you have?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: It brings back a lot of memories. Each time that I went back, when approaching the house or coming up to it, I – it brings back memories of certain things that happened to me when I was very young. For example, I had an uncle that worked in the – Sherman was this uncle – that worked in the – worked for a candy company. In those days they had a wagon driven by a mule – a mule-driven wagon. When I was a youngster, I would wait for him to come by the house for lunch. I would go up the street and meet him – up the block and get on the wagon and then drive the mule – sit at the driver’s seat and drive the mule down to the edge of the street – to the end of that block, where then he’d put his feedbag on him and hook him up there for his lunch. Then he’d get out and come in the house. So any time I go there, I always see that picture.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What is – your recollection of the neighborhood – what did it look like? What did it – visually – and maybe, how has it changed from . . .? How does it look today?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: The neighborhood looks pretty much the same as it did then. When I went back for the Heritage festival, they had paved the streets. That’s the only changes that had [been] made, because this was dirt road. The street was dirt. Dirt-road streets with gutters. Very – I wouldn’t say primitive, but not very modern or anything. It was pretty much the same. The houses look pretty much the same. Still standing. Looked okay. We lived in what is called – I guess it’s called a two-storey – there’s another name for it, but I can’t think of what that – the title of that name.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Is it a duplex?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: It’s like a duplex, but we called it a half a house. That’s what they called it, because half was one side and the other half was the other side. But you could hear people in the next house – next place. It was all in one. You had two separate entrances and the wall between them, but it was like one house split right down the middle.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What were some of the things you might hear from the other house?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: You hear just about everything.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I don’t know whether I should pursue that any further. Was there music coming from . . .?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah, you could hear just about everything. I recall that. The neighbor was a teacher, like a private school teacher, what we would call now kindergarten classes at a private school. That’s what this woman did for a living. People left their children there – very young kids there, and they were taught there. I used to go over and sit in. I wasn’t one of the – you might call the pupils that was hired – that the people brought over. I was much younger than most of the students that this woman taught, but I’d go over there and sit in class with them. I learned to read pretty young.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Do you remember in terms of what you learned? Was it your numbers? Your alphabet?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I learned numbers very well, and I learned the alphabets, like they were taught: a-b-c-d-e­ f-g-g-h-i-j-k-l-m-n-o-p-q-r-s-t-u-v-w-x-y-z period. And from 1 to 100 and from then on.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: With being an only child and with both parents working, would you be considered middle class or would you be considered fairly well to do or certainly not wanting for anything? How would you describe your [?] in that sense?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: In today’s world it would be considered middle class, I would think, because you didn’t want for anything. You had clothing. You had food. You weren’t on any kind of a welfare. There was no – you had all of the things that were – that people had for that time. There was no electricity in that house. There was an outhouse. You cooked on a wood stove, that kind of thing. There was no gas. But everything was everything was okay.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I know this is early, but in terms of your recollection, what role did church play in your life in those early years?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Church played – church in that period played a very important part, because it was everything, really. It was your entertainment, and of course, naturally, it was your religion, and it was your music. Music was very dominant in the church with the choirs, with the different things that happened in the in the church

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I’m assuming that you went to Sunday school there?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: You went to Sunday school and you came back – then you went back again in the afternoon for what was B Y P U, which was – I’m trying to remember what that really meant at the time. But I remember that title. And then there was the morning service. There was morning service. There was evening – first there was a service before, for the children. Then there was the regular 11 o’clock in the morning service. Then there was that afternoon service. Then there was the night service. A lot of times children didn’t go to the night service. That was the Sunday thing. Of course there was choir practice during the week. There was a lot of different things going on.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Do you remember the name of the church.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Right off the top of my head, at this point, I don’t. I don’t remember.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: We can come back to that.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: But I remember that one of my chores at the church was to ring the bell. There was a bell in a bell tower. Every morning, one of the things that I had to do was to go and pull this thing. It had a big bell – clanging bell, and it would go up and down. I did that. I recall that.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: One of the interesting things – you left New Orleans at five, so one would assume that you may have had some early friendships, maybe some early confrontations, maybe some early flirtations.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: The only friendship or contacts that I recall – because I wasn’t in public school yet – was the neighbors. The neighbors were Italian. Not at the half a house. This was down the block that I recall going to these neighbors. There were an Italian family. I remember the boy’s name. Goodie was my age, so Goodie and I were pretty much – we’d go inside each other’s house and they’d come in my house and we’d have – so I didn’t really run into anything in prejudice that made me being alerted to what segregation was, because on that block, or in that particular area, it was sort of mixed.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: So neighborhoods – it was probably typical for the South in that period of time – neighborhoods weren’t segregated . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No. They weren’t segregated.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: . . . in the South.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No. That’s right. Not in New Orleans, anyway.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Right.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Not in that area. I don’t know about any other part of the South, but in New Orleans, it wasn’t. The first sense of segregation, or that there was some form of segregation, came to me through my godfather, who was a French Creole, but very light skinned. He passed for white. He would take me into town to shop for me, for a birthday or for whatever holidays. I don’t recall the exact holidays, but I do recall the incident of getting on the streetcar and him going all the way up to the front where the motorman was. There was a motorman and a conductor. They had these signs where you put up in between each section – you could move – for example, if there were more white people on the streetcar at the time, then this sign would be moved back. Each seat had a little hole in [it] where you could stick this sign in. I had to stay behind that sign, and he would go up front. Then he’d come back and make a joke out of it, but I realized then there was a difference, that me being black, I couldn’t go past that sign. Whites sat in the front end of it and blacks sat in the back end of it.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Can you describe how you felt even at that early time about that? Or did you have a sense of anything?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I felt very hurt about the whole thing, because I felt that I wanted to go up front, like any kid would like to do: go to the front of the streetcar and stand up and watch the motorman or whatever. I couldn’t do that. So I really felt – it gave you a feeling of rejection. That was the first time I realized there was a difference, because on the block and in the street, the neighbors and the grocery store we went to – later on – which is much later, after I’d come to Chicago – I went back to spend some time with my grandmother, who was still living there. Then I realized there was this segregation in the movie houses, where we had to sit way up top – on the top of the house. [We] couldn’t sit on the main floor of the theater. It was like you being in the gallery.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: When you would come South to visit your grandmother?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah. I only made one trip South. I must have been around 11 years old – somewhere around that time. I even went to school for a short period of time. I don’t quite know why it was done that way at the time. All I know [is that] I went to visit and then stayed there for at least one semester of schooling.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: This is around when you were 11 years old?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah. I was around 11 years old.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What – how do you – when you think of yourself as a child, how do you picture yourself? Were you an antsy kid? Were you a thoughtful, pensive kid? Or somebody who was always worrying the elders because you were likely to get into stuff? Or did you regularly get “whippin’s,” as they . . .? How do you describe yourself?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I think I was . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Mischievous, or what?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: . . . very well disciplined, because, for one thing, there were certain rules laid down for you. You had to follow those rules. For example, if I went out, I had to be back in the house before dark and I couldn’t go off of my block, the block that I lived on. I could go from one corner to the other, but I wasn’t supposed to cross the street.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: You had boundaries.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah. So that was rules. You had rules and those kind of things. So I wasn’t into that much. I wasn’t much of a – but I was spoiled as far as having, for example, the food you’d want to eat. They’d fix something special for me, because I didn’t eat what everybody else wanted. I could eat red beans and rice every day, and plantains and that kind of stuff is what I – but I didn’t like vegetables. Still don’t.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No okra?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No. I didn’t eat that stuff. I didn’t even eat potatoes, except sweet potatoes. That was the only time – as what we used to call it, Irish potatoes – what we call white potatoes now. It was called Irish potatoes.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Devra has encouraged me on flipping streetcars. I’m not sure what that means, but maybe you can explain it.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Flipping streetcars? Streetcars had a little step on the rear end of the car. To enter the rear of the streetcar, there was a step. You went up on the step, then into the back of the streetcar where the conductor was, which he would take your fare and then you’d go and sit down. There was just a little platform at the rear end. That was where the step was, where you stepped to get on. The same thing was at the front end if you got out. The funny thing about thing: you could get off the streetcar on the front end, but you couldn’t get on at the front end.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Okay. So what does flipping mean?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: As the car’s coming up to the station, you could stand in line along the way, and as the car is approaching, you could flip it: you jump on and grab the thing and flip it and get on ahead of the crowd that’s waiting when the streetcar stops.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I see. I got you.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: So that’s what that means.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I want to get some sense of the early sense of music or where the roots of your music talents, in the sense that: was it the family? Was it in Thompson Methodist Church, where you used to go?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah, that’s it. Thompson’s Church. Thompson’s Methodist Church . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Thank you, Devra.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: . . . was the church, yeah. I had forgot the name of it.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Where do you trace those roots?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: The roots, really, for the music and everything else, actually came from the church – basically from the church. Of course we did have – I guess you call it a graphophone [sic: gramophone] that then you wind up. It had a horn and you had records. We had records of classical music.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: You had records. Okay.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yes, yes. We had records of – I can’t remember the names of some of the classical people at that time, but we could hear all that type of music.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What about your mother and father? Were they musically inclined?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My mother was. My father wasn’t.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Okay. How was your mother . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My mother was musically inclined. I had an uncle who sang in the choir, and as I said, they all went to church and sang – the whole congregation. But I had one uncle – the youngest uncle – Nathaniel, the youngest one. He was a bass singer. He sang bass. He was in the choir.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Your mother sang? Did she play an instrument or anything like that?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No. Nobody played an instrument.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: People often talk about their being family gatherings in the South and singing at Thanksgiving or dinners. Was there that kind of – were those kind of things happening in your home, where people would gather and sing spirituals or anything like that?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No. No, I didn’t have that. All the singing was done pretty much in the church.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: And long hours in the church I think.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah. You spent a lot of time in church. That was your social life, really, in the church. But I heard music almost every day, because practically every day there was parades and stuff. There was also – a form of advertising was music. They had a float – they had floats to advertise different events, like fish fries that were coming up the weekend, the movie – in fact there was a regular movie float that came on with the whole side of – each side of this float was pasted like we call “billboards” now. It was pasted [with] a billboard of what was appearing at the movie that week. On the float was a group of musicians. They’d have a bass player, which was on the end, a trombone player, a trumpet player, and usually a clarinet player. That was your sound. That was where you got your sound to bring the people out. They’d be playing music as they came along. They’d be playing all kinds of popular music. You could run out and see what’s happening and follow – I would follow them down the block – not past that corner – coming right back after that. Also if there was a funeral on the way to the cemetery, the band would be playing, and the family followed behind this parade. Here again, I’d follow that to the corner. Then when they came back through the same street – they’d come back after the funeral – then they’d be swinging. I’d go out and watch them, check up on the floats.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: This was pretty much the emergence of jazz that had started years before but was taking shape, I’m sure, in the years after 1912. This is still early jazz, I would imagine.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: It was only music. It was called “dixieland.” It wasn’t really – it wasn’t called jazz at that time. It wasn’t particularly considered jazz music. The beginning of the thing was more like what was termed “dixieland.” I don’t know how that term came about, how they named it [at] that

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: particular time. But these people played a type of music which developed into what is today called jazz. These were the pioneers of that type of music. Right.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: So you were a child . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I was fascinated by the bass player, because he was on the rear end of this float with a bow. He would hit his thing and play it. And the trombone player was on the rear end. That’s why they call the trombone player [“tailgate”] – on the end, so he can have room for the slide, the trombone. These two people were on the rear. Then the other people were in the other parts of the float.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: In essence, this was the early – your early sense – your curiosity of music. Am I correct?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Right. But by my parents listening to classical music and religious music, they decided to get me a violin. That was my first thing about music. They got a violin for me. I started some lessons very, very young, but I didn’t stay with the instrument at all. But I did get a sense of the instrument, of what it was, and playing, but I didn’t particularly care for it. I didn’t like it.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Was this still in New Orleans?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: This was in New Orleans.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: You were first introduced to an instrument at that stage?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: At a very early age, yeah. So here again it shows that my parents weren’t exactly poor, because I don’t know where it came from or who bought the instrument and all that, but you had to buy it, I’m sure . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Were there lessons as well?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: . . . because nobody else was playing any instrument in my home at that time.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Were there lessons as well?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah. I recall some lessons. Somebody came to the house. This is my best recollection of it at that time. They came to the house and [I would] take lessons, but I didn’t practice very much with it. I didn’t care much for practicing. But it stayed with me later on, when I started with the string bass, because actually a violin – the bass is just tuned – the strings are backwards – in other words, it’s E – A – D – G [on] the bass. The violin was just the opposite [g – d – a – e], but in a different clef. It was bass clef and then standard [treble clef].

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I just want to go back to the family one more time in the sense of – it seemed like on your mother’s side there were plenty of uncles and aunts.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: On my father’s side, practically – very little communication with them. My grandmother – my father’s mother – I never quite understood her, because she was what was called “patois.” She spoke a broken French. I never could communicate with her very much. She was real black as you could get, from that side of the family. I didn’t spend much time with them, because naturally children in most families go toward the mother’s side of the family. It’s usually the stronger side than the father’s side of the family.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Were there first cousins?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yes. I had a couple of cousins, but I don’t – we didn’t keep a close contact with each other, ever. I recall there was two girls and there was two boys. I think there was a son, Paul – and Nelson. Paul and Nelson were the two boys I recall. I think there was two girls on that side from my father’s brother, but there wasn’t much contact. Anything you want to say? I didn’t hear you. Devra Hall Levy: No. I’m ready to move North. Do you want the names of things before you start?
[recording interrupted]

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Okay. We can move on. What I’m curious about at this point is the moment in time when the family is deciding to move North, what prompts that decision, and to what extent you as a five-year-old might be aware of what energies are going on, because you’re getting ready to start this journey.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Let me say this. There was not – there was only two people – that was my father and my youngest uncle – came up to Chicago first and established – came there to work. Then the family – other parts of the family moved up to Chicago. That’s when my aunt and my mother – but my father and my uncle went first. My father went into the stockyards. They both did. They both went into the stockyards. The youngest uncle referred to just now was Uncle Nat.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: In Chicago.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: In Chicago. They had jobs offered them as soon as they got there.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What did they do in the stockyards? Slaughtering?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I don’t know what my uncle did, but my father worked in the hides cellar. He skinned the hides from the cow. That was his job mostly, working with the hide. He did that, after that, his whole life until he died – until he died or retired.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: So at some point what you probably noticed – or did you notice that your father was no longer at home?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Oh yeah, but I was aware of what happened. I was aware that they were going away – that father and my uncle were going away, north to Chicago, because they’d been offered jobs. You could do much better. But I didn’t have any thought about why they were doing it or why they had moved or any reason about it.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Was there a sense of his absence in the house?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: With my father, there wasn’t much difference, because there wasn’t much family thing with my father. He went to work at 5 o’clock in the morning. When he came home from work, he ate his dinner and went to sleep – went to bed. I had very little communication with my father, period, over my whole lifetime.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Let’s talk about the communication you did have.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: He took me to the roundhouse one time, I recall, and showed me what he did, when I was very young. [He] showed me how he stoked the fire engines, so the firemen could get it, and showed me the roundhouse. [He] explained that to me one time. That’s the only time I remember anything like that. I never went anywhere with him, never did any traveling or did anything. He never took me any places. My father didn’t have much of an education. He just barely could read and write, which was an odd situation, considering that everybody on my mother’s side of the family was well educated. My mother had an excellent education. My uncles had an education.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Well educated for the time meant . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: For the time. For the time.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: . . . meant what?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: As far as you could go.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Meaning high school? Meaning elementary school? Meaning . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah. However it was graded. They all could read and write and communicate and all that. Where and how, I don’t know.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I understand.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I wasn’t too familiar with the schooling they went through to get – where my mother went through to get her learning. To be able to be a nurse and to deliver babies and that kind of thing, you had to have some medical training in some medical school somewhere. I don’t know. But I wasn’t familiar with it and never bothered to try to find out later on in life. I’m not too inquisitive about things, in reality.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Throughout your whole life, you’re not?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My whole life. Yeah.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Why do you think that is?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Because I’m just not. For example, people talk about – different subjects come up, and people say, did you know so-and-so’s wife? or did you know this? No. I didn’t know that, because unless in some way I was in a direct contact with someone about something or with a subject or a reasoning, I didn’t inquire much about anything. I read a lot and tried to learn everything I could about everything from reading, and then finally when I got into school, but not very – kids are inquisitive. They like to find out about what makes this work. I didn’t have any of that going on for me.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: So you weren’t taking the wings off of butterflies?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No, nothing like that.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: And taking things apart and putting them back together.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I remember the only pet I had was a rabbit, and I didn’t want to touch him. I came back in the backyard one day in New Orleans and the rabbit was dead. I started screaming and crying and going on about it. I remember that. But I didn’t want to touch him. I didn’t like the food they had him on.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Who handed the discipline – your discipline?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My grandmother.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: So neither your mother or father disciplined you.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No. I got more discipline from my mother in the later years when in my teen age and everything. That was in Chicago.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Is it fair to say that in your early years you were closer to your grandmother than to either parent?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Absolutely. My whole – yeah. I was closer to my grandmother – as long as she was living – than I was to my mother – my grandmother and grandfather.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What was it about them?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: They were the ones that practically raised me. The other people weren’t around me that much. They were working or doing their thing. But I was every day with Grandma and Grandpa. I learned how to cook. I learned how to wash clothes. I learned how to clean house. I learned all of the domestic things that a person would learn from childhood from my grandmother.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Do we have your grandmother and grandfather’s names? I don’t think so.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My grandmother was Carolyn Hagen. My grandfather was Thomas Hagen.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What did Carolyn Hagen do, and what did Thomas Hagen do?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My grandmother did nothing. She was a housewife – took care of the house, took care of the kids, managed the family. My grandfather, when he was functioning, when he was working, was a longshoreman, which was the same thing a couple of my uncles did. They worked out on the docks unloading ships when they came in. That was the work they did, except the one that drove the candy wagon, one of the uncles.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Do you know approximately how long they lived.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Not really. No. My father lived to be about 72, I recall – in his seventies, but the uncles, I don’t know how old they were.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: And Mom lived how long?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: My mother died when she was in her fifties. She died from pneumonia in Chicago.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: And Dad was living in Chicago at that time?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah. They were living in Chicago, living together. They were always together.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What do you recall and think about the journey to Chicago? I want to bring us to Chicago now. Do you remember that train ride, anything about it?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I don’t recall much of anything of the train ride going from New Orleans when the family as a whole took, except I know we had a lot of food. I didn’t pay any attention to the fact or think

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: too much about it. Later on, there was excursions that ran from Chicago to New Orleans. There – my mother participated in these organizations that had these train rides – there I learned a lot about what you could do and you couldn’t do on a train, and the travel between Chicago and New Orleans. Along the way – we picked up people along the way on the way back – not so much on the way going, but on the way back. We had one – I remember we had one car with a piano in it, and drums and bass, and the people – it was like – that was a social thing. They ran these excursions just like we have excursions on ships now. You go on a ship – to an excursion on a ship – travel like we do today. In those days it was on the railroads. You travel – people had what they call excursions – train excursions – and organizations would somehow – I don’t know how it worked – but they would rent these from the railroad. The railroad would have – you’d have so many cars for people and so many cars for entertainment. In one car would be – they’d [be] dancing and music would be playing and everybody having a good time. But it was in a sense private, because it was just those people from that organization. There was no other people on the train. This particular train would go to – we spent a lot of time on the sidelines letting the other trains go by, in order to get where we would go. It took us a long time to get to New Orleans. Then coming back was where, whenever we’d stop, people would come along. We’d pick up people. Just come along. They’d stop and they’d get on the train.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: The train would stop like a local stop?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah, stop – local stop, to get water and coal and everything. When they’d stop at those particular stops, people would just get on the train and ride on back with us, back to Chicago.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: To what extent were the trains segregated back then.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: See, this wasn’t segregated, because this train was hired. It was as if you hired your own bus, or you go on a ship and it’s a jazz cruise, so everybody on there is jazz people for that cruise. In that way, everybody [who] was on the train was black. There was nobody else on there, except [the] conductor, a motorman, and the engineer.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: And they would often be black as well.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No. No. They’re all white. There was no black engineers, train engineers.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Okay, but there would be black porters.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No. The only thing they had was the conductor and a motorman, but they were white.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Would families bring their own food on the trains?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah. Oh, you’d bring a lot of food on the train. Everything you brought. We didn’t have a dining car. No, we didn’t have a dining car. They brought food on the train.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What kind of food?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What do you think? Fried chicken, ribs, ham – a lot of soul food. That was it. They’d have a good time, eating and drinking. They had big tubs of – where you had ice in there and all of the drinks were in there. I assume they had a little liquor going too, but being so young, I wasn’t participating in that part of it. In fact the only reason why I was even on there is that my mother was a socialite. She was into this social thing.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What do you mean by social?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I mean she belonged to clubs and organizations – social organizations that black people had to communicate with each other and to have their parties and enjoy each other. Just like – in Chicago it was like – this is where the name the “chitlin’ circuit” comes – the name comes about, because every weekend it was a chitlin’ dinner in Chicago, now where in New Orleans it was a fish fry. Every weekend is a fish fry, usually on Friday. They socialize. They come there and they’ve got fish – they sold fish sandwiches. You would eat fish and drink. You had the soda. They’d make a little money off of that. Then the next week it’s at your house. Then you make a little money off of it. That was the social thing. You had no ballroom you’re going to go to do anything. That was the social life of these people at the time.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Clearly they were having fun.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: They were having a great time.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What was life like for a five-year-old, traveling north? Were you bored? Were you . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: See, I don’t recall much of that first trip north.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Okay. All right.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I learned more about traveling on the road later on. After I – we came back and I made a couple [of] trips, then I knew about the segregated section and knew you couldn’t go in the dining car and all of that. I knew that. But we always – when we got on the train, we got on with them baskets – baskets of food, and as I said, most of it was something that was – could stay over. You’d have baked ham, which – something that could last the two or three days you travel. Fried chicken. That kind of stuff.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: So your father and uncle were already up there in Chicago . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah, and once they got settled and everything there – my uncle is very hip. He was well- educated [and] very hip. [He] got an apartment and everything for us. We all lived together. He had his wife come up. He and his wife – everybody – that’s the way the whole thing lined up. When we came, we came to an apartment. It was there. That was it.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Do you recall that apartment?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Oh yes. I recall the first place we moved in was an apartment on 31st Street. It was in a building. In this building on the main floor was a nightclub, which they called a cabaret. In this cabaret King Oliver’s band played, and it had the signs in the lobby of this building that we lived in. That’s where I first heard or knew about King Oliver. We could hear the music when you came in. Like when the thing was going on, we could hear the music, go to rehearsals and that stuff, because it was right on the main floor. Part of it – this nightclub place – was on the main floor of this building that we lived in, the first place we moved in. Then later on – I think after a couple of years there – we moved to a larger apartment, because some of the other parts of my family decided to come up. I think that’s when my grandmother and grandfather and all them came up. See, actually, my mother and father and that part of it came up first. Then the older people came up much later. When my grandmother and grandfather came up, we were on Cottage Grove – 2934 Cottage Grove, which was between 31st and – it was the lakefront. We could walk to the lake. Just go past the railroad tracks, which was where the Illinois Central ran, and there you were right at the lake. The tracks and everything were right on Lake Michigan, right on the lakefront.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: This is where the cabaret was?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No, no. The cabaret scene was in the first place, when we first – the first place I lived there.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Where was the Royal Garden Club?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: That’s it. That’s where – it was in that building. That was the Royal Gardens.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What street was that on?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: 31st and, I guess, Calumet.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Right. So basically you moved along 31st Street from – I think you said . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: From New Orleans.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah. From 2934 Cottage Grove . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No, I think it’s the other way around.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: From 31st Street to Cottage Grove.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: To Cottage Grove. Right.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: I’m assuming that that wasn’t far. Each place . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: No. 29 – 30 – 31. Three blocks. But, a few blocks east. Cottage Grove was a few blocks east of Calumet.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: What did the few blocks east represent, in terms of . . . ?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: It’s just like . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: A bigger place?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah. It was three blocks. The blocks in Chicago going from east to west are long. North to south are short.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Do you remember King Oliver playing.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Oh yeah. I remember hearing him. I didn’t go in. I was just a child. I wasn’t allowed to go into the nightclub or see him at that stage in my life, but I could hear him.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Can you – what do you imagine the influence that had on your development as a musician?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: They played a lot of the stuff that I heard as a child in New Orleans in those parades when – they played a lot of that music, because that was their music. They created that stuff. They played a lot of those tunes. Like one of the basic things – tunes they used to play coming back from the funeral – was Didn’t He Ramble. I remember the title of that. That was like they were talking about his lifestyle, whoever was buried. They made all kinds of songs about somebody’s life and sang and played tunes about this person that was buried. Most of the people were buried above ground, because of New Orleans being so low, as we’ve heard a lot at Katrina and all that – that level.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Often what happened with people migrating north, they tended to move from the neighborhoods where they lived in the South to specific areas in the North, so that the communities that they lived in were among – were folks from New Orleans, for example.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Pretty much. Pretty much.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Was that the case with you?

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Yeah, and this is why – there was no segregation per se in Chicago. Say, you can’t live here. You can’t live there. You can’t [do] that. But they tended to live in certain areas. They just did that, because it’s like they wanted to be close to each other and close together and all that. So most of them that came up – and it was no big problem, because blacks were in a minority. There weren’t that many black people coming up. They were coming up from the South. They were beginning to work in the stockyards, basically. It was one of the main places. Then later on, Gary, Indiana, and the steel mills and all those places came up – later on, for them to work in. There was another migration, which was much later. The original migration was basically to work in the stockyards, in the food industry.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: So from New Orleans you moved to Chicago to a neighborhood that was kind of like a little New Orleans, in a sense that the people – the neighbors had the same kind of food. They listened to the same music. It sounds like King Oliver came up and the musician had a . . .

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: They migrated to Chicago for the same reason we did.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Mitchell
Levy_John_Transcript.text: Right, right.

Levy_John_Transcript.speaker: Levy
Levy_John_Transcript.text: There was work for them there. They made money there. They recorded there. They did all the things. So naturally they had – that’s where they came to play. People didn’t – musicians didn’t move around. You worked in a place, and you worked there for years. You didn’t work there for two weeks here and two weeks there.
