As a 15 year old kid, I’m still working up until – I went to New York when I was 22. I was in no rush for anything national. It didn’t occur to me that it would not be. If I got the things, surrounded myself with what I thought would work, I knew that it would be more than just what I was doing. I also knew that I was successful enough, I could come back and pick up. I would never be a failure. I was already a success before I ever left and went to New York, looking for, specifically, John Levy, Capitol Records, and I knew that if I was John, I could – John – I was basically known as jazz, but I wasn’t a jazz singer. I was singing pop. I just knew that John Levy had the reputation of being a person of great integrity, and I did not want show business on a larger scale if I did not have security and peace around me.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: How did you know so much about John and also about Capitol Records?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That was kind of obvious. If you knew Cannon, if you knew the musicians. I knew who John Levy managed. He had George Shearing. He had the Three Sounds. I just knew that I liked a lot – I liked the people that he managed, that he handled, and I knew that I would fit in, or could expand John’s – I wouldn’t be working in a jazz room. I would be working in a nice supper club, and John saw that too. That was a way for him to move on up and do something different, to get out of jazz rooms and get into the Coconut Grove with a singer. John was not looking for a singer. The last thing in the world John Levy wanted was a singer. Oh no, no. Girl singers? Oh, John did not want to hear. Everybody was coming from Ohio, telling John about this kid in Ohio who sings. John couldn’t care less. John’s assistant was from Cleveland, and he must have bugged – I know he bugged John about it a lot. He just got tired one day, I guess. What happens, I finally got a showcase where I did come to New York. I knew Cannonball, and I knew a girl named Sonja LaForte Sandra Lefort, who was the singer with Johnny Hammond Smith. So I stayed with her and hung out. We went to a couple of the clubs. We went to a club called the Blue Morocco. Irene Reid was the featured singer. I can’t remember. I can see the drummer, but I can’t remember his name. Arthur Jenkins was on piano. I do remember going there. I went to the Blue Morocco and sat in. A

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: couple of weeks after I had sat in, had been up there, Irene Reid broke her ankle, and they called me to replace her. That gave Chuck Taylor and everybody who – and Cannon – who knew – they knew I was in the city. That’s the way we can get John there to hear you.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Back up, just a sec. This idea of what it would mean to go national, of liking who you were, are – what do you attribute that kind of – at the age of 20, 21, 22 – that kind of self insight and level-headed thinking? Where does that come from?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s part of the gift. I was fortunate. He gave me the singing gift. He gave me the storytelling part of all of this. He also gave me a little bit of common sense. I did not see a lot of females in show business who were happy. I did not see any of that. So why would I want to jump in there, when I didn’t see, I didn’t – everybody I knew that was married and divorced and struggling and drugs. I didn’t want any part of that, and I didn’t think that at 15, 16, 17, I was ready to deal with that. I needed to wait until I got to know who I was first. That’s just me. That’s part of the gift. It was one thing for Him to give me the signing voice, but I really appreciate God giving me some common sense.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: So you formulate a plan. You set parameters, as I recall. You gave yourself a certain amount of time. You knew Sandra. So that’s how you felt okay to just go.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yeah, and Cannon. Those are the only two people I really knew.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You got a job.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Came and went and learned how to work a pbx board.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Switchboard?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Um-hmm. Gave myself six months to get John Levy and Capitol Records. But I knew that I needed to support myself while I was there. So I worked at a handbag company for a few minutes as a pbx operator, and then I went to the New York Institute of Technology. They were very, very kind. I worked – my hours were such that I could do work at night. I didn’t have to be at work until 12. They gave me time off for photos and all the things that I needed. I ended up doing, in longhand, a textbook for the dean. I can’t remember his name. But New York Institute of Technology was very kind to me. They really – they stuck by me. The thing was that I gave it six months, but everything happened and was solidified in five weeks. What can I say? It was just supposed to be.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Did your coworkers know that you were a singer?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Did anybody come out to hear you?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes. Richard Griffin was the librarian. He came to just – I was pretty much working at the Blue Morocco then. Then I went to – in October of ’59 I went to New York. In December of ’59 I was recording for Capitol. The first album was done.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: So you were up at the Blue Morocco. John Levy arrives. I want to talk about your signature song, Guess Who I Saw Today. It not only became your signature song, ongoing to this day, but that’s the song that won John over.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Now, Carmen McRae had recorded it.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s where I heard it. I was 15 when I heard it.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Even Eydie Gormé, I think, had recorded it.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: She did it first, Eydie Gormé.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: So how is it that that’s the song that John says, Nancy sounded most like Nancy.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Well, I don’t know if he’d heard the others sing it. I had heard Carmen sing. I hadn’t heard Eydie Gormé sing. Everybody was surprised at me singing a song that heavy, at such a young age. I had been singing Guess Who I Saw Today for a long time before John heard it. So I had a habit down pat. I had my little shtick that went with it. I don’t remember what I was singing at that time. I do know that Guess Who I Saw Today has always done – it doesn’t matter when I sing it. It always – I love it to this day and have never gotten tired of it. It’s fresh and new all the time. I see a different man every time. Different audiences. I mean, I don’t see the particular man. But the bottom line is, it’s a play. Guess Who I Saw Today is like a – literally like a small play. I’ve always looked at it like that.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Are ballads your forté?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes. I always loved the ballads. I like uptempo things, but give me a heavy ballad with a message, and I’m – that’s me. Give me a ballad that says something, that tells a story, and I can get my teeth into that. Sometimes with uptempo songs, it’s almost like you’re throwing them away. That’s just me. There’s no uptempo song that I would say was my top 10 songs, favorites. I used to love – I’m trying to remember the song I

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: used to open with. Fireworks. That was a great chart. It was a great way to get on stage. It was a great way to get to where you wanted to go, which was, eventually, Guess Who I Saw Today. I’m thinking of the Coconut Grove album, and I can’t think of all the songs that were on it.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: We’ll get to that album, and I’ll give you a list.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Good, because I truly do not – Don’t Talk, Just Say, I remember that. That’s the kind of think that I like. I never professed to be a great jazz singer. I’ve always been a song stylist, to me. I still feel that, to this day, and that was how I looked at the music, is in the story that it told. I’m still that way. Trying to find a song today, oh boy.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: We’ll come back to that subject too. What do you remember about – we know that John was impressed. He signed you.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: No, we never signed anything, to this day. I don’t remember ever signing anything. I’ve been with him for, what?, 50-some years. If there ever was a contract, it was 50-some years ago and never renewed.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s true. There is, actually, on file, at the Smithsonian, a copy of your first management contract.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s probably the only one.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It is indeed the only one. We will come back and talk more about John and what that means, because it is very important that both of you feel that there was no contract and what that means. But let’s get a little more history down before we get into that. You did a demo very shortly after that night at the – with Ray Bryant, I believe.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yeah, Ray Bryant’s trio. Right.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Do you remember anything about the session, the demo.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I remember the two songs that I did. There might have been four, but I remember Sometimes I’m Happy and Guess Who.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Did you know Ray?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: No, John Levy set all that up. I did not. I didn’t know anybody in New York except Cannonball and Sandra, and Nat, of course.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: So what was it like to walk into this demo session knowing that you were this far from getting the other half of what you wanted?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I never gave it a thought. To this day I don’t think about stuff like that.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: No nervousness?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: No. I don’t know what it is to be nervous. I never did know what it was to be nervous. I found out later – when you start out doing what you do at three, by the time you realize you’re supposed to be nervous, it’s a little too late. I don’t remember ever being nervous about anything.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: So, you do your demo session, and now you have to sit and wait for Capitol to respond..

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Which didn’t take but a minute. Dave Cavanaugh heard the demo, then called John, told him to don’t let anybody else hear it. That was it.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Then what did you do? Did you go back to work for a while?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I worked the whole time. I told you, New York Institute of Technology was wonderful. They gave me the time off to go do photos, to do – I could do anything during the week. I wasn’t locked into the job. So I kept the job until all through – I went to California and recorded the album. I still was working at New York Institute of Technology.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: So you flew out to Los Angeles . . .

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: . . . to record at Capitol Records.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Right.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You flew out alone, as I recall.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Right. I was met at the airport by Ernie Andrews, who took me to this little hotel I stayed at. I don’t think my mother was in California then. At some point she was in California when I was out there. But it was a piece of cake. I just don’t – I just never felt that I was supposed to be nervous or anything. I figured that if Dave Cavanaugh didn’t want anybody else to hear it, that was good enough for me, and I loved the people that David Cavanaugh produced. I loved the production values.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Okay. We’ll start talking about albums in a minute. John had this notion, and he sent you out of the country.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yeah.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: So you go into the studio, record your album. Now the world is waiting for it to come out.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Um-hmm. But he did not want me to be in the States when it came out. So I went to Australia.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What was that about?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You ask John Levy that. I don’t have a clue.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Okay. He sent you to Australia.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I went to Australia, and we worked for three months. When I came back – it was the second album that Guess Who I Saw Today was in. When I came back, Guess Who I Saw Today had made its mark. I stayed in Australia for three months, I believe.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It was a Hotel Chevron?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Chevron Hotel, yeah, both in Melbourne and Sidney.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Any memories of that time?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Just that the little room in Melbourne we got, once my bags got in, I couldn’t get in. That’s all I remember about it. Then I actually moved out of the hotel into a bed and breakfast or whatever, something like that, because the hotel room was not working.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Somewhere around this time you also managed a whirlwind romance, married a drummer.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Oh, I met him before that. He was the only person who wrote to me in Australia. I met him when he was with Sonny Stitt. Remember I told you earlier that I had met Sonny? I went to see certain people. So I had met Kenny [Dennis] with Sonny Stitt.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Back in Ohio.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Back in Ohio. We stayed in touch and wrote. Basically, I’ve done that twice.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes, I know.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Jesus. That’s just occurred to me, that I’ve done that twice. Came back from Australia, got off the plane, and got married before I got back to New York. Then, when I met Wiley [Burton], I met him on April 22nd and was married on May 22nd. That’s the same thing. Wow. I’ll have to think about that. I’ll really have to think about that.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: In the midst of – really, everything’s building up, and you get married to a drummer. Did he work with you?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes. I remember him working with me at Lake Tahoe. We had a nice rhythm section. I don’t remember who else was in it, but I do know that – basically, I was working in rooms that had big bands.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: How soon did you start a family?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Got married in 1960. Kacy was born in 1963.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: This was part of what you set out wanting from the get-go, if I’m not mistaken.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I was going to have lived a life that included a family, and they would be first. The business would be second. I always put the children first. I was fortunate to have some fairly decent children, too.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Was that a difficult sell to the people around you? Was that hard to accomplish back then?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What, to have a baby? It was nobody’s business. It never would have occurred to me, what other people would think. Me getting pregnant didn’t have anything to do with the jobs. The jobs were still there. I worked pregnant. I took a few months off, after I had the baby. Took the baby with me. Never had – there was no difficulties with that. It never would have occurred to me to wonder, should I ask somebody? It’s my life, and I’ve always put that first. It’s my life. It’s nobody else’s. I have to do what’s right for me. And we were very happy, had this beautiful boy, this little child who is so cute. The problem, I think, that happens in the marriage – in fact I don’t recall Kenny and I ever having any argument. I just didn’t like – I didn’t like the way I saw the public perceiving him. If you notice, a lot of female singers, their husbands are dogged. I’d seen that in other people’s marriages and didn’t like that, and I found that people would – we had a production company. Instead of people listening to the president of the company, who was my husband, it would be, ask – you have to ask Nancy. I thought that was

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: disrespectful. I thought it was harmful to him emotionally. So we decided to – well, we’re still friends to this day.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What was it like to travel with a small child? Was – you just did what you did.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You just did what you did. I had someone with me, obviously, to take care of him when I was on stage. But the bottom line was, it was a piece of cake. He was fun to have on the road. I had all of my kids out on the road at some point. We’ve been out there, and I’ve taken somebody with me to see to it that they were there when I – but my girls, especially, they could care less about who was supposed to be there watching them. When they got up in the morning, they woke me up. It did not matter that there was somebody who was supposed to do be there to do – no, no, no. Mom would have to get up and make sure they had their breakfast and stuff. But it was fun. I wouldn’t have had it any other way. There was a time when there was too much work for me, I thought, and I took off and said no, no, no, no, no. This is getting out of hand. When you’re working 48 weeks out of a year, that is not fun, and that had to stop. So I called an abrupt halt to that. Nobody understood it, but then, it wasn’t for them to understand. It was for me to do what was right for me. When you work 56 nights straight, it’s like – two shows a night? Oh no, no, no, no.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Let’s take a quick break.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Okay.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Over the coming years, from ’60 to 1980, you would record, give or take, 48 to 51 complete albums. It’s been difficult to parse that, because there were some reissues, and things got listed twice. But I’m pretty confident that it was 49 or 50 complete albums for Capitol. What role did you play in planning those albums and selecting the material?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: A lot. David Cavanaugh was a wonderful man to work with, and John – between John and David and I, we really were able to have a lot of fun picking the songs. There were little meetings where we would sit down and decide which direction we were going for the next one. Is it going to be about a specific thing? Usually I did not do albums that were about one particular subject. Generally, I – we’ d just – we’d sit down, me, John, Dave, sit at my house, go over the music, and Dave would have music to bring in. We would listen, and we would choose.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Where was your house?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: At that point in time I was living in Viewpark [California], on Monteith [Drive].

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You would sit in a living room? The kitchen? What kind of . . . ?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: The living room, where the piano was.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Did you listen to a lot of material?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes. By the time it got to me, it had pretty well been honed down. There was – I had – I was new and fresh. I had all of Cole Porter to look forward to and all George Gershwin to look forward to. So it was easy to find material then, because there were such great writers of renown. It was wonderful to be able to sit there and pick twelve of the best tunes you’ve ever heard. Not that many originals, new things that were coming up. I just was grateful to be able to sing all the good stuff that I’d ever heard.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: In those years, you recorded at least two albums a year, and in some cases, three and four. That seems unimaginable today. Tell us what you did, what that was like.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It just was. You couldn’t do it today.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Why?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That industry’s changed dramatically. There’s no – you can’t compare today to 1960, can’t compare it at all. It just is no comparison. Today’s music is not – I feel sorry. If I were me, today, and I was 22, if there were not a John Levy, I would not do it. I would not attempt to do it. There just is not – the market is not the same, because I keep saying that the music that I was singing then was the pop music of the day. That is not the case today. So I would not be able to be myself if I were starting to do it today. So, I would finish college.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: And be a teacher.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Or go to Carnegie Tech. Right.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Going into a studio, back in the day, in the good old days, if you would allow that – I heard you do an interview once, and you kept referring to 8:01. There would be an 8 o’clock call time for the session, and at 8:01 the music began.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You’ve got that right, exactly, downbeat, we were doing the first song. We would do three songs, if not four, a night. We completed an album in three nights, because everybody was prepared. The music was written. We weren’t – people weren’t going in there, figuring out what to do, in the studio. You already had everything written out. Everything was done. I pretty much knew my music. I had it in front of me, but the

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: bottom line is, I knew what I was singing. It just never occurred to me that that would be – nobody would even try to do it today. But when you have the arrangers that I had, who wrote such beautiful charts – Jimmy Jones – it was just easy, a piece of cake.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: The arranger on the first two albums was Billy May.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Billy May, um-hmm.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I don’t know if this is a fair question, because this is what people who aren’t singers just want to know: what does it feel like to hear and feel an orchestra behind you, beneath you, an arrangement?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Oh that’s still my favorite. My favorite thing is a full orchestra, symphony orchestra. One of the dreams as a kid was to be standing on a mountaintop with a symphony orchestra behind me, the wind blowing my hair. That was – there’s nothing – nothing could take the place of that. That’s unique and beautiful. As much as I love working with a rhythm section – you notice that through the years I’ve either worked with a big band or three pieces. I have never really – except for Cannonball, I’ve never worked with quintets. Give me the three, just the basics, or give me all of it. And there’s nothing like hearing that full orchestra behind me.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Does it change your – the performance?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I have no idea. It just makes me feel good inside to hear the band. I don’t know that it changes what I sing, because I’m pretty sure that’s pretty much – that’s the same, but it’s just what it does for me to hear that full orchestra. It doesn’t – I would like to be in the audience, watching, sometimes, especially when you have one of those great orchestras. I would love to be one of those people sitting in the seats, to see it.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Having come out from – basically all this time with a trio or with the band, and now you’re in a studio with Billy May and an orchestra.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: With an orchestra, yes.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What was that like?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It was what it was supposed to be.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It’s exactly what you expected?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yeah, except that Billy May did not do the right – he didn’t write the chart for one of the songs. He had taken it and made it something else. It never occurred to me,

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: never occurred to me, that you’re going to question Billy May? You’re going to question? Yeah, I questioned it. I didn’t like the arrangement.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s interesting.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: So it was rewritten, because that is not what you got from Ray Bryant. That is not what was the demo. That was not what it was supposed to be. It never occurred to me that I had no – who did I think I was, telling Billy May the chart is not right? But I did. I just never think about stuff like that.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: And this is based on your gift. You did not have any musical training?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: No. When my parents took me to a singing teacher, they said I was too young and my voice would change, which it did not. So I never really had any musical training.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: When you were in a studio, when you heard whatever you heard, were you able to say anything besides, “This isn’t it?” How do you communicate when you don’t have the technical training? How do you communicate with the people that are working with you?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: If you have good people – like Billy May, Dave Cavanaugh, John Levy, and I, we all sat down together. It was no – it never occurred to me that it should be any different. This to me was the way it was supposed to be.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Favorite arrangers?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Gerald Wilson and Jimmy Jones. I got a letter from Billy May once. It said that he was glad that God allowed him to live at a time when we could record. I’m trying to remember the song that it was about. But that was nice to hear.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: He did your Lush Life album.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That was what he was talking about. That was the one. That’s still my favorite album.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: John Levy’s too.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yeah, that’s my favorite album.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Even Shearing came on board for an orchestration.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Hello Young Lovers, George Shearing. Beautiful charts. I’m trying to remember who worked with him, who wrote the charts out. I can see him, but I can’t call his name.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: But I loved George Shearing. He was precious. We did – when we worked at Carnegie Hall – I think it was – I don’t know who we were celebrating. Celebrating somebody’s birthday. I don’t think it was mine. Anyway, Shearing played the music that many years later exactly the way it was played on the record.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That was Shearing’s birthday.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Okay. That’s what I thought.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: His 80th.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes, Shearing’s 80th birthday. That he would come in and play the things that we did 40 years ago.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Let’s talk about that album and also about the Cannonball album. The Shearing album was ’61, the Cannonball album was in 1962, and suddenly, Nancy Wilson is a jazz singer. How did you feel about that?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I wasn’t that thrilled. I was not thrilled. And I have not changed my mind about that. I’m a song stylist. Whether I recorded with Cannonball Adderley and George Shearing or not, I’m still a song stylist. I didn’t – I knew who the great jazz singers were.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Which were who, in your opinion?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Ella. And Sarah Vaughan had pipes that – you know, please God. But they all went in a different way. They would go with the music. They knew more about music than I did. I don’t know squat about music. I don’t know anything about it. I don’t read it. I can’t play it. I just have ears. They were more musicians. And Carmen was a musician, Sarah. They were jazz singers, to me. Then, as I say, I sang a lot of pop things. But it took a long time before the jazz singer happened. They didn’t – I was still working in supper clubs for many, many years after that.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: In addition to Guess Who I Saw Today, there are a lot of songs that are still in your rotation, if you want to call it that, today. I’m thinking about – I don’t know – Green Dolphin Street.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Never Will I Marry, Save Your Love for Me, Masquerade.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Sleeping Bee.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yeah, that’s an easy one when you need something uptempo to break with.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Do you ever get tired of these songs?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: No, no.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: How can that be?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I pick songs that are good. If you pick songs that are good, you don’t get tired of them. If you pick a song that works – especially with the rhythm section that I have, Sleeping Bee would be – with a bass player, when you have a great bass player, Sleeping Bee works every time. I don’t remember half of the material I’ve recorded. That’s for sure. People keep asking me, do you remember a certain – no, I don’t. And I don’t feel bad because I don’t. I can’t retain all of this. It’s impossible. When you realize how much there has been, there’s no way I could remember all of these things.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: And yet I’ve heard you pull a few out of the hat.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s God. That’s not me, because I can’t remember – getting older is – my memory was never that great to begin with. In fact, because I didn’t – all of it was so natural that it didn’t register. Do you understand what I’m saying? It was a natural kind of thing, the work, the singing, the songs that were picked, and it wasn’t something that I gave a lot of thought to. It was just there.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: So you don’t have to work at keeping material fresh for yourself or for the audience?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: If I were working 40, even 36 weeks a year, maybe I would do a lot of changing. But I’m only working four times a year. What – no, I’m not . . .

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: At this point.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: At this point, I’m not going to . . .

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: But back then.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Back then, if it was working, we left it alone.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What does it mean when you say, it worked, the song works?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It’s got a great story. It’s more than just singing notes. It’s telling a story.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Your manager at the time, still your manager today, but back then, he signed with you with an agent at General Artists Corporation, a guy named . . .

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Jerry [?C].

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Jerry [?Florencia].Perrenchio I remember reading something about a difference in marketing, that he wanted the slinky, sexy, low-cut, that you had a closet full of, if I have this right, Walter Bass matte jersey dresses with Dolman sleeves, in every color. First, the lighter side of this. Talk to us about your taste in clothes, then and now.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It’s pretty much the same. I just saw an ad in – when I was being honored, there was an ad with the Walter Bass – no, no, the content page of Ebony magazine has me, full page picture of Nancy Wilson in a Walter Bass. I bought it. I remember that I bought it at Sidney’s. Someone said, how could you remember something like that? But it was me in a Walter Bass matte jersey gown, and it’s a full page on the table of contents. That’s the background on the table of contents, is a picture of me in that gown. I’ve always liked good clothes, though. I love beautiful gowns.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Do you – where do you shop?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I haven’t been in a store in so long. When I was shopping, I shopped at Sax Fifth Avenue and Neiman Marcus, when I was shopping. I have no desire. I don’t have the patience anymore to shop, and I don’t really need to. I have so many things that I’ll never get around to. Nothing’s worn out. I have two cargo vans full of things, that are on my property. Then every closet in the house is full. So I don’t think I’ll be doing any shopping anytime soon.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Do you have any favorite designers?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: These days – well, Angela Dean, who has been very good to me. B. Michael. I used to love Halston. And that’s – what’s the guy’s name who used to do Halston? He’s got his own, and he – oh, wow, I can’t think of his name. Cannot think of his name.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You’re out of my league now.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Oh, wow. Well, I can’t remember his name, but anyway, he used to – after Halston wasn’t there, he was there. [Ms. Wilson later remembers Kevan Hall.]

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Your taste, is that also part of the gift? Who did you – how did you come to develop such a sense of presentation?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It wasn’t anything that you think about. It’s really kind of natural. It wasn’t something that I – today, there’s somebody around you to tell you when to open your

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: mouth, when to – back in the day, you were your own person. You were your own self. Nobody was sitting there telling you how to dress and what to do, not really.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Magazines? Television? Where did you – I mean, you didn’t learn about this picking tomatoes.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I’ve never even thought about it. I’ve always worn nice clothes. Even in the pictures I see of myself as a kid, my jeans were just so. I just never – it wasn’t something that you consciously thought about. It just is.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: When you launched this career, let’s say in the ’60s, and things are hot and happening, and you’ve already expressed some business savvy here – you knew what you wanted, you knew who you wanted, you knew why you wanted – did you give any conscious thought to shaping your image? Or what today they might call branding?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: No. I never had a stylist. I didn’t have someone to tell me which way to go and what to do. We didn’t do that, back in the day. That’s a new thing. That was not something ever that I – I just never had that kind of sense that I needed someone to tell me what to wear, what to do.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: But you told you those things.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I just did it, yeah. I know what is pleasing to my eye, and if I like it, I think that the rest of the fans will like it. I don’t like every gown I see. I’ve just been lucky to have a sense of taste.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What draws you? Color? Shape? Texture?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: No, I haven’t ever thought about it.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You just like it and you . . .

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I just see it. I see it and I like it or I don’t.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: If you’re not paying any particular attention to what, as you say, today they call it branding, I have heard you over the years, at different times and different circumstances, say, no, Nancy Wilson doesn’t do that, or Nancy Wilson wouldn’t say that, or Nancy Wilson wouldn’t sing that. Are there Nancy Wilson rules? Or is it just all gut?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It’s all gut. There’s no rules. It’s all – it’s natural. It’s not something that I’ve ever consciously sat down and thought about.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I’ve heard you referred to, these are some great phrases, “a professor emeritus of body language,” “a consummate actress,” or in your own words, a ham. Is there a way that you approach a song?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I’ve never given it any conscious thought.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Is there a difference for you, singing on stage versus in the studio?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What is the difference?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: One can be quite boring.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Which one?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: The recording can be very boring. I like to get on the stage and do the thing and just get it, just do it. In the studio it’s a lot different. I rarely ever do more than three takes of a song.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Maybe it depends on what day that question gets asked of you, because I have heard a different response from you on this. I have heard you talk about being able, in the studio, without an audience, to “go there.”

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Oh, that’s the same thing as being the actress, the song stylist, the singer. She goes there. That’s on stage and in the studio. Go inside that song and make it happen.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: So you don’t have to have an audience to make it happen?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: No, no.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: And you never had acting lessons either.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: No. I did ask a prominent actor, when I was getting ready to do something for television, a dramatic role, what is there about it? He gave me the words, “Just go there.” I’ve used that. It was [?] who told me that. He said, “Just go there.” So that’s what I do when I sing. There’s no way to prepare to go into an acting role without ever having done it before. So he just said, just go where the lyric, where the – what is the word I’m trying to think of? What were the words that are on the paper? Go where they take you.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: So, in the studio, you can go there, if you need to. With a live audience, that gives you a little something else. Let’s talk for a minute about some of the camaraderie and the

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: shows, packages, that you got to participate in the ’60s, where, say, John put together a show with different people on the bill. I haven’t seen anything like that in recent years. Tell us a little bit about that camaraderie, what it does for you as a performer, in terms of, it’s a different kind of a show.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: When we would do shows together, it wasn’t – they weren’t separated. I did what I do, Cannonball did what he did, and then we would do a few songs together. But you didn’t have to change in order to – because I always had my own rhythm section. The only time that that did not happen is when I would come back out with Cannonball. We would use his quintet. The bottom line is, I didn’t have to change and adapt to somebody else’s – the way they were. We – I had my own, and that always worked out nicely. I remember waiting with George Shearing back in the day. I always had – I remember Jimmy Bond not – that’s the only time I was ever really upset before going on stage. The bass player wasn’t there. So I used Shearing’s. I’m trying to remember who it was. Jimmy Bond’s name comes to mind. But I think Jimmy was playing with Shearing, and he played for me that night. I can’t remember who my bass player was or who was not there.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Did that kind of camaraderie give you a different feeling? Do you miss that sort of thing today? It just seems like such a different sense of time and place.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It wasn’t, not really. I don’t change from day to day. I am what I am, and that’s whether I was working with Cannonball or Shearing or Ramsey [Lewis]. I love Gene Harris of the Three Sounds. We never got a chance to work together too often, but when we did, it was memorable. But I don’t change up, just because it’s different people. I’m still who I am and do what I do and was very blessed and fortunate that it is what it is.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Do you remember anything about the shows at the Apollo?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I remember the chair with Oscar Brown, Jr., in it.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Tell us what that means.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Oh God. We were doing a thing called The Free Sounds.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s right. Free Sounds of ’63.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It was Oscar Brown, Jr. I can’t remember. It was Cannon?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Um-hmm.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Oscar did what he did. I did Miss Otis. No, not Miss Otis – Just Because We’re Kids. I had on sneakers. Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Cosby – Bill – and Robert Culp.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That was fun. That was a lot of fun.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What makes a show like that fun for you?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That Emmy nomination also says a lot about your dramatic skills, yet another gift with no training. The other story at that time also was Police Story. Were those guest spots a big deal for a singer, a black woman, back in that time?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Did you enjoy that kind of work?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You did?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Luther King. Those are my – Dorothy Height was just phenomenal. I think she would be the person that I would say inspired me the most.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You’ve been blessed in so many ways, but among them, it seems that you didn’t really experience too much of the racial color barrier career-wise.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You escaped the color barriers.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I really did. Like I said, there’s only the one time at Kitty’s Show Bar, when I said, “If you need reservations, I’m making them,” and that was the end of that. But in the job area, in working, everybody had already paved the way.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: And yet, in the ’60s and ’70s, you felt it important to be very involved in civil rights activities.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes, because I also felt and knew that I’m being treated one way while my brother is being treated another. See, Nancy Wilson’s been Nancy Wilson for a long time. But I don’t believe that doors were as open, as wide, for my brother as they were for me. And midwest Ohio was not notorious for being segregated. It was always kind of integrated. I grew up where the whites down the road, you didn’t have a problem with them, because they were your cousins. So I was just blessed. Came along at the right time.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What activities did you involve yourself in?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: We’re not going to go there, are we? Jesus.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: At least go to the march.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: The march was one thing, but then the funeral was another thing, and then the Poor People’s march. That one – and being there for Martin’s lieutenants, making sure that they were housed and fed, and going to the Justice Department to make sure that they

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: were protecting blacks running for elected office, just to see to it that these things were done. And going to Selma. As one of the first 30 footsteps in the Martin Luther King walk of fame, that’s because – they said, they were looking for artists and people of prominence to show up, and they couldn’t find me. They realized they couldn’t find me, because I was already there.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You were what I might describe as a quiet activist. I don’t think many people are aware of all the behind-the-scenes things that you did. How did you come to be a member of the Minority Business Advisory Council under the Nixon administration?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Nixon appointed me. Don’t ask me why. I was also on the education, when Lyndon Johnson appointed me. And I didn’t do anything to work at it. It just was offered. It was there. I guess they thought I might be too quiet, and they found out I wasn’t.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What was involved in these things?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: A lot of meetings, and what I found out was going over things that the previous group of people had done, and I saw no reason. Why are we going over their work? Let’s move forward instead of standing still and keeping repeating the same thing over and over. There was one other person on the board who felt the way I did. We made a little stink about it. Why are we going over the work that the last three years of people had done? Let’s take it from there and move on. That was my only fault with all of that. They were just repeating the same thing over and over.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: But you felt you were able to make a difference?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: In a lot of young people. I went into high schools, and I did a radio show called To Your Baby’s Health, when Samantha was little. That helped young women who were pregnant and didn’t have anywhere to turn and whatnot. That was sponsored by Johnson & Johnson. That was fun, but I remember being someplace, and a youngster – little – I’m talking young girl asked me about having a baby and leaving it in a trash can and whatever. Oh, it broke my heart. It’s like, what? What could she be thinking about at that age? She couldn’t have been more than 10, 11 years old. So that’s why I did To Your Baby’s Health.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: And even though this is jumping ahead a bit, most recently you were involved in the National Minority AIDS Council.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes. That’s necessary, and a lot is being done, thank God, finally, but it isn’t in the forefront the way it was. Everybody feels that because we have some medications and

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: whatnot, it’s not that big a problem. It should not be happening. It should not be being transmitted at this point. We’ve been – we’ve known it’s around long enough to understand that this is a dangerous situation, and we’re still getting so many people who are being infected. That distresses me. It really bothers me.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What have I missed here in the causes that you have championed over the years? What are the things that Nancy Wilson is passionate about?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: The high schools. I’ve gone into just about every major high school system in L.A. I went into – and as I said, just being concerned about babies, young girls having babies out of wedlock, this whole welfare system that perpetuates the same thing, over and over. That bothers me quite a bit.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Let’s talk a little bit about some of the organizations whose work you’ve quietly supported. Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Oh yes. I did the very first telethon. I was the hostess for the first UNCF telethon. My co-host was Clifton Davis, before Lou Rawls got involved. So that was a special thing for me. And having been on many of the black campuses, it’s just wonderful to support them. I’ve also discovered that – and it disturbs me – that 80% of black students in college are female. There’s a problem there. That’s not – where are my men? Where are my guys? That’s distressing. I found that out going to meetings. I find out stuff like that. That threw me for a loop. I was at Howard University when I got that information. Wow. Well, at least I’m remembering some of the things.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What do you say to a young person who says, “Well, you didn’t finish school”?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes, but I am also a doctor. I have doctorates, two. I have been a professor at a university. So I did finish school. I finished my school. Since my work was already formed, it was – it would have been – it was selfish of me, I think, to continue school, because I had already – I was already doing what I was going to be doing. Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: In an interview recently, a gentleman wrote, “There is always a ministerial quality to your approach,” the ministry of Nancy Wilson. Is there a message that you feel should be shared?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: John B. Williams on bass, Roy McCurdy on drums. • Lou Llew Matthews, we’re getting up there in time, 18 years or so. He’s my conductor, and he has produced and arranged a lot of the things I’ve done for MCG – Manchester Craftsmen’s Guild. I got that part right. Ronnell Bright, I remember well. I can’t remember too many. The guys have been with me for so long that for me to try to remember who was with me 40 years ago is . . .

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yeah. The main ones were Don Trenner, Ronnell, and Mike Wolff.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Michael was with me five or six years.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Phil Wright.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: He was with me five years or so, yeah. See, I wouldn’t have thought of that. I’m glad you got all that together.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: But tell me about what “my gentlemen” really means, because it’s not just a phrase you throw away.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: They’re with me. They allow me to feel comfortable enough to arrive onstage without a rehearsal, without worrying about anything, knowing that I can change the show if I want to. I can switch stuff around, because they’re there, and they’ve been there with me and supported me, supported both emotionally and physically. They’ve been there. I know my guys well. And when I say gentlemen, I mean that. They are gentlemen, as opposed to just “the fellows.” They are cordial, always dress nice. I remember, back in the day, when people would go on stage without anything on. Most people expect to see my trio in a tuxedo, but once in a while – once in a while – if we’re doing a jazz thing, we don’t have to wear the tuxedos. But they are – it’s a presentation. I want them to look like gentlemen with their tuxedos. That’s the difference. I didn’t want to work in the sawdust, years ago. I wanted to be in a supper club. I did not want to be in the rooms that had sawdust on the floor and whatnot. I just couldn’t see that. If I didn’t have to do it at 15, why would I want to do it at 25?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What stands out for you in your memory – and I can give you songs if you need it – but I’m thinking about some of those lush albums that Kiyoshi produced with charts by Masahito Satoh. There are four or five, six albums in that batch that were almost harkening back to the early ’60s Capitol material. What stands out for you in those days and memories and times?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Right now, just that we did them. Don’t start me lying about how we did – well, a lot of them were done in Tokyo. That’s what stands out, that they were done in Tokyo, that Kiyoshi also liked the same kind of music that I liked. We did a couple of things in Los Angeles, but the bottom line was just to continue to do good material. That was my – that’s always been my – about recording – is recording material that’s substantial.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You also did some music videos with Kiyoshi. My recollection is that the – this is when MTV – or VH1 . . .

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: VH1.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: . . . was starting up, so that we finally had some “jazz” on t.v. in a music video format. Isn’t Forbidden Lover around the time when you finally got a chance to actually lay down on the piano?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Was it Forbidden Lover or was it that song . . .

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I’ll Be a Song? No, it was the music video with Carl Anderson. We did two songs from Forbidden Lover.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: See, you remember more than I do. I don’t remember. I don’t remember it at all. I remember recording with Carl – singing with Carl, not necessarily recording with him.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It was a studio in Culver City, and the director with the frizzy hair, and Doug Dilge.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Okay. You lost me.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: What I remember, because I’ve heard you talk about it in interviews, but not related to this video, was the vision you had of draping yourself across a piano, the drama of it all, and for the first time, Nancy Wilson got to do a music video that was all of that.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Okay. I need to see it.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You need to see it.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s for sure.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You’ll love it. I promise. You did some live concert video performances that Kiyoshi was involved in.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Carnegie Hall.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes, the Carnegie Hall show, and then one down at the Bottom Line in the Village, East Meets West. [Ken, there may be video of one or both of these shows in the Levy archives]

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I don’t remember that one. The Bottom Line? Did I work the Bottom Line?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I think that’s where it was. It was a public show. It was for the video.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I don’t remember that.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Remember anything about the Carnegie Hall gig?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yeah. Purple dress.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: We’re back to the style.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Back to the style. Purple gown. It was gorgeous. Lew Llew [Mathews] was around then too, and Masahiko. I had both of them out there.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s right. And Carl Anderson was on [?].

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I love Carl Anderson. His voice is like – there would be a time when you couldn’t tell where his stopped and mine started. We sang – we were singing – what was Carl’s big song?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Ferris Wheel.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes, we sang Ferris Wheel at Carnegie Hall, and Carl and Nancy left the building. I’ve never been that involved in the music. We were not there. We were someplace . . .

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: On a ferris wheel.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: On a ferris wheel. It was the first time I can remember really saying, I left the building. I was – we were somewhere else, and it was magnificent. It was wonderful. I loved working with Carl.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: A good place to jump off to some other people that you’ve worked with over the years.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You come up with the names if you’re expecting me to remember.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: James Ingram.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: See, that’s what I’m saying. Thank you. Let’s see. Daryl Coley.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Peabo and Daryl Coley, the two vocalists.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Daryl Coley, Peabo Bryson. Daryl Coley was on the Ramsey Lewis album. Where’d I work with Peabo?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I forget which album.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It was on an album, really?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I think there’s one track on an album.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You sure about that?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: No.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I’m not either.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I’ll look it up for you.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I remember doing a couple of shows with Peabo, but I don’t remember recording with him.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That would be it. Is it hard to sing with another person?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Well, let’s put it this way: before Daryl Coley, Bernard Benard– what was his last name?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: [?Ardmer] Igner

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Bernard Benard[?]. They had brought him in to sing this song with me, which I had no clue what ever possessed them to think that that would work. There’s such a big, big difference in the tonal qualities and all that. So that didn’t work at all. That’s how I found Daryl Coley, because that was – oh, I love his voice, and we mesh, we blend. And James Ingram and I are like – it’s like, on fire. I love singing with James Ingram. He’s a dynamite – he’s a great, great singer. I love him a lot.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You’ve done some unusual collaborations, unusual in that they were just one-offs. You did some things with the Crusaders.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That was big. That was big. What was the name of the song? It was big. I know that.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It went right out of my head.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Oh, I sang it for years. Oh God – what? – The Way It Goes?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Whew. That would have broken my heart, if I didn’t remember that. That was – that got – that was big for the Crusaders. That was big.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Who else did I work with?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: There was some unusual compil- – Chick Corea, Return to Forever.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I’m glad that you’re remembering – have all this written down.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: You were invited to do one or two songs, [Stephen] Sondheim, in the collection, which was . . .

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That was where Peabo Bryson came in. It was a Sondheim song we did together. Don’t ask me the name of the song.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I won’t ask.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: But when you mentioned Sondheim, I remembered, that was where Peabo Bryson came in, and I don’t remember the name of the song. [The duet was Loving You on Color and Light: Jazz Sketches on Sondheim, Sony 1995]

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: There was the Boston Pops. That was a recording.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes. It was fun. That’s my big orchestra. That’s my milieu.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Then there was a very unusual album with Barry Manilow.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It was big.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: It was very big. It was very unusual . . .

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: With My Lover Beside Me.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s right. What do you remember about that album?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That there was Mercer lyrics – Johnny Mercer lyrics. Barry is delightful, fun to work with, easy. I was asked to do this album in an elevator in Osaka.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Really?

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Ran into the producer on an elevator, and he told me that Manilow was getting ready to have this thing he wanted to do and would I be interested in doing a Mercer album with Barry Manilow? Who’s going to say no? Barry’s delightful to work with. This was easy, a piece of cake. Here again, you get to know the material.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s some beautiful material

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: When October Goes. Oh, wonderful, wonderful material.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s one of the ones I heard you pull out of the air at an audience request, after not doing it for many, many years.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I did it not too long ago.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Yes, in Oakland.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I hadn’t done it in forever – in years.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Actually, it was Seattle. In late ’80s and ’90s, you kept doing television, but you also did another show of your own. This time it was a syndicated program.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Right, Red, Hot, and Cool.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Tell us about that show.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: We filmed it at the Biltmore Hotel. It gave – there was no doubt about it. It was a jazz show, because we had an awful lot of jazz artists on. One of the reasons that I liked doing it so much, is it exposed the audience to – because I was in a position to do this show, I could bring people on who were in the jazz field, who didn’t get exposure. That was one of the good things about it. It was fun to do.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Do you remember the format? You always did a song. Then you would showcase the guest . . .

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: Somebody else.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: . . . somebody else, the guest. Then sometimes you would do something with them. I can’t remember if it was a half hour or an hour.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: That’s what I – you just read my mind. I was trying to think if it was a half hour or an hour.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: I think it was a half hour, and I think we might have done two a day in that time. I do remember some of the guests. There was some obvious – Joe Williams was one. You might have had Lou Rawls also.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Wilson
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: We did.

Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.speaker: Levy
Nancy-Wilson-Transcription-2020_0.text: But we had Gerald Albright, and we had Supersax.
